The trumpet of Jubilee is a wonderful sound. But do not miss the silence wrapped inside it, the year the fields were allowed to rest, and the freed people learned, at last, that they were free.

pieces.title: Praise Is the Sound a Cancelled Debt Makes
pieces.imagePrompt: An intimate close portrait of a radiant person mid-shout of joy with head thrown back, eyes bright with grateful tears and arms flung wide in warm backlight, an overjoyed crowd blurred behind them, light scattering upward like released confetti, pure relief and celebration; vivid cinematic film-still quality, warm gold and glowing amber tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: There is a note in the singing of a forgiven person that no untouched voice can reach. You cannot fake it, and you cannot earn it. It is the specific sound a person makes when they know exactly what they were let off of.

body.text: You can hear the difference. You have always been able to hear it, even if you never had words for it.

There is a way that some people sing which does not sound like the others. It is not about the quality of the voice, this has nothing to do with pitch or training or whether they could hold their own on a stage. It is something underneath the voice, in it and behind it, a kind of weight or release that some singers carry and others simply do not. You have been in a room where one person was singing and you found, without deciding to, that your eyes had gone to them, and your throat had tightened, and you could not have told anyone why. They were not the best singer in the room. They were singing about something. And whatever it was, it had cost them, and it had been paid, and you could hear the whole transaction in a single held note.

I have come to believe that this sound has a source, and the source is forgiveness. Praise, real praise, the kind that stops a room, that is the sound a cancelled debt makes when it finally gets a voice.
The math of gratitude

Yeshua once said something about this so plainly that we tend to slide right past it. He was at a dinner, and a woman with a bad reputation came in and wept at His feet and poured out expensive perfume on them, and the respectable people in the room were scandalized that He would let such a person touch Him. And Yeshua, reading the room exactly, told a small story. Two people owed money. One owed a little, one owed an enormous amount. Neither could pay. The lender forgave them both. Now, which of them will love him more?

The answer is obvious, and that is the point. The one who was forgiven more. Whoever has been forgiven little, Yeshua said, loves little. And whoever has been forgiven much, loves much. He was explaining the woman at His feet. She was not weeping and pouring out everything she had because she was more emotional than the dignified men reclining at the table. She was doing it because she knew the size of her debt, and she knew it had just been erased, and the only sane response to a cancellation that large is a love that looks, to everyone who does not understand, like too much.

That is the math behind the sound. The intensity of a person's praise is not a measure of their personality. It is a measure of how clearly they see what they were forgiven. The quiet, careful worshiper is very often not the mature one. They are frequently the one who has not yet reckoned with the size of their own debt. And the one who worships like the woman at the feet, who does not seem to care how it looks, is very often the one who has done the terrible, freeing arithmetic and knows exactly the number that was written off.
Why the never-broken cannot fake it

Here is the hard and beautiful thing. You cannot manufacture this sound. You cannot practice your way into it or borrow it from someone who has it. It comes from one place only, and there is no shortcut to that place.
It comes from having been genuinely down, and genuinely let off.

This is why some of the most powerful worshipers I have ever encountered are people whose stories you would not want for your children, people who wandered into a far country, who wrecked things, who ran up a debt so large they had given up any hope of ever paying it. When such a person finally understands that the debt is gone, not reduced, not deferred, gone, something happens in their worship that the carefully-behaved among us simply cannot reproduce. There is a floor of relief under everything they sing. Every note stands on top of the memory of what they were spared. And so their praise has a bottom to it, a depth, that a person who has never been broken has not had the chance to develop.

I am not romanticizing the far country. The debt was real and the ruin was real and I would not wish either on anyone. But I have to be honest about what grace does with a wreck, because it is the entire reason I have hope to offer. Grace does not merely repair the person who fell the furthest. It gives them a voice that can reach a note the rest of us cannot, and then it stations them in the choir precisely so the rest of us can hear it and remember that we, too, owed more than we ever admitted.
The debt you keep forgetting the size of
Which means the real problem, for most of us, is not that we have sinned too much to sing like that. It is that we keep forgetting the size of what we were forgiven.

We drift. It is the most natural thing in the world. The memory of the debt fades, the way any memory fades, and as it fades our praise flattens out, and we do not even notice it happening. We start singing carefully again. We start watching how it looks. The perfume stays in the jar. And the flatness is not a sign that we have matured past all that emotion. It is a sign that we have lost sight of the number, that the cancellation has become a fact we affirm rather than a rescue we feel.

So the work of a worshiper, and I mean work, is to keep the size of the debt in view. Not to wallow in the old sin, not to drag the forgiven wreckage back out and roll around in it, but to remember. To remember honestly what you were, what you owed, what it would have cost you to pay it, and what it cost the One who paid it instead. Because that is where the sound comes from. Not from working up an emotion, but from telling yourself the truth about the transaction until the gratitude rises on its own, the way it must have risen in the woman at the feet the moment she understood she was free.
The one debt none of us could ever pay

And underneath the woman's debt, and the far country, and every specific thing any of us has run up. There is the one debt that gathers all the others into itself, the one none of us could ever pay, the distance between what we are and what we were made to be. That is the debt the whole story is about. That is what the trumpet of Jubilee was always pointing toward, and what Yeshua stepped into the world to settle. He did not renegotiate it. He did not lower the number. He paid it, in full, with everything He had, and then He tore the record of it up so completely that it cannot be produced against you again.

That is why we sing. Not as a duty we owe, not as rent on our salvation, but as the only fitting sound a cancelled debt can make when it finally finds a voice. Praise is what happens when relief that large runs out of quiet ways to express itself.

So if your worship has gone flat, do not go looking for a better song or a bigger feeling. Go back and look at the number. Sit with the size of what you were forgiven until it lands on you again the way it landed the first time. And then open your mouth, and let the room hear the specific, unfakeable sound that only a freed debtor can make.
That sound is the truest thing about you. It is the debt, cancelled, learning to sing.

pieces.title: The Song in the Drawer Is Not a Dead Song
pieces.imagePrompt: An Indian songwriter smiling warmly over a drawer full of handwritten sheet music in a sunlit writing room, golden afternoon light and drifting dust motes glowing around his content, hopeful face, a guitar resting nearby; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, warm honey and soft green tones, authentic and tender, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I have written far more songs than anyone has ever heard. For a long time that felt like failure. Then I understood what a seed is for, and why the dark is not the end of it.

body.text: Let me tell you something I do not usually say out loud.

I have written far more songs than you will ever hear. Whole albums of them, melodies with every note settled, verses that took me weeks, choruses I still hum walking to the kitchen. Most of them have never been sung by anyone but me, alone, into the quiet of a room. They exist the way a letter exists in a sealed envelope no one has opened. Finished. And silent.

For a long stretch of my life this felt like the plainest kind of failure. You are supposed to have something to show. A song that no one has heard can feel like a song that does not quite count, a tree falling where no ear is standing, making, they say, no sound. I would open the drawer, look at all that work, and feel the particular ache of the maker whose making has gone nowhere anyone can see.

Maybe you know a version of that drawer. It does not have to hold songs. It can hold the degree you never used. The business plan in a folder. The apology you wrote and never sent. The child you raised who cannot see yet what your years cost. The prayers you have prayed for a decade with nothing visible to point to. There is a particular loneliness in having poured yourself into something real, and watching it go quiet, and wondering if quiet is the same thing as wasted.
I want to sit with you in front of that drawer, because I have learned something there that I did not expect.
The difference between a grave and a garden

Jesus told a story about a man who took a seed and threw it into the ground. And then, this is the part I love, the man went to bed. He slept and rose, slept and rose, and the seed sprouted and grew, and he could not have told you how. The earth did it. Quietly, in the dark, without asking his permission or requiring his attention. He woke one morning and there was a blade where there had been bare dirt, and all he had done was trust the ground with something and walk away.

Here is what stopped me the first time I really heard that. A seed only works when it is buried. You cannot keep it on a shelf where you can see it and admire it and know it is safe. Kept in the light where nothing can touch it, a seed simply stays a seed forever, hard, whole, and utterly barren. The burial is not the enemy of the seed. The burial is the beginning of the wheat.
So the drawer is not automatically a grave. It might be a garden. And the difference between the two is not whether anyone is watching. The difference is what put the thing in the dark.

Jesus told another story, and I have to be careful with this one because it cuts the opposite way. A master gave his servants money to steward, and one of them was so afraid of losing it that he dug a hole and buried it and gave it back untouched, and the master was not pleased. People sometimes read those two stories together and get frightened: is my drawer the seed that will rise, or the coin I buried out of fear?
The answer is in the reason you put it there.

The seed goes into the dark in hope. It is an act of trust. You commit something you love to a process you do not control, believing the ground will do what you cannot. The coin went into the dark in fear. The servant said as much: I was afraid, so I hid it. One burial is faith. The other is dread wearing the costume of caution. And you always know which one you are doing, if you are honest, because faith plants and then rests, while fear buries and then keeps checking the hole.
The song was never only for the room
I used to believe a song was not finished until a crowd had heard it. Now I am not so sure the crowd was ever the point.

Something happens in me when I write a song that is true, whether or not it is ever performed. It changes the writer. The reaching-for-God that a melody requires, the honesty it drags up out of you, the way you cannot fake a chorus you do not mean, that work is done in me the moment the song is made, in the empty room, with no one there. The audience was never the only thing being formed. I was.
And there is a listener in every empty room.

The Scriptures say that God sings over his people, that he quiets them with his love and rejoices over them with singing. I take enormous comfort in that image, because it means the direction of song is not only from us upward. There is singing coming the other way. And a God who himself sings over the ones he loves is not a God who needs a stadium to count a song as heard. He was there in the room. He heard the one no one else heard. He does not measure a life's work by the size of the audience, because he has been, from the beginning, an audience of One who misses nothing.
What the dark is doing

I cannot promise you that every song in your drawer will one day fill a room. I will not lie to you like that. Isaiah says God gives seed to the sower and bread to the eater, and that his word does not come back to him empty. It does what he sends it to do. But he never promised the sower he would get to watch. Some seed rises in a season you can see. Some rises after you are gone, in soil you will never visit, in a life you will never meet. The farmer sleeps. The growing is not his job.
So this is what I do now, in front of the drawer.

I stop asking whether anyone has heard it. I ask instead whether it was true, whether it was made in hope, whether it was given honestly to the ground. If it was, then it is not dead. It is planted. And a planted thing keeps its own clock, underground, in the patient dark, doing the one thing a seed knows how to do.

You have a drawer too. Before you decide it is a grave, look again at how the thing got in there. If you buried it in fear, there is grace to dig it up and try. But if you planted it in hope, if you gave your real work to God and could not make it grow and finally, exhausted, let the ground have it, then hear me.
That is not a wasted song.
That is a seed.
And the One who tends that field has never once forgotten what is coming up in the dark.

pieces.title: The Shape of a Melody Is a Story Your Body Already Knows
pieces.imagePrompt: A young Black man wearing headphones at home, eyes closed and face breaking into a delighted smile as the music moves through him, gently swaying, warm golden light across his joyful face; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, warm gold, soft peach and blue tones, authentic and emotionally compelling, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: Why does a rising line feel like hope and a falling one like grief, before a single word is added? Take a melody apart and you find longing built into its very bones, by a hand that was there before the first song.

body.text: Hum the first three notes of a song you love, not the words, just the tune, and watch what your body does before your mind catches up.

Somewhere in those three notes, without your permission, you brace or you soften. A phrase that climbs makes your chest lift a little, like standing on your toes. A phrase that falls settles you, or saddens you, or lets a breath out you did not know you were holding. No one taught you this. No one sat you down as a child and explained that up means hope and down means home. You simply knew, the way you knew to reach for a hand in the dark. The shape of a melody is a language you were fluent in before you had words at all.
I want to take a melody apart in front of you, gently, the way a watchmaker opens the back of a watch, because I think what is inside will tell you something about the One who built the ear it fits.
What a melody is actually made of

Strip a tune down and you find it is almost nothing. A handful of pitches. The distances between them. The order they come in, and the length each one is allowed to last. That is essentially all. A melody has no pictures, no story, no argument. It cannot tell you a single fact. And yet a good one can walk into a locked room in a grown man and open a door he has kept shut for forty years.
How? Consider just one piece of it: the interval, which is only the gap between one note and the next.

Some gaps feel like rest. Two notes close together, or spaced in the ways we call consonant, and something in you unclenches. It sounds like agreement, like two people who finish each other's sentences. Other gaps feel like a question left hanging. The note lands somewhere unresolved, leaning, and your whole body leans with it, waiting for the note that will set it right. That leaning has a name. Musicians call it tension, and its release is called resolution, and I promise you that you have felt both a thousand times in songs you could not name, in the exact place your throat tightened and then let go.

Now here is the strange, holy thing. Tension and resolution are not decorations we add to music. They are the engine. A melody with no tension is not restful. It is dead. It goes nowhere because it wants nothing. Every tune that has ever moved you did it by setting up a longing and then satisfying it: raising a question in sound and then, a few beats later, answering it. The pleasure of a melody is the pleasure of a homesickness that gets to come home.

Sit with that, because it is not a small thing. The mechanism by which music moves us is longing followed by fulfillment. Ache, then rest. The tune takes you out and brings you back, and the coming-back is sweeter for the going-out.
Where did we learn to want the note that hasn't come?

I cannot fully explain why a suspended note makes you hunger for its resolution. Neither can anyone, all the way down. We can describe it. We can chart the physics of vibrating strings and the ratios that sound sweet and the ones that sound sour. But underneath the description is a mystery no ruler reaches: why should a creature of blood and bone care at all whether a sound resolves? Why should it feel like anything? A stone dropped in a certain order of pitches feels nothing. You weep.
I have come to believe the ache in a melody is not an accident of our wiring. I think it is a signature.

The Scriptures open with a God who speaks and then, having made a world, calls it good, who is, from the first page, an artist standing back from the work with pleasure. And they say we are made in his image. If that is true, then the part of you that leans toward the unresolved note, that cannot bear a question left hanging, that aches for the coming-home built into every good tune, that part did not come from nowhere. It is the fingerprint of a Maker who wrote longing and resolution into the very grammar of sound, because he wrote it first into us.

We are the creatures who are homesick for a home we have not clearly seen. That is the human condition in one sentence, and it is also, note for note, the shape of a melody: taken out, held in tension, aching for the resolution that is surely coming. When a tune reaches the place a sermon cannot, this is why. It is not sneaking past your reason. It is speaking to something older than your reason, the part of you that was built leaning forward, waiting for a note to land.
The tune reaches where words can't because it is shaped like you
A word has to be understood to work. It knocks on the door of your mind and waits to be let in, and if the mind is tired or defended or does not speak the language, the word stands out in the cold.

A melody does not knock. It is already shaped like the thing it wants to reach. Its rising is your hope, in sound. Its falling is your grief, in sound. Its unresolved note is your unanswered prayer, in sound, and its resolution is the answer arriving, felt in the body a full second before the mind can say what happened. That is why the same tune can move a scholar and a child and a person whose language you do not speak. It is not arguing with any of them. It is holding up a mirror to something all of them already carry.

I write melodies for a living, and I will tell you honestly that the best ones do not feel invented. They feel found, as if the shape was already there, humming under the floor of the world, and my only job was to get quiet enough to trace it. When I finally catch one, the feeling is never pride. It is recognition. Oh. There you are. Like meeting something that was true before I arrived.

So the next time three notes lift your chest without your consent, do not hurry past it. That is not a trick of the ear. That is your own design, singing back to you. The longing built into the tune is the longing built into you, and both of them lean the same direction, toward a resolution that has not fully come.
Hold that leaning gently. It is not a flaw in you. It is a homing signal.
And the One who set it there does not intend to leave the note hanging forever.

pieces.title: A Song Will Not Be Bullied Into Being
pieces.imagePrompt: A peaceful older Scandinavian songwriter seated by a bright window with a guitar and open notebook, a patient, contented smile on his face and a steaming mug beside him as warm sunrise floods the room, the quiet gladness of waiting on a song; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, amber and soft cream tones, authentic and human, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: You cannot order a melody to arrive. Writing taught me that the deepest work is half discipline and half surrender, showing up every day to wait for a thing you cannot command.

body.text: Here is a scene from my actual life, repeated more mornings than I can count.

I sit down to write a song. I have the time blocked out. I have the coffee, the quiet, the instrument in my hands. I have decided, by an act of will, that today a melody will come. And I play, and nothing comes. Or worse, something comes and it is stale, a tune I have clearly heard before, warmed over and served back to me by a tired imagination. An hour passes. Two. I have done everything right, and the room stays empty.

Then, three days later, standing in a grocery line with no instrument and no intention, a whole melody arrives at once, fully formed, unbidden, almost rude in its timing, and I am fishing for my phone to hum it into a voice memo before the person behind me thinks I have lost my mind.

Anyone who makes things knows this maddening arrangement. The song will not come when summoned and will not stay away when it is finally ready. And for years I thought this meant I was doing it wrong, that a real professional would have mastered the machine by now, would be able to turn the crank and produce inspiration on a schedule. It took me a long time to understand that there is no crank. A song will not be bullied into being. And that is not a defect in the process. That is the process telling you the truth about how the deepest things actually come.
Two things at once, and you need both
The work of writing is discipline and surrender held together, and the mistake is always to try to get away with only one.

Surrender alone is a person who waits for the mood to strike and writes twice a year. They love the idea of being a songwriter. They are precious about inspiration, they talk about their gift a great deal, and they produce almost nothing, because they have confused waiting with laziness and dressed it up as artistic temperament. The muse, they say, has not visited. The muse is not the problem. The problem is they were not at the desk when she came by.

Discipline alone is the other failure, and it is subtler because it looks so responsible. It is the person who grinds, who forces, who fills the page by sheer effort and manufactures something technically complete and completely dead. You can hear it in a song. Craft with no breath in it. A tune that was assembled rather than received. It is the sound of a person who showed up but would not wait.

The truth sits in the tension between them, and it is exhausting because you cannot resolve it. You show up every single day, on schedule, with your hands ready, that is the discipline, and it is not optional; the melody in the grocery line only found me because I had spent a hundred fruitless mornings training my ear to catch it. And then, having shown up, you let go of the outcome. You wait. You cannot make the thing come. You can only be the kind of person, in the kind of posture, that it can come to.
I did not learn that framework from a music book. I learned it from the way God seems to work with people who are trying to follow him.
The cave was a studio

We have a whole book of songs in the middle of our Bible, and a great many of them were written by a man on the run. David wrote in caves, hunted, exhausted, frightened, some of his psalms marked in their very headings as songs from the days he was fleeing for his life. And what strikes me, reading them, is that he clearly did both things I have been describing. He showed up. He kept writing, kept turning his fear into structure, kept the discipline of putting the ache into ordered lines even when God felt absent. And he surrendered. He let the songs go where they wanted, into complaint, into terror, into a trust he could not manufacture and had to wait to feel arriving.

He did not bully those psalms into being. You can tell. The most famous of them do not read like a man forcing an upbeat feeling he does not have. They read like a man who kept showing up to the page and waiting, honest, until the resolution came, and sometimes it came within the same psalm, the tune turning from grief to trust in the last few lines, and sometimes it did not come at all and the song simply ends in the dark, still waiting.

That, to me, is the whole discipline of the spiritual life in miniature. You cannot command God to show up on your schedule. You cannot crank the handle and produce an experience of him. Anyone selling you that machine is selling you a counterfeit. But you can do the one thing that is actually yours to do: keep showing up. Keep your hands ready. Keep the quiet. Be at the desk when he comes by.
The waiting is not the enemy of the work
I want to say a hard and freeing thing to whoever is reading this in a dry season, of writing, of prayer, of faith, of any real work that has gone silent.

The empty mornings are not wasted. This is the part nobody tells you. All those hours I sat with an instrument and nothing came. I used to count them as loss. I no longer do. Those hours were not failure to produce a song. They were the training that made me able to receive one. The waiting was doing something in me the whole time, tuning the instrument that I am, so that when the melody finally passed by, I was ready to hear it instead of missing it entirely.

The ground looks idle in winter. It is not idle. It is working in a way that produces nothing you can point to, and that quiet, apparently fruitless labor is the exact condition of the spring. A farmer who dug up his field every February to check for progress would kill the harvest. The waiting is not the interruption of the work. The waiting is the work, done in a form your impatience cannot recognize.

So if you have been showing up faithfully to a thing that will not come, the prayer that stays unanswered, the calling that stays unclear, the healing that stays out of reach. I do not want to hand you a false promise that if you just try harder the crank will finally turn. It will not. There is no crank. But I will tell you what I have staked my working life on.

Keep showing up. Keep your hands ready. Do not force the false, stale, forced thing just to have something to show. And do not walk away from the desk in the dry season, because the whole point of the dry season is that it is making you into someone the true thing can finally reach.
The song is coming. Not on your schedule. But to the one who kept showing up to wait for it.

pieces.title: You Are a Song God Hasn't Finished Writing
pieces.imagePrompt: A hopeful teenage girl at a piano in warm afternoon light, a half-filled page of handwritten music on the stand and a bright, expectant smile on her face as she plays a song still being written, golden light glowing across the keys; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, soft gold and rose tones, authentic and uplifting, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I know the ache of a half-written song abandoned on the piano, and the difference between the ones I quit on and the ones I only stepped away from. You are not a discarded draft. You are an unfinished one, and the Composer has not left the room.

body.text: There is a particular sadness that only songwriters know, and I want to describe it to you, because I think you have felt its cousin.

It is the half-written song. Not the one you finished. Not the one you never started. The one that sits open on the piano with a great verse and a chorus that will not come, a beginning full of promise and then a cliff, a place where the music simply stops mid-thought. You walk past it for days. Every time you see it, it accuses you a little. There it is, that good beginning, going nowhere. And a quiet voice suggests the obvious: maybe it was never going to be anything. Maybe you should throw it out and stop pretending.

I have a stack of those. And I have learned, over years, that the stack is really two stacks wearing the same clothes. There are songs I truly abandoned, walked away from, gave up on, decided were not worth finishing. And there are songs I only stepped away from, set down not in defeat but because they were not ready, because I was not ready, because the ending had not arrived and forcing it would have ruined it. From the outside, on the piano, the two look identical. Both are unfinished. Both are silent. But one is a corpse and the other is a person asleep, and everything depends on which you are.

I think a great many people walk around convinced they are the first kind, an abandoned draft, a song God started and thought better of, when the truth is they are the second. Unfinished. But not abandoned. Not for one moment.
Unfinished is not the same as failed

Somewhere along the way we absorbed the idea that a good life is a finished one, resolved, arrived, all its questions answered, its loose threads tied. And so the unfinished places in us feel like evidence against us. The relationship still broken. The habit still winning. The dream still out of reach. The version of yourself you meant to become by now, still unbuilt. You look at the open page of your life, all that promise and then the cliff, and you hear the same accusing voice I hear over the piano: maybe this was never going to be anything.

But listen to what the accusation actually assumes. It assumes the Composer has left the room. It assumes the song is being judged in its current state, as a finished object, and found wanting. And that is precisely the lie.

The Scriptures make a promise I hold onto on my worst days. Paul writes to a young church that the One who began a good work in them will carry it on and complete it, will keep at it, faithfully, all the way to the end. Read the shape of that sentence carefully. It is addressed to people mid-song. People with the verse written and the chorus missing. It does not say you are finished. It says you are being finished, that the gap between the promising beginning and the completed whole is not a verdict against you but a description of where you are in a process that has an Author who does not walk away from His drafts.
He is not standing over the piano deciding whether to keep you. He is sitting down at it. Still writing.
The bridge is always the ugliest part on the page

I have written enough songs to tell you a secret about how they look while they are being made: the unfinished middle is almost always the ugliest part on the page. Crossed-out lines. Notes that do not resolve. A section that seems to have lost the thread entirely and wandered somewhere dark and strange. If you found that page and did not know it was a work in progress, you might conclude the writer had failed.

But that dark, wandering, unresolved middle is not the failure of the song. In the finest songs it is the most important part, the place the music leaves the safety of what it already knows and goes out into tension so that the last chorus, when it finally lands, can mean something it could not have meant before. The struggle in the middle is not a sign the song is broken. It is the reason the ending will be worth hearing.

I do not say this to make light of the hard middle you are living in. I say it because I have watched, over and over, the exact passage that felt like proof the song was ruined turn out to be the passage that made the ending land. The Composer works in tension. He is not afraid of the unresolved measure. He is, in fact, doing something there that could not be done in the easy, resolved, finished-looking parts, deepening the thing so that its resolution, when it comes, will carry a weight it could never have carried if He had let you skip straight to the last chorus.
He does not lose the thread
Here is the difference between the songs I abandoned and the songs I only stepped away from, and it comes down to one thing: whether the writer forgets.

The songs I truly lost are the ones I forgot, set down and never thought of again, the thread of what I was reaching for gone from my mind entirely. But the songs I only stepped away from stayed with me. I would be walking, months later, and the missing chorus would surface, because some part of me had never stopped holding the shape of what that song was trying to become. I did not abandon it. I was carrying it the whole time it lay silent on the piano.

Now hear the thing I most want you to hear. God does not forget the thread of you. The Scriptures say He knit you together, that He knew you before you were born, that the days of your life were written before one of them came to be. Whatever He began in you, He is still holding the shape of what it is meant to become, not vaguely, not distantly, but the way a writer carries an unfinished song in the back of his mind through every ordinary hour, waiting for the measure that will complete it. You are not a page He walked past and forgot. You are a work He is still composing, and the reason the ending has not come is not that He lost interest. It is that He is not done.
So when you look at the open, unresolved page of your own life and the accusing voice tells you it was never going to be anything, I want you to answer it with the truth about who is holding the pen.
You are not a discarded draft.

You are an unfinished one, which means the best of you is not behind you in the crossed-out lines. It is ahead of you, in the chorus that has not landed yet, being written by a hand that has never once abandoned a song it began.

pieces.title: A Melody Is Older Than Its Words

pieces.excerpt: Most of my songs arrive as a wordless tune long before a single lyric comes, a melody humming for years, waiting for the words that will finally give it a home. There is a kind of prayer that works exactly the same way.

body.text: I want to let you in on how a song is actually born, because it is almost never the way people think.

People imagine you sit down with something to say, and then you find a tune to carry it. Words first, music second, the melody as a kind of delivery truck for the message. And sometimes it happens that way. But far more often, for me and for most writers I know, it is the reverse. The tune comes first. A melody arrives, wordless, humming itself in the back of the mind on a walk or in the shower or in that strange floating minute before sleep, and it means something, powerfully, urgently, but it does not yet know what it means. It has a shape and a feeling and no words at all. It is a question in the form of a tune, waiting for the sentence that will finally answer it.

I have melodies I have been humming for years that still have no words. Wordless the whole time. I catch myself singing one in the kitchen, no lyric, just la, just the shape of it, and I know it is about something. I know it is reaching for something true. I simply have not yet found the words that fit it, and I have learned not to force them, because a lyric jammed onto a melody it does not belong to is one of the most obvious lies in all of music. So the tune waits. It hums in me, older than its own words, patient, unhurried, sure of what it feels long before it can say what it means.
I have come to believe this is not only how songs work. It is how the deepest part of a human being works when it turns toward God.
The feeling that arrives before the words
There is a kind of prayer you have prayed that had no words, and I want to name it, because you may not have known it counted.

It is the ache you cannot articulate. The groan at the hospital bedside when language has completely failed. The wordless swell in your chest at a sunrise, or over a sleeping child, or in a moment of grief so total that every sentence you reach for feels like an insult to the size of it. It is the hum with no lyric, a feeling reaching for God that is absolutely real and absolutely wordless, and because you could not put it into a proper sentence, you may have decided it did not count as prayer at all.
Hear me. It counted. It counted more than the polished sentences.

The Scriptures say something about this that I find almost too kind to believe. Paul writes that we do not even know what we ought to pray for as we should, that we come to God not knowing the words, and that in exactly that place, the Spirit himself takes up our cause and intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words. Read that slowly. There is a wordless prayer being prayed. And it is not a lesser prayer, a failed prayer, a prayer that did not make it to the level of language. It is the Spirit of God himself, praying the melody underneath your words when you have run entirely out of words to sing.

That means the hum in your chest at the bedside was not nothing. It was a tune God was already carrying, older than any lyric you could have managed, and he did not need you to finish the sentence to know exactly what it meant.
The tune knows before you do
Here is the mystery that keeps me humble as a writer: the wordless melody almost always knows more than I do.

When I finally find the words to a tune I have been humming for years, the experience is never that I invented a meaning and pasted it on. It is that I discovered the meaning that was always in there, that the melody had been about this all along, and I simply had not been ready to understand it. The feeling came first and led the way. The words came later and caught up. The tune was the truth; the lyric was me finally learning to read it.

I think your wordless longings work the same way. That ache you cannot name, the homesickness for a home you have never quite seen, the reaching that has no object you can point to, the tune that has been humming in you since you were a child and that no achievement or relationship has ever fully set to words. I do not think it is confusion. I think it is a melody that knows more than you do. It is reaching for something real. It has a shape and a direction and a certainty, long before you can say what it means. And the great error is to decide that because you cannot name it, it must not be pointing at anything.

It is pointing at Someone. The wordless tune in you was always a tune about God, the way my kitchen melodies are always about something true before I can say what. You have been humming your way toward him your whole life.
He hears the tune, not just the lyric

There is a picture in the Scriptures I return to constantly: God singing over his people. The prophet says the Lord will quiet you with his love and rejoice over you with singing. And I notice he does not tell us the words. There is no lyric printed. It is described simply as singing, a wordless, exulting melody that God sings over the ones he loves, the way you hum, without words, over something too precious to reduce to a sentence.

If God sings over you wordlessly, then he is not a God who only hears the lyric. He hears the tune. He hears the melody underneath your fumbling sentences, the hum you cannot finish, the ache you cannot name, and he understands it completely, because it is, in the end, a song about him, and he has known its meaning since before you first began to hum it.
So I want to give you back something you may have thrown away.

The prayers you could not put into words were still prayers. The longing you cannot name is not a confusion to be solved but a melody to be trusted. It knows where it is going even when you do not. And the wordless hum in your chest, the one that rises at sunrises and bedsides and in the dark before sleep, is not proof that you have failed to pray properly. It is the oldest and truest song you sing, older than any words you will ever find for it, and it is being heard, every note of it, by the One who has been singing back to you, wordlessly, this whole time.
You do not have to find the words tonight.
The tune is already enough. The One it is reaching for has understood it all along.

pieces.title: A New Star Is Just an Old One Catching Fire
