pieces.excerpt: My name means new star. But the astronomers taught me something that undid me, a nova is not a young thing at all. It is an old star, given up for dead, suddenly ablaze. That is the only kind of newness God has ever promised you.

body.text: When my parents named me, they reached for the sky. Nova. A new star. For years I carried it the way you carry a name you have never questioned, proudly, a little vaguely, the way you'd wear a coat handed down from someone who loved you.
Then one winter I actually looked it up. Not the pretty version. The real one, in the language of the people who spend their lives staring at the dark.
And it took my breath.

A nova, it turns out, is not a young star. It is not a fresh thing newly lit, a bright infant hung up in the black. A nova is an old star. An ancient one. So old, in many cases, that it has already died once, collapsed into a small, dense, cooling ember that any casual observer would write off as finished. A cinder. A has-been. The kind of star you would never name a child after, because there is nothing left of it worth pointing at.

And then, from that ember, without warning, comes the light. A star that had been given up for dead suddenly floods with fire, brightens by thousands of times in a matter of hours, and burns so brilliantly that people on a planet unthinkably far away look up and say, with wonder, *there is a new star.*
There isn't. There never was. It is the old one. It only looks new because it is finally, gloriously, on fire again.
I have not been able to unhear that since.

Because we throw the word *new* around in church as though it means *replacement.* As though God's promise to make all things new were a promise to throw you out and start over with someone less disappointing. We read the ancient line, *behold, I make all things new*, and some tired part of us braces, certain it means the old self will be discarded like a first draft, that the real gift is that He will finally be rid of the person we have actually been.
But that is not how He works, and the stars have been telling on Him the whole time.

The Scriptures do not say He makes *all new things.* They say He makes *all things new.* The very same things. This chest. This history. This name you have been dragging around, heavy with everything that happened under it. He does not import a stranger to live your resurrection for you. He reaches into the specific cinder of *your* life, the collapsed place, the part everyone quietly filed under *finished*, and He sets it alight.
Newness, in the hands of God, has never meant erasure. It has always meant ignition.

I want to be careful and honest here, because ruin is real and I will not skip over it to get to the pretty part. There are seasons that genuinely collapse. Not metaphorically. A marriage that goes cold and then goes out. A calling that seemed sure and then just, stopped, and you stood in the silence where the music used to be and wondered if you had imagined the whole thing. A faith that burned bright at twenty and by forty had cooled to a dark, dense little coal you kept in your chest and did not show anyone, because who wants to admit their star went out.

I have pastored people in exactly that place. I have been in exactly that place. And the cruelest lie whispered there is always the same one: *this is what you are now. Cold. Small. Done. The bright version was the anomaly. This is the truth of you.*

But collapse is not the end of a star's story. In the physics of the thing, collapse is the *setup.* The cinder is not the failure of the star. It is the pressure the fire will come out of. The very density everyone mistook for death is the thing that makes the eventual blaze possible. Nothing is wasted in the dark. The years you thought were you cooling into nothing were you being compressed into something that could hold a fire again.

There is an old scene in the Scriptures I keep returning to for this, the prophet standing in a valley full of dry bones, so long dead they had gone white in the sun. Not wounded. Not sleeping. *Dry.* And the question put to him is almost unbearable: *can these bones live?* Every honest instinct says no. Dead is dead. Old is old. Cinders do not sing.

And then the wind comes, and the breath comes, and the valley of the unmistakably finished stands up as an army. Not new bones. *Those* bones. The same ones, reassembled and set ablaze with breath they had long since surrendered.
That is the only kind of new God has ever dealt in.
So I have made a kind of peace with my own name, and I want to offer you the peace under it, because I don't think it was ever meant to be only mine.

If you are in the cinder season, if you have been told, or have told yourself, that the luminous years are behind you and this cooled and quiet thing is the final draft. I want to say something to you with all the tenderness I have. You may not be extinguished. You may be *compressed.* You may be in the part of the story that looks, from the outside and even from the inside, exactly like the end, and is actually the pressure the fire is gathering under. The dark you're in is not proof the light is gone. It is the only sky against which the ignition would ever be seen.

And here is the wonder that steadies me on the hard nights: the fire does not have to come from you. The nova does not manufacture its own blaze by trying harder to be a star. Something comes to it. Something reaches the cold, dense, given-up-for-dead core and awakens what was there all along. You do not have to relight yourself. You were never asked to. You only have to still be there in the dark when the breath arrives, and, when it does, to stop insisting you are only a cinder, and let yourself catch.

Somewhere far off, on the other side of a distance you cannot picture, there is a table where they know your name already. And I have started to believe that on the day the breath finds you and the long-cold thing floods with light, no one there will call it a replacement. They will do what people have always done when an old star suddenly burns.
They will look up, and their faces will open, and they will say, *a new star.*
It won't be new. It will be you. Finally, and at last, on fire again.

pieces.title: Every Note Is Hiding a Chord
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful, diverse small-group Bible study gathered around a wooden table in a warm home, laughing together over open Bibles and mugs of coffee, faces bright with delight and warmth as golden lamplight glows over the whole circle; wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, inviting and radiant, premium worship-brand cinematic film-still warmth, authentic and natural, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: Pluck one string and you think you hear one note. You don't. You hear a crowd, a whole hidden choir stacked inside a single sound, singing whether you notice or not. And I cannot stop believing that says something true about how God is present in the plainest moments of your life.

body.text: Pluck a single string. Just one. A guitar, a piano key, the low string of a cello. It doesn't matter. You will tell me, and you will believe it, that you heard one note.
You didn't.
You heard a crowd.

This is one of those facts that sounds like a riddle until someone shows you, and then you cannot un-know it. When a string vibrates, it does not only vibrate as a whole. In the same instant, it divides itself and vibrates in halves, and in thirds, and in quarters, and in fifths, on and on, each division singing its own higher, fainter note *at the same time* as the low one you thought you were hearing. Musicians call them overtones, or harmonics. They are always there. Stacked inside every single note you have ever heard is a whole ladder of quieter notes, a hidden chord, a small choir folded into what you took for one lonely voice.
You have never in your life heard a single sound. You have only ever heard a fullness so seamless it disguised itself as simplicity.

I learned this properly as a grown woman and I actually laughed out loud, alone in a room, because it felt like being let in on a secret the universe had been keeping in plain hearing the whole time. And then, the way these things go with me, it stopped being about music and started being about God, and I have not been able to send it back.

Because we are forever pressing God to *show up*, as though He is somewhere else and must be summoned, as though the ordinary moment is one note, thin and alone, and holiness would be the arrival of a second thing from outside. We stand in a plain Tuesday, a plain sink of dishes, a plain drive home in traffic, and we think: there is nothing of God in this. It is one note. It is just my life, and it is not enough, and where is He.
But what if the plain moment is a plucked string?
What if it was never one note?

The old Scriptures make a claim that most of us nod along to and none of us can quite live inside, that God fills all things. Not visits. *Fills.* That there is no ordinary place He is absent from, no plain Tuesday emptied of Him, no low and lonely note of your life that is not, right now, carrying a hidden ladder of His presence, singing at a pitch you have simply not yet learned to hear. The psalm-writer, dizzy with it, tries to name a single location God isn't, the heights, the depths, the far side of the sea, the dark itself, and gives up, because there isn't one. Every note is hiding a chord. Every moment is stacked with a fullness you took for emptiness because it was too seamless to notice.
Here is the part that undoes me, and I want to slow down for it.

You can learn to hear the overtones. It takes almost nothing, a quiet room, a still mind, and the willingness to stop listening for the obvious note and start listening *underneath* it. Pluck the string, and then don't reach for your certainty about what a string sounds like. Wait. Listen past the top of the sound, into it, and one by one the higher voices begin to lift out and become audible, the ghostly fifth, the shimmering octave above, the faint sweet third, notes that were *there the entire time,* singing over you, waiting only for your attention to turn.
The presence of God is very often like this. Not a new note added to your day. The undertone of the day, finally heard.

I think of the ancient prophet who ran for his life into the wilderness and stood on the mountain waiting for God to arrive in the obvious way, in the earthquake, in the wind that tore the rocks apart, in the fire. Everyone would call *those* the sound of God. The loud note. The unmistakable one. And He was not in any of them. He came, instead, in something the old translators reached for and could barely hold, a sound of thin silence, a still small voice, a whisper you would only catch if you had already gone quiet enough to hear underneath the noise you were expecting. God, it seems, prefers to be an overtone. He is forever singing in the register we have not tuned our attention to yet.
And I find this unbearably tender, because of what it means for the days that feel like nothing.

The season where nothing is happening. The stretch of faith where the loud, obvious notes of His presence, the goosebumps, the answered prayer you can point at, the mountaintop feeling, have all gone quiet, and you are standing in what feels like a single thin note, a life with no chord in it, sure that He has left the room. I have pastored so many people through that exact silence, and I have stood in it myself, and the temptation is always to conclude from the missing loud note that there is no music at all.

But a string that seems to be sounding one bare note is, in physical fact, at that very moment full of a hidden choir. The fullness does not depend on your hearing it. The overtones sing whether or not anyone in the room has learned to listen. And the invitation, in the dry and silent season, is not to manufacture a louder note to prove He is near. It is to go quiet. To stop straining for the obvious arrival, and to listen down, patiently, into the plain note of your ordinary life, until, faint and then unmistakable, the ladder of His nearness begins to lift out of it, and you realize with a rush that it was singing the whole time, and the only thing that ever changed was you.

So the next time your life sounds like one lonely note, I would be very slow to trust that impression. Every note you have ever heard was a fullness dressed as a single sound. And the God who fills all things has never once been a second thing arriving from outside the moment.
He is the chord already inside it.

Go quiet. Listen under the note. He is nearer, and richer, and more crowded with His own presence, than the surface of your day will ever let on. There has only ever been one thing to do about a hidden choir: get still enough to finally hear it singing over you.

pieces.title: The Rest Is Part of the Song
pieces.imagePrompt: A young woman resting on a couch in a peaceful sunlit room, earbuds in and eyes gently closed, a soft radiant smile of contentment on her face as she savors a quiet moment of music, warm golden light and drifting dust motes around her; wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, tranquil and tender, premium worship-brand cinematic film-still warmth, authentic and natural, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: On the page, a rest is not the absence of music. It is written in, counted, and held, as deliberate as any note. And I have come to believe the silent seasons of your life are not gaps in the song God is composing through you. They are the song. Notated, on purpose, in His own hand.

body.text: There is a mark in written music that most people, if they ever notice it, mistake for nothing. It sits on the staff where a note ought to be, and it tells the musician to make no sound at all. A rest.
Here is what I love about it, and what I think we have almost entirely missed.

A rest is not the music stopping. A rest is *written in.* Someone composed it. It has a shape on the page, its own particular symbol, and it has a length, a whole rest, a half, a quarter, that must be *counted,* held for exactly as long as the notes around it are held. The player does not get to skip it, or rush through it, or treat it as the part where nothing is happening and they can relax. A great musician plays the silences with the same care as the sound. Ask any conductor: an orchestra that cannot hold its rests cannot make music at all. The stillness is not the absence of the piece. The stillness is *in* the piece. It was put there on purpose, by the one who wrote it.
I want to hand you that, gently, because I think you are living inside a rest right now and grieving it as a gap.

We do not know what to do with the silent seasons. The stretch where the doors that used to open have all quietly closed. The year after the diagnosis, or the loss, or the ending, when the momentum of your life just, stopped, and you found yourself holding a strange, unbearable stillness where the music used to be. We are certain, in those seasons, that we have fallen out of the song. That the melody of our real life is on pause, waiting somewhere ahead for us to get back to it. That God is composing everyone else and we are the one measure where nothing is written.

But I don't think the silence is a gap in the composition. I have come to believe it is *part* of it. Notated. Counted. Held for exactly as long as it needs to be held, by a hand more careful with your stillness than you are.

The Scriptures are far more honest about this than we tend to be. At the very beginning, before the story of the world has barely begun, God does something that must have looked, to any watching eye, like stopping. Six days of unimaginable making, light, sea, sparrow, star, the whole singing torrent of it, and then, on the seventh, He *rests.* Not because He was tired; the One who spoke galaxies does not need a nap. He rested to write the rest *into the score,* to build a silence into the very structure of time and call it holy. The pause was not the failure of the work. It was the crown of it. He made a measure of stillness and declared it good, and then He asked His people, forever after, to learn to hold it too.

And they resisted it exactly the way we do. Keep the rest, He kept telling them. Stop the striving one day in seven. Let the field lie fallow one year in seven. And every generation heard it as a threat, surely the music of provision stops if we stop playing; surely we fall behind, surely the song unravels if we dare to hold the silence. It takes enormous trust to play a rest. You have to believe the piece is still going when you have gone quiet. You have to believe the Composer is still counting even though your instrument has fallen still.
That is the whole test of a rest. Can you stay in the measure without making noise to reassure yourself the song is still there?

Because here is what the rushing musician never learns: the rest is not empty. It is doing something the notes could never do. In music, silence is where a phrase gets its shape, the held breath before the return, the space that makes the next entrance land like sunrise instead of just more sound. Take the rests out of a great piece and play every note back to back with no gaps, and you do not get *more* music. You get noise. An exhausting, shapeless wall of it, with nothing to lean into and nothing to long for. The silences are what make the sound mean anything. Remove them and you have not added to the song. You have destroyed it.

I say that as someone who spent years believing my worth was measured in unbroken sound. If I was producing, creating, moving, making, then I was the song. And when a season finally came that stopped me, and the noise I had mistaken for my whole identity fell away, I was sure I had gone silent because I had failed. It took me a long time, and a lot of tenderness from God and from people who loved me, to hear it differently: that I had not fallen out of the music. I had reached a rest He had written in with His own hand, and my only task, the hardest one, was to hold it without panicking, and trust that He was still counting.

Something happens in the held silence that cannot happen anywhere else. It is where the next thing gathers. The old poets knew it, those who wait, they wrote, *those who wait* will find their strength renewed, will rise up on wings like eagles. Not those who never stop. Those who wait. The waiting is not the punishment before the strength. The waiting is where the strength is made.

So if you are in the quiet measure right now, if the noise of your busy, useful, sounding life has gone still and you have been reading that stillness as proof that God set your song aside. I want to offer you the truest thing I know. You may not be in a gap. You may be in a rest. And a rest is not the absence of the music. It is the music, in the one form that shapes everything the notes will later mean.

Do not rush it. Do not fill it with anxious noise to convince yourself the song survives. Hold it, the way a good musician holds a silence, fully present, quietly trusting, eyes on the One still keeping time. He has not stopped composing you. He has written you a measure of rest, and He is counting every beat of it, and when the silence has done its slow and shaping work, the next note will come.
And it will land the way a return always lands after a well-kept rest, not as an interruption of the quiet, but as the thing the quiet was making room for all along.

pieces.title: The Realest Thing You'll Never Hold
pieces.imagePrompt: A diverse outdoor worship gathering at dusk with hands raised toward a warm glowing sky, faces radiant with awe and joy as string lights and golden haze drift over the crowd, an emotionally compelling sense of something unseen yet unmistakably alive; wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, marketable and uplifting, premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, authentic and natural, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: You cannot hold a song. It has no weight, no place, no edges. It exists only while it is moving and dies the instant it stops, and yet it can wreck you, heal you, and outlast the ones who first sang it. Music may be the most honest teacher we have about the things that are most real and least holdable.

body.text: Try to hand me a song.

Not the recording. Not the sheet music, not the file, not the vinyl. The song itself, the thing that made you cry in the car, the thing that got a room of strangers to lift their hands at the same moment. Put *that* in my palm.

You can't. Nobody can. It has no weight. It has no color. It has no location. You cannot point to where the song is in the room, only to where the air is moving. It has no edges. And most unsettling of all, it does not even fully exist in any single instant. A song only *is* while it is going. Freeze it, stop time on one note, and you don't have a song, you have a pressure. The song lives only in motion, only across time, dying continuously into the note behind it and being reborn continuously into the note ahead. It is never all there at once. And the moment it stops moving, it is simply gone.
By almost every test we use for whether a thing is *real*, can you hold it, weigh it, keep it, point to it, stop it and still have it, a song fails completely.
And yet.

And yet a song can take you apart. A song can reach a grief you had bricked up for twenty years and open it in four bars. A song can walk a terrified person through a night they were sure they would not survive. A song sung by people long dead can arrive, intact, in a room they never imagined, and do its full work on hearts that were not born when they sang it. The most weightless, un-holdable, cannot-be-frozen thing in your whole day may also be the thing that changed you most.

I think about this more than is probably reasonable, because I make my living inside it, and because I have come to suspect that music is not just beautiful. I think it is *telling us something*, quietly, constantly, about the whole architecture of what is real. And the thing it is telling us runs exactly opposite to what our hands believe.

Our hands are convinced that real means holdable. Solid. Weighable. Ownable. The whole grabbing logic of a human life runs on it: get your hands around enough solid things, money, property, security, the visible and the verifiable, and you will have gotten your hands around reality itself. We stake our peace on what we can grip.

But a song will not be gripped, and a song is undeniably real, and once you have really noticed that, a crack opens in the whole assumption. Because a song is not the only thing like this. Neither is love. You cannot hand me a pound of it. Neither is courage, or forgiveness, or joy, or grief. None of them can be held, weighed, or frozen. All of them exist, like music, only *in the motion*, love only while it is being given, forgiveness only while it is being extended, joy only while it is being lived. And every one of them is more real, and more powerful, and more permanent than the solid things we spend our lives clutching. The most world-changing forces you will ever encounter all share the song's strange nature: weightless, un-holdable, alive only in motion, and truer than the floor under your feet.

The old Scriptures were saying this long before anyone measured a sound wave. *The things that are seen are temporary,* they insist, *but the things that are unseen are eternal.* We read it as a poetic flourish and go back to trusting our hands. But it is not a flourish. It is the plainest description of reality on offer, and music has been demonstrating it in every worship set, every lullaby, every song at every funeral, the entire time. The holdable things are the passing ones. The un-holdable ones are the ones that last.

Which is why I have come to love, rather than resent, that you cannot hold a song. It is training. It is God teaching the grabbing creature, gently and over a lifetime, that the realest things were never meant to be gripped. They were meant to be *received while they move,* and then passed on while they are still warm.
And this is where it turns from philosophy into something I would kneel down and say to you softly, because it is the whole point.

The God the Scriptures describe is, Himself, exactly this kind of real. You cannot hold Him. You cannot weigh Him or freeze Him or set Him on a shelf and own Him. Every attempt in the ancient story to reduce Him to a holdable object, to cast Him in gold, to nail Him down to one mountain, to get a grip on Him and keep Him, ends in ruin, not because He is less real than the idol, but because He is *more* real, in precisely the way a song is more real than the speaker it comes out of. He will not be held. But He can be *received while He moves*, met in the going, encountered in the living current, known the way you know a song: not by seizing it, but by letting it move through you and take you somewhere you could not have carried yourself.

I find that unbearably hopeful, especially for the people who are certain they have missed Him because they cannot point to Him. If you have ever felt disqualified from faith because you could not produce God as a holdable fact, could not weigh the evidence in your palm and be done, then hear this: you were trying to hold a song. That is not how songs are known, and it was never how He was meant to be known. He is not less real for being un-holdable. He is real the way the truest things are always real, the way the music is real, undeniable in its effect and impossible in your grip.
So here is what I would leave in your open, empty hands, which is the only honest place to leave it.

Stop trying to hold the song. Let it move. Stop demanding that the realest things become solid before you will trust them. The song was weightless and it healed you anyway. Love has no edges and it is the strongest force in your life. And the God you cannot get your hands around is not far away because you cannot grip Him. He is near in exactly the way music is near, filling the room you are standing in, moving through the very air, asking only that you stop grasping long enough to let Him wash over you and carry you where you could not go alone.
The realest thing you will ever know is the one thing you will never hold. Open your hands anyway. That was always how it was going to be received.

pieces.title: The One Word Nobody Translates
pieces.imagePrompt: A radiant global montage of worshippers from many nations, an African congregation, a South Asian gathering, a Latin American crowd, an East Asian fellowship, hands lifted and faces bright with the same joy, all bathed in warm golden light as if singing one word together across the earth; wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, diverse and uplifting, premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, authentic and natural, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: My songs travel into six languages, and almost every word gets remade at the border. But there are one or two that refuse. Hallelujah crosses untranslated into nearly every tongue on earth, and I think the reason is the most hopeful thing I know about where all of this is going.

body.text: When one of my songs crosses a border, almost everything about it gets remade.

I have watched it happen. A line I wrote in English is carried into Japanese, into Dutch, into Romanian, into Swedish, into Thai, and the translators, who are artists in their own right, take it apart and rebuild it. The rhymes vanish and new ones are found. The images bend to fit a different sky. A metaphor that sings in one tongue lands flat in another and has to be replaced with something a grandmother in that language would actually feel. By the time the song arrives in a new mouth, nearly every word has been through customs and come out changed. That is not a loss. That is the miracle of translation, love, taking the trouble to become local.
But there are one or two words that refuse.

They reach the border, and the border waves them through unchanged. The translator sets down the pen. Because some words cannot be improved by remaking, and everyone who works with language for long enough eventually meets them.
*Hallelujah* is the great one.

Follow it around the world and it will astonish you. In English we sing it. But so do worshippers in Japanese, and in Dutch, and in Romanian, and in Swedish, and in Thai, and in nearly every other language that has ever lifted a song to God. Not a translated version. The *same word*, Hebrew at the root, *hallelu-Yah,* praise Yah, carried whole and un-remade across thousands of years and thousands of miles into mouths that share almost nothing else. A word so full that no language felt it had the right to replace it, only to receive it. *Amen* does the same thing. So does the older *alleluia.* A tiny handful of words that the whole singing world holds in common, untranslated, unchanged, passed hand to hand across every border on earth like a coin everyone already recognizes.
I cannot tell you how much this moves me, and I want to try to tell you why, because I think it is pointing at something enormous.

We are a scattered species. That is the plain fact of us. Thousands of languages, and most of them cannot understand each other at all. The old Scriptures tell a piercing little story about how it happened, a tower, a proud people determined to make one name for themselves and climb to heaven on their own engineering, and a God who, rather than let that pride harden into something monstrous, scattered their speech until they could no longer understand one another and had to spread out across the earth. Ever since, we have lived behind the walls of our own tongues. It is why translation is holy work and heartbreaking work at once, every act of it is a small, tender attempt to reach across a divide that runs right down the middle of the human family.
And yet, here is the wonder, through all that scattering, one word got through the walls intact.

Not a word of commerce. Not a word of conquest. Not the name of an empire. A word of *praise.* The single thing the scattered languages of the earth still hold in common, unchanged, is the word we use to worship. When we go to lift something up to God, we reach past all our different vocabularies and find, waiting in every one of them, the same untranslated sound. It is as if the scattering that runs through everything else stops at the door of worship, as if, at the exact point where humanity turns together toward its Maker, the confusion of tongues quietly lifts, and for one word we are one people again.
I don't think that is an accident of history. I think it is a rumor of the ending.

Because the Scriptures do not leave us scattered. They open, at the very end, onto a scene that has kept singers like me awake at night with longing, a vast crowd that no one could number, from every nation and tribe and people and language, standing together before the throne, and out of that impossible diversity comes not chaos but a *song.* And what does the great multitude of every tongue on earth cry out together in that final scene? The old writers tell us plainly. *Hallelujah.* The one word that never needed translating turns out to be the first word of the world made whole. The sound the scattered languages kept in common all along was the sound of where they were always heading.

So every time you sing that word, in whatever language you were born into. You are doing something far larger than you know. You are rehearsing the reunion. You are speaking the one syllable that the Japanese worshipper and the Romanian worshipper and the Thai worshipper and the Swedish worshipper and the Dutch worshipper are speaking too, in the very same form, so that in that single word, and, for now, almost only in that word, the scattering is already undone. Worship is the place where the walls of Babel go transparent. It is the one room where we already understand each other.
I find that unspeakably hopeful, and I want to hand the hope to you directly, because I think some of us have quietly given up on ever belonging to the whole.

You may feel like the odd voice. Wrong language, wrong background, wrong story to ever fully fit the great human choir, always translating yourself, always at the border, never quite waved through. But there is a word that was made for exactly you, and it asks nothing of your accent, your fluency, your pedigree, or your past. It has crossed every border ever built between people, and it will cross the ones inside you too. You do not have to learn a new tongue to belong to the song at the center of everything. You already know the word. You have probably already said it. It is the one nobody translates, because everybody is welcome to it, because it was always meant to be the sound of the whole family finding its way home.
That is the whole promise, folded into four syllables the world could not stop passing along.
The scattering is not the last word. *Hallelujah* is.

Go ahead and say it, in your language, which is also, in this one word, everyone's. You are not only praising. You are rehearsing the day the walls come down for good, and the numberless crowd of every tongue on earth turns toward the throne and discovers, with joy, that they all know how the song begins.

pieces.title: The Procession That Would Not Stay Indoors
pieces.imagePrompt: A jubilant worship procession pouring down the middle of a warm-colored barrio street at golden hour, people of every generation singing and clapping with hands raised and faces radiant, banners and marigolds and drifting light with painted walls glowing amber, unstoppable joy in the air; luminous cinematic film-still quality, warm gold coral and terracotta tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: In my barrio the worship never fit inside the building. It spilled out the door, down the middle of the road, past the fruit stand and the mechanic, and turned the whole street into a sanctuary with no walls.

body.text: The first thing you should know about where I come from is that the worship never once fit inside the building.

We had a room. A small one, with plastic chairs and a fan that lost the argument with the heat by ten in the morning. And every week the singing would start in there, polite enough, and then something would happen that I have watched my whole life and still cannot fully explain. Somebody near the door would prop it open for air. And the sound would find the gap. And once the sound found the gap it was gone, out the door, into the street, past the fruit stand where Doña Marta stacked her mangoes, past the mechanic wiping his hands on a rag, out into the whole barrio, which had never agreed to be quiet in the first place.

We called it *la calle canta*. The street sings. And I do not mean it as a poem. I mean that on the right day, in the right season, the actual road, the asphalt and the potholes and the tangle of wires overhead, became the sanctuary, and it had no walls, and that was the point.

I want to tell you why a faith like that will not stay indoors, because I think somewhere along the way a lot of good people were taught that worship is something you do in a room and then carefully carry home in your pocket, and I think that idea has made them smaller than God ever intended them to be.
Here is what the procession knows that the pocket does not.
Praise was always meant to take up space
When you read the old accounts honestly, the worship in them is almost never a private, indoor thing. It is loud, and it is outside, and it takes up an embarrassing amount of room.

There is the day the ark of God came home to the city, the sacred thing carried back through the streets after years away, and the king himself went out in front of it. Not seated on a throne watching a program. Out in front, in the road, dancing before Yahuah with everything he had, whirling and leaping down the public street while the whole house of Israel came up behind him shouting, and the horns blowing, and the whole city turning out to see it pass. His own wife watched from a window and was embarrassed for him. And he told her plainly that he would be more undignified than this, that he did not care who saw. The procession did not stay indoors. It went down the middle of the road, and the king led it there.

Go back further and you find the same thing at the edge of the sea, when a company of freed slaves came up out of the water alive and free, and the very first thing they built was not a shelter. It was a song. Miriam took a tambourine in her hand and the women came out after her with tambourines and dancing, and the whole desert, the wide, open, roofless desert, heard a sound it had never heard, because there was no building anywhere for miles and the praise did not wait for one.

This is the tradition I was born into without knowing it had a pedigree that old. In the barrio we did not invent the procession. We inherited it. When we carried the song out the door and down the block, we were doing the oldest thing the people of God have ever done, refusing to let the praise be smaller than the God it was aimed at.
The street needs to hear it more than the choir does
There is a reason it matters that the worship goes outside, and it is not about volume.

Inside the room, everyone already agrees. That is a beautiful thing and I would never take it from you, the gathered people, the shared song, the roof over the family. But the mechanic wiping his hands on the rag did not come to the room. Doña Marta is minding her mangoes. The old man who has not darkened a church door in thirty years is on his step, and he is not going to walk in.
But the procession walks *past* him.

I have watched it a hundred times, and it undoes me every time. The song comes down the street, and the man on the step who would never have come inside, something in his face changes. He does not stand up. He does not raise a hand. But he goes quiet, and he watches it pass, and I have seen his lips move. Because the worship came to *him*. It did not wait behind a door for him to find the courage to open it. It came out into his ordinary afternoon, into the exact street where he actually lives, and it sang the great deeds of God right there in front of his fruit crates and his broken-down car.

That is the whole heart of the thing. Yeshua did not set up a booth and wait for the crowds to file in and take a number. He went *out*, into the streets, the roads, the hillsides, the shoreline where the fishermen were already working. He met people in the middle of their Tuesday. The Gospel has feet. It was always meant to move.
Your ordinary road is holier than you think
So here is what I want to leave with you, whether you were raised in a barrio or a suburb or a place where nobody sings in the road anymore.

The distance you have drawn between the sacred room and the ordinary street is a distance God does not recognize. He was never content to be worshiped only under a roof, by people who already agreed, behind a door propped open just enough for air. He is the God who went out in front of the ark and danced down the public road. He is the God who filled a roofless desert with tambourines. He is the God who walked the dusty streets of small towns and called it His Father's business.

And your street, the real one, the one with the traffic and the neighbor you avoid and the shop on the corner, is not a lesser place. It is the exact place the procession is trying to reach. The worship you keep so carefully indoors was never meant to live there full-time. It was meant to find the gap in the door, and go.

So let it out. Hum it on the walk to the bus. Sing it under your breath at the market. Carry the joy down the middle of your ordinary road where Doña Marta and the mechanic and the old man on the step can see it pass. You do not need a permit and you do not need a stage. You need only to stop believing that praise belongs inside.

*La calle canta.* The street is waiting to sing. It has been waiting for someone to prop the door open and let the song find the gap. Let it be you. And watch what happens to the faces along the road when the worship of God finally comes out to where the people actually live.

pieces.title: The Cross That Learned to Dance
pieces.imagePrompt: A radiant crowd dancing at dusk in a warm plaza strung with glowing lights, arms lifted and skirts spinning in a blur of color, faces turned upward in fierce joy as a simple wooden cross rises above the movement catching the last gold light, celebration forged out of struggle; luminous cinematic film-still quality, warm gold magenta and amber tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: Someone once told me my people worship too joyfully for how much we have suffered. He had it exactly backward. The joy is not in spite of the suffering. The joy is what the suffering became.

body.text: A man said something to me once that I have never been able to put down.

We had just come off a long night of worship, the kind where the room is soaked through, where the drums have been going so long the walls have a pulse, where old women who buried husbands are up on their feet with their eyes shut and their arms open, dancing. He watched all of it from the back with his arms crossed, and afterward he came to me, and he was not unkind, but he was troubled. He said: *your people worship too joyfully for how much you have suffered. It does not add up. Where is the grief? How can a people who have lost so much dance like that?*

I did not have a clean answer for him that night. I have one now, and it took me years, and it is this: he had the arithmetic exactly backward. He thought the joy came *in spite of* the suffering, a bright coat thrown over a cold body, a denial, a way of not looking at the wound. But that is not what he was watching. He was watching something much stranger and much older.
He was watching a cross that had learned to dance.
The two things the world keeps in separate rooms

The world I grew up in, and maybe the one you did too, is very sure that suffering and joy live in separate rooms, and that you can only be in one at a time. Grief is for the dark room with the door closed. Celebration is for the good days, when nothing is wrong. Keep them apart. Do not mix them. It is not appropriate to dance at a wound.

But my grandmother mixed them her whole life, and she was not confused. She would light a candle for the dead and then turn on the radio. She would weep at the grave and cook a feast that same afternoon and mean both. She was not being inconsistent. She knew something the man with the crossed arms did not: that in the kingdom of God, the deepest joy is not the absence of suffering. It is what suffering becomes when it is handed over to a God who raises the dead.

That is the whole scandal at the center of our faith, and we have gotten so used to it that we have stopped being scandalized. The most joyful symbol the world has ever known is an instrument of torture. A cross. A slow public killing. That is what we hang in our homes and wear around our necks and lift up over the dance floor. Think about how insane that is for a moment. It would be like a people making a party out of a gallows.

And yet. When Yeshua went to that cross, He was, the account tells us plainly, going *for the joy set before Him*. Not around the suffering. Not in spite of it. *Through* it. He endured the cross, despising its shame, for a joy He could already see on the far side of it. The suffering was real. The nails were real. And it was the very road the joy came by.

That is the cross that dances. It is not a cross that forgot it was a cross. It is a cross that went all the way down into the worst the world could do, and came up on the third day with the music still in it.
Joy forged in the fire is a harder joy
Here is what the man in the back could not see about the old women dancing with their eyes shut.

Their joy was not cheap. That is the thing he mistook. He saw the lightness and assumed it was ignorance, that they danced because they did not know how hard life was. But those were the women who *knew*. They had buried children. They had gone hungry so the little ones could eat. They had scrubbed other people's floors and come home to sing. Their joy was not the thin, nervous happiness of people whom life has not yet found. It was the deep, unbreakable joy of people whom life found early and often and could not finish.

There is a kind of joy you can only get one way, and it is not the easy way. The Scriptures are strangely insistent on this, in a way that offends our comfort. They say to count it all joy when you meet trials, because the testing of your faith produces something that ease never could. They say that the sorrowful can be, at the very same moment, always rejoicing. They say weeping may last for the night, but joy comes in the morning, not instead of the weeping, but *after* it, on its far side, arriving in the same body that did the weeping.

This is why the songs of a suffering people hit different. There is a reason the deepest worship music on earth has so often come up out of the hardest ground, out of slavery, out of the barrio, out of the margins, out of exile. It is not a coincidence and it is not a tragedy. It is the design. Joy that has never been near a cross is a pretty thing, but it is light. It floats off in the first hard wind. Joy that has been *through* the cross and come out singing, that joy has weight. It has scars. It has, if you look closely, holes in its hands. And it cannot be talked out of the dance, because it already knows the worst and has decided to praise anyway.
Dance at the wound, because of Who is coming for it
So I will say to you what I wish I had said to the man that night.

You are not being asked to pretend the wound is not there. That is not what the dancing means. The Gospel is not a denial. It looks the grave full in the face. It wept at the grave of a friend before it raised him, and it does not lie to you about how much it costs to be alive in a broken world. If you are in the dark room right now with the door closed, hear me: the dance is not an accusation against your grief. Grief is holy. Weeping is a form of faith. There is a time for the candle and the closed door, and God is in that room with you, and He is not asking you to fake anything.

But do not believe the man with the crossed arms when he tells you that your joy has to wait until the suffering is over. It does not. The cross did not wait. The cross went down into the very center of the suffering and turned it, from the inside, into the doorway of resurrection. That is what our God does with the worst things. He does not delete them. He raises them. He takes the instrument of death and teaches it to dance.

So when your night comes, and it will, and it may already be here, do not think you have to choose between the tears and the tambourine. My people never did. They wept *and* they danced, sometimes in the same hour, because they had staked their whole lives on the promise that the story does not end at the cross. It ends at the empty tomb. And a people who believe that can dance at a wound without lying about the wound, because they can see, past it, the One who is coming to raise them.
*La cruz que baila.* The cross that dances. Lift it up over your hardest season. And let your feet believe, before the rest of you catches up, that Sunday is coming.

pieces.title: The Theology My Grandmother Hummed at the Stove
pieces.imagePrompt: A warm kitchen in morning light where a smiling abuela hums at the stove, steam rising and catching gold sunbeams, a wide-eyed grandchild seated close and watching her with delight and wonder, worn hands and simple dishes glowing in tender inheritance and belonging; warm cinematic film-still quality, warm amber honey and soft green tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: My abuela never read a page of theology in her life. She hummed it. And the songs she pressed into me at the stove have held under pressure that the books I later studied never could.

body.text: My grandmother could not have told you what the word *theology* meant. She left school young to work. She read slowly, and mostly she read one book, and she read it out loud with her finger under the words. If you had put a shelf of doctrine in front of her she would have dusted it and made you lunch.
But she hummed.

She hummed at the stove in the mornings, low, with her back to the room, stirring something that had been simmering since before I woke. She hummed on the bus. She hummed folding the laundry and hummed walking to the market and hummed at the sink at night when she thought the house was asleep. And here is the thing I did not understand until I was grown and had studied the books she never opened: every one of those hums was a sermon. She was preaching the whole time. She just did it in a key instead of a paragraph.

I want to tell you about the theology my grandmother hummed, because I have come to believe that some of the deepest truth any of us will ever hold got into us exactly this way, not through the front door of the mind, but through a side door somebody left open with a song, when we were too small to guard it.
What a song does to a child who is not listening

I was not trying to learn anything. That is the first thing to understand. I was a boy underfoot in a small kitchen, waiting for food, thinking about the street. I was not listening to my grandmother's humming the way you listen to a teacher. I would have told you I did not hear it at all.

But it went in anyway. It went in the way rain goes into ground you did not till. Years later, grown, far from home, in a season so dark I could not have told you my own name, a melody surfaced in me from nowhere, unbidden, and I found my mouth moving to it before my mind had agreed to anything, and it was hers. The exact tune she hummed at the stove. And riding underneath that tune, carried on it like a boat on a river, was a truth about God I had apparently believed my whole life without ever deciding to: that He is good, that He does not leave, that the morning comes. I had not learned it. I had absorbed it. She had pressed it into me with a melody when I was too young to argue, and it had waited, folded up small, for the exact day I would need it.

The Scriptures actually command this, though we have mostly forgotten it is a command. Fix these words in your heart, they say, teach them to your children, talk of them when you sit at home and when you walk by the road, when you lie down and when you get up. Sit and walk and lie down and rise. That is not the schedule of a classroom. That is the schedule of a kitchen. That is a grandmother at a stove. God's chosen delivery system for the deepest things was never mainly the lecture. It was the ordinary day, sung over and over until the truth became part of the furniture of a child's soul.
Honest about what was hers and what was His
Now I want to be careful here, because I love my grandmother and I will not lie for her, and love that lies is not love.

Not everything she hummed was Scripture. Some of it was her people's tradition, the old songs handed down, the rhythms of a faith carried across an ocean and worn smooth by generations of hands. Some of it, if I am honest, I could not find a chapter and verse for, and I have looked. There was folk faith mixed in with the true faith, the way there is in every family that has loved God for a long time in a hard place. I am not going to pretend the humming was flawless. It was human.

But here is what I have learned to say plainly. The *core* of it was true, truer than a lot of the polished things I was taught later by people who could cite every reference. Underneath the folk melodies and the borrowed customs, the thing she was actually pressing into me was the real Gospel: that God came down, that Yeshua carried what I could not, that grace is real and free and mine, that death does not get the last word. That part was not tradition. That part is the solid rock the whole thing stands on. And she had it. She had it in her bones, in her humming, in the way she cooked and forgave and kept getting up in the dark to pray.

So I do the work she could not. I take what she gave me and I hold it up against the Book she read out loud with her finger under the words, and I keep what is gold and I let the rest go with gratitude. That is not a betrayal of her. That is the most faithful thing a grandson can do, to love the inheritance enough to sort it honestly, to carry forward what was truly the Lord's and lay down gently what was only ours.
You are humming something right now
Here is what I most need you to hear, and it is not really about my grandmother at all. It is about you.

You are humming something over the people around you right now. Whether you sing or not. Whether you have children or not. There is a tune your life makes, a repeated melody of what you fear and what you trust and what you believe about God when you think no one is listening, and the small ones underfoot are absorbing it exactly the way I absorbed hers. Not through your lectures. Through your kitchen. Through the thing you hum at the sink at night, the mood you carry to breakfast, the truth or the lie about God that rides underneath your ordinary day.

That should frighten you a little, and it should also set you free. It should frighten you because they are learning your real theology, not your stated one, the God you actually trust, not the one you can define. But it should set you free because you do not have to be a scholar to hand down the deepest thing there is. My grandmother proved that. She could not have passed a doctrine exam. She passed on the faith anyway, whole and load-bearing, by humming the goodness of God over a boy who was not even listening, until the day the darkness came for him and the song was already there.

So hum the true thing. Learn it well enough, from the Book she read with her finger under the words, that what you press into the ones you love is gold and not just custom. And then trust the side door. Trust the melody to go in where the lecture never could, and to wait, folded up small, for the exact morning it will be needed.

My grandmother is with the Lord now. But I still catch myself humming at the stove. And when I do, I know exactly what I am doing, and exactly who taught me, and exactly Who was in the song the whole time.

pieces.title: The God Who Was Already in the Margin

pieces.excerpt: We keep talking about taking God to the margins, as if He waits in the nice parts of town for us to carry Him out. But every time I have gone looking for Him in the overlooked places, He was already there, and He had been for a long time.

body.text: We have a way of talking in the church that I have finally decided I no longer believe.

We talk about *taking God to the margins*. Taking Him to the poor, to the barrio, to the forgotten street, to the people the world has written off. And I understand what we mean by it, and the heart behind it is often good. But there is a lie folded up inside that language, so small you can miss it your whole life, and it is this: that God is here, in the comfortable center, in the nice part of town, in our clean and well-lit rooms, *waiting for us to carry Him out* to the poor like a package we deliver.

I do not believe that anymore. I have gone looking for God in too many overlooked places, and I have found the same thing every single time. He was already there. He had been there for a long time. And more often than not, He was waiting for *me* to arrive, not so I could bring Him to the margin, but so the margin could show me a face of Him I had never seen in the center.
*Dios en el margen.* God in the margin. Not carried there. Native there.
Where He actually kept turning up
If you read the accounts looking for where God locates Himself, you will notice something that ought to unsettle the comfortable and comfort the overlooked.

He is born, not in the capital, not in a palace, not among the people who mattered, but in a feeding trough in a nowhere town, and the first ones told are shepherds, night-shift laborers, ceremonially unclean, the sort of men no one would have chosen as the honored first witnesses of anything. Heaven throws open the greatest announcement in history, and it sends the invitation to the wrong side of the tracks first.

He grows up and does the same thing on purpose, over and over, until it becomes the most obvious pattern of His life. He eats with tax collectors, the collaborators everyone despised. He lets a woman with a reputation wash His feet in a room full of respectable men who are scandalized by it. He touches the leper the whole society had exiled. He stops the entire crowd for a blind beggar that crowd was actively shushing. He is forever wandering off toward exactly the people the center had decided did not count.

And then He tells a story that gives the whole game away. A man throws a great banquet, He says, and the invited guests, the respectable, the busy, the ones who assumed the feast was for people like them, all make their excuses and do not come. So the master is angry, and he sends his servant out into the streets and the alleys of the town, and then out along the country roads, with a strange and specific command: bring in the poor, the crippled, the blind, the lame. Fill my house with *them*. Go out to the margins and the hedges and compel them to come in, because I tell you, my house will be full, and it will be full of the ones the first list left off.

That is not a marginal story. That is the story. The banquet of God fills up from the outside in. The honored seats go to the overlooked. And the ones who assumed they were the center discover, too late, that the center of God's love was never where they thought it was.
What the margin taught me that the center never could
I did not learn this from a book. I learned it in rooms the wider church has never heard of and never will.

I have worshiped in places with dirt for a floor and a single working light, with people who had every earthly reason to be bitter and were instead so full of joy it embarrassed me. I have watched a woman who cleaned houses all day lift her hands in praise with a freedom I have rarely seen in any beautiful sanctuary. I have heard the poor sing about the goodness of God with a conviction that the comfortable simply cannot manufacture, because they were not singing a theory. They were singing about a God they had actually needed, actually leaned their whole weight on, actually found holding them up when there was nothing else.

And every time, I came in thinking I was bringing them something, and I left knowing they had shown me the Lord. Not a smaller, poorer version of Him for people who could not afford the real thing. The real thing. A face of God, tender, near, unmistakably present among the overlooked, that I had somehow missed in all my well-lit rooms.

Because here is what the margin knows that the center keeps forgetting: God is not most at home where things are comfortable. The Scriptures say it flatly, and we keep flinching from it. He is near to the brokenhearted. He lifts the poor from the dust and seats them with princes. He has chosen the foolish things to shame the wise and the weak things to shame the strong and the things that are not, to bring to nothing the things that are. He resists the proud and gives grace to the humble. There is a bias in the heart of God, and it does not run the direction the world's does. It runs *down*, toward the low place, the last seat, the forgotten street, the ones no one counted.
Stop delivering Him and start meeting Him
So here is what I want to say to you, whichever side of this you are standing on.

If you are one of the overlooked, if you have spent your life in the margin the world drew, assuming that the real presence of God was happening somewhere else, in someone else's nicer building, among people who matter more than you. I need you to hear the banquet story correctly. You are not on the substitute list. You are not the afterthought the master settled for. You are the ones the feast was *filled with on purpose*. The seat at the table is not a consolation prize. It has your name on it, and it was always going to, and the God who set it there has been in your margin the whole time, closer to you in your low place than He ever was to the comfortable in theirs.

And if you are in the center, comfortable, resourced, well-lit, then stop talking about delivering God to the poor like a package. He is already there. He beat you to it by a lifetime. Go, yes, go out into the streets and the alleys and the country roads, because the going is holy and the servant in the story was sent. But go as one who is arriving where God already lives, not as one who is bringing Him somewhere new. Go to *meet* Him in the face of the overlooked. Go to be shown the part of Him you have been missing. Go humble, and go ready to worship, because I promise you the singing you find out there will teach you things about the goodness of God that your comfort never could.

The margin is not the edge of God's kingdom. It is, more often than we dare admit, the center of it. He was already there. He is there now. And the only real question is whether we will finally go and join the feast that has been going on, gloriously, without us, among the very people we thought we were coming to save.

pieces.title: The Drum Was Praying Before the Words
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful circle of friends clapping and drumming congas at golden hour, heads thrown back in laughter and praise, bodies leaning into the rhythm as warm light catches their radiant faces and the blur of moving hands in embodied uninhibited celebration; luminous cinematic film-still quality, warm gold amber and rich brown tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: Long before I had the words for worship, my body already knew the beat. And I have come to believe that God gave us the drum, the clap, and the swaying hip on purpose, because there is a praise the body can offer that the mouth cannot.

body.text: Before I knew a single word of any prayer, I knew the beat.

I could keep the clave before I could read. My hand knew where the accent fell, that off-kilter pattern that runs like a heartbeat under so much of my people's music, years before I could have told you what it was called or why it mattered. My mother says I was patting it out on the side of the crib. I believe her, because I have watched every child in my family do the same thing: the words come late, but the rhythm is there almost from the beginning, wired in, waiting.

And I have come to believe that this is not a small or accidental thing. I think God put the beat in us before the words on purpose. I think there is a kind of praise the body can offer that the mouth simply cannot, and that a whole tradition raised on stiff, seated, neck-up worship has been quietly starving for it without knowing what was missing.
The oldest instrument is the one you were born holding

Here is something worth sitting with. The very first rhythm any of us ever heard, we heard from the inside. Before light, before language, before a single thought, a heartbeat. Your mother's, steady and close, the metronome of the whole world you lived in for nine months. We are, all of us, rhythmic creatures before we are anything else. We were kept alive by a beat before we ever drew a breath of our own.

So when the drum starts, and something in you answers before you have decided anything, that is not a shallow response. That is the deepest and oldest part of you recognizing a language it spoke before it spoke any other. The beat is not beneath the words. The beat came *first*.

And the Scriptures, which we have somehow managed to read as though God only wanted our minds, are full of bodies. The final Psalm, the great crescendo the whole book has been climbing toward, does not say *think about God quietly in a chair*. It says praise Him with the trumpet, with the harp, with the tambourine and *dancing*, with strings and pipe, with loud clashing cymbals, with the loud crashing cymbals, as if once was not enough to say it. It ends with everything that has breath. That is not a quiet room. That is a body, all the way in, hands and feet and lungs, holding nothing back.

Go back to the sea again and you find Miriam with a tambourine in her hand and all the women behind her with tambourines *and dancing*. Go to the day the ark came home and you find the king himself leaping and whirling down the public street with all his might, so undignified his wife was ashamed of him, and God was not. God was not ashamed of the dancing king. It was the watching, sneering wife whom the account leaves empty. Heaven took the side of the body that praised over the mind that judged it.
What the mouth cannot say, the body can
I want to be careful, because words matter and I am not against them. The mouth is a glorious instrument. But the mouth has a limit, and you have felt it.

There are things too big for a sentence. Real joy is one of them. Have you ever tried to *say* how glad you were? The words come out small and flat next to the size of the gladness. But a body does not have that problem. When the joy is too big for the sentence, the hands come up on their own. The head goes back. The feet start to move. The hips sway before the brain has signed off on any of it. And that motion says the thing the sentence could not. It says *this joy is bigger than my words, so I am going to hand it over with my whole body instead.*

This is why I refuse to be embarrassed by embodied worship, and why I grieve a little for traditions that trained it out of their people. When my grandmother swayed with her eyes shut, she was not performing and she was not out of control. She was saying, with the one instrument she had owned since before she could talk, a thing about the goodness of God that no sentence in any language could have carried. Her body was praying. It had been praying since before she had the words, and it never forgot how.

And I will tell you plainly what I think the resistance to this really is, underneath. It is not reverence. We tell ourselves it is reverence, that stillness is holier, that a moving body is somehow less serious about God. But often it is not reverence at all. It is *pride*. It is the fear of looking foolish. It is the sneering wife at the window, worried about dignity, while the king dances his heart out before the Lord. The mind that will not let the body praise is very often not being holy. It is being self-conscious. And self-consciousness is just pride that has learned to sit still.
Let the body pray, and let it be loud
So here is my invitation, and I mean it for the stiff and the shy as much as for anyone.

Stop making your body wait for your mind to give it permission. That order is backwards. The mind is slow and cautious and worried about the neighbors. The body is honest. When the beat rises and something in you wants to move, to clap, to sway, to lift a hand, to let your feet believe the good news before your head has finished analyzing it, that is not a distraction from worship. That may be the truest worship in the room. The child patting the clave on the crib rail had it right before any of us confused ourselves with dignity.

And do not be afraid of it being loud. We have made *quiet* a synonym for *reverent*, and the Bible simply does not agree. The Bible ends its songbook with clashing cymbals and everything that has breath. There is a hush that is holy. I know it, I love it, there are nights the only right response is silence. But there is also a shout that is holy, a clap that is holy, a drum that is holy, a dance down the middle of the street that Heaven applauds while the watchers at the window sniff. Do not let anyone convince you that God only accepts the neck-up, seated, silent version. He made the heartbeat. He wired the rhythm in before the words. He is not offended by the body He designed doing exactly what He built it to do.

*Corazón latino*, the Latin heart, did not invent embodied praise. We just never let the world talk us out of it. And there is room at that party for you, whoever you are, whatever tradition trained your hands to stay in your lap. The drum was praying before you had the words. It still is. Let your body join it. And discover, maybe for the first time, how much of the praise inside you has been waiting, not for better words, but for permission to finally move.

pieces.title: The God Who Was Not in the Fire
pieces.imagePrompt: A young person seated at a quiet mountain overlook at first light, earbuds in and eyes closed with a gentle joyful smile, leaning in to listen as the last storm clears and warm gold spills across the ridgelines below, hushed delight and peace, premium cinematic film-still quality, authentic and natural; wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: A prophet climbed a mountain expecting thunder and got a whisper instead. What if the reason your worship feels thin is that you keep listening for the wind, and Yahuah keeps speaking under it?

body.text: There is a version of the story we all secretly prefer, and it is the loud one.

The prophet Elijah had just lived the loud one. Fire had fallen on a soaked altar in front of a whole nation. He had outrun a chariot. He had, by every measure a ministry would use, arrived. And then a queen sent word that she would have his head by the next evening, and the man who called down fire ran like a boy from a dog. He ran until the towns gave out, and then he ran into the wilderness, and then he sat down under a lonely broom tree in the desert and asked Yahuah to let him die.
I want you to sit under that tree with him for a moment before we climb, because most of us skip it.

This is a man at the very top of his powers, empty. Not backslidden. Not in scandal. Faithful, and finished. He had spent everything he had on one enormous, spectacular day, and now there was nothing in the tank and a threat at the door, and the only prayer he could find was a request to stop existing.

If you have ever done the big, visible, faithful thing and then found yourself hollowed out on the other side of it, you already know this desert. The applause does not follow you into it. The fire does not warm you here.
What the wilderness fed him first

Notice what Heaven did not do. It did not rebuke him. It did not hand him a strategy. An angel woke him, and there was bread baked on hot stones and a jar of water, and a word as plain as a mother's: eat, and sleep. He ate. He slept. The angel came a second time and touched him and said the journey was too great for him, so eat again.

Before Yahuah said a single deep thing to this prophet, He fed his body and let him rest. I have pastored long enough to tell you that some of you are not in a crisis of faith. You are in a crisis of sleep. You have made your exhaustion into a spiritual problem, and Heaven keeps trying to hand you bread. Eat first. The mountain will still be there.

On the strength of that food he walked forty days and forty nights, all the way to Horeb, the mountain of God, the same slopes where the whole covenant had once been thundered down in smoke. He came to a cave, and he spent the night, and there in the dark the question came: what are you doing here?

And out it poured, the self-pity, the accounting, the lonely math of a man who believed he was the last one left who cared. *I have been zealous. They have torn everything down. I alone am left, and now they want me too.* It is not a noble speech. It is an honest one. And Yahuah did not argue with it. He said: go stand on the mountain, because I am about to pass by.
The wind, the quake, the fire, and then
Then came the thing every one of us would have staged.

A wind tore through, so violent it split the mountains and shattered the rocks. It was the kind of power that would end any argument about whether God is real. And the account says, carefully, that Yahuah was not in the wind.
Then an earthquake, the ground itself convulsing. Not in the earthquake.
Then fire, the very signature that had won Mount Carmel days before. Not in the fire.

Read that slowly, because it is almost rude how deliberate it is. The three loudest phenomena in the ancient imagination, the exact special effects Elijah's whole prophetic career had been built on, and Heaven walks past all three like an empty stage. God is not in the show. Not this time. Not for this man.

And after the fire, a low whisper. Some render it a gentle stillness, a sound of fine silence, the smallest voice imaginable. And *that* is when Elijah moved. Not during the earthquake. He had presumably braved plenty of drama. But when the whisper came, he pulled his cloak up over his face, because a man can stand in front of God's fireworks and stay a spectator, but nobody stays a spectator in front of God's whisper. The quiet is more exposing than the fire ever was.
Why the whisper does the deeper work
Here is what I have come to believe on my own high, quiet mornings, and I offer it to you as a pastor and not a theory.

The loud manifestation confirms that God is powerful. The whisper confirms that God is near. And a wounded person does not most need to be reminded that God is powerful. Elijah knew that. He had just watched water-logged wood ignite. Power was never his problem. His problem was that he felt alone, and power at a distance cannot cure loneliness. Only nearness can, and nearness, it turns out, does not shout. Nearness leans in.

This is why so much worship leaves us strangely unfed even when it is loud and even when it is true. We have trained ourselves to measure a service by its wind and quake and fire, the swell, the key change, the moment the room lifts. Those are good gifts and I am not against them; I have wept in them. But if the loud is the only place you have learned to find Him, then every quiet season will feel like abandonment, when it may in fact be the most intimate thing He has ever tried to do with you. He turned the volume down because He was finally about to say the thing that was only ever meant for you.
The wind is for the crowd. The whisper is for the son.
Come down off the noise for a minute
So let me speak plainly to whoever is reading this hollowed out under their own broom tree.

You may have decided that the quiet in your life is God's silence. I want to gently propose it is His whisper, and that you have simply been listening in the wrong register, straining for the earthquake while the low voice waits under it for you to stop straining.

Try worship that does not perform. Not the anthem. The sound just under the anthem, a spoken sentence, a hummed line with the lights off, the kind of praise that has no audience and no swell and would embarrass you in public precisely because it is so bare. Wrap your face, the way the prophet did, and get low, and say the true thing quietly. That is not lesser worship. On the mountain of God it was the whole point.

And notice what the whisper actually did for Elijah when it came. It did not leave him on the summit to glow. It gave him a road, a task, and, the detail that undoes me every time, the news that he was not alone after all, that there were seven thousand others who had never bent the knee. The nearness came first. Then the truth that his loneliness had been a lie. Then the way forward.

That is still the order. He does not shout you back to life. He gets close, in a voice pitched just for you, under all the noise you keep waiting on, and He tells you to eat, and to rest, and then to walk.
You were never the last one left. Pull the cloak back, and listen lower.

pieces.title: Every Song Is First Sung to Rocks
pieces.imagePrompt: A solitary young woman singing on a wind-swept high desert plateau at golden hour, arms loose and face lifted in unguarded joy, pouring her song toward the empty sunlit ridges with no audience but the light, warm cinematic worship-brand glow, authentic and natural; wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: Before a song ever reaches a crowd, it is sung alone to stone and wind and no one. The wilderness is not the delay before your worship. It is the room where your worship becomes real.

body.text: Every song you have ever loved was first sung to rocks.

I mean that almost literally. Long before a worship song reaches a room full of raised hands, it is sung by one person, badly, into the air of an empty kitchen or a parked car or a trail switchback where the only listeners are stone and wind. The version the crowd hears is the polished descendant of a hundred private, unwitnessed rehearsals sung to nobody. And I have come to believe that the private ones, the ones with no audience, are not the practice for the real thing. They *are* the real thing. The crowd just gets to visit it later.
We have this backwards, and it costs us.

We assume the wilderness is the waiting room. The dry stretch you endure until the door opens and the calling begins. Obscurity as the long, unfortunate hallway before the platform. So we spend our desert seasons the way you spend a layover, restless, checking the clock, treating the whole thing as time to be gotten through rather than a place to be shaped.

But look at how Heaven actually spends people, and you will notice a pattern so consistent it cannot be an accident. Almost everyone Yahuah has ever used at scale, He first sent somewhere with no scale at all.
The pattern nobody would design

Moses did not step from the palace to the deliverance. He stepped from the palace to forty years of somebody else's sheep on the back side of the desert, until the man who once acted on impulse had been slowed down enough to notice a bush that would not stop burning. Forty years. To lead a people out of Egypt, God apparently first needed a man who had learned to pay attention to something small in a place where nothing happened.

John, the one sent to prepare the way, grew up in the wilderness and became a voice crying out from it, out where there were no synagogues to preach in and no crowds to build. His whole ministry was formed by wide silence before it was ever heard by a single pilgrim.

And Yeshua Himself, this is the one that stops me, before the miracles, before a word of public teaching, the Ruach drove Him out into the wilderness for forty days. Hungry, alone, tested, with no ministry to point to and no one watching but the accuser and the wild animals and the angels. The most important life ever lived began with more than a month in the emptiest place available, singing, we might say, to rocks.
