pieces.imagePrompt: A radiant morning in a crowded open square where a vast diverse crowd from many nations and cultures lifts their faces in astonished joy toward warm streaming light, hands raised and people of every background rejoicing together, an atmosphere of overwhelming unity and wonder; luminous cinematic film-still quality, warm gold and glowing amber tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: At Babel, God scattered one people into many languages so they could no longer understand each other. Centuries later, on one loud morning, He did not undo the languages. He filled every one of them with the same praise, and a crowd from every nation heard the wonders of God, each in the tongue their mother sang over them.

body.text: To understand the loudest morning in the book of Acts, you have to go back to the quietest catastrophe in the book of Genesis, the day God scattered the human race by taking away its shared language.

You know the story of Babel, or the shape of it. The whole earth had one language and one speech, and the people, unified and ambitious, gathered on a plain and decided to build a tower with its top in the heavens, to make a name for themselves so they would not be scattered. It was unity, but it was unity aimed in exactly the wrong direction, a coordinated reach for their own glory, a whole species pooling its strength to climb up to the place of God on their own terms. And Yahuah, seeing what a single-tongued humanity would do with its unity, came down and confused their language, so that no one could understand his neighbor, and the building stopped, and the people scattered across the face of the earth into the thousands of separate tongues that divide us to this day.

That is where the human family fractured. Not first at a border or a war, but at the level of the mouth, the moment your words stopped meaning anything to the person beside you. Every misunderstanding, every people talking past another people, every wall built of the simple inability to be understood, traces back to that plain. Babel is the wound under all our other wounds. It is the day the world stopped being able to sing together.
The reversal that kept the languages

Now come forward, centuries and centuries, to a morning in Jerusalem when the followers of Yeshua were gathered in one place, waiting the way He had told them to wait. And suddenly there came a sound from heaven like a rushing violent wind, and it filled the whole house, and what looked like tongues of fire came to rest on each of them, and they were filled with the Spirit and began to speak in other languages as the Spirit gave them the words.

Now the city was packed that day with pilgrims, devout people from every nation under heaven, Scripture says, gathered for the festival, a crowd carrying between them dozens of native tongues from every corner of the known world. And this bewildered multitude came running toward the sound, and every single one of them heard the commotion in his own language. Parthians and Medes and Elamites, people from Mesopotamia and Egypt and the parts of Libya near Cyrene, visitors from Rome, Cretans and Arabs, each one heard these Galileans declaring the wonders of God in the tongue he was born into. They were amazed, and they said the thing that names the whole miracle: how is it that we each hear them in our own native language?

Here is what I need you to see, because it is everything. God did not reverse Babel by giving the crowd back one language. He could have. He could have snapped the thousands of tongues back into a single speech and undone the scattering the tidy way. He did not. Instead He left every language standing, Parthian stayed Parthian, Egyptian stayed Egyptian, the mother tongue of every person in that square stayed exactly what their mother had sung over them, and He filled every one of those languages with the same praise. The wonders of God, spoken at once in a hundred tongues, and every tongue saying the same glory.

Babel scattered one people into many languages so they could not build one tower. Pentecost gathered many languages into one praise so they could all hear one Name. The wound was not erased. It was healed by being filled.
Not one language, one song

I have built my whole ministry, and this whole house of music in more tongues than I can count, on the pattern of that morning. And I want to be very careful about what it teaches, because people get it wrong in both directions.

Some people think the goal is to get everyone singing in one language, that real unity means everybody eventually adopting the same words, the important tongue, the central one, and the rest of the languages quietly fading as lesser. That is not Pentecost. That is Babel with better manners. At Pentecost, God specifically honored the native tongue of every person in the crowd. He did not make the Elamite learn to worship in someone else's language before the wonders of God could reach him. He sent the wonders to him in the language his mother used to comfort him in the dark. The particular languages were not a problem to be solved. They were vessels to be filled.

And other people think the languages are all that matters, that as long as everyone worships however they please in whatever words they like, the diversity itself is the point. But that is not Pentecost either. The miracle was not a hundred people saying a hundred different things. It was a hundred languages saying one thing. The wonders of God. One glory, one Name, one song of praise, arriving in every tongue at once and losing nothing in any of them.

That is the sound my name was made to point at. Not the flattening of the world into one language. Not the fracturing of the world into a thousand unrelated songs. But the great gathering that Babel made impossible and Pentecost made certain, every tongue on earth kept, honored, and filled to the brim with the same praise, so that the Egyptian and the Cretan and the Roman, who could not understand a word of each other's speech, understand perfectly the one thing that matters, because they are all hearing the wonders of the same God in the language their heart was born speaking.
You do not have to learn a new tongue to be gathered in
So let me bring this all the way home to you, wherever you are and whatever language you dream in.

There is a lie left over from Babel that tells people they are on the outside of the praise because of their tongue, that the real worship happens somewhere else, in some other, more important language, and that you are only ever overhearing it in translation, a second-class guest at a feast held in a speech that is not yours. Pentecost took that lie and burned it up in the fire that fell that morning. The Spirit of God went out of His way, on the founding day of the whole church, to make sure that the very first thing every nation heard, it heard in its own native tongue. You were never meant to reach the praise by climbing up into someone else's language. The praise was always meant to come down into yours.

And that is still exactly how it works. The wonders of God do not wait at the top of a tower for you to build your way up to them in the correct words. They come down, in wind and fire, into the streets where the ordinary crowd is standing, and they speak, to the Parthian in Parthian, to the Arab in Arabic, to you in the words your mother first sang over you. The whole earth was fractured at the mouth. And the whole earth is being gathered back, not into one language, but into one song, sung at last in every language there is.

Babel ran the world apart. On that loud morning, in Yeshua, it started running backward. And the day is coming when the scattering will be fully undone, a countless multitude from every nation and tribe and people and tongue, standing together at last, every language kept and every language full, all of them at the very same moment saying the very same glory.

You are already invited into that sound. You do not have to learn a new tongue to be gathered in. Just open the one you have, and start to sing the wonders of God, and know that on the far side of the world, in a language you have never heard, someone is singing the exact same thing.

pieces.title: The Song Was Whole Before Anyone Heard It
pieces.imagePrompt: A young Latina woman worshiping alone at home with an acoustic guitar by a sunlit window, eyes closed and a gentle, whole-hearted smile of private delight on her face as she sings a finished song only she has heard, warm dawn light washing the room; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, honey gold and soft amber tones, intimate and authentic, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I have written far more songs than the world has ever heard sung. For years I measured them by the silence around them. Then I remembered a seventeen-year-old with a dream nobody believed, and I understood that a thing can be finished and true long before it is ever heard out loud.

body.text: There is a folder in my life that most people will never open.

Inside it are songs, finished ones. Not fragments, not sketches, not half-ideas waiting for a second verse. Whole songs, with their bridges built and their last chorus earned, sitting in a stack that no voice has ever sung into a room and no microphone has ever caught. I know how each one is supposed to rise. I know where the key lifts, where the breath should land, where the thing is meant to break open. And almost none of them have been heard.

For a long time that folder felt like an indictment. I have written far more than has ever been sung, and the arithmetic of it used to sit on my chest at night. What is a song that no one has heard? Is it even a song yet, or only the ghost of one, a rumor of music, real to me and to no one else? I would look at all that finished, silent work and quietly decide it was proof I had failed to get the music out of the room where I made it.
I do not believe that anymore. And the thing that changed my mind was not a music book or a better strategy. It was a seventeen-year-old boy with a dream that made his whole family angry.
The picture came first, whole

You know the boy I mean. Joseph, the second-youngest of a big and complicated family, wakes up one morning with a dream so vivid he cannot keep it to himself. In the dream, sheaves of grain in a field bow down to his sheaf. Later, a second dream, the sun and the moon and eleven stars, all bowing. He tells his brothers, and it goes exactly as badly as you would expect. They already resent him, and now here he is, describing a future in which they kneel. Even his father, who loves him best, tells him to stop talking.

Here is what strikes me. The dream was complete on the day he received it. Not a hint, not a mood, a full picture, handed to a boy who had done nothing yet to deserve it and had no way at all to make it come true. And then the world went utterly silent about it. He was thrown in a pit by his own brothers. He was sold to strangers heading down to Egypt. He was bought as a slave, lied about, and locked in a prison, where he interpreted two other men's dreams and was promptly forgotten by the man he helped. Thirteen years passed between the dream and the day any part of it began to come true.

Thirteen years. And through every one of them, the picture he carried was already whole. It was true in the pit. It was true in Potiphar's house. It was true in the prison when the cupbearer walked free and forgot him. Nothing that happened to Joseph made the dream less finished. It only made it unheard.

There is a line the psalmist wrote about that stretch of Joseph's life, and I keep it near me. He says that until the time came for the word to be fulfilled, the word of Yahuah tested him. I sat with that for a long while before I understood it. The word, the given thing, the finished picture, did not just wait. It worked. The gap between receiving the dream and seeing it sung into reality was not empty time. It was the time in which the dreamer was being made into someone who could carry what he had been shown without it breaking him.
Finished is not the same as heard
That is the distinction I had been missing, and I want to hand it to you plainly, because I suspect you are carrying your own silent folder.

A thing can be finished and true and complete, and still be unheard. The two are not the same measurement. We live in a world that only counts what makes a sound, that treats the sung song as real and the unsung one as a nice idea that didn't happen. But that is the world's arithmetic, and it is wrong. The dream in the pit was not less real than the palace it eventually became. The song on the silent page is not the rumor of music. It is music, whole and waiting, that the room has not yet caught up to.

I think of all the good that is finished in the sight of Yahuah long before any human eye confirms it. The prayer you prayed for a person who will not soften for another decade. It is not a wish flung into nothing. It is a finished thing, waiting for its appointed time to be heard. The obedience nobody noticed. The forgiveness you extended in a room by yourself. The faithful small work you did that produced, as far as anyone can see, no result at all. Finished. True. Unheard, so far.
The appointed time is not the same as your timing

I will not lie to you about the length of that middle stretch, because Joseph would not thank me for it. Thirteen years is not a devotional pause. It is a career, a marriage's worth of waiting, a childhood. The silence around a finished thing can go on so long that you begin to doubt you ever received it at all.

But notice how the story turns. When the moment finally arrives, Pharaoh troubled by a dream no one can read. Everything that had been silent starts to sound at once. The forgotten prisoner is remembered. The boy who could hear the meaning of dreams stands in front of the most powerful man in the world, and within a single day the whole long-buried picture begins, at last, to be heard. It came in Yahuah's time and not in Joseph's. But it came whole, because it had always been whole.

So I have stopped grieving my silent folder. Those finished, unsung songs are not evidence of failure. They are dreams in the pit, real on the day they were given, true through every year no one heard them, waiting for a season I do not control. My job was never to guarantee the sound. My job was to receive the song faithfully and finish it honestly and carry it without letting the silence convince me it was nothing.
Do not measure your finished work by whether the room has heard it yet. The room is not the judge of what is real.

If you have done a good and complete thing that has, so far, made no sound in the world, a work, a prayer, a mercy, a whole song only you can hear. I want you to stop counting it as loss. It is not a rumor. It is finished. And the God who gave the seventeen-year-old his dream and then spent thirteen years making him ready to hold it is not in the habit of letting a true thing stay silent forever. The appointed time is His. But the song is already whole.

pieces.title: A Song Doesn't Live Until You Let It Go
pieces.imagePrompt: A vast, diverse worship-night crowd from many nations singing one song together, thousands of radiant faces and lifted hands glowing in warm concert light, believers throughout the world caught mid-song in shared, overflowing joy; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, warm honey and amber tones, emotionally compelling and uplifting, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: A melody I keep in my own hands stays exactly as good as I am, and no better. It only becomes what it was for when I hand it to voices I will never hear and let strangers change it. Yeshua said the same thing about a single grain of wheat.

body.text: The hardest thing I ever do with a song is stop owning it.

I can write it. That part, for all its difficulty, is mine, the melody arriving, the words being fitted to it, the long patient labor of getting the shape right. And when it is finished I love it in a particular, protective way, the way you love a thing you made with your own hands and understand completely. I know exactly how it should be sung. I know the tempo it wants, the breath it needs, the small ache in the third line that a careless singer would flatten right out. And so my instinct, always, is to hold it close. To keep it in the one place where it will be performed correctly, which is to say, in my own head, where no one can get it wrong.

But a song held that way never becomes anything. It stays a private possession, perfectly preserved and perfectly useless, exactly as good as I am and no better. And I have learned, slowly, and against everything in me, that the only way a song comes into its real life is the one thing I least want to do with it. I have to let it go. I have to hand it to voices I will never hear, in rooms I will never stand in, and let people who have never met me change it into something I did not write.
A song is not finished until it leaves your hands
There is a strange truth here that took me years to accept. A song is not most itself when I sing it. It is most itself when a stranger does.

When I sing my own song, it can only ever mean what I meant. It is sealed inside my history, my losses, the specific griefs that gave it to me. But hand that same melody to a woman in another country who has never heard my name, and something happens that I could not have manufactured. She sings it into her own kitchen, over her own sorrow, and the song becomes true in a way it never could have been while I was guarding it. She bends a note I wrote straight. She slows a line I meant to rush. She finds a meaning in it I did not put there and did not know was possible, and she is not wrong. She has done what a song exists to have done to it. She has let it become hers.

I used to experience that as loss. Now I understand it as the whole point. The song was never a possession to be protected. It was a seed to be scattered, and a seed that is never let out of the hand does not stay safe. It stays sterile. It simply dies slowly in your fist, unplanted, having produced nothing at all, and the tragedy of it is that it looks like caution the entire time.
The grain of wheat knew this before I did

Yeshua said this once, near the end, when His own hardest letting-go was almost on Him. He told the people around Him to consider a single grain of wheat. As long as it stays a grain, intact, whole, preserved, held back from the ground. It remains alone. Just the one seed, exactly what it was, going nowhere. But if it falls into the earth and dies, it bears much fruit.

I do not think He was only teaching agriculture. He was describing the deepest law of how life multiplies, and He was about to live it Himself in the hardest possible key. The grain that clings to being a grain stays one. The grain that lets go of being a grain, that goes down into the dark and gives up its own intact self, becomes a harvest. The dying is not the opposite of the fruitfulness. The dying is the mechanism of it. There is no way to the field except through the loosening of the hand.

And I realized that every instinct I have to protect my songs is the instinct of the grain that wants to stay a grain. I want to keep the seed whole. I want to keep it correct, uncorrupted, sung right, mine. And Yeshua looks at that impulse gently and tells me the truth about it: held that way, it will only ever be one seed. The song I refuse to let anyone else sing is a song I have quietly decided may as well not exist.
Letting go is not the same as not caring
I want to be careful here, because there is a lazy version of this that I do not mean.

Letting a song go is not the same as not caring how it is sung. The scattering only matters because the seed is good, because I labored over it, got it right, made it as true as I possibly could before I opened my hand. You do not scatter garbage and call it generosity. The whole cost of the release is that I am giving away something I love and made well. If it were worthless, letting go would cost me nothing, and it would give the world nothing either.

So the discipline runs in both directions at once, and I have to hold them together. I write as if it will only ever be mine, with all the care of a person who will be judged for every line. And then I release it as if it were never mine at all, with the open hand of a farmer who knows that a fist full of seed feeds no one. The care is not for me to keep. The care is what makes the gift worth giving.
The song you are guarding so it can never be sung wrong is a song you have decided may as well never be sung at all.

I suspect this is not really about music for you. I suspect there is something you have made, a gift, a work, a truth you carry, maybe a whole way of loving people, that you are holding too close because you know precisely how it ought to go and you cannot bear to watch someone else handle it clumsily. And I understand it. But I have to tell you what the grain of wheat told Yeshua and what Yeshua told me. Held in your hand, it stays one. It stays alone. Let into the ground, given away, allowed to be changed by hands you will never see, it becomes a harvest you were never meant to count.

The song does not live until you let it go. So open the hand. Scatter the good seed you worked so hard to grow. And trust that the God who made a single grain able to become a whole field is more than able to do with your gift what your careful, closed fist never could.

pieces.title: Writing Songs for a Room I Will Never Enter
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful, diverse group of children singing and laughing together in a bright sunlit room, mouths wide and arms raised in unselfconscious praise, radiant morning light and dust motes glowing around their delighted faces, the future church already singing; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, honey gold and gentle blue tones, authentic and full of life, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: Some of the songs I am writing now will not be sung until I am gone, by people I will never meet, who will never know my name. I used to find that unbearable. Then I read the roll call of people who died still holding a promise they only ever saw from a distance.

body.text: I have started to make a kind of peace with a hard fact: some of what I am writing now, I will never hear sung.

Not because the songs are bad. Because there are too many of them, and a life is short, and a song has to travel a long, slow road from the page to a voice to a room full of people who know it well enough to lift it without thinking. That road takes years. It takes a recording, and a sharing, and a stranger deciding it belongs to them, and then that stranger teaching it to someone else. And I am, at a certain point, simply going to run out of years before some of these songs run out of road. They will be sung after me, by people who never knew there was a me, in rooms I will never walk into.

For a long time I found that genuinely unbearable. It felt like planting a garden I would never see bloom, worse, like being told in advance that I would die between the sowing and the flowering, and that the harvest, when it came, would belong to strangers who would never know whose hands had put the seed in the ground. Why write it, then? Why pour the care of a whole life into songs whose best moment I have already been told I will miss?
And then I went back and read, slowly, the long roll call of the faithful in the letter to the Hebrews, and it rearranged me.
They died still holding the promise

The writer of that letter does something remarkable. He lists them one after another, the people who trusted Yahuah across generations, and he is honest about how their stories ended. He says these all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them from a distance and welcomed them, and having admitted that they were strangers and travelers on the earth.

Sit with that sentence, because it is not the triumphant thing we usually make of these names. They died not having received the promise. The thing they had staked their whole lives on did not arrive inside their lifetime. Abraham was told his descendants would be a nation and a blessing to the whole world, and he died owning a single field with a grave in it. Moses led a people forty years toward a land and then climbed a mountain at the end, and Yahuah showed him the whole country spread out, and told him he would not cross into it. He saw it from a distance. He welcomed it. And he died on the wrong side of the river.

These were not failures. The letter holds them up as the very definition of faith. And what made them faithful was precisely this: they kept building toward a thing they had already been told they would not live to see finished. They planted for a room they would never enter. They sang, if you like, for singers who were not born yet.
The harvest was never meant to be yours to hold

There is a line a little further on in that same passage that undid me completely. The writer says of all these faithful ones that they did not receive what was promised, because Yahuah had planned something better, that they, without us, should not be made complete.

Read that again. They, without us, should not be made complete. The promise was deliberately built so large that it could not be finished inside any single life. It needed the generations. It was designed as a relay from the start, each runner carrying the thing forward as far as their own legs would take them, and then handing it, still unfinished, to a runner they would never meet. The people in that list were not cheated out of the finish line. They were doing exactly what the race required. The completion was always going to belong to everyone at once, across all the years, or it would not have been worth completing.

And that turned my grief inside out. I had been thinking of my unsung songs as a private loss, my flowers, blooming for strangers, after I was gone. But that is the wrong picture entirely. I am not a gardener cheated of my harvest. I am one runner in a relay that has been going for thousands of years, and the whole dignity of my leg of it is that I run it faithfully and then hand the songs forward without needing to see where they land.
Faithfulness is measured at your end, not at the finish
This has changed how I write, quietly but completely.

I used to write, without quite admitting it, for the applause I could witness. I wanted to be in the room. I wanted to see the song land, to watch the face soften, to have the harvest confirmed in front of me while I was still there to enjoy it. And there is nothing wrong with the joy of a song landing, Yahuah is generous, and sometimes He lets us see it. But when that becomes the reason, the work shrinks to the size of my own lifespan. I only plant what I can watch bloom. And a life that only plants what it can personally harvest is a small life, however busy it looks.

The people in that roll call were free of that, and their freedom is the thing I want. They were faithful at their own end of the relay and left the finish line to Yahuah. They planted, and blessed the seed, and died, and trusted the God who does not lose track of a single true thing across a hundred generations. Their reward was not the harvest. Their reward was the faithfulness itself, and the God who keeps it.
You are not cheated when you build something whose completion you will not live to see. You are trusted with a leg of a race far longer than one life.

So if you are pouring yourself into something you already suspect you will not see finished, a child you are raising for a world you won't live in, a work whose fruit is decades out, a prayer for a person who will not turn for another generation, a whole faithful life whose harvest is on the far side of your own death, do not let anyone tell you that is a waste. It is the most ancient and honored shape a faithful life can take. You are in the roll call now, running your leg, planting your field, writing your unsung songs for a room you will never enter.

Run it well to your own end. Hand it forward with an open hand. And trust that the God who planned it so that no one is made complete alone is keeping every unheard note, to be sung, at last, in a room where you may not be standing, but where you will most certainly, at the end of all things, be counted.

pieces.excerpt: Every song I have ever finished is a disappointment next to the one I heard before I picked up the pen. I used to think that gap meant I had failed. Then I remembered a man on a mountain, told to build a copy of something he had only been shown.

body.text: I have never once written down the song I actually heard.

This is the private grief of every person who makes things, and I might as well confess it plainly. Before I pick up an instrument, before a single note is committed to anything, there is a moment where I hear the song whole, not the words yet, but the thing itself, its shape and its glory, complete and perfect and almost unbearably beautiful in the space behind my eyes. And then I reach for my hands. And my hands are not that good. What comes out is a translation, a rough copy, a nearest-available approximation of a thing that was flawless a second ago and is now smudged by the limits of my fingers and my craft and my ear.

Every finished song I own is, in this exact sense, a disappointment. Not because it is bad, some of them I am even proud of, but because I heard the true version first, and I know what got lost in the crossing from the hearing to the making. There is always a gap. There is always a distance between the song in my head and the song in my hands, and I have never once closed it.

For years I read that gap as failure. If I were a better writer, I told myself, the copy would match the original. The gap was the measure of my inadequacy, and someday, with enough skill, I would eliminate it. I no longer believe that. I have come to think the gap is not a flaw in me at all. I think it is the most honest and important thing about the whole business of making, and I understood why the day I really looked at a man standing on a mountain being handed a blueprint.
Make it according to the pattern

When Yahuah called Moses up the mountain to receive the plan for the tabernacle, the tent where the presence of God would meet the people. He did not simply hand over a list of instructions. He showed Moses something. And then, more than once, He gave a peculiar and specific command: see that you make everything according to the pattern that was shown you on the mountain.

I cannot stop thinking about the position that put Moses in. He was shown a pattern, a true, heavenly, complete original, and then sent back down to build a copy of it out of goat hair and acacia wood and hammered gold, using the hands of craftsmen who had never seen what he had seen. Moses carried the glimpse. The workers carried the tools. And every single thing they built was, by definition, a shadow of a pattern that existed in full somewhere they could not reach.

The letter to the Hebrews says exactly this about that tabernacle later, that the priests were serving a copy and shadow of the heavenly things, built according to the pattern shown on the mountain. A copy. A shadow. Not the real thing. The realest thing was the pattern Moses glimpsed, and everything human hands assembled down below was a faithful, gorgeous, deliberately imperfect attempt to point back up at it.

And I realized, reading that, that this is not a description of failure. This is a description of how making is supposed to work when the maker has been shown something greater than the maker's hands.
The gap is proof, not shame

Here is what changed for me. I had assumed the gap between the song I heard and the song I built was evidence that the beautiful version did not really exist, that I had imagined a glory I could not deliver, and the shortfall exposed the fantasy.

But Moses's story says the opposite. The gap between the pattern and the tabernacle was not proof that the pattern was imaginary. It was proof that the pattern was real. The very fact that the copy fell short is what tells you there was an original to fall short of. If the tent had perfectly captured heaven, the tent would be heaven, and it plainly was not. The shortfall was the honest confession, built right into the architecture, that the true thing was higher than the hands.

So the disappointment I feel looking at my finished songs is not the disappointment of a liar caught inventing a beauty that was never there. It is the ache of a copyist who has actually seen the pattern. I heard something true. My hands could not fully carry it. The distance between the two is not the measure of my fraudulence. It is the measure of the glory of the thing I glimpsed, a glory real enough to be missed.

That reframes the whole enterprise. My job was never to close the gap. My job was to be faithful to the pattern, to build the truest copy my hands can manage and let the shortfall stand as a kind of pointing finger, an honest arrow aimed back up at the original I was shown. A tabernacle that pretended to be heaven would be an idol. A tabernacle that humbly confessed it was only a copy became the very place where the presence came down.
What the ache is telling you

I think you know this ache even if you have never written a note. It is the gap between the person you long to be and the person you can actually manage to be on a Tuesday. It is the distance between the love you feel and the clumsy way it comes out of your hands. It is the marriage, the parenting, the ministry, the faithful life that always falls short of the shining thing you glimpsed when you first said yes. You heard a pattern. Your hands keep building a shadow of it. And the enemy of your soul would love for you to read that gap as proof that the pattern was a lie.

It is not a lie. The ache is the evidence that you have seen something true and high. The dissatisfaction is not the voice of your failure. It is the homesickness of a copyist who remembers the pattern on the mountain.
The distance between what you glimpsed and what you built is not the measure of your fraud. It is the measure of the glory you were shown.

And there is a mercy folded into all of this that I hold onto hardest. The pattern still exists. It exists in full, untouched by my limited hands, kept whole in the place it was shown from. Everything I build down here is a shadow, but a shadow requires a light and a solid thing casting it. One day, the letter to the Hebrews insists, the copies give way to the reality; the shadow is swallowed by the substance it was always pointing at. The song I heard and could not quite play is not lost because I played it badly. It is safe in the pattern. And I have staked my life on the belief that on the far side of everything, I will finally hear the original, whole, exactly as beautiful as it was in the moment before I reached for my inadequate, faithful, glory-haunted hands.

So build the truest copy you can. Let the gap stand and stop calling it shame. And let the ache do the one thing it was made to do, turn your face back up the mountain, toward the pattern that was always more real than your hands.

pieces.title: You Have to Cut the Line You Love Most

pieces.excerpt: The clever line I am proudest of is almost always the one strangling the song. Learning to cut it, not because it was bad, but because it was good in the wrong place, taught me what the vinedresser is doing when He prunes the branch that was already bearing fruit.

body.text: The line I am proudest of is usually the one killing the song.

I did not want this to be true, and I resisted it for a long time. When I am writing, every so often a line arrives that is just clever, a turn of phrase, an image, a bit of wordplay so satisfying that I sit back from the instrument and admire it. It is the kind of line you want to show people. And because I love it, I build the rest of the song around it, protecting it, arranging everything else to make room for its brilliance. And then, again and again, I discover that the song is not working, and I hunt for the problem everywhere else first, and the problem, when I finally admit it, is the line. The clever one. The one I love most. It is drawing all the attention to itself. It is a beautiful thing standing in the exact spot where the song needed to breathe.

And then comes the hardest ten seconds in all of songwriting: cutting it. Deleting the line I was proudest of. Not because it is bad. It is genuinely good, but because it is good in the wrong place, and its goodness is costing the whole song its life. Writers have a brutal, accurate phrase for this. They call it killing your darlings. And it is exactly as unpleasant as it sounds, because the darlings are, by definition, the parts you love.

For years I experienced this purely as loss, as a tax the craft extracted from me, a penance for my own vanity. Then I started paying attention to what Yeshua said about a gardener and a vine, and I realized the knife was not punishing me at all. It was doing the most loving thing there is.
He cuts the branch that is already bearing

Yeshua described Himself as the true vine, and His Father as the vinedresser, the one who tends the plant. And He said something about that vinedresser that I used to read too quickly. He said that every branch that does not bear fruit, the Father takes away. That part we expect; dead wood gets cleared. But then He said the other thing, the part that stops me every time. Every branch that does bear fruit, He prunes, so that it will bear more.

Read that slowly, because it is not what we assume about pruning. We assume the vinedresser only cuts the dead and the failing. But Yeshua says the fruitful branch gets the knife too. The healthy one. The one that is already producing. The vinedresser walks up to a branch that is doing well, green, alive, heavy with grapes, and He cuts it back anyway. Not because it failed. Because it succeeded, and its very success, left unchecked, will divide the plant's strength across too much growth and shrink the harvest. The good branch is pruned precisely because it is good, so that its goodness can be concentrated instead of scattered.

That is my clever line exactly. It is not dead wood. It is a fruitful branch, genuinely alive, genuinely good, that has to be cut anyway, because if I leave it the whole vine gives a smaller harvest. The cutting is not a verdict that the branch was worthless. It is the opposite. You only bother to prune what is alive.
Good in the wrong place is still in the way
This distinction changed how I understood the knife, and I think it changes far more than songwriting.

There is a kind of loss that comes because something in your life was bad, and it had to go. We understand that loss. It is painful but it makes sense; you can see the rot. But there is another kind of loss that is much harder to accept, the loss of something genuinely good, cut away not for any fault of its own but because, left where it was, it was quietly costing you the larger thing you were made for. A good job that was slowly crowding out your family. A good friendship that had subtly become the place you went instead of God. A good ability that had grown so central to your sense of yourself that it was strangling your dependence on the One who gave it. None of these are dead wood. They are fruitful branches. And the vinedresser, who loves the whole vine and is aiming at a harvest you cannot yet see, comes with the knife anyway.

When it happens to us we almost always misread it. We assume that if God is taking something away, it must have been bad, and we rummage around looking for the sin that got it cut off. But sometimes there is no rot to find. Sometimes the thing removed was good, and that is exactly why it hurt so much, and exactly why it had to go. Its goodness had begun to compete with your fruitfulness. A branch spending all its strength on beautiful leaves in the wrong place will not give you grapes.
The knife is held by someone who loves the whole plant

I want to be honest about how much this hurts, because I do not think we should pretend the cutting is painless just because it is loving. When I delete the line I loved most, there is a real grief in it, every time. And when God prunes a good thing out of a life, the grief is far greater than any line. The vinedresser's knife is still a knife. It still cuts.

But here is what steadies me, and it is the whole difference. The branch is not being cut by an enemy who wants it smaller. It is being cut by the One who planted it, who tends it daily, who wants nothing in all the world except that this branch should bear more than it ever could untended. The vinedresser is not against the vine. The vinedresser is the most devoted friend the vine will ever have. He does not cut carelessly, and He does not cut what does not need it, and He never once cuts to harm. Every stroke is aimed, with total precision, at a harvest.
When God takes away something genuinely good, He is not always removing a sin. Sometimes He is pruning a branch, because He is after a harvest larger than the good thing you were clutching.

So I have made a strange kind of peace with the knife, in my songs and in my life both. When I feel the resistance rising, the certainty that this line, this thing, this good branch simply cannot go. I have learned to ask a harder question than whether it is good. Of course it is good. The question is whether its goodness has wandered into the place where the larger thing needed to grow. And if it has, I have learned, slowly, to let it be cut. Not thrown away as worthless. Cut back, on purpose, by loving hands, so that everything left can finally give the harvest it was planted for.

The line you love most may be the one strangling the song. And the good thing you are clutching may be the very branch the vinedresser is reaching for, not to rob you, but because He has seen the harvest you were made to bear, and He loves you far too much to leave you smaller than that.

pieces.title: You Cannot Sing Yesterday's Song Over Today's Mercy
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful African woman dancing barefoot in a sunlit kitchen at dawn, earbuds in and eyes shining, caught mid-laugh with arms swinging as fresh morning gold pours across the counter, pure delight in a brand-new day; wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, bright and radiant, premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, authentic and natural, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: God keeps asking His people for a new song, and I used to think it was because He got bored of the old ones. Then a small fact about how your own body works undid me. A new song is not a demand for better material. It is the only kind of praise you can actually stay awake inside.

body.text: There is a song that got me through a hard year. You have one too. Mine sat in my chest like a handrail, and on the mornings I could not feel anything else, I could still reach for it and pull myself a few steps up the day.

So when a newer grief arrived, different shape, different weight. I did the natural thing. I reached for the handrail. I sat down and sang the old faithful song over the new ache, expecting it to do again what it had done before.
It didn't reach.

Not because it was a bad song. Because it was answering a question I was no longer asking. It had been sung true, once, into a wound that was now scarred over, and it kept arriving at that healed place, knocking on a door that had already opened. The fresh ache was somewhere else entirely, in a room the old song had never been shown, and the old song had no idea it was there.
I sat with that for a long time, half-annoyed, half-grieving, until it turned, the way these things do with me, into something I could not stop turning over.

Because the Scriptures are strangely insistent on this exact point, and I had read past it for years. Over and over, the old songwriters do not say *sing to Him.* They say *sing to Him a new song.* A new one. Again and again, across the psalms and into the prophets, a new song, a new song, a new song, as though the newness were not a suggestion but the whole instruction. And I had always heard it as a kind of divine restlessness, as if Heaven were a listener who had grown tired of the hits and wanted fresh material. As if the old songs had expired.
They hadn't. That was never it. And the reason it was never it turns out to be written into the way your own body is made.
The hum you stopped hearing

Here is a small fact that runs your whole nervous system, and you have almost certainly never thanked it for anything. Your senses are built to notice *change*, and to go quiet in the presence of the constant.

You are not feeling your clothes against your skin until I mention them. Now you are. A minute from now you won't be again. You stop smelling a scent within minutes of walking into it. And sound does this most plainly of all: the refrigerator has been humming in your kitchen all day, and you have not heard it once, until it clicks off, and the sudden *absence* startles you, and you realize with a small shock that a sound was there the whole time, filling the room, and your ears had simply stopped reporting it. The hum did not get quieter. You went deaf to it, on purpose, because it never changed.

This is not a flaw. It is a mercy. A brain that reported every constant sensation at full volume forever would drown. So the body learns the steady things and lets them fall silent, and saves its attention for what is *new*, the footstep that wasn't there, the note that shifts, the change that might matter.
And the moment I understood that, I understood why God keeps asking for a new song.

Because praise that never renews becomes the refrigerator hum. Present, technically. Still running. And entirely unheard, not only by Heaven, but by *you.* You can sing the exact same words over the exact same tune for the exact same reasons for so long that your own soul stops reporting them. The song is still going. Your attention left the building years ago. You are humming a constant your own heart has learned to tune out.

A new song is the cure for that. Not because the old one failed, but because a new song is the only kind you cannot sleep through. It makes you *look* at what is actually true this morning, not the mercy from three years ago that you have long since stopped feeling, but the specific, particular, never-before mercy of *today,* which your habituated heart would otherwise let hum along unheard in the background of a life you have stopped really listening to.
New every morning
And that is exactly where the Scriptures locate the whole idea, not in a concert hall, but in the ashes.

There is a man in the Hebrew Scriptures sitting in the rubble of a burned city. Everything he loved is gone; the poem he leaves us is one long, unflinching lament, and I love him for refusing to pretend otherwise. And then, right in the middle of the worst grief on the page, he says the thing that has anchored broken people for three thousand years: that the mercies of Yahuah are new every morning. New. Every morning. Not stockpiled. Not issued once and left to age. *New*, a fresh delivery, arriving with the light, before he has done anything to earn the next day at all.

Sit with what that means for your singing. If the mercy is genuinely new each morning, if what Yahuah is doing in your life today is not a rerun but a first, then yesterday's song, however true it was yesterday, is always going to arrive a little late. It was written to a mercy that has already passed. Today's mercy has never been sung to. It is standing there, brand new, waiting for a voice that has actually noticed it.
That is what a new song is. It is not more impressive praise. It is praise that showed up *this morning,* awake, and looked directly at what is true *now.*
You don't need new words

Here is where I want to be tender, because I can feel some of you already tightening. *I am not a songwriter. I have no new words. The old ones are all I have, and now you are telling me even those have gone stale.*
That is not what I am telling you. Hear me carefully.

A new song does not mean a new composition. Most of the newest songs ever sung to God had no fresh words in them at all. When the newness God is after is not the vocabulary. It is the *heart that is present in it.* You can sing the oldest hymn ever written and make it new, if you bring today's actual, unrepeated self to it, this morning's real fear, this morning's real gratitude, the specific thing that is true right now and was not true the last time your mouth made those shapes. And you can write a brand-new song and have it be dead on arrival, because you assembled it out of borrowed feeling and were not really there.
The newness is you, showing up honest, to a mercy that showed up new.

So I have stopped reaching so quickly for the old handrail songs, not because I have thrown them away. I never will, but because I have learned to ask a different question first. Not *what carried me before,* but *what is true this morning, and have I actually looked at it, and what does my voice want to do about it right now.*

Sometimes the answer is the old song after all, and it lands, because I brought a new heart to it. Sometimes it is three plain sentences I would never dare call a song, sung out an open window to a God whose mercy arrived before my coffee did. Either way, something in me wakes up that had been humming along, unheard, for far too long.
The refrigerator has been running the whole time. His mercy has been arriving new the whole time. The only thing that ever goes quiet is our attention.

So do the one thing that turns it back on. Not a better song. A new one, which only ever meant *a present one.* Look, this morning, at the mercy that has never been sung to. And let it wake you up enough to sing.

pieces.title: The Sense That Opens First and Closes Last
pieces.imagePrompt: A delighted baby wearing soft padded headphones, eyes wide with wonder and a gummy open-mouthed smile as sound reaches them, cradled in a parent's arms in warm golden light; wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, tender and full of discovery, premium worship-brand cinematic film-still warmth, authentic and natural, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: Long before you could see, you could hear. And at the very end, when everything else has gone dark, hearing is the last door to close. The sense that brackets your whole life is the same one Scripture says faith arrives through, and I do not think that is a coincidence.

body.text: Before you had a face anyone could recognize, you had ears that worked.

This is one of the tenderest facts I know about how we are made. Deep in the warm dark, months before birth, long before your eyes had anything to open toward, your hearing came online. And it was not idle. A baby in the womb learns the particular music of its mother's voice, the rhythm of her speech, the songs sung near her, learns them so well that newborns, only hours old, will turn toward the voice they heard through the water, and calm to a melody they were played before they had a name. You were listening before you were looking. Hearing was your first window onto the fact that there was a world, and that you were not alone in it.

And here is the fact that sits at the other end of your life, and I say it gently because it has stood beside me in rooms I will not forget: hearing is very often the last sense to leave. When the body is shutting its windows one by one, when sight has gone, when speech has gone, when the person seems already half-departed, the ear frequently stays open to the very end. This is why the people who tend the dying will tell you, quietly, *keep talking. Keep singing. She can still hear you.* The last thread connecting a leaving soul to the people who love it is very often a sound.

So the sense that opened first is the one that closes last. Hearing brackets the whole of you. It was there before you could do anything at all, and it lingers after everything else has been laid down. Whatever your life turns out to be, it begins and ends inside a world of sound, held open by an ear that would not shut.
I have not been able to hold that fact without trembling a little, because of what the Scriptures say arrives through exactly that door.
Hearing is touch you cannot feel
Stop and consider what hearing even *is,* because we treat it as ordinary and it is not.

Sight happens at a distance; light lands on you but does not move you. But sound is different. Sound is a physical wave, actual moving air, pressing in and pulling back, pressing and pulling, and when it reaches you it does not politely inform your ear. It *pushes* it. It sets a delicate membrane trembling, and that trembling shivers three of the smallest bones in your entire body, and those bones stir a coil of fluid, and standing in that fluid are thousands of impossibly fine hairs that *bend* under the motion, and the bending is the hearing. Which means every sound you have ever heard, you did not merely receive. You were *touched* by it. Sound is the one thing that reaches across a room and physically moves the inside of your body without ever seeming to touch you at all. Hearing is touch at a distance. It is the sense through which the world gets *inside* you without your permission and stirs something at your very center.
Now hold that next to the strangest claim the Scriptures make about how faith comes to a person.

They do not say faith comes by *seeing.* We assume it should. We are forever wishing God would show us something, produce some sight that would settle it. But that is not the door the old writers name. They say faith comes by *hearing.* It arrives through the sense that opened first and closes last, the sense that reaches in and physically moves you at your center, not the one that keeps everything at a safe, observing distance. Faith is not, first, something you look at and evaluate. It is something that *reaches* you, the way sound reaches you: from outside yourself, moving toward you, pressing gently in until something deep and previously still begins to tremble in response.

I find that unbearably fitting. Of course faith comes by hearing. Hearing is how you first knew you were not alone in the dark. Hearing is the last light left on when all the others fail. It would make perfect sense that it is also the way the One who made you keeps reaching in.
Hear, O Israel
And this is why the most important sentence the Hebrew people ever carried does not begin with *look.* It begins with *hear.*

*Hear, O Israel*, that is how it opens, the confession they were told to bind to their hands and speak over their children and say lying down and rising up. Not *see, O Israel.* Not *understand, O Israel.* *Hear.* Before you are asked to grasp anything, before you are asked to see anything, you are asked to open the one sense that was open before you could do anything else, and to let a word reach in and move you. Yeshua Himself kept pressing the same door. Again and again He would finish a hard and wonderful thing by saying, *whoever has ears to hear, let them hear*, as though the whole matter came down not to how clever you were or how much you could see, but to whether you would keep the oldest window in you open, and let the sound in.

Because it is possible to have working ears and hear nothing. That is the ache underneath all of it. You can be present at every service and let the whole thing hum by like a refrigerator. Hearing that reaches the soul is not automatic; it is a kind of consent, a decision to stop merely processing the air and to let a word actually *touch* the center of you, the way sound was always designed to.
Keep the window open
So here is what I want to hand you, tenderly, especially if you are in a season where God has felt far and silent.

You may be straining to *see* Him. Waiting for a sign, a proof, a sight that would finally settle the matter, and finding only more distance, because sight keeps everything at arm's length and that is exactly what it is for. But you were not built to meet Him first with your eyes. You were built to meet Him through the door that opened before your eyes ever did, the one that reaches in and moves you from within. Stop straining to see, for a moment, and simply *listen.* Not for something loud. For something that reaches. A word read slowly until it stops being ink and starts being a voice. A song that presses gently in and stirs the thing at your center that has been still too long. That trembling is not nothing. That is the sense that opened first, doing again what it was made to do: telling you that you are not alone in the dark, and that Someone is near enough to reach you.

And if you are keeping watch beside someone who is leaving, if the doctors have gone quiet and the room has gone still, hold onto this. The window is very likely still open. So do the thing love does when words have run out and hearing is the last thread left. Sing over them. Say the old true things. Let sound do the one work it has done since the warm dark before any of us were born, and will do until the very last door closes: reach in, across the distance, and let a soul know it is held.

You began your life inside a sound you did not choose, that told you you were not alone. It is fitting beyond words that you might end it the same way, and that in between, the God who made the ear would come to you through the one window He made sure would open first and close last.
Keep it open. Faith comes by hearing. It always has.

pieces.title: The New Name No One Else Can Pronounce
