pieces.excerpt: My name means new star, and for years I introduced myself by my worst season instead. Scripture keeps promising ruined people a new name, written on a white stone, known only to the one who receives it. I think there is a name being sung over you that you have never once answered to.

body.text: For a long stretch of my life, if you had asked me who I was, I would have answered with the worst thing that had happened to me.

Not in those words. I was subtler than that. But the season I was in, the one that had failed, the one where something I loved came apart, had quietly become my name. I introduced myself by it without meaning to. It was in the way I held my shoulders, the way I hedged when people asked what I did, the small reflexive apology I attached to my own presence in a room. If my life had a nameplate on it in those years, it would not have read *Nova.* It would have read the name of my ruin.

And the strange thing is that my given name means *new star.* I was walking around every day answering to *cinder* while carrying a name that meant *light.* I had let the wrong word become the sound I turned toward when someone called.

I think a great many people are living this way, and do not know there is another option. So let me tell you what I have come to believe about names, because the Scriptures do something with them that changed how I understand my own.
A name is a sound you turn toward

Consider, first, what a name actually is. Strip away everything else and a name is simply a *sound*, a small arrangement of air that someone makes, and that you, out of the whole roar of the world, have learned to answer to. It is remarkable, really. In a crowded room full of noise, you can be deep in conversation, hearing none of it, and the instant someone across the room says your name, you turn. Your whole attention pivots toward it before you have decided anything. A name is the one sound that reaches past all the other sound and finds you.

Which means the name you answer to has enormous power. It is the sound that owns your turning. And here is the quiet tragedy: you can train yourself, over years, to turn toward the wrong one. Say *failure* over a person often enough, or let them say it over themselves, and eventually that becomes the sound their attention pivots to. They stop turning toward their real name because they have stopped believing it is still theirs to answer.
The Scriptures are full of people exactly there. And what Yahuah does with them, over and over, is the same startling thing.
He changes their name.
The renaming God

There is a man in the old story who wrestles all night with God by a river, and he does not come away with a trophy. He comes away with a limp, and a new name. He had spent his whole life being *Jacob*, a name that meant something like *grasper,* *heel-grabber,* the one who takes what is not his. He had earned that name; he had lived down to it since birth. And in the dark by the water, wounded and clinging and refusing to let go, he is renamed *Israel*, one who has struggled with God and prevailed. He limps into the morning with a wound and a new word for who he is, and the old name, the one that had been his shame his whole life, is not the sound he answers to anymore.

It keeps happening. An old man past all hope of a future is renamed from *Abram* to *Abraham,* father of a multitude, decades before there was a single child to make sense of it, named for the promise, not the present. A rough, unreliable fisherman who would go on to fail badly, at the worst possible moment, is given a new name to his face, *Cephas,* *Peter,* the rock, named for what grace would make of him, not for what he actually was that afternoon.

And then there is the woman who tried to do the renaming herself. She had lost her husband and her sons, lost everything, and she came home hollow, and she said to the whole town: *do not call me by my name anymore.* Her name meant *pleasant,* and she could not bear the irony of it. *Call me Bitter,* she said. *Call me by my ruin, because the Almighty has dealt bitterly with me.* She did exactly what I did. She renamed herself after her worst season, out loud, and asked everyone to use it. And the tender thing is that the story does not honor her request. It keeps calling her by her real name. And it does not end in bitterness at all; it ends with a child laid in her lap, and a line running from that lap all the way down to a shepherd-king and, in time, to the Messiah. The name she gave herself in her grief was not the name God was writing. She could not see her own ending, and she got her own name wrong.
We so often do.
The name on the white stone
But the promise that undoes me most is a small strange one, tucked near the end of the Scriptures, and I have carried it for years.

To people who had held on through everything, the worn-down, the ones who had every reason to answer to their ruin, Yeshua makes a promise that sounds almost like a secret passed hand to hand. He says He will give them a white stone, and on the stone a *new name written, which no one knows except the one who receives it.* A name known only to you and to the One who gives it. A private word, spoken over you alone, that no one else can even pronounce, because it is not a public label at all. It is the name that says who you actually are underneath every name the world assigned you, every name your failures pinned on, every name you assigned yourself in a bitter season and asked everyone to use.

Sit with how personal that is. Not a category. Not *forgiven sinner,* said over everyone at once. A name *no one else knows*, the sound that Heaven has for *you,* specifically, that has never been said over anyone else in the history of the world. There is, the promise insists, a word being held for you that is not your wound, not your worst season, not the diminished thing you have been answering to. And on the day you receive it, you will finally hear the sound your whole life was meant to turn toward, and know it instantly as your own.
Stop answering to the ruin
So here is what I want to say to you as tenderly as I know how, especially if, like me, you have been answering to the wrong name.

The name you have been turning toward, the failure, the diagnosis, the label someone hung on you young that you never took down, the bitter word you gave yourself when a season fell apart, that is not the name written on your stone. It may be the loudest sound in your life right now. It is not the truest one. Somewhere, being held for you and spoken over you, is a name that is not your ruin, a name the God who renames graspers and bitter widows and unreliable fishermen has already chosen, a note that only you will ever sound.

You do not have to keep pivoting toward the old word every time it is called. You can begin, even now, to stop turning your head when your ruin says your name, to let it call and not answer, because it is not your name and it never was. And you can start listening, instead, for the sound your life was actually tuned to. It is quieter, for now. It is being sung over you in a register you are still learning to hear. But it is yours, written down and waiting, in a hand that has never once gotten a name wrong.

I walked around for years answering to *cinder* while my name meant *light.* Do not do what I did. There is a new name with your whole true self folded into it, held on a white stone by the One who made you, and He is not going to call you *Bitter,* no matter how many times you have asked Him to.

pieces.title: Keeping Step With a Rhythm You Didn't Set
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful, diverse crowd at a worship night clapping and moving as one, hands up and faces radiant with delight under warm golden stage light and drifting haze, a palpable sense of many hearts falling into one beat; wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, celebratory and uplifting, premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, authentic and natural, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: Your foot starts tapping before you decide to tap it. A whole crowd's clapping drifts into one beat that no one is conducting. We are built, strangely and beautifully, to fall into step with a rhythm outside ourselves, and Scripture keeps asking us to do exactly that with God.

body.text: Watch your own foot sometime when a good rhythm comes on.

You did not decide to tap it. You will catch it already going, already keeping time with something outside you, a beat it locked onto without consulting you at all. And if you try to stop it, you can, for a few seconds, by main force. Then your attention drifts, and there it is again, tapping, pulled back into step by a pulse it simply could not leave alone.

There is something almost comic about it, and something profound. Because this small helpless thing your foot does is one of the stranger facts about human beings, and once you see how deep it runs, it stops being small.

We fall into rhythm. Not just as a preference, as a reflex, a pull we are built to obey. Put a group of people in a room with a steady beat, and their bodies begin, without instruction, to organize themselves around it. It is why a crowd's scattered clapping, after a great performance, so often collapses on its own into a single unified pulse that no one is leading, thousands of hands that were each keeping their own time, drifting, drifting, and then suddenly *together,* one beat, as if a conductor had walked out, when in fact the only thing that happened is that human beings cannot easily stand near a rhythm and keep their own. We reach for the shared pulse. We fall into step.
I love this so much I could talk about it all day, but let me give you the fact that made me actually sit down.
The rhythm that could shake a bridge
The pull to fall into step is so strong, and so physical, that armies have to be *ordered out of it.*

For a long time, soldiers crossing a bridge have been commanded to break step, to stop marching in unison and walk in a deliberate, ragged, out-of-time shuffle. Not for show. Because a column of people all striking the ground on the very same beat can set a whole bridge swaying in sympathy with their rhythm, and the swaying can build, and build, until the structure is in danger. The unified human pulse is powerful enough to move something enormous. So the command goes down the line: *break step.* Scatter the rhythm. And soldiers, who have trained their whole bodies to fall into the shared beat, have to consciously fight the very thing they were drilled into, because the pull toward the common rhythm does not politely switch off.

Think about what that means. We are not neutral timekeepers, each of us privately ticking along at our own rate, occasionally choosing to coordinate. We are built to *entrain*, to lock onto a rhythm outside ourselves and be carried by it, so readily that it takes discipline to resist. A pulse outside you wants to become the pulse inside you. Your body is on its side.
And the instant I understood that, a whole line of Scripture I had read a hundred times lit up from underneath.
Keep in step

The apostle who wrote to the churches in Galatia was not, as far as I know, thinking about marching bands. But he reached for exactly this image, and I do not think it was an accident. Live by the Spirit, he wrote, and then, *keep in step with the Spirit.* Keep in step. Match your stride to a rhythm that is not your own. Let the pace of the Spirit of God become the pace of your body and your days, the way your foot lets a song become its beat.

Once you feel the weight of how *physical* that word is, it stops being a vague spiritual instruction and becomes something almost tender. He is not asking you to invent a holy rhythm out of your own effort, gritting your way into godliness by private willpower. He is telling you that there is already a pulse, steady, external, going, and that you were made, in the very grain of you, to fall into step with it. The same reflex that catches your foot before you decide, the same pull that folds a scattered crowd into one clap, that is the faculty you were given so that a life could be carried along by a rhythm larger than itself. You do not have to generate the beat. You have to *stop keeping your own* long enough to feel His, and let the built-in pull do what it already wants to do.

The prophet Amos asked it as a question that only sounds simple: *can two walk together, unless they have agreed to meet?* You cannot keep step with someone whose rhythm you have never fallen into. Walking together is not two people privately marching in the same direction. It is two rhythms become one. And the whole ache of a distracted, exhausting faith is the ache of trying to walk *with* God while insisting on keeping your own tempo, hurrying when He is unhurried, stalling when He is moving, always a half-beat off, always tired, because nothing wears a body out like fighting the pull to fall into step.
Of one accord
And here is why it was never meant to be only *you* and the rhythm.

There is a moment in the early days of the church that the old account describes with a phrase worth slowing down over. Before the great thing happened, before the wind and the fire and the sudden speech, the whole gathered company was, it says, *of one accord.* One accord. The word underneath it carries the sense of many becoming a single motion, many rhythms fallen into one. They were not merely in the same room. They had entrained. They had become, for a while, a single pulse, and it was into *that* unified rhythm, not into a room of soloists each keeping private time, that the Spirit came like a rush of wind.

I think that is how it usually goes. We were not built to keep step with God entirely alone, any more than a single clapping pair of hands can pull a crowd into unison by itself. Something happens when a body of people fall into the same rhythm together, the beat gets *strong,* the way a scattered crowd's clap gets strong once it converges, strong enough to carry the ones who were drifting, strong enough, like an army in step, to move things that no single person could budge. This is not a threat, the way the bridge is a threat. It is the promise. A people who have truly fallen into step together generate a pulse that can hold up the weak and shake loose what needed shaking.
Stop keeping your own time
So here is what I would leave with you, especially if you are worn out from a faith that has felt like effort.

You may be exhausted because you have been trying to *set* the rhythm, to manufacture, by your own private willpower, a holiness and a peace and a pace that were never yours to generate. Stop, for a moment, and notice: there is already a pulse going. Steady. Patient. Not frantic like your calendar, not stalled like your discouragement, a rhythm of grace that has been keeping perfect time the whole while you were fighting to keep your own. You do not have to invent it. You have to fall into it. And the very thing that catches your foot before you decide, the pull you could not resist if you tried, is the faculty God gave you precisely so that a whole life could be carried by a beat larger than itself.

Let your own tempo go for a little while. Get near enough to His that the built-in pull can take over. And if you can, do it near other people who are trying to do the same, because the beat gets strong when we fall into it together, and a body in one accord can carry you through stretches you could never have marched alone.
Your foot already knows how to do this. It has been showing you all your life. There is a rhythm you did not set, going right now, and you were made, down to the reflex, to fall into step.

pieces.title: The Song That Remembers You
pieces.imagePrompt: An elderly East Asian grandmother and her young grandchild sharing a pair of headphones by a bright window, both faces glowing with wonder and quiet joy as a beloved melody plays, warm afternoon light and gentle smiles of recognition between them; wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, dignified and radiant, premium worship-brand cinematic film-still warmth, authentic and tender, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: In the care home, she no longer knew her daughter's name. But when the old hymn began, every word came back, in order, sung true. Music is stored somewhere deeper than the memories that fail, and I think that deep place is telling us something about a God who does not forget.

body.text: Her daughter told me the story with her hand pressed flat against her own chest, the way people do when they are holding something in.

Her mother had been slipping for a long time. The names had gone first, then the faces, then the thread of a sentence, then the daughter's own name, which was the hardest morning of all: to walk into the room she had walked into a thousand times and be met with the polite, pleasant, terrible smile you give a kind stranger. The woman who had raised her no longer knew who she was. There is no gentle way to carry that.

And then one afternoon someone in the care home began to play an old hymn. One of the ancient ones, the kind that woman had sung every Sunday for seventy years, back when Sundays and years and everything else still held together.

And her mother sang it. Every word. In order. All the verses, the ones nobody remembers past the first, the ones you have to read off the page even when your mind is whole. Sang them through, in tune, with feeling, her face open and unclouded, as though the fog had rolled back for exactly the length of the song and set her down, whole, in a place she still completely knew. She could not name her own daughter sitting beside her. But she knew every word of the song.
Her daughter said, *it was like she was still in there. Like the song went and found her.*
I have not stopped thinking about it since, because there is a real reason it happened, and the reason is one of the most quietly staggering things we have learned about how we are made.
Stored somewhere deeper

The kind of memory that fails first in a mind that is coming apart, the names, the appointments, the faces, the what-did-I-come-into-this-room-for, is stored in one region of the brain. It is fragile. It is often the first thing the disease takes.

But music does not live only there. A deeply known song, one sung a thousand times, bound up with melody and rhythm and emotion and the movements of your own mouth, gets laid down in *many* places at once, woven through parts of the brain that the disease reaches late, or sometimes never. Which means a person can lose the memory of their own wedding and still sing every word of the song that was played at it. The song is not filed with the facts. It is written deeper, in a place the erosion does not reach, held by a self that is still there long after the surface has gone quiet. This is not sentiment. It is why music therapists can walk into a locked and wordless silence with a familiar tune and watch a person surface, eyes clearing, mouth moving, *someone home*, for as long as the music lasts.
The song outlives the memory of the song. What you sang deeply enough, long enough, gets stored below the water line, where the storms that take everything else cannot get to it.
And the moment I understood that, I understood something about worship I had never had words for, and something about God I badly needed.
What you sing gets stored below the waterline

The Scriptures talk this way about the deep things, as buried treasure, planted seed, words hidden down where they cannot be stolen. One of the old songwriters said he had *hidden God's word in his heart*, not memorized it for a test, *hidden* it, buried it somewhere internal and safe, so that it would be there when he needed it and could not have reached for it deliberately. I always read that as a discipline, a technique. Now I read it as a mercy built into the architecture of a human being. There is a place in you below the waterline, and the things you put there, sung, repeated, loved into the deep grain of you, get held in a keeping that outlasts the parts of you that fail.

This is why I have stopped being embarrassed about repetition in worship. There is a modern nervousness about singing the same true things over and over, as if depth required constant novelty. But you are not only enjoying a song when you sing it for the hundredth time. You are *burying* it. You are lowering it, word by word, past the fragile surface memory and down into the deep keeping, laying up something that will still be there on a day you cannot picture, a day when the surface has gone dim and you can no longer reach for God on purpose, and something older than your failing mind will start to sing, and the song will come and find you.
You are, right now, choosing what your soul will still know when it can no longer know much. That is not a small thing to be doing on an ordinary Sunday.
He does not forget
But here is where the whole thing turns, and where I would sit down beside you and say it softly, because it is the part that steadies me most.

The terror underneath a story like that woman's is not really about melody. It is the fear of being *forgotten*, of a self dissolving, of a person you love vanishing behind their own eyes, of one day being someone no one recognizes, and worse, of being someone who no longer recognizes God, whose faith fades along with the faces, who reaches the end unable to hold onto the One they spent a life holding.

And to that specific fear the Scriptures speak with a tenderness I can hardly get through. Yahuah says, to His people growing old: *even to your old age I am He, and to your gray hairs I will carry you. I made you, and I will bear you; I will carry, and I will save.* Hear the direction of it. It does not say *keep holding on to Me.* It says *I will carry you.* The strength in that promise is not your grip on Him. It is His grip on you, and His does not loosen when yours does. Another of the old songs pleads, *do not cast me off in the time of old age; do not forsake me when my strength is spent*, and the whole weight of Scripture answers: He won't. He cannot forget you, because you were never being held by your memory of Him. You were being held by His memory of you, and His does not fail.

That is the deepest thing the song in the care home was telling us. When that woman sang every word she could no longer explain, it was a picture, in miniature, of a rescue larger than the song. Something in her was still held, still whole, still reachable, waiting below the waterline the whole time the surface was failing, and a familiar melody was enough to reach down and touch it, and prove it was still there. Even in her, even then, someone was home. And if a mere song, buried deep enough, can go and find a person the world had given up as gone, how much more the God who buried Himself deeper still, who wrote His own faithfulness into a place no disease can reach, and who has promised to come, at the very end, and carry home the ones who can no longer carry themselves.
Bury the true things now
So here is what I want to leave with you, whether you are young and whole or already watching the surface of someone you love begin to go.

Sing the true things now, and sing them deep. Not for the feeling of the moment, for the keeping. Bury them below the waterline, in the place the storms cannot reach, so that on the day you cannot summon a single fact about God on purpose, the deep grain of you will still know how the song goes.

And do not be afraid of the fog, for yourself or for the ones already in it. The self you fear losing is held lower than the part that fails, in a keeping older than your memory, by a God who has promised to carry you when your strength is spent and to come, at the last, and sing you the rest of the way home.
The song remembers you when you cannot remember it. And He remembers you even then, especially then, most of all then.

pieces.title: Nobody in the Barrio Sings the Whole Song Alone
pieces.imagePrompt: A warm crowded barrio courtyard at golden hour alive with call-and-response singing, one radiant song-leader with open mouth and lifted hand while a sea of joyful faces of every age answers back with raised palms, everyone singing as one in shared voice and belonging; luminous cinematic film-still quality, warm gold amber and terracotta tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: The night my voice gave out in the middle of a song, the whole room finished the line for me. That is when I finally understood what call-and-response was always for. Nobody was ever supposed to carry the melody by himself.

body.text: There was a night my voice simply quit on me in the middle of a song.

We had been going for hours. It was one of those gatherings in the courtyard behind my tío's house, the kind that starts with a few people and a guitar and somehow, by midnight, has the whole block leaning over the wall. I was leading, calling out the lines the way I had learned to, the way my people have always done it, and somewhere in the third hour my throat closed up on me. Nothing came out. I opened my mouth to sing the line and there was only air.
And here is what I will never forget. The song did not stop.

Because I had just sung the call, the room already had the answer ready in their mouths, and they gave it back to me full and loud without me, a hundred voices carrying the line I could not carry, holding it up in the air where I had dropped it, waiting, patient, for me to find my voice again and throw them the next one. I stood there with my hand on my chest, undone, listening to a song I was supposedly leading go on perfectly well without me. And I understood something in my body that night that I had somehow never understood in my head, though I had done it my whole life.
Nobody in the barrio was ever supposed to sing the whole song alone.
The call was always built to be answered

The way I was raised to sing is called *llamada y respuesta*. Call and response. One voice throws out a line, and the crowd throws it back. The leader sings the verse nobody knows yet, and the people answer with the *coro*, the chorus, the part everyone owns, the line so worn-in and familiar that a child half-asleep on a shoulder can still murmur it.

For years I thought this was just a style. A flavor. Something my people did because it was lively and it kept the tired ones awake. I did not realize it was theology until I started reading the old songs honestly and found that God's own songbook was built exactly the same way.

There is a psalm, the long one that walks all the way back through the whole story of everything, and it is impossible to read it right and miss what it is doing. It names the making of the sun and the moon. It names the sea splitting open and a people walking through on dry ground. It names the bread in the wilderness and the enemies overthrown. And after every single line, without fail, the same answer comes back: *for His mercy endures forever. For His mercy endures forever.* Over and over, more than twenty times, like a tide coming in.

That is not a poem meant to be read by one man alone in a quiet room. You cannot read it that way without it feeling strange, like clapping with one hand. It was written for a leader and a crowd. Somebody up front sang the deed of God. He made the heavens, He brought us out, He remembered us when we were low, and the whole assembly of the people roared the answer back: *for His mercy endures forever.* The verse changes every time. The answer never does. The leader carries the story. The people carry the faithfulness. And neither one of them is singing the whole song alone.

That is call and response. It is the oldest way the people of God have ever worshiped, and my barrio did not invent it. We inherited it, the same way we inherited the procession and the drum. We just never let anyone talk us out of it.
Why the answer has to come from the crowd
I want to tell you why this matters, because I think a lot of good people have been quietly taught to worship as soloists, and it is wearing them out.

There is a moment recorded from the day they finished the great house of God, when the singers and the players had been going and going, and the account says something I find almost unbearable in its beauty: they were *as one.* One sound. The trumpeters and the singers made themselves a single voice to praise the Lord, and it was in that exact moment, when the many became one sound, that the glory came down and filled the house so thick the priests could not even stand to do their work. It was not the skill that brought the glory. It was the *oneness.* It was the many voices agreeing to become one song.

You cannot do that alone. That is the whole point. There is a kind of worship that only happens when you stop being a soloist and let yourself become one voice in a crowd of voices, when you sing the line you know and trust the person beside you to sing the line you have forgotten. The barrio understood this instinctively. When my voice gave out, nobody panicked, because nobody had ever believed the song depended on me in the first place. The song belonged to the room. I was just one throat in it.

And that is the thing I most want you to hear, because I think you may be tired in a way you have not named. If you have been carrying your faith like a solo, like the whole melody rests on you, like you have to hit every note and never lose your voice and never drop the line, then hear me: that was never the arrangement. You were written into a *coro.* You were meant to sing your part and let the room carry what you cannot. When your voice gives out, and it will, everyone's does, the people around you are supposed to already have the answer in their mouths, holding it up in the air where you dropped it, waiting for you to come back in.
Throw the line, and trust the room
So here is what I would say to you, wherever you sing.

Stop trying to be the whole song. It is not humility to insist on carrying every part yourself; it is exhaustion dressed up as strength, and it was never asked of you. The God who wrote His own songbook for a leader and a crowd did not design you to worship as one lonely voice straining to hold the whole melody in the air. He designed a call and a response. He designed a people who finish each other's lines.

There will be seasons you are the caller, when your voice is strong and the story is fresh in your mouth and you get to throw the great deeds of God out over the crowd. Do it. Sing the verse nobody knows yet. And there will be seasons you are only the *coro*, when you are too tired or too broken to carry anything new, and all you can do is stand in the crowd and answer, *for His mercy endures forever,* over a story someone else is strong enough to sing. Do that too. It is not a lesser worship. It is the answer the whole song was waiting for.

And on the night your voice quits altogether, the night nothing comes out but air, do not be afraid. Look around. The room already has your line. They have been holding it for you the whole time. *La respuesta ya viene.* The answer is already coming. It is coming from the crowd God set around you on purpose, so that no one in the barrio, and no one in His whole wide family, would ever have to sing the whole song alone.

pieces.title: They Took Our Drums, So We Drummed on the Box
pieces.imagePrompt: An older Afro-Peruvian percussionist rides a simple wooden cajón in warm golden light, eyes closed and face lit with fierce joy, hands blurred mid-strike as a delighted circle of onlookers claps and cheers around him in triumphant praise forged out of hardship; luminous cinematic film-still quality, warm gold amber and rich mahogany tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: They outlawed the drums to break the people. So the people sat down on the shipping crates meant to carry them and drummed on those instead. The instrument of their captivity became the heartbeat of their praise, and that is exactly the kind of thing my God does.

body.text: The first time I really *saw* a cajón, not just heard it, but saw what it was, an old man was sitting on one in a doorway, playing it with his bare hands, and I could not for the life of me figure out why a grown man was drumming on a wooden crate when there were real drums in the world.

It looks like nothing. That is the first thing you have to understand about it. A cajón is a box. A plain wooden box, about big enough to sit on, which is exactly what you do. You straddle it like a stool and lean forward and strike the front face with your palms and your fingers, and out of this humble nothing of a box comes a whole kit's worth of sound: a deep boom near the bottom, a bright crack up top, a rattle and a slap and a heartbeat. A grown man on a wooden box, and the whole street starts to move.
I asked the old man where the box drum came from. And he told me a story I have never been able to shake, and it changed the way I understand praise itself.
The box was never supposed to be an instrument
The cajón was born in chains.

When my brothers and sisters were carried in ships to this side of the ocean and sold, the drums came with them in their memory, the drums were the language, the drums were the prayer, the drums were how a people talked to God and to each other across the whole long dark of what was being done to them. And the ones who bought and sold human beings understood this perfectly. So they banned the drums. Outlawed them. Took them away, because a people who can still drum is a people who can still gather, still remember, still hope, and you cannot fully own a people who can still hope.
So they took the drums.

And the people sat down on the shipping crates, the very boxes that had been used to move goods and move bodies, the boxes of their captivity, and they drummed on *those.* On the fruit crates. On the dresser drawers. On whatever wooden thing was too ordinary and too useful to be forbidden. They could not stop a man from sitting on a box. And out of the box, the banned heartbeat came back. The prayer they had tried to outlaw simply changed its address and kept right on praying, from inside the very object that was meant to keep the people down.

The old man in the doorway told me this and then he hit the box once, hard, and let it ring, and he said something I have carried ever since. He said: *they gave us the crate to break us, and we made it sing.*
I sat with that for a long time. Because I realized I was looking at more than a clever instrument. I was looking at the whole shape of the Gospel, carved in wood.
This is exactly how my God works

You do not have to look far in the old accounts to find that God is forever doing this same thing, taking the object meant for harm and turning it, from the inside, into the instrument of praise and rescue.

Think of the boy sold by his own brothers. They hated him, and they threw him in a pit, and they sold him off to strangers headed for a far country, and everything after that was a box built to break him, the false accusation, the prison, the years forgotten in the dark. Every single thing that happened to that boy was a crate of someone else's cruelty. And when he finally stood in front of the brothers who had done it, grown now, holding their lives in his hand, he did not say what they were braced to hear. He said: *you meant it for evil. But God meant it for good.* The same events. The identical crate. Meant one way by the ones who built it, and meant another way entirely by the God who was quietly turning it into the salvation of nations the whole time.

That is the cajón. That is the whole thing. The box does not stop being a box. Joseph's pit was a real pit; the chains were real chains; the ban on the drums was a real, cruel, bitter ban. My God does not pretend the harm away. He does something stranger and far greater than pretending. He reaches into the very instrument of the harm and pulls praise out of it. He lets the thing that was meant to silence a people become the thing that carries their song farther than the old drums ever could.

And the cross itself. I have to say it, because it is the same story one more time and the largest one. The cross was a crate built to break a man. It was the empire's box, its instrument of shame and silence, designed for exactly one purpose: to end you publicly and make sure everyone got the message. And God sat down on it. And made it sing. The most terrible object the world could build became the most joyful symbol the world has ever known, and we hang it in our homes and lift it over our dancing, because our God specializes in exactly this, taking the crate that was meant to break the people, and turning it into the heartbeat of their praise.
Whatever they gave you to break you, make it sing
So here is what I want to leave with you, and I want to say it gently, because I do not know what box you are sitting on tonight.

There is something in your life right now that was built to break you. Maybe someone handed it to you on purpose, the way the brothers handed Joseph the pit. Maybe it was just the crate that life ships everyone in, the loss, the poverty, the wound that will not close, the years you feel you have lost in some prison nobody remembers you are in. And the whole world's counsel is the same: get rid of it. Escape it. Wait for it to be gone before you dare to make any joyful sound.

But my people learned something better in chains, and I am handing it to you. You do not always get to throw the crate away. Sometimes the box is the only wood you have. So do not wait for the drums to come back. Sit down on the very thing that was meant to keep you down, and drum on it. Let the God who meant it for good pull a heartbeat out of it. Let the object of your captivity become the instrument of your praise, because that is the exact miracle He is best at, and He has been practicing it since a boy in a pit and a man on a cross.

*Le quitaron los tambores, y él hizo cantar la caja.* They took the drums, and he made the box sing. That is not just the story of an instrument. It is the story of everyone my God has ever gotten His hands on. And it can be your story too. Sit down on the box. And play.

pieces.title: The Homesickness That Turned Out to Be Faith
pieces.imagePrompt: A young woman sits on a warm porch at dusk cradling a guitar, her face lit with a peaceful, hopeful smile as she gazes toward a horizon glowing golden, an ache of longing softening into quiet joy as the far sky turns to gold; warm cinematic film-still quality, warm amber rose and deep indigo tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: The Brazilians call it saudade. The Romanians call it dor. It is the ache for something you cannot quite name and cannot get back. I used to think it was a wound to be healed, until I realized it was a compass, and it was pointing home.

body.text: There is a word in Portuguese that does not have a real translation, and I have spent years trying to explain it to people who did not grow up with it.

*Saudade.* The Brazilians will tell you it is the closest thing their language has to a soul. It is the ache for something absent, a person, a place, a time, a version of your own life, that is somehow sweet and sad at the very same moment. It is not simple sadness. Sadness wants the pain to stop. Saudade almost does not; it holds the ache close, because the ache is the last thread still connecting you to the thing you loved. You feel saudade for your grandmother's kitchen. For the country you left. For a song you cannot find again. For a happiness you are no longer sure was ever fully real, but you miss it anyway, with your whole chest.

And here is what struck me when I first started traveling and singing among other peoples: it is not only the Brazilians. The Romanians have their own word for it, *dor*, and they will tell you the very same thing, that no one from the outside really understands it, that it is the particular homesickness of their whole people, an ache in the shepherd's song that goes back further than anyone can remember. Two peoples, an ocean and a continent apart, both certain that they alone carry this untranslatable longing.

Which made me think it is not Brazilian and not Romanian at all. I think it is human. I think everyone has it. And I have come to believe it is one of the most important things about us, because for most of my life I treated saudade as a wound to be healed, and I was completely wrong. It is not a wound. It is a compass. And it is pointing somewhere.
The ache that no arrival can cure
Here is how I finally figured it out.

I noticed that the longing never actually got satisfied by the thing I thought it was for. I would ache for home, and then I would finally go home, and home was good, home was real, but the ache did not close. It moved. It stood just behind the reunion I had wanted, whispering that even this, even this good thing I had missed so badly, was not quite the thing. I would get the very object of my saudade in my two hands, and discover that it had never been the real object at all. It had only been pointing past itself.

The old songs describe this exact thing, and once you see it you cannot unsee it. There is a psalm that begins with a thirst so deep the writer reaches for the picture of a deer in a drought, a hunted, exhausted animal panting for the streams, its whole body one single want for water. And he says: that is my soul. That is what I am. My soul thirsts for God, for the living God. He is not describing a bad day. He is describing the deepest structure of a person, a thirst too large for any river he had yet found.

Another of those songs was written by a man out in an actual desert, on the run, hiding in the wilderness, and he says his soul is thirsting for God in a dry and weary land where there is no water. He is homesick. But notice what he is homesick *for.* Not his palace. Not his old comfort. For God Himself. He had learned to read his own thirst correctly. He knew the ache was not really about the missing water or the missing home or the missing throne. It was about a Presence he had tasted and could not stop wanting.

That is what saudade is, underneath. That is what dor is. It is the soul thirsting for the living God and mistaking it, for years, for a hundred smaller things, the kitchen, the country, the childhood, the face. All of those were real, and all of them were loved, and none of them was ever the true country the ache was pointing to.
The longing is not a defect. It is evidence

We treat this homesickness as a problem to be solved. The whole modern world is one enormous machine for numbing it, a thousand ways to stop feeling the ache, to fill the quiet before it can whisper, to keep so busy and so entertained that saudade cannot find you. And I understand why. It hurts. It is a strange, sweet, bottomless hurt, and nobody wants to sit in it.

But I want to tell you that the ache is not a defect in you. It is one of the truest things about you. The old letters put it plainly: the people of faith confessed that they were strangers and exiles on the earth, that they were looking for a homeland, not the one they had left behind, but a better country, one they had never yet seen. They were homesick for a place they had never been. Think about how strange that is. You cannot be homesick for somewhere you have never lived, unless something in you belongs there already, unless you were made for a country your feet have not yet touched.

And there is a place in the letters where it says that the whole creation is groaning, the entire world straining and aching like a mother in labor, waiting for something not yet born. And that we ourselves groan inside, waiting. The ache is not a sign that something has gone wrong with you. It is a sign that something is not yet finished, that you and the whole aching world are pregnant with a homecoming that has not arrived. Saudade is not the wound. It is the labor pain. It is the not-yet, felt in the body, because the redemption is real and it is coming and it has not come *yet.*

This is why the deepest worship songs of every people carry that minor-key thread even in their joy, why the Brazilian celebration has a tear in it and the Romanian melody bends downward even when it lifts. It is not because these peoples are sad. It is because they are honest. They are singing the true condition of every human heart: made for a home we have not reached, aching for a Presence we have only tasted, and refusing to pretend the ache away.
Follow the ache all the way home
So here is what I want to say to you, if you carry this longing and have never known what to do with it.

Stop trying to kill it. Stop treating your homesickness like a malfunction. That sweet, bottomless ache you feel on certain evenings, when a song comes on, when the light goes gold, when you miss something you cannot even name, that is not you being broken. That is the truest compass you own, and it is not lying to you. It is pointing, past your grandmother's kitchen and your lost country and your gone childhood, past every good thing you have loved and buried, to the one Home that was underneath all of them the whole time. The ache is not for the water. It is for the Living God who is the source of every stream you ever drank from.

So follow it. Let saudade do its real work. Let the homesickness lead you all the way to the One it was always about, the God who put eternity in your chest so you would never quite settle for less than Himself, and who has prepared a country you have never seen but were somehow, all along, homesick for.

*Saudade. Dor.* The ache that has no cure on this side. Do not be afraid of it. It is not a wound. It is a promise, felt before it is kept, and the One who planted it in you is also, at this very moment, on His way to keep it.

pieces.title: The First Miracle Was Saving a Party
pieces.imagePrompt: An exuberant outdoor wedding feast at golden hour in a warm courtyard, a diverse crowd of guests dancing with arms raised and cups brimming, faces radiant with laughter beneath lights strung overhead and long tables of abundant food, pure overflowing celebration that will not run dry; luminous cinematic film-still quality, warm gold amber and deep rose tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: Of all the things Yeshua could have chosen for His first miracle, He chose to keep a wedding from running dry. I think we have badly underestimated what that tells us about the heart of God.

body.text: I once watched a whole neighborhood save a wedding.

The family did not have much. They had put everything they had into the day, the dress borrowed, the chairs borrowed, the whole barrio pitching in the way it does, and somewhere in the late afternoon, with the dancing already going strong, the word went quietly around that the food was running short and the drink was nearly gone. It is a particular kind of quiet panic, that one. Because it is not really about the food. It is about the shame. In my culture, to run out at your own celebration, to have the joy stop dead in front of everyone because you could not provide, is a wound a family carries for years.

And I watched the neighborhood move. Somebody went home and came back with a pot. Somebody's tía appeared with more of everything. A cousin ran to the store. Quietly, without a word said out loud about what was happening, the whole street closed ranks around that family and refilled the celebration before it could die, so that the couple dancing in the middle never even knew how close their joy had come to running out. Nobody was shamed. The party went on until dawn.

I did not think of it as a holy thing at the time. I thought of it as just what you do. It was only years later, reading slowly through the account of the first miracle Yeshua ever performed, that I sat straight up in my chair. Because He did the exact same thing. And I realized we have badly, badly underestimated what it means that this, *this*, is the thing He chose to do first.
He could have chosen anything, and He chose the wine
Think about it honestly for a moment.

The first public miracle. The opening act. The very first time He pulls back the curtain and lets a little of the glory show. Of all the things He could have chosen, a healing, a resurrection, a storm stilled, a demon cast out, some thunderous sign to announce who had arrived. He chose to keep a wedding from running out of wine.

The setting is a village celebration. A young couple, a big crowd, days of feasting the way they did it back then, the whole town packed in. And partway through, the wine runs out. Now understand what that meant. It was not an inconvenience. It was a humiliation waiting to happen, the family's joy about to collapse into public shame, the celebration about to die in front of everyone, the young couple's happiest day about to become the story people told for the wrong reason. His mother notices before almost anyone, the way mothers do, and she comes to Him. And she does not even really ask. She just tells Him the trouble: *they have no wine.*

He tells the servants to fill the great stone jars with water, ordinary water, the kind kept for washing, and when they draw it out, it has become wine. And not just enough wine to get by. Not cheap wine to quietly cover the gap. The man in charge of the feast tastes it and is astonished, and says what nobody ever says: usually you serve the good wine first and bring out the cheap stuff once everyone is too far gone to notice, but you have saved the best wine for *now,* for the end, for last. The finest wine of the whole celebration arrived after everyone thought the celebration was already over.

That is the first thing Yeshua ever chose to show the world about Himself. Not power for its own sake. Not a warning. He chose to be the one who keeps the joy from dying, and who, when He steps in, does not merely patch the gap but floods it with more and better than anyone dared hope for.
God is not embarrassed by your celebration

I need to say this plainly, because somewhere along the way a great many sincere people got the idea that God is fundamentally suspicious of joy. That the parties, the feasting, the dancing, the abundance, the music going till dawn, that all of it is a slightly guilty thing, tolerated at best, and that the truly spiritual life is thin and quiet and a little grim, forever apologizing for any happiness it cannot fully justify.

The first miracle demolishes that. God did not send His Son to a wedding to frown at it. He sent Him there to *rescue* it. To make sure the music kept going and the cups stayed full and the young couple was not shamed. The whole of Heaven's power, unveiled for the first time in human history, went toward keeping a celebration alive.

This is the God my people have always known in their bones, even when the wider church tried to make Him respectable and sad. He is the God of the feast. His own book is full of them, the appointed festivals, the harvest joy, the fatted calf killed for the son who came home, the promise held out at the very end of everything of a wedding supper where the tears are wiped away for good. Joy is not a distraction from God. Joy is *aimed* at God. The celebration is not the opposite of the sacred. On the day He chose to first reveal Himself, the celebration was the sacred thing, and He gave His power to keep it going.

And notice how He did it. He took the water meant for washing, the plain, the functional, the ordinary substance of a working household, and He turned it into the wine of joy. That is His signature. He is forever taking the ordinary stuff of an ordinary life and turning it into gladness nobody saw coming. He does not import joy from somewhere else. He transforms what is already in the room.
Bring Him your empty jars
So here is what I want to leave with you.

If your celebration has run dry, if the joy that once filled your life has quietly gone, and you are standing in the middle of what should be a feast, ashamed, hoping nobody notices how close to empty the cups have gotten, then you need to know exactly who this God is. He is not standing at the edge of the party with His arms crossed, waiting for it to end so the serious business can begin. He is the one who *saves* parties. His very first act was to keep the joy alive for a family that had run out and could not fix it themselves.

Bring Him your empty jars. That is all His mother did. She did not have a plan, she did not have more wine, she just brought the emptiness to Him and told Him plainly: *they have no wine.* You can do the same. You do not have to manufacture the joy back yourself, or perform a happiness you do not feel, or borrow gladness from the neighbors. You bring Him the empty. You fill the jars with whatever plain water you have left, the ordinary, the functional, the tired remains of your day, and you let Him do the thing only He can do.

And here is the promise buried in the story, and I want you to hold it close: He saves the best wine for last. The finest joy of your whole life may still be ahead of you, waiting on the far side of the moment you were sure the celebration was over. That is not how the world serves it. But it is exactly how He does.
*El vino nuevo llega tarde y llega mejor.* The new wine comes late, and it comes better. Bring Him your empty jars, and let the party go on till dawn.

pieces.title: The God Who Got Turned Away at Every Door
pieces.imagePrompt: A candlelit posada procession of joyful families winding through a warm narrow street at dusk, faces of every age glowing with candlelight and delight as they sing toward a doorway swinging wide, warm light pouring out to welcome them in after long searching; luminous cinematic film-still quality, warm gold amber and candlelit rose tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: In the posada, we act out the couple going door to door, singing to be let in, and being turned away again and again. I used to think it was just a game for the children. Then I understood we were rehearsing the deepest thing about our God.

body.text: Every year of my childhood, for nine nights running, we walked the street to be turned away.

That is the *posada.* It is one of the oldest and most beloved traditions my people keep, and if you have never seen it, let me tell you what it looks like, because it is stranger and more beautiful than most people realize. A little procession forms in the evening, candles, a couple of children dressed as Mary and Joseph, the rest of us following behind, singing. And we go from house to house. And at each house we sing a song asking to be let in. *We are weary. We have traveled far. Please, is there room? Will you open the door?*

And the people inside the house sing back. And what they sing, at first, is *no.* No room here. Go somewhere else. We do not know you. Move along. So the procession moves on to the next door, and sings the same plea, and gets the same refusal. Turned away. Turned away again. Nine nights of it, walking the cold street, singing to be let in, and hearing *no* through door after door after door.

As a boy I thought it was mostly a game, a bit of theater with candy at the end, because eventually one door does open, and when it does, everyone pours inside for the feast. But I am grown now, and I have walked that procession too many times, and one year it stopped being a game. One year, singing outside a closed door in the cold, I understood what we were actually doing. We were not playing. We were rehearsing the truest and most heartbreaking thing there is to know about our God.
He knows exactly what it is to be turned away at the door. Because it happened to Him.
There was no room, and it was written down

We have made the birth of Yeshua so pretty that we have sanded the hard fact right off of it. But the account does not hide it. It says it flat and cold: when the time came for the child to be born, they laid Him in a feeding trough, because there was no room for them. No room. The doors were full, or the doors were shut, or the doors simply did not care, and the God of all creation entered His own world through the one gap left over after everyone with a bed had been accommodated. The King of everything was born in the space nobody else wanted, because there was no room.

Think about what the posada is actually doing, then. It is not inventing a sad story for the sake of drama. It is putting our own bodies inside the true one. When we walk that cold street and sing to be let in and hear *no* through the door, we are not pretending. We are remembering. We are feeling in our own feet what it cost, that the Maker of the world came to the world and knocked, and the world, busy and full and asleep, told Him there was no room.

And it did not stop at His birth. That was only the first door. He grew up and went from town to town, and His own people would not receive Him. He came to what was His, the old letter says, and His own did not take Him in. He stood outside the hearts of the very ones He had come to save, and knocked, and was told again and again: no room. The turning-away at the inn was not a one-time accident of a crowded night. It was the shape of His whole life. He is, in a way we do not like to sit with, the God who spent His days on the wrong side of doors, singing to be let in.

That is who we are walking with, out there in the cold of the posada. Not a God who has always been safely, comfortably inside. A God who knows the exact feeling of the closed door, because He stood outside it Himself, and was turned away, and kept knocking anyway.
He is still standing at the door
Here is the part of the posada that broke me open, once I finally saw it.

The whole thing turns on a knock and a plea from *outside.* And there is a line in the very last book of the Bible where the risen Yeshua, glorified, seated over everything, needing nothing, describes Himself, and of all the images He could have chosen, He chooses this one. He says: *look, I am standing at the door, and I am knocking. If anyone hears My voice and opens the door, I will come in and eat with him.*

Sit with how astonishing that is. The God who was turned away at the inn did not respond by kicking the doors down. He could. He is not weak; He is the one who made the wood and the hinges and the hand that bolts the latch. He could break into any life He wanted, take any room by force. And He will not. He stands outside, as He always has, and He knocks, and He sings the plea, *is there room? will you open?*, and He waits for the door to be opened from the inside. He turns the whole story of the closed inn around and makes Himself, forever, the one on the doorstep asking to be let in. The God who was refused a room now refuses to force one.

This is why the posada always, always ends with a door that opens. Because that is the Gospel. After nine nights of *no,* one household sings back a different word, *come in, come in, there is room here, you are welcome, this is your home*, and the door swings wide and the cold street pours into the warm house and the feast begins and nobody is turned away anymore. The whole tradition exists to teach the children, in their bodies, that the turning-away is not the end of the story. The story ends with a door thrown open and a weary traveler brought in from the cold, and it turns out the weary traveler was the Lord all along.
Open the door
So here is what I most need to say to you, whoever you are and whatever household you keep.

He is still on the doorstep. That is not a memory from a stable long ago; it is a fact about right now. The God who was turned away at every door has come to yours, and He is doing the same thing He has always done, not breaking in, not forcing the latch, but standing in the cold of your ordinary evening and knocking, and singing the same patient plea He sang outside the inn. *Is there room? Will you open the door?*

And you know how full the house gets. You know all the reasons the innkeeper gave, no room, too busy, too late, we do not know you, come back another time. I have given every one of those reasons myself. But the posada taught me, one cold night outside a closed door, that the saddest role in the whole story is the one who keeps the latch shut while the God of glory sings on the step. And the most joyful role, the one every version of the tradition builds toward, is the household that finally sings back *come in,* and swings the door wide, and lets the feast begin.

You do not have to have a fine house. The first door that opened to Him opened onto a room with animals in it. He is not inspecting your accommodations. He only wants in. So open the door. Sing back the welcome. Let the God who was turned away at every other door be received, at long last, at yours.
*¿Hay posada?* Is there room? He is asking it of you right now, in the cold outside your heart. And there is only ever one answer that ends in a feast. Open the door.

pieces.title: The Long Walk to Moriah
pieces.imagePrompt: A father and his young child hiking hand in hand up a golden mountain trail at dawn, both smiling with quiet delight as warm first light breaks over the peaks ahead, tender resolve and gentle joy, premium cinematic worship-brand quality, authentic and natural; wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: Before Abraham ever built the altar, he had to walk three days toward it, carrying the fire past the same fear every morning. What if the worship God is forming in you is not the moment on the mountain, but the long obedient walk it takes to get there?

body.text: We always tell this story as if it happened in an instant, and it did not. It took three days.

You know the shape of it. An old man is asked to give up the one thing his whole life had been aimed at, the son of the promise, the boy he waited a hundred years for, and to give him up on a mountain, as an offering. It is the hardest command in all of Scripture, and we tend to fast-forward through it to the knife and the ram, because the ending is where the relief is. But I want to slow the account down to the pace it actually moved at, because between the command and the mountain there is a road, and the road is three days long, and I think the road is where the real thing happened.

The account says Abraham rose early in the morning. He split the wood for the offering himself, an old man, at dawn, cutting the very wood his son would be laid on, with his own hands. He saddled the donkey. He took two servants and the boy, and he set out toward the place God had told him about. And then comes the line that undoes me every time I sit with it: on the third day, Abraham looked up and saw the place in the distance.

The third day. Which means the first day, and the second day, he woke up with it. He walked all day with it. He lay down at night still carrying it, and got up in the morning and it was still true. Whatever he had settled in his heart back home in the first terrible hour of obedience, he had to re-settle it every single mile, for seventy-two hours, with the mountain getting slowly closer the whole time.
Worship is mostly the walk

Here is what I have learned climbing real mountains, and it is exactly the same thing: the summit is a moment, but the climb is the mountain. You do not become the kind of person who can stand at the top by standing at the top. You become that person on day two, on the switchback nobody photographs, when the peak is still a far grey shape and every part of you is negotiating whether to keep going. The mountain is not the last hundred feet. The mountain is all of it.

We have almost the opposite idea about worship. We think worship is the moment, the altar, the raised hands, the surrender that finally breaks. And it is that. But before Abraham ever built a single altar on Moriah, he called what he was doing by its name. He turned to the servants at the foot of the mountain and told them to wait, and said, in effect: *the boy and I are going over there to worship, and we will come back to you.*

Sit with the word he used. Not "I am going to go through the worst thing a father can do." He called it *worship*. He had been calling it worship for three days of walking. Which means the worship was not only the knife on the altar. The worship was the whole obedient trudge toward a thing he could not understand and did not want and would not stop walking toward. The surrender was already happening at three miles an hour, in the dust, with a boy asking questions.

And notice what else he said to those servants: *we* will come back. Not "I will come back." He was climbing toward what looked like the end of everything, and somehow, out of a faith I can barely comprehend, he had already decided that the God who gave the promise would keep the promise on the far side of the altar, that he would come down the mountain with his son somehow, some way. He did not have the answer. He had the God. And he started walking, and he told the truth about the God before he had any evidence for it.
The provision was already on the mountain
Here is the mercy hidden in the long walk, and I do not want you to miss it.

The whole way up, Abraham did not know how it ended. The boy carried the wood. Abraham carried the fire and the knife, the dangerous things, the things a father would never let a son carry. And the boy, no fool, finally asked the question that must have gone through the old man like a blade: *father, here is the fire and the wood, but where is the lamb?* And Abraham said the truest thing he knew: *God will provide the lamb, my son.* He did not know that yet. He believed it. He spoke it uphill into the silence, and kept climbing.

And then, at the very top, after the altar was built and the boy was bound and the hand was raised and Heaven itself stepped in to stop it, Abraham looked up, and there in a thicket was a ram, caught by its horns. The provision was not sent from somewhere far away in the nick of time. The ram was already on the mountain. It had been up there, in the brush, the entire three days Abraham had been walking toward the place, terrified and obedient and not knowing. The answer was ahead of him on the trail the whole time. He just could not see it until he had climbed all the way up to where it was waiting.

He named that place a name that God's people have carried ever since: *Yahuah will provide.* Or more literally, *Yahuah will see to it*, on the mountain of Yahuah, it will be seen. And the name is not really about a ram. It is about a discovery you can only make by walking the whole road: that the God who asks you to climb toward the impossible has already gone up ahead of you and put the provision in the thicket, out of sight, waiting for the exact altitude where you will finally need it and finally find it.
For the one on day two
So let me speak to whoever is somewhere in the middle of their own three-day walk, not at the command anymore, and not at the altar yet, but out on the road in between, where it is hardest.

You said yes to God about something a while ago. You surrendered it in a rush of grace, and you meant it. And now you are on day two, and the mountain is still far off, and you have discovered the thing nobody warned you about: that you have to keep surrendering it. Every morning it is still true. Every mile you carry the fire again. The obedience did not finish when you decided; it just began, and now it is a long walk, and part of you wonders whether all this trudging even counts, because nothing dramatic is happening. You are just putting one foot in front of the other toward a thing you do not fully understand.

Hear me as a pastor who trusts this metaphor with his life: the walk counts. The walk is the worship. What you are doing on the ordinary, undramatic, third-day road, getting up, carrying it again, speaking the truth about God's faithfulness before you can see it, keeping your feet moving toward the mountain, that is not the delay before the real surrender. That *is* the surrender, stretched out to the size of your actual life so that it can go all the way down into you.

And the provision you cannot see yet is already up ahead. The God who asked you to climb did not send you toward an empty summit. He went up first, and He has put in the thicket, at the exact altitude of your need, the thing you will require when you get there, which you will not find one step sooner and do not need to. Your job is not to see the ram. Your job is to keep walking, and to tell the truth about Him on the way up, and to trust that on the mountain of Yahuah, it will be seen.
Keep climbing. Say it out loud like Abraham did, into the silence, before you have any proof: *we will worship, and we will come back down.* Then take the next mile. The ram is already there.

pieces.title: The Song That Called the Water Up

pieces.excerpt: Deep in the wilderness, a tired nation gathered around a dry hole in the ground and did something strange before there was any water in it. They sang. Here is what happens when a people learns to sing over the well before it fills.

body.text: There is a moment in the wilderness wanderings that most people read straight past, and it is one of the only places in all of Scripture where the text stops the story to hand you the actual song.

The people of Israel had been in the desert a long time by then. They had complained, they had wandered, they had buried a whole generation in the sand. And they came to a place the account simply calls Beer, which is the Hebrew word for *well*. It was there that Yahuah said to Moses: gather the people together, and I will give them water. And then the text says something that ought to make anyone who leads worship sit up straight. It says: *then Israel sang this song.* And it gives you the words. Spring up, O well, sing to it, the well that the leaders dug, that the nobles of the people hollowed out with the scepter and with their staffs.

I want you to picture the scene precisely, because everything is in the details. A worn-out desert people, gathered around a hole in the ground. The leaders down in the dirt, digging, not with shovels and machines, but with the very staffs of their office, the walking sticks that marked them as princes, driven into the sand like tools. And the whole crowd around them, not silent, not grumbling for once, but *singing to the well.* Singing at it. Singing water up out of the dry ground.
Worship over the empty place
Now think about the order of things, because the order is the whole lesson.

They did not wait until the water came and then throw a celebration. That is how we usually do it. We keep our praise in reserve until the provision arrives, and then, once the well is full and we can see it and touch it and drink from it, we sing our thank-you. That is real, and it is good, and there is a place for it. But it is not what happened at Beer. At Beer, the singing came *while* the ground was still dry and the leaders were still digging. The song was not a response to the water. The song was sung over the absence of water, into a hole that had not yet given anything, as an act of expectation. They were singing to summon what they could not yet see.

I have spent enough of my life in high, dry, wilderness places to tell you this is one of the hardest kinds of worship there is, and one of the most important. It is easy to sing over a full well. Anyone can rejoice at a spring that is already flowing. But to gather around the dry place, the marriage that has gone quiet, the body that will not heal, the calling that has borne nothing yet, the child who has not come home, to gather around the dry hole and *sing to it*, sing over it, sing as though water were on its way when there is no evidence in the sand that it is, that takes a faith the comfortable never have to develop. That is desert worship. And the desert is the only place it can be learned.

Notice, too, that Yahuah had already spoken. He said, *I will give them water.* The song was not a technique to twist God's arm; the song was the people agreeing with a promise already made. That is the difference between anxious wishing and worship. Worship over the empty well is not you trying to force something out of God by the force of your singing. It is you taking a word He has already given and setting it to music before it comes true, so that your heart lives in the promise while your eyes still see only sand.
They dug it together

And do not miss the other thing, because it is easy to miss. *The well that the leaders dug, that the nobles hollowed out with their staffs.* This was not a miracle that dropped from the sky onto passive spectators. The people sang, and the leaders dug, and both were happening at once.

There is a false spirituality that says if God is going to provide, then I should sit still and wait and touch nothing, and any effort of mine only gets in the way of grace. And there is an opposite lie that says it is all up to my effort, my strategy, my sweat, and God helps those who help themselves. The well at Beer refuses both. The song rose *and* the staffs went into the ground. The people worshiped over the dry place *and* the leaders got down in the dirt and dug. The provision was God's. He said plainly, *I will give them water*, and yet He gave it through singing people and digging hands, and He did not seem to think the digging insulted the gift.

This is how it almost always works in the high country of faith. You sing over the dry place, and you also pick up the staff and dig. You worship expectantly, and you also do the next faithful thing in front of you. You go to the appointment, you make the call, you keep showing up, you drive the plain ordinary tool of your obedience into the ground where you are believing for water. And somewhere down in that dark, out of your sight, the source God had already placed there begins, at last, to rise toward the light.

And it was *together.* The leaders did not dig a private well for themselves. The nobles hollowed it out for the whole thirsty nation, and the whole nation sang over it as one. Nobody in that crowd was drawing water alone. That is the church at its best in a dry season, not every person frantically digging their own hole in isolation, but a people gathered around the same empty place, some singing when others have no voice left, some digging when others have no strength left, all of them believing for the same water, all of them about to drink from the same well.
For the one standing over a dry well
So let me speak to whoever is standing over an empty place right now, exhausted, with no water in sight.

You have prayed over it for a long time and nothing has risen. The ground is dry and it stays dry, and you have started to go quiet, because it feels foolish to keep singing over a hole that gives you nothing back. The silence feels more honest than the song. And a voice keeps telling you that when there is finally something to celebrate, then you can worship, but not before, not over sand, not over nothing.

Hear me: sing over it now. Not because pretending will make it so, and not to perform a happiness you do not feel, but because Yahuah has spoken over your desert the same kind of word He spoke over Beer, and worship is simply the sound of a heart that has decided to trust the word before it sees the water. Sing to the dry well. And then pick up your staff, the plain, ordinary tool of your next act of obedience, and put it in the ground, and dig where you are, and do not despise how unmagical it looks. The well the leaders dug with their walking sticks still gave a whole nation water.

The source was already there. Yahuah had placed it under that dry ground before the people ever arrived, and He placed it under yours too. Your singing does not manufacture the water. Your singing calls it up, agrees with the God who promised it, and lives inside the promise while the ground is still bare. So gather at the dry place with whoever will stand there with you, and lift the song the desert people lifted, and dig, and wait, and watch.
Spring up, O well. It is already on its way to the surface.

pieces.title: Moving at the Speed of the Cloud
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful small group gathered on a high sunlit ridge at dawn, a diverse handful of friends resting together with an open book, faces content and glad as they wait beneath a glowing pillar of cloud, patient expectancy and warm fellowship, premium cinematic worship-brand light, authentic and natural; wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: For forty years an entire nation lived by one rule in the wilderness: when the cloud lifted, they walked, and when it settled, they stayed, for a night or for a year, whatever it did. Here is what that ancient discipline has to teach a generation that cannot stand to wait.

body.text: Anyone who has spent real time on a mountain has learned to obey the weather, and it humbles you the first time.

You want to summit today. Your body is ready, your schedule says today, everything in you says *go*, and the mountain wraps itself in cloud and wind, and any climber worth trusting says the same flat, maddening thing: not today. We wait. And you sit in the tent, fully capable, fully willing, and you do not move, because the mountain does not care about your timeline, and the people who ignore the mountain's timeline are the ones they go looking for later. The hardest discipline of the high places is not effort. It is the discipline of not moving when everything in you wants to.
Israel lived that discipline for forty years, and the account of it is one of the quietest, strangest, most beautiful passages in the whole wilderness story, and almost nobody preaches it.
The one rule in the wilderness

When the tabernacle was set up, the account says, a cloud covered it. By day it looked like cloud, and at night it looked like fire, so that whether the sun was up or down, the presence of Yahuah was visible over the camp. And the whole ordering of the nation's life came down to a single rule, repeated over and over with a kind of patient insistence, as if the text knows we will resist it: whenever the cloud lifted from over the tent, the people set out; and wherever the cloud settled, the people camped. When the cloud stayed, they stayed. When it lifted, they moved.

And then the passage does something remarkable. It walks you through all the different lengths of the waiting, one by one, so you cannot miss the point. Sometimes the cloud remained over the tabernacle for only a few days, and they camped a few days and then moved. Sometimes it remained only from evening until morning, and when it lifted in the morning, they packed and walked.
