You have almost certainly slept through more of the presence of God than you have ever noticed, and the invitation of this whole story is not guilt about the nights you missed. It is the gasp Jacob gasped at dawn, the awe that finally sees, and the small holy stubbornness that says: God was here, and I will not walk away from it unnamed.

pieces.title: The Ear Was Consecrated First

pieces.excerpt: On the day the priests were ordained, Moses put blood on three places, the right ear, the right thumb, the right big toe. Not the mouth. Before Yahuah would trust a man to speak or sing for Him, He consecrated the ear that would have to hear first. The set-apart life begins where you did not expect it to.

body.text: The day Aaron and his sons were made priests, there was a moment in the ceremony so specific and strange that it stops you cold if you slow down enough to see it. Moses took a ram, the ram of ordination, the ram of consecration, it is called, and after it was offered, he took some of its blood and did something with it you would never invent on your own.

He put the blood on the tip of Aaron's right ear. Then on the thumb of his right hand. Then on the big toe of his right foot. And he did the same for each of the sons, one by one, ear, thumb, toe, marking the three points with blood before the anointing oil came.
The ear. The hand. The foot. Of all the places on a man you might consecrate to serve the Holy One, Yahuah named those three. And He named the ear first.
Not the mouth

I keep circling the omission, because it is the loudest thing in the ritual. This was the ordination of the priesthood, men who would spend their lives speaking blessings, teaching the law, pronouncing what was clean and unclean, leading the singing in the house of God. If ever a consecration should have begun at the mouth, it was this one. The mouth was the tool of the trade.

And the mouth is not touched. Yahuah does not begin with the instrument that speaks. He begins with the instrument that listens. Before He will trust a man to say one word on His behalf, He consecrates the ear that will have to hear the word first.

That order is not an accident, and it is not only about ancient priests. It is a diagnosis of every one of us who has ever wanted to serve God with our voice. We are so eager to speak, to sing, to declare, to lead. We treat the mouth as the frontier of ministry. And Yahuah quietly reaches past the mouth to the ear and says, this comes first. What you say for Me will only ever be as true as what you have first heard from Me. A consecrated mouth over an unconsecrated ear is how a person ends up saying sincere and beautiful things that God never actually said.

The whole life of Israel was built on a single command that begins with that same word, Hear, O Israel. Not speak first. Not act first. Hear. The set-apart people were a people defined by an ear turned toward God before it was a mouth turned toward the world. And on the day their priests were ordained, the blood went on the ear to seal exactly that: you are, before anything else, a listener now. You belong to the voice of Yahuah before you belong to your own.
Then the hand, then the foot

Only after the ear came the thumb, the hand, the part that does the work. Everything the priest would ever lift, arrange, offer, carry, and touch in the service of God was claimed by that mark. His labor was no longer his own to spend however he pleased. His hands had been bought for a purpose. What they reached for now had to answer to the One who had marked them.

And then the big toe, the foot, the part that goes. Wherever the priest walked from that day forward, he walked as a consecrated man. His steps had an owner. He could not carry a blood-marked foot into just any place and pretend the mark came off at the door. Where he went, he went as one set apart, and the ground under him had to reckon with that.

Do you see the whole man being claimed? Ear, hand, foot, what he hears, what he does, where he goes. This is not the tidy modern arrangement where God gets the religious compartment and the rest of the man runs on his own steam. Consecration in the tabernacle was total. It reached the extremities. It went all the way to the tip of the ear and the very end of the toe, as if to say: there is no outermost edge of you that this does not touch. You are set apart to the last inch.
The cost and the belonging

We should be honest that this cost something. To have your ear, hand, and foot marked with blood is to lose a certain kind of ownership of yourself. The consecrated man cannot listen to whatever he likes, do whatever he likes, go wherever he likes, and remain what he was ordained to be. There is a real surrender at the center of it. Worship that costs nothing was never the biblical kind. The ram had to die. The blood had to be applied. Something was given up so that these men could be brought near.

But do not read the surrender as loss, because it was the opposite. To be marked was to belong. These men were not being diminished; they were being brought closer to Yahuah than any Israelite outside their line would ever come. The blood on the ear was not a leash. It was a wedding band. It said: you are Mine now, and being Mine, you may stand where no one else may stand. The cost and the nearness were the same transaction. You cannot have the second without the first.

And here is where the whole ceremony finally opens up and pours out toward us. The Scriptures tell us that in Yeshua we too are made priests, a whole kingdom of them, drawn from every nation, given real access to the Holy One. The blood that marks us now is better than the blood of any ram, and it does the same three things it did on the day Aaron was ordained. It claims the ear, so that we become people who hear the voice of God before we speak for Him. It claims the hand, so that our work has an owner. It claims the foot, so that everywhere we walk we walk as those set apart.

So if you long to sing for Him, to speak for Him, to serve Him with your voice, start where He starts. Give Him the ear first. Let it be marked before the mouth ever is. Become, before you become anything else, a listener consecrated to His voice, and you will find that the singing takes care of itself, because a mouth that belongs to God has first been fed by an ear that heard Him. The whole of you is being claimed, out to the last inch, and to be claimed by Yahuah is not the losing of your life. It is the finding of it.

pieces.excerpt: A dying man in a foreign palace made his family swear an oath about a box of bones, and for four hundred years a nation carried that promise like a refrain no one would let die. This is a song for the ones who are handed a hope they may never live to see fulfilled.

body.text: There is a request at the very end of the book of Genesis that I have never been able to read without going quiet, and I want to sit with you in that quiet for a while, because I think it is one of the bravest things anyone in the whole Bible ever said.

Joseph is dying. He is a hundred and ten years old, and by every measure the world keeps, his life has been an enormous success. He is second only to Pharaoh. He has a house, a name, honor, a family, granaries full of grain, a whole civilization that owes him its survival. He is the most Egyptian a Hebrew has ever been. He could be buried like a prince of Egypt, in a tomb carved for eternity, in the only country his children and grandchildren have ever known as home.

And on his deathbed, he asks for none of it. He gathers his family and he makes them swear an oath. Yahuah will surely visit you, he tells them, and bring you up out of this land to the land He promised. And when He does, carry my bones up from here. Do not leave me in Egypt. When you go, I go with you.

Think about what he is really doing. He is looking at a promise that has not moved an inch in his lifetime. Yahuah had sworn a land to Abraham, and to Isaac, and to Jacob, and here at the close of Genesis not one family owns so much as a field of it, except a burial cave. They are guests in someone else's country, comfortable for now, and every visible fact says they will stay. Joseph will die without seeing the promise. He knows it. And instead of making peace with Egypt, he stakes his own body on a homecoming he will not be alive to attend.
Faith you can carry
I keep thinking about what that oath cost the ones who had to keep it.

Because here is the part the story does not narrate but I cannot stop imagining. Joseph dies. They embalm him, the way Egypt embalms its great ones, and they place him in a coffin. And then that coffin does not go into the ground. It waits. It waits through the good years and then through the years that turn bitter, when a new Pharaoh rises who does not remember Joseph and turns a favored family into a slave nation. It waits through generations of brickmaking and grief. Mothers die who told their daughters about the box and the oath. Old men who could point to it die, and younger men take their place, and somebody in every generation has to keep knowing what it is and why it must not be buried and forgotten.

For four hundred years, a people who owned almost nothing held on to a coffin and a promise. Slaves with no reason left to believe kept alive the memory that they were only passing through. Every year that box said the same stubborn thing: *this is not our home. We are going up. He will visit us. Carry the bones.*

That is faith handed from hand to hand across four centuries, and it is the exact shape of what I do for a living. Because a song is a coffin like that, in the best possible sense. A song is a promise you can carry when you cannot carry anything else. A grandmother hums it over a crib in a language the child will only half-learn, and the child does not understand the words, but the child understands the shape, and forty years later in a hard country the shape comes back and it still says *we are going up, He will visit us, this is not the end of the story.* I have watched faith travel across three languages and two oceans exactly like Joseph's bones traveled across four hundred years, not because anyone could see the promised land, but because somebody refused to stop carrying the box.
The night the box finally moved
And then, one night, everything the box had waited for happens all at once.

The plagues break Egypt open. The blood on the doorframes. The cry that goes up at midnight. Pharaoh finally saying go. And in the middle of that chaos, a whole nation packing in the dark, dough on their shoulders, children half-asleep, the greatest night of deliverance in their history unfolding around them, the Scriptures pause to tell us one small, deliberate thing. Moses took the bones of Joseph with him.

He did not forget. In the rush of the Exodus, with a sea still to cross and an army still to fear, someone made sure the box came too. Four hundred years of waiting, and the oath held. Joseph goes up out of Egypt with his people, carried on their shoulders through the parted water, out into the wilderness, and eventually, after forty more years, after a whole generation more, his bones are laid down in a plot of ground at Shechem that his father Jacob had bought long before. He comes home. Late. So impossibly late. But home.

The letter to the Hebrews looks back on all of it and says something I find almost unbearably tender. Of everything Joseph did, ruling Egypt, saving the world from famine, forgiving the brothers who sold him, the one act it lifts up as his great deed of faith is this: at the end of his life, he spoke about the exodus and gave instructions about his bones. That was the faith. Not the power. Not the success. A dying man betting his own body on a rescue he would only reach as freight.
For the ones who won't see it
I want to say something to whoever is reading this from inside a promise that has not moved.

You may be carrying a hope you will not live to see arrive. A prayer for a child, a people, a country, a healing, a homecoming that keeps not coming in your lifetime. And the temptation, the very old temptation, is to make peace with Egypt. To decide that comfortable-for-now is the same as home. To quietly bury the box, because holding it hurts and it never seems to move.

Joseph is here to tell you not to bury it. Keep the oath. Keep the song. Hand it forward even if all you can hand forward is the shape of it. The whole story turns on the fact that a dying man was willing to be freight in someone else's exodus, and that ordinary people he never met kept faith with him for four hundred years until Yahuah did exactly what He said He would do.

He will visit you. It may be after you. But the God who kept an oath sworn over a deathbed for four centuries is not going to drop yours. So carry the box. Sing the song your grandchildren will finish. This is not your home, and He has not forgotten which way is up. When the night of deliverance finally breaks, someone is going to remember to bring you along, and you, too, will come home. Late, maybe. But home.

pieces.title: The Torch Was Useless Until the Jar Broke

pieces.excerpt: Three hundred men surrounded an army in the dark holding a trumpet in one hand and a clay jar in the other, and the light that won the night was the light they had been hiding inside the jars the whole time. The breaking was never the accident. The breaking was the plan.

body.text: I want to take you to a hillside at night, in the hours before dawn, and put a strange pair of objects in your hands, because I think you may be holding them right now without knowing what they are for.

The army of Midian is spread across the valley below, so many that the old account says they were like locusts, their camels beyond counting. And on the ridges above them stand three hundred men. Not three hundred thousand. Three hundred. Gideon started with thirty-two thousand, and Yahuah kept saying *too many*, too many for the victory to look like anything but Him, until He had whittled a nation's army down to a number that could not possibly work. Three hundred men against a valley full of locusts.

And here is what Gideon puts in their hands. Not swords, not first. Each man gets a trumpet, a ram's horn, a shofar, and a clay jar, an empty pitcher, and a torch to hide down inside the jar. That is it. That is the arsenal. A horn, a pot, and a light shut up in the dark where no one can see it. If you were one of those three hundred, standing on that ridge with a jar in your arm while an army breathed in the dark below you, you would be forgiven for thinking you had been handed the most useless weapons in the history of war.
The light you were told to hide
Sit with that jar for a second, because I think most of us are living inside this exact instruction and hating it.

The torch is already lit. That is the part that gets me. The fire is real, it is burning, it is right there in your hand, and you are told to put it down inside a clay pot where it cannot be seen. Carry the light hidden. Cross the dark ridge with the flame muffled and covered, giving off nothing, warning no one, changing nothing. To anyone watching, you are just a man walking in the dark with a pot. The light does the enemy no damage at all as long as it stays in the jar.

I have carried that jar. You have carried that jar. There are seasons when Yahuah has clearly put a fire in you, a calling, a word, a song, a thing you know you were made to give, and the instruction, for now, is *hide it*. Walk the ridge. Get into position. Do not let it show yet. And it is a strange, aching obedience, to hold a burning thing under a lid and give off nothing, and to trust that the covering is not a burial. It feels like the light is wasted. It feels like maybe the fire will just go out down there in the dark of the jar, unseen, unspent.
But watch what the covering is actually for.
The breaking was the plan
Gideon gives the signal. And on that signal, three hundred men do the same three things in the same instant. They blow the trumpets. They smash the jars. And they lift the torches high and shout.

Feel the order of it. The light does not come out gently. Nobody tips the jar and slides the torch out with care. They break the pitchers. They shatter them, all at once, three hundred clay jars exploding in the dark, and in the same heartbeat the hidden fire that was doing nothing a second ago is suddenly blazing on every hill at once, and the horns are screaming, and a whole valley of sleeping locusts jolts awake to find themselves ringed by fire and sound with no idea how small the circle really is. The Midianites turn on each other in the panic. The army destroys itself. Three hundred men, a pot each, and the night is won.

Here is the thing I need you to see, the thing I have staked real hope on. The breaking of the jar was never the accident. It was not the plan going wrong. It was the plan. The whole point of the pitcher was to hold the light hidden *until the moment it was meant to be broken open*, and the breaking is what let the light out all at once, together, blinding. The jar had to be covered so the fire could arrive as a shock instead of a warning. And the jar had to shatter for the fire to do a single thing.
I cannot tell you how much of my life this has explained.

Because there are two lies that come at you when you are carrying a covered flame. The first lie says the light does not matter, since no one can see it, put it out, stop carrying it, it is going nowhere. The second lie comes later, when the jar finally cracks, and it says *this is the end of you.* The breaking feels like ruin. The loss, the grief, the thing that shattered the vessel you had built your life inside. It feels like the light is spilling out to be lost. And it is exactly then, in the sound of your own jar breaking, that the fire you were told to hide finally gets to do what it was lit for.
Trumpets and torches, not swords

I love that these three hundred never actually swung a weapon at the height of it. Their hands were full. One hand held a horn, a sound. One hand held a torch, a light. There was no hand left for a sword. The victory came through worship and testimony, through the noise you make and the fire you carry, not through the strength you bring. That is the ministry, all of it. A sound lifted in the dark and a light that will not stay covered. I make music for a living, and this is the whole picture of it: my hands are full of a trumpet and a torch, and there is deliberately no room left for a sword, because the battle was never mine to win with force. It was won by the God who likes the number to be small enough that no one can mistake whose fire it is.
So let me say it plainly to whoever is holding a covered flame tonight.

If He has told you to hide it for now, the hiding is not the waste. You are getting into position on the ridge. The fire has not gone out inside the jar; it is being kept for a moment you cannot see yet, a moment when it will do far more blazing out all at once than it ever could have leaking out slow. And if your jar is breaking right now, if the vessel you carried the light in is cracking and you feel the whole thing coming apart, hear me: that may not be your ruin. That may be the signal. The God of the three hundred does not shatter His people to lose them. He breaks the jar so the light can finally get out. Lift the torch. Blow the horn. The valley is smaller than it looks, and the dark cannot survive what you have been carrying all this time.

pieces.excerpt: After three rainless years, a prophet told a king he could hear a downpour coming, and then bowed his face to the ground and sent a servant to look at an empty sky seven times. This is a song for everyone who has been asked to keep believing the rain while the horizon stays stubbornly blue.

body.text: There is a scene tucked just after one of the most famous days in the whole Bible, and almost nobody lingers on it, because it comes right after fire fell from heaven and it is hard to compete with fire. But I want to linger on it with you, because the quiet minutes after the fire have taught me more about faith than the fire ever did.

The land has been in drought for three and a half years. No rain, no dew, the ground cracked, the brooks gone to dust, a whole nation slowly starving under a hard bright sky. And on Mount Carmel, Yahuah has just answered the prophet Elijah with fire in front of everyone, settling the question of who is God. It is a mountaintop day in every sense. But the drought is not over. The fire proved who reigns; it did not put water in the wells. The people still need rain.
And Elijah turns to the king and says the strangest thing. He tells Ahab to go up, eat and drink, *because I can hear the sound of a heavy rain coming.*

There is not a cloud in the sky. There has not been a cloud worth the name in three and a half years. The horizon is the same merciless blue it has been all along. And the prophet says he can *hear* it. Not see it. Hear it. Somewhere below the register of the visible, in a place that has nothing to do with what the eye can confirm, Elijah has caught the sound of an ocean of water that is not there yet.
Faith with its face in the dirt
Here is what he does next, and this is the part I have built a lot of my hope on.

He does not stand there triumphant, arms wide, declaring the rain over a dry sky and waiting to be proven right. He climbs to the top of Carmel, bends all the way down to the ground, and puts his face between his knees. The man who just called down fire folds himself into the dirt like a woman in labor and prays. The one who heard the rain does not act like he has already got it. He gets low. He travails. He asks.

And then he sends his servant to go look toward the sea. The boy goes, scans the whole flat horizon, comes back: nothing. And Elijah, still folded on the ground, says the word I want to give you tonight. *Go again.*

Seven times. The servant walks out to the edge, searches the empty sky, walks back with nothing, seven times over. And I want you to feel how that would wear on you, because I have lived inside those seven trips. You heard the sound. You are sure you heard it. You have committed yourself out loud. You told the king it was coming, and now you are on your face in the dust and the report keeps coming back *nothing, still nothing, the sky is exactly as blue as it was before.* Six times the evidence says you were wrong to hope. Six times the horizon calls you a fool. And the prophet does not get up, and does not take it back, and does not stop sending. Go again.
A cloud the size of a hand
The seventh time, the servant comes back and says there is a little cloud rising out of the sea, small as a man's hand.

That is all. Not a storm front, not a black sky, not thunder, one small smudge of cloud the size of a fist held up at arm's length, the kind of thing you would never notice if you had not been told to look for it. And Elijah does not wait for it to grow. He knows. He sends word to the king: *harness the chariot and get down the mountain before the rain stops you.* And before long the sky goes black with clouds and wind, and a great rain comes, and a man who had been folded in the dust runs ahead of the king's chariot in the downpour with the hand of Yahuah on him.

I love that God did not answer with the whole sky at once. He answered with a hand-sized cloud. He gave Elijah just enough to run on, the smallest possible confirmation, a thing you had to be looking for to even see, and Elijah treated that fist of vapor like the flood it was about to become. He did not despise how small it was. He recognized the down payment on the roar he had already heard.
For the ones on the seventh trip
Let me tell you why this is a musician's story, and why I carry it.

Long before a song is finished, before there is a single line anyone can sing, you can *hear* it. It arrives as a sound with no shape yet, a rain you catch below the register of the visible, and you commit yourself to it out loud with nothing on the page to show for it. And then comes the labor of it, the getting low, the sending, the going again, and trip after trip the report comes back *nothing, still nothing, this is not becoming anything.* That is the actual work of faith: to keep sending, to keep looking, to stay folded in the dust believing the sound you heard was real when the sky refuses to confirm it. Prophets do not just announce the rain. They travail for it. They hear it first, and then they pray it down, and then they wait through six empty trips for one hand-sized cloud.
So here is my word to whoever has been sent to look at the horizon one more time.

You may have heard the rain. Somewhere in a place deeper than sight, over a marriage or a child or a calling or a country, you caught the sound of an ocean that is not visible yet, and you said so, and now you are on trip number four, or five, or six, and every report comes back dry. Do not get up. Do not take it back. The blue sky is not the verdict; the sound you heard is the verdict. Send again. And when the answer finally comes, do not be surprised that it is small, a cloud the size of a hand, a thing so easy to miss you would have overlooked it if you had not been looking. That fist of cloud is not the disappointment. It is the down payment on the downpour. Harness the chariot. The One who lets you hear the rain before He shows you the cloud is not toying with you. He is teaching you to run in faith before the first drop lands, and the rain is already on its way up out of the sea.
