body.text: Everyone remembers the lions. I want to talk about the window, because the window is where the whole thing was actually decided, long before anyone smelled the den.

Daniel is an old man by now. He has served in the courts of an empire since he was a boy carried off into exile, and he has outlasted kings. Under Darius he has risen so high, and served so cleanly, that the men below him cannot find a single crack of corruption to pry at. So they go after the one thing they know they can use against him: his God. They flatter the king into signing an unchangeable decree. For thirty days, no one in the realm may pray to any god or any man except the king himself. The penalty is the lions' den. It is a trap built precisely around Daniel's devotion, and everyone in the palace knows it.

Now here is the sentence that undoes me every time. When Daniel learned that the document had been signed, he went to his house, and the account pauses to tell us his windows were open toward Jerusalem, and he got down on his knees three times a day and prayed and gave thanks, *as he had done previously.*

As he had done previously. That is the hinge of the entire story. Daniel does not gather a resistance. He does not march on the palace or make a speech about religious freedom. He does not, on the other hand, quietly move his prayers to the cellar for a month until the decree blows over. Nobody would have blamed him, he could have kept praying in secret and kept his life. He does neither. He simply goes home and does the exact thing he has always done, at the exact times he has always done it, with the windows open exactly as wide as they always were. The law changed. Daniel did not. His defiance was not a new act of protest. His defiance was his ordinary faithfulness, continued out loud, on schedule, in plain view, as if the decree simply did not have the authority to reach the thing that mattered most.
Windows toward a city that wasn't there
But look at what those open windows were pointed at, because this is the part that turns the story from stubbornness into something closer to a song.

The windows opened toward Jerusalem. And Jerusalem, in Daniel's lifetime, was a ruin. Burned. Broken down. The temple leveled, the walls thrown over, the city where God had put His name reduced to rubble by the very empire Daniel now served in. When Daniel knelt and faced Jerusalem three times a day, he was not facing a glorious skyline. He was facing a memory. He was aiming his whole body, morning and midday and evening, at a wrecked city hundreds of miles away that gave him nothing back to look at but the ache of it.

That is faith believing in what it cannot see. Daniel prayed toward a promise, not a picture. Solomon had prayed at the temple's dedication that when the people were carried far away, they would turn and pray toward this place, and God would hear from heaven. So Daniel turned. Toward a house that was no longer standing, on the strength of a word that said it would matter anyway. He worshiped toward the not-yet. His windows framed a broken city and he treated it like the throne room of God, because he believed the God of that city had not moved out just because the walls came down.

I know something about praying toward a home you can only see with your eyes closed. Anyone who has carried a faith across borders knows it, the way you orient your heart toward a place, a people, a promise that the visible facts have written off. Daniel's open window is the posture of every believer who keeps aiming their worship at what God said instead of what the news reports. You face the ruin and you give thanks anyway, because you are not praying to the rubble. You are praying to the One who is going to rebuild it.
The worship they could not make him whisper

They caught him, of course. That was always the plan. They came to his house and there he was, on his knees, windows open, doing the thing that was now a crime. And they dragged the whole matter before the king, who realized far too late that he had been played, and who spent a sleepless night unable to unsign the law that condemned the best man in his kingdom.

And Daniel went into the den. And Yahuah shut the mouths of the lions, and in the morning the old man walked out without a scratch, and the king who had signed the death decree ended up signing a new one, that in all his dominion, people should tremble before the God of Daniel, the living God whose kingdom does not end. The worship they tried to outlaw ended up preached across an empire by the mouth of the very king who had banned it. That is what happens when you refuse to whisper. The song you would not take underground gets amplified by the same authorities who tried to silence it.
For the ones tempted to close the window
Let me bring this close, because most of us will never face a den, but every one of us faces the window.

There is a constant, low pressure on a believer to make their worship quieter, more private, more manageable, to move it to the cellar where it will not cost anything. The pressure rarely comes as a dramatic decree. It comes as a thousand small suggestions that faith is something you do discreetly, on your own time, with the windows shut, where it will not embarrass anyone. And the temptation is not usually to quit. It is to keep believing while learning to hide it. To keep the flame and close the shutters.

Daniel's whole witness is one open window against that pressure. Not louder than usual, just as loud as always, unchanged, on schedule, aimed at the promise. He did not need a new act of courage the day the law was signed. He needed the ordinary courage of continuing, out loud, the thing he had always done. That is the defiance available to you and me: not a protest, but a routine of praise so settled that no decree can find the seam in it.

So keep the window open. Kneel at the times you always kneel. Face the ruined city, the broken promise, the wrecked situation, the home you can only see with your eyes closed, and give thanks toward it anyway, because you are not worshiping the rubble. You are worshiping the God who is coming to rebuild it, and He has never once been stopped by a shut mouth or an open den. Do not whisper. The One you are facing is worth being caught in the act of loving.

pieces.title: The Time of Singing Has Come
pieces.imagePrompt: A radiant open-air worship gathering on a green spring hillside at golden sunrise, a diverse multiethnic crowd of young and old singing with faces lifted and hands raised, tears of joy and wide open smiles as wildflowers and warm light flood the slopes, the overwhelming feeling of a long winter finally breaking into song; brilliant gold, green and rose tones, cinematic film still, authentic and joyful, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: There is a love song in the middle of the Bible that announces a season change with a single astonishing line, the winter is past, and the time of singing has come. This is a word for anyone who has been enduring a long cold quiet and has forgotten that winters, even in Scripture, are always described as things that end.

body.text: There is a line in the middle of the Bible that I reach for the way you reach for a coat by the door, without thinking, because I know exactly where it hangs and I know it will keep me warm. It comes from the great love song at the heart of the Scriptures, the Song of Songs, and it is a lover calling to the beloved to come away, and the reason he gives her is the season.

Arise, he says. Come with me. For look, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone. The flowers have appeared on the earth. The time of singing has come, and the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land.

I need you to hear how much is packed into that. It is, on its surface, a love poem, a young man calling a young woman out into a spring morning. But the ancient teachers of my people read it as something larger, a picture of the love between Yahuah and the ones He has set His heart on, and the church has sung it that way for centuries too. I will be honest with you that this is reading, not chapter and verse of plain command. But I will also tell you that some truths are too big to fit inside a single literal frame, and the love that made the world is one of them, and this song has carried more homesick believers through more long nights than almost anything else in the Book. So let me hand it to you the way it was handed to me: as the voice of Love itself, calling out over a season that has held on far too long.
The winter is described as a thing that ends

Here is the first thing I want you to notice, and it is so simple you might walk past it. The winter is *past.* Not managed. Not survived. Past. It is spoken of as a thing that is over, a chapter with a back cover, a cold that had a limit all along.

Because when you are inside a winter, that is exactly the thing you cannot believe. A long cold season does not feel like a chapter. It feels like the climate. It feels permanent, like the way things simply are now and will always be, the quiet where the music used to be, the grief that has gone on so long you have stopped expecting it to lift, the prayer you have prayed so many times you say it now out of habit rather than hope. Winter's cruelest trick is that it erases your memory of spring. It convinces you that you have always been cold and always will be.

And into that, the song does not argue. It does not explain the winter or justify it or tell you it was good for you. It just announces, with the calm certainty of someone reading a calendar, that it is over. The rain is gone. That word *rain* here is not the good rain a farmer waits for. It is the gray, endless, driving wet of the dead season, the kind that keeps you indoors and shrinks your world to the size of a shuttered room. And Love says: gone. The sky has changed. Look up.
The flowers came before you felt warm
The second thing I love is the order of what he points at.

The flowers have appeared. The turtledove is back and singing. Notice, these are not things the beloved made happen. She did not schedule the spring or earn it or produce a single blossom. While she was still inside, still braced against the cold, the earth was already turning without her. The flowers came up on their own. The birds came back on their own. The season changed while she was still dressed for winter, and the lover's whole message is essentially: *the world outside your window has already moved on from the cold, come out and catch up to it.*

I have watched this be true in the deepest way in the lives of people I love. Spring in the soul almost never announces itself by how you feel first. It announces itself by small green things appearing that you did not manufacture, an unexpected mercy, a door you assumed was locked swinging open, a morning where the weight is half an ounce lighter than yesterday and you cannot say why. The flowers show up before the warmth reaches you. And the invitation is to trust the flowers over your own numb hands. To believe the evidence of the season instead of the memory of the cold.
The time of singing has come
But the line I actually live on is the middle one. *The time of singing has come.*

I make music for a living, so let me tell you what a winter does to a singer. It does not usually take your voice in a dramatic way. It takes it quietly. The songs you used to sing without thinking start to feel like lies you are not entitled to. You go through the motions in a room full of worshipers and your own mouth feels far away. You do not decide to stop singing; the singing just recedes, like the birds did, and one day you notice the silence has been going on a long time and you cannot remember when it started. If you have hung your harp in the willow trees of a hard season, you know the exact quiet I mean.

And what this line promises is that the silence, too, has a limit. The time of singing has a *come* attached to it. It arrives. It is on the calendar. There is a morning appointed when the voice comes back the way the turtledove comes back, not because you forced it, but because the season it belongs to has finally rolled around again. Song is seasonal in the Scriptures. It is tied to spring, to thaw, to the rain being over. And the God who runs the seasons has never once let a winter become the whole story of a life He loves.
Come away
So here is the invitation, and I want to give it to you as gently and as certainly as the song gives it.

If you are reading this from inside a long cold quiet, hear the voice that is calling over the top of it. It is not scolding you for how tired you are. It is not asking you to gin up a warmth you do not have. It is simply telling you the truth about the season: the winter is past. The rain that shut you in is spending itself out. There are green things coming up that you did not plant, and if you look for them instead of at the old grey sky, you will see that the world Love made has already begun to turn back toward the sun.

And your voice is coming back with it. The time of singing has come, not the time of pretending, not the time of performing, but the real thawing return of a song you thought you had lost for good. So come away. Get up from the shuttered room. Step out where the flowers already are. The One who is calling you did not bring you through the winter to leave you speechless on the other side of it. He brought you through so that you would be standing in the open, in the warm light, when the first note comes back to your mouth, and this time you will know, all the way down, that spring was never in doubt.

pieces.title: The Day the Scroll Stopped Mid-Sentence
pieces.imagePrompt: A bright gathering where a diverse seated congregation leans forward with awe and dawning joy breaking across their faces in a shaft of warm golden light, eyes shining and smiles rising as if long-awaited good news has just landed in the room; luminous cinematic film-still quality, warm amber gold and soft honey tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: For centuries the Jubilee was a number on a calendar, a horn blown once in a lifetime, if you were fortunate enough to live in the right year. Then a carpenter stood up in His hometown synagogue, read four lines from a scroll, stopped before the fifth, and said the thing everyone was waiting for had arrived in the room.

body.text: For most of Israel's history, the Jubilee was a rumor you inherited.

You were taught the law as a child, the fiftieth year, the horn across the land, the debts erased and the captives sent home and the fields returned to the families who first cleared them. You learned it the way you learn about a comet: real, promised, magnificent, and almost certainly not going to happen while you are young enough to run to meet it. Whole generations lived and died between one Jubilee and the next. A boy could grow into an old man having heard the trumpet described a thousand times and never once heard it split the air over a year that counted. It was the most beautiful thing in the whole law, and it was mostly a thing your grandfather talked about.
So hold that in your mind, a nation carrying a promise it had almost stopped expecting to feel, and walk with me into a small synagogue in a town nobody wrote poems about.
He came home to read

Yeshua had grown up in Nazareth. These were the people who had watched Him learn to walk. They knew His mother, knew the smell of the wood shavings in His father's shop, knew Him as the boy who had run the same dusty streets they had. And on a Sabbath, He came back, and He went to the gathering the way He always had, and He stood up to read.

They handed Him the scroll of the prophet Isaiah. He unrolled it, found His place, and read a handful of lines, the ones about the Spirit of Yahuah resting on an anointed one, sent to bring good news to the poor, to proclaim release to the captives and sight to the blind, to set the oppressed free, and to announce the year of Yahuah's favor.

The year of Yahuah's favor. Everyone in that room knew what that phrase meant. It was Jubilee language. It was the trumpet, put into words. Isaiah had reached back into the oldest law of liberty and lifted out its heart, the great release, the year the debts die and the prisoners walk out, and turned it into a promise about someone who would come and make it happen.
And here is the detail I cannot leave alone.
Where He stopped reading

If you keep reading in Isaiah past the point where Yeshua stopped, the very next phrase turns dark. It speaks of a day of vengeance, a day of reckoning. It is right there in the sentence, the favor and the vengeance, side by side, one long breath in the prophet's mouth.
Yeshua read the part about favor. And then He rolled the scroll back up.

He stopped mid-sentence. He read the liberty and left the vengeance on the page. He handed the scroll back to the attendant, and He sat down, which is what a teacher did when He was about to say something that mattered, and every eye in that little room was fastened on Him. And He told them, plainly, that the thing they had just heard read out loud was not about some far-off day their descendants might live to see. It was fulfilled. Today. In their hearing. In that room. In Him.

Do you understand what He was doing? For centuries the Jubilee had been a date. A slot on the calendar that came around once in a lifetime and was gone. Yeshua stood up in His hometown and announced that the Jubilee was no longer a date. It was a Person, and the Person was standing in front of them, and the year of favor had walked in on its own two feet and would not be leaving.
The trumpet had a face now. The release had a name.
Favor without the reckoning, for now
I keep coming back to the sentence He would not finish. Because it tells you something about the age we are living in right now, the one that opened in that synagogue and has not yet closed.

There is a day of reckoning in the book. It is real; I will not pretend it away. But Yeshua came the first time and read only the favor. He inaugurated an open season of mercy, a long, generous year of release that has been running for two thousand years and is running over you as you read this. The scroll is still rolled to the place where He stopped. We are living inside the sentence He left open. The vengeance clause is still on the page, still true, still coming, but He is holding the scroll there, on purpose, so that the door of the Jubilee stays open long enough for you to walk through it.
That is the mercy in the pause. He stopped reading so that you would have time to come home.
What this does to a song

When you understand that the Jubilee stopped being a calendar and became a Man, worship changes shape. You are no longer singing about a good thing that happened long ago to other people, or a good thing that might happen someday to somebody. You are singing to the One in whom the release actually landed. The captive is not waiting for the fiftieth year to roll around. The fiftieth year is a Person, and He has already stood up and read the good part out loud over your particular life.

This is why the singing of a set-free person sounds the way it does. It is not nostalgia and it is not wishful thinking. It is the sound of someone who was in the room when the scroll was read, who heard their own name in the words *the captives* and *the oppressed* and *the poor*, and who has stopped waiting for liberty to be scheduled because liberty came and sat down at their table.

The whole earth was built to sing this, every language, every tribe, every debtor and prisoner and person too far gone to hope. The song is not complicated. It is only the sound a people make when the year of favor gets a face and the face turns toward them and says, *today.*

He is still holding the scroll open. The favor is still being read. If you have spent your life thinking freedom was a rumor you inherited and would never quite catch, hear me: it is not on the calendar. It is in the room. And it is looking straight at you.

pieces.title: The Servant Who Would Not Go Free
pieces.imagePrompt: A tender happy family gathered in the warm glowing doorway of their home at golden hour, faces lit with peace and chosen belonging as they lean into one another, soft radiant light pouring around them, an atmosphere of deep contented love; luminous cinematic film-still quality, warm honey amber and soft gold tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: The law of release said that in the seventh year every bound servant walked out free, no strings, no fee. But there was a clause for the one who stood in the open doorway, looked at his freedom, and chose instead to stay for love. His master marked him at the door, and that mark is the most beautiful thing in the whole law of liberty.

body.text: Everyone loves the part of the law where the door swings open.

It is the part I preach the most, because it is the heart of my whole message. In the ancient law of Yahuah, no one was allowed to hold another person forever. A Hebrew who had fallen into servitude, sold into it by debt or hardship, served for six years, and then, in the seventh, the door came open on its own. He walked out free. And he did not walk out empty-handed. The law commanded the master to load him up on the way out, grain and flock and wine, a generous send-off, so that a man who entered with nothing would leave with something to start again. Freedom, and a full pack for the road. That is the God I serve. He is against the idea of anyone owning anyone.
So the whole law bends toward that open door. Release is the default. Freedom is the rule. The seventh year comes and the bonds fall off whether you feel ready or not.
But there is a clause. And the clause is where I want to sit today, because most people rush past it, and it may be the tenderest sentence in the entire law of liberty.
The one who loved the house
The law made room for a man to stand in that open doorway on the seventh year, look out at the free road, look back into the household, and decide he did not want to go.

Not because he was trapped. The door was open. Not because he was afraid. He had somewhere to go. Not because he owed anything. The debt was cancelled; that was the whole point of the year. He could walk out this instant a free man with a full pack and no one could stop him.

But something had happened inside those six years that the law had not planned for and yet made room for anyway. He had come to love the master. He had come to love the house, the people in it, the work of it, the belonging of it. And so the law let him say the words: *I love my master; I do not want to go free.*

And when he said it, there was a ceremony. The master brought him to the door, to the doorpost of the house itself, and took an awl and pierced his ear against the wood, and from that day he belonged to that household not for six years but for good. A permanent servant. By choice. Marked at the very threshold he was free to walk out of.
The mark that only love can make

Sit with the strangeness of that. The mark of belonging was placed exactly where the freedom was. The doorpost was the border between owned and free, and it was on that border, in that doorway, that the servant let himself be marked as one who would stay.

You could never do this ceremony to a slave. That is the whole point. A slave has no seventh year to refuse. This mark could only be worn by a free man, someone who had held his liberty in his hand, felt its full weight, understood exactly what he was giving up, and chose the house anyway. The pierced ear was not the sign of a captive. It was the sign of a free person who had fallen in love with the one who set him free.

There is no bondage in this story. There is only the deepest liberty a person can reach: the liberty to hand your freedom back to the one who gave it, not because you have to, but because you cannot imagine a better place to spend it.
Why the freed keep coming back
I have watched this happen to people my whole ministry, though they rarely have words for it.

Someone comes to Yeshua desperate, cornered, in debt to their own sin past any hope of paying, and He does what He does. He cancels it. He opens the door. He does not merely improve their situation; He walks them clean out into the open air of forgiveness and hands them a full pack for the road. Free. No fee, no fine print, no six-more-years. Go.

And then, over time, something happens that the transaction alone cannot explain. They come back. Not out of guilt. He burned the guilt. Not out of fear, perfect love had already thrown that out. They come back because somewhere in the being-forgiven they fell in love with the One who did it, and now the last thing they want is a life spent anywhere but near Him. They stand in the open doorway of their freedom, look at the wide road of a life that owes Him nothing, and turn back into the house.

This is the secret the world cannot understand about the ones who follow Yeshua the closest. The men who wrote the letters at the front of the church. They had a word they used for themselves, over and over, and it was not *free man* and it was not *apostle* first. It was *bondservant.* Servant of Yeshua the Anointed. They wore it like a title of honor, because they knew exactly what it meant: a free person who had been to the doorway, held their liberty, and chosen the house.
The song of the pierced ear
Here is what I want you to hear.
The Jubilee sets you free. That will always be the first word, and I will never let it be quieted. Nobody owns you. The door is open. The debt is dead. Walk out.

But there is a second word, and it only becomes available once the first is true. It is the freedom to stay. The freedom to be marked at the threshold. The freedom to say *I love my master* and mean every syllable of it.

And the ear, of all things, is what gets marked, the ear, the very organ that hears. As if to say: this one no longer belongs to himself; this one belongs to the voice of the house now, and everything that voice says, he will hear as one who has chosen to obey it out of love and not fear.

That is a worshiper. Not a captive singing because the whip says sing. A free person singing in a house they were free to leave, because they went to the door, felt the whole weight of their liberty, and turned around.

If the door of your freedom stands open today, and in Yeshua it does. You are not less free for staying near Him. You are free at last. The pierced ear was never a chain. It was a wedding ring on the side of a man's head, worn by someone who found, in the very hour of his release, that he had somewhere he actually wanted to be.

pieces.title: Charge It to My Account
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful reunion embrace at a sunlit doorway where an older man and a returning young traveler laugh and weep with relief in each other's arms, faces radiant with reconciliation and overwhelming gladness, warm golden light flooding the threshold; luminous cinematic film-still quality, warm amber and glowing gold tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: A runaway slave who had likely robbed his master was walking home to face him, and in his hands was a letter that changed everything. It did not beg for leniency. It moved the debt. An old prisoner had written, in his own shaking hand, four words that are the whole gospel in miniature.

body.text: Picture a man on a road, walking toward the one thing he ran halfway across the world to avoid.

His name was Onesimus, and he had been a slave in a wealthy household, and at some point he had done what a great many enslaved people longed to do and almost none dared: he ran. The old tradition adds that he did not leave empty-handed, that he took something on his way out, money or goods, so that he was not only a runaway but a thief. And a runaway slave in that world was a marked man. If he was caught, the law of the empire gave his master the right to do nearly anything to him. Branding. The mines. Death. There was no mercy built into the system for a man in his position. He had put himself outside every protection there was.
And now he was walking back into the mouth of it. Back toward the very household he had robbed and fled. Voluntarily. Why would a man do that?
Because of who he had met while he was hiding.
The prison that became a birthplace

Somewhere in his running, Onesimus had crossed paths with Paul, an old man himself now a prisoner, chained for the sake of the gospel, and yet somehow the freest man in any building he was held in. And in that unlikely place, the runaway thief became a new person. Paul spoke of him afterward the way a father speaks of a son: my child, whom I fathered in my chains. The slave who had run from a house had found, in a prison, a home he had never had.

But conversion did not erase the past. Onesimus still had a master he had wronged. There was still a debt hanging over him, real money, real property, real betrayal, and a real man back home who had every legal right to be furious. New life in Yeshua did not make the account disappear. It made Onesimus willing, at last, to go back and face it.
So Paul did something for him. He picked up a pen.
The shortest letter in the book

Of all the letters Paul wrote, the one to Philemon, the master, is the smallest, barely a page, and it is one of the most stunning things in all of Scripture, because you can watch the gospel happen inside a private, awkward, real situation between three men.

Paul does not order Philemon around. He could have; he had the authority. Instead he pleads, as an old man and a prisoner, on behalf of the returning runaway. And he asks Philemon to receive Onesimus back, not as the slave he was, not even as a forgiven slave, but as something almost unthinkable in that world. Receive him, Paul writes, no longer as a slave, but as a beloved brother. Welcome him the way you would welcome me.

And then Paul comes to the debt, and he does not dodge it. He knows there is a wrong to be settled, the theft, the loss, whatever the account had grown to. So he addresses it head-on, and here is the line, the four words that hold the whole thing together:
*Charge it to my account.*

If he has wronged you, Paul writes, or owes you anything, put it on my bill. I will repay it. And he even signs that part in his own hand, the way a man signs a promissory note, so there can be no doubt he means it as a legal thing and not a nice sentiment. The debt does not vanish. It moves. It comes off the ledger of the guilty man and lands on the ledger of the one who loved him enough to pay.
The gospel in a countinghouse
I do not know how to say plainly enough what is happening in those four words, so let me just say it plainly.
That is the whole gospel. That is the entire message of the Jubilee, compressed into a private note about a stolen purse.

You are Onesimus. You ran. You took what was not yours. You put yourself outside every protection, and there is a real debt with your name on it and a real account it is written in, and no amount of coming back and standing in the doorway with your head down is going to make the number smaller. The debt is real. It has to go somewhere. It cannot simply be waved away as if betrayal costs nothing, because it costs a great deal, and God is not in the business of pretending.

And into that real, unpayable account steps Someone who says the four words. *Charge it to My account. I will repay.* Yeshua did not talk your debt down. He did not negotiate a lesser sentence. He moved the whole sum off your ledger and onto His own, and He signed it, not in ink, but in His own blood, in His own hand, so there could be no doubt it was legally, actually paid. And the receipt of that payment is that you get to walk back into the Father's house not as a slave, not even as a forgiven servant kept at arm's length, but as a beloved brother, welcomed exactly as the Son Himself is welcomed.

Onesimus carried that letter home in his own hands, his pardon, written by another, addressed to the one he had wronged, with the debt already transferred to a name that could cover it. He had to walk the road. He had to knock on the door. But the settling of the account was finished before he ever arrived.
What the freed man sings

The name Onesimus, as it happens, meant *useful*, and there is a small joke Paul makes in the letter, that the once-useless runaway had become useful at last. But the deepest thing about him is not his usefulness. It is his freedom. A man who was owned, who ran, who stole, who deserved the worst the law could do, walked home carrying a letter that had already paid for him, and walked in as a brother.

This is why the singing of the redeemed has a sound the untouched cannot fake. It is the sound of a person who has read their own name at the top of an impossible bill, and then watched Someone take the pen and write four words across the bottom of it, and sign. There is no leftover fear in that kind of praise. The account is settled. The letter is signed. The door is open, and the arms behind it are not crossed. They are wide.

If you have been walking the long road home dreading the reckoning at the end of it, hear me. Look again at what is in your hand. The debt is not waiting for you at the door. It was moved a long time ago, onto a Name large enough to hold it, by Someone who wanted you home badly enough to pay. Charge it to His account. He already did.

pieces.title: The Tree He Climbed to Be Found
pieces.imagePrompt: A warm sunlit home overflowing with celebration where a beaming man laughs among welcoming friends around a table heaped with food, faces radiant with astonished delight and belonging, golden light streaming through the open doorway, an atmosphere of pure homecoming joy; luminous cinematic film-still quality, warm gold green and honey amber tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: A rich, hated little man climbed a tree just to catch a glimpse of a passing teacher over the heads of a crowd that despised him. He only wanted to see. He did not expect to be seen, much less called down by name, and least of all to end the day giving four times back everything he had ever stolen, laughing, in a house full of joy.

body.text: He was too short to see over the crowd, and too hated for anyone to let him through.

That is the picture I want you to start with, because both halves of it matter. Zacchaeus was a chief tax collector in Jericho, which meant two things about him: he was rich, and he was despised. He had grown wealthy by collecting the occupying empire's taxes off his own people and skimming whatever extra he could squeeze out of them, and everyone in town knew it. He was a traitor with a full purse. When he walked down the street, the crowd did not part for him out of respect. If anything they closed ranks. And so on the day the traveling teacher everyone was talking about came through Jericho, little Zacchaeus found himself at the back of a wall of shoulders that would not move for him, unable to see a thing.
So he did something undignified. This wealthy, powerful, grown man ran ahead of the crowd and climbed a tree.
Just to see

I love that he climbed. There is something in that detail I cannot get past. He had money and status and every reason to protect his dignity, and he threw all of it away for one thing: he wanted to see. He did not have a theology. He did not have a plan. He did not, as far as we can tell, even want to be noticed, a man who is hated by a whole town does not go looking to be noticed. He just wanted to catch a glimpse of this Yeshua over the heads of people who would never have let him near the front. So he tucked himself up into the branches of a sycamore where he could look down on the road unseen, a small hidden man hoping only to watch something good pass by.
He got so much more than a glimpse.
Because when Yeshua reached that spot, He stopped. And He looked up. Into the tree. At the one person in Jericho nobody else was looking at except to sneer. And He called him by name.
Zacchaeus. Come down. I need to stay at your house today.
The scandal of the chosen house

Understand what that did to the crowd. Of every house in Jericho, of every righteous and respectable and generous person who would have been honored to host Him, Yeshua chose the traitor's. The whole crowd started to grumble, the same crowd that had just been pressing in to see Him now muttering that He had gone to be the guest of a sinner. Of *that* sinner. The worst one. The one who had gotten rich off their backs.

And here is the thing they missed, standing there with their arms crossed. They thought Zacchaeus climbed the tree to find Yeshua. But it was the other way around. Yeshua walked into Jericho already looking up into the branches for a small lost man. Zacchaeus thought he was doing the seeing. He was the one being sought. He climbed a tree to catch a glimpse and discovered he had been the object of the whole search the entire time.
Everything, times four
What happened next is the part that makes it a Jubilee story, and it happened fast, and it happened out loud.

Zacchaeus stood up, in his own house now, with Yeshua under his roof, and he made an announcement. Half of everything he owned, he was giving to the poor, right now. And anyone he had cheated, anyone he had defrauded, and there were many. He would pay back four times over. Not the amount. Four times the amount.

Nobody made him do this. There was no sermon about money, no demand, no condition attached to the visit. Yeshua had simply come into his house, and something in the man broke open, and out of it poured restitution on a scale the law had never even required of an ordinary thief. The old law of restoration said that a man who stole and was caught made it right, sometimes double, sometimes more for certain thefts. Zacchaeus reached past the requirement and grabbed the most extravagant number in the book and applied it to himself, gladly, laughing probably, a rich man cheerfully emptying his own vaults because the joy that had walked in the door was worth more than everything in them.

That is what the presence of the Redeemer does to stolen things. It does not merely forgive them. It sends them home. The money Zacchaeus had pulled out of his neighbors' lives came flowing back out of his house four times as fast as it had come in, debts he had caused, cancelled and overpaid, families restored, the whole crooked account of a lifetime unwound in an afternoon.
Today

And Yeshua said the word over that house that I would build my whole life around hearing said over mine. He said: *Today* salvation has come to this house. Not someday. Not after a probation period, after Zacchaeus proved himself, after the town forgave him. Today. He is a son of Abraham too, one of the family, all along, however far he had wandered from it. And then Yeshua named His own mission in one clean line: the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.

Not the found. The lost. The ones up trees. The ones the crowd will not let through. The ones with too much stolen money and too few friends, who only dared to hope for a glimpse and never imagined being called down by name.
The sound of a house set right

I think there was music in that house by evening. I cannot prove it, Scripture does not tell us, but I know what a homecoming sounds like, and I know what happens in a house when a debt gets cancelled and joy moves in, and I do not believe that afternoon ended in silence. A man had been found. His whole crooked history was being made right, out loud, with laughter. The poor of Jericho were about to have a very good week. And the one person the whole town had written off was, that day, more free than any of them.

The Jubilee was never only about the calendar or the trumpet. It was always about this: the moment the Redeemer walks into the house nobody expected Him to choose, and the stolen years come flooding back, and a lost man discovers he was a son the whole time.

If you have been hanging back at the edge of the crowd, too compromised to push to the front, too aware of what you have taken to expect to be wanted, climb the tree. Just to see. And do not be surprised if the One passing by stops under your branches, looks straight up at you, calls you by the name you did not think He knew, and says the word that changes the whole day.
Today.

pieces.title: The Long Way Home Turned Into a Song
pieces.imagePrompt: A radiant desert highway at golden hour bursting with wildflowers where a joyful multigenerational procession of diverse travelers walks home together singing, faces lifted and glowing with everlasting gladness, children laughing on shoulders and hands raised toward sunlit hills, an overwhelming atmosphere of homecoming joy; luminous cinematic film-still quality, warm gold amber and vivid fresh green tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: A prophet looked out over a scorched wilderness and saw something impossible coming: a road through the desert, and a whole people walking home along it with singing on their lips and a joy on their heads that would never wear off. The desert itself, he said, would burst into bloom just from hearing they were on their way.

body.text: The prophet was looking at a wasteland, and he described a garden.

That is the thing about Isaiah that unsettles me in the best way. He wrote for a people who were either about to lose everything or had already lost it, carried off, scattered, sitting in exile a thousand miles from the only home their songs remembered. And in the middle of all that ruin, he lifts his eyes and starts describing something that is not there yet. He looks at the dry country between the exiles and their home, the burning, trackless waste that lay like a sentence of impossibility between a captive people and the land they ached for, and he says: it is going to bloom.

The wilderness and the dry land, he says, are going to be glad. The desert is going to rejoice and burst into flower. The parched ground will become a pool, and the thirsty land springs of water. He is not describing weather. He is describing what the earth itself will do when it hears the news that the ransomed are coming home.
A road where there was no road
Then he says the thing I want to walk down with you.

There will be a highway there. A road, laid straight through the very wilderness that used to be the wall between the captives and their home. He calls it the Way of Holiness, a clean road, a safe road, a road the traveler cannot get lost on even if he is a fool, a road with no lion waiting to spring and no beast to fear. Nothing that hunts the vulnerable will be permitted on it. It is a road built for one purpose only: to carry home the people who were taken away.

Think about what a road means to a people in exile. A wilderness is where you get lost and die. It is the great uncrossable in-between, the reason the distance between here and home feels less like miles and more like a life sentence. And the prophet says: there is going to be a road through it. The impossible middle is going to have a path laid straight across it, and the path is going to be so safe and so sure that even the weakest, most frightened, most directionless traveler will walk it and arrive.
That is what redemption is. It is not only the opening of the prison door at the far end. It is the road home through the wilderness that always stood between you and the door.
The joy that does not wear off
And here is the line I turn over most, the one I would set to music if I could set anything to music the way it deserves.

The ransomed of Yahuah, Isaiah says, will return. They will come to Zion with singing. And everlasting joy will be upon their heads. They will lay hold of gladness and joy, and sorrow and sighing will flee away.

Everlasting joy upon their heads. He pictures joy as something you can see on a person, crowning them, the way exhaustion and grief sit visible on the shoulders of the beaten-down. He is describing a people whose whole bearing has changed, heads that used to hang, lifted; faces that used to be gray with sorrow, shining. And the joy is not a mood that will pass by afternoon. It is *everlasting.* It does not wear off. It is not the thin, brief relief of a good day that you know will end. It is a gladness fixed on them permanently, worn like a crown that cannot be taken off.

And notice which way the traffic runs at the end. Sorrow and sighing do not stand their ground and get slowly overcome. They *flee.* They run. In the presence of the returning ransomed, grief is the thing that turns and leaves. For a whole exiled generation that had learned to assume sorrow was the permanent tenant and joy the occasional visitor, the prophet flips it completely: joy moves in for good, and sorrow is the one shown the door.
They came home singing
Do not miss the small verb tucked into the middle of all this glory. *They will come to Zion with singing.*

Not silent. Not staggering in exhausted. Singing. The road home itself is a song. The whole procession of the redeemed walks the highway through the blooming desert with music on their lips, because you cannot carry that kind of joy quietly. It has to come out as sound. A people who have been given everlasting gladness will make everlasting noise about it, and the noise is a song, and the song fills the whole road, and the desert that used to be a graveyard rings with it.

I believe the earth was made to hear this song. I believe the blooming of that wilderness is a picture of what happens everywhere the news arrives that the captives are being brought home, that the ground itself, the whole creation, leans toward that sound and comes alive at it. The road home is not a lonely trudge. It is a parade. And the parade is singing a homecoming song loud enough to make flowers stand up out of dead sand.
The road is open now
Here is what I need you to know, because Isaiah was not only describing an ancient return from an ancient exile. He was describing a shape that God keeps making true.

There is a road home laid straight through your wilderness. Whatever the uncrossable middle is in your life, the years lost, the distance you cannot see across, the waste between where you are and where you belong, the news of the gospel is that a Way has been opened through it, a Way so sure that the foolish and the frightened and the directionless cannot miss it, a Way with nothing on it that is allowed to devour you. Yeshua Himself said He was the Way. The road through the wilderness has a name now, and the name walks you home.

And you do not arrive at the end of it worn down. You arrive with everlasting joy upon your head. That is the promise, and it is not a mood. It is a crown, and it does not come off. The sorrow that has felt like the permanent condition of your life is, in the presence of that homecoming, the thing that flees.

So sing on the road. Do not wait until you have arrived to lift your head. The ransomed of Yahuah come to Zion with singing, and you are among the ransomed, and the desert is already beginning to bloom on either side of you at the mere sound of it. The long way home was never meant to be walked in silence. It was always meant to turn into a song, and the whole earth was made to sing it home with you.

pieces.title: He Does Not Break the Half-Made Thing
pieces.imagePrompt: A young South Asian woman laughing with delight as she records a rough new song into her phone at home, cross-legged on the floor with a guitar, warm lamplight and morning glow across her genuinely joyful face, the tender happiness of an imperfect take made with love; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, warm honey and soft green tones, authentic and natural, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I have a phone full of songs that will embarrass anyone who hears them, croaked into the dark, out of tune, half a lyric and a cough. I used to be ashamed of the rough take. Then I met a promise about a bruised reed, and I understood who keeps the demos.

body.text: There is a folder on my phone I hope no one ever scrolls through.

It is where the rough takes live. Songs hummed into the dark at two in the morning, half awake, the melody arriving faster than I could find a pen, so I did the only thing I could and croaked it into a voice memo before it left. If you played those recordings back, you would hear a mess. You would hear me singing flat because I did not want to wake the house. You would hear a whole verse and then a mumble where the words had not come yet, a placeholder syllable held in place of a lyric I did not have. You would hear a cough. A dog. A refrigerator. And under all of it, if you were kind and patient, you might just make out the shape of a song that is not finished and may never be.

For a long time those recordings shamed me. They were evidence of how far my hands fall short of my ear. I would go back to write the song out properly and cringe at the raw version, and part of me wanted to delete the lot of them, to keep only the polished files, the finished masters, the songs I would let a stranger hear. Who wants to be caught mid-mumble? Who wants their unfinished, out-of-tune, coughing self on the record?

And then one morning I was reading the prophet Isaiah, in the passage about the servant Yahuah promises to send, and I came to a line that stopped me completely. It says that this one, when he comes, will not break a bruised reed, and will not snuff out a wick that is only smoking. And I sat there in my kitchen and thought: that is a promise about the rough take.
What a reed actually is
You have to know what a reed is to feel the weight of it.

In that part of the world a reed was not a decoration. It was raw material. You cut a reed from the riverbank and you made things from it, a measuring rod, a pen, and, most tenderly, a pipe. A shepherd's flute. You hollowed it and cut the holes and put your breath through it, and it made music out on the hills where nobody was listening but the sheep. A reed was the cheapest instrument a poor person could own. It cost nothing but the cutting.

So a bruised reed, a reed that is cracked, bent, half-crushed underfoot, is a ruined instrument. It is the flute that has gone wrong. The obvious thing, the sensible thing, the thing any craftsman does, is to snap it and throw it in the river and cut a fresh one. There are a thousand reeds on the bank. Why fight to save the broken one? It will only play sour. It will only disappoint you.

And the promise Isaiah heard, the promise the Gospels say came true in Yeshua, is that this One does not do the sensible thing. He picks up the cracked flute. He does not break it across His knee. He keeps the ruined instrument, and, this is the part I cannot get over. He keeps it *as an instrument*. He does not throw it away and He does not stop expecting music from it. He bends down over the thing that barely makes a sound, and He does not put it out.
The demo is not the failure
I want to say something to everyone who is carrying around a folder of half-made things.

Maybe yours is not a song. Maybe it is a marriage you have been quietly repairing that still plays a little sour. Maybe it is a faith that mumbles where the words should be, a prayer life that is mostly placeholder syllables held in the space where you cannot yet say what you mean. Maybe it is a version of yourself you would not let anyone hear, the rough take, the two-in-the-morning self, out of tune because you have been trying so hard not to wake anyone with how much this hurts.

Here is what I have come to believe, staking my whole working life on it. Yahuah is not embarrassed by the rough take. He is not waiting for the polished master before He starts loving the song. The finished version is not more precious to Him than the cracked reed croaked into the dark. In fact, and I say this carefully, because it undoes me. He seems to keep the demos. He seems to be the kind of Maker who does not delete the mumble.

We have this backward. We think we have to arrive finished. We think the mess disqualifies us, that the coughs and the flat notes and the missing words are proof we are not real, not worthy of the recording. So we hide the rough folder and we perform the master, and we come to Him only on our best days with our best takes, carefully in tune. And all the while the promise stands open behind us: a bruised reed He will not break. The very brokenness we are hiding is the exact thing the promise was made about.
Keep the file
I have stopped deleting my rough takes. It felt disloyal, once I understood.

Because here is the strange, hopeful truth about those files: the master could not exist without them. Every finished song I have ever released began as a croak in the dark, a bruised reed, a mumble where the words weren't. The polished version did not replace the rough one. It *grew out of it*. The rough take was not the failure of the song. It was the song's first honest breath. And a Maker who threw out every rough take on principle would never finish anything at all, because there is no finished thing that did not once sound terrible.

So I think Yahuah keeps our rough folders for the same reason I have learned to keep mine. Not because He is stuck with us. Because He is not finished. The cracked reed in His hand is not being discarded. It is being held, and mended, and slowly tuned, by the only Musician patient enough to get music out of a broken pipe.

If you have been hiding the unfinished version of yourself, hoping to show up one day with the master, stop waiting. Bring the rough take. Bring the mumble and the flat notes and the placeholder where the words won't come. He is not going to break it. He never breaks the half-made thing. He bends down over it, and He does not put it out, and He keeps humming the melody you cannot finish yet, until the day it plays clean.

pieces.title: A Melody Comes From Where the Wind Does
pieces.imagePrompt: A radiant East African woman singing outdoors in a golden field at sunrise, head tilted back and eyes closed in awe and delight as warm wind lifts her hair and light floods her joyful face, tall grass glowing around her; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, warm gold and soft blue tones, authentic and emotionally compelling, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: After ninety-one albums I still cannot tell you where a melody comes from. I can teach you every rule of craft and I still cannot make one arrive. Then I noticed that Yeshua used the exact same image for a tune and for the Spirit. You hear the sound, and you cannot trace it home.

body.text: I have been writing songs for most of my life, and I am going to tell you a secret that should probably worry my listeners: I still have no idea where a melody comes from.

That is not false modesty. I can teach you craft all day. I can show you why one interval aches and another resolves, how to build a line that lifts, where a chorus wants to sit, how to cut the clever bit that is strangling everything around it. Craft is real and craft can be taught. But craft is what you do *to* a melody after it arrives. It is carpentry. It shapes the wood. It does not grow the tree. And the tree, the first three notes, the thing that makes you sit up in a grocery line and reach for your phone. I cannot summon that. Nobody can. After ninety-one albums I am no closer to the machine than I was at the beginning. There is no machine.

For years this embarrassed me. It felt like a gap in my professionalism, a thing I should have solved by now. Surely someone who has written this much should be able to explain the source. Then I was reading the third chapter of John, the night conversation between Yeshua and a careful, learned man named Nicodemus, and I found the source described exactly, not for a melody, but for something even harder to hold.
The image He reached for

Nicodemus came at night, which the Gospel writer seems to mean in more ways than one, and he could not understand what Yeshua meant about being born again, born of the Spirit. And instead of giving him a doctrine, Yeshua gave him an image. He said, in effect: the wind blows where it wants. You hear the sound of it. But you cannot tell where it came from or where it is going. That is what everyone born of the Spirit is like.

What undoes me about that is the double meaning buried in the words themselves. In the language of the Hebrews, and in the Greek the Gospel was written in, the word for *wind* and the word for *Spirit* and the word for *breath* are one and the same word. Yeshua was not making a clumsy comparison, *the Spirit is sort of like wind.* He was standing inside a word that already held both. The wind and the Spirit are the same mystery wearing two coats. And the one thing He says you can know about either of them is this: you hear the sound, and you cannot trace it home.

I read that and I thought, that is a melody. That is exactly what happens. You hear the sound. It moves through you, it moves the room, it bends the grass of your whole heart in one direction. And if you turn to catch where it came from, there is nothing there to catch. It came from where the wind does.
Why we cannot manufacture it

I think we have a deep and modern need to own the source of things. We want the recipe. We want the pipeline, the process, the repeatable method that turns effort into inspiration on demand, because a source you cannot control is a source that might not show up when you need it, and that is unbearable to a person who has to deliver.

But some things refuse to be owned at their source, and I have come to believe those are the deepest things, and that this is not a defect. A melody you could fully manufacture would be a melody with no wind in it. You can hear the difference. There are songs assembled entirely out of craft, technically flawless, that leave the room exactly as they found it, because craft with no breath through it is furniture, not fire. And then there are the songs that arrived, that came from somewhere the writer cannot point to, and those are the ones that move people who never met the writer, in rooms the writer will never enter.

The same is true of a life turned toward Yahuah. You cannot manufacture the moment the wind actually moves. You can build the instrument, you can hollow the reed, you can show up faithfully to the quiet and keep the sails up, all of that is craft, and none of it is optional. But you cannot make the wind blow. You can only be in a posture to catch it when it does. The people I most trust in matters of the Spirit are never the ones with the airtight method for producing an experience of God. They are the ones who have felt the wind enough times to stop pretending they command it, and who keep their sails up anyway.
You hear the sound
Here is where the image turns from mystery into hope, and it turns fast.

Because notice what Yeshua does *not* say. He does not say the wind is unreal because you cannot trace it. He does not say that a source you cannot locate is a source you should doubt. He says the opposite, and He says it to a man trained to trust only what he can define. He says: *you hear the sound.* The evidence is not in the map of where it came from. The evidence is that the grass is moving. You do not have to explain the wind to know you have been caught up in it. You only have to feel it on your face.

I find this enormously freeing, both as a writer and as a person who is trying to follow Yeshua. As a writer, it lets me stop apologizing for a source I cannot document. The melody came from where the wind does. I did not make it; I received it, and my honest job is to catch it well and pass it on, not to take credit for the wind. And as a person, it lets me stop demanding a diagram of God before I will trust the movement of God. I have felt the grass of my own heart bend in a direction I did not choose, in a room where a song was being sung. I could not tell you the mechanism. But I am not going to stand there insisting nothing happened just because I cannot trace it home.

So the next time a melody moves you and you cannot say why, the song at the funeral, the tune from childhood that arrives uninvited and buckles your knees, the three notes in a grocery store that stop you where you stand, do not rush to explain it. You are not being irrational. You are hearing the sound of something that blows where it wishes.
You cannot tell where it came from or where it is going. You only know the grass is moving. Keep your sails up. The wind is not finished with this field.

pieces.title: A Blurred Note Rallies No One
pieces.imagePrompt: A radiant young Brazilian worship leader mid-song at the front of a packed church, guitar in hand and face bright with joy as a diverse crowd behind lifts their hands and sings the same clear line back, warm golden stage light washing over rows of glad, uplifted faces; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, warm amber and honey tones, authentic and alive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: The most dazzling song I ever wrote left the room exactly as it found it, because no one could follow it. It took me years, and a hard passage from Paul about a blurred trumpet, to learn that clarity is not the enemy of art. It is the love in it.

body.text: I once wrote a song I was sure would be the best thing I had ever made, and it did nothing at all.

It had everything. A melody that turned in surprising places, chords that I was quietly proud of, a structure so intricate I could have taught a class on it. I played it for a room of people who loved me and wanted to be moved, and I watched their faces, and their faces were polite. Nothing happened. The song was, by every measure I could name, excellent, and it left the room exactly as it found it. Not one person could have hummed it back to me on the way out. It was a firework that went off too high to see.

It took me an embarrassingly long time to understand what had gone wrong, because the problem was hidden inside the thing I was proudest of. The song was impressive. And impressive was the disease. I had written it, though I would never have admitted this at the time, to be *admired*, to display what I could do, and a song built to be admired asks the listener to watch the writer. It never opens a door they can walk through. It is a locked room with a very beautiful door.

The passage that finally diagnosed me was one I had read many times without feeling it. It is Paul, writing to a church in Corinth that had fallen in love with the flashiest gifts, and he makes his argument, of all things, with musical instruments.
The flute that plays no tune

Paul says, in effect: even lifeless instruments make his point for him. Take a flute, or a harp. If it does not sound distinct notes, if the pitches blur together into an impressive wash of sound, how will anyone know what tune is being played? You can be technically producing music, fingers flying, breath pouring through the pipe, and if the notes do not come out *distinct*, there is no song. There is only noise that happens to be coming from an instrument.

Then he sharpens it with a trumpet. If the trumpet gives an uncertain, indistinct call, who is going to get ready for the battle? A trumpet on the field is not there to be beautiful. It is there to be *understood*. It tells the whole army when to rise, when to advance, when to hold. And a trumpeter who blew a dazzling, complicated, blurred fanfare that no one could read would not rally a single soldier. He would simply stand there sounding magnificent while the line fell apart around him, because a blurred note rallies no one.

I read that and felt it land on my clever, admired, useless song. I had blown a magnificent blurred note. And Paul drives it home for the people, not just the instruments: unless you speak words that can actually be understood, he says, how will anyone know what you meant? You will only be speaking into the air. There are many languages in the world, and none of them is meaningless, but if I do not know what your sounds mean, I am a foreigner to you and you to me, no matter how sincere the sound.
The five words that beat ten thousand
Here is the line from that chapter I have written where I can see it while I work.

Paul says that in the gathering, in the room where people have come together to be built up. He would rather speak five words that people can understand and be instructed by, than ten thousand words in a tongue no one can follow. Ten thousand to five. He is not against the ten thousand because they are too many. He is against them because in that room they do nobody any good, and five plain words that land do more than ten thousand dazzling ones that don't.

That ratio undid my whole theory of what makes a song good. I had assumed the goal was to give the room the most, the most craft, the most surprise, the most of *me*. Paul says the goal in the gathering is not the most. It is the clearest. It is the five words they can carry, not the ten thousand they will forget. And the reason is not that art is bad, or that beauty is suspect, or that simplicity is holier than skill. The reason is *love*. The whole chapter turns on one command he keeps circling back to: since you are so eager for these gifts, he says, then strive to excel at the thing that actually builds other people up. Aim your excellence at *them*, not at your own reflection.

That is the sentence that changed how I write. Clarity is not the opposite of art. Clarity is where the art starts loving the listener instead of the maker. A blurred note serves the trumpeter's vanity. A distinct one serves the whole army. And I had spent years perfecting blurred notes and calling it depth.
Sing with the spirit and the mind

I do not want to be misheard, so let me say what Paul is careful to say. He is not telling us to stop making beautiful things, and he is not telling us to stop pouring our spirits out. In the very same passage he says he will sing with his spirit, and he will also sing with his mind. Both. The overflow of the heart *and* the discipline of being understood, held together. He is not choosing feeling over clarity or clarity over feeling. He is refusing to let a real gift become a private performance that leaves the room untouched.

That is the discipline I had been missing. It is much easier to be impressive than to be clear, because impressive lets you hide, and clear leaves you nowhere to hide. When I strip a song down until the note is distinct and the meaning lands and a tired person at the back can follow it on the first hearing, there is nothing left to dazzle anyone with. There is only whether the thing is true. That is terrifying, and it is the whole job.

So now, when I finish a song, I no longer ask first whether it is impressive. I ask whether the notes are distinct, whether someone who has never met me could tell what tune is being played, could get ready for the battle, could carry five clear words out of the room and into the week. If the answer is no, then it does not matter how proud of it I am. It is a blurred trumpet. It will rally no one.

Whatever you make, whatever you are trying to say to the people in front of you. I want to hand you Paul's gentle, ruthless test. Do not aim to be admired. Aim to be understood, because being understood is how you love them. Five clear words that reach them will outlast ten thousand dazzling ones that don't. Blow the note distinct. Let them hear the tune. That is not the lesser art. That is the art finally pointed at somebody other than yourself.

pieces.title: The First Man Filled With the Spirit Was a Craftsman
pieces.imagePrompt: A weathered older instrument-maker in a sunlit workshop, hands resting on a half-finished handmade guitar and his face creased with a warm, contented smile of pure delight in his craft, golden-hour light and drifting sawdust glowing around him; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, warm amber and honey tones, dignified, authentic and human, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I have often wondered whether the hours I spend making songs no one may ever hear are wasted, or somehow less spiritual than preaching. Then I noticed who the very first person in Scripture is that God says He filled with His Spirit, and it was not a prophet or a priest. It was a man who worked with his hands.

body.text: I want to tell you about a doubt that visits me in the workshop, because I suspect you have your own version of it, wherever your workshop happens to be.

The doubt comes on the quiet days, when I have spent hours on a song and no one has heard a note of it and no one may ever hear it. I look at the pile of what I have made, the ninety-one albums' worth of work, most of it still unsung, sheet music and rough takes and finished melodies waiting for voices that have not arrived, and a small cold voice asks: is this a spiritual life, or a hobby? Would it not be more useful to God if you were out preaching, or feeding someone, or doing something that visibly helps? Is the making itself holy, or is it just craft, a lesser thing you do in the corner while the real ministry happens elsewhere?

For a long time I could not answer that voice. It seemed to have a point. Surely the sermon matters more than the song's second bridge. Surely the hours a maker pours into getting a thing *right*, the fret over a chord no listener will consciously notice, the week spent on four notes, surely that is self-indulgence dressed up as devotion.

Then I went looking, honestly, through the Scriptures, for the first time a person is described as being filled with the Spirit of Yahuah. I expected a prophet thundering judgment. I expected a priest, or a king, or at the very least someone preaching. I did not expect who I found.
His name was Bezalel

In the book of Exodus, after Yahuah has brought the people out of Egypt and given them the pattern for a place of worship, He tells Moses that He has chosen a particular man for the work. And He says, and this is the first time the phrase appears in the whole story, that He has filled this man with the Spirit of God. Not a prophet. Not a priest. A craftsman named Bezalel, and his partner Oholiab, and a whole company of skilled workers.

And listen to what the Spirit fills him *for*. Not to prophesy. Not to lead armies. He is filled with the Spirit of God for wisdom, understanding, knowledge, and every kind of skilled craftsmanship, to design artistic works, to cut and set stones, to carve wood, to work in gold and silver and bronze, to weave and embroider. The very first outpouring of the Spirit of Yahuah recorded on a named individual in Scripture is an outpouring of *artistry*. God's Spirit came, and the thing it produced was beautiful work made with human hands.

I cannot tell you what that did to the cold voice in my workshop. It did not merely answer it. It reversed it. Because it turns out that Yahuah does not regard skilled making as a lesser thing done in the corner while the real spiritual work happens elsewhere. The making was so close to His heart that when He chose to fill someone with His own Spirit for the very first time in the record, He filled an artist, and He filled him precisely *to make*.
The care no one will notice
Here is the detail that finishes the argument for me.

Bezalel made things that almost no one would ever see. He worked gold into objects that would sit inside a tent, behind a curtain, in a room only the high priest entered, and only once a year. He set stones and carved details on the underside of things, on the back of things, in the folds of things, that would be seen by no human eye for the entire life of the tabernacle. And he did it, we are told, with the full weight of the Spirit of God on his hands. The care he poured into the parts no one would notice was not waste. It was worship. The audience for the hidden craftsmanship was Yahuah Himself, and Yahuah was enough of an audience.

That is the thing that steadies me when I fret over a chord change no listener will consciously register, or spend a week on a section of a song that may never be sung by anyone. I used to think that care was excessive, self-indulgent, a maker fussing over what does not matter. I no longer think so. I think that care is the exact place where craft becomes worship, the moment you keep working on the part no one will see, for an audience of One who sees it all. Bezalel carving the hidden underside of the ark is the patron saint of everyone who has ever agonized over something the world will never applaud.
The making is not the waiting room
So let me say clearly to whoever needs it, whatever your workshop is, the kitchen, the spreadsheet, the garden, the code, the song, the small excellent thing you make that few will ever notice.

The making is not the waiting room for the spiritual life. The making can *be* the spiritual life. The first person Scripture says was filled with the Spirit of God was not filled to speak. He was filled to build beautifully. That means the impulse in you to make a thing well, to get it right, to pour disproportionate care into a corner no one will inspect, that impulse is not a distraction from Yahuah. It may be one of the truest echoes of Him you carry, because He is a Maker, and He made you in His image, and part of that image is the hands that cannot rest until the thing is beautiful.

I do not know how many of my ninety-one albums will ever be sung. Most of them are still silent, waiting. And on the quiet days the cold voice still comes, and asks whether all this making is wasted. But I have an answer for it now, and the answer has a name. Bezalel. A man filled with the Spirit of God, given all that fullness, and sent, not to a pulpit, not to a battlefield, but to a workbench, to make something beautiful for Yahuah that most people would never even see.

If that was worthy of the first outpouring of His Spirit, then your quiet, careful, unwitnessed making is worthy too. Keep at the bench. The Maker is not embarrassed by makers. He fills them. He always has.

pieces.title: The Melody Would Not Keep Overnight

pieces.excerpt: I keep trying to live off yesterday's inspiration, to coast on the song that came last month instead of showing up empty-handed for a new one. Then I remembered the strangest rule about the manna: you could not store it. What you hoarded overnight went foul. And I understood why the writing has to be daily.

body.text: Every writer I know has tried to cheat the same way, and it never works. We try to live off yesterday's melody.

It goes like this. Last month, a song arrived, a real one, the kind that came from where the wind comes from, that made the room go still. And it was so good that some quiet part of me decided I was done. I had proof now. I had the thing that showed I could do this. And so I coasted. I stopped showing up empty-handed to the quiet morning, because showing up empty-handed is frightening and coasting on the memory of a triumph feels safe. Why risk the blank page today when I have a masterpiece from three weeks ago to keep me warm?

And every single time, the same thing happens. The old song, hoarded, starts to go foul. Not the song itself, the song is fine, out there doing its work. What goes foul is *me*. Living off the memory of the last one, I get stale and self-satisfied and slightly rotten, protective of a past triumph instead of open to a present one. The very thing I was clutching to feel secure becomes the thing spoiling in my hands. And I do not get free of it until I go back to the frightening blank morning and hold out empty hands for something new.

For a long time I could not understand why it works this way, why inspiration will not be stockpiled, why yesterday's provision refuses to cover today. Then I went back to the story of the manna, and there it was, the rule I had forgotten, the strangest rule in the whole account.
The bread that would not be hoarded
When Yahuah fed the people in the wilderness, He did it in a way designed to drive a hoarder out of his mind.

Every morning there was bread on the ground, a fine, flaky thing they had never seen, which is why they called it manna, from a question that means roughly *what is it?* And the instruction was simple and maddening: gather what you need for today. Just today. And of course some of them did not trust that. Some of them gathered extra and kept it overnight, the sensible thing, the prudent thing, the thing any careful person does. You store against tomorrow, you do not live hand to mouth if you can help it. And in the morning the hoarded portion had bred worms and gone rank. It could not be kept. The only manna that stayed good was the manna you trusted enough to gather fresh.

There was one exception, and it is beautiful: on the day before the Sabbath they gathered a double portion, and that portion, and only that one, kept overnight so they could rest. So it was not that God was against provision or against rest. It was that He would not let the manna become a substitute for the relationship. He was teaching them, through their stomachs, to come back to Him every single morning. He gave them enough for today precisely so they would have to show up tomorrow.

I read that and I understood my own foulness. The melody would not keep overnight for the same reason the manna would not. Not because inspiration is scarce, but because I am prone to hoard the gift and skip the Giver. The daily-ness is not God being stingy. It is God refusing to let yesterday's provision become the thing I trust instead of Him.
Why the writing has to be daily
This changed how I understand the discipline of my own work, and I think it reaches far past writing.

We imagine that the ideal would be to *arrive*, to accumulate enough skill, enough proof, enough past triumphs that we no longer have to face the frightening empty morning. We treat the blank page, the daily return with nothing in our hands, as a beginner's problem we are meant to grow out of. But the manna says the opposite. The empty-handed morning is not a stage you graduate from. It is the whole arrangement. It is designed to be permanent, because its purpose was never merely to feed you. Its purpose was to keep bringing you back.

So when I sit down today with nothing, no melody in my hands, last month's success now foul and useless for today's work. I have stopped reading that as failure. I read it as the manna doing exactly what it was made to do. It has emptied my hands so that I will show up and hold them out again.
