The daily fear of the blank page is not a flaw in the creative life. It is the creative life keeping me honest, keeping me dependent, keeping me coming back to the only source that actually has anything.

And the same is true of walking with Yahuah, which is why He taught it through bread. You cannot live this year on the strength of a spiritual experience you had five years ago. You cannot store last summer's sense of His nearness against this winter's silence. People try, constantly. They hoard an old encounter, a season when God felt close, and try to make it cover the long ordinary stretch, and it goes foul in their hands, and they wonder why their faith feels rank and stale. It is the manna rule. Yesterday's portion was never meant to feed today. He gives you enough for today so that tomorrow you will come back to Him and gather again.
Come back empty-handed
So here is what I do now, and what I would hand to you if you are living off an old portion that has quietly gone foul.

I come back every morning with empty hands. I stop trying to coast on the last good thing. I treat the blank page and the silent room not as evidence that the gift has left me, but as the daily invitation it has always been, the ground scattered again with what I did not make and could not have stored, waiting to be gathered fresh. Some mornings there is a feast. Some mornings there is just enough, an omer, barely a song, only enough for today. But it is always there, and it is always new, and it is never the same as what I gathered yesterday.

The melody would not keep overnight. I used to grieve that. Now I am grateful for it, because a melody that could be hoarded is a melody I would have used to stop needing the Giver. Instead I am kept poor in the best way, sent out every single morning, empty-handed and expectant, to gather what has fallen fresh in the night.

Do not try to live off yesterday's bread. Let it go foul if it has to. Get up, hold out your hands, and come back to the ground where the new thing is already lying, waiting for you, glowing in the early light. There is enough for today. There will be enough tomorrow. There always has been.

pieces.title: The Voice You Could Pick Out of Ten Thousand
pieces.imagePrompt: A radiant mother lifting her laughing baby high in a sunlit nursery, both faces alight with pure delight and recognition, warm golden morning light pouring through the window; wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, tender and joyful, premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, authentic and natural, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: In a ward full of crying newborns, a sleeping mother wakes to one cry and one only, her own. Your brain performs a daily miracle of picking a single known voice out of a roar of others, and I think it is quietly teaching you how faith learns to hear.

body.text: There is a room in every maternity hospital that no one photographs, and I think about it more than you would expect a songwriter to.

It is the middle of the night, and the room is full of cries. Newborns, a dozen of them, each one working its small lungs at full volume, and to any stranger walking past it is simply noise, an undifferentiated wall of the same sound, indistinguishable, a siren with no center. But down the hall there is a mother who has slept perhaps forty minutes, and she is sleeping through all of it. The crying does not wake her. Not the loud one, not the closest one, not the twelve strangers' children an arm's length from her own exhaustion.

And then one cry lifts out of the wall of sound, and she is awake before she has decided to be. Not startled, *summoned.* Something older than her tiredness has already sorted the entire roar and found, in it, the one voice that is hers. She could not have described the difference. If you played her a recording and asked her to explain what set that cry apart from the other eleven, she would have no words for it. But her body knew instantly, and it did not consult her, and it did not make a mistake.
That is one of the quietly staggering things about how you are made, and it has a name, though the name is less beautiful than the thing.
The miracle you perform without trying

Sound does not arrive at your ears in tidy separate streams. It arrives as one thing, a single, churning pressure, every voice and engine and rustle in the room folded together into one wave that hits your eardrum all at once, mixed beyond any hope of sorting. By all rights you should hear only mud.

And yet you can stand at a crowded party, in a genuine roar of overlapping conversation, and follow the single thread of the one person speaking to you. You can lose it, and find it again. You can be only half-listening to the person in front of you and get yanked clear across the room by a familiar voice you were not even trying to hear. Somewhere behind your attention, tirelessly, your brain is taking the one impossible mixed wave and pulling it back apart into voices, separating, tracking, choosing, holding on to one and letting the rest fall away. It does this so constantly and so well that you have never once thanked it, because you never noticed it was hard.

But it is hard. It is so hard that we have spent decades and fortunes trying to teach machines to do it, and they still stumble at what a tired mother does in her sleep. The ability to lock onto one known voice inside a crowd of others is not a small trick of hearing. It may be one of the most sophisticated things a human being does, and most of us do it a hundred times a day without ever turning around to look at it.
And the reason it undoes me is what it means to be *known* well enough to be heard that way.
My sheep hear my voice
There is an image Yeshua reached for that I did not understand until I understood this.

He said He was the good shepherd, and He described His people as sheep, which sounds, to modern ears, faintly insulting, until you learn how it actually worked. In that country, several flocks would be folded together at night in one enclosure, mixed the way those newborns are mixed, indistinguishable to any outsider. And in the morning the shepherds would come, and each one would simply *speak*, and out of the tangled mass, his own sheep would lift their heads and come to him, sorting themselves from the others by nothing but the sound of a voice they knew. A stranger could stand in the same gate and call in the same words, and they would not come. They did not know that voice. They knew *theirs.*

He said it plainly: My sheep hear My voice, and they know it, and a stranger they will not follow, because they do not recognize the stranger's voice. He was describing exactly the faculty in that hospital ward. Not cleverness. Not theological expertise. *Recognition*, the deep, wordless, cannot-explain-it knowing of one particular voice out of a roar of others.

And then He said the thing that steadies me on the days I feel lost in the crowd of the world. He said the shepherd calls His own by name and leads them out. He does not call to the flock in general. He knows which cry is which. In the whole indistinguishable wall of human noise, billions of us, crying at once. He is not overwhelmed the way a stranger is overwhelmed by that nursery. He hears *you.* Specifically. He has never once mistaken your voice for someone else's, and He never will.
Learning to hear one voice in the roar
Here is why I wanted to hand you this, especially if your life right now is loud with voices that are not His.

Because it is loud, isn't it. The accusation that runs on a loop. The fear dressed up as prudence. The old verdict someone spoke over you when you were young that still calls your name in the dark. The endless commentary of a world with an opinion about everything you are. It can feel like that nursery, a wall of sound with no center, every voice equally urgent, no way to tell which cry to answer. And in that roar it is easy to conclude that God has gone silent, when the truth may be that He is speaking in the register you have not yet learned to pick out.

But recognition can be trained. That is the hope folded into the fact. A mother does not know her newborn's cry on the first night by magic; she learns it, fast, because she stays near it, because she listens for it, because it matters more to her than any other sound in the world. And you can learn His voice the same way, not by straining harder to hear over the noise, but by getting near enough, often enough, to the places He actually speaks, until the shape of that one voice becomes so familiar that it lifts out of the wall on its own and your whole attention turns before you have decided to. The Scriptures read slowly until the ink becomes a voice. The song that says something truer than the accusation. The quiet that is not empty. You are not being asked to silence the crowd. You are being invited to know one voice well enough that the crowd can no longer drown it.

And on the nights you cannot find it at all, when the roar wins and you strain and hear nothing you can trust, remember which direction the miracle actually runs. You do not hold your place in that flock by the sharpness of your hearing. You are held there by *His.* The tired ear may lose the voice for a while. The Shepherd never loses the sheep. He knows your particular cry out of ten thousand, He has known it since before you had a name, and He is not, even now, mistaking you for anyone else.

You could pick one voice out of an impossible crowd because you were made by a God who does exactly that with you. Get near enough to learn the sound of Him. And on the nights you cannot, rest in the better half of the promise: you were already picked out, already named, already heard, one cry, unmistakable, in a nursery the size of the world.

pieces.title: The Throb That Means You're Almost in Tune
pieces.imagePrompt: A happy young couple leaning close on a park bench at golden hour, sharing a single pair of earbuds and grinning at each other as a song lands just right, faces bright with shared delight and easy laughter; wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, warm radiant sunlight, premium worship-brand cinematic film-still warmth, authentic and natural, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: When two notes are nearly the same but not quite, they fight, a slow, restless throbbing you can hear and feel, that vanishes the instant they lock together. A piano tuner listens for that beat on purpose, and I have come to believe it explains the ache of a soul that is close to God but not yet at rest.

body.text: The first time I watched a piano tuner work, I expected him to listen for beauty. He listened for a fight.

He would strike two strings meant to sound the same note, and instead of the single clean tone I anticipated, the air would do something restless, a slow *wah, wah, wah,* a throbbing that swelled and faded and swelled again, as if the sound itself could not settle. He would turn his wrench a hair. The throbbing would slow down. Another hair, and it slowed further, the pulses stretching further apart, *wah . . . wah . . . wah,* until, at some invisible threshold, they simply stopped, and where two strings had been quarrelling a moment before, there was suddenly one still, pure, unwavering tone, so at peace it seemed to open a window in the room.
He did not tune by chasing the pretty sound. He tuned by hunting the throb and driving it out.

I have never forgotten it, because that throb turns out to be one of the most honest things in all of music, and once you understand what causes it, you start hearing it everywhere, including in yourself.
The sound of almost
Here is what is actually happening in that *wah, wah, wah.*

When two notes are pitched at exactly the same frequency, their waves rise and fall together, perfectly in step, and you hear one smooth tone. But when they are *almost* the same, close, but off by a hair, something strange occurs. The two waves drift slowly in and out of alignment with each other. At the moments they line up, they reinforce, and the sound swells louder. At the moments they oppose, they cancel, and the sound thins to nearly nothing. Loud, soft, loud, soft, a slow pulse that is not in either note by itself. Musicians call it a *beat,* and the closer the two pitches get to each other, the slower the beating goes, until at true unison it disappears entirely.

Sit with what that means, because it is quietly profound. That restless throbbing is not the sound of two notes that are *far apart.* Two notes far apart do not beat at all; they simply clash, or they make a chord, and each keeps its own life. The beat only happens when two notes are *nearly the same and not yet the same.* It is the specific, physical signature of *almost.* The throb is the sound of closeness that has not yet become oneness, of two things reaching for the same pitch and not quite arriving.
And the moment I understood that, a whole kind of spiritual restlessness I had felt for years, and misread for years, finally made sense.
The ache is not distance
There is a certain unrest that the closest people to God often carry, and almost always misdiagnose.

It is not the numbness of someone far off. It is not the cold indifference of a heart that has stopped caring. It is something more agitated and more tender than that, a person who prays and still feels a pull, who has surrendered and senses there is more surrender being asked, who loves God genuinely and yet cannot shake the low, throbbing sense that they are not quite *there,* not yet fully at rest, not yet all the way in tune. And that unrest torments them, because they read it as evidence of distance. *If I were really close to Him,* they think, *I would feel settled. This restlessness must mean I am far.*
But the beat only happens when you are near.

The soul that is genuinely far from God does not throb. It clashes, or it goes quiet, or it hums along contentedly in its own key, undisturbed. The throb, that restless, swelling, will-not-settle ache for a rest you can almost taste, is not the signature of distance at all. It is the signature of *almost.* It is what closeness sounds like before it becomes union. The very unrest you have been taking as proof that God is far may be the surest evidence that He is near, and getting nearer, two pitches sliding toward each other, the beats slowing, the gap closing, the stillness just ahead.

A man who lived long ago and thought hard about God, and here I am telling you a piece of Christian tradition, not a line of Scripture, is remembered for saying that God has made us for Himself, and our hearts are restless until they find their rest in Him. I used to hear that as a diagnosis of the far. Now I hear it as a description of the *almost.* The restlessness is not the absence of God. It is the sound a heart makes while it is being tuned toward Him and has not yet come to rest.
Rest for your souls
And here is the mercy that makes the whole picture bearable: you do not close the gap by straining.

Watch the tuner again. The two strings do not come into unison by trying harder, by throbbing more sincerely, by wanting it more. Someone turns the peg. The pitch is *brought,* gently and from outside, until it matches, and at the moment it matches, the effort ends, and there is nothing left to do but sound. The stillness is not achieved by the string. It is received.

Yeshua said something to the restless that I now hear in exactly this key. He said, Come to Me, all of you who are weary and heavy-laden, and I will give you rest. And then He said the strangest, tenderest thing, that if we would take His yoke and learn from Him, we would find rest for our souls. Not rest *from* Him. Rest *in* Him. The unrest that has been throbbing in you was never going to be silenced by you generating a purer note through willpower. It goes still the way two strings go still, when the distance closes, when the pitch is brought home, when *almost* finally becomes *one.* And that closing is His work, offered to you, not a performance demanded of you.

So if you are carrying that restless throb tonight, the ache of a faith that is real and yet not at rest, close and yet not settled, wanting God and somehow still swelling and fading and swelling with an unrest you cannot name. I want to hand you the tuner's secret.

Do not despair of the throb. It is not the sound of a soul that has missed Him. It is the sound of a soul that is *nearly there.* The beating you feel is the beating of *almost,* and *almost* is only ever a hair away from unison. You are not far. You are close enough to hear the pulse of your own nearness. Stop straining to manufacture the stillness, and simply come, near enough, and often enough, and honest enough, that the One who tunes can turn the peg. The throb will slow. The pulses will stretch further and further apart. And one day, at a threshold you will not see coming, they will simply stop, and where there was quarrelling there will be one still, pure, unwavering tone, the sound your whole restless life was reaching for, finally, and at last, in tune.

pieces.title: You Have Never Actually Heard Your Own Voice
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful Latina woman singing wholeheartedly in a bright church, head tilted back and one hand lifted, her face luminous with unguarded delight and freedom, surrounded by fellow worshippers glowing in warm morning light; wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, radiant and uplifting, premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, authentic and natural, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: The voice you hear in your own head is not the voice anyone else hears, and the recording that makes you cringe is closer to the truth than the one you carry inside. You are the single worst-positioned person to judge your own sound, and I think that is one of the most freeing facts God ever built into a body.

body.text: Almost everyone has had the small, specific horror of hearing themselves played back.

A voicemail you didn't know was recording. A video someone took at a birthday. A voice memo you meant to delete. And there it is, your voice, coming out of the speaker, and it is *wrong.* Too high, or too thin, or too nasal, some quality you do not recognize and immediately dislike. *That's not what I sound like,* you think, with a flush of embarrassment. *Do I really sound like that?*

Yes. You do. That is exactly what you sound like, to everyone. To your mother, your best friend, the person you married, the strangers on the bus. That cringe-inducing recording is the true one. The voice you have loved and lived inside your entire life, the one in your head, the one you think of as *yours*, that is the one no one else has ever heard, and never will.
I find this quietly astonishing, and the older I get the more I think it is a mercy dressed as an embarrassment.
Two roads into one ear
Here is why the recording sounds like a stranger.

When you speak, the sound reaches your own ears by two completely different roads at once. Some of it travels the ordinary way, out of your mouth, into the air, around and back into your ear, exactly the path everyone else's version of your voice takes. But a great deal of it never goes into the air at all. It travels *through you*, through the bone of your jaw and your skull, conducted directly to the inner ear as a trembling in the very structure of your head. And bone carries sound differently than air does. It favors the low, warm, resonant frequencies. It adds a richness, a depth, a fullness that is not in the sound anyone else receives.

So the voice you hear when you speak is a blend of two things: the air version everyone hears, *plus* a private, bone-deep, low-end fullness that is for you alone and can never leave your own head. Strip that hidden layer away, record just the part that made it into the air, and what is left sounds thinner and higher and stranger than the voice you know, because you have never once heard your voice without the secret warmth your own skull was adding to it.

Which leads to a conclusion I cannot stop turning over. Of every single person on earth, *you* are the only one who has never heard your real voice. Everyone else knows it. You are the one it is hidden from. You are, by the plain architecture of your own head, the least reliable judge of your own sound in all the world.
The eye that cannot see itself
I want to sit with that, because we build so much of our lives on the opposite assumption.

We assume we are the experts on ourselves. We assume the voice in our own head, the running self-assessment, the verdict we have reached about our own worth, our own gifts, our own likeability, is the accurate one, the inside track, the true report that outsiders only glimpse. And so we walk around trusting our own most private estimate of ourselves as if it were the last word.

But the body is telling on us. The one voice you can never hear correctly is your own. The one face you can never see except backwards in a mirror or frozen in a photo is your own. You are, structurally, the person with the worst seat in the house for the show that is *you.* And I think that goes far deeper than acoustics, because the harshest, most confident, most authoritative judge most of us ever listen to is the voice in our own head passing sentence on ourselves, and that judge is sitting in the exact seat that cannot hear the true sound.

The person who refuses to sing because they *hate their voice* is trusting a judgment made from the one position that cannot hear it. The person convinced they are unlovable, or useless, or too far gone, has reached that verdict from inside the skull that distorts everything before it arrives. We are so sure our self-assessment is the accurate one. It is the one measurement we are structurally least equipped to take.
The Lord looks at the heart
The Scriptures say this in a way I did not connect to any of it until recently.

There is a moment when a prophet named Samuel is sent to find a new king among a father's sons, and one by one the impressive ones are paraded before him, tall, strong, the obvious choices. And each time Samuel is sure he has found the one, God stops him. Do not look at his appearance or his height, He says, for I have refused him. And then the line that has outlived three thousand years: *man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahuah looks at the heart.* The one they finally send for is the youngest, still out with the sheep, the one no one in the room thought worth calling in, and he is the one God had chosen all along.

Hear what that is actually saying. There is a way you are seen and heard by others, and it is partial. There is a way you see and hear *yourself,* and it is distorted, filtered through a skull that adds and subtracts before you ever get the sound. And then there is the way *God* perceives you, which is the only undistorted hearing in the universe. He is not fooled by the air version the way your neighbors are. He is not fooled by the bone-deep private version the way *you* are. He hears the actual sound, the true voice, the true worth, the real self underneath every distortion your own perception laid over it. He looks past the outward, and past your own crooked report of your inward, straight to the heart.
Sing anyway
So here is what I want to leave with you, tenderly, especially if you have gone silent because of a verdict you passed on yourself from the one seat that cannot hear.

You may have decided your voice is not worth lifting, that it is too thin, too broken, too unlovely to add to the song. I want you to notice *where that judgment was made.* It was made from inside the one head that has never once heard your voice as it truly is. It is the least trustworthy assessment available anywhere, delivered with total confidence by the one witness structurally guaranteed to be wrong. You are not the authority on your own sound. You never were. The body made sure of it.

The voice that makes you cringe on a recording may be the very voice that steadies someone else in a room. The self you have quietly written off may be the one God looked past every taller, stronger option to choose. Do not let the distorted judge have the last word. Sing the true thing anyway, out an open window, into an ordinary morning, badly if you must, and let the One who hears you without distortion do what He has always done with voices the singer thought were nothing.

You have never actually heard your own voice. But He has. And He is not embarrassed by it. He made it, He hears it true, and He has been waiting for you to stop trusting the cringe and start trusting the One who has loved the sound of you from the beginning.

pieces.title: The Gap Between the Flash and the Thunder
pieces.imagePrompt: A delighted grandfather and his young grandchild together on a porch at golden hour, both smiling with warm wonder as they watch a distant summer sky, gentle radiant light glowing at the horizon; wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, safe and tender, premium worship-brand cinematic film-still warmth, authentic and natural, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: The flash and the thunder leave in the very same instant, but the light arrives at once and the sound takes its time, so you count the seconds and measure the distance. I have come to believe the silence after you have seen God move, before you hear it land, is not His absence. It is travel time.

body.text: My grandmother taught me to count the storm, and I did not know she was also teaching me how to wait on God.

We would sit on the porch as the weather moved in over the fields, and when the lightning cracked she would take my hand and start counting, low and unhurried, *one, two, three, four*, until the thunder finally rolled in behind it, and then she would tell me how far off the storm still was. If the count was long, the storm was miles away, and I could be unafraid. If the count grew shorter each time, it was coming closer. The gap between the flash and the sound was how you knew where the storm really stood, and whether it was moving toward you or away.
It was years before I understood what a strange and beautiful thing that gap actually is.
Light comes at once; sound takes its time

The lightning and the thunder are the same event. They happen together, in the same instant, born of the same violent tearing in the sky. They leave at the same moment. But they do not arrive together, because they travel at wildly different speeds.

Light is almost unimaginably fast, for any distance you could see across, it arrives essentially the moment it leaves. But sound is slow. Sound lumbers. It moves through the air at a pace you could very nearly track, taking a full five seconds to cross a single mile. So the flash reaches you instantly, and then you wait, one, two, three, while the sound of the very same event is still crossing the distance toward you, still on its way, still *coming.* The thunder you finally hear is the sound of something that already happened. You are, in a small and literal way, always hearing the past. The sound is real, and true, and dispatched. It is simply still in transit.

And that gap, that strange silent interval between seeing and hearing, is not a sign that the thunder isn't coming. It is the measure of how far the sound still has to travel. The silence *is* the distance. Nothing is missing. Something is on its way.
I cannot tell you how much this reframed a certain kind of spiritual waiting for me, the hardest kind, the kind that comes *after* God has already moved.
The silence after the flash

There is a particular anguish we do not talk about enough, and it is not the anguish of a God who seems absent. It is the stranger ache of having genuinely *seen* Him, a prayer clearly answered, a door unmistakably opened, a moment you knew beyond argument was Him, and then finding yourself in a long, ringing silence where nothing further seems to arrive. You saw the flash. You know it was real; you were there; the light landed and lit up your whole sky for an instant. And now you are sitting in the quiet that came after, counting, and the thunder has not rolled in, and you begin to wonder whether you imagined the lightning altogether.

That is a brutal place to sit, because the silence tempts you to unsee the flash. *If it were really Him,* the doubt whispers, *wouldn't the whole of it have arrived by now? Wouldn't I still feel it? This quiet must mean it wasn't real.*

But the porch taught me otherwise. The gap after the flash is not evidence that nothing happened. It is the sound still crossing the distance. What you saw was real and instantaneous, the light does not lie, and now you are simply in the interval, the travel time, the space between the seeing and the full arrival. The silence is not the absence of the thunder. It is the measure of a sound still on its way to you.
The voice still crossing the distance
The Scriptures are full of the voice of God described as exactly this, as thunder.

There is an old song, one of the psalms, that does almost nothing but stand in awe of it: the voice of Yahuah over the waters, the voice of Yahuah in power, the voice of Yahuah that breaks the great trees and shakes the wilderness and makes the whole earth answer. The God of glory, it says, thunders. And I notice that the writer does not reach for lightning, for the silent flash. He reaches for *thunder*, the sound that takes its time, that rolls in after, that fills the sky once it finally arrives. As if the word of God were less like a flash that is over in an instant and more like a sound still traveling toward you across a distance, gathering, coming.

And another of the prophets puts words in God's own mouth about exactly this, that His word goes out from His mouth and does not come back to Him empty, but accomplishes what He sent it for and succeeds in the thing He dispatched it to do. Hold that next to the storm. A word *goes out.* It is sent. And a thing that has been sent, and has not yet arrived, is not a thing that failed. It is a thing in transit. When God has spoken over your life, when you saw the flash of Him promising, calling, beginning something, that word did not evaporate in the silence that followed. It is crossing the distance. It is still coming. The quiet you are counting through is not proof it will never land. It is the travel time of a thunder that left the same instant the light did and is, even now, on its way.
Count the gap and take heart
So here is what I want to hand you, if you are sitting in the silence after you were sure you saw God move.

Do not unsee the flash. The light does not lie, and you were not making it up. Something real happened, and it happened all at once, and it happened *for you.* You are not in an absence. You are in an interval, the counted, aching, faith-stretching gap between the seeing and the full arrival, which is not empty at all but full of a sound still traveling toward you.

And here is the tender part my grandmother knew that I did not, sitting small beside her in the dark. The gap tells you not only that the thunder is coming, but *where the storm stands*, and a storm that is genuinely of God is a storm moving toward you, not away. Every silence you count through is one you will not have to count again, because what has been sent does not turn back. The word is on its way. The sound left when the light did. And one day, at the end of a count you did not think you could hold through, the thunder of it will finally roll in and fill your whole sky, and you will know that the quiet was never the end of the story, only the distance a faithful sound had left to travel to reach you.
Count the gap. Take heart in it. It is not silence. It is thunder, still on its way.

pieces.title: The Same Song in a Lower Key
pieces.imagePrompt: A young Black woman curled on a sofa in a sun-drenched living room, warm headphones over her ears and eyes closed in serene delight as a favorite song washes over her, a soft radiant smile of peace and quiet joy on her face; wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, bright golden-hour light, premium worship-brand cinematic film-still warmth, authentic and tender, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: Move a melody into a different key and every single note changes, and yet the song stays unmistakably itself, because a tune lives in the relationships between its notes, not in the notes themselves. I think that is exactly how a life can be transposed into the darkest season and still be the same song God has been playing all along.

body.text: A singer once told me, apologetically, that she could not reach the top of a song I had written. It sat too high for her; the climbing notes strained and cracked, and she was embarrassed, as if the failure were hers.

So I sat down at the keyboard and moved the whole thing down. Not a little, a long way down, into a register her voice could live in comfortably. And here is the thing I want you to notice, the thing so ordinary that we forget how strange it is: *every single note changed.* Not one pitch from the original remained. The song she sang was, note for note, a completely different set of sounds than the song I had written. And she knew it instantly. She started singing on the first chord, no music in front of her, because it was, obviously, unmistakably, without a shadow of doubt, the *same song.*
I have done this ten thousand times. It is the most routine thing a musician does. And I still find it quietly miraculous, because it means a song is not what I always assumed a song was.
The song is not in the notes
You would think a melody *is* its notes. That "the tune" means these particular pitches in this particular order, and change them and you have changed the song.

But that is not how it works, and almost no one has the kind of hearing that would even let them believe otherwise. A tiny handful of people have what is called perfect pitch. They hear a note and know its exact name, its precise frequency, the way you know a color on sight. But the overwhelming majority of us, nearly everyone reading this, do not hear that way at all. We have *relative* pitch. We do not recognize a melody by its absolute pitches. We recognize it by the *relationships* between the notes: this one higher than that one by a certain reach, this one falling to that one by a certain step, the shape of the rises and drops, the pattern of the intervals. The song lives in the *relationships,* not in the notes.

Which is why you can begin a familiar tune on any note in the world and everyone still knows it at once. Move the whole thing up, move it down, every pitch is now different, and as long as the *relationships between* the notes are kept, the song is perfectly, undeniably intact. You can transpose a melody into a key with not one note in common with the original, and it survives completely, because its identity was never in the pitches. Its identity was in how the notes stood in relation to one another. Change all the notes, keep the relationships, and you have not lost the song. You have only moved it.
And the day that truly landed on me, I understood something about the hardest seasons of a life that I had needed for years.
When your whole life is transposed
Because a life gets transposed. That is what a hard season actually is.

One day you are living in a certain key, a comfortable register, the notes falling where you expected them, the melody of your days in a range you could sing without strain. And then something moves the whole thing down. A diagnosis. A loss. A door that closed. A grief that dropped your entire life into a lower, darker key overnight, and suddenly *every note is different.* The mornings feel different. The prayers sound different. The future you were humming is in a register you do not recognize, low and heavy and strange in your mouth. And it is so easy, in that transposition, to conclude that the song is *over*, that because every note has changed, the melody itself has been lost, that whatever God was playing through your life has stopped and something else, something worse, has taken its place.
But every note changing is not the same as the song ending.

If the *relationships* hold, if the shape of the thing endures, if the way the notes stand toward one another is kept even as the pitches all drop, then it is the same song. Transposed into a key you never wanted, yes. Harder to sing, lower, aching, unfamiliar under your fingers, absolutely. But the same melody God has been playing through your life all along, now sounding in a register you did not choose. The theme did not die when the key changed. It only moved. And a melody in a minor, low, sorrowing key is not a broken melody. Sometimes it is the same beloved theme finally sounding at the depth it always had in it.
The theme He never abandoned
The Scriptures give us a whole life shaped exactly like this, and his name was Joseph.

Consider the key changes. A favored son in his father's house, then, in a single afternoon, thrown in a pit and sold, his whole life dropped into slavery. A trusted servant rising in a foreign house, then falsely accused and dropped again, lower still, into a prison with no visible bottom. Every stretch of his story is a transposition, always downward, every note changing, nothing where it was before. And if you had asked him in the pit, or in the cell, whether God was still playing his song, I do not think he could have heard it. The key had changed too many times.

And yet, at the end, standing before the very brothers who had thrown him down, he says the sentence that reveals the melody was never lost: *you meant it for evil, but God meant it for good.* The same events. He does not deny a note of the darkness. He names it plainly, *you meant it for evil.* But he had come to hear that underneath every brutal key change, one theme had been sounding the whole time, and the relationships had held, and it was, from the pit to the palace, the same song. God had never stopped playing it. He had only kept transposing it into keys Joseph could not yet sing.

There is a line late in the Scriptures that I read now as the deepest promise of all to a transposed life: that Yeshua the Messiah is the same yesterday and today and forever. The keys of our lives change constantly, up in the bright years, down in the dark ones, restless and modulating through every season. But the One the song is truly about does not change. He is the theme that holds through every transposition, the constant relationship every note in your life is measured against. And as long as He holds, the song holds, in any key, however low, however far from where it began.
Sing it in the key you're in
So if your life has been dropped into a key you never wanted, if every note is different now and you have been grieving it as the end of the music. I want to offer you the songwriter's truest secret.

You have not lost the song. You have been transposed. Every pitch may have changed; the melody has not, because the melody was never in the pitches. It was in the relationships, and the deepest relationship. You to the God who is the same yesterday, today, and forever, has not moved an inch. The theme He has been playing through your whole life is still playing. It is only sounding, for now, in a lower and more aching key than you would have chosen, and one day you will hear how much depth that key gave it.

Do not wait for the old bright key to return before you are willing to sing. Sing it low. Sing it in the register you are actually in, with all the notes changed and your voice cracking on the reach of it. It is still the same song. He is still the one composing it. And a melody transposed into the dark and sung anyway is not a lesser music. It may be the truest performance of the theme your life was ever going to give.

pieces.title: The Vendor Whose Whole Day Was a Song
pieces.imagePrompt: A beaming Latin street vendor pushes his steaming cart up a sunlit market lane at golden hour, one hand cupped to his mouth mid-song and his whole face alight with joy, while smiling neighbors lean from bright doorways and windows to answer his call amid glowing baskets of fruit; luminous cinematic film-still quality, warm gold amber and terracotta tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: Before I knew there was such a thing as a worship set, I knew the tamale man's cry that came up the street at dawn. It took me thirty years to understand that he was teaching me where God actually raises His voice.

body.text: Before I knew there was such a thing as a worship set, before I could have told you what a bridge was or why a key change lifts you off your feet, I knew the tamale man.

He came up our street every morning while the light was still gray and thin, pushing a cart that squeaked on one wheel, and he sang. Not a song exactly. One long word, stretched and bent until it filled the whole block, *tamaaaaales*, rising at the front, falling soft at the end, a little cracked from the cold. My abuela knew his cry the way you know a voice on the phone before anyone says a name. She would already be reaching for coins before he came into view.

There was the knife-sharpener too, who did not sing at all but played a little wooden flute, five falling notes, the same five every time, and everyone on the street knew what those five notes meant: bring me your dull blades. There was the woman with the basket of *pan dulce* balanced on her head, calling in a voice that could carry three streets. There was the man who bought old iron, and the man who sold brooms, and each of them had a melody that belonged to no one but them. You could stand in our kitchen with your eyes closed and know exactly who was passing, and how far away, and whether they were coming or going.

I thought this was just noise. The soundtrack of being poor. It took me a long time, thirty years and a great deal of travel and study, to understand that the whole street was singing, and that it was teaching me something the sanctuary never quite got around to saying out loud.
The song was the invitation

Here is what I finally saw. The vendor did not sing because he had leisure. He sang because he had bread to sell and mouths to feed at home, and the song was how the bread found the mouths. The melody was not decoration on the labor. The melody *was* the labor. It went ahead of him into houses he would never enter, up stairs he would never climb, and it said, in a form no closed door could keep out: *there is something here for you, come and get it while it is warm.*
That is not far at all from how the Scriptures describe the voice of God.

We tend to picture Wisdom as a quiet thing, a scholar in a still room. But the Proverbs put her somewhere else entirely. They say she does not whisper in the seminary. She stands at the busiest corner of the city, at the head of the noisy streets, in the gates where the traffic is thickest, and she *raises her voice*. She calls out over the haggling and the cart wheels and the arguments. She cries aloud in the one place respectable people assume God would never lower Himself to shout, the marketplace, the barrio, the ordinary grinding street where people are just trying to make it to the end of the day.

I grew up thinking the holy voice was the hushed one. The one you had to go inside and be quiet to hear. And there is a real and precious quiet with God, I will not take that from you. But the tamale man taught me the other half. Sometimes the voice of God is not the one that waits for you to come and find it. Sometimes it is the one that comes up your street before you are even awake, cracked from the cold, stretched out over one long word, refusing to let a wall or a door or your poverty keep it from you.
He sold to everyone the same

I noticed something else as a boy, though I did not have language for it then. The vendor's cry did not change based on who lived in the house. He sang the same word up at the fine painted door and the leaning tin one. He did not lower his price for being liked or raise his voice only for the customers who could pay the most. The song went out over the whole street, indiscriminate, generous, the same warm offer to every window.

The prophets caught this and would not let it go. There is a passage where the invitation is thrown wide open. Everyone who is thirsty, come to the water; you who have no money, come, buy and eat without money and without price. That is not the pitch of a merchant protecting his margin. That is a vendor who wants his cart empty by noon not because he was paid but because everyone got fed. That is the strangest economy in the world, and it is the economy of Yahuah. He is out in the street at dawn calling the whole barrio to a table where the poorest can eat first.

We forget this in our buildings. We build the worship for the ones already inside, already fed, already able to read the bulletin and follow the changes. And the song God keeps singing is out on the corner, aimed at the window that never comes in, cupping its hands and calling one more time toward the people the market forgot.
Your ordinary labor is already a melody
Here is where I want to land it, because I think many of you reading this are tired, and are working jobs that feel about as holy as a squeaky cart.

You have believed a lie that the song and the labor are two different things, that worship is the part where you finally stop working and lift your hands, and the rest of the day is just survival. The vendor never believed that. For him the cry and the work were one motion. The song was how the work reached people. The work was what gave the song something to carry.

I think Yeshua worked a trade with sawdust in His hair for most of His years, and I do not believe He stopped worshiping the Father when He picked up a tool. I think the swing of the hammer had a rhythm and the rhythm had a prayer in it, the same way the drum was praying in me before I had the words. The sacred was not waiting for Him at the synagogue on the seventh day only. It was in the grain of the wood on the second day too.

So sing your street. Whatever your cart is, the cash register, the classroom, the bus route, the sink full of dishes at midnight. There is a melody the Father is asking you to carry up it, an invitation your ordinary passing can push under doors you will never open. You do not have to be inside a sanctuary for your voice to be holy. The tamale man never was. He just came up the street at dawn, cracked and generous and unashamed, and made a whole barrio hungry for something warm.
That was worship. I have been trying to learn his song ever since.
Come and get it, mi gente. It is still warm.

pieces.title: The Carol That Walks Into the Cold
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful band of Romanian village carolers in heavy coats and scarves singing down a snow-covered lane at blue dusk, cold-reddened cheeks and faces bright with delight, breath fogging the freezing air as a handmade star glows warm gold above them and lantern light spills from a cottage door thrown open in welcome; warm cinematic film-still quality, gold lantern light against deep blue snow tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: In the Romanian villages, the carolers do not sing where it is warm. They put on their heaviest coats and walk out into the snow to sing news too big to keep inside a house. I have never forgotten what that taught me about the shepherds.

body.text: The first time I heard the *colinde* I was a long way from any barrio I knew, in a Romanian village where the snow came up over my boots and the cold got into the seams of my coat and stayed there. I had come to learn how these people worshiped, because I had been told their winter songs were among the oldest in the Christian world, and I wanted to hear them where they lived and not on a recording.
What I did not expect was that they would make me go outside to hear them.

I had assumed, coming from a warmer place, that a winter carol would be an indoor thing, that you would gather around a fire with something hot to drink and sing where it was comfortable. That is not how the *colindători* do it. When the light goes blue in the late afternoon they put on their heaviest coats, the ones that smell of woodsmoke and sheep, and they gather at the edge of the village. Someone carries a star made by hand, a great wooden star on a pole with a candle glowing inside it, and they walk. House to house, through snow that squeaks under the boots, breath fogging in front of every face, they walk out into the cold and they sing.

They do not wait for people to come to the church. They carry the song to the door. And at each house the door opens, and warmth and lantern light spill out into the freezing dark, and the people inside stand in the doorway and receive the news as though they had not heard it in a thousand years, though of course they hear it every winter of their lives.
I stood in that snow with my feet going numb and I understood something I had read a hundred times and never once felt.
The shepherds could not keep it indoors

Think about how the news of Yeshua's birth actually broke, the first night. Yahuah did not announce it in the palace. He did not send it to the temple first, to the men with the credentials and the good chairs. He sent it to men who were outside in the cold at that very hour, out in the fields at night, keeping the sheep because someone has to and it is not going to be anyone who can afford not to.
The heavens opened over the *shepherds*. Over the ones on the night shift. And the sky filled with a song so enormous that the men fell down in terror before they could take in that it was good.

Here is the part I want you to hold. When the light closed up again and the field went dark and ordinary, the shepherds did not go home and keep the wonder to themselves. The account says they went with haste to find the child, and then, this is the line that undid me in that snow. They could not stop talking about it. They told everyone. They made known abroad what had been said to them about this child, until everyone who heard them was amazed. Men whose whole job was to stay put with the flock got up and became the first carolers in the history of the world, walking from person to person in the cold with news too big to keep inside.

That is exactly what the Romanian village was doing in front of me. They were not putting on a concert. They were being the shepherds. They were rehearsing, in the oldest way they knew, the truth that this news does not belong to the warm room. It belongs to the doorway. It belongs to the cold lane and the far house and the neighbor you have not spoken to since the argument last spring. You carry the star to them. You do not make them come find the light. You bring it, glowing on a pole, out into the dark.
Worship that costs you the warm room
I have thought about those numb feet for years, and I have decided the cold was not incidental. It was the whole point.

It is easy to sing where it is comfortable. It costs you nothing to lift your hands in a heated building among people who already agree with you. But the *colinde* asks something of the body. It asks you to leave the fire and go out into the weather, to sing badly through chattering teeth, to walk to a door that might not open and knock anyway. The discomfort is not a flaw in the tradition. It is the tradition telling the truth about what the news is worth. You do not carry a small thing into the snow. You only walk out into the cold for something you cannot bear to keep to yourself.

I come from a people who worship loudly and in the street, who let the procession spill down the middle of the road and turn the whole barrio into a sanctuary with no walls. I felt the same Spirit in that frozen Romanian lane, wearing a heavier coat. Different weather, same refusal to let the praise stay indoors. My people carry it out into the heat and the dust; theirs carry it out into the snow and the dark; and in both places the song is saying the same thing to the closed door, *He is born, He is here, come and see, we could not keep it to ourselves.*
Your song was never meant to stay in the building

Maybe you have made worship a warm-room thing. I understand the pull of it. The world outside is cold in more ways than the weather, and the gathered room is one of the few places you feel safe. Sing there. Be warmed there. God meant that room to hold you.

But do not let the door become the border of your praise. There is someone on your street tonight who has not heard the news in a way that reached them, someone whose door has not opened to real warmth in a long time, someone who would never in a thousand years walk into your building but who might stand in their own doorway if the song came to them. The shepherds did not wait to be qualified. They were the least qualified people in the story and they became the first evangelists in it, simply because they could not shut up about what they had seen.
Put on the heavy coat. Pick up the star. The news is too big for the warm room, and it always was.
Walk it out into the cold, mi gente. Somebody's door is about to open.

pieces.title: The Accordion Breathes Both Directions
pieces.imagePrompt: A weathered accordionist with eyes closed and a wide joyful grin plays at a warm outdoor family dance at golden hour, bellows pulled wide with sunlight glowing through the pleats, while multigenerational couples laugh and spin beneath strings of warm lights behind him; luminous cinematic film-still quality, warm gold amber and rich red tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: An old accordionist told me his instrument had one rule I would never outgrow. It only makes music when the air is moving, and it has to move both ways. I have been thinking about that rule ever since, because I am fairly sure it is also the rule for a soul.

body.text: There is an old man in my memory who played the accordion at every wedding, every quinceañera, every backyard where enough folding chairs could be borrowed, for as long as anyone could remember. His instrument was older than my father. The bellows were patched with tape in two places and it wheezed a little between phrases, like it was catching its breath, which as it turns out is exactly what it was doing.

I asked him once, when I was young and thought I was clever, why he did not get a better one. A keyboard, maybe. Something that did not have to be squeezed. He looked at me the way you look at a boy who has just told you he would rather not breathe so much, and he said something I did not understand for many years.

He said the accordion only makes music when the air is moving. And here was the part that stayed with me. He said it has to move *both ways*. Pull the bellows open and it sings. Push them closed and it sings again. There is no such thing as an accordion note that does not involve air passing through the reed. Stop the air in either direction and the instrument goes silent. It is not really a keyboard at all, he said. It is a pair of lungs with buttons.
I have been thinking about that rule ever since, because I am fairly sure it is also the rule for a soul.
The whole thing starts with borrowed air

Go back to the very beginning, to the making of the first man. The account is startlingly physical about it. Yahuah forms a shape out of the dust of the ground, no life in it yet, just clay in the shape of a person, lying there. And then He does the tenderest thing in all of Scripture. He bends down and breathes into it. He puts His own breath into the dust, and only then does the man become a living soul.

You were clay with the breath of God moving through you. That is not poetry I am adding. That is the diagnosis. Every note your life has ever made, every good thing that ever came out of you, was the reed of you vibrating because His air was passing through. The accordion does not manufacture its own wind. Neither do you. The old man's patched bellows and your patched-up heart run on exactly the same principle: no borrowed breath, no music.

I think we forget this constantly. We start to believe the sound is coming *from* us, that we are the source, that the reason there is music in our lives is that we are, at bottom, talented. And then a season comes when the air stops moving, grief, or exhaustion, or the long gray silence where God feels far off, and we panic, because we discover we cannot make a single true note on our own. We were never the wind. We were always the reed. And the reed is a beautiful thing, but it is silent until something greater than itself decides to breathe.
Praise on the way in and the way out
Here is where the accordion's second rule undid me, the both-ways rule.

We are good, in the church, at teaching people to breathe in from God. Receive His grace. Take in His word. Draw on His strength. Inhale. And that is true and we should never stop. But the accordion will not let you leave it there, because a pair of lungs that only ever pulls air in bursts. You have to push it back out. The instrument sings on the exhale as truly as on the inhale, and a soul that only receives and never returns anything is a soul holding its breath until it turns blue.

The last line of the Psalms is not complicated. It says let everything that has breath praise Yahuah. Everything that has breath. Which means the very evidence that you have received the gift, the fact that air is in your lungs at all, is the reason and the material for giving something back. Every breath is on loan, and praise is simply the exhale of a life that noticed. You pull His mercy in. You push His praise out. In, out, in, out, and the music is happening the entire time, on both halves of the motion, and there is never a moment where you are not either receiving or returning.

The old man understood this in his body without ever putting it in a sentence. Watch an accordionist and you will see it, the constant motion, open and close, open and close, never resting on one, because the second you stop moving the air the joy stops. He was not playing a machine. He was demonstrating a theology of the breath, all night, for people who only wanted to dance.
The music is for the dancing

And they *did* dance. That is the part I do not want to lose. This was not a lesson delivered from a stage. It was a wheezing patched-up accordion at a backyard party, and the whole reason the man kept the air moving both directions was so that his cousins and his neighbors and the shy teenagers along the wall would eventually get up and move.

I love that the breath God put in the first man was not given so that man could sit very still and think holy thoughts. It was given for *living*, for working and laughing and weeping and holding people and, yes, for dancing at your niece's wedding until your feet hurt. The breath is for the celebration. Worship at its fullest is not a solemn withholding of the exhale; it is a body given permission to move because it finally understands where the air came from and Who keeps sending more.
So let me ask you plainly, because the accordion asks it of me. Which direction have you stopped breathing?

Some of you have stopped pulling air in. You have been giving and serving and pouring out for so long that the bellows are collapsed and there is nothing left to push, and you are trying to make music on empty. You do not need to try harder. You need to open back up and let Him breathe into the dust of you again. That is not weakness. That is the first thing that ever happened to you.

And some of you have stopped pushing air out. You have received and received, sat under good teaching, taken in more grace than you will ever use, and gone silent, a lung holding its breath, a reed with all that wind sitting motionless behind it. The exhale is waiting. Some praise, some service, some love pushed back out toward God and toward the people He put in front of you.
The rule is the same as it was for the patched old accordion in my memory. The music only happens when the air is moving, and it has to move both ways.
Breathe, mi gente. In and out. That is where the song lives.

pieces.title: We Came in the Dark to Sing You Awake
pieces.imagePrompt: A small band of joyful friends with guitars gathered beneath a lit second-story window in the deep blue hour before dawn, their upturned faces radiant and laughing in the first blush of rose-gold sunrise, breath visible in the cool air as they serenade a beloved awake; warm cinematic film-still quality, deep indigo giving way to warm rose-gold dawn tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: In the serenata you do not wait until morning to sing. You gather under the window while it is still dark, and you sing the person awake, and the day begins with a voice loving you before your eyes are even open. I think David knew that secret, and I think God still practices it.

body.text: The serenata always begins as a conspiracy.

You gather in the dark, several of you, while the person you have come for is still deep asleep and knows nothing. You keep your voices down on the way. Somebody carries the guitar; somebody else is only there to clap and cannot be trusted to stay quiet; there is always one cousin who insists he is going to sing the high harmony and always one who begs him not to. You arrive under the window while the street is still that deep blue that is not quite night and not yet morning, and you look up at the dark glass, and on a breath, all together, you begin.

And here is the thing about the serenata that I have never gotten over, even after singing dozens of them. You do not sing to a person who is awake. You sing to wake them. The whole point is that the first thing they experience of the new day, before their eyes are even open, before they have washed their face or remembered their troubles or braced for whatever the day holds, is a voice, several voices, under their window, in the cold and the dark, telling them they are loved.
The day begins with a song that got there before they did.

I have sung a girl awake on her birthday and watched the lamp come on behind the curtain and then the curtain move and then a face appear, sleep-creased and startled and slowly breaking into the kind of smile you do not get any other way. I have sung *Las Mañanitas* to an old woman who wept in her doorway in her robe because no one had done it for her in forty years. And every single time, the miracle is the same and it is this: love arrived while she was still asleep. She did not earn it awake. It was already outside her window, tuning up in the dark, before she had done one single thing that day to deserve it.
David woke the dawn on purpose

There is a line in the Psalms that I did not understand until I had sung enough serenatas, and now I cannot read it any other way. David, in a season when his heart is fixed and steady, calls out to his own soul to wake up, and he tells his instruments to wake up, and then he says the most audacious thing, *I myself will awake the dawn.*

Not: I will wait for the dawn and then praise. Not: when the sun comes up I will feel like singing. He says he is going to get up before the light, while it is still dark, and sing so early and so fiercely that his song will be the thing that rouses the morning. He is going to serenade the sunrise. He is going to sing the day awake instead of waiting for the day to grant him permission to sing.

That is the boldest posture of worship I know, and it is exactly the posture of the serenata. You do not sing because conditions are good. You sing *into* the dark to make the good conditions arrive. You get up before there is any evidence of morning and you lift your voice as though the light were already on the way, because it is, because it always is, because the God who made the mornings has never once failed to send one.

I think many of us have it backward. We wait to feel the dawn before we will sing. We say, when this lifts, when the diagnosis is better, when the money comes, when I feel God again, then I will worship. David says no. Awake the dawn. Be the voice under the window of your own dark night, singing the morning up before it has shown its face. The song does not come after the light. In David's practice, the song comes first, and the light comes because someone was willing to sing in the dark.
He is already outside your window
But here is the turn I most want you to have, because it is the sweeter half.
You are not only meant to be the one who sings the serenata. You are meant to know that one is being sung *to you*.

There is a mercy in the Scriptures that arrives fresh every single morning, before you have done anything to earn the day. The prophet says it plainly: the compassions of Yahuah are new every morning, and great is His faithfulness. New every morning. Which means that while you were asleep, while you were doing nothing, while your troubles were still waiting for you on the other side of waking, the mercy for this exact day was already being prepared and set outside your window. You did not wake up and then receive it. It was there before your eyes opened, like a voice in the dark street, like cousins with a guitar who could not wait for you to be ready.

And there is another word, one of my favorites, that says Yahuah your God is in your midst, and He will rejoice over you with gladness, and He will quiet you with His love, and He will sing over you. He sings over you. The God of the universe conducts serenatas. While you sleep in your worst season, convinced you are alone and unwatched and unwanted, there is a voice under the window of your soul, and it is His, and it is singing you toward a morning you did not believe would come.
Sing into the blue hour
So let me leave you where the serenata always leaves me, standing in the cold blue dark, before there is any light, with a song on my lips anyway.

If you are in a night right now, one of the long ones, I am not going to tell you the sun is out. It is not. But I am going to tell you what the serenata knows and what David practiced and what the mercies of God prove every single day: the song does not have to wait for the morning. You can sing the morning up. You can stand under the window of your own dark and lift your voice as though love were already on its way, and it will feel like a conspiracy, and it will feel too early, and your voice will be a little cracked from the cold.

Sing anyway. That is how the dawn has always been woken. And listen, under the noise of your own singing, listen close. There is another voice out there in the dark that got to your window first, and has been singing over you the whole time, waiting for you to wake up and hear it.
The lamp is about to come on, mi gente. Keep singing. Morning is closer than the dark would have you believe.

pieces.title: The Dance That Leads the Drum
pieces.imagePrompt: A radiant open-air bomba celebration at golden hour: a beaming Afro-Caribbean woman in a swirling white-and-gold skirt caught mid-spin, arms flung high with pure delight lighting her face, while a grinning barrel-drummer leans in watching her feet to follow her lead and a ring of laughing neighbors of every age claps in the warm light; luminous cinematic film-still quality, warm amber and deep coral tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: In the bomba, the drummer does not lead the dancer. The dancer leads the drummer. I did not believe it until I saw it, and once I saw it I could not stop seeing it in the story of a king who danced so hard his own dignity could not keep up.

body.text: The first time someone explained the bomba to me, I was sure I had misunderstood the words.

I know drums. I come from a people whose worship has a heartbeat in it, who drummed on shipping crates when the drums themselves were taken away. In almost every music I had ever played, the drummer keeps the time and the dancer follows. The rhythm is the floor and the dance is the house you build on it. The drum leads. Everyone knows this.

So when the old players told me that in the bomba it is the other way around, that the *dancer* leads and the *drummer* follows. I laughed, because I thought it was a joke or a translation problem. Then they took me to see it, and it was neither.

The dancer steps into the center of the ring. The lead drummer, on the barrel drum they call the *primo*, fixes his eyes not on his own hands but on her feet, her hips, the sudden fling of her skirt. And she begins to challenge him. She throws a movement, a stamp, a turn, a snap of the cloth, and it is his job to catch it, to answer that exact gesture with a strike of the drum that lands in the same instant. She feints and he must not be fooled. She holds and he must hold with her. She explodes and he explodes under her. The whole ring is watching a conversation where the body speaks first and the drum has to keep up, and the drummer who cannot follow is the one who is embarrassed, not the dancer.
I stood there and something in my understanding of worship turned over on its side and never turned back.
Sometimes the body has to go first

We have a deep instinct, especially those of us who lead worship for a living, to make everything wait for the music. The band sets the tempo, the singer sets the feel, and the congregation is expected to *follow*, to fall in line behind whatever we have prepared, to keep step with a rhythm we set for them. And there is a place for that. Order is a gift.

But the bomba insists on a truth that the polished stage tends to bury: sometimes the praise in a person's body has to be allowed to lead, and everything else has to learn to follow *it*. Sometimes the Spirit moves in the least prepared person in the room, the grandmother in the third row, the man who cannot carry a tune, the child who does not know it is not the moment, and their whole body says *He is worthy* before the song has gotten there, and the honest thing, the holy thing, is for the music to catch up to them rather than the other way around.

The dancer in the bomba is not showing off. She is expressing something that must come out, and the drum's entire dignity is spent in trying to honor it. I have come to believe that is a picture of how Yahuah receives our worship. He is not up in heaven insisting we all stay on His tempo before He will pay attention. He is the *primo* drummer, leaning in, watching the feet of the least likely dancer in the ring, delighting to answer the movement of a heart that could not hold still.
The king who danced ahead of the music
There is a day in Israel's history when the body of the king led and the whole nation's music had to follow, and it cost him something, and he did not care.

The ark of God was coming home at last. David had it carried into the city with an entire orchestra, harps and lyres and tambourines and cymbals and the ram's horn, the full sound of a people who had waited too long for this. And in front of all of it, out ahead of the musicians, went the king himself. He danced. The account does not say he danced with restraint appropriate to his office. It says he danced before Yahuah with all his might. He had stripped off the royal robes and put on a simple linen garment, and he leapt and he whirled at the head of the procession like a man who had forgotten there was such a thing as a throne.
He was the dancer in the ring, and all the drums of Israel were behind him, and the movement of his worship set the pace for the whole city.

His wife Michal watched it from a window, and the Scripture is careful to tell us what was in her heart: she *despised* him. When he came home glowing she met him with contempt, sneering that the king had made a fool of himself in front of the servant girls, uncovering himself like one of the vulgar people who did not know any better. She wanted the dignity kept. She wanted the body kept still and the office protected and the worship kept at a respectable distance.

And David's answer is one I have leaned on my whole life. He told her that it was before Yahuah that he danced, the God who chose him over her father's house, and that he would be even more undignified than this, and humble himself even further in his own eyes, and that the very servant girls she was ashamed of him in front of were the ones who would hold him in honor. He would not shrink the dance to fit her window. He would let his body lead, and let the drums of an entire nation follow, and let his dignity land wherever it landed.
Let the drum catch up to your joy

I have met so many people who worship like Michal is watching. They keep the body still. They keep the joy at a respectable volume. They will move only after they are certain everyone else has decided it is acceptable, only after the music has clearly given permission, only after the risk of looking foolish has passed. And I understand it, because the barrio taught me long ago that a joyful people are always being told they are too much.

But the bomba, and the dancing king, keep pressing the same question on me. What if your praise was never meant to wait for permission? What if there is a movement of gratitude in you that is supposed to go *first*, ahead of the polished band, ahead of the acceptable moment, ahead of your own carefully guarded dignity, and the honest thing is to let it out and trust that heaven will answer it, that the drum of God will lean in and catch every stamp and turn of a heart that finally stopped holding still?

The dancer does not fear the drum. She trusts that it will follow her. And the God I serve is not standing back waiting for you to compose yourself. He is leaning in, watching your feet, ready to answer the smallest true movement of your joy with a strike that lands in the very same instant.
So step into the ring, mi gente. Let the body say it. The drum will catch up. It always has, it always will, and it will be more undignified than this before it is done.

pieces.title: The Blessing That Falls While the Mountain Sleeps
pieces.imagePrompt: A delighted family with young children waking at a mountain campsite at first light, laughing as they discover the whole dew-jeweled alpine meadow glittering silver-gold around them, warm radiant dawn, tender and euphoric, premium cinematic worship-brand quality, authentic and natural; wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: You go to sleep on the high ground and no rain falls all night, and yet at first light everything is soaked, the grass, the rope, your own hair. There is a blessing that works like the dew, and the oldest song about unity says that is exactly how it comes.

body.text: The first time it happened to me I thought it had rained.

I had gone up alone, the way I still do when I need the noise of my own life to stop, and I had slept the thin, cold sleep you sleep at altitude, and when I unzipped the tent at dawn the whole world was wet. The grass was bent under water. The rope I had strung between two rocks was strung with beads instead. My hair, where it had touched the fabric, was damp. And there had been no cloud all night. I had watched the stars until they blurred. Not a drop had fallen from the sky.

It was dew. Up high, the cold reaches into the air itself and pulls the water out of it, and it settles, not by falling, exactly, but by gathering, silently, on every surface willing to hold still long enough to be found. You do not hear the dew arrive. You do nothing to earn it. You go to sleep tired and wake up drenched in something you did not make and could not have stopped.
I have never read Psalm 133 the same way since.
The shortest song about the hardest thing

It is one of the songs the old pilgrims sang going up to the feasts, and it is short, only three verses, and it is about the one thing that is nearly impossible for people to do, which is to live together without tearing each other apart. How good and how pleasant it is, the song says, when brothers dwell together in unity. Anyone who has been part of a family, or a village, or a church, or a band, knows that the song is not describing something common. It is describing a miracle. Unity is not the natural state of people. It is the rare and lovely exception, and everyone who has tasted it knows they did not manufacture it.
So the song reaches for two pictures, and both of them run downhill.

The first is oil. The precious oil poured on the head of Aaron, running down over his beard, running down onto the collar of his robes. It is a strange image to modern ears, but the point is the direction. The oil is poured at the top and travels down, covering everything below it, until the whole man is glistening and fragrant and set apart. Nobody rubs the oil upward. It comes from above and it descends.

The second picture is the one I woke up inside of on that cold morning. Like the dew of Hermon, the song says, coming down on the mountains of Zion. Hermon is the great snow-crowned mountain in the north, the tallest thing in that whole country, and its dew is famous, heavy, generous, the kind that soaks a man to the skin. And the song imagines that abundance settling all the way down onto the lower hills, as though the wealth of the high mountain were being shared with everything beneath it. There, the song says, Yahuah commanded the blessing. There, life that does not end.
You cannot rub it upward
I have spent a lot of years around people who are exhausted from trying to generate the dew.

They want unity, and they are right to want it, because it really is good and really is pleasant, and where it is missing everything else curdles. So they organize. They strategize. They call the meeting and give the speech and draft the values and hang them on the wall. And none of it is wrong, exactly, but none of it is dew, either, because dew does not come from horizontal effort. It comes down. It is commanded from a height. It settles in the dark on whatever held still long enough to receive it.

This is the quiet, humbling thing the mountain teaches you about blessing, and about worship, and about the love between people that God calls good. You cannot climb to it and you cannot squeeze it out of the air by wanting it badly enough. You can only make yourself the kind of surface it is willing to settle on. You can hold still. You can stay out under the open sky through the cold hours when nothing seems to be happening. You can stop thrashing.
The dew does not fall on the tent that is being packed and unpacked all night by an anxious hand. It falls on the grass that stayed where it was.
What forms in the dark

Here is what struck me most, out there, and what I keep bringing back down the mountain with me. The dew forms while you sleep. It does its whole silent work in the exact hours when you are least able to help. You contribute nothing but your presence.
