pieces.excerpt: There is one line in the Psalms that tells you exactly where Yahuah chooses to sit down. Not on gold. Not on clouds. On the praises of His people. Which means a room full of worshippers is not just singing. It is building a throne.

body.text: If you could see it, you would never sing a lazy note again.

Because there is a moment in every gathering of praising people when something is being *built*. Not felt, built. A structure rises in the room, invisible to the eye but real as timber, and Yahuah walks in and takes His seat on it. He does not bring the throne with Him. He builds it out of what comes out of your mouth.

I am not being poetic for effect. This is one of the most staggering sentences in the whole songbook, and most people read right over it because the English goes soft exactly where the Hebrew goes electric.
The line hiding in the darkest psalm
The sentence lives in Psalm 22, and you should feel the weight of *where* it sits.

Psalm 22 is the psalm of abandonment. It opens with the cry that Yeshua Himself would later scream from the cross: *My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?* It is the lowest note in the entire book, a song sung from the very bottom of feeling forgotten. And then, one breath after that cry, before any rescue has arrived, the singer says something that turns the whole psalm on its hinge. He says: *but You are holy, enthroned on the praises of Israel.*
In the pit, with no answer yet in sight, he reaches past his own feelings and grabs onto a fact about God, and the fact is this: *You sit down on our praise.*
The Hebrew is *yoshev tehillot Yisrael*. Let me open it up, because both words are doing something English flattens.

*Yoshev* comes from *yashab*, to sit, to dwell, to remain, to be *enthroned*. It is the same posture word used elsewhere of the One who *sits enthroned* above the cherubim, the King taking His royal seat. It is not a casual sitting. It is a monarch lowering Himself onto his throne to reign. And what is the throne, in this line? *Tehillot*, praises. The plural of *tehillah*, a song of praise. That word is so central to Israel's worship that the entire book of Psalms is called *Tehillim* in Hebrew, the Praises. It is cut from the same ancient root as *hallelu*: to shine, to boast, to make a radiant, unashamed noise over God.

Put it together and the sentence says: *the King takes His royal seat on the shining, boasting praises of His people.* Where a normal king's throne is built of cedar and gold, this King's throne is assembled out of worship. He sits down on the sound.
He does not haul in the throne. We raise it.
Stop and let that reorder your whole idea of a worship service.

We tend to imagine that Yahuah arrives already enthroned, and our praise is just the polite noise we make in the presence of a King who was seated whether we showed up or not. And it is true that His majesty needs nothing from us. He was King before the first star and will be King after the last one burns out.

But this line tells you something He has *chosen*. When it comes to His dwelling *among a people*, His manifest, felt, come-close reign in an actual room full of actual human beings. He has decided to make Himself at home on their praise. He inhabits it. He settles onto it. The tehillot are the seat.

Which means a gathering of worshippers is not merely admiring a King who is already comfortable. It is *raising the platform of His reign in that place*. Every honest line of praise is another beam laid, another plank set, until there is a throne standing in the middle of the room and the King steps forward and sits.

You have felt this. You have been in the ordinary room, folding chairs, tired people, a leader a little nervous, and somewhere in the third or fourth song the whole atmosphere changed. It got *heavier* and *lighter* at the same time. People stopped watching the stage and started meaning the words. And what you were feeling was not the sound system. It was the King taking His seat on a throne the room had, without knowing it, been building the whole time.
A crowd that praises is not decorating His presence. It is constructing His throne, one line at a time, and summoning His reign into the room.
Why this makes your worst days matter most
Here is the part I cannot get over, and it comes straight back to *where* the line sits.

The throne-building sentence is not spoken from a mountaintop of feeling. It is spoken from the pit, *why have You forsaken me?*, one breath earlier. The singer builds the throne with a voice that is still shaking. He does not wait until the rescue comes to declare that God is enthroned on praise. He declares it *in the dark*, and the declaring is itself the first plank.

So do not believe the lie that your praise only counts when your heart is full. The most load-bearing worship in any room is almost always coming from the person who has the least reason to give it, the one singing through the divorce, through the diagnosis, through the silence where an answer was supposed to be. When *that* voice says *You are holy, You are worthy, You reign*, that is not a weak note. That is the strongest beam in the whole structure. Heaven knows exactly what it cost, and the King is drawn to sit precisely there.

This is why the enemy of your soul works so hard to keep you quiet on your hardest days. He is not afraid of your feelings. He is afraid of your *building*. He knows that if a hurting person opens their mouth and boasts on Yahuah anyway, a throne goes up in a place the darkness was counting on to stay empty, and the King moves in.
So sing like you are building something
I want you to walk into your next gathering and see it for what it is.

You are not an audience. You are a construction crew. Every person who came in carrying a hard week, every voice that decides to lift the shout whether it feels it or not, is laying material for a throne that the King of the universe has *promised* to come and sit on. That is not a metaphor to make you feel better about singing. It is the mechanics of the room. He said He would inhabit the praises of His people, and He does not go back on where He said He would sit down.

And notice, the line says *the praises of Israel*, not *the praise of one Israelite*. It is a people's word. One plank does not make a throne. But a *gathering*, a whole company lifting the shout at once, the strong covering the weak, the full-hearted carrying the empty-handed, that raises a seat wide enough for the King to reign over the entire room, and everyone in it goes home having been ruled by the very thing they built.

So do not mumble. Do not save it for when the mood is right. Somewhere in your city tonight a handful of ordinary people are about to open their mouths and raise a throne out of nothing but worship, and the King of Heaven is already on His way to take His seat.
Build it well. He is coming to sit down.

pieces.excerpt: We think of joy as a mood that can strike anywhere. But the Psalms insist that worship has a geography, a mountain, a city, a gathering-place the poets called the joy of the whole earth. And they say something wild about where it keeps everyone's happiness stored.

body.text: We talk about joy as if it has no address.

We say it *strikes* us, *washes over* us, *comes and goes*, as if it were weather, drifting in from nowhere and out again, and the best we can do is stand in the open and hope some of it lands on us. Joy, we assume, is a mood, and moods have no map.

The poets of the Psalms would have found that idea strange to the point of sadness. Because they knew something we have almost entirely forgotten: worship has a *geography*. Joy has a mountain. There is a place on the map where the springs of gladness rise, and the whole song of Israel keeps pointing back to it with an almost unbearable homesickness.
They called it Zion. And what they said about it will change how you think about where your own joy is supposed to come from.
A mountain called the joy of the whole earth

In one of the great Zion psalms, the poet stands and looks at the city set on its hill and reaches for the biggest thing he can say about it. He does not call it the joy of Israel. He does not call it the joy of Jerusalem. He calls Mount Zion *the joy of the whole earth*.

The Hebrew there is *mesos kol ha'aretz*, the exultation, the glad shout, of *all the land*, of the entire earth. Not one people's happiness. Everybody's. He is looking at a single ridge of rock in a small, contested country and declaring that the gladness of the *planet* has its source right there.

You have to understand what Zion actually was to feel the audacity of that. Zion started as a *fortress*, a stubborn hill the city was built on, a stronghold that had to be taken by force before it could become the city of the great King. It was stone and slope and hard-won ground. And the poets looked at that fortified rock and said: this is where the joy of the world lives. Not a feeling. A *place*. Beautiful in its height, they sang, the crown of the earth's gladness, this mountain, this city, this exact spot where Yahuah had chosen to set His name and gather His people.

Worship, to them, was never a free-floating mood. It had a *there*. And the whole nation oriented its year around going *up* to it, walking the roads to the mountain, singing songs written for the climb. They did not wait for joy to find them. They went to where it was kept.
Where everyone's happiness is stored
Now the second Zion psalm turns the astonishment all the way up, and it does it with a single image about water.

This psalm is doing something the ancient world found almost scandalous. It runs down a list of the great foreign nations, the proud empires, the old enemies, the far-off peoples on the edges of the map, and instead of cursing them, it *registers* them. It says that of Zion it will be recorded: *this one was born there, and that one was born there*, that people from every hostile nation would one day be counted as native-born citizens of the city of God, entered in the registry as if they had always belonged.

And then, at the very end, comes the line that I cannot read without my chest tightening. The singers and the dancers together, celebrating in the city, cry out one thing: *all my springs are in you.*

The Hebrew word is *ma'yan*, a spring, a fountain, a source of living water. In a dry land, a spring is not a luxury. It is *survival*. It is the reason a city exists at all. And the worshippers point to Zion and say: every fountain I have is *here*. Every source of my life, every wellspring of my gladness, rises in *this* place. Not in my circumstances. Not in my success. Not scattered across a hundred things that come and go. *All* my springs, every last one, are in *you*.
They did not say joy visited them. They said the *source* of their joy had a location, and the location was the gathering-place of God.

Read that as a diagnosis of your own restlessness. You have been chasing joy the way you chase weather, standing in field after field hoping the good feeling lands on you. The psalm says stop. The springs are not scattered. They are *gathered*. There is one place where every fountain of your gladness rises, and it is the place where God gathers His people to Himself.
The gathering was always the point
Here is what pulls the whole thing together, and it is the part I was made to tell you.

Zion was never mainly about the *rock*. The rock mattered because of what happened *on* it, a people, gathered, before their God, praising. The mountain was the joy of the whole earth because it was the place where the *whole earth was invited to come home*. Every foreign nation entered in the registry, every stranger reckoned as native-born, every pilgrim who walked the long road up the slope singing, the geography existed to *gather*. Zion is what you call the spot where everyone is finally in the same room with God and with each other.

And that is why this ancient mountain leans forward into something even bigger. The New Testament takes the old geography and lifts it: it tells believers that they have already *come* to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, to countless angels in joyful assembly, to a festival gathering of the redeemed from every nation. The address did not disappear. It *opened up*. The springs that once rose on one hill in one country now rise wherever Yahuah gathers His people to worship, and the registry of the native-born has been thrown open to every tribe and tongue on earth.
Which means the homesickness you feel, that ache for a joy that stays, a gladness with a *there* to it, is not a flaw. It is a compass. It has been pointing you home the whole time.
So come up to the mountain
Stop trying to be happy in the field alone.

The design of worship was never that joy would rain randomly on scattered individuals. It was that a whole earth of gathered people would climb the same mountain, walk into the same festival, and discover that every spring they had been chasing separately was pooled in one place all along, the place where God draws His people together and dwells among them in their praise.

That is what a gathering of worshippers *is*. It is Zion breaking out wherever the redeemed assemble. It is the joy of the whole earth finding its address again in an ordinary room full of extraordinary homecomings. The springs are there. They always were. You just have to come up.

So come. From whatever far country, under whatever old name, carrying whatever thirst, come up to the mountain of gathering, and put your name in the registry of the joyful, and say what the singers and dancers have always said when they finally arrive: *all my springs are in You.*
The city is on the hill. The fountains are running. And there is a place at the celebration with your name already written in.

pieces.imagePrompt: A warm, radiant multiethnic congregation mid-song seen from within the crowd, diverse joyful worshippers packed shoulder to shoulder with lifted hands, a sense of one unseen voice leading from the very center of the gathering as golden light glows outward from among the people rather than from a stage; intimate, familial, jubilant, premium cinematic worship-brand film-still quality, warm gold and amber tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: We picture Yeshua as the One we sing to, up front, on the throne, receiving the worship. But there is a verse that puts Him somewhere we never expect: standing in the middle of the congregation, one voice among us, leading the song and calling us family while He sings.

body.text: Ask most believers where Yeshua is during worship and they will point up.

He is on the throne. He is the audience of One. He is the King we sing *to*, seated above us, receiving the praise. And all of that is gloriously true. But it is not the only place the Scriptures put Him, and the other place is so tender it can undo you if you actually stop and picture it.

There is a line, quoted in the New Testament and lifted straight out of an ancient psalm, that puts Yeshua not above the congregation but *inside* it. Not receiving the song from a distance, but *starting* it from the middle of the crowd. Not the One we sing to, the One singing *next to us*.
The verse the letter puts in His mouth

The letter to the Hebrews is building a breathtaking case: that the Son who made the worlds was not too proud to become one of us, bone of our bone, brother of our brothers. And to prove He is unashamed to call us family, the writer does something remarkable. He reaches back into the Psalms, takes an old line, and puts it directly into Yeshua's mouth.
The line is this: *I will declare Your name to My brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will sing Your praise.*

Sit with the setting of that quotation, because it is almost too much. It comes from Psalm 22, the very psalm that begins with the cry Yeshua screamed from the cross, *My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?* The song that opens in total abandonment does not end there. It climbs. And by the time it reaches the line the letter quotes, the forsaken One has come through to the other side and is doing something with His rescued breath: He is turning to a *crowd* and starting a song.
The One who was forsaken becomes the One who leads the worship. And the first word out of His mouth on the far side of the cross is *brothers*.
Where Hebrew puts Him: in the middle
Look hard at the geography of that sentence, because English rushes past the most important word in it.

*In the midst of the congregation.* The Hebrew is *b'toch qahal*, in the *middle*, the very center, of the *qahal*. And *qahal* is the great gathering-word of Israel: the assembly, the called-out ones, the whole company summoned together before God. When the ancient translators carried the Hebrew into Greek, the word they reached for to render *qahal* was *ekklesia*, the exact word that would later come to mean *the church*.

So read the verse again with that in your ear. Yeshua says: *in the midst of the ekklesia, in the dead center of the gathered church. I will sing.* And the verb the New Testament uses is not a distant, kingly word. It is *hymneo*, to sing a hymn, to lift the song. The King does not merely accept the worship of the assembly from above it. He steps into the middle of the assembly and *sings*.

He is not the guest of honor watching the choir. He is *in* the choir. He is the voice that starts the line you follow. Where we imagined Him seated at the front receiving, He is standing in the crowd *leading*, the firstborn among many brothers, and He has taken the lead part.
The One worthy of every song has chosen to sing one with us, from inside the huddle, close enough to hear.
Unashamed, and you need to feel the weight of that
Here is the word the whole thing turns on. The letter says He is *not ashamed* to call us brothers.

Feel how much that word is carrying. To be *unashamed* to stand with someone is only remarkable when there would be every reason to be ashamed. And there is every reason. He is the sinless Son; we are the ones who denied Him at the fire, ran in the garden, wasted the years, showed up to the gathering with our failures barely hidden under our sleeves. If anyone in the history of the universe had grounds to keep His distance, to stand apart, to be worshipped from a careful, dignified separation. It is Him.

And He will not do it. He steps down off the platform of pure majesty, walks into the middle of a crowd of forgiven failures, throws His arm around us, calls us *family* in front of everyone, and *starts the song*. He is not embarrassed to be found singing next to the recovering addict. He is not too holy to lead the tune standing beside the doubter, the divorced, the barely-holding-on. He put Himself in the *midst* of exactly those people on purpose, and He is not ashamed of a single one of them.

That is the God we actually have. Not one who tolerates our worship from a safe height, but one who came all the way down into the assembly to *worship with us*, because worship, done right, is not a performance we offer to a distant King. It is a family lifting its voice together, and the eldest Brother has taken His place in the middle of the room.
So look around. He is in the room
I want to change how you walk into your next gathering forever.

You have always looked *up* to find Yeshua in the worship, and you should. He reigns. But start also looking *around*. Because the same Scripture that seats Him on the throne also plants Him in the middle of the congregation, leading the song, unashamed of the company He is keeping. When the room lifts its voice, He is not only receiving it from above. He is *in it*, at the center, His voice under yours, His breath in the line, carrying the part when yours falters.

And notice how this completes the whole psalm. Psalm 22 does not end with one Man singing. It ends with the song spreading outward until *all the ends of the earth* remember and turn to Yahuah, until families of every nation bow, until a people not yet born is told what He has done. The lead voice in the middle of the qahal was always meant to become a *global* chorus, the one Brother starting a song that every tribe and tongue would eventually join.

That is the gathering you were made for. Not a room of individuals performing for a faraway King, but a family singing shoulder to shoulder with the risen Yeshua Himself standing unashamed in the middle of them, calling every last one *brother*, *sister*, and leading the tune home.
So sing like He is beside you. Because He said He would be, right there in the midst of the congregation, one voice among the ransomed, not ashamed to be found singing next to you.
He took the lead part on purpose. All you have to do is come in on His line.

pieces.title: A Scream and a Song in the Same Breath

pieces.excerpt: We keep trying to decide whether Hosanna is a desperate cry for help or a shout of triumph. The ancient word refuses to choose. It is both at once, a scream and a song fused into one syllable, and that refusal is the most honest thing worship has ever done.

body.text: We keep trying to make *Hosanna* pick a side.

Is it a happy word or a hurting one? Is it the triumphant shout of a festival crowd, or the raw scream of people who have run out of options? Preachers argue it. Worship leaders lean it one way or the other depending on the song. And the whole time, the word itself is standing there refusing the question, because it was never one *or* the other.
It is both. In the very same breath. And once you hear it that way, it becomes the most honest sound a human being can make.
The word that will not choose

*Hosanna* is a lightly worn-down form of two Hebrew words: *hoshia na*. *Hoshia* is a command form of the verb *yasha*, to save, to rescue, to deliver. *Na* is the little particle Hebrew adds when a request goes past politeness into pleading. We reach for it with words like *please*, or *now*, or *I beg you*. Put together, *hoshia na* means *save, please, now*. It is not a decoration you drape over a triumphant chord. On its face it is a cry for help.

So far, so desperate. But here is where the word does the thing no English word can do. That desperate cry is *also*, at the very same time, an act of *praise*, because of *who* you are screaming it at, and *where* the crowd learned to scream it.

Think about what it means to yell *save me now* at a specific person. You do not beg rescue from someone you doubt. The scream is itself a confession of confidence. Every decibel of the plea is also a declaration: *You can do this. You are the one who saves. I am staking everything on You.* The cry for help and the shout of trust are not two different sounds. They are the *same* sound. To beg Him that loudly is to boast in Him that loudly. *Hosanna* is a plea with the muscles of a victory shout, because the desperation and the confidence are pointed at the same rescuing God.
That is why it will not pick a side. It was built to hold both.
Where the crowd learned the cry

The people waving branches on the road into Jerusalem did not invent that word on the spot. They were quoting a song they had sung every year of their lives, and knowing *which* song is the key to the whole scene.

*Hoshia na* comes from Psalm 118, and Psalm 118 is the climax of the *Hallel*, the great cluster of praise-psalms sung at Israel's feasts, and above all at *Passover*. Every year, at the meal that remembered the night the blood on the doorposts turned death aside, families sang their way through these psalms. The Hallel was the soundtrack of *rescue already accomplished*, the exodus, the sea split open, a nation walking out of slavery. And it was, in the same songs, the cry for rescue *still to come*. The Passover table held both: the God who *had* saved and the ache to be saved *again*.

And listen to what Psalm 118 itself actually does. It swings, verse by verse, between the pit and the mountaintop. *Out of my distress I cried to Yah*, that is the scream. *Yah answered me and set me in a wide open place*, that is the song. *Yahuah is my strength and my song; He has become my salvation*, a line lifted straight out of the Song of the Sea that Israel sang on the far shore with the water still draining off their sandals. The psalm does not resolve the tension between anguish and triumph. It *braids* them. It teaches a whole nation to cry for help and celebrate rescue in one continuous breath.

So when the Passover crowd grabbed that psalm's most desperate line and hurled it over the head of a man on a donkey, they were not confused about whether they were begging or praising. Their oldest worship had already fused the two. They were doing what the Hallel had trained them to do their entire lives.
*Hosanna* is what you get when a people who know how to celebrate rescue and a people who still desperately need it turn out to be the same people, shouting at the same God.
The Name hiding inside the plea
And here the scene tips into something almost too beautiful to say plainly.

The word the salmists used for the rescue they longed for is *yeshuah*, salvation, deliverance. It is the very word Psalm 118 uses when it says *He has become my salvation*. Now hold that beside the name of the Man the crowd was screaming at. *Yeshua*, the name means *Yahuah saves*; it is built from that same root of rescue. The crowd was crying *save now!*, *hoshia!*, straight into the face of the One whose very name *is* the answer to the cry.

Do you feel the collision? The plea and the answer met on that road. A whole nation's ancient scream for salvation reached the end of its long journey and landed on a Person named Salvation. The word had been traveling for a thousand years looking for an address, and it finally found one, riding low and humble into the city on a borrowed colt. *Save now* had come face to face with *Yahuah saves*.

That is why the palm branches make sense. The crowd tore down the green branches and waved them high, and branches like that were the gesture of *festival*, of *victory*, of celebration. So there they stood, waving the signs of triumph while screaming the cry for rescue. Victory palms in the air; desperate plea in the mouth. If you ever needed a picture of what *Hosanna* is, it is that: a crowd celebrating and begging in the same motion, because the One who could answer the beg was finally in the road.
Why your worship needs a word this big
Here is why I refuse to let anyone flatten this word into just a cheer or just a plea.

Because your real life is not one or the other, and neither is anyone's in the room with you. You come to the gathering carrying triumph *and* trouble in the same chest. There is something you are thanking God for and something you are still desperate for, and most worship songs make you pick which one to bring. *Hosanna* refuses to make you choose. It is the one word wide enough to hold the whole truth of you, the gratitude and the groan, the answered prayer and the open wound, the *He has saved me* and the *I still need saving*, all in a single breath.

And notice. It is not a solo. Psalm 118 was sung by a *crowd*. The road into Jerusalem roared with it because a whole multitude lifted it together. This is a word made for a *gathering*, a room full of people who each carry a private scream and a private song, discovering that when they lift them together, the desperation and the joy come out as one enormous, unstoppable shout aimed at the God who saves.

So the next time you sing it, do not decide first whether you are happy enough or desperate enough to mean it. You are both. That is exactly the point. Bring the scream. Bring the song. Bring them in the same breath, like the crowd on the road, and aim the whole thing at the One whose name has always been the answer.
*Hoshia na.* Save now. And He is already coming up the road.

pieces.excerpt: Again and again the songbook of Israel calls for a *new* song, never the old reliable one, never the favorite you already know by heart. There is a reason Yahuah keeps asking for the one you cannot sing yet. And the Hebrew word for "new" is hiding it in plain sight.

body.text: There is a small command tucked into the songbook of Israel that most of us read straight past, and I want to slow down on it, because it has been quietly shaping the way heaven asks to be worshiped for three thousand years.
Sing to Him a *new* song.

Not a good song. Not the beloved one everybody already knows the words to. A **new** one. And it is not said once, as a passing suggestion. It is said again and again, across the Psalms, until you start to notice it is a pattern and not an accident. The prophets pick it up. The last book of the Bible closes with it, a song no one had ever sung before, rising in a room full of the redeemed.

Here is the thing that used to trouble me about it. We have old songs that work. We have the reliable ones, the ones that have carried us through funerals and midnight and the long grey Tuesdays of a life. Why would the God who never changes keep asking for something we have never sung? Why new, over and over, from the One who is the same yesterday and forever?
The answer is buried in the Hebrew word itself. And once you see it, you cannot unsee it.
The word for "new" is the word for the moon coming back
The Hebrew word is *chadash*. New. Fresh. And it comes from a root, the letters *chet, dalet, shin*, that carries the sense of renewing, of making fresh again.

From that very same root comes another word you would never expect to be related: *chodesh*. It means *month*, and more precisely, the *new moon*, the sliver of light that returns to the black sky after the moon has gone completely dark.
Sit with that picture, because it is doing theology.

To the ancient Hebrew ear, *new* did not mean *never existed before*. It did not mean novelty, the shiny thing off the shelf, the trend that will be old by autumn. *New* meant what the moon does. The moon is not replaced every month. There is no second moon. It is the *same* moon, renewed, brought back around, filled again with light after the dark had swallowed it whole.
A new song, in Hebrew, is not a stranger. It is the old faithfulness, come back around, filled with light again after the dark.

So when Yahuah asks for a *shir chadash*, a new song, He is not asking you to invent a God you have never met. He is asking you to sing the same steadfast One as He shows up *again*, freshly, in a place He has not yet been thanked for.
You cannot sing a new song about nothing
Now the command starts to make a different kind of sense.

You cannot manufacture a new song. Try it. Sit down and decide to be freshly amazed at a rescue that has not happened yet, and all you will produce is performance, a pretty imitation of wonder with nothing underneath it. A true new song is not something you generate. It is something that *arrives*, pressed out of you by an act of God recent enough to still be warm.

The songbook says it almost exactly like that in one place. A man is sunk in a pit, mud, silence, no bottom to stand on, and he waits, and waits, and then Yahuah reaches down and lifts him out and sets his feet on rock. *And then*, the song says, He put a new song in my mouth. The new song did not come first, to talk him into hoping. It came *after*. It was the sound a real deliverance makes on the way out of a real body. He did not choose it. He could not have. It was given, because something had genuinely changed.
That is why the new one and not the old reliable one.

The old song is a monument, precious, load-bearing, true. It remembers what He did *back then*. But the new song is a witness. It testifies that He is *still doing it*. That the same steadfast love that split a sea is, this very week, splitting something in your own life wide open. A God who only earned old songs would be a God who used to be good. The relentless call for a new one is not Yahuah being restless. It is Yahuah promising you He has not finished. He keeps asking for a song you don't have yet because He keeps intending to do something you haven't seen yet.
New every morning, and the same root every time
There is one more place that root shows up, and it undoes me every time.

A man who had watched his whole city burn, who wrote an entire scroll of nothing but grief, stopped in the exact middle of the ashes and said this: the mercies of Yahuah never run out; they are *new* every morning. Great is His faithfulness.
That word, *new* every morning, is the same root. *Chadash.* Renewed. The moon coming back.

Which means the mercy that finds you on Monday is not a fresh batch of a different substance. It is the *same* everlasting kindness, renewed to the day you are standing in, arriving with the sunrise, unspent, as if it had been saving itself for exactly this morning. His mercy renews the way the moon renews. The way a new song renews. Same faithfulness. New light.

And that is why He can honestly ask you for a new song even on your hardest day. Not because you are supposed to fake a brightness you do not feel. But because His mercy showed up *new* this morning, before you woke, and a new mercy has a right to a new song.
So sing the one you don't know yet
Here is the door I will leave open for you, gently.
If the only songs you can find in your mouth right now are the old ones, sing them. They are holy, and they will hold. There is no shame in the reliable song; it is reliable because it is true.

But do not close your heart to the new one. Keep a corner of you listening for it. Because the new song is not a demand that you become a more creative worshiper. It is a *promise* that Yahuah is not done renewing you, that there is a rescue still coming that will need a sound you have never made, a mercy arriving tomorrow morning that the old words cannot quite hold.
The moon goes dark. And then, without fail, it comes back full of borrowed light.
So will you. And when you do, you will not have to reach for the new song.
It will already be rising in you, the same faithful God, sung *new*, because He just did it again.

pieces.title: They Titled the Book of Tears "Praises"
pieces.imagePrompt: An intimate evening worship service lit by candlelight, a diverse circle of people of many ages and ethnicities singing together with tears and gentle smiles on their faces at the same time, one older Asian woman with her eyes closed and a hand on her heart, warm flames glowing across their faces in the dark; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, deep amber and soft gold tones, tender and reverent and alive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: The Hebrew name for the book of Psalms means, simply, "Praises." Yet open it and you will find it soaked in tears, more laments than hymns, more *how long* than *hallelujah*. Israel did not misfile its grief. It made a daring claim about what praise actually is.

body.text: I want to tell you the real name of the book you think you know.

We call it Psalms, an old Greek word for songs played on strings. A fine name. But it is not what the people who wrote it called it. In Hebrew the book is *Tehillim*. And *Tehillim* does not mean "songs." It means, flatly and unmistakably, **Praises**. The Book of Praises. That is the title Israel gave it, the sign over the door.
Now here is what should stop you in your tracks. Walk into that book expecting praise, and you will spend most of your time inside weeping.

You will find a man asking Yahuah, out loud, why He has forgotten him. You will find *how long* asked so many times it becomes a refrain. You will find someone whose only companion, he says, is the darkness. You will find betrayal, and sickness, and enemies, and the specific loneliness of praying into what feels like an empty sky. Scholars who count these things will tell you the single largest category in the Book of Praises is not the hymn. It is the *lament*. The book named for praise is, by volume, a book of tears.

Israel was not careless. Israel was not confused about which songs were happy. They looked at their collected grief, the raw, the furious, the inconsolable, and they wrote **Praises** over the top of all of it on purpose.
I think that is one of the bravest things any people has ever done. And I think it will change how you worship if you let it.
What the word underneath is actually saying

The word *tehillah*, praise, comes from a root you already know without knowing it: *halal*. It is the *hal* in *hallelujah*. And its oldest sense is not "to compliment." It is closer to *to shine*, to flash out light, to make a thing radiant and seen.
To praise, in that root, is to make Yahuah *visible*, to lift Him up where the whole room can see how bright He is.
Hold that next to the tears, and something quietly enormous happens.
A lament, sung to His face, is not the absence of praise. It is praise refusing to shine a false light. It is the radiance of a God trusted enough to be told the truth.

Because think about what a lament in that book actually is. It is not a complaint muttered *about* Yahuah to someone else. It is a cry brought *to* Him, addressed to His face, in His hearing. And you do not pour out your worst hour to a God you believe has left the room. You only cry *how long* to Someone you are certain is still listening. The lament is soaked in an unspoken faith the griever may not even notice he is confessing: *You are here. You can do something. You are the One I bring this to.*

That is why they could file the tears under Praises and not be lying. The tears *are* a form of shining. They make visible a God so trustworthy that His people will hand Him their unedited anguish and expect to be held.
A praise big enough to carry sorrow without lying
Here is what we have often done instead, and I say it with tenderness, because I have done it too.

We have built a kind of praise that can only hold good weather. Bright, quick, resolved, a praise that needs you to feel fine first, or at least to fake it convincingly by the second chorus. And so the moment real sorrow arrives, that praise has no room for you. You have to leave your grief in the car and put on a face at the door, because the only worship on offer cannot carry what you are actually holding.

The Book of Praises will not allow that. It is *praise built wide enough to walk your grief straight through the front door.* It hands you words for the valley of the shadow and never once demands you pretend the valley is a garden. It lets you say *my tears have been my food day and night*, and counts that, too, as praise, because it was sung to His face and not away from it.

This is the mercy of it: you do not have to lie to worship the God of the Bible. You never did. The most honest thing you can do with your sorrow is not to hide it from Him until it clears up. It is to *bring it to Him as a song*, to let even the ache be a way of making Him visible, a way of saying, without saying it, *I still believe You are the One who hears.*
Notice how the tears travel
Read those grieving songs to their end and watch what happens, because they are teaching you the shape of a sung sorrow.

So many of them begin underwater, *why, how long, where are You*, and somewhere in the middle, without the circumstances changing at all, the language turns. *Yet I will trust.* *But You, O Yahuah.* The problem is not solved. The enemy has not left. The night is exactly as long as it was. But the griever has been *sung* somewhere. In the act of pouring it all out to a listening God, the weight redistributed. The song became the hand that reached in and held on.

That turn is not decoration. It is the whole architecture of praise that tells the truth. It does not leap over the grief to get to the light. It carries the grief *toward* the light, at grief's own pace, and lets the light find it there.

And a handful of them do not turn at all. One ends in the dark, with the last word being *darkness* itself. Yahuah kept that one too. He did not require every song to arrive somewhere bright before it was allowed into the Book of Praises. He knew some nights do not end by morning, and He wanted His people to have a song even for those. Even the unresolved cry, aimed at Him, is praise.
So bring the whole book of you
If you have been holding a sorrow you did not think you were allowed to sing. I want to lift that off you.

You are allowed. The oldest worship book in the world was named **Praises** by people who filled it mostly with tears, precisely so you would know that your grief has a place at the front of the sanctuary and not out in the parking lot. Praise, it turns out, was never the sound of a life with nothing wrong. It was the sound of a God made visible, even, and especially, by the ones who came to Him with wet faces and told Him everything.
So sing the ache. Address it to His face. Let it shine.
They titled the book of tears *Praises*, and they were not wrong. They just understood, long before we did, that a praise too small to carry sorrow was never really praise at all.

pieces.title: The God Who Hands Out Songs in the Dark
pieces.imagePrompt: A diverse group of friends worshiping together outdoors at night under a vast starry sky, faces upturned and glowing with quiet joy, a young Middle Eastern man singing with his eyes closed and a peaceful smile while others sway beside him, soft warm lantern light catching their features against the deep blue dark; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, midnight blue and warm amber tones, hushed and hopeful and luminous, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: An almost-forgotten line in the book of Job asks a question no one ever asks: where is the God who *gives* songs in the night? Not who explains the night. Who hands you a melody in the middle of it. There is a Hebrew word for that gift, and it changes what the dark is for.

body.text: There is a line in the book of Job that almost no one quotes, and I have come to think it is one of the most tender things in the whole Bible.

It is not spoken by Job. It comes from one of the younger men circled around him in the ash-heap, trying to make sense of a suffering too big for any of them. And in the middle of his speech he lets slip a description of God so gentle it does not fit the argument he is making. He asks: where is *Eloah my Maker*, who **gives songs in the night**?
Read it slowly, because every word is carrying weight.

Not the God who *ends* the night. Not the God who *explains* the night, or shortens it, or tells you what it was for. The God who *gives you a song in it.* Who reaches into the black hour where you are still very much awake and very much afraid, and presses a melody into your hands that was not there a moment before.
I did not know God did that until I needed Him to. And then I found out that Israel had known it all along, and had a word for it.
The word for a night-song

The Hebrew here is *zemirot*, songs. It comes from the root *zamar*, which is one of the great music-words of the Scriptures: to make melody, to pluck the strings, to sing praise with an instrument in your hands. When the Psalms say *I will sing praises*, over and over, in every mood, that is often this word. *Zamar.* Music made on purpose, plucked out into the air.
And Job's young friend attaches it to *laylah*, the night.

Put them together and you have something startling. The songs Yahuah gives are not only for the bright temple courts at noon, with the choirs assembled and the harvest in. He is, this line insists, a *giver of night-music*, a God who composes specifically for the dark, who has melodies that only work at all when the lights have gone out.
He does not merely permit songs in the night. He *gives* them. The melody in your worst hour is a gift, handed down, not something you had to manufacture to prove your faith.

That word, *gives*, is the whole comfort. Because when the dark is genuinely dark, you cannot make a song. You know this if you have been there. In the deep of a grief, there is nothing in you to compose *with*. The well is dry. And a faith that told you *you must summon praise from your own strength at 3 a.m.* would be a cruelty, not a comfort.

But Job's friend does not say *sing a song in the night*. He says God *gives* one. It comes down. It arrives from outside your empty hands. All you have to do, all you *can* do, is receive it and let it be sung through you.
By day His steadfast love, by night His song
There is another place this exact idea appears, and the two verses lean on each other like they were written to be read together.

In one of the Psalms, a man who is drowning in his own sorrow, the same song where he says his tears have been his food, where he asks God why He has forgotten him, stops and says something almost defiant. *By day Yahuah commands His steadfast love, and by night His song is with me.*

Look at the pairing. The daylight has the *chesed*, the covenant kindness you can see, the mercies you can point to when the sun is up. But the night gets its own provision, and it is a *song*. His song. *With* him. In the exact stretch of hours when the evidence goes quiet and the arguments fail and the enemy's questions get loudest, this man is not left with silence. He is left with a melody God put there for the watch.
That is not a man who felt like singing. That is a man being *carried* by a song he did not write, through a night he did not choose.

I love that the two places agree, one in the oldest book of the Bible, one in the middle of the songbook. Both of them are saying the same quiet, enormous thing: **the God of Scripture keeps different music for the dark.** He is not only the God of your celebrations. He is the God of your night-watch, and He does not send you into it empty-handed.
What the night-song is for
Here is what took me years to understand, and I want to hand it to you so it does not take you as long.

The night-song is not given to *lift* the night. If it were, it would only ever be a failed sunrise, and you would judge it by whether the darkness left, and it usually does not leave on schedule. The night-song has a different job.
It is given to keep you *company* until the watch is over.

A song in the night does not argue with the dark. It does not pretend the dawn is closer than it is. It does something better. It accompanies you. It reminds your own body, from the inside, that you are not alone in here, that Someone is awake with you, that the God who could have sent an explanation sent a *melody* instead because He knew a melody could go where an explanation cannot. An explanation talks *at* your fear. A song sits *down inside* it and holds on.

And there is a strange grace in the fact that night-songs are usually quiet. You do not belt them. You barely sing them above a breath. But that is not weakness, that is the sound of worship made for a room where everyone else is asleep and the only audience is the One who gave you the tune. The quietest song you will ever sing may be the truest, because there is no one there to sing it *for* except Him.
So keep your ear open on the watch

If you are in one of those nights right now, the kind that does not end when the clock says morning. I am not going to tell you it will be short. Job's friend did not lie to him about the dark, and I will not lie to you.

But I will tell you what he told a suffering man in the ashes: your Maker *gives* songs in the night. He has one for this one. You do not have to be strong enough to compose it. You do not have to feel like singing. You only have to keep the ear of your heart open, because a melody is coming to you from outside the dark, put there on purpose, by a God who stays up through every watch and never once leaves His people to face the black hours without a song.
Listen for it. It is already on its way down to you.
And in the morning, whenever the morning finally comes. You will realize you were being sung *through* the whole time.

pieces.title: The Woman Who Sang the Magnificat First
pieces.imagePrompt: A radiant woman of color standing with her arms raised and her face lifted in triumphant joyful song, tears of gladness on her cheeks and a fierce bright smile, surrounded by a diverse crowd of women of many ages and backgrounds worshiping jubilantly around her, warm light breaking across the scene like a sunrise; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, warm gold and rose tones, powerful and jubilant and tender, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: A thousand years before Mary sang the Magnificat, a mocked and childless woman named Hannah stood up and sang almost the same song, a fierce, prophetic praise that reached far past her own rescue. Her worship did not begin when the answer came. It began in the anguish, while her mouth was still moving without a sound.

body.text: Most of us know the Magnificat. A young woman in an obscure town, told she will carry the Messiah, opens her mouth and pours out one of the most beautiful songs in all of Scripture, *my soul magnifies the Lord.* He scatters the proud. He topples the mighty from their thrones. He lifts the lowly and fills the hungry and sends the rich away empty.
What most of us do not know is that Mary was singing a **cover**.

A thousand years earlier, another woman stood up and sang almost the same song, the same reversals, the same toppled strong and lifted low, the same fierce, holy joy. Her name was Hannah. And when you set her song beside Mary's, side by side, the family resemblance is unmistakable. Mary, steeped in the Scriptures of her people, reached back across ten centuries and picked up a melody a heartbroken woman had left for her.
I cannot stop thinking about that. The most famous song of the New Testament was first sung by a woman the whole town had written off.
The song that started before the answer did
Here is what you have to understand about where Hannah's song came from, because it is the whole scandal of it.

Hannah was barren, in a time and place where that word was a verdict on your worth. And she was not left in peace about it, the other wife in her household, who had children, provoked her, needled her, made a sport of the one wound Hannah could not heal. Year after year. Hannah wept until she could not eat.

She went up to the house of Yahuah at Shiloh, and she prayed the way you pray when you have run out of composure. Her lips moved, but no sound came out. She was so far into her grief that the old priest watching her assumed she was drunk and told her to sober up. She had to explain to him that she was not drunk. She was pouring out her soul before Yahuah. (It is a beautiful footnote of history that Israel later looked back at that scene, lips moving, no voice, the whole heart poured out in silence, as a picture of how prayer is meant to be prayed. That is tradition remembering her, not Scripture commanding it. But I think the tradition saw something true.)
Now here is the part that undoes me.

The song of triumph in the next chapter, the fierce one, the prophetic one, Hannah did not sing it because life had finally become easy. The child came, yes. But she sang it while handing that only son *back*, leaving him at Shiloh to be raised by the very priest who had misjudged her, walking home to a house where her rival still lived. Her circumstances were nowhere near tidy. The mockery had not been fully answered. And she stood up anyway and sang the biggest song of her life.
Her praise did not wait for the ending. It began in the anguish, in the silence where only her lips moved, and it grew into a song too large for the room she was standing in.
A song bigger than her own story
If Hannah's song were only about a baby, it would be sweet, and small, and we would have forgotten it. It is not small.

Listen to what she actually sings. *There is none holy like Yahuah; there is no Rock like our God.* The word she reaches for is *tsur*, a rock, a crag, an immovable place to stand. A woman who had been standing on nothing for years names Yahuah her unshakeable ground.

And then she says, *my horn is exalted in Yahuah.* The horn, *qeren*, is the ancient image for strength, for lifted-up power, the way an animal carries its head high and unafraid. The woman who came in with her head bowed by shame sings that her strength has been lifted where everyone can see it.

But she does not stop at her own reversal. She widens out, and this is where it becomes prophecy. The bows of the mighty are broken, she sings, and the stumbling are girded with strength. The full sell themselves for bread, and the hungry hunger no more. Yahuah brings down to the grave and raises up; He lifts the poor from the dust and the needy from the ash-heap and seats them with princes. One barren woman's answered prayer becomes, in her mouth, the whole pattern of how God runs His universe: **He lifts the low and He topples the high.**

And then her song does something it has no business doing. In the very last line she prophesies a *king*, *He will give strength to His king and exalt the horn of His anointed*, when Israel had no king yet. There was no throne. There was no crown. Hannah, a private woman singing over a weaning child, reaches forward into a future that did not exist and names the Anointed One, the *Messiach*, before there was anyone to wear the word.

That is why Mary could pick this song up and it fit her perfectly. Because Hannah had not been singing only about herself the whole time. She had been singing about the God who does exactly this, who chooses the overlooked woman, the empty womb, the ash-heap, the nobody, and lifts her up to announce the way the whole story is going to end. Hannah sang the shape of the gospel a thousand years early, and Mary, carrying that gospel in her own body, sang it back.
Praise is the seed you plant in the anguish
Here is what I want you to carry out of this.

Hannah teaches us that the fiercest praise is not grown in the good season. It is grown in the barren one. The song that would echo down ten centuries and land in the mouth of the mother of the Messiah was *seeded* in a woman weeping so hard she could not speak, in a sanctuary where the only witness misread her as a drunk. The praise did not come *after* the pain as a reward. It grew *up through* the pain, like something green forcing its way through cracked ground.

And notice. She did not sing to convince herself. She sang to *testify*. She had met the God who lifts the low, in the one place she had been low the longest, and once you have met Him there, you cannot keep the song in. It gets bigger than your own story. It starts prophesying over other people's ash-heaps. It starts announcing the King.
So sing from where you actually are
If you are in a barren season, a prayer unanswered so long you have stopped saying it out loud, a wound the mockers keep finding, do not wait for the ending to sing.

Hannah didn't. She poured out her soul in silence, and then she stood up and sang a song so true it outlived her, so wide it prophesied a King, so trustworthy that the mother of Yeshua would one day borrow it word for word. Her circumstances were not finished when she sang. But her God was already the Rock, already the Lifter of the low, already the One who was going to turn the whole world right-side up.
He still is. And the song you sing from inside your barren years, before the mockery ends, before the answer comes, may turn out to be the truest one you ever sing.
Somebody a thousand years from now might just be singing it back.

pieces.title: The Abyss in You Was Built to Answer His
pieces.imagePrompt: A diverse group of worshipers standing at the edge of a misty lake or waterfall at dawn, faces lifted and glowing with peaceful longing and joy, a young South Asian woman with her eyes closed and hands open at her sides breathing in deeply, soft golden mist and first light rising off the water around them; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, soft teal and warm gold tones, vast and hushed and yearning, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: "Deep calls to deep," the psalmist writes, *tehom el tehom*, the same word Genesis uses for the primeval abyss. He is drowning, and he calls it worship. What if the ache you keep trying to fix is not a failure of faith at all, but the deepest part of you singing back to the deep in Him?

body.text: There is a song in the middle of the Psalter that opens with a picture so tender it has been carried in people's hearts for three thousand years, and then, a few lines later, it says something so strange that most of us skate right over it without noticing what we just read.

It begins with a deer. *As the deer pants for streams of water, so my soul pants for You, O God.* A parched animal, sides heaving, driven half-mad by thirst, searching the dry hills for the sound of water. That is what my longing for You feels like, the psalmist says. Not calm. Not settled. *Panting.*
And then, a little further down, when the same man is describing how far under he has gone, tears for food, God seeming absent, waves closing over his head. He says this: **deep calls to deep.**

In Hebrew it is *tehom el tehom qore.* And I need you to know what *tehom* is, because English hides it. *Tehom* is not just "the deep water." It is *the* deep, the primeval abyss, the vast dark formlessness that Genesis says lay over the face of the earth before there was any light at all. The unfathomable. The bottomless. The same word for the depths that burst open in the flood.

So read what he is actually saying. Drowning, undone, waves going over him. He does not say *I have lost my faith.* He says the *abyss* in his circumstances is calling out, and something just as bottomless in him is answering. And he includes the whole thing in a song of worship.
That single line rearranged how I understand longing. Let me tell you why.
The deer is not doing anything wrong

We tend to treat spiritual longing as a symptom, a sign that something has gone wrong, a deficiency to be cleared up as fast as possible. If I still *ache* for God, we think, then I must not have enough of Him yet. The ache is the problem. Get more, and the ache should go quiet.
But look again at the deer.

The word for what the deer is doing, *ta'arog*, to pant, to long, is a rare and physical word. It is the sound of a creature that wants water *with its whole body*. And the psalmist does not present that panting as a failure. He presents it as the truest possible picture of a soul in the right relationship with its God. The deer is not broken because it is thirsty. The thirst is what proves it is *alive*, and it is what drives it, straight and unerring, toward the only thing that can save it.
Your longing is not the evidence that God is far. It is the compass He built into you so you would keep running toward the water.

And notice the word the psalmist uses for the part of him that pants: *nephesh.* We translate it "soul," and that is not wrong, but it is thin. *Nephesh* is the whole living self, and its most physical sense is the *throat*, the seat of thirst and hunger and breath. So *my nephesh pants for You* is not a delicate, disembodied sentiment. It is a throat gone dry. It is the wanting that lives in your body, below your arguments, older than your theology. That is the part of you that longs for God, and Scripture treats that raw, bodily wanting not as a weakness to apologize for, but as worship.
The depths were made to answer each other
Here is the line I keep returning to. *Deep calls to deep.* Abyss to abyss. *Tehom* to *tehom.*

There is a bottomlessness in God, an inexhaustible vastness we will be exploring for all of eternity and never reach the floor of. The Scriptures reach for the biggest words they own and still come up short: His understanding is unsearchable, His riches unfathomable, His depths past finding out. He is, in the truest sense, an abyss of glory. There is no bottom to Him.

And the astonishing claim buried in this psalm is that *there is a matching depth in you.* You were made in His image, and part of what that means is that He put a bottomlessness inside you too, a capacity for Him so vast that nothing smaller than God will ever fill it. You have tried to fill it with smaller things. We all have. And the ache never quite goes, because you were built with an *abyss* in you, and only *the* Abyss can answer it.

That is what *deep calls to deep* means when the waves are going over your head. The bottomless longing in you is not malfunctioning. It is doing exactly what it was made to do, *calling*, across the dark, to the only Deep that can hold it. Your emptiness is not the opposite of worship. Your emptiness, turned toward Him, *is* worship, the deepest part of you singing the one note it was tuned to sing.
Longing itself is a form of praise
This is the thing I most want to leave with you, because I think it will set some of you free.

You do not have to wait until the ache is gone to worship. You do not have to manufacture a feeling of fullness you do not have. The longing itself, the panting, the reaching, the *God, where are You*, is already a form of praise, because it is your whole *nephesh* aimed, with everything in it, at Him.

Watch how the psalmist handles his own drowning. Three times in that song he turns and speaks to his own downcast soul: *Why are you cast down? Hope in God.* He does not scold the longing away. He does not pretend to be fine. He simply keeps aiming the ache in the right direction, *for I shall again praise Him.* He worships in the future tense, from the bottom of the present tense, while the waves are still coming. That is not a man who has stopped worshiping. That is worship in its rawest and most honest form: a deep that will not stop calling to the Deep, no matter how long the answer takes.

And here is the mercy hidden underneath the whole picture. A call implies a hearer. *Deep calls to deep* only makes sense if the other Deep is listening, if your longing is not flung out into an empty void but received by a God whose own depths rise to meet it. The panting deer is not chasing a mirage. There *is* water. The thirst was never a cruelty. It was the surest sign that the streams are real.
So let yourself want Him
If you have been treating your longing for God as a spiritual failure, a sign you must not have enough faith, or enough of Him. I want to hand you a gentler and truer word.

That ache is holy. It is the deep in you calling out to the Deep in Him, exactly as you were designed to do. It is the deer running toward the water it can already smell on the wind. It is worship in the form of thirst.

So do not silence it. Do not be ashamed of it. Turn it, like the psalmist did, straight toward His face, and let the bottomless place in you go on calling, unashamed, across every dark, to the only One deep enough to answer.
He hears the call. He always has. And the depths in Him are already rising, at the sound of the depths in you.

pieces.title: The Ringing Cry That Won't Stay Inside You
pieces.imagePrompt: A jubilant multiethnic crowd erupting in joyful shouts of praise outdoors under a bright sky, a beaming Ghanaian woman and a young Filipina and a Brazilian grandfather with heads back and mouths open in ringing joy, arms raised, trees and open fields behind them, light pouring over everyone; exuberant, radiant, premium cinematic film-still, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: There is a Hebrew word for praise that does not describe a decision to worship. It describes joy that has run out of room. It rings. It overflows. It is the sound a heart makes when gladness gets too big to hold, and the Psalms command the trees themselves to make it. Let me open the word.

body.text: Some joy you can manage. You can feel it, appreciate it, keep it in a reasonable voice. And then there is the other kind, the kind that gets too big for the body that is holding it and comes *out,* whether you gave it permission or not. A laugh you could not swallow. A shout you did not plan. The sound a crowd makes when the thing they were hoping for actually happens.
The Hebrews had a word for that, and they used it for praise. The word is *ranan.*
A word for a sound, not a decision

Most of our praise vocabulary in English names an intention. *I will worship. I choose to praise.* And there is a place for the deliberate, the willed, the disciplined offering brought when you do not feel like bringing it.

*Ranan* is not that. *Ranan* names a **sound**, specifically, a ringing, shrill, overflowing cry of joy. The lexicons reach for words like *to cry aloud, to shout for joy, to give a ringing cry, to sing out.* It is high and bright and unmistakable. It is not the low rumble of solemn reverence; it is the ringing top note of a heart that cannot contain itself.

Notice the difference from its neighbors, because the Hebrew keeps them distinct. *Halal* leans toward boasting, making a radiant show. *Shabach* is the loud, commending shout that declares who God is. *Teruah* is the blast, the alarm, the war-cry that goes up before the battle. *Ranan* is none of those exactly. *Ranan* is the **ringing overflow**, joy that has become audible because there was simply no more room for it inside.
You do not *decide* to *ranan* the way you decide to be quiet or to sing a planned song. You *ranan* the way a full cup spills. The word describes praise as a consequence of fullness.
The command that lands on the trees
Here is where the word does something that should stop you.

The Scriptures do not only tell *people* to *ranan.* In the songs of Israel, the command lands on creation itself. The daughter of Zion is told to sing aloud, to cry out with this ringing joy. And then, in one of the most startling pictures in the whole songbook, the *trees of the forest* are summoned to do it too. The fields, the sea, the hills. The poet turns to the woods and commands them to *ring out* before Yahuah, who is coming.
Sit with that image. A God so worth rejoicing over that the created world is called to make the ringing cry, and the trees, if they could, would break into it.
Ranan is the sound gladness makes when it stops asking whether it is allowed. It is the note a full heart hits on the way out.

Why the trees? I think because the command is not really about vocal cords. It is about *fullness meeting worthiness.* When something is truly and overwhelmingly worthy of joy, the fitting response is not measured approval. It is overflow. And if human throats fell silent, the poet insists, the sheer worthiness of Yahuah would be enough to set the forest ringing. The joy has to go *somewhere.*
The overflow you keep corking
Now let me bring this close to home, because I think many of us have a problem *ranan* was made to cure.

We have learned to cork our joy. We feel the gladness rise, at the answered prayer, at the song that lands, at the sudden awareness of how good God has been, and we clamp it. We keep it dignified. We let a little escape, tastefully, and we press the rest back down. We have been trained to believe that maturity means keeping our worship at a moderate volume.
But a corked bottle is not more mature than an open one. It is just under pressure.

*Ranan* is the songbook's permission, no, its **command**, to take the cork out. To let the ringing joy do what ringing joy does, which is to *sound.* The word is telling us that there is a kind of praise God actually asks for that cannot be produced by trying harder to be reverent. It can only be produced by letting the fullness overflow.

And here is the tender part: you cannot fake *ranan.* You cannot manufacture a ringing cry of joy on command out of an empty heart. Which means the very existence of this word is a promise. It assumes there will be fullness. It assumes that if you stay near Yahuah long enough, honestly enough, the day will come when the joy is simply too big for the container, and the ringing cry will come out on its own, and when it does, you are not to be ashamed of it. You are to let it ring.
When you have no ring left
I would be a poor teacher if I left it there, because you may be reading this from a season with no ringing cry in you at all. The cup is not overflowing; it feels bone dry.

Hear this gently. The Psalms that command *ranan* sit in the same book as the psalms of the pit, the tears, the *how long.* The songbook never pretends the ringing cry is always available. What it does is keep the word *there,* on the page, waiting, a memory of overflow past and a promise of overflow to come. There is a beautiful line in the Psalms about those who go out weeping, carrying seed, who will come home with this very ringing cry of joy, bringing in the harvest. (I am paraphrasing the picture, not quoting a verse number to you, but that is its shape.) The ringing cry is promised on the far side of the weeping. It is coming. The word is holding a place for it.
Let it ring

So the next time the gladness rises in you and your first instinct is to clamp it, do not. That instinct is trained, not holy. Let the joy get loud. Let it reach the ringing top note it was always trying to reach.
You were not made to keep your best gladness at a manageable volume. You were made, like the daughter of Zion and the trees of the wood, to *ring out* before a God who is worth every decibel of it.
The cup is meant to overflow. When it does, do not apologize for the spill. Let it ring.

pieces.title: There's a Thrown Hand Buried in the Word "Thank You"
pieces.imagePrompt: A radiant multiethnic worship crowd with open hands thrown upward and outward, a beaming Kenyan grandmother beside a young Korean woman and a Guatemalan father lifting his child, palms open to the sky, warm light spilling across their faces; uplifting, tender, premium cinematic film-still, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: The Hebrew word your Bible prints as "give thanks", and, strangely, also as "confess", is built out of the word for a hand. Not a folded hand. A thrown one. Once you see the gesture hiding inside the verb, you cannot un-see why your arms want to move when your heart is full.

body.text: Watch a room full of people receive good news. Watch what the arms do before the mouth catches up.

The hands go up. They open. They throw themselves outward, palms to the sky, as if the body cannot contain the gladness and has to spill it somewhere. Nobody teaches a toddler to do this. Nobody has to. It is older than language.
The Hebrews knew that. And so when they built their word for *giving thanks*, they built it out of the very gesture your body already makes.
The hand hiding in the verb
The word is *yadah*. Your Bible renders it, most often, as *give thanks* or *praise.* But listen to what it is made of. At its root sits *yad*, the ordinary Hebrew word for *hand.*

And *yadah* is not a still hand. The verb carries the sense of *to throw, to cast, to shoot*, the motion you would use to fling a stone, to hurl something out and away from you. Elsewhere in the Scriptures the same root shows up describing hands that cast down, that throw out. So the picture inside the word for thanksgiving is not a hand laid politely on the heart. It is a hand *flung open and up.*
To *yadah* is to give thanks with your arms, to throw your hands toward Yahuah the way you would throw them toward someone you had not seen in years and could not reach fast enough.
The gesture is not a bonus we add to the gratitude. The gesture *is* the word.
Why your arms know before you do
This is the part I love, and it is not sentiment. It is anatomy meeting theology.

The Hebrew mind did not file "thanksgiving" as an idea that lives in the head and might, optionally, produce a bodily response. It named the whole thing by the body. In that world, gratitude is not something you feel privately and then decide whether to express; the expression is baked into the name for it. The thrown hand is not the overflow of thanks. It is what thanks *is.*

So when you feel your arms twitch upward in a song and some cautious voice inside asks whether you are being excessive, understand what is happening. The word for what you are doing is telling your hands to do exactly that. Your body is not getting ahead of your worship. Your body is speaking the word correctly.
You do not raise your hands *because* you are thankful. In Hebrew, raising your hands *is* the thankfulness. The verb is a gesture that learned to be a word.
The strangest thing about this word
Here is where *yadah* opens into something I did not expect the first time I traced it, and it has stayed with me for years.
The same verb, the thrown, open hand, is also the word for **confession.**

In one grammatical form, *yadah* means to give thanks. In another, closely bound to it, it means to confess sin, to own it, to bring it out into the open before Yahuah. And once you see that, the connection is almost unbearably beautiful.

Think about what both acts require of the hands. Thanksgiving throws the hands open to say: *look what You have done, I am holding nothing back from my praise.* Confession throws the same hands open to say: *look what I have done, I am hiding nothing from You.* Both are the identical posture, empty palms, nothing concealed, the whole self exposed and reaching. One says *here is my gratitude.* The other says *here is my guilt.* Same hands. Same word. Same refusal to keep anything in the pockets.

That is why the deepest thanksgiving and the most honest confession feel so oddly alike in the body. They are, in Hebrew, the same motion. You cannot truly *yadah* Yahuah with clenched fists. Praise and confession both require an open hand, and the word knew it before we did.
Closed hands cannot do this

We live in a culture that trains the hands to close. To grip, to hold, to keep, to protect what is ours. A closed fist is ready to fight and ready to hoard. And a closed hand, whatever else it can do, cannot *yadah.* It cannot throw thanks upward and it cannot lay guilt down. It is too busy holding.

I think that is why so many of us find both gratitude and confession so hard. It is not only a matter of the heart. It is a matter of the hand that the heart has trained. We have spent years teaching our hands to grip, and now, in the one place where they most need to open, they do not remember how.

The good news is that the body relearns quickly. The gesture is still in you. It is the same one you made as a child receiving good news, before anyone taught you to be careful. It is waiting under all that gripping.
Throw your hands
So here is the invitation, and it is not a technique. It is a homecoming.

The next time gratitude wells up in you and your arms want to move, let them. Do not sit on your hands out of some inherited fear of drawing attention. Throw them open. That is the word doing its work through your body.

And the next time you come to Yahuah with something to confess, notice what your hands are doing then, too. If they are clenched, open them. You cannot lay it down with a closed fist. The same thrown, empty, honest hand that says *thank You* is the one that says *I hid this and I am hiding it no longer.*

There is a hand buried in the word for thanks, and it was never meant to stay folded in your lap. It was made to be thrown wide open toward the One who gave you both the gladness and the mercy, sometimes in the very same breath, with the very same hands.

pieces.title: The One Word the Translators Refused to Touch
pieces.imagePrompt: A diverse congregation caught in a held moment of stillness mid-worship, eyes closed and faces peaceful, a young Indian woman and an elderly Black man and a Middle Eastern family breathing together in a shaft of warm light, hands lifted but motionless as if the room is holding its breath; reverent, radiant, premium cinematic film-still, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: Scores of times, right in the middle of a psalm, a single word appears that the translators quietly gave up on. They did not render it. They just left it standing there, untranslated, in the middle of the song, Selah. Here is what the honest scholarship can and cannot say about it, and why the mystery might be part of the music.

body.text: Open the Psalms and read one aloud, really aloud, the way they were always meant to be sounded rather than skimmed. Somewhere in the middle of the song, you will hit a word that does not belong to the sentence. It does not finish a thought. It is not addressed to anyone. It just sits there, mid-stream, like a stone in a river.
*Selah.*

Your English Bible printed it, but notice what your English Bible did *not* do. It did not translate it. Across scores of appearances in the songbook, and a handful more in the prayer of the prophet Habakkuk, the translators reached this one small word and, in effect, laid down their pens. They left it in the Hebrew. They did not know what to make of it, and, to their great credit. They refused to pretend that they did.
I want to honor that honesty, and then I want to show you what the mystery might be *for.*
What we actually know, and what we don't
Let me be a careful teacher here, because this is exactly the kind of word where enthusiasm outruns evidence.

The plain truth is this: **no one is certain what *selah* means.** It is one of the genuine unsolved words of the Hebrew Scriptures. What follows are the serious proposals scholars have offered, and I will label them as proposals, not facts, because that is what they are.

One line of thought connects *selah* to a root meaning *to lift up* or *to raise.* On this reading it might be an instruction to the musicians, lift the voices here, raise the instruments, bring up the volume, or lift up the One being sung to.

A second proposal links it to the idea of *weighing*, to measure, to give something its full weight. On this reading, *selah* is a marker over a line that says: *do not rush past this. Weigh it. Let it register at its true heaviness before you move on.*

A third, and perhaps the most widely felt, treats it as a musical or liturgical direction meaning something like *pause*, a suspension, a held rest, an interlude where the singing stops and perhaps the instruments carry on, or where everything falls silent for a breath. Notably, the ancient Greek translation of the Psalms rendered it with a word suggesting an instrumental interlude, which tells us that even in antiquity, centuries before us, its precise meaning was already being guessed at.

Here is what I will not do: I will not pick one of these, hammer it flat, and hand it to you as *the* meaning of *selah.* The most honest thing I can tell you is that the word probably lived at the intersection of all three, lift, weigh, pause, and that the certainty some teachers project about it is not coming from the evidence.
The mystery is doing something to the song
