pieces.excerpt: Right in the middle of the Passover instructions, the most Israelite of all Israel's feasts, the Torah stops to make a provision almost nobody notices. If a foreigner wanted in, there was a way in. And then it says something the ancient world simply did not say: one law, one Torah, for the native and the stranger alike. The feast of a chosen people always had a place set for the outsider.

body.text: If you wanted to build a feast that shut foreigners out, Passover is exactly the feast you would build.

Think about it. This is the meal that remembers the night God chose *this* family and not that one, the night He set a difference between Egypt and Israel, the night He carried His own people out of a nation that was not theirs. It is the most tribal, most in-house, most *ours-and-not-yours* moment in Israel's whole calendar. A birthday of a single people. You would expect its instructions to draw the circle tight and keep it that way.

And that is what makes the small print of Passover so astonishing. Because right there, tucked into the very laws for keeping the feast, the Torah stops and does something the ancient world almost never did. It makes a doorway for the outsider. It says, in effect: if a foreigner among you wants to keep this feast, here is how he may. There is a way in.
Most of us read straight past it. But it is one of the most tender sentences in the Law of Moses, and I want to slow all the way down on it.
The stranger who wanted in

The Hebrew word running through this passage is *ger* (גר), the sojourner, the foreigner who lives among you, the resident outsider with a different birth and a different past. And the instructions about Passover deal with him directly. A foreigner, the Torah says, may keep the Passover.

There is a condition, and I will not hide it from you, because the Word does not hide it. The *ger* who wanted to eat the Passover had to enter the covenant fully, the males were to be circumcised, the sign that marked a man as belonging to Abraham's household. This was not a low fence. It was the real thing: not a guest pass, but full covenant membership. But look closely at what that condition actually says. It does not say the foreigner may *never* come in. It says the opposite. It says the door is real, the way is open, and once he has come all the way in, the Torah's own words are these, *he shall be as one born in the land.* As a native. As family. No lesser tier. No side table.
And then, as if that were not enough, comes the line that I think the ancient world could not have written on its own:
One Torah shall be for the native and for the stranger who sojourns among you.

*One law.* Ezrach and ger, the homeborn and the foreigner, under the same instruction, at the same table, keeping the same feast, with the same standing before the same God. In a world where every people group ranked itself above the peoples around it, where the foreigner was by definition a lesser being with fewer rights, the God of Israel wrote into the founding feast of His nation that there would be *one* standard, and the outsider who came in would live under it as an equal.
A place was always set

I have eaten at a lot of tables in a lot of countries, in guarded places where an outsider is watched at the door, and I know the difference between a table that has a chair for you and a table that merely lets you stand near it.

What moves me about the Passover law is that it does not merely permit the foreigner to exist at the edge of the feast. It sets him a place. It hands him a way to move from the doorway to the table, from *watching* the family remember its rescue to *being* one of the rescued. The circumcision was not a barrier meant to keep him out; it was the covenant meant to bring him all the way in, to make sure that when he sat down, he sat down as a son of the house and not as a tolerated guest who might be asked to leave when the real family got serious.

Do you feel how deliberate that is? Yahuah did not have to say any of this. He could have made Passover a closed door. Instead, on the way *in* to the story of His chosen people, He wrote a standing invitation to the un-chosen, a place always set, a law that made no distinction, a table where the stranger who came in was simply *one of us.* The feast of a particular people carried, from the start, the heart of a God who was never only after one people.
The table where the outsider becomes kin
Now carry this to the upper room, because that is where the whole provision finally opens all the way.

Yeshua keeps this same feast on the last night before the cross, and He takes the ancient Passover and stretches it to the size it was always straining toward. He lifts the bread and the cup and makes them the sign of a new covenant in His own blood, and the sign of entry is no longer a knife. It is faith. The covenant that once asked the *ger* to be marked in the flesh now asks the outsider to be marked in the heart, circumcised inwardly, brought near not by the blood of his own body but by the blood of the Lamb. And the promise on the far side of that entry is the very promise the Torah made at the first Passover: you shall be *as one born in the land.* No lesser tier. No side table. Kin.

This is why the message of Yeshua could walk out to every nation without betraying a word of the Torah. The Passover always had a door for the foreigner. Yeshua simply flung it as wide as it was built to open. The stranger who once had to travel the whole distance into a single nation is now brought near, in Him, from wherever on earth he stands, and seated, as family, at a table that always had a place set.
For the one still standing at the door
So hear this, you who have been hovering at the edge of the room, sure that the real feast belongs to people with a longer history and a purer pedigree than yours.

The most in-house feast in all of Scripture wrote you a doorway on its very first page. The God who set apart one people also declared, in the same breath, *one law for the native and the stranger*, one welcome, one standing, one table. He never intended the outsider to press his face to the window and watch a family he could not join. He intended the outsider to come in and become the family.

The place has been set for longer than you have been alive. The Lamb has already been given, and the only entry He asks now is your trust. So come in from the door. Sit down. There has been a chair at this table with your name on it since the very first night the blood went up over the frame, and the God of this feast has been keeping it for you.

pieces.title: The Feast Built on a Scroll That Never Names God
pieces.imagePrompt: A jubilant multi-ethnic crowd celebrating in a city square at golden hour, people of many nations dancing, embracing, sharing food and gifts, faces flushed with relief and laughter as mourning turns to festival, a rescued people feasting together in the open air; premium cinematic worship-brand film still, warm festive gold light, exuberant and joyful, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: There is one book in the Bible where the name of Yahuah is never spoken. Not once, from the first line to the last. And yet an entire feast, Purim, was born out of it, a feast of the far-off exiles whose rescue came without a single visible miracle. It is the feast for everyone who has ever wondered whether God was still there when they could not see His hand at all.

body.text: There is one scroll in your Bible where the name of God is never written.

Not shortened, not hinted, not tucked into a corner, simply absent, from the opening word to the last. No booming voice from heaven. No prophet standing up to say *thus says the Lord.* No parted sea, no fire on an altar, no angel with a sword. Just a story about exiles in a far-off empire, a beauty contest, a paranoid official, a sleepless king, and a series of coincidences so precisely timed that by the end you cannot breathe. The book is *Esther.* And out of this one book, this book where God is never named, an entire feast was born.

The Hebrews call it *Purim* (פורים). And I have come to love it more than almost any feast on the calendar, because it is the feast for everyone who has ever wondered whether God was still in the room when they could not see His hand at all.
The feast named after a gambler's dice
The name itself tells the story, and it is right there in the text, so I can hand it to you without inventing a thing.

In the book, a powerful man named Haman sets out to destroy every Jew in the Persian empire, the whole scattered nation, far from home, living at the mercy of a foreign throne. And to choose the day for the slaughter, he casts lots. The word for that lot is *pur*, a Persian word, a foreign word, the very dice of the empire that wanted them dead. He rolls the *pur* to pick the date the Jews will die.

And when the whole thing is turned upside down, when the gallows Haman built for his enemy becomes his own, when the scattered people are not destroyed but delivered, the feast that remembers it is named, of all things, after his dice. *Purim.* The *lots.* As if to say: the very instrument the enemy used to seal our doom is the name we now shout at our party. The empire rolled its dice against a far-off people, and the dice came up rescue.

There is a defiant joy in that name that I cannot get over. The feast is not called *the deliverance* or *the victory.* It is called *the lots*, a permanent, laughing reminder that what looked like blind chance in the hands of a tyrant was something else entirely.
The hidden hand
Here is why the missing name is not a flaw in the book but the whole point of it.

In every other great rescue in Scripture, you can see the hand of God move. The sea splits. The walls fall. The fire comes down. But the exiles in Persia did not get a visible miracle. They got a *chain of coincidences.* The right woman happens to become queen. The king happens to have a sleepless night. He happens to call for the royal records. The records happen to fall open to the one page that mattered. The timing happens to line up so perfectly that the villain walks into his own trap at the exact moment he means to spring it.

Read it as luck, and it is the luckiest story ever told. But nobody who reads it carefully believes it is luck. The absence of God's name is not His absence from the story. It is a summons to *look harder*, to see that when there is no pillar of fire out front, there is a hand underneath, moving every piece into place without ever showing its face. The book leaves His name out so that you will find Him in the pattern. And once you have seen it, you cannot un-see it: this is what God's care looks like when it works in the dark.

The name of Yahuah is never spoken in the whole scroll, and His fingerprints are on every single page. That is not the story of His absence. It is the story of how He rescues the ones who cannot see Him work.

There is one line the whole feast hangs on, and I will paraphrase it rather than risk bending the words: a relative says to Esther, in her moment of terror, that perhaps she has come into the kingdom *for such a time as this*, that maybe the whole strange arrangement of her life, the exile and the palace and the crown she never asked for, was quietly aimed at this one hour when a scattered people needed someone on the inside. Neither of them can see the hand. But both of them bet their lives that it is there.
From mourning to a good day
And then comes the turn that gives the feast its flavor forever.

The book says the month that was meant for the people's grief was turned for them from sorrow into gladness, from mourning into a good day, and so they were told to keep it every year as days of feasting and joy, of sending portions of food to one another and gifts to the poor. Sit with that. The command at the heart of Purim is not merely *remember.* It is *feast, and make sure the outsider and the destitute are feasting too.* The rescued people are told to turn around and fill the hands of the ones who have nothing. A grief that was flipped into gladness overflows, by command, to the far-off and the poor.

I have to say honestly where this feast comes from: Purim is not one of the appointed times commanded at Sinai. It was established later, by a scattered people in exile, inside the book of Esther itself, to mark a rescue that happened far from the temple, far from Jerusalem, far from every familiar sign of God's presence. It is, from its very origin, the diaspora's feast, the feast of the ones who were too far away to see the fire fall, and who learned to trust the hidden hand instead.
For the ones who cannot see His hand
Which is exactly why I want to put it into the hands of anyone reading this from a far country, a hard place, a season where God seems to have gone silent.

You may be living in a stretch of your life with no visible miracle in it, no voice, no sign, no sea splitting in front of you, just a run of ordinary days and unexplained turns and a quiet ache to know whether He is even there. Purim was made for you. It is the feast that celebrates a rescue no one saw coming, worked by a God who never once stepped into the frame, on behalf of a people who felt utterly forgotten at the edge of an empire.

The greatest hidden hand of all finally showed its face in Yeshua, the God who had been working underneath the whole story stepped into it in the flesh. But even now He often works the Esther way: unseen, patient, arranging the sleepless nights and the strange timings of your life *for such a time as this.* The absence of the name was never the absence of the God. He is closer to your dark season than the fire ever was to theirs.

So keep the feast in your heart, wherever you are. Send a portion to someone poorer than you. And trust the hand you cannot see, because the whole book was written to tell the far-off exile one thing: mourning does not get the last word. The last word is a feast.

pieces.title: The Winter Feast of Lights He Chose to Walk Into

pieces.excerpt: There is a feast in the Gospels that was never commanded in the Torah. It was born in the darkest chapter of Israel's history, out of a defiled temple and a fight for survival. The Hebrews call it the Feast of Dedication. And John tells us, almost in passing, that Yeshua walked into it one winter, in the temple's colonnade, and said the most staggering sentence of His life. Why there? Why that feast?

body.text: There is a feast that shows up in the Gospels almost by accident, and once you know its story, you cannot read the scene the same way again.

John is telling us about a day in the life of Yeshua, and he sets the stage with two small details that most of us slide right past. It was the *Feast of Dedication,* he says, and it was *winter.* Yeshua is walking in the temple, in the sheltered colonnade named for Solomon, and a crowd presses in around Him and demands, plainly, that He tell them who He is. And there, at that feast, in that cold, He says the sentence that got Him nearly stoned on the spot and has echoed for two thousand years: *I and the Father are one.*

The Hebrews call this feast *Hanukkah* (חנוכה). The word means *dedication*, the same root as the verb for consecrating, setting apart, inaugurating something for holy use. And I want to be honest with you about where this feast comes from, because its story is not like the others, and the honesty makes the Gospel scene burn brighter, not dimmer.
A feast the Torah never commanded

Passover, Shavuot, the Day of Atonement, these were appointed at Sinai, commanded from the mouth of Yahuah in the Torah. Hanukkah was not. It is not one of the *moedim,* the feasts fixed in the Law of Moses. It was born centuries later, in one of the darkest chapters Israel ever lived, and I will tell it to you as history, because that is what it is.

Long after the last prophet fell silent, a foreign king ruled over Judea, a Greek ruler named Antiochus who set out to erase the faith of Israel altogether. He outlawed the Torah. He forbade the covenant. And in the deepest wound of all, he marched into the temple in Jerusalem, the one place on earth set apart for the presence of Yahuah, and defiled it, desecrating the altar, turning the holy house over to the worship of his own gods. The heart of the nation's worship was profaned. The lamp went out.

And then a small, outmatched family of priests and their followers refused to accept it. Against every reasonable odd, they fought and they resisted, and eventually they took the temple back. And when they had it again, they did the only thing that mattered: they *cleansed* it and *rededicated* it. They gave it back to Yahuah, relit the lamp, and set the defiled house apart for holy use once more. That rededication is *Hanukkah.* A feast not of a battle won, but of a defiled thing made holy again.

There is a beloved tradition attached to it, that when they went to relight the temple lamp they found only one small jar of undefiled oil, enough for a single day, and that it burned miraculously for eight until more could be made. I tell you plainly that this is a later tradition, treasured and retold for centuries, and I will not hand it to you as though the Scriptures recorded it. But whether or not the oil stretched, the meaning of the feast is fixed and unshakeable: a house that had been profaned was purified, and the light that the darkness tried to put out was lit again. That is why it became known as the Feast of *Lights*, a winter festival of lamps kindled against the longest nights of the year.
Why He chose that feast to say it
Now stand back inside John's scene, because the timing is not decoration. It is the sermon.

Here is Yeshua, at the feast that celebrates a defiled temple made holy again, walking in the very temple courts, and He begins to speak about Himself in a way that keeps circling one idea. He is the shepherd. He gives His life for the sheep. No one takes it from Him. He and the Father are one. He is standing in the rededicated house, on the feast of its cleansing, quietly presenting Himself as the true temple, the real dwelling place of God among men, the one place where Yahuah's presence has come to live in full.
They gathered that winter to celebrate a house made holy again. And the true House was standing in the middle of them, in the flesh, saying: the Father and I are one.

Feel the layers of it. The feast remembered a lamp relit in the dark. And here was the One who would soon call Himself the light of the world, saying the light shines and the darkness cannot overcome it. The feast remembered a temple purified and given back to God. And here was the One in whom the whole fullness of God was pleased to dwell, the true and final temple that no Antiochus could ever defile. He did not stumble into that feast by chance. He walked into the Feast of Dedication and let its every image gather around Him like a garment, because He *was* what the feast had been reaching for all along. Every relit lamp in every winter window was a small rehearsal for the day the true Light walked into the courts and refused to be put out.
The house they meant to defile is being rededicated in you
And here is where it comes all the way home, to you and to me.

Because the story of Hanukkah did not end in that temple, and it did not end in that colonnade. The New Covenant says something that should take your breath: *you* are now a temple. The Ruach HaKodesh dwells in the one who trusts Yeshua, making the body a holy house, a dwelling place for the presence of God. Which means the whole drama of the feast, a sacred house defiled by an enemy, and then cleansed, and then rededicated, and then relit, is the drama Yeshua wants to work in you.

Maybe you know exactly what a defiled temple feels like. Maybe something marched into the holy places of your life and profaned them, and you have assumed the lamp is out for good and the house is beyond reclaiming. Hear the feast. Hanukkah exists to tell you that a desecrated house is not a lost house. It can be taken back. It can be cleansed. It can be *dedicated again*, that is the whole meaning of the word, and the light that the darkness tried to extinguish can be kindled once more, and burn.

That is what the One walking in the winter colonnade came to do. He is the Light that the longest night cannot swallow, and He is not ashamed to walk straight into the defiled and reclaim it for Yahuah. So let Him. Let the true Temple make His home in you, cleanse what was profaned, and relight the lamp. There is no winter dark enough, and no house too far gone, for the God who turned a desecrated temple into a festival of lights, and who said, in the middle of it, *I and the Father are one.*

pieces.title: Four Cups, Because He Said "I Will" Four Times
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful multigenerational family of many nations gathered close around a candlelit Passover table lifting small cups of red wine together with radiant faces and open-mouthed laughter, grandmother and children and guests leaning in beneath warm hanging lights, a table crowded with matzah and bright dishes; luminous cinematic film-still quality, warm gold amber and deep ruby tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: There are four cups on the Passover table, and every one of them is named after a promise. Most people at the meal never notice that they are drinking their way through the very sentence God spoke to a nation of slaves. And there is a fifth thing hiding in the story, a cup Yeshua lifted, and a cup He refused to finish.

body.text: Let me tell you about a table where nobody drinks just once.

At the Passover meal, the *Seder*, which simply means "order," because the whole night follows a set path like a song follows a melody. There are four cups. Not one. Four. And here is the thing that took my breath away when I first understood it: those four cups are not four refills of the same happy toast. Each one has a name. Each one has a job. And when you line the four names up in a row, you find that the family gathered around that table is drinking its way, cup by cup, straight through a promise God made to a people who had nothing.

The four cups are tradition, mi gente. Let me say that plainly so nobody accuses me of smuggling. You will not find "drink exactly four cups" written as a command in the Torah. What you *will* find is a sentence, spoken to a nation of slaves who had forgotten how to hope, and the tradition of the four cups is built right on top of that sentence, one cup for each promise inside it. So this is a case where the custom is faithful. It took a word of God and turned it into something you could hold in your hand and lift to your mouth.
The sentence the cups are made of

Go back to Egypt. The people are crushed. The bricks never stop. And Yahuah sends word to them through Moses, and inside that word there are four things He swears He will do. *I will bring you out.* *I will deliver you.* *I will redeem you.* *I will take you to be My own people.*
Four verbs. Four "I will" promises, stacked one on top of the next like a man building a staircase up out of a pit. And the tradition took each of those promises and gave it a cup.

The first cup they call the cup of **sanctification**, *I will bring you out.* This is the cup that sets the night apart, that says: something holy is starting here, we are not who we were an hour ago.

The second is the cup of **deliverance**, *I will deliver you from their bondage.* This is the cup you lift over the memory of the plagues, over the night the whole machinery of slavery finally cracked.

The third is the cup of **redemption**, *I will redeem you with an outstretched arm.* And that word, redeem, is *ga'al*, the word for a kinsman buying back what his family lost. This is not a rescue by a stranger. This is family reaching into the slave market and paying to bring you home.

And the fourth is the cup of **praise**, *I will take you to be My people.* This is the cup where the story stops being about escape and becomes about belonging. You did not just get out. You got *taken in.*
Four cups. Four promises. One staircase out of Egypt. And every family that lifts them is rehearsing, without always knowing it, the exact shape of how God saves.
The cup He lifted
Now come with me to a different upper room, on a different Passover night, generations and generations later.

Yeshua, Jesus, if that is the name you learned Him by first, is at this same table, keeping this same order, lifting these same cups. His friends have done this every year of their lives. They know which cup comes when. They could do it half-asleep. And that is exactly why what He does next lands so hard.

The tradition holds that it was at the **third cup**, the cup of redemption, the *ga'al* cup, the kinsman-buys-you-back cup, the one lifted after the meal, that He picked it up, and instead of saying the words they had all expected, He said something no one at any Passover table had ever said before.
This cup is My blood. Poured out for you.

Think about *which* cup. Not the first. Not the second. The **redemption** cup. The cup that for a thousand years had meant *I will redeem you with an outstretched arm*. He lifted that one, and He said: this. This is how the arm gets outstretched. This is the family member reaching into the slave market. The price is not going to be gold. The price is going to be Me.
Every year they had been drinking a promise. That night He told them the promise had a body, and it was sitting at their table, and it was about to be poured out.
The cup He would not finish
But there is one more thing, and this is the part I cannot get over, the part that makes me want to stand up from my chair.

There are four cups. He lifted the third and made it His blood. But the tradition, and the accounts of that night agree, is that after that cup, Yeshua said something strange about the *next* one. He said He would **not drink of the fruit of the vine again** until He drank it new in His Father's Kingdom.
The fourth cup. The cup of **praise**. The cup of *I will take you to be My people.* He would not finish it.

Do you feel the weight of that? The story of salvation has four movements, and He drank three of them to the bottom, the sanctifying, the delivering, the redeeming, all of it, He drained the cup of what it cost to buy you back. But the fourth cup, the cup of the family fully gathered, the cup of *you are finally, wholly Mine*. He set that one down. He left it unfinished on the table. On purpose.

Because that cup is not for an upper room. That cup is for a wedding feast that has not started yet. He is saving it. He looked His friends in the eye and told them, in effect: I am going to drink the whole bitter price now, alone, but the cup of joy, the cup of belonging, the cup where the whole family is finally home, *I will not lift that one without you.* I will wait. I will hold it, untouched, until the day we can raise it together in the Kingdom.
Mi gente, He is still holding it.
Drink like the promise is coming true
So here is why I love this table with my whole heart.

Most of the world thinks Passover is a history lesson, a sad, solemn remembering of something that happened to somebody else a long time ago. But that is not what those four cups are. Those four cups are a promise you drink. They are Yahuah's own "I will," turned into something warm and red that you lift with people you love, so that the saving does not stay an idea in your head but gets down into your body, into the muscle of your arm, into the taste on your tongue.

You were brought out. Lift the cup. You were delivered. Lift it again. You were redeemed, bought back by family that came looking for you in the market, lift it a third time and let it be His very blood. And the fourth cup, the one He set down and would not finish?

That one is still on the table. It has your name near it. He is not going to drink it alone. And on the day the whole familia is finally gathered, when there is not one empty chair left, He is going to reach for that fourth cup at last, the cup of *you are Mine and you always will be*, and we are going to lift it with Him, and we are going to drain it to the bottom, and the joy of that toast is going to shake the whole house of God.
¡Salud, familia! Keep your cup ready. The best one is still to come.

pieces.title: The Song That Cannot Stop Saying "It Would Have Been Enough"
pieces.imagePrompt: A warm crowded Passover table of many nations mid-song with faces thrown back in laughter and joy, hands raised and clapping, an old man beating time and children bouncing in their seats, everyone singing together beneath golden lamplight over matzah and bright dishes; luminous cinematic film-still quality, warm gold amber and honeyed tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: There is a song at the Passover table that keeps interrupting itself with the same three words: it would have been enough. Stanza after stanza, the family piles up everything God did, and after each gift they stop and confess that this one, by itself, would already have been more than they deserved. It is the loudest math lesson in the world, and it will undo you.

body.text: There is a song at the Passover table that does not know how to end.

It is called *Dayenu*, and if you have never heard a room full of people sing it, I am sorry, because it is one of the most joyful sounds a human family makes all year. The word itself is simple. *Dai* means "enough." *-enu* means "for us." Put them together and you get the whole song in a single breath: **it would have been enough for us.**

And that is the entire trick of the thing. It is a gratitude song built like a staircase, and on every single step the family stops and sings the same three words. The tradition strings together a long list of everything Yahuah did for His people, one gift per stanza, a good long pile of them, and after each one, the whole table sings back, *dayenu, dayenu, it would have been enough.*

Had He brought us out of Egypt but done nothing else, *dayenu*, it would have been enough. Had He split the sea but not led us through on dry ground, *dayenu*. Had He fed us in the wilderness but given us nothing more, *dayenu*. Had He brought us to the mountain but never spoken, *dayenu*. On and on it climbs, stanza after stanza, gift stacked on gift, and after every one the room roars back the same impossible confession: *this one, all by itself, would already have been too much.*
The math that makes no sense
Now listen, because I want you to feel how strange this song actually is.

*Dayenu* is not true. Not literally. If Yahuah had split the sea but left His people standing on the wrong shore of it, that would **not** have been enough. They would have died on the beach with the water in front of them and the army behind. If He had brought them to the mountain but never spoken a word from it, they would have had a pile of rock and no covenant. The song knows this. Everybody singing it knows this. That is the whole point.

The family is not doing accounting. They are doing worship. They have stopped trying to calculate what they were owed, because the second you start calculating, gratitude dies. What *Dayenu* does instead is take each individual mercy, lift it up all by itself into the light, and say: *look at just this one. Even if the story had stopped right here, even if this were the only kindness we ever got, it would already be more than we could ever deserve.*
That is a people who have completely lost their grip on the idea that God owes them anything.

And do you know what a people like that becomes? **Too thankful to stop counting.** That is the whole theology of the song. Once you truly believe you were owed nothing, then everything, *everything*, becomes a gift so outrageous you have to name it out loud. You cannot just say "thank you for everything" and move on. That is too cheap. You have to slow all the way down and go one at a time. This. *Dayenu.* And this. *Dayenu.* And also this. *Dayenu.* You keep going because you cannot bear to lump the mercies together into a blur when each one deserves its own line.
Why the counting never runs out
Here is what breaks me open about this song, mi gente.

The reason the family cannot stop counting is not that they are performing. It is that once you start seeing gifts as gifts instead of as your due, you discover there is no bottom to the pile. You reach for what you thought were three or four big rescues, and underneath every big one you find ten small ones you had never even noticed. He brought them out, but who softened Pharaoh's heart to finally let them go? He fed them, but who kept the bread coming *every* morning, and not just the morning they remembered to be grateful? Start pulling on one mercy and a hundred more come up attached to it, like roots.
A grateful heart does not run out of things to count. It runs out of *breath* before it runs out of reasons.

I think a lot of us pray the exact opposite of *Dayenu*. We pray a song I would call *"lo dai"*, "not enough." God, this is not enough. God, You gave me the job but not the raise. You healed the body but not the marriage. You brought me out of the old bondage but I am not in the promised land *yet*. We stand on step three of the staircase, arms crossed, refusing to sing, because we are staring up at all the steps we do not have. And the whole time, the family beside us is singing their hearts out over the step we are standing on and cannot even see.

*Dayenu* is the cure for that. It does not deny that there is more you long for. It just refuses to let the longing rob you of the joy of what is already in your hands. It takes the one gift you *do* have and says: even this. Even *only* this. *Dayenu.*
The God who never stops at "enough"
But now here is the turn, and this is where I want you on your feet.

The whole song is the *people* saying "it would have been enough." Stanza after stanza, *we* would have been satisfied here, *we* would have called it more than fair. The family sets the bar of "enough" lower and lower, humbler and humbler.
And Yahuah blows straight past every single one of them.

That is the secret joke buried in the joy. The people keep saying "this would have been enough", and God keeps not stopping. He brings them out; that would have been enough; He does not stop. He splits the sea; that would have been enough; He does not stop. He gives the mountain, the bread, the land, the promises, and He *keeps going*. The song is a running list of all the places God could have reasonably quit being good to them, and refused to.

And then, when the fullness of time came, when a people who kept singing "it would have been enough" had every reason to expect God to finally rest. He gave His own Son. Yeshua. The gift after which there is no next stanza, because there is nothing left in heaven to give. If Yahuah had only made us. *Dayenu.* If He had only spoken to us. *Dayenu.* If He had only forgiven us. *Dayenu.* But He came down. He wore our skin. He took our death. He rose. And there is no honest way to sing *dayenu* after **that**, because "enough" is a word that finally breaks in your mouth.

So sing the old song, familia. Count your mercies one at a time and refuse to blur them. Say *dayenu* over the small bread of this ordinary morning. Say *dayenu* over the step you are standing on. And then let the song turn around on you and realize the beautiful, staggering truth it was always pointing at:
You keep saying it would have been enough. He keeps deciding it isn't. *¡Aleluya!*, the counting is never going to be finished, because the giving never was.

pieces.title: The Holiest Noise You Will Ever Make
pieces.imagePrompt: A riotous joyful festival crowd of many nations in bright costumes and masks laughing and cheering, children shaking noisemakers with open-mouthed delight, hands lifted, baskets of pastries and fruit passed between neighbors, confetti in warm evening light; luminous cinematic film-still quality, vivid festive jewel tones with warm gold, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: Once a year the most sober people on earth put on costumes, hand out baskets of food, and scream their heads off in the middle of the reading. It looks like chaos. It is actually the loudest theology of joy anyone has ever written, a whole people staging a party on the exact spot where they were supposed to be buried.

body.text: There is one day on the calendar where the rule is: be as loud as you possibly can.

Not quiet. Not solemn. Not heads-bowed. *Loud.* On the feast called Purim, the most reverent people you will ever meet put on costumes and masks, load up baskets of pastries to carry to their neighbors, dig into their pockets for the poor, sit down to a feast that is meant to run long and joyful, and then, right in the middle of the sacred reading, when a certain villain's name is spoken aloud, the whole room *erupts*. Stamping. Shouting. Spinning noisemakers as hard as their arms can go. They blot the man's name out under a wall of sound.

I need to be careful and honest with you before I go one word further, because the house I write in does not let me fudge. Most of what I just described, the masks, the noisemakers, the wild carnival mood, is **tradition**, mi gente. Later custom. You will not find "wear a costume and scream" written into the story itself. What you *will* find written into the story is the reason for every bit of it. And the reason is so good that once you see it, you will want to grab a noisemaker too.
The day everything flipped
The story is the book of Esther, and it is one of the great reversals in all of Scripture.

A man named Haman, powerful and poisoned with hate, cast lots to choose the day he would wipe out an entire people. That is where the name Purim comes from, *pur* is the word for the lot he cast, and *Purim* is just the plural, "lots." The feast is literally named after the dice of the man who wanted them all dead. Sit with that. They named their biggest party after his murder weapon.

Because the dice did not land the way he threw them. A young woman named Esther, hidden in a palace, and her cousin Mordecai, standing at the gate, ended up in exactly the right place at exactly the right hour. The scheme turned inside out. The very gallows the villain built got used on the villain. The day appointed for slaughter became the day of rescue. The book says it plainly: the thing was **turned around**. What was meant for their mourning became their feasting; what was meant for their end became their beginning.

And so the celebration was born, not as a party thrown *after* the danger, in some safe calm afterward, but as a party staged *on the very ground where the graves were supposed to be.* That is what makes the noise holy. They are not being loud because everything is easy. They are being loud on the exact spot where the enemy planned their silence.
Joy as an act of war
This is the thing most people miss about Purim, and it is the thing I most want to put in your hands.

The riot of joy is not silliness. It is **defiance.** When that whole room stamps and shouts and drowns the villain's name in noise, they are doing something ancient and fierce: they are declaring, out loud and in public, that hate does not get the last word and its author does not even get to keep his name. The tradition of blotting out the name under a wall of sound is a people saying, *we will not let this word stand in the air unanswered.* It is worship shaped like a battle cry.
The devil can survive your fear. He has trouble with your feasting. Nothing enrages the accuser like a rescued people throwing a party on the grave he dug for them.

And notice what the celebration is actually made of, because this is where it stops being a show and starts being the gospel. The heart of the day is not the costumes. The heart of the day, and this part is right there in the story itself, is **giving.** The rescued people are told to make it a day of sending portions of food to one another, *mishloach manot*, the baskets carried neighbor to neighbor, and of giving gifts to the poor. The joy is not allowed to curl up private and self-satisfied. It has to spill. It has to get up, put on shoes, and walk a basket of sweet things to somebody else's door, and it has to find the person with nothing and make sure they feast too.
Do you see the whole shape of it now? A people who were nearly erased spend their rescue day making *sure no one around them goes without joy.* That is not a party. That is a sermon you can eat.
The King hidden behind the mask
Here is the part that undoes me, and it is the reason I put on the mask myself.

The book of Esther has a famous secret: the name of God is never written in it. Not once. In the whole story of the great rescue, Yahuah is never mentioned by name. He is *everywhere*, in the timing, in the sleepless night of a king, in the girl who "happened" to be queen, in the reversal no human could have arranged, but His name is hidden. He is working the entire miracle from behind a mask.

And I think that is why the tradition of the costumes is so beautiful, whether the ones who started it knew it or not. On the one day we celebrate the God who saved us without ever showing His face, we all put on faces too. We hide, because He hid. We mask up, in a holy joke, honoring the King who ran the whole rescue from behind the curtain and let a servant girl and an old man at the gate take the visible risk.

But mi gente, the mask is not the end of the story. Because the God who hid His name in Esther eventually stepped out from behind the curtain entirely and *put on flesh.* Yeshua is what happens when the hidden Deliverer finally shows His face, when the reversal we celebrate at Purim becomes a Man who takes the gallows meant for us, and turns the very instrument of death into the instrument of our rescue. Haman's gallows became his own; the cross meant to end Yeshua became the thing that ends *our* death. The pattern is the same pattern. What was built to destroy us got turned around and used to save us. The lots the enemy cast did not land the way he threw them.
So make the noise
Here is what I want you to take from the loudest, most riotous day on the calendar.

There is a kind of joy that is a weapon, and you are allowed to pick it up. When the accuser whispers your name over the grave he has been digging for you, you do not have to answer him with fear. You can answer him with a *feast*. You can drown his voice under praise the way that room drowns the villain's name under noise. You can put on the garment of gladness on the exact ground where you were promised despair, and you can look the whole scheme in the eye and laugh, because the dice already landed and they did not land his way.

And you do not celebrate alone. You fill a basket. You find the one with nothing and you make sure they feast too, because joy that does not spill is not the joy of the redeemed. The redeemed always throw the party wide open.

So make the noise, familia. Make the holiest, gladdest, most defiant noise you have ever made. The name of the enemy is being blotted out. The King who hid His face has shown it. And the day the graveyard turned into a fiesta is a day worth screaming about.

pieces.title: The Day They Dance With the Book in Their Arms
pieces.imagePrompt: A jubilant crowd of many nations dancing in circles holding wrapped scrolls tenderly against their chests like beloved children, faces lit with pure joy, arms lifted, elders and children spinning together beneath warm festive lights, movement and celebration everywhere; luminous cinematic film-still quality, warm gold amber and joyful bright tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: Once a year a whole community lifts the Torah scrolls out of the ark, wraps them up in their arms like children, and dances. Circles and circles of it, laughing, all night, holding the Word against their chests. They have just finished reading the whole thing, and the first thing they do is start it over. Who dances because they love a book this much?

body.text: Imagine a party thrown for a book.

Not a book launch, not a quiet reading, not a lecture with folding chairs. A *party.* Music. Circles of dancing that go on for hours. People taking the scrolls out of the cabinet where they are kept, wrapping them up carefully, holding them against their chests the way you hold a sleeping child, and then *dancing* with them. Spinning. Laughing. Passing the scrolls from arm to arm so everyone gets a turn to carry the Word around the room. Circuits and circuits of it, sometimes late into the night, on a day whose entire purpose is to be glad about the Scriptures.

The day is called *Simchat Torah*, the words mean "the joy of the Torah," or "rejoicing in the Torah." And before I say one more glorious thing about it, let me be straight with you the way I am required to be: this feast is **later tradition.** It is not one of the appointed times commanded in the Torah itself. It grew up long after, as a joyful cap on the fall festival season. So when I tell you about the dancing and the scrolls in the arms, hear me clearly. I am describing a beautiful custom, not a command from Sinai. But mi gente, sometimes a custom captures a truth so well that heaven must smile at it. And this one does.
Finishing the book so you can start it again
Here is the reason for the whole celebration, and it is one of the most tender ideas I know.

The people who keep this feast read through the Torah, the five books of Moses, on a schedule that takes an entire year. A portion each week, faithfully, all the way through the seasons, until the very last week when they reach the end. And the end of the Torah is not a happy ending, not on the surface. It closes with the death of Moses, the greatest prophet, standing on a mountain looking at a promised land his own feet will never walk into. That is where the scroll runs out. On a grave, and a longing.
So what do they do when they reach that last, aching word?

They do not close the book and put it away for a rest. On the very same day, in the very same breath of celebration, they **roll the scroll all the way back to the beginning and start reading it again**, *"In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth."* From the death of Moses to the making of the world, with no gap in between. They finish and they begin in the same joyful hour, so that there is never a single day when the reading of the Word has stopped.

Do you feel how gorgeous that is? They refuse to let the story ever be *over.* The last word hands you straight back to the first word. The grave hands you back to *let there be light.* And the joy of the day is the joy of a people who cannot stand the thought of a single day without the Word open in front of them, so they make sure the ending is also a beginning, and they dance in the seam between the two.
Loving the Word with your whole body
I have to sit with what it means that they *dance* with it.

Not study it. Not merely revere it from a respectful distance. They pick the scrolls up, hold them close, and *move.* This is worship done with the feet and the arms and the sweat of the whole body, not just the head. And I love that with everything in me, because a lot of us have been quietly taught that loving the Word is a serious, seated, silent activity, something you do with a furrowed brow and a highlighter, alone.
The Word of God was never meant to be only studied. It was meant to be *embraced*, carried, held against the chest, danced with until your feet hurt from gladness.

The tradition of the circuits, the going around and around the room with the scrolls, turns loving the Scriptures into something a child can join, something an old woman can join, something the shy man at the back can be pulled into whether he understands every verse or not. You do not have to be a scholar to dance. You just have to be glad. And there is a kind of knowing the Word that only opens up to you when you have held it in your arms and celebrated it with your whole body, that will never open up to you from a chair.
I think heaven is far more like the dancing than like the folding chairs.
The Word you can finally hold
But now I have to tell you the thing that makes me want to jump into the circle myself, because for those of us who follow Yeshua, this feast points at something almost too good.

They dance holding the Word wrapped in their arms like a beloved child. And there came a day, mi gente, when the Word stopped being only ink on a scroll and became a Man you could actually hold. Yeshua is called the Word, the Word that was in the beginning, the Word through whom the heavens and the earth were made, the very "in the beginning" that the scroll rolls back to. The Word did not stay on the page. The Word put on skin and walked into the world, and there was a night when an old man in the temple named Simeon literally took the Word of God up into his arms, held Him, an infant, against his chest, and blessed God that his eyes had seen the promised rescue.

That is Simchat Torah made flesh. The joy of holding the Word became the joy of holding *Him.* And notice what the scroll was always telling us with its beautiful refusal to end: it closes on a death and reopens on creation, over and over, year after year, because the story of God has never once been allowed to stay at the grave. It always rolls forward into new beginning. And Yeshua is the One in whom that pattern stopped being a poem and became history, the death that turned straight into a new creation, the last word that became the first word, the tomb that opened onto *let there be light.*

So when I picture them dancing with the scrolls in their arms, I do not see a quaint old custom. I see a whole people acting out, without always knowing it, the deepest joy there is: the Word of God is not a distant thing to be feared. It is something, *Someone*. You get to hold.
So take Him in your arms and dance
Here is what I want you to carry away from the gladdest day on the calendar.

Stop keeping the Word at arm's length. Stop treating it like a stern examiner you have to satisfy. The people who dance with the scrolls have understood something the anxious student never will: the Word is not against you. It is *for* you, it is *yours*, and it wants to be held close and celebrated, not filed away and feared.

And when you get to the hard endings, the pages that close on a grave and a longing, the seasons where the story seems to run out on a mountain looking at a land you will not reach, do what they do. Do not close the book. Roll it forward. Trust that in the God of Yeshua the last word is always secretly the first word of something new, and let the ending hand you straight back to the beginning.
Then get up. Take the Word into your arms. And dance, familia, dance until your feet hurt, because the Word came near enough to hold, and that is worth every circle you can make around the room.

pieces.title: Even the Poorest Servant Leans Like a King
pieces.imagePrompt: A warm candlelit Passover table where a joyful family of many nations reclines back against cushions in ease and delight, leaning on their elbows and on one another with radiant relaxed faces, a servant and a child leaning like everyone else, abundance spread across the table; luminous cinematic film-still quality, warm gold amber and soft ruby tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: At the Passover table there is one instruction that sounds almost scandalous: everyone must lean. Not sit up straight and dignified, lean, sprawl, recline against the cushions like nobility, even the poorest servant in the room, even the child. There is a whole gospel hiding in that posture, and once you feel it in your own back you will never sit at His table the same way again.

body.text: There is a moment at the Passover table that would have shocked me if I had grown up outside it.

The instruction, at the meal where a whole people remembers being slaves, is not "sit up straight." It is not "be respectful." It is, of all things: **lean.** Recline. Sprawl back against the cushions. Get comfortable. And not just the head of the house, not just the honored guest, *everyone.* The tradition is emphatic and almost defiant about this: even the poorest man in Israel, even a servant, even the smallest child at the table, must recline. Nobody eats this meal sitting bolt upright. Everybody leans.

Let me name the thing honestly, the way I am bound to. The custom of reclining at the Seder is **tradition**. It is written into the old rabbinic teaching about how to keep the meal, not spelled out as a command in the Torah itself. But it is not a random tradition. It is one of those customs that reaches down and grabs the deepest truth of the whole night and puts it in your *body.* Because there is a reason free people lean. And there is a reason it undoes me that they make the servant lean too.
Why leaning meant everything
You have to understand what reclining meant in the ancient world to feel the weight of it.

In the world where this custom took shape, the way you ate told everyone exactly who you were. Slaves and servants **stood.** They stood at the edge of the room, ready to run, ready to fetch, ready to serve. You do not sit down when your body belongs to someone else. And the free, the noble, the master of the house, *they* reclined. They stretched out on cushions, propped on one elbow, at ease, in no hurry, because a free man does not have to be ready to jump. His time is his own. His body is his own. Reclining was the physical signature of freedom. It was the posture of a person who is not afraid of being told to get up.

So when the tradition says *everyone leans tonight*, even the servant, even the poorest, even the child. It is staging a small, glorious revolution at the dinner table. For this one meal, the man who stands and serves all year is told: not tonight. Tonight you lean. Tonight you take up the posture that says *I am free, I belong here, my time is my own.* The people at that table spent generations being told to stand at the edge and be ready to run. And the meal that celebrates their rescue orders them, with tender insistence, to *stop standing.* To lie back. To take the posture of the redeemed.
The question the child asks
There is a beautiful thing built into the Seder about this very posture.

Part of the tradition of the night is that the youngest child asks a set of questions, the "why is this night different" questions, and one of them is exactly this: *why is it that on all other nights we eat sitting or reclining however we please, but on this night we all recline?* The child names the strangeness of it out loud. Why is everybody leaning tonight?

And the answer the night gives is the whole point of Passover: **because we were slaves, and now we are free.** We lean because free people lean. We recline because the God who brought us out did not bring us out to make us slightly-more-comfortable slaves. He brought us out to make us sons and daughters, people with a place at the table who do not have to stand ready to bolt. The posture *is* the theology. You cannot lean back in ease and still believe, in your body, that you are on the edge of the room waiting to be dismissed. The leaning tells your own muscles the truth your fear keeps trying to forget.
Fear stands at the edge of the room, always ready to be sent away. The redeemed lean back into the middle of the table, because they finally believe they are allowed to stay.
The night He leaned with them
Now let me take you to the table I cannot stop thinking about.

When Yeshua kept the Passover with His friends on the last night, the meal we call the Last Supper, the accounts tell us something we skim right past in our paintings and our imaginations. They did not sit at that table on chairs, upright and formal, the way the famous pictures show them. They **reclined.** The word used for how they were at the table is the word for leaning back, stretched out on the low couches around it. This is why, on that very night, the disciple Yeshua loved could lean his head back against Yeshua's chest to ask Him a question. You cannot do that sitting in a chair. You can only do that when you are already reclining beside Him, close, at ease, leaning.

Think about what that means. On the night He was betrayed, on the night the whole weight of the world's rescue was about to fall on His shoulders, Yeshua and His friends took the posture of *free people.* They leaned. And one of them was so unafraid, so at home, so certain of his welcome, that he let his head fall back onto the Lord's own chest. That is the posture Yeshua invites His people into. Not standing at the edge, anxious, ready to be dismissed. *Leaning*, close enough to feel Him breathe.

And here is the wonder of it: He was about to become the servant. On that same reclining night, He got up from the leaning and took a towel and washed feet like the lowest slave in the house, and then He went out and poured His whole life out so that *we* could stop standing at the edge forever. He took the servant's place so that the servant could take the free man's cushion. He stood and served so that you could lean.
Come and lean
So here is what the reclining puts into my very back, and what I want it to put into yours.

A great many of God's own children are still eating at His table standing up. I do not mean literally. I mean in their spirit. They are at the meal, they are technically invited, but they are perched on the edge of the chair, ready to be told they do not really belong here, braced for the moment somebody notices they snuck in. They serve and serve because they are secretly sure their welcome depends on it. They have been rescued out of Egypt and they are still standing like slaves.

Mi gente, **lean back.** The whole scandalous instruction of the night is aimed straight at you: even the poorest servant reclines tonight. Not because you earned the cushion. You did not, none of us did, but because the Master got up and took the servant's towel so that you could take His place at ease. Your time is your own now. Your body is your own now. You are not on the edge of the room. You are in the middle of the table, and there is a chest to lean your tired head against, close enough to feel Him breathe.
You are not a slave who got a nice meal. You are a free child of the house. So do the bravest, most believing thing there is to do at the table of a God who set you free.
Stop standing. Lean.

pieces.title: The Day Jubilee and Hallelujah Became One Word
pieces.song: The King Is At The Door
pieces.imagePrompt: A packed worship-night crowd of many nations under warm stage light, hands lifted, faces mid-shout in pure joy, a multigenerational gospel choir behind them with a grandmother and a small child both dancing, confetti caught in the beams, cinematic worship-brand film still, bright and emotive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I made a whole album out of a word that does not exist. JubiLujah is Jubilee and Hallelujah fused into one breath, because when the King is this close to the door, the right response to waiting is not a furrowed brow. It is a party that refuses to end.

body.text: A Word That Wasn't in the Dictionary Yet
I did not sit down to invent a word. I sat down to praise, and the word arrived before the morning did.

I was somewhere between two of the oldest ideas the faith owns. On one side was **Jubilee**, the fiftieth year of Leviticus 25, when the trumpet sounds, the debts are cancelled, the slaves walk off the auction block, and the land comes home to its family. On the other side was **Hallelujah**, the Hebrew shout that simply means *praise Yah*, the word heaven itself keeps repeating over the marriage of the Lamb in Revelation 19. I had a hand on each of them, and my mouth would not keep them apart. They collided. And out came a word that has never been in any dictionary: *JubiLujah*.

Jubilee plus Hallelujah. Release plus praise. The year of freedom married to the shout that freedom makes. I said it once and I could not un-say it. So I built twelve songs around it, and the first sung word of the whole record is the made-up word itself, landing at the count of zero.
Why a Coined Word and Not a Careful One

People ask why I would risk a nonsense word on the most joyful album I have ever released. The honest answer is that the old words had gotten too comfortable. We say *hallelujah* the way we say *bless you* after a sneeze, reflex, not release. I wanted a word that had no worn groove in anybody's mouth. A word you have to lean into. A word that makes a stranger turn and ask, *what did you just say?*
Some folks wait for a Sunday to start. JubiLujah is a Tuesday in the heart.

That is the thesis of the whole thing. I am tired of joy that keeps office hours. The freedom Yeshua bought was not filed under Sunday morning; it followed the released captive into the carpool line and the diner and the ordinary Wednesday. So I wrote a wake-up call, a song that says *sing it now*, don't wait for the perfect building or the robed choir or a reason that will pass an inspection. The waiting itself had become a thief. It kept telling me *tomorrow* when today was the day the King had already set.
Kairos, Not Chronos

There is a song on this record that unpacks the one idea that convinced me the celebration could not wait. The Greeks had two words for time. *Chronos* is the clock, the watch on the kitchen wall, tick by tick, the years that quietly make you small. And *kairos* is the other kind: the appointed moment, the ripe hour, the instant heaven breaks into the ordinary and everything changes.
Chronos was the line, and kairos was the rhyme. The line keeps ticking, but the rhyme breaks the floor.

I had been living by chronos, waiting for a calendar to grant me permission to rejoice. But the gospel does not run on chronos. It runs on kairos. The Scripture keeps calling this *the acceptable year*, the fullness of time, the day of salvation that is always *today*. When I understood that the right time was not something I was waiting for but something that had already arrived in **Yeshua**, the whole reason to postpone joy collapsed. The watchers get paid. The waiters get to speak. The kairos hour is not coming. It is here.
The Reason Underneath the Party
Here is what I need you to understand, because a celebration this loud can look naive from a distance: I did not make a shallow record. I made an *earned* one.

Right in the middle of all the noise, everything strips back to a single breath and a testimony. I remember the floor. Three in the morning, the tile cold against the cheek, a photograph on the dresser of who I used to be. And then the morning the laughter came up out of my chest without my trying to push it. That song is quiet on purpose. The joy on the rest of the album is only believable because that one song admits where the joy was born.
And the joy that I sing did not start in the sun. JubiLujah was earned where the night was begun.

That is why I can dance. Not because I have never been on the floor, but because He brought me *off* of it. Celebration is not a reaction to a victory I am hoping for. It is the strategy of someone who already knows how the story ends. **Yeshua** said *it is finished* from the cross, and He sat down. The war was already won before I started singing about it. So the dancing is not denial. It is memory.
The Moment the King Is at the Door
Every album has one song that is the reason the album exists. On this one it is the eighth track, and I will not pretend I wrote it calmly.

The whole band drops to silence. A choir whispers three words, *listen, footsteps, the door*, and everything the record has been building toward lands on a single revelation: the King is at the door *right now*. Not someday, not at a safe theological distance. Now. Revelation 22 ends with Yeshua saying *surely I am coming soon*, and the Bride answering *come*. That answer is the whole album compressed into one breath. When the band comes crashing back in after the silence, that is what heaven's arrival sounds like to me, the held breath and then the flood.

I felt the floor tremble where the tile had been. The years He brought me out of folded thin. And the joy I earned in the dark finally put on a crown. That is the arc: the pit, the deliverance, and then the King at the threshold, and every one of them is a reason to make the noise louder, not softer.
Who I Made It For

I made this for the person stuck in a waiting room who has been told to be patient one more time. For the believer in traffic who forgot that the kingdom is already here and not-yet at the same time. For every tribe and tongue that will one day stand before the throne in Revelation 7. I even wrote a song where the word gets sung in Swahili in the morning, Mandarin at noon, Spanish in the evening, because a coined word belongs to everybody or it belongs to no one.

And I built the record to loop. The last song's final chord is engineered to drop a half-step and land exactly on the first song's opening note, so that on repeat the album never actually stops. That is not a production trick for its own sake. That is the point. The party of the Lamb does not have a closing time. It just keeps going.

So here is my invitation, and it is the only one I know how to give. Say the word out loud once, even if you feel foolish. *JubiLujah.* Feel how it makes you lift your head. That lift is the whole gospel in your neck muscles, freedom looking up because the One who bought it is almost at the door. The waiting is nearly over. You are allowed to start the celebration early. In fact, I think that is exactly what we were made to do.

pieces.title: I Stopped Asking God to Erase My Wasted Years
pieces.imagePrompt: A warm recovery-community gathering of diverse adults and elders and a few children in a bright hall, a middle-aged man being embraced by friends with tears and laughter, hands raised in a modest congregation, sunlight through tall windows, a sense of years redeemed, cinematic worship-brand film still, bright and emotive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: For years I prayed the wrong prayer, Lord, delete my lost decade, let me start over clean. He never subtracted a single day. He does something the calendar cannot do: He repays. This is the album I built on the one verse that says the stolen years come back larger than they were taken.

body.text: The Prayer I Prayed for Years, and It Was the Wrong One

For a long time I prayed a prayer I was certain was faith. *Yahuah, erase it. Delete the lost decade. Take the wasted years, the wrong room, the silence I chose, and let me start over at the age I was before it all went sideways.* I wanted the calendar rewound. I wanted a clean page, as if the mercy of God were an eraser.
He never once did it. Not a single day subtracted. And it took me an embarrassingly long time to hear what He kept saying underneath my request: *child, I do not erase. I repay.*

That word broke something open in me, and the album grew out of the crack. I found it in the prophet Joel, chapter two, in a promise so specific it almost sounds like an accountant wrote it: *I will restore to you the years that the locust has eaten.* Not I will pretend they did not happen. Not I will look away from them. Restore. Give back. Repay.
Four Kinds of Locust, Because He Does Not Lump Your Grief Together

The first thing I loved about that prophecy is how *particular* it is. Joel does not say a bug ate your crops. He names four devourers, the palmerworm, the locust, the cankerworm, the caterpillar. What one left, the next one took. It is grief in stages, and the God who inspired that verse refused to lump the stages together.
That mattered to me more than I can say. When I sat down to actually count my own losses, I did not want a vague pile called *the bad time*. I wanted honesty.

Twenty-three to the depression I could not name. Fourteen to the wrong man I should not have chosen. Ten to the silent profession that was not the same. Five to the prodigal child whose phone was frozen.

I put that kind of counting into a song on purpose, with a blank left open so you can name your own. Because **Yahuah** is not a Father who says *they are all the same thing*. He saw every stage, and He did not flinch at any of them. He keeps a ledger, not to accuse you, but because you cannot repay a debt you refuse to count. Year by year, He knows the date the season started and the date it broke.
The Twist: I Stopped Asking Him to Erase

The turn of the whole record, the song the whole thing is built to arrive at, is the one where the prayer finally gets corrected. I had spent so long asking for subtraction. And one day the answer came back inverted.
I stopped asking You to erase, and You started showing me repay. You don't subtract the locust years. You add the wondrous days.

Sit with the difference, because it is enormous. Subtraction shrinks your story down to the parts you are proud of. Repayment lets the whole thing live, even the wreckage, and then *pays interest on it.* The Hebrew verb under the promise is *shalam*: to make whole, to complete, to pay back in full. It is the root behind *shalom*. Repayment is not damage control. It is peace poured back into the exact place the damage happened.
You Were Not Absent From Those Years

There is a quieter song in the middle of the record that I almost did not include, because it names a grief people rarely say out loud, the shock of the mirror. You catch your reflection one morning and the face is older than the story in your head. You went in young. Where did the time go?
I needed to answer that honestly, because the cheap answer, *don't dwell on it*, is a lie that leaves people ashamed. Here is the true one:
The years did not skip me. I was inside them. I was breathing while the locust ate. I was praying while the seasons hardened.

You were not absent during the wasted years. You lived every one of them. And more to the point, so did **Yahuah**. He did not skip the seasons either; He was in the waiting room the whole time. The locust ate the calendar, but it did not eat the breath of the believer, and it did not touch the prayers you prayed with no visible answer. Those were not lost. They were seed in the ground. When I finally believed that the Father saw the *inside* of my years and not just the wreckage on the surface, the shame around the lost time began to lift on its own.
Larger Than Was Taken
Here is the part that still makes me want to shout. When Yahuah repays, He does not hand you back the same amount the thief took. He gives it back *larger*.

I wrote a whole song around a man I will call Brother Calvin, a composite of a hundred real recovery testimonies I have sat inside of. Sixteen to thirty-nine gone to addiction, a couch, a needle, a daughter he lost the right to visit. Then, slowly, a turning. And by his fifties: eight landscaping trucks, and eight recovering brothers driving them. Three foster boys tucked in at night on the same couch his own mother once tucked him into. Fifty regulars at a Wednesday recovery circle he leads.
Father, You did not give me back my twenties. You gave me a season larger than the theft. I have repaid people in my fifties more than I damaged in my twenties.

He did not get his calendar back. He got a repayment that dwarfed the loss. That is the pattern all through Scripture, the God who takes what the enemy meant for evil and makes it *feed multitudes*. What the locust ate did not exhaust His treasury.
Never Ashamed Again

Joel does not stop at the repayment. He adds a line that is really the reason I could put my own name on this record: *and my people shall never be ashamed.* That is the closing note of the whole album, not merely that the years come back, but that the shame attached to them finally has to leave.

The final song ends with a picture I cannot get out of my head. The Father wears the locust years now. I wear His wondrous vow. The exchange is complete. He does not ask you to hide the decade you lost; He asks you to wear the testimony of how thoroughly it was repaid, out loud, forehead-high.

I made this for the person who is convinced the best chapters are already behind them. For the one doing the math on wasted time and coming up short and ashamed. Stop praying my old prayer. He is not going to erase it, and thank God for that, because erasure would rob you of the very testimony He intends to make larger than the loss. Bring Him the honest count. Name the years. Then watch what a Father does who has never once dealt with His children in any way but wondrously. The locust does not get the last word. He does. And the last word is *repaid*.

pieces.title: I Wrote a Whole Album for Holy Saturday
pieces.imagePrompt: A small diverse group holding a quiet candlelight vigil at dawn, a widow and a young man and an elderly couple with heads bowed and faces soft with grief turning to hope, first light breaking through a window behind them, warm and tender and cinematic, worship-brand film still, emotive low light lifting toward morning, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I am the loud one, the praise-break psalmist. So people were surprised when I made a record that refuses to rush to the morning. The brass does not sound until the very last song, on purpose. This is the album for the day between the cross and the empty tomb, when Sunday has not come and Friday is over and you are just sitting in the silence.

body.text: The Loud One Made a Quiet Record

I am the psalmist of the praise break. I am the one who turns waiting rooms into worship rooms and ordinary Tuesdays into celebrations. So when I told people I was making an album that spends its first three songs in a minor key and does not let a single trumpet play until the very last track, some of them thought I had lost my nerve.
I had not lost my nerve. I had finally found my honesty.

Because here is a thing the loud church does not always admit: roughly a third of the Psalms are laments. The songbook God authored is full of grief that never once loses its address to Him. And most of us live a great deal of our lives not on Friday, where the sacrifice is clear, and not on Sunday, where the tomb is empty, but on *Saturday*. The day in between. The day when the cross is over and the resurrection has not arrived yet and you are just sitting in the silence, holding a question no one can answer.
So I wrote a whole album for Holy Saturday.
Holding the Question Open

The record opens with the oldest honest prayer in the world: *how long, O Lord?* It is Psalm 13, verse one, the question David asked and did not get punished for asking. I set it at two-fourteen in the morning, an unanswered text glowing on a screen, a worn Bible page, an empty chair at the breakfast table.
I did not resolve it quickly, and I want to tell you why. If I rush you to the answer, I am not comforting you. I am dismissing you.
He is in the "how long." He hears the unwhispered song.

That is the theology holding up the whole first act. **Yahuah** is not embarrassed by your question. He is *inside* it. The second song leans on the hardest verse in the Bible, Psalm 22, verse one, *my God, my God, why have You forsaken Me?*, and reminds you that **Yeshua** Himself sang that exact line from the cross. He did not float above the abandonment. He prayed it. Which means when you pray it, you are not falling out of faith. You are standing in the footprints of the Son of God.
Why the Brass Waits
The most deliberate decision on this record is one you feel before you can name it: the instruments are rationed.

There is no Hammond organ, no brass, no arena drums for the first five songs. The cello carries the weight alone. The Hammond does not arrive until the sixth track, on the exact line where the album turns, *yet I will trust*, borrowed from Habakkuk, who looked at the fig tree that would not blossom and the empty stall and chose praise anyway, and from Job, who said *though He slay me, yet will I trust Him.* That is not triumph. That is gritted teeth. So the first warm sound on the whole album is the sound of trust decided in the dark, not felt in the light.

And the brass, the full, blazing, celebration brass that people expect from me in the first thirty seconds. I held it back for eleven songs. It does not sound until the final track. The first trumpet on the entire album *is* the morning. I wanted you to have to wait for it the way grief makes you wait for joy, so that when it finally breaks, your body knows it was earned.
Weeping for a night, but joy comes in the morning.
That is Psalm 30, verse five. But I refused to let the morning cheat the night out of its due.
The Song I Could Not Sing Twice

Every honest lament record has a track that costs the writer something. On this one it is a song about an empty cradle, a nursery painted yellow at the twenty-second week, a hand-stitched name-blanket folded on a changing table, a pregnancy lost. I built it on Psalm 139, the passage that says we are knit together in the secret place, because I needed the God who does the knitting to be the one holding the loss.

In the middle of that song the whole band cuts out and a father's voice speaks over the silence. *I held the baby before you did. I am holding the baby now. I am holding you. The empty cradle is not the end of the story.* I have watched that moment undo rooms of people who were told to *stay strong* when what they needed was permission to grieve in the presence of God. Lament is not the absence of faith. It is faith refusing to let go of God's sleeve while it weeps.
The God Who Was Not in the Earthquake

Near the end of the journey there is a song that resolves the whole ache in the quietest possible way. It goes to Elijah, in 1 Kings 19, the prophet in the cave on the mountain, burnt out and wanting to die. A great wind tears at the rocks, but the Lord is not in the wind. An earthquake shakes the ground, but the Lord is not in the earthquake. A fire passes, but the Lord is not in the fire. And then, a still, small voice.
Not the earthquake, not the storm, not the fire. The still small voice transforms.

I wanted that song on the record because so much of our grief is spent waiting for **Yahuah** to show up in the spectacular, the sudden healing, the loud deliverance, the earthquake that fixes everything. And He so often comes instead as a hush after the hard week, a whisper the storm could not drown. Being held in that hush is not a lesser answer than the fireworks. It is frequently the truer one.
