The Trinidadian heart that pours into the road already knows how to do that. I am simply pointing the parade at the throne.

The album also has a hymn on it, and I chose it on purpose. **Amazing Grace on the Shuffle** carries the melody the whole diaspora knows, but I sing it remembering that the man who wrote those words wrote them out of his own turning from the slave trade. That is real history, and I hold it honestly. The same grace that turned that ship's captain crossed the same ocean that carried the stolen, and met the descendants of the stolen on the Caribbean shore, and it is *the same grace* still. *Same grace then, same grace today.* When a steelpan plays that melody on a Sunday morning in Port-of-Spain, the whole terrible and redemptive weight of that water is being sung over into something free.
The Wisdom Was Already Walking the Islands

The boldest thing I say on this record is on **Wisdom Walked the Caribbean,** and I want to be precise about it because it is easy to misuse. When the missionary boats came, some arrived with the assumption that they were *bringing* God to a godless place. But Scripture names **Yeshua** as *the wisdom of God* (1 Corinthians 1:24), the One *in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge* (Colossians 2:3). The Wisdom of God is not a Western possession that had to be imported. Christ was Christ before any steamship sailed. **Yahuah** was already sovereign over those islands, already the sea's Lord, already the One toward whom every genuine longing for truth was straining, long before the colonial chaplaincy arrived.

I do not say that to erase the missionaries who genuinely carried the good news. I say it to heal a wound, to tell the Caribbean believer that she was never outside the reach of the Wisdom of God, and that her hunger for truth was itself evidence He had already been near.
Holy Spirit knew the islands first, and now the islands know Him better.
Bright Joy Marches Home

The album ends where the whole story ends. Isaiah promises that *the ransomed of the Lord shall return, and come to Zion with songs and everlasting joy upon their heads* (Isaiah 35:10). **Bright Joy Marches Home** is that verse with a brass band, the diaspora, the ransomed, marching from the panyard to the altar to the throne, joy on our heads like a crown, the whole scattered family coming home. Isaiah even foretold the sound: *Sing unto the Lord a new song... from the ends of the earth,* from *the isles* (Isaiah 42:10, 12). The islands were written into the choir from the beginning.
Who I Made This For

I made *Calypso Consciousness* for the one who thinks their culture and their Christ live in separate rooms. For the calypsonian, the panman, the artist who suspects their gift is too worldly to be wanted. For the diaspora believer who was told, in a hundred quiet ways, that God arrived on the islands by boat and might still consider them a mission field rather than a home.

Hear me. Your consciousness was made for **Yeshua.** The truth you were always trying to tell has a name, and He is the Truth Himself. The Wisdom you were reaching for walked your waters before anyone taught you His name. So bring the whole tradition home, the pan, the shuffle, the truth-telling lyric, the joy on your head, and lay it at the throne where it was always headed.
Calypso was always telling the truth. It just took me a while to hear Who the truth was about.

pieces.title: The Dust Has to Rise Before the Glory Falls
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful sunrise gathering of many families of every nation around a rough timber altar on a high mountain ridge, thin gold smoke rising into a bright sky, hands lifted and faces radiant with hope, children on shoulders, a fiddle and a banjo in the circle, warm dawn light spilling across the grass; cinematic worship-brand film still, bright and emotive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I made a whole record out of the smoke that comes off a frontier altar at dawn. Here is why the dust rising is not the opposite of the glory falling. It is the invitation for it.

body.text: I built this record around a picture I could not shake: a rough altar of stacked timber on a high ridge, first light coming up cold and clean, and a thin line of smoke climbing off the offering into a sky that has not decided yet whether it will answer.

That smoke is the whole album. Not the fire that falls, the smoke that rises before it. I named the thing *Altar Dust & Glory* because I had come to believe those two words belong on the same breath, and most of us have been taught to keep them apart.
Why I had to make it

I grew up around people who thought worship was what you did after the glory showed up. You wait for the goosebumps, the swell, the moment, and then you lift your hands. But out on the frontier, in the log-house meetings and the clearing revivals, I watched something older. I watched people bring the offering first. Before they felt a thing. In the cold, in the dark, with the lanterns held low, they laid it down and they let the dust rise, and they did not demand that heaven hurry.

That order matters. The dust goes up before the fire comes down. Every single time. I have never once found it reversed in the whole record of Scripture, and I have looked, because there were seasons I badly wanted it to be reversed, seasons I wanted the glory first, as proof, before I risked the offering. It does not come that way. The altar gets built in the dark, and the smoke goes up while you are still cold, and only then does the sky decide to answer.

Exodus chapter twenty-nine calls the burnt offering a sweet savor to **Yahuah**, the smoke itself is the thing that pleases Him. Not the ash left over. The rising. The part where you can still smell the cedar burning and you do not yet know what He will do with it. I wanted a record that lived right there, in the ache between the offering and the answer, because that is where most of my life actually happens, and I suspect it is where most of yours does too.
What the title means

"Altar dust" is the residue of a real sacrifice. You cannot get it without giving something up, the bullock, the timber, the morning you would rather have spent asleep. It is dirty. It gets on your boots. The opener, *Altar Dust Rising*, puts a plain altar "on the high ridge" and lets the "dust of the offering" climb "into the dawn," and I sing it the way I mean it: every offering my frontier heart could carry, smoking on the timber of the cross, lifted in the glory at no cost.

"Glory" is what **Yahuah** does with the dust that we could never do ourselves. In Second Chronicles chapter seven, when Solomon finishes praying, the fire falls and the glory fills the house so thick the priests cannot even walk back in to do their jobs. That is track eight of this record, *Glory Filled the House*, the whole assembly thrown to the floor, not because they worked it up, but because He came down.
The dust is yours to raise. The glory is His to send. Do not confuse the two, and do not skip the first one waiting on the second.
The heart under the songs

The center of this album is a fire on a mountain. Track nine, *Cedar Fire Cinematic*, is Elijah on Carmel, and it opens with the plain words of First Kings chapter eighteen: the fire of **Yahuah** fell and consumed the sacrifice, and the wood, and the stones, and even the dust. I put that verse right up front on purpose. The dust that Elijah had raised, the offering he built with his own hands and then drenched in water until it looked impossible, that same dust is what the fire came for. Heaven did not answer his cleverness. It answered his altar.

But I did not want a record that only shouted. So I hung the quiet tracks around the fire like lanterns. *I Will Lift My Eyes* is Psalm one hundred twenty-one sung almost in a whisper, the pilgrim song, "I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help." I wrote it for the bedside and the night watch, for the one who cannot raise a shout right now and needs to be told that the Keeper of Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps. And *Holy Holy Holy on the Mountain* takes Isaiah chapter six, the seraphim covering their faces, and drops that trembling awe down into an Appalachian valley where the cedars bow in the wind of the Spirit.

Then there is the trail. *Wagon Trail Hallelujah* and *Cloud of Witnesses* both stand on Hebrews, the strangers and pilgrims of chapter eleven, the great cloud of chapter twelve cheering us on. Because an altar is not a destination. It is a place you stop on a long road to lay something down, and then you get back on the wagon and keep moving toward home. I wanted the record to feel like that: fire, then dust, then wheels turning again at dawn.
Who I made this for
I made *Altar Dust & Glory* for the ones who are tired of manufacturing a moment.

For the mother holding a lantern who brought her offering before she felt a thing. For the man whose sacrifice this year cost him more than anybody in the room will ever know, and who is standing at the timber in the cold wondering if the fire is ever going to fall. For the pilgrim who has been on the trail so long the dust has settled into his skin, and who needs to be reminded that the dust on him is not proof he is far from the altar. It is proof he has been near it.

Hear me on this, because it is the thing I most want you to carry off this ridge: you do not have to feel the glory to raise the dust. You raise it in the dark. You lay the offering on the timber before the sky answers. And the record of **Yahuah**, from Elijah's soaked altar to Solomon's finished prayer to the cross where **Yeshua** became the offering Himself so we would never have to earn the fire, that whole record says the same thing every time. The One who told you to build the altar has never once let the dust rise for nothing.
So build it. Raise your dust into the cold dawn. Sing it before you feel it.
And then watch the ridge. Because the fire that fell on Carmel is the same fire that fills the house, and it is still, this very morning, looking for an altar to answer.

pieces.title: The Mountain Was Always Meant to Shake
pieces.imagePrompt: A jubilant Pentecost-style revival packed with believers of every nation on a green Appalachian mountainside at golden hour, hands thrown high, tambourines shaking, mouths open in a shout of joy, older saints and children dancing together, mist rising off the ridges behind them like smoke, radiant faces lit with fire-warm light; cinematic worship-brand film still, bright and emotive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: This is my loudest record, and it is loud on purpose. The Spirit that fell at Pentecost did not come to make us comfortable. He came to shake the mountains, and He is not tame.

body.text: I will tell you straight: *Appalachian Shout* is the loudest thing I have ever made, and I made it loud on purpose.

Somewhere along the way the church talked itself into believing that reverence means quiet and maturity means restraint. I do not find that in the record. I find a wind so violent it filled a whole house. I find a room so full of the Spirit that the building itself shook on its foundations. I find people so undone that the watching crowd accused them of being drunk before nine in the morning. That is the mountain I come from, and that is the mountain this album climbs.
Why I had to make it

I come out of the holiness-Pentecostal hollers of the high country, brush-arbor meetings, foot-stomped floors, the shout that starts in one voice and rolls down the ridge until the whole valley is on its feet. And I watched that fire get sanded down into something polite. Something scheduled. A worship set with a curfew.

So I built a record with no restraint in it. The opener, *The Spirit Moves*, starts a cappella, one tenor voice, no band, just "the Spirit moves, the Spirit shakes", and then the whole mountain comes in behind it. I wanted the first thing you heard to be a voice with nothing to hide behind, because that is how it started in the upper room. Joel had promised it: in the last days, says **Yahuah**, I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh. Not a trickle. A pouring. And when it came in Acts chapter two, it came as wind and fire and unstoppable speech.
What the title means
A shout is not noise for its own sake. In the record, a shout is a body agreeing with its Maker out loud.

Psalm forty-seven says it plainly, clap your hands, all ye people; shout unto God with the voice of triumph. Psalm one hundred opens the same way: make a joyful noise. The shout is what happens when the good news gets bigger than your composure. Track nine, the title cut, *The Appalachian Shout*, is that exact moment, the point in a mountain meeting where the singing stops being a song and becomes a roar, where the congregation quits performing worship and starts erupting with it.
A shout is the sound faith makes when it finally believes what it has been singing.

And "Appalachian" matters. I did not want a generic revival record. I wanted the fiddle and the clawhammer banjo and the ten-voice congregational holler of my own people, because the Spirit who fell at Pentecost fell on every man in his own tongue. That is the miracle nobody slows down for, the fire did not make them all sound the same. It let each man hear the wonderful works of God in the language of the country he was born in. Fire does not erase where you are from. It sets it ablaze. So I sang it in mine, high and lonesome, off the ridges, on purpose.
The heart under the songs

The engine of this album is *Pentecost Fire*, the third track, and the one I would point a stranger to first. It is Acts chapter two set to a fiddle scream: the fire that descends, fills the vessels, and "can't be contained." I built the whole song around that last idea. You cannot contain Pentecost. The minute you could manage it, schedule it, keep it inside the lines, it would not be the fire that fell in the upper room anymore.

*Shake the Mountains* comes right behind it, and it is a prayer straight out of Acts chapter four, the believers pray, and the place where they are gathered is shaken. But I aimed the shaking inward on purpose: shake the comfortable, shake the complacent, shake the church, shake the nation. Isaiah cried, "Oh that thou wouldest rend the heavens, that thou wouldest come down, that the mountains might flow down at thy presence." That is not a tame request. That is a man asking **Yahuah** to tear the sky open. I wanted a whole record that dared to pray it.

Now, a word of honesty, because the record earns it. There is a track called *Snake Handlers and Saints*, and I need you to hear how I hold it. Mark chapter sixteen does say signs will follow them that believe, and in my mountains some took up serpents from that verse literally. I sing about those saints with love, because they were hungry for a power the flatland church had forgotten. But I will tell you what the Scripture actually promises and what is only mountain tradition: the promise is that the Spirit is real and present and moving. Handling serpents to prove it is a tradition some of my people built on top of the text, and more than one of them died doing it. I honor their hunger. I do not command their method. The fire never asked us to tempt it, only to receive it.
Who I made this for
I made *Appalachian Shout* for the ones who have been told to settle down.

For the young man whose praise is too big for the room he is standing in. For the grandmother who remembers when the meetings ran till midnight and nobody wanted to leave, and who has been quietly grieving a church that watches the clock now. For the tired believer who has been running on a program instead of a presence, and who needs to be reminded that the Spirit of **Yahuah** is not a mood you set with lighting. He is a fire that fell on real people in a real room and shook the walls.

And for the one who is afraid of it. I know you are out there. You have seen the fire counterfeited and you have grown suspicious of loud. I understand. But hear me: the answer to counterfeit fire is not no fire. It is the real thing, tested against the Word, aimed at the glory of **Yeshua** and no one else.

That is the whole safeguard on this record, every shout on it lands on His name. The Spirit did not come at Pentecost to make people spectacular. He came to make them witnesses. The fire sat on their heads and then sent them into the street to talk about a risen Savior.
So let the mountain shake. Let the shout rise up out of you like it rose off the ridges of my childhood. Do not apologize for the size of it.
The wind that filled the house is still blowing. And the mountain, all along, was always meant to shake.

pieces.title: Your Calluses Are Consecrated Ground
pieces.imagePrompt: A radiant, globally-diverse crowd of working people gathered at golden hour, farm workers, a coal miner, a mother with a baby on her hip, a mill hand, calloused hands lifted together in joyful praise, work tools set down beside them, warm dust and light in the air, faces lit with dignity and gladness; cinematic worship-brand film still, bright and emotive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I made a record with a hammer for a heartbeat. It is for the farm worker, the coal miner, the single mother, the millhand. Everyone the church has quietly treated as a lower kind of saint. Your labor is not the opposite of your worship. It is your worship.

body.text: The heartbeat of this record is a hammer.

Not a kick drum dressed up to sound like one, a real hammer on a real downbeat, an anvil, a mill bell, the percussion of people who make their living with their hands. I built *Working Hands, Faithful Heart* on that rhythm because I got tired of a church that treats the calloused as a lower kind of saint.
Why I had to make it

Somewhere we got the idea that there are holy jobs and ordinary jobs. That the man behind the pulpit is doing the Lord's work and the man behind the plow is just paying his bills until Sunday. I have stood in too many rooms where the farm worker, the miner, the millhand, the woman raising kids on two jobs, all got the quiet message that their real life happens elsewhere, that the sacred is somewhere they visit, not something their hands already touch.
That is a lie, and it is old, and I wanted to burn it down with a record.

Because the very first thing **Yahuah** did with the man He made was give him work. Genesis chapter two. He put him in the garden to dress it and to keep it, before the fall, before sin, in the middle of paradise. Labor was not the curse. Labor was the assignment, handed out in Eden while everything was still very good. The sweat got hard later. The dignity was there from the beginning.
What the title means
*Working Hands, Faithful Heart.* I put those two together because the world keeps trying to pull them apart.

It will tell you the hands are for the marketplace and the heart is for the sanctuary. But the second track on the record says the thing I most believe: *Working Hands Are Holy.* Not holy someday, when you finally get into ministry. Holy now, in the field, at the rig, on the line. The opener, *These Hands Know the Way*, traces it back through a family, my father's hands, my mother's hands, all of them knowing the work, all of them knowing God through it, because faith in my country got handed down calloused palm to calloused palm.

Moses prayed it in Psalm ninety: "establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it." He asked twice in one breath. He was not asking **Yahuah** to bless his church service. He was asking Him to make the daily labor count for something that lasts. And think about who prayed it, a man who had spent forty years on the backside of the desert keeping another man's sheep before God ever spoke to him from the bush. He knew what it was to labor in obscurity, to work hard at something nobody was watching. When he finally asked heaven to make the work of his hands stand, he was asking for every calloused, unnoticed year of it.
The question was never whether your work is holy. The question is whether you will believe Him when He says it already is.
The heart under the songs
This record has a lot of faces on it, and I put them there on purpose.

There is *Farm Worker's Prayer* and *The Migrant's Song*, because Scripture is not shy about the ones who stoop in other people's fields. *Coal Dust and Gospel*, for my own mountains, where men went down into the dark and came up singing. *Single Mother's Blessing*, because raising children alone is some of the hardest and most invisible labor there is, and heaven sees every hour of it. *The Mill Bell Rings* and *Hands That Build*, for the ones who make the things the rest of us use without a second thought.

And then there is *Wage Theft and Justice*, and I will not apologize for it. James chapter five says the wages of the laborers, kept back by fraud, cry out, and the cries have reached the ears of the Lord of Sabaoth. That is not my opinion. That is the Word raising its voice on behalf of the underpaid. A record about the dignity of work that stayed silent about the theft of a paycheck would be a coward's record. So I named it, and I set it to the same hammer as the rest, because justice for the worker is not a distraction from worship. It is the shape love takes when it has skin in the field.

The whole thing rests on one verse more than any other. Colossians chapter three: "whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men." Paul wrote that, remarkably, to slaves, to people whose labor was stolen from them by definition, and he told them their work could be aimed straight past their masters at **Yeshua** Himself. If the most exploited workers in the ancient world could hand their labor up to the Lord and have Him receive it as worship, then so can you, at whatever bench you are standing at tomorrow morning.
Who I made this for
I made *Working Hands, Faithful Heart* for the ones the church forgot to disciple because they showed up tired.

For the man who comes home with dirt he cannot fully scrub out and wonders if God notices a life spent that way. He does. *Faithful Hands Forever* closes the album for exactly him. For the woman who has never once felt like the "spiritual" type because her days are spent doing and lifting and cleaning and providing, and who needs to hear that her doing is her devotion. For every saint who suspected the real Christians were the ones who got to sit in a study all day, and quietly counted themselves out.

Hear me. Hebrews chapter six says **Yahuah** is not unrighteous to forget your work and the love you have shown toward His name. He is not unrighteous. He does not forget. Not the field, not the shift, not the double, not the night feeding, not the thing nobody thanked you for. He keeps a record calloused hands never see, and He keeps it faithfully.

The first man the Bible ever says was filled with the Spirit of God was not a preacher. He was a craftsman, Bezalel, filled to work gold and stone and wood for the tabernacle. The Spirit's first named skill was the skill of the hands. That has never stopped being true.

So set the hammer down for one minute and look at your own palms. The lines in them, the calluses, the wear, that is not evidence of a lesser life. That is consecrated ground. And the God who worked the world into being with a word is not the least bit embarrassed to call your labor holy.

pieces.title: Every Handful of Red Dirt Belongs to Him
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful, diverse gathering of ranch families and farmhands on wide West Texas red-dirt land at golden hour, first rain clouds breaking on the horizon, hands raised in gladness, a rancher lifting a laughing child, dogs and horses nearby, red earth glowing warm under a vast open sky, faces bright with hope and relief; cinematic worship-brand film still, bright and emotive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: Texas red dirt taught me two things I could not have learned in a pew, that I am made of the ground, and that the ground was never mine to begin with. It all belongs to Him, and He is coming back like rain to redeem it.

body.text: Red dirt gets in everything. It works into the creases of your boots and the knees of your jeans and the grain of your skin until you cannot tell anymore where the land stops and you start. Out on the West Texas frontier, that is not a metaphor. That is Tuesday.
And it taught me two things I could never have learned sitting still in a pew, that I am made of the ground, and that the ground was never mine.
Why I had to make it

I wanted to make a gospel record that smelled like actual dirt. Not a sanitized country album with a cross stamped on the cover, but something that came up out of the soil the way the people I love came up out of it, ranchers, roughnecks, border-country farmers, folks whose faith is inseparable from the land they break their backs on.

Because the land is where the whole story starts. Genesis chapter two says **Yahuah** formed man of the dust of the ground and breathed into him. We are red dirt with the breath of God in it. The opener of the record just says it flat, "red dirt, Texas, that's where I come from, red dirt in my blood, red dirt, gospel, home." I meant it as theology, not just geography. You are dust He decided to love. So is the man on the rig next to you.
What the title means
Here is the turn the album is built on, and it took me years to make peace with it: the redemption in *Red Dirt Redemption* is not just mine. It is the land's too.

We think redemption is a private transaction, my soul, my rescue, my ticket out. But Leviticus chapter twenty-five, in the law of Jubilee, has **Yahuah** saying something that stops a landowner cold: "the land shall not be sold for ever: for the land is mine; for ye are strangers and sojourners with me." Every deed you have ever signed, every fence you have ever strung, and the ground underneath it belongs to Him. You are a guest on it. Psalm twenty-four opens the same way, the earth is the Lord's, and the fulness thereof. Even the cattle on a thousand hills are already His.
You do not own the red dirt. You were entrusted with it. Those are very different jobs, and only one of them lets you sleep at night.

That reframes everything a working man does with land. *The Rancher's Prayer*, *The Rancher's Covenant*, *The Land Is the Lord's*, those tracks are all wrestling the same holy fact: I do not possess this place. I keep it for the One who does, and one day I hand it back.
The heart under the songs

The center of the record is the title cut, *Red Dirt Redemption*, and I built it on the way rain comes to dry country. If you have never watched a real drought break, you have not felt the thing this album is chasing. Joel chapter two promises **Yahuah** will send the rain, the former rain and the latter rain, and restore the years the locust has eaten. Hosea says He will come to us as the rain, as the latter and former rain unto the earth. On hard land, redemption does not arrive as an idea. It arrives as weather. As mercy you can smell before you can see.

So the record moves like a rainstorm. *Oil Rig Gospel* and *Border Country Gospel* are the dry, dusty, working-hard middle, grit and diesel and heat, the long stretch where you are doing everything right and the ground gives you nothing back. *Red Dirt Repentance* is the turning, the moment a hard man finally goes to his knees in the field, and I put it there deliberately, because on real land repentance and rain tend to show up in the same week. Something in the human heart cracks open right about the time the sky does. And then the sky opens.

There is a thread through the whole thing I did not want anyone to miss. *Matthew* chapter twenty-five, "I was a stranger, and ye took me in." Border country is a place where strangers cross hard land, and I wanted a gospel record from that country to remember what **Yeshua** said about the stranger. On land that is not finally ours anyway, hospitality is not charity. It is just telling the truth about who owns the place.

And the record does not end on the dirt. It reaches past it. Romans chapter eight says the whole creation groans, waiting, the land itself is aching for the day the children of God are revealed and everything gets set free. Revelation chapter twenty-one promises a new heaven and a new earth. So *Red Dirt Forever* closes the album not with the land as it is, cracked and thirsty, but the land as it will be, redeemed, watered, restored, belonging fully and finally to the One who formed it.
Who I made this for
I made *Red Dirt Redemption* for the ones whose faith grew up outdoors.

For the rancher who has prayed for rain until his voice gave out, and who needs to know that the God he is praying to owns the sky and the pasture and him. For the roughneck who thinks a man that dirty and that far from a church could not possibly matter to heaven, when heaven made him out of the same red dust it made kings from. For the farmer watching a drought take everything he built, who needs to hear that the years the locust ate are exactly the years **Yahuah** specializes in restoring.

And for the wanderer. Border country is full of them, and so is this record. If you have felt like a stranger on ground that will not claim you, hear the deepest thing on the album: you were always a sojourner here. Every one of us is. The dirt is on loan, the days are numbered, and the only permanent inheritance is the one **Yeshua** went ahead to secure, a land where nothing dries up and no deed ever expires.
So go on and get the red dirt in your creases. Work the ground you were given. Pray for the rain like it is coming, because on His land, it is.

And when it breaks over you, and it will, remember that the redemption running down your face was never only about you. It was the whole thirsty earth getting a taste of what its Maker has been planning to do with all of it.

pieces.title: He Drove Me Past the Last Fence Line
pieces.imagePrompt: A small, tender gathering of diverse pilgrims at dawn in a vast high desert canyon, kneeling and standing together with faces turned upward in peace and relief, soft amber light spilling over red rock, one figure with arms open wide, a sense of hard-won joy and homecoming after long solitude, warm wind moving through sparse brush; cinematic worship-brand film still, bright and emotive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: This is my quietest record, and it cost me the most. It is about the wilderness, the place the Spirit drives you to strip away everything you perform, until the only voice left is His and the only word you own is His name.

body.text: Every other record I have made shouts. This one whispers, and it cost me more than all the loud ones put together.

*Prophetic Wilderness* is sparse on purpose, one weathered baritone, an open-tuned guitar, a harmonica drifting in from two canyons over, and a lot of wind in the gaps between the lines. I stripped the band out because the wilderness strips you out. That is the whole point of the place. And I could not make an honest record about it with a full arrangement covering for me.
Why I had to make it

I had gotten good at sounding sure. That is the danger of doing this long enough. You learn to perform certainty, to preach with confidence you have not actually paid for. And **Yahuah** loves you too much to let you keep doing that forever.

So He does what He did to His own Son. Luke chapter four says the Spirit led **Yeshua** into the wilderness, Matthew says He was driven up into it, and He was there forty days. Notice who did the driving. Not the devil. Not a bad season. The Spirit. Sometimes the emptiness you are standing in is not punishment and it is not failure. It is direction. The opener of the record starts right there: "Jesus, You led me out past the last fence line, the Spirit drove You before He drove mine." I followed His footprints out past the last thing I could control.
I had to make this record because I went out there myself, and I came back different, and I did not want to lie about the trip.
What the title means
A wilderness in Scripture is not just scenery. It is the place where **Yahuah** does the deep, quiet, private work that a crowd would only get in the way of.

Hosea chapter two has Him say something almost tender about it, "I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak comfortably unto her." He does not drag you to the desert to break you for sport. He takes you somewhere quiet enough that you can finally hear Him say something kind. But you cannot hear it over the noise you carry. So the desert takes the noise first.

That is track two, *Silence Speaks*, the song people keep coming back to. I went out hunting a word, some ringing declaration my pride could have used, and He kept the quiet until the third day. And then His silence turned out to be louder than the noise of men. It comes straight from First Kings nineteen, where Elijah looks for God in the wind and the earthquake and the fire, and **Yahuah** is in none of them. He is in the still, small voice, the one you cannot hear until everything louder has burned off.
The wilderness is not where God goes quiet. It is where He gets you quiet enough to notice He never stopped speaking.
The heart under the songs

The song I would hand a stranger first is *Wilderness Prayer*. It is just a man on his knees where nobody can see, "no one to perform for, nobody but Thee." It leans on the hardest picture in the Gospels, **Yeshua** in Gethsemane praying "not my will, but thine," and it lands on the one word I most wanted this whole record to reach: *Abba.* Father. The intimate name. Out in the waste, with the audience gone and the performance impossible, His "Abba" finally became my own. That is what solitude is for. Not to make you lonely, to make you His.

And I will not pretend the desert is gentle. The center of the album is *Prophet Breaking*, and it is the altar of the whole record. It is seven minutes of a man coming apart in the best possible way, "every idol I'd carried I laid at Your feet, every sermon I'd preached lost its old counterfeit." I sing there that the breaking was kind, though not mild. That is the truest line I know how to write about God. He does not break you because He is cruel. He breaks the thing in you that was never load-bearing, the reputation, the act, the self you built to be admired, and He does it so gently and so completely that you come up off the ground with your hands empty and your heart free, saying the only thing left that is actually yours: His name.

I anchored it all on the Baptist. Isaiah chapter forty and Matthew chapter three, the voice crying in the wilderness, prepare ye the way of the Lord. Every prophet God ever used, He seasoned in a desert first. Even **Yeshua**, who needed no correcting, went to the solitary place a great while before day to pray, as Mark chapter one tells it. If the sinless Son sought the wilderness on purpose, then the wilderness is not a detour off the road of faith. It is on the road. It may be the most important stretch of it.
Who I made this for
I made *Prophetic Wilderness* for the ones who are in the dry place right now and cannot figure out what they did to deserve it.

Maybe you did nothing to deserve it. Maybe the Spirit drove you here the way He drove **Yeshua**, not to punish you, but to prepare you. For the man who used to feel God easily and now feels nothing, and has quietly concluded that something is wrong with him. Nothing is wrong with you. You are in the school every prophet before you attended. For the woman worn hoarse by everyone else's voices, every opinion, every expectation, who needs the desert to make those voices go quiet so she can hear the One at the source.

And for the one who is breaking. I know how that feels from the inside, and I will tell you what I learned face down in the sand: the breaking is a kiss from His hand. Everything you thought you were, you are not, and that is the beginning of freedom, not the end of you. Hebrews chapter eleven honors the ones who wandered in deserts, of whom the world was not worthy. Heaven has never once looked down on a wilderness saint.
So if He has driven you out past the last fence line, do not run back too fast. Let the silence do its work. Let Him take the noise, the act, the borrowed certainty.
Because on the far side of the quiet, "Abba" is waiting to become your own word, and a man who has learned to say that in the dark can say it anywhere for the rest of his life.

pieces.title: Thirty-Seven Dollars in the Drawer and the Only Name That Paid
pieces.song: I Don't Need a Backup Plan
pieces.albumTitle: The Only Name You'll Ever Need
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful multi-generational family of many nations gathered close on a sunlit front porch, a silver-haired grandmother with her hand on a young grandchild's shoulder, faces lit with peace and laughter, a worn family Bible open on a small table between them, warm golden late-afternoon light, believers leaning in as one story is passed down; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still warmth, bright and emotive, hope steadying every face; wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: My grandmother died with thirty-seven dollars in the kitchen drawer and not one unpaid debt, because the Name of Jesus had covered every bill she ever couldn't. This is the album I made about the one Name that holds when every backup plan you built runs out.

body.text: Let me tell you about a kitchen drawer.

When my grandmother passed, we opened the drawer by the stove where she kept her important things, and inside there were thirty-seven dollars, a folded church bulletin, and a pencil worn down to almost nothing. That was the accounting of her estate. Thirty-seven dollars. And here is what undid me as I stood in that kitchen: she did not owe a single soul a single cent. Every bill that had come to that house across a long life had been paid, and not because she had the money, because most seasons she plainly did not. It was paid because when the letters came and the balance was more than the drawer could cover, she did the only thing she knew to do. She called on a Name.

That is the whole album. I called it **The Only Name You'll Ever Need**, and I made it because I have spent my life watching people build backup plans out of everything except the one thing that actually holds.
The world will sell you a Name and a hundred fallbacks

We are taught, almost from the cradle, to keep a Plan B in our pocket. Better have a savings account. Better have a contingency, a network, an exit door, a fallback in the wallet, in case the prayer doesn't reach and you're left with nothing to do. I wrote a song about exactly this and called it "I Don't Need a Backup Plan," because somewhere along the way my grandfather leaned back in his rocker, shook his head at all of it, and told me the truth: *the Name of Jesus has never needed a backup plan, and neither do you.*

I want to be careful here, because I am a teacher and not a fool. Wisdom saves and plans are good; Scripture praises the ant that stores in summer. But there is a difference between stewarding a resource and worshiping a fallback. The heart will always try to lean its full weight on *something*, and the tragedy is how many believers lean on the backup and merely tip their hat to the Lord. Psalm 20:7 puts the sorting line right down the middle of the human heart: *"Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God."* Chariots were the backup plan of the ancient world, the fastest, surest thing a nation could buy. The psalm doesn't mock them for being weak. It exposes them for not being **Yeshua**.
Why a Name, and not just a feeling
Here is the doctrine underneath the whole record, and I made twelve songs about it because it took me twelve songs to say it plainly.

A whisper can comfort you for an evening. A Name can carry a family for a hundred years. The opening song on the album is called "Whispers Don't Work Like His Name Does," and it came from my grandmother handing me sweet tea on the porch and saying, *the world will give you whispers, soft and sweet, but when the storm comes rolling through the valley of your living, only the Name of Jesus is the rock beneath your feet.* That is not sentiment. That is Proverbs 18:10, *"The name of the LORD is a strong tower; the righteous run into it and are safe."* A tower is not a mood. You cannot lean your weight on a mood at three in the morning. You can run into a tower.

And the reason His Name works is not magic; it is identity. Matthew 1:21 tells us why He was even given the Name: *"you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins."* The Name is a description of a rescue already accomplished. So when Acts 4:12 says *"there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved,"* it is not being narrow to be cruel. It is being honest about the only door that actually opens. Philippians 2:9-11 says **Yahuah** exalted Him and gave Him *the name that is above every name*, above every diagnosis, every deadline, every debt in every drawer.
A whisper fades with the evening breeze on the windowsill. A Name has been carrying my grandmother's grandmothers, and it is the strong tower where the family begins.
The songs are a map of when you'll need it
I built the record as a journey through the hours a person actually reaches for the Name, because doctrine you can't find in the dark isn't doing its job.

There's "I Called on Jesus (And Everything Changed)", a Tuesday in October, a doctor's letter in the mailbox by the gate, and a woman sitting on the kitchen step with her mother's Bible. The letter still said what it said. But she called, and the Name walked into the kitchen and stood by the bed. That is Psalm 50:15 lived out in a farmhouse: *"call upon me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you."* Notice the song does not pretend the letter changed. It says the *room* changed. The Name doesn't always rewrite the report; it rearranges who is standing in the room with you while you read it.

There's "Power in the Middle of Nowhere," out on a two-lane road where there's no cell tower and no neighbor close enough to holler, and my grandfather cutting the engine to say, *this is where the Name has the most power, where there ain't a single soul but Jesus and the trees.* There's "That Name Found Me First," a cradle song built on the astonishing truth that before you ever called on Him, He was already calling, that the Name searched you out before you could spell your own. And there's "The Devil Flinches When I Say It," which I will defend to anyone: it is not about naming the enemy, it is about naming the One who emptied his tomb. The devil flinches at the Name because the Name has the keys.
Who this album is for

It is for the woman with the letter in her hand. It is for the man at the kitchen table with the bills he can't quite pay. It is for the one in the hallway with the phone call she's been dreading, which is why the tenderest song on the record is "Just Say the Name (Even If You're Broken)." You don't need a script. You don't need a steeple or a prayer-book or a good Sunday hat. Psalm 34:18 promises *"the LORD is near to the brokenhearted,"* and Romans 10:13 makes it as plain as a Name can be: *"everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved."* Everyone. Even if your voice is shaking. Even if your knees won't hold.

My grandmother left thirty-seven dollars. But she left me the drawer's real inheritance, the thing that had quietly paid for everything: she left me the Name. And I have spent a life discovering she was right. It is the only Name you'll ever need, because it is the one that's still standing in the room after every backup plan you ever built has run clean out.
Say it again, even if you're broken. He is right there at that.

pieces.title: Forty Years of Prayers Still Sit on My Shelf
pieces.imagePrompt: A radiant grandmother of deep brown skin seated in a circle of laughing grandchildren of many nations in a warm sunlit living room, an old leather prayer journal open in her lap, a wall of framed family photographs behind them glowing in golden light, faces full of wonder and belonging as stories pass between generations; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still warmth, bright and tender, legacy and joy shining on every face; wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: My grandmother's prayer journal still sits on my shelf, forty years of intercession in her own hand. I made this album because faith is not a feeling that happens to you; it is a watch that was kept over you, by name, before you were born.

body.text: There is a leather book on my shelf that is worth more to me than anything I own, and it is not for sale at any price. It is my grandmother's prayer journal. Forty years of intercession in her own careful hand, names, dates, the tired scrawl of nights I never saw. My name is in there. It was in there before I could read. And when I take it down and turn the pages, I am not reading a book. I am hearing a watch that was kept over my whole life while I slept.

That book is why I made **Keeper of Stories**. Because somewhere along the way I understood a thing that reorganized my faith entirely: I did not arrive at belief on my own. I was prayed here. And the moment you understand that, you stop being only a *receiver* of faith and you become what my grandmother was, a keeper of it.
Faith did not start with you, and it will not end with you

We talk about faith as though it were weather, something that happens to a person, privately, on the inside. But Scripture almost never talks about it that way. It talks about faith as something *handed*, carried, kept, and passed. When Paul writes to Timothy, he doesn't say, "I admire the faith you generated." He says, *"I am reminded of your sincere faith, which first lived in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice, and now, I am persuaded, dwells in you as well"* (2 Timothy 1:5). Three generations, named, in one sentence. A grandmother is the headwater. That is the whole architecture of the album, the opening song is "Lineage of Light," and it says the plainest true thing I know: *we are not alone; the cloud of witnesses is gathered round.* That line is Hebrews 12:1 set to a porch rhythm. You are surrounded. You always were.

The second song is the one I chose to carry this whole story, "The Faithful Kept Watch." It came straight off my shelf. *My grandmother's prayer journal still sits on my shelf, forty years of intercession.* They kept the watch when the night was long. They knelt by bedsides praying Scripture over people not yet born. And here is the turn the song makes, the turn every believer eventually has to make: *the faithful kept watch, and now it's me.* The watch does not end when the watchman dies. It gets handed to whoever is still awake.
What a keeper actually keeps
I want to be precise, because "legacy" is a word people use to mean nothing. A keeper of stories is not a nostalgic person. A keeper is a *teacher under orders.*

Psalm 78 gives the job description, and it is not gentle. *"We will not hide them from their children, but tell to the coming generation the glorious deeds of the LORD"* (Psalm 78:4). Not hide them. The default, if no one keeps watch, is that the stories go quiet in one generation. Psalm 145:4 says *"one generation shall commend your works to another, and shall declare your mighty acts."* Commend, hand across, on purpose, out loud. This is why I wrote songs like "Witness of Generations" and "Blessing Forward." The blessing was never meant to pool in you. It was meant to move *through* you, forward, to a face you may never see.
Blessed by the prayers they whispered in the dark, blessed by the courage that refused to break, and now it is my turn to keep the watch and pass the flame to those who come behind.

And Joshua tells us *how* to keep it: with stones. After Israel crossed the Jordan, **Yahuah** told them to pile up twelve stones so that *"when your children ask in time to come, 'What do these stones mean to you?' then you shall tell them"* (Joshua 4:6-7). A keeper builds things that provoke the question. A journal on a shelf is a stone. A song your granddaughter can't get out of her head is a stone. You are stacking memory where the next generation will trip over it and have to ask.
Glory hides in the ordinary

The song on this record I most want you to hear is "Glory in the Ordinary." Because we imagine legacy is built by the dramatic saints, the martyrs, the missionaries, the platform names. But my grandmother's monument was flour on her hands and a whispered blessing over a pot on the stove. The most faithful watch I have ever witnessed was kept in a kitchen, at four in the morning, by a woman nobody outside our county ever heard of.

This is doctrine, not sentiment. Lamentations 3:22-23 says His mercies *"are new every morning; great is your faithfulness."* Every *morning*. The faithfulness of God is delivered in daily, ordinary portions, and the keepers who catch it are almost always doing something ordinary when they do, turning a page, setting a table, sitting at a sickbed. "Memory and Grace" on this album is a whole song about a photograph on the wall, about my mother young, before the weight of years, carrying something precious she knew I'd inherit. What I remember of her isn't always clear. But what she deposited is always near.

I put a song near the end called "Rise and Celebrate," and I want you to know it is there on purpose. Because keeping stories is not a mournful business, and legacy is not a museum you tend in the dark. Every name in that journal is a name **Yahuah** answered, is answering, or has promised to answer. When I read the pages, I am not grieving a woman who is gone. I am reading a ledger of a faithfulness that never left. The proper response to a well-kept watch is not a sigh. It is a shout. The keepers who came before us are not asking us to be sad that they're gone; they are handing us a reason to celebrate that He is not.
Who this is for, and what I'm asking of you

This album is for the woman who feels like the last believer in her family and wonders if the line stops with her. It does not have to. And it is for the woman on the *other* end, the grandmother who thinks her quiet prayers accomplished nothing because she never saw the fruit. Sit down with me. You have no idea what your journal is doing on a shelf you cannot see yet.

I called the record **Keeper of Stories** because that is the office every one of us is quietly ordained into whether we accept it or not. Someone kept watch over you. Someone's forty years of prayers are the reason you can read this at all. The only question the album asks is the one the second song asks: the faithful kept watch, *and now it's me.*
Take the book down off the shelf. Read a name. Then go add your own.

pieces.title: We Are Always One Silence Away From Losing It
pieces.imagePrompt: A warm home Bible study of globally-diverse believers of every age gathered around a kitchen table in golden lamplight, an older woman guiding a teenager's finger along an open page while younger children listen wide-eyed, an aunt with her arm around a laughing child, faces full of discovery and belonging; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still warmth, bright and hopeful, the passing-down of faith made visible; wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: Faith is never automatically inherited. It is handed, deliberately, hand to hand, or it is dropped in a single generation. This is the album I made about the actual mechanics of how belief moves from one set of hands to the next.

body.text: I want to begin with the most sobering sentence in the Bible about faith and family, and it is not the one you'd expect. It is Judges 2:10: *"there arose another generation after them who did not know the LORD or the work that he had done for Israel."* Read that again slowly. This was Israel. This was the generation *right after* the one that walked through the parted sea and ate manna in the desert. One generation. That is all it took for the whole thing to go dark, not because of a war, not because of a plague, but because of a silence. Somebody stopped handing it down.
I made **Hand-Me-Down Faith** because I have watched that verse come true in living rooms. And I refuse to let it come true in mine.
Faith is not inherited. It is handed.
Here is the distinction the whole album turns on, and it is the difference between a wish and a work.

We *hope* our children will believe. But hope is not a plan, and belief does not travel by bloodline. There is no such thing as automatic faith, transmitted quietly through the DNA like eye color. Scripture never assumes it. Every single time it speaks of faith crossing to the next generation, it commands an *action*, a handing. *"Teach them diligently to your children,"* Deuteronomy 6:6-7 says, *"talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise."* Four settings. All of them ordinary. None of them a Sunday service. The opening song on the record is called "Teach Them Well," and its whole refrain is a job I take with the seriousness of an ordination: *you're the bridge between the ages, the keeper of the flame, teach them well, pass along the Name.*

A bridge is a good picture, because a bridge only works if it actually touches both sides. Faith that stays in your generation, however sincere, is a bridge built halfway out over the water. It is beautiful. It also goes nowhere.
The mechanics: how it actually moves hand to hand

I did something unusual on this album. I did not just sing *that* faith gets passed down. I tried to sing *how*, because I think we have kept the mechanics a secret and then acted surprised when the young ones didn't catch what we never actually threw.

The second song, "Word to the Next Generation," is built on a woman in our family who had no children of her own, and who poured her faith into every young person in reach. She's telling them the stories. She's teaching them the truth. That is Titus 2:3-5 in a housedress: *the older women are to train the younger.* Notice: spiritual motherhood is not restricted to the ones who bore children. The mantle goes to anyone willing to open their hands. Joel 1:3 lays out the relay across *four* runners, not two: *"Tell your children of it, and let your children tell their children, and their children another generation."* You are not just handing to your kids. You are handing to a runner who will hand to a runner you will never meet.

But the song I most needed to write is the third one, "Questions in the Quiet." Because here is the mechanic nobody wants to teach: *you do not need to have all the answers.* My own father couldn't answer half of what I asked him. What he did was better. He showed me how to seek, how to let faith outlast the question. The song sits right on Mark 9:24, the most honest prayer in the Gospels: *"I believe; help my unbelief."* If you have been silent with the young ones because you're afraid of their hard questions, hear me: your fear is the only thing that can actually drop the baton. A child does not need a parent with every answer. A child needs a parent who is not afraid of the question, and who knows Who to bring it to.
I don't have all the answers, but I know enough to say the Lord is good, and He will light the way. Questions in the quiet are the places where faith grows.
What we hand down, we do not water down
I am a teacher, so let me be exact about *what* moves down the line, because you can hand a child a hollow thing and think you did your job.

We do not hand down mere manners, or a denomination, or a nostalgia for how church used to feel. We hand down the *Word* and a living *testimony*, the two rails of the bridge. Paul reminds Timothy that *"from infancy you have known the Holy Scriptures, which are able to make you wise for salvation"* (2 Timothy 3:15). The Scriptures. Actual content. And alongside the content, the story: this record has a song called "The Testimony I Carry," because a child needs to know not only that the Bible is true but that it was true *in this house, for these people, with this last name.* Proverbs 22:6, *"train up a child in the way he should go"*, uses a word that pictures a mother placing something in an infant's mouth so it learns the taste. That is intimacy, not instruction from a distance. You are giving them the flavor of faith before they can define it.

And you hand it down while you yourself are still learning, which is why one of the tenderest songs on the album is "Learning as I Go." The keeper of the flame is not a finished person. She's just a person facing the right direction, close enough for the young ones to walk in her footsteps and see where she trips and how she gets back up.
Who this is for

This is for the exhausted parent who feels unqualified. You are not unqualified; you are just next in line. It is for the grandmother who thinks her window has closed. It has not, Lois discipled Timothy from a grandmother's chair. It is for the aunt, the mentor, the Sunday-school teacher, the older friend with no children who quietly disciples the whole block. And it is for the young one wondering whether any of this is really theirs to carry. It is. The final song says it flat out: *we are passing it down.*

Judges 2:10 is not a prophecy over your family. It is a warning you get to answer. The faith does not survive on autopilot; it survives on the deliberate, unglamorous, hand-to-hand work of teaching one more child one more true thing about **Yeshua**, today, at the table, before the light goes out of the room.
Hand it down. There is a set of small hands waiting, closer than you think.

pieces.title: The Master Weaver Wastes Not a Single Broken Thread
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful circle of globally-diverse women of many generations quilting together around a large frame in warm afternoon light, brown and fair hands weaving bright mismatched threads into one radiant cloth, grandmothers guiding young women, faces full of tenderness and belonging as a broken pattern becomes whole; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still warmth, bright and emotive, mending and unity made visible; wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: My grandmother taught me to see a torn life the way a weaver sees a loose thread, not as ruined, but as unfinished. This is the album I made about the Master Weaver who takes every broken, mismatched, unraveled strand and works it into one whole cloth.

body.text: My grandmother could not pass a loose thread without reaching for it. A frayed hem, a pulled stitch, a quilt corner coming apart, her fingers found it before her eyes did. And she taught me something at her sewing basket that took me fifty years to understand was theology: a broken thread is not a ruined thread. It is an *unfinished* one. The weaver does not throw it out. She works it back in.

That is the whole of **Hands That Mend**. I made an album about weaving because I had run out of gentler ways to say the truest thing I know about **Yahuah**, that He is a Weaver, that nothing torn is beyond His loom, and that He is patient enough to work a whole life back into the cloth one strand at a time.
We are threads, and He is the loom

Start with the picture Scripture itself hands us. Before you were anything you could name, *"you knit me together in my mother's womb... I am fearfully and wonderfully made"* (Psalm 139:13-14). Knit. Woven. You did not assemble yourself; you were *made* by hands that knew the pattern before the first row. The song at the center of this record is "The Master Weaver," and its confession is exactly that: *the Master Weaver knows the pattern from the start, knows the secrets of my heart... surrendering to the weaving of His hand and of His will.* That is not a passive resignation. It is the deep rest of a thread that has stopped fighting the hands that are trying to place it.

And here is why the picture matters so much for the broken among us. A single thread is a fragile, useless thing. It snaps at the lightest tug. But **Yahuah** does not leave any of us as single threads. Ecclesiastes 4:12 says *"a threefold cord is not quickly broken."* The opening song, "The Tapestry Begins," is built on that verse and on Dorcas, Tabitha, the seamstress of Joppa, *"full of good works,"* who sewed garments for the widows until the whole grieving town stood holding up the coats she had made (Acts 9:36-39). A woman with a needle preaching the gospel in thread. The tapestry begins, the song says, *with a single thread of faith*, but it never stays single. Faith woven to faith is what holds.
The unraveling is not the end of the weaving

I will not sell you a soft record. The song on this album I most needed to write is track six, "The Unraveling and Re-weaving," and it is honest about the thing every one of us dreads: *sometimes the tapestry unravels. Plans fall through.* My grandmother lost much across her years, more than I knew as a child. But here is the line that carries the whole album: *she lost much, but she never lost her faith. In the unraveling, she found grace and grace.*

This is doctrine, and it is precise, so hear me as a teacher. **Yahuah** is not only the One who wove you in the beginning; He is the One who *re-weaves* what has come apart. Psalm 147:3, *"He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds."* Binds. That is a weaver's word, a mender's word. And Isaiah 61:1, the very passage **Yeshua** stood up in the synagogue and claimed as His own mission, says He was sent *"to bind up the brokenhearted."* Your unraveling is not proof the pattern failed. In the hands of the Master Weaver, the unraveling is the part of the work where the loose strand gets picked back up. The song says it plainly: *in the breaking and the mending, we discover what we're made of.* You do not learn what a cloth is made of until a thread is pulled, and neither do you.
Sometimes the tapestry unravels, plans fall through, but in the unraveling we find what's true. The unraveling and re-weaving is how we learn to love.
Many colors, one cloth
Now the picture opens outward, because a tapestry is never one color, and this is where the album turns from the private ache to the whole household of God.

We are, the second song says, "Many Colors", *beautiful and broken*, every one of us a different strand, and the church has too often tried to sort us by shade before letting us into the weave. But that is not how the Master works. First Corinthians 12 is the loom laid bare: *"the body is one and has many members... the eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of you"* (1 Corinthians 12:12, 21). Different threads, one cloth, and *"individually members one of another"* (Romans 12:5). That is why the songs on this record are called "Patterns of Belonging" and "We Are One Cloth", because belonging is not something you earn by matching the threads around you. It is what happens when the Weaver runs your strand *through* theirs. "Through and Through," I called one of them. That is how cloth is made: over and under, through and through, until you cannot pull one life out without pulling on all the others.

And what binds the whole thing so it does not fall apart? Not our compatibility. Paul tells us the binding thread by name: *"above all these put on love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony"* (Colossians 3:14). Love is the strong cross-thread. The knots are not flaws in the cloth, the song "Knots and Strength" is exactly right, the knots are where two lives got tied and the whole thing got *stronger*. We spend so much energy trying to hide the knots in our story. The Weaver builds the cloth's strength out of them.
Who this is for

This album is for the person who has looked at the underside of a life, theirs, or someone they love, and seen nothing but a chaos of loose ends and cut threads and thought, *there is no pattern here, only a mess.* I wrote every song on this record to say: you are looking at the back of the tapestry. Of course it looks tangled from there. Only the Weaver sees the front, and He *"knows the pattern from the start."* He does not make a mistake, and He will not let you break.

It is for the woman walking through a divorce, a grief, a diagnosis, anyone whose plans just fell through, and it is for the one in the pew who feels like the wrong color thread in a cloth that never wanted her. And it is for the mender: the grandmother, the quilter, the caregiver, the one whose whole calling is picking up loose threads in other people's lives and working them gently back in. There was a woman who was sure she was too unraveled to be worth the Healer's time, so she only reached for *the fringe of His garment*, the very edge of the weaver's cloth, and He turned and said, *"take heart, daughter; your faith has made you well"* (Matthew 9:20-22). Even the hem of Him mends.

The last song is "Forever Woven," and it looks all the way down the loom to the finished piece: *"a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, tribe, people and language,"* standing together before the throne (Revelation 7:9). That is the cloth He has been weaving the whole time, every color, every broken strand, every re-worked thread, whole at last and never coming apart again.
So bring Him the frayed edge. Bring Him the part that came undone. The Master Weaver wastes not a single broken thread. He picks it back up, and He works it into the whole.

pieces.title: Not Borrowed, Not Begged For, Not Loaned by a Man
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful multi-generational circle of women of many nations standing together in warm morning light inside a simple country church, an older woman with an open Bible laying a hand of blessing on a younger woman while others sing with lifted faces, daughters and grandmothers commissioned side by side, faces full of courage and tenderness; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still warmth, bright and emotive, holy commissioning made visible; wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: The voice a woman carries in the kingdom was not loaned to her by a committee, and no silence can un-sign what Christ has commissioned. I made this album about the daughters He calls, and the borrowed authority they carry from the King who gave it.

body.text: I want to sing you a line before I explain it, because the line is the whole argument. In the first song on this album, a woman stands up and says of the voice in her chest: *not borrowed, not begged for, not loaned by a man, Jesus, You gave the voice.* Given from heaven and held in His hand.

I made **Women's Authority and Wisdom** because I have spent a lifetime watching gifted daughters wait for a permission that was never theirs to wait for. And I have watched them mistake the source. So let me be a teacher and get the source exactly right, because everything. Everything, depends on where a woman believes her authority comes from.
All authority is His before it is anyone's

Here is the doctrine that keeps this whole record from tipping into something it is not. This album is not about a woman seizing authority. It is about a woman *receiving* it from the only One who has any to give. The second song, my hit single, says it in a way I cannot improve on: *all authority is Yours, Lord, not taken, not stolen, not seized by a hand, and You commission whoever You want to in the land.*

That is straight out of the mouth of **Yeshua**. On the mountain, before He sends anyone anywhere, He says: *"All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore..."* (Matthew 28:18-19). Read the order carefully. First He claims *all* of it. Then He sends. Which means every calling that any of us carries, man or woman, is a *loan from the King*, not a possession we generated and not a prize we wrestled from someone else. This matters enormously for a woman, because the moment she understands her authority is borrowed from Christ, two things happen at once: she stops begging men for what only God can give, and she stops swaggering, because you cannot be arrogant about something you're only holding. The song's own line: *I don't carry a single thing that's mine.*
He has been calling daughters the whole time
Now, the Scriptures. Because I do not build songs on feeling; I build them on the text, and the text is fuller than the church has often let on.

When **Yahuah** poured out His promise through the prophet Joel, He did not restrict the microphone: *"I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; your sons and your daughters shall prophesy"* (Joel 2:28). Daughters, named, in the same breath as sons. And the Bible does not leave that as a theory. It gives us the women who lived it. Deborah *was judging Israel* under her palm tree, a prophetess leading a nation (Judges 4:4). When King Josiah needed a word from God about the newly found Book of the Law, he sent the priests to *Huldah the prophetess*, and she spoke, and the reformation of a kingdom turned on her word (2 Kings 22:14). That is why one of the songs is "Jesus Called the Elders", because the elders He called into my own life were women like Grandma Ruth, up at four in a cold house with a shawl and His Word, who never preached from any stage I knew but poured half of what I carry into me.
Jesus, You called Deborah. You spoke through Huldah's mouth. You anointed Priscilla, You sent Phoebe to the south. What Jesus has commissioned, no silence can un-sign.

The song names these women on purpose, and I want you to know they are really there in the text. Priscilla, with her husband, *"explained to Apollos the way of God more accurately"* (Acts 18:26), a woman correcting the theology of a powerful preacher, and the Spirit saw fit to record it. Phoebe is commended as a *servant of the church at Cenchreae*, entrusted by Paul (Romans 16:1). And in that same chapter Paul greets Junia, *"outstanding among the apostles"* (Romans 16:7). Now, I am a careful teacher, so I will tell you the plain truth: the church has argued over that phrase for centuries. But the name is in the text, and the honor attached to it is in the text, and I will not pretend the Word is quieter than it actually is.
Wisdom, not just a platform

But notice I did not title the album *Women's Authority* alone. It is **Women's Authority and Wisdom**, and the second word is the guardrail, because authority without wisdom is a loud, dangerous thing in anyone's hands.

The wisdom on this record is not the wisdom of the boardroom. It is the wisdom of the kitchen door. "Jesus, Teach Through Me" tells where my own theology actually began: *my first theology was Your voice at a kitchen door, where my mama opened Scripture and You walked across the floor. She didn't have a seminary, she had a worn-out King James book*, but the Spirit of the Living God put the fear of the Lord in it. That is the deep water this album swims in. The daughters God commissions are not usually the ones grasping for a stage. The chorus says it: *not from a podium, not from a stage, Father, write Your Word on the life I turn the page.* Real authority is a life you can read, long before it is a voice you can hear.

And there is a tenderness threaded all through the strength, because commissioned women get tired and shaken like anyone. "Jesus, You Hold Me Steady" is on this record right beside the fierce ones, because the same Christ who says *go* is the One who *holds*. His authority in Matthew 28 comes with a promise in the very next breath: *"I am with you always, to the end of the age."* You are not sent out alone to fend for the calling. You are held while you carry it.
Who this is for

This is for the daughter who has been sitting on a gift, waiting for a man to hand her a permission slip. Sister, hear the first song: you do not need it. What **Yeshua** commissioned, no committee convenes to un-sign. This is for the older woman who thinks her season of usefulness has passed. It has not; Huldah's greatest word came late. It is for the young bride who found courage on a gravel road, and for every woman who quietly discipled a preacher and never got the credit. And it is written, deliberately, so that the men who love these women can stand next to them and sing it too, because in Christ *"there is neither male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus"* (Galatians 3:28), and a household strong in the Lord raises its daughters, it does not silence them.

I built this record as a chapter-close, a passing of the mantle. Because that is what wisdom does with authority. It does not hoard it, it hands it on. The last song simply says *Jesus, You are forever*, and that is the anchor under all of it. The authority is His forever. He only lets us carry it for a while, in our own hands, for His own glory.
So stand up, daughter. Use the voice. It was given from heaven and held in His hand, and He gave it to you on purpose.

pieces.title: The Anchor Was Already Set Before the Storm Had a Name
pieces.imagePrompt: A multigenerational, multiethnic congregation gathered close around one weary man in a hospital waiting room, hands resting on his shoulders and clasped in his, faces steady and full of quiet strength as morning light breaks through tall windows behind them, a grandmother's hand over a younger hand; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, warm amber and steel-blue tones, tender and alive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I wrote this album for the hour after the 2:47 phone call, the drive to the hospital, the kitchen floor at 4 a.m., the parking-lot cry before you go in and pretend to function. It is not an album that stops the storm. It is an album that puts a rope in your hand and tells you the truth: the Anchor was set in the deep long before the wind ever learned your name.

body.text: The phone rang at 2:47 in the morning, and the clock became a character in the room.

I have sat with too many people in that exact hour to pretend I don't know it. The biopsy came back. The marriage is over. The child is in the emergency room. The voice on the other end says something you cannot unsay, and the floor you were standing on goes sideways while you are still holding the receiver. I wrote *Anchor in the Storm* for that hour, and for the twelve weeks that come after it, because that hour deserved better than a platitude, and the people living in it deserved a song that would not lie to them.
I refused to write an album that ends the storm

Here is the thing I decided before I wrote a single line: this record would not pretend the wind dies down by track four. It doesn't. The waves are still breaking at track nine. I have watched well-meaning faith promise people that if they believe hard enough the weather will change, and then I have watched those same people drown in shame when the weather didn't. So I made a different promise. The storm on this album is real, and it is allowed to be real. What changes across the twelve songs is not the weather. It is your relationship to the deck under your feet.

That is why the opener, "The Phone Call," names an actual time. Not "hard times." Not "the valley." *Two forty-seven.* The cup of cold coffee. The chair turned to the wall at 4 a.m. Grief does not arrive in the abstract, and neither should the God who meets you in it. Underneath every track there is a slow, steady kick drum we called the anchor pulse, a heartbeat that will not move even when the melody tears. That was on purpose. The production itself is the theology: the storm is audible, but it is never the loudest thing in the room.
What the title actually means
An anchor is not an explanation. It is a weight in the deep and a rope in your hand.

The whole album stands on one verse, the writer of Hebrews calling our hope "an anchor for the soul, firm and secure" (Hebrews 6:19). I love that he does not say the anchor calms the sea. He says it holds the soul. There is a world of pastoral difference between those two things. So on "Hold the Rope" I tried to write the plainest song I could, the one a hospice nurse could play for a family while a non-religious spouse in the corner quietly starts to cry. *You don't have to see the Anchor yet. You just have to hold the rope He put in your hand.* You can hold that rope with your eyes closed. You can hold it when you are too tired to say one word to God. He is not asking you for a theology. He is asking you for your hand, and the Spirit of **Yahuah** will carry the rest.

Then, three songs later, the whole record turns over on itself. On "You Were the Deep All Along" the man in the boat stops waiting for the anchor to be thrown and looks down, and realizes it was already set, in the deep, before the storm ever came. The rescue did not arrive from the horizon. It rose from underneath. **Yeshua** was not a rescue coming; He was the floor that had been there the whole time. That is the sentence I most wanted to hand you: you are not catching up to grace. Grace has been under you since before the wind knew your name.
The Anchor never had to be thrown, Lord. You were already the floor.
The songs are a slow walk from thrown to held

The middle of the album is where the wind does its worst. "When the Wind Tears at Me" is the altar, a man with the rope going taut in his fists, soaked but not drowned, tossed but not thrown, discovering that grace is deeper than the wind. I sang it low and rasped and let my voice crack, because a voice that never breaks cannot minister to people who are breaking.

But I could not end the record with one man alone on a deck. That is not how rescue actually works. So "Not Alone in This Storm" is the moment the cabin door opens and there are other hands on the rope beside yours, the friend who showed up with soup, the brother who texted at 2:14 a.m., the elder's worn hand on your shoulder in the back of the sanctuary. And "We Hold On Together" says the part pride never lets us say out loud: *when my hands are tired, your hands take the rope; when yours are tired, mine take it.* The church is not a building. It is the hands **Yahuah** sends. Then "Scars Are Evidence" reframes the whole ordeal, your wounds are not your shame, they are the receipt that the rope was in your hand. And "After the Storm" walks you out changed, the deck steady, humming an old and true line: *it is well with my soul*, not because the sea was always calm, but because He walked the deep with you.
Who I made this for
