I made this for the exhausted one reading a diagnosis they can't pronounce. For the parent in the parking lot who has to fix their face before they walk back inside. For the pastor whose public role won't let them fall apart in private. For the believer whose theology promised no storms and whose storm came anyway, and who has been quietly terrified that God moved, or was never there. Hear me: He did not move. He was already in the room the morning the phone rang.

You do not have to hold the rope alone, and you do not have to hold it well. You just have to hold it. The Anchor was set in the deep before you were old enough to reach for it, and the same hands that set it are the ones now closing around yours. The storm does not get the last word. He does, and He is holding you here.

pieces.title: The Call Came In Through a Friend, and It Was God the Whole Time
pieces.imagePrompt: A diverse circle of people in a warm church basement recovery meeting, folding chairs and coffee cups, one man mid-embrace with an older mentor while others clap and beam around them, a sobriety token catching the light in an open palm, faces lit with relief and joy; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, warm amber and honey tones, raw and hopeful, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: This is the album for anyone who has been drawn up out of a pit and is still shaking from how close it was. It is built on one verse. He drew me up from the slimy pit and set my feet on a rock, and on a truth I could not shake: that God keeps coming through the people He sends. The rescue was His. The man on the phone was a man. And it saved a life.

body.text: There is a kind of rescue that happens through a telephone at three in the morning, and I have made a whole album about it.

*Rescue Story* is twelve songs for the person who has been drawn up out of a pit and is still standing on the shore, still shaking, still doing the math on how close it actually was. I did not write it from the high ground. I wrote it from the low ground, from the basement folding chair, the guardrail, the waiting room, the kitchen table with divorce papers on it, because those are the rooms where **Yahuah** does His most stubborn work, and I refuse to sing about rescue like a man who has never needed one.
The whole record stands on one sentence

David wrote it, and I have never gotten over it: *He drew me up from the pit of destruction, out of the miry bog, and set my feet upon a rock, making my steps secure, and he put a new song in my mouth* (Psalm 40:1–3). Read that slowly. The man does not climb out. He is *drawn* out. The verb belongs to God. That single reversal, from "I saved myself" to "I learned the language of the saved", is the spine of the entire album, and it is the difference between religion and rescue.

So the opener, "The Call That Saved Me," is exactly what it sounds like. A voice on the line at 3 a.m., *"brother, talk to me instead"*, a bottle in one hand, a name I would not say. And the truth the song keeps circling back to: **Yeshua** came in through a phone, through a voice that was not His, and He was His the whole time. That is the miracle I most wanted people to see. God is not too proud to arrive wearing a friend's voice. He sent a man, and His Son was on the line.
The pit has a Person already sitting in it

The album refuses to make the rescue distant or clean. On "From the Brink" it is a cold guardrail and a whispered name, and a nail-marked hand already pressed into the metal where mine had been. On "Rock Bottom Found You" it is the burned-coffee smell of a recovery room and the shock of realizing the chair you dreaded was holy ground: *what I thought was the floor was the front pew of Your love.* That song leans on the most audacious line in the Psalms, *if I make my bed in Sheol, behold, You are there* (Psalm 139:8). You cannot dig low enough to get below God. He is already at the bottom of the pit, sleeves rolled up, dirt on His hands.

Because that is the image I keep returning to on "The God Who Digs Me Out", a Rescuer who does not shout instructions from above but comes *down*, with a shovel and dirt on His sleeves. The Carpenter has soil on Him from a Garden and a Cross. He is not afraid of yours.
I did not climb out. I was lifted out. I did not save myself. I learned the verb of the saved.
Rescue is not always the news you wanted

I could not write an honest rescue record without the song that admits the news sometimes goes dark. "Rescue in the Waiting Room" is the album's peak, and it is set in those chairs you cannot sleep in, the styrofoam coffee left over from shift change. Sometimes the rescue was not the surgeon's report, sometimes the rescue was the company that waited with you. Whether the doors opened onto joy or onto grief, He did not stand up and leave. *Wait for the Lord; be strong, and let your heart take courage* (Psalm 27:14). The Comforter stays through both endings. That is a harder gospel than the one that promises only good outcomes, and it is the only one strong enough to hold real people.

And then the album turns outward, because rescued people are the loudest witnesses there are. "Testimony Over Trauma" is built on Revelation 12:11, *they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony*, sung in a folding-chair circle where saying it out loud is the beginning of not being held by it anymore. "My Scars Tell Your Story" takes the marks I used to hide under long sleeves in July and calls them a sermon, because **Yeshua** wears His own scars on the throne and does not hide them either. The scar is not a shame. It is the signature of the Surgeon on the skin of the saved.
Who this album is for

It is for the one holding a number they have not let ring in years. For the person on the guardrail who needs to stay one more hour. For the father who almost gave it all away and got interrupted by grace wearing a four-year-old's pajamas at the door. For anyone who has quietly believed that grace is for the weak and is finding out that the strong need pulling out too.

I built the finale, "Still Being Rescued," to answer the very first song, because the 3 a.m. call was the door, not the destination. Salvation is not a single night you can frame and hang up. It is a Person who keeps showing up. *He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion* (Philippians 1:6). The Rescuer who drew you up the first time is not done, and His hand does not get tired, and the road does not run out.

So take the chip. Take the chair. Take the call. If you are on the line tonight and you can barely get the name out, get it out anyway, one word, almost a whisper, almost not at all. He drew me up. He will draw you up too. The story is not over, and the One who is writing it has never once let go.

pieces.title: I Kept Looking for a Shelter, and the Shelter Turned Out to Be a Person
pieces.imagePrompt: A diverse group of weary travelers of many nations stepping in from a rainstorm through a warm open doorway, shaking off the cold as unseen hands welcome them into golden lamplight, a mother holding a sleeping child, an old man exhaling in relief, faces softening as they cross the threshold; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, warm amber and rain-blue tones, tender and safe, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: Refuge is the album I made for the person who is tired of running in the storm and cannot find a door. Its whole discovery is that the walls of the fortress are not stone. They are Him. From My Refuge and Fortress to the cleft of the Rock that bled, this is a slow walk from exposed to sheltered, hidden not in a place, but in a Person who does not expire.

body.text: For years I looked for refuge the way you look for a building, some fixed place I could get to, lock behind me, and finally rest inside. *Refuge* is the album I wrote when I finally understood that I had been looking for the wrong kind of thing.
The shelter is not a place. The shelter is a Person. And once that lands in you, it changes everything about how you survive.
Stepping through the door

The record opens exposed, a man who has been running in the storm too long, the rain soaking the worn Bible in his hand, seeing at last a lamp in a window and a door. "My Refuge and Fortress" leans on the verse my grandmother taped to her kitchen window: *God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble* (Psalm 46:1). But here is the turn the whole album is built on. I step through the door, and I discover the walls of the fortress are not stone. *You are the shelter and the One sheltered with me.* **Yahuah** is the door and the room. That is not a location you flee to. That is a Presence you dwell inside.

From there the album goes deeper into the house, room by room. "Safe in Your Shadow" sits under Psalm 91, *he who dwells in the secret place of the Most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty*, and the relief of it is that inside the shadow you do not have to perform. You do not have to explain why you are tired. The shelter never asked for your credentials.
The tenderest shelter in Scripture

Then comes the song I can barely sing without my voice going soft. "Under Your Wings" takes the mother-hen image, *he will cover you with his feathers, and under his wings you will find refuge* (Psalm 91:4), and holds it next to the moment **Yeshua** wept over Jerusalem and said He had *longed to gather your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings* (Matthew 23:37). Do you feel the weight of that? He did not say "find shelter elsewhere." He said come under My wings, come under My body, the body that opened wide on a cross. The shelter is His own wounds welcoming you in.

That is the theology the album keeps pressing toward, and it peaks on "The Cleft of the Rock." When Moses asked to see the glory of God, **Yahuah** set him in a cleft of the rock and covered him with His hand while the glory passed by (Exodus 33:22). I sang that image straight into the gospel: the cleft of the Rock is the wounded side of the Son. The Rock the prophets struck for water in the wilderness is the Rock struck for me at Calvary, and the bleeding is the shelter.
Jesus, I am hidden in the Rock that bled for me, and the bleeding is the shelter, Lord.

I anchored that song to a hymn the saints have sung for two hundred years, *Rock of Ages, cleft for me, let me hide myself in Thee*, and I want to be careful and honest here: that line is Augustus Toplady's hymn, not chapter and verse. But the hymn is standing on solid Scripture, and the saints were right to sing it. The Rock of Ages is real, and He is the hiding place.
Refuge is not a bunker. It is a river

Here is where I most wanted the album to surprise people. It would have been easy to make "refuge" mean a locked bunker, a hiding-away from a raging world. But "When the Nations Rage" takes the panic of the headlines and sets it under Psalm 2, *why do the nations rage? He who sits in the heavens laughs*, and refuses to let the news dethrone the King. And "River of Refuge" flat-out rejects the bunker: *there is a river whose streams make glad the city of God* (Psalm 46:4). The shelter is not walls. It is a current. It runs through the food pantry on Tuesday, the recovery meeting on Thursday, the church kitchen on Sunday, the prison Bible study on Monday. Every congregation is a tributary of that river. Refuge that only hides you is not the refuge of **Yahuah**, His shelter carries you forward, and then it flows through you to someone else.

The album also had to make room for stillness, because so many of us are holding the world together with our anxiety as if our worry were a load-bearing wall in the universe. "Be Still and Know" (Psalm 46:10) and "Selah Refuge" (Psalm 62:8, *pour out your heart before him; God is a refuge for us*) are the quiet center of the record. The Selah, the pause between the verses, is not the interruption of the work. The pause *is* the work. It is the breath that lets Him become the refuge in your body.
Who I made this for

I made *Refuge* for the one who is soaked and out of breath and cannot find a door. For the person doom-scrolling at 2 a.m. convinced the raging of the nations is stronger than the throne. For the striver who cannot stop holding the universe together long enough to be held. For the griever who needs a place that will not ask them to explain.

The finale, "Forever My Refuge," rests on David's old prayer: *be to me a rock of refuge, to which I may continually come* (Psalm 71:3). The point of the whole album is right there in one word, *continually*. The refuge is not a season of your life. It is His own Self, and His Self does not expire. The fortress is forever. The shadow is forever. The wings, the tower, the cleft of the Rock, forever.

So come inside. You do not have to be clean first, and you do not have to be strong first. Step through the door. The lamp has been on the whole time, and the One who left it burning is the shelter and the Sheltered, the cover and the covered, and when you finally walk back out into your week, the refuge walks out with you.

pieces.title: There Is a Chair at the Table With Your Name Already On It
pieces.song: Pull Up a Chair (The Table's Wide)
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful, richly multiethnic congregation packed shoulder to shoulder at a long welcome table that stretches from a church kitchen out to a sunlit porch, people of every age laughing and passing food, an usher pulling out a folding chair for a newcomer being embraced at the door, hands raised, wide grins everywhere; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, warm golden and honey tones, exuberant and full of life, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: This is my loud, hand-clapping, Hammond-and-horns album about the ache of arriving alone and the God who throws the door open before you can knock. It is the gospel that you who were far off have been brought near, that strangers become sisters and brothers in a single service, and the table just keeps getting longer. Come on in. The coffee is ready.

body.text: I know the specific ache of walking into a room full of people and being sure not one of them was expecting you. So I made a loud album about the God who opens the door before you can even knock.

*The Gospel of Belonging* is twelve tracks of Hammond B3 and horn stabs and hand-claps on the two and the four, the sound of a family that cannot whisper. I built it that way on purpose. Most of my records are pastoral and hushed, sung close to the microphone at three in the morning. This one is a front-porch light and a screen door swinging wide and somebody hollering, *"Come on in, the coffee's ready!"* Because belonging is not a quiet doctrine. When it finally happens to you, it is the loudest thing in your life.
The gospel is a welcome before it is anything else

The opener, "Knock on the Front Door," has a man coming up the walk with his Bible in his hand, bracing to be evaluated, and the whole house is already singing his name. That is the theology of the entire album in one image. **Yeshua** throws the door open before you knock. The house of the Lord already has a chair with your name on it. You are not auditioning for a seat. The seat was saved.

And I wanted the welcome to have texture, the deacon who walks over and puts a hand on your shoulder in "Hallelujah Hand on My Back" and says *"welcome home, brother, you are family today."* That hand had **Yahuah's** fingerprints on it. This is how God most often welcomes people: through the hand of someone who decided you belonged before you proved it.
Pull up a chair. There is always room

The heart of the record is "Pull Up a Chair (The Table's Wide)," and it is the song I would play for anyone who has ever felt like the extra person nobody planned for. The table was already long when I got there, stretched from the kitchen straight out to the porch. Somebody grabs a folding chair. Pastor says, *"Bring three more, the doorbell ain't done ringing."* There is no such thing as crowded at His feast.

That is not sentiment. It is the mechanics of grace. The table of **Yahuah** was carved wider than the world, and every chair has a name on it He already knew. When people ask me what the church is *for*, this song is most of my answer: it is the place where every stranger is a brother and every visitor is kin, and the bread that gets passed is Christ Himself.
Every chair has a Name on it Jesus already knew, pull up a chair, the family is full.

I built the album's peak, "Doors Thrown Open for Everyone," around the widest word in the gospel. Every fence the church ever raised, He knocked down for love, *every tongue and tribe and color and history.* The widow walks in beside the prodigal son; the pastor beside the man just released from prison; the grandmother brings the grandson she has prayed for forever; the skeptic walks in just to see what the singing is about. I anchored it to an old altar-call hymn, *whosoever will may come*, and I'll be plain that the exact phrase is a hymn, not a chapter and verse. But it is standing on the true ground of Revelation 22:17, and the *whosoever* really is the heartbeat of the gospel. It is sitting in the front pew tonight.
Stranger to sister, stranger to brother

The reason this album matters to me is a single sentence from Paul: *you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ* (Ephesians 2:13). He is writing to people the world had sorted into insiders and outsiders, and he tells them they are now *the household of God*, no longer strangers and aliens, but family. That is not a metaphor I take lightly. It is the actual work of **Yeshua**, and it happens fast. "Stranger to Sister Stranger to Brother" watches it happen inside a single service: she walked in the door not knowing a single face, and by the closing prayer she was trading numbers with new friends. *God sets the lonely in families* (Psalm 68:6), the college kid alone in a new city finding a Sunday family, the single mom finding aunties to hold her babies, the widower finding a table of brothers.

And I saved the tenderest song for near the end, on purpose. "I Was the Outsider" is the one quiet moment on a celebration record, because I needed to tell you the truth about myself before I told you anything about you. *I was the boy who counted his reasons You'd say no. I was the man who rehearsed all the doors that had closed.* And then He opened the door and called me by my name. I tell it so you will know He will do it for you too, for the one on the curb, the one in the parked car, the one in the back row hoping no one notices.
Who this album is for

It is for the newcomer standing at the back with a visitor card in his hand. For the person who has been burned by a room that pretended to be family and wasn't. For everyone who has ever slipped in late and slipped out early so no one would have to make space. For the tired one who has stopped believing there is a table where they would actually be wanted.

The finale is called "The Family Won't Stop Singing," and it ends the way I want your whole life to end, with a song that outlasts every voice that gives out, because the Lamb is on the throne and *a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, tribe, people, and language* is standing before Him (Revelation 7:9). The doors are wide. The welcome is loud. The table keeps on growing.

So hear me, wherever you are reading this: the chair has your name on it, and it has had your name on it longer than you have been alive. You do not have to clean up first. You do not have to arrive with anyone. Come up the walk. The porch light is on, the house is already singing, and there is a seat that has been waiting for exactly you.

pieces.title: The Chief Who Sent Everyone In Could Not Reach Himself
pieces.imagePrompt: A diverse gathering of rescued people of many nations standing in warm dawn light outside a firehouse, a weathered older fire chief among them with his arm around a young survivor, hands lifted and faces streaked with relief and wonder, an unburned white coat draped over one shoulder, embraces and quiet joy all around; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, warm amber and first-light gold tones, cinematic and reverent, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: This is my firehouse album, one fire chief telling his rescue to a hushed room. He runs toward the smoke his whole life, until the night the floor gives way and he becomes the one trapped in the dark. It is about the Firefighter in white who reaches the rooms no hose can reach, and the terrible mercy of discovering you cannot save yourself. You can only cry out.

body.text: I wanted to tell the story of salvation to people who think they are too strong to need it. So I wrote a whole album in the voice of a fire chief.

*Jesus Saves from the Fire* is staged like an intimate piece of theatre, one hardened man alone in a warm pool of light, felt piano and cello underneath, telling his rescue to a small, hushed house. No stadium, no choir wall. Just a survivor at the edge of the stage who has something he cannot stop saying. I built it that way because the truth at the center of it is too personal to shout. It has to be leaned in and told.
A man who runs toward the smoke

The opening songs are the chief in his element, and they are proud in the best sense of the word. "The Bells Go Off", two in the morning, boots by the bed, out the door. "Run Toward the Smoke". Everybody on the street is running out, and here come the engines against the current, the only ones driving in. *I don't run away, I run toward. I don't stand back, I kick the door.* That is a real and holy courage, and I honored it, because I have known people who spend their whole lives being the running-in, reaching-in hand for everyone else.

But every one of those early songs has a crack in it, a rumor the chief keeps hearing. A survivor comes out of a sealed room no hose could reach, no soot on her cheek, no smoke in her hair, and she points back into the flame and says, *"He was in there."* A Firefighter in white. White gear with no soot, no name, no crew. There and then gone. And He gets to the ones the chief never could. This is the God of Isaiah, the One who says *when you walk through the fire you shall not be burned* (Isaiah 43:2), and He is the fourth man Nebuchadnezzar saw walking loose in the furnace with the three who would not bow (Daniel 3:25).
The honest ceiling of human strength

I could not write this record without the song that admits the job has a limit. "Some Don't Come Out" is the chief telling the truth the posters never show, the night the stairwell folded early, the night he was one room too slow, the list of names he carries alone. *The chief is not a god in a yellow helmet, the chief is a man with a job he can't always do.* And that admission is not despair. It is the crack where the wonder starts. Because if he could not reach them, then who was walking in?

The middle of the album is the evidence piling up. "They All Describe the Same", three strangers who never met, three different fires, and every statement describing the identical impossible figure. A courtroom would call that corroboration. "The Crew Says It's Jesus", the rookie coming out grinning, the older men who have buried friends nodding along, a name written in the corner of the whiteboard that nobody erases. And then, because I will not cheapen anyone's real struggle, "Hard to Believe", the chief alone in the empty bay at midnight, wanting it to be true and unable to make himself pretend. *It's not that I'm against You, it's not that my heart is hard. It's just I've buried too many to be careless.* I gave doubt its dignity there, in the honest cry of the father in the Gospel: *I believe; help my unbelief* (Mark 9:24).
The night the rescuer became the rescued

Everything turns on track eight. "When I Cried Out" is the album's peak, and it is the moment the man who sent everyone into the danger becomes the one trapped in it. The warehouse floor gives way and drops him to the basement, the heat pressing him flat, his low-air alarm chirping in the dark, the one sound a firefighter is trained to dread. He keys his radio and gets static. His own call sign goes out unanswered. *The chief who sent everyone into the danger couldn't reach himself, couldn't reach a thing on his own.*

And there it is, the terrible, saving mercy of the whole gospel. There is a rescue your own arms cannot manage. So he goes down on a floor too hot to kneel on, and every word he ever doubted comes up out of him at once as a single word, a name, and a glove he has never felt closes around his wrist. *I could not reach myself, so I cried out, "Jesus", and the One I couldn't believe came down for me.* That is 2 Samuel 22:17 made flesh in a basement: *he reached down from on high and took me; he drew me out of many waters.* And it is the promise that holds the entire record: *everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved* (Romans 10:13).
I could not reach myself, so I cried out, and the One I couldn't believe came down for me.
The proudest thing he will ever say

The last act is the chief owning the reversal. "The Chief Got Rescued" is a man laying down twenty years of being the strong one, *I used to think the strong don't need it, I used to think that grace was for the weak*, and calling his rescue the proudest thing he will ever talk about. There is no helmet, no rank, no record of valor that saves a man the way grace does. He did not earn it and he did not deserve it, and that is precisely the point (Ephesians 2:8–9). **Yeshua** is the Son of Man who *came to seek and to save the lost* (Luke 19:10), and there is no such thing as being too far gone for the One who runs the wrong direction, toward the screaming, when the world runs away.
Who I made this for

I made this for the person who has fixed everything for everyone and cannot reach the one thing that matters, the addiction they cannot beat, the diagnosis, the marriage that is all smoke in the kitchen, the grief they cannot get out of their head. For the skeptic sitting in the cold bay at midnight, half-doubting and half-leaning toward the fire. For everyone who has been the strongest person in the building and is quietly running out of air.

Hear me the way that chief would tell it to one person across a table: you do not have to clean up first, and you do not have to crawl out on your own. You just have to cry the name. There is a hand in the smoke. The same door **Yahuah** opened for a hard old fire chief is open still, the same door, the same hand, the same rescue, and somewhere the bells are going off right now, and He is already running toward you.

pieces.title: You Can Sing Before the Chains Come Off
pieces.imagePrompt: A jubilant globally-diverse congregation dancing at first light, believers of many nations with hands raised, faces streaming with joy, the stone wall behind them glowing gold as sunrise breaks over a courtyard, tambourines lifted, a great crowd caught mid-shout in the warm dawn, cinematic worship-brand film still, bright and emotive, radiant amber and rose light, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I built a whole record around the hour most people give up, midnight, with the chains still on. Paul and Silas didn't wait for the doors to open before they sang. Neither do we. This is the story of the night the foundations answered a song.

body.text: Two-fourteen in the morning, the phone is face-down on the nightstand, and you cannot sleep. The list of names you are carrying is longer than the hours left in the dark. That is where I wanted this record to find you, not on Sunday with your good clothes on, but on the kitchen floor at the exact minute you decided nobody was coming.
Because somebody is. And you can sing before the chains come off.

That is the whole confession of *Earthquake at Midnight*. Twelve songs that start in the hush of a sleepless house and end with the sun climbing a prison wall. I did not want to hand you a victory song and pretend I skipped the night to get there. I wanted to walk the night with you, minute by minute, and show you what I have learned on that floor: the praise comes first, and then the ground moves.
Why the Album Is Named for a Prison

There is a story in Acts 16 I have never been able to leave alone. Paul and Silas, beaten, backs torn open, feet locked in wooden stocks in the innermost cell of a Philippian jail. Every reason to be silent. And Scripture says, *"And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them"* (Acts 16:25).

Read the order slowly, because the order is the sermon. They sang **while bound**. The song went up before a single lock had moved. And then, *"suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken: and immediately all the doors were opened, and every one's bands were loosed"* (Acts 16:26).
The earthquake did not come to *start* the worship. It came to *answer* it.

That is why the album is named for an earthquake and not for the morning. I did not want to name it after the outcome. I wanted to name it after the moment your faith is tested hardest, the moment the room is still dark, the stocks are still on, and you decide to open your mouth anyway. **Yahuah** is not moved by the volume of the crowd. He is moved by the saint who will worship in the inner cell.
Walking the Night, Track by Track
I built this one as a real night, in three acts, so you would know exactly where you are standing.

It opens in the tarrying. *"Midnight Finds Me Praying"* meets you at your own 2:14 AM and tells you the truth the enemy hides: midnight is not where the prayer goes to die, midnight is where the Helper meets your cry. *"The 3 AM Watch"* takes you to the hospital corridor and the cold coffee and the hand you are holding that will not warm up, and it stands on Psalm 63:6, *"when I remember thee upon my bed, and meditate on thee in the night watches."* Then *"Tarry With Me Holy Ghost"* plants both knees on the linoleum and refuses to leave, because **Yeshua** Himself told the disciples to *tarry* in the city until they were endued with power from on high (Luke 24:49).

The middle act is the long haul, and I did not make it pretty. *"Persistent Widow Prayer"* is the woman in Luke 18 who would not stop knocking, and the whole point of her, Yeshua said, is *that men ought always to pray, and not to faint* (Luke 18:1). *"Groanings Too Deep for Words"* is for the night your chest is heaving and no sentence will come, and Romans 8:26 promises that the Spirit Himself makes intercession for us *with groanings which cannot be uttered.* You do not have to have the words. He is praying the ones you cannot say.
Then comes the hinge of the whole record: *"Sing Hymns At Midnight."* This is the model. This is Paul and Silas. Sing even when the chains are on. The praise will be the dawn.
The bound singing until the bound come alive, that is not a strategy. That is the oldest weapon the church ever carried into a dark room.

*"The Watchman Does Not Sleep"* holds the last tension, Habakkuk on his tower saying *"I will stand upon my watch"* (Habakkuk 2:1), and then the floor drops out. *"Earthquake (At Midnight)"* is forty-five seconds of held breath and then the whole room breaks: *Earthquake! At midnight! Every chain falls off!* I wrote it so the music itself would be the quake, so your body would feel the *suddenly* before your mind caught up.
Who I Made This For

I made it for the intercessor nobody sees. The one on the floor at 3 AM with a list of names and a chest that will not breathe. The mother praying for a child who has not called in a year. The chaplain on the night shift. The saint who has held a wall so long she has started to wonder if the morning is a rumor.

And I made it because the breakthrough is bigger than your one prayer. Watch how Acts 16 ends. The chains fall off, and then the jailer, the very man who locked them in, falls down trembling and cries, *"Sirs, what must I do to be saved?"* And Paul says, *"Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved, and thy house"* (Acts 16:30–31). That whole household came home that night. *"Jailer Saved Tonight"* on this record is me telling you: you thought you were praying for your one thing. **Yahuah** was setting a whole house free while you sang.

The album does not end at the earthquake. It ends at sunrise. *"Morning Has Broken Through"* names the real content of the breakthrough, not just that He answered, but that He *stayed.* He did not leave when the words ran out at three. And *"Sunrise on the Prison Wall"* lifts the very first line of the album, *midnight found me praying*, into celebration, because the woman who walked in on the bedroom floor walks out at the open door, and the other prisoners walk out with her.

Here is what I need you to hear tonight, wherever the dark has you. The chains are real. I am not going to sugar it. But you were never meant to wait for the morning to start the song. Open your mouth in the inner cell. Sing before anything moves. The foundations of that prison are closer to shaking than they have ever been, and the God who answered at midnight in Philippi has not aged a day, has not cooled, and has not run out of *suddenly.*
Sing, beloved. The morning is already on its way to you.

pieces.title: The Fire Still Doesn't Skip a Single Head
pieces.imagePrompt: An ecstatic globally-diverse congregation mid-praise-break, believers of many nations packed shoulder to shoulder with hands lifted and mouths open in shout, a young woman in the front row caught in a spin of joy, elders and children and visitors of every skin tone radiant under warm light, tambourines and raised palms everywhere, cinematic worship-brand film still, bright and jubilant, glowing gold and ember tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: They told us Acts 2 was a historical event. I made a whole double-time record to argue back. The wind that filled the upper room never packed up and left Jerusalem, and when the fire divided that morning, it sat on every single head. It still does. Yours included.

body.text: Somebody taught you that Pentecost was a Sunday on the calendar. A red banner, a memorial service, a nice sermon about something that happened a long time ago to people you will never meet. I made *Pentecost Fire* to walk into that room and turn the lights all the way up.

Because Acts 2 is not a museum. It is an address. And the wind that filled that upper room is not a memory. It is weather that is still moving through buildings, and kitchens, and bus stops, and this exact room.

I built this record fast on purpose. Double-time, the Hammond Leslie spinning at the top of its speed, the kick on eighth-notes, tambourine in sixteenths, brass stabbing every "Holy Ghost." I wanted the *tempo* to preach. Pentecost was not a slow, cautious thing. When the fire fell, they came out of that room spinning so hard the crowd thought they were drunk. I wanted your feet to feel that before your head could argue with it.
What the Title Is Really About
*Pentecost Fire.* Two of the most misread words in the whole church.

Here is what actually happened, straight from the text. The one hundred and twenty waited in the upper room, just like **Yeshua** told them to, *tarry ye in the city of Jerusalem, until ye be endued with power from on high* (Luke 24:49). And then: *"suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind... And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost"* (Acts 2:2–4).

Read that last part again, because it is the whole album. The fire *divided.* It took a shape you could see. And *it sat upon each of them.* Not on the leaders only. Not on the ordained, the polished, the ones with the right last name. Each of them. The fire did not skip a single head.

That is the line I could not get past, and it became the beating heart of the whole record. On *"Fall on Me (Fall on Me!)"* I say it plain, the fire didn't skip a head. It fell on the daughter in the third row who has never felt it. It fell on the first-time visitor. It fell fresh on the grandmother who has been singing about the fire for forty years. **Yahuah** does not hand out His Spirit by seniority.
The Wind Was Already Moving

The first thing I wanted you to know is that you are not begging a closed heaven to crack open. On *"The Wind Is Already Moving"* I lean all the way into Acts 2:2 and connect it back to the very beginning, the same Spirit that *moved upon the face of the waters* in Genesis 1:2 is the wind in the upper room. It is not a different Spirit than the beginning. The air pressure drops before the fire falls. He announces Himself like weather.

Then the fire itself. *"Tongues of Fire"* stands in Acts 2 and marvels at the thing the crowd could not explain, Parthians, Medes, Elamites, the visitor from Cappadocia, every one of them hearing the wonderful works of God in his own mother tongue. The Spirit does not translate through the brain. He speaks from love, in a language you never studied.

And when the room caught, they *danced.* On *"Dance Till the Room Spins"* I put David in the frame, *David danced before the Lord with all his might*, and Michal despised him from the window (2 Samuel 6:14–16). The world will always call the Spirit-dance foolish. Peter stood up on that first morning and told the mockers exactly what it was: *this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel* (Acts 2:16).
The dance the world thinks is drunk is the oldest evidence in the book. Let them look out the window. Keep spinning.
The Daughters Were Moved to the Front

I could not make a Pentecost record and leave out the line that changed everything for women like me. Peter, quoting Joel, preached it over the whole crowd: *"And it shall come to pass in the last days, saith God, I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh: and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy"* (Acts 2:17).

*"Your Sons and Daughters"* is my favorite corner of this album. The synagogue used to seat the women behind. The upper room sat them in the front. The fire fell on Mary the mother. It fell on the back-row daughter who was told to be quiet, and on the grandmother who has been dreaming for thirty years. The prophecy does not check your gender at the door. If you have breath, you have a portion.

And then the cinematic center of the whole thing, *"Acts 2 Right Now"*, where the record refuses to keep the story in the past tense. The Spirit is falling in the kitchen, the parking lot, the kid's bedroom, the dorm room, the hospital chapel, the sanctuary at midnight. I built that song so you would hear your own kitchen on the list. That is not poetry. That is Acts 2:39, *the promise is unto you, and to your children, and to all that are afar off.* That is *you.*
Who I Poured This Out For

I made this for the believer who thinks the fire has an expiration date, and it ran out before she was born. For the visitor in the back who is sure the encounter is for everybody but her. For the young ones the church keeps telling to wait their turn. For the tired saint who has been to a thousand services and never once let herself believe the flame could fall on her own head, fresh, tonight.

The album does not end in the upper room. It never could. *"The Church Was Born Today"* remembers that three thousand were added in a single afternoon (Acts 2:41), the same crowd that had screamed *crucify* seven weeks before became the harvest field. And *"Fire in the Streets"* opens the door, because the upper room *had* a door. Peter lifted his voice in the street (Acts 2:14). The fire that fell was never meant to stay in the room. It was meant to walk out onto your commute, your cubicle, your corner store, carried in the pocket of an ordinary saint who finally believed it was hers.

So let me say to you what the fire said to that whole room, all at once, skipping no one: *fall on me.* You are not too late, too ordinary, too far back, or too far gone. The same wind is in the building. Lift your head. It has always been the heads He was looking for, and He still does not skip a single one.

pieces.title: The Same Spirit Walked Into Six Rooms
pieces.imagePrompt: A radiant intercontinental celebration of many nations worshiping together, a joyful crowd blending African, diaspora, Latin American, South Asian and Western believers, hands raised under an open sky, talking drums and tambourines and colorful fabrics, dancers mid-motion, a great multiethnic congregation glowing in golden hour light, cinematic worship-brand film still, bright and euphoric, warm amber and sunset tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: A Lagos crusade square, a 6:47 kitchen, a Soweto sunrise, a locked room in Mumbai, a São Paulo hillside, an Atlanta church basement. Six rooms, six cities, one Person. I made this record to prove He never broke the link, and that the encounter is portable.

body.text: I want to take you to six rooms.

A crusade square in Lagos at the dusk hour, stage lights on the field, hundreds of thousands gathered, vendors selling plantain, children on shoulders, the talking drum preaching to an orange-burning sky. A kitchen at 6:47 in the morning, coffee pot on, cabinets still yellow, a woman wiping down the counter with the radio low. A Soweto sunrise service, dew on the tin roof, the choir humming in Zulu before the rooster. A room in Mumbai, twelve faces, one lamp, the window covered and the door locked. A hillside favela in São Paulo where the city wouldn't go. A church basement in Atlanta on a Friday night, folding chairs in a circle, a sixteen-year-old in the back with her phone face-down.

Six rooms that could not be more different. And the same Person walked into every single one of them without changing His name. That is *The Holy Ghost Walks Africa*, and that is why I had to make it.
The Wind Never Signed a Peace Treaty With Geography

The thesis of this whole record is one sentence: **He came down again.** The first track says it plainly. He didn't close the upper room, He didn't lock the door. The wind that fell on the one hundred and twenty back then is on my kitchen floor right now. Acts chapter two is still open, and *the pouring never quit.*

I know the temptation. We read Acts 2 like it was a one-time storm, a beautiful weather event that happened over Jerusalem and then the sky cleared for good. But **Yeshua** did not describe a single afternoon. He described a range: *"ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth"* (Acts 1:8). That verse is a map. Jerusalem was the first room. Africa and the diaspora and the uttermost parts are the rooms He was always walking toward.

And the promise underneath it is Joel's, quoted by Peter on the day itself: *"I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh"* (Joel 2:28; Acts 2:17). All flesh. Not one nation's flesh. Not one continent's. He does not carry a passport, and He does not need a visa.
He Doesn't Need a Pulpit

The song I love most on the front half is *"Holy Ghost in the Kitchen,"* and it is the least dramatic room on the record on purpose. A woman with suds still on her wrist, eggs on the plate, and the Spirit walks through her right beside the stove. The line is: *the pulpit don't define the cloud.* He didn't wait for Sunday. He didn't need a date. The floor became a sea and the yellow light got brighter, and there was not a candle lit.

We have trained the church to believe the encounter belongs to the platform, the big stage, the anointed man, the crusade square. And He *is* in the crusade square. *"Lagos Crusade"* is one of the most electric things I have ever recorded, a hundred thousand hands going up like a wave while the talking drum opens the altar call in Yoruba. But the whole architecture of this album is built to say: the same Spirit who fills the square fills the kitchen, and He plays no favorites between them.
He met me on the highway, and He met me at the sink, and He did not act any smaller in the small room.
The Room the World Locked, and the Room the City Forgot
There are two rooms on this record I could not leave out, because the church needs to hear them.

*"Mumbai Underground (He Came Anyway)"* is the persecuted church. Twelve believers, the door locked against the threat on the street, no music, no raised voices, and the Holy Ghost steps through the wall anyway. I anchored it in Acts 4, where the early church prayed under real pressure and *the place was shaken where they were assembled together; and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost* (Acts 4:31). He does not ask the regime for permission. He came past the lock.

And *"São Paulo Favela Fire"* is the room the city wrote off, the hillside the elites avoided, the corner nobody counts. I say it in the bridge and I mean it as theology: *the Holy Ghost loves the margin most.* He climbs the hill the avenue ignores. That is not a slogan; that is His whole pattern, all the way back to a manger in a town nobody expected anything from.

Then the cinematic turn, *"Same Spirit, Every Country,"* where all six rooms collapse into one recognition. The talking drum in Lagos and the Hammond in the South are calling the same Person through a hundred different mouths. The whispered *Holy Ghost* in Mumbai and the Soweto morning hum are reaching for the same Spirit who has always been the One. Same wind. Same fire. He never broke the link. **Yahuah** is not a regional deity who changes His character at the border.
Who I Carried This Record For

I made it for the believer who thinks revival only happens somewhere else, some other country, some other era, some more spiritual people than her. For the saint in the small kitchen who assumes the good stuff is reserved for the stage. For the underground church holding on behind a locked door. For the ones the city forgot on the hillside. And for the whole beautiful, scattered, many-tongued family of God, so we would recognize each other as carriers of the *same* flame.

Because the record does not end in any of the six rooms. It ends in *you.* *"Carry the Fire Out"* remembers that the encounter always opens onto a street, the Holy Ghost is portable, He is not staying with the building. *"Release Him in the Room"* puts the fire in your own mouth: the conference room, the classroom, the hospital ward, the hard conversation in the kitchen, open your mouth, speak the Name, and the atmosphere shifts. And *"We Are Encounter-Carriers"* closes the loop, answering the very first song. He came down in Lagos, He came down in my house, He came down again in me, *and now I walk Him out.*

That is where you come in. You are the next square. The next kitchen. The next locked room where He steps through the wall. The wind that walked into six rooms on this record is looking for a seventh, and it has your address. Open your mouth wherever you are standing. The same Spirit, in every country, and He is already in yours.

pieces.title: He Named Me Prophet Before He Named the Stars
pieces.imagePrompt: A jubilant multigenerational congregation of many nations with hands lifted in prophetic release, a young woman near the back caught mid-shout with an elder's hand on her shoulder, a choir in robes behind her, grandmothers and youth and children radiant together, brass players and raised tambourines, warm sanctuary light breaking through high windows, cinematic worship-brand film still, bright and stirring, golden and warm-amber tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: A Black Baptist youth conference, a grandfather-deacon laying his hand on a daughter near the back, and a whole church going up. I made this record for every saint who was told the Voice belonged to somebody else. Measured Baptist gravity, Pentecostal fire, and daughters rising to speak.

body.text: Let me tell you about the moment this whole record was built to reach.

A youth conference. A prophet steps to the door of the auditorium, walks past the platform, past the polished ones, and lays a word on a daughter near the back, the kid nobody was watching. Her grandfather, an old deacon who has sat in a measured Baptist pew his whole life, catches it. His hand goes to her shoulder. And he leans in and says the four words that break every ceiling: *"Speak, daughter. You're bolder than you know."*
That is *Prophecy Rising (Bapticostal).* And I made it for every believer who was quietly, politely, over a lifetime, taught that the Voice of the Lord belonged to somebody else.
Two Traditions, One Fire

The word *Bapticostal* is a made-up handshake between two rooms I love. The Baptist room gave me gravity, the closed hymnal, the reverence, the weight of a Word that does not need a hype man. The Pentecostal room gave me the fire, the Hammond leaning into the Leslie, the brass, the praise-break, the daughter going higher. I did not want to choose. I wanted the measured Baptist verse to *erupt* into the Pentecostal shout, because that is exactly how the Word moves when it finally lands on somebody who was told to stay quiet. It sits still. And then it can't.

The album opens with the Voice arriving. *"The Voice of the Lord Arrives"* stands on Psalm 29, the Voice of the Lord that breaks the cedars and shakes the wilderness. A woman is reading her Psalter on a Saturday morning and the Word comes near like it never had before, and the Father says the tenderest, most dangerous thing: *Daughter, let it go.*
The Word Was Never Meant to Stay in the Pulpit
Here is the theology I fought for on this record, and I will put it in front of you plainly.

The Spirit of prophecy is not a title for the few. On the day the fire fell, Peter quoted Joel over the entire room: *"your sons and your daughters shall prophesy... and on my servants and on my handmaidens I will pour out in those days of my Spirit"* (Acts 2:17–18). Handmaidens. Servants. The people who were never given a microphone. And Revelation puts it beyond argument, *the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy* (Revelation 19:10). If you carry the testimony of **Yeshua**, you already carry the thing.

That is why *"Every Saint A Prophet"* stands on 1 Peter 2:9, *ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation.* You do not need a pulpit. You do not need a stage. The Holy Ghost will turn your kitchen into a prophetic age. The brother in the back pew has a word in his bones. The sister in the choir stand is not there to fill a robe. **Yahuah** hands out the gifts (1 Corinthians 12), and He did not run out before He got to you.
Prophesy to the Bones, Even the Ones in Your Own Chest
The single I would put in your hand first is *"Prophesy Over The Bones,"* and it comes straight out of the strangest, most electric prophet story in the book.

Ezekiel is set down in a valley full of dry bones and **Yahuah** asks him a question no reasonable person answers with hope: *"Son of man, can these bones live?"* And the prophet, humble, says, *"O Lord God, thou knowest."* Then comes the command: *"Prophesy upon these bones... O ye dry bones, hear the word of the Lord"* (Ezekiel 37:3–4). He speaks. Bone comes to bone. Sinew, flesh, breath, and an exceeding great army stands up out of a graveyard.

I wrote that song so you would understand the valley is not always out there. Sometimes the valley of dry bones is *in your own chest.* A dead marriage. A cold call. A dream you buried and marked with a stone. And the Holy Ghost is standing next to you asking the same question, *will you prophesy?* Not wait for the bones to look alive. Speak first. **Yeshua** is *the resurrection and the life* (John 11:25), and He puts the breath in your mouth before the graveyard has moved an inch.
Open your mouth over the deadest thing you own. The command came before the miracle every single time.
The Daughters Have Their Say
I will not pretend this record is neutral about who gets to speak. It is not.

*"I Hear Him Say (My Daughter)"* is a woman at 5 AM with a journal open and the pen mid-air, and the Father whispers over her the thing He whispered before the world began, *I knew you before the world began; I named you Prophet, and the call still stands.* That is the title of this whole reflection, and it is the ground I stand on. He named the calling before He named the stars. Your gift is not a late idea. It is older than you are.

*"Open My Mouth"* is Isaiah at the throne, undone, *woe is me, for I am a man of unclean lips*, until the seraph takes a live coal from the altar and touches his mouth, and the Voice asks *whom shall I send?* and the trembling prophet says the bravest words in the Bible: *Here am I; send me* (Isaiah 6:5–8). And *"Speak, Lord, Your Servant Hears"* is little Samuel in the temple, learning to answer the Voice in the dark (1 Samuel 3:9), because before the prophet ever pours, the prophet listens.

I made this for the quiet one. The back-row daughter. The grandmother whose word lay buried in the pew for forty years. The grandson the church didn't know how to receive. The saint who has felt something rising for years and kept swallowing it because nobody handed her permission.

And I made it as a covenant word, too, because the calling was never only about you. *"Prophecy Over The Bloodline"* takes a pencil to butcher paper and names the generations, the ones who carried trauma and the ones who carried gold, and stands on the promise that **Yahuah** keeps *covenant and mercy... to a thousand generations* (Deuteronomy 7:9), while every curse the enemy tried to hand down is crossed out at the cross (Galatians 3:13). When you finally open your mouth, you are not just speaking for yourself. You are prophesying up a family tree and down into children not yet born.

Consider this your permission. The album ends where it began, *"Sons and Daughters Speak"* lifts the Voice that arrived in Track One and says it now lives in every mouth, on the strong and the weak alike, the last-days promise finally landing on the ones who were told to wait. The coal is already on the altar. The command has already come. So lift your head, open your hand, and speak the thing He put in you before the foundation of the world. Heaven has been waiting a long time to hear your voice, and it was always yours to lift.

pieces.title: The Floor Beneath the Floor
pieces.song: The Bottom Fell Out for Good
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyous multiethnic block party of praise at golden hour, people of many nations dancing in the street, a woman in a bright robe with arms thrown wide mid-spin, neighbors and elders and children celebrating together, horns and hand-drums, tables set on the pavement, warm string lights, confetti of light, everyone caught in unguarded joy, cinematic worship-brand film still, bright and celebratory, warm sunset gold and amber tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I made a reggae-soaked, block-party record about the worst night of a life, because the pit is where He does His best work. When the floor of the bottom finally gave way, I didn't fall further. I found out He was the floor beneath the floor. This is the story of the funeral He turned into a party.

body.text: Here is the image the whole record hangs on, so I will give it to you first.

You are already at the bottom. You made your peace with it, the pit is a basement with no ladder and no friend, and you have decided this is where the story ends. And then the floor of the pit itself gives way. You brace to fall further, to hit something harder, to lose the little ground you had left. And instead of falling. You *rise.* Because it turns out there was a floor beneath the floor, and it had a name, and it was holding you the whole time.

That is *Pit To The Party.* And I dressed the worst night of a life in a warm reggae one-drop and a block-party groove on purpose, because I refuse to let the enemy have the only soundtrack for the low place. He does not get to score your bottom. I do.
Why the Pit Earns Its Own Album

I could have started at the celebration. Plenty of gospel does. But I did not want to hand you a party and pretend I skipped the pit to get there, because that is a lie, and lonely people can hear a lie a mile off.

So the record starts *in the miry clay.* Track one plants you at the bottom where the concrete met your back, cellphone at four percent, a message you could not send, and then a voice in the dark says *your bottom is not the end.* That is Psalm 40, and I built the whole album on it: *"He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings"* (Psalm 40:2). Notice **Yahuah** does not shout down instructions from the rim of the pit. He reaches *into* the clay. He gets His own hands dirty pulling you out.

And when He pulls you up, He does not leave you standing there ashamed in your rags. He runs. *"Best Robe On"* is the prodigal, the son who rehearsed a servant's speech the whole way home, and *while he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him* (Luke 15:20). The best robe. The ring. The fatted calf. *Let us eat, and be merry* (Luke 15:23). He did not make you earn it. He wrapped you in the best before you got your apology out.
The Party Is a Doctrine, Not a Mood
I want to be careful here, because "party" can sound like I mean a vibe. I do not. The party in this record is theology.

When **Yeshua** told the prodigal story, He was answering people who were scandalized that He ate with sinners. And the point of the whole story is that heaven *throws a feast* when the lost come home. The celebration is not decoration on top of the grace, the celebration *is* the grace, made loud enough for the whole block to hear. That is why *"Mourning Into Dancing"* stands on Psalm 30:11, *"thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing; thou hast put off my sackcloth, and girded me with gladness."* He does not just dry the tears. He unbuckles the sackcloth you tied around your own waist and hands you a dance.
Beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness, Isaiah 61:3 is not a metaphor. It is a trade, and He always overpays.

*"New Creation Now"* is the same grace in a different key, the torn-up ID that doesn't fit the face anymore, the same address with a brand-new tenant and a new lock on the door. *"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new"* (2 Corinthians 5:17). Old you couldn't stay. That is not you working harder. That is Him rewriting the story and showing you how.
The Bottom Fell Out for Good
The peak of the whole record, and the reason for the song I put in the frontmatter, is *"The Bottom Fell Out for Good."*

Everything you clung to comes apart in your hand, job, pride, reputation, slipping like desert sand. And you are certain this is the end of you. But *the losing of the bottom was the finding of the Rock.* Every door you thought was slamming shut was **Yahuah's** hand turning a lock you couldn't reach. He was the floor beneath the floor. He caught the falling and turned it into flight.

I have lived that verse. Most people who will ever love this album have lived it too. The night the last thing gave way and you found out you were not going to keep falling, because underneath the bottom of your bottom was the everlasting arms, and they do not have a lower limit. He turned the pit into a *door.*

That is why the tenderest song on the record, *"Mama's Kitchen Prayer,"* matters so much to me. Not everybody at the party got there by their own testimony. Some of us got carried on somebody else's knees, a mother at the burner turned to low, cornbread in the oven, praying for a child longer than that child had been gone. And **Yeshua** followed every syllable of that prayer down every dark road until He brought the runaway home. If you are still out there, hear me: somebody's kitchen prayer has a homing signal on you, and He is honoring it right now.
Who Gets an Invitation
Everyone. That is the whole point of the last act.

Once you have been pulled out of the clay, you cannot keep the address to yourself. *"Whole Block Invited"* is the overflow, if He did it for the girl on the curb outside the store, He can do it for the whole block that got counted out. His grace is not rationed to the righteous, and it is not a private feast. The table is set for the greatest and the least, the corner boys and the church folk and the sister who lost hope and the auntie on the stoop. *"Beauty for the Ashes"* carries it across generations, grandmama came up out of her own valley and told me how He turned her ashes into gold, and now my daughter is watching the beauty get rebuilt in me. And *"Dance Out the Door"* sends the whole thing back onto the avenue, because the grace that found you at the bottom was always meant to send you out.

I made this record for the one who is sure the pit is the last chapter. For the runaway rehearsing a speech she will never need. For the person who has already braced for the floor to give way again. Hear the good news in the groove: the bottom is not the end, the funeral is about to become a party, and the God who reached into the clay is the floor beneath every floor you will ever stand on.
So dust off. Put the robe on. The music has already started, the whole block is invited, and there is a plate at the table with your name on it. Come on to the party. He has been holding your seat.

pieces.title: One Word, One Name, One Undivided God
pieces.imagePrompt: A globally-diverse congregation of many nations standing together at dawn with hands raised and mouths open in a single sung word, an elder and a small child side by side, warm light washing across joyful upturned faces; uplifting emotionally powerful premium cinematic worship film-still, bright golden tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: Twelve songs, and every one of them is chasing a single Hebrew syllable, echad, One. I made this record because I kept meeting people who could shout the Name in a crowded room but had never once whispered it at their own bedside. This is the story of the word I could not stop singing.

body.text: I once spent an entire recording session on one word.

Not one song. One word. Twelve tracks, an oud, a darbuka, a room full of singers from four countries, and the whole apparatus was built to carry a single Hebrew syllable across the finish line: **echad**. One. I know how that sounds. Who writes an album to say a word a toddler could learn in an afternoon? But I had been teaching for years, and I kept running into the same quiet emergency: people who could sing loud, dense, wonderful worship, and had somehow never let the smallest true thing land on them. That the God they were praising is not one god among a shelf of options. He is One. And that changes the size of a life.
So I made *Echad, the Name Is One* to say the word properly, from the top of my lungs and from the edge of a pillow.
The word that is also a confession

The album opens where every faithful Hebrew day has opened for thousands of years, with the Shema. "Hear, O Israel: **Yahuah** our God, **Yahuah** is one" (Deuteronomy 6:4). The first track is called *Shema Yisrael*, and it does the thing I wanted the whole record to do: it starts as an unaccompanied voice, then the drum enters, and suddenly a confession becomes a body moving. Because that is what the Shema actually is. It is not a doctrine you file away. It is a summons you answer with your feet.

Here is the part I never want a listener to miss. In Hebrew, *shema* does not only mean "hear." It means hear-and-do, to listen in a way that reorganizes your life around what you heard. So the very first word of the confession is already asking for everything. And the next verse tells you how much everything is: "You shall love **Yahuah** your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength" (Deuteronomy 6:5). Track three carries that line, *All My Heart, All My Soul, All My Strength*, and I wrote it as a checklist you can't get out of. Heart, soul, strength. Nothing held back. The One asks for the whole.

When **Yeshua** was asked which command was greatest, He did not invent a new one. He reached back and quoted the Shema, "Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one" (Mark 12:29). The Messiah's answer to the biggest question was the oldest sentence His people knew. That is not a small thing to build an album on.
Why "One" is bigger than a number

There's a track in the middle I fought hardest for. It's called *Compound Unity*, and it's the teaching heart of the record. Because the moment you sing "the Name is One," an honest person asks: then what do we do with Father, Son, and Spirit?

Here is where I have to be a careful teacher and not a sloppy one. The Hebrew *echad* is a rich word. When Genesis says a man and his wife become "one flesh," the word is *echad* (Genesis 2:24). It is a word that can hold a togetherness inside its oneness. Now. I want to be plain: the Bible does not hand us a tidy sentence that says "echad proves the Trinity." That reading is a teaching tradition, and I'll name it as one. But I'll also tell you what Scripture shows me directly. At the Jordan, when **Yeshua** came up from the water, the Father spoke, the Spirit descended like a dove, and the Son stood dripping in the river (Matthew 3:16-17). Three, present, in one scene, and no crack in the oneness. So the song does not lecture. It simply sings:
The mystery is not a math, the mystery is a path.
I am not asking you to solve the One. I am asking you to love Him.
The shout and the whisper
If the album has a secret, it's the eighth track, *Echad, Hear Me Whisper His Name*. I built the whole record to arrive there.

Because I had watched something over the years that undid me. The Shema is a shout when a congregation stands together. I've heard rooms roar it. But there is an old, tender Hebrew custom of making the Shema the *last* words a person speaks before sleep, and the last words breathed at the end of a life. That's tradition, not commandment, but it is a holy tradition, and it taught me something the loud rooms never could. I have sat beside people at the end and sung *echad* slowly while a hand went still. I have watched a man who spent his whole life chasing a dozen different names finally weep over the discovery that there is only One.

So the song strips down to a single held note, a voice whispering the Name that holds the world, and then it rises back into full sound. Shout and whisper, the same word. That is the whole Christian life in one track. The God who is loud enough to shake a festival is close enough to be your last breath.
The Name on the doorpost, the Name on the children

The Shema doesn't stay in the sanctuary. Deuteronomy 6 tells the household to bind these words on the hand, set them between the eyes, write them on the doorpost, and teach them to the children when you sit at home and walk by the way (Deuteronomy 6:7-9). Two tracks live right there in the kitchen and the hallway, *Mezuzah on the Doorpost, Mezuzah on the Heart* and *Teach the Children His Name*.

I put those songs on the record on purpose. Because a confession that only works in a crowd is not yet yours. The Name has to make it onto your doorframe and into your bedtime and into the small ears at your table, or it stays a performance. The album closes with a lullaby, *Bedtime Shema*, and then a benediction, *Adonai Echad*, that carries the Name back out the door into an ordinary Tuesday. The first track and the last track are the same confession, the bookends of a whole life. You open your eyes with the Name and you close them with the Name, and the day in between is just the space you get to love Him in.
Who I made this for

I made *Echad* for the person who is tired of a faith that feels like a menu. Who suspects, correctly, that being pulled in twelve directions is not the same as being whole. The Shema is the cure for a divided life, because a God who is One asks for a heart that is one, undivided, unhedged, unashamed.

And I made it for the person at the bedside. The one holding a hand that is going still, reaching for words holy enough for the moment and finding only one. There is one. It is the smallest true thing and the largest. **Yahuah** is one, and **Yeshua** is His salvation, and the Name is close when the room is quiet.
So yes. I wrote a whole album to say one word. I'd do it again tomorrow. Some words are worth a lifetime of saying, and this one you can carry all the way home.

pieces.title: The Countdown Hidden in the Verses You Skip
pieces.albumTitle: The Line That Leads To Yeshua
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful multi-generational, multi-ethnic family gathered around an open Bible in warm lamplight, grandparents and grandchildren of many nations leaning in and smiling, one child pointing at the page in delight; uplifting emotionally powerful premium cinematic worship film-still, warm amber tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: You already know the reflex, the reader hits "begat, begat, begat" and the whole room quietly checks out. I made an album to argue the opposite: that the genealogy nobody reads is Yahuah counting down to a manger, and that the broken names left in it are the best news in the chapter.

body.text: Watch a congregation the moment the reader begins Matthew chapter one. Something happens to the room. Shoulders soften, eyes drift, a page rustles ahead to the "good part." Begat, begat, begat, forty-two links of ancient names, and the whole pew goes flat.

I have watched it my entire teaching life, and I finally got tired of it. So I made a record whose only argument is this: the list you skip is not a phone book. It is a countdown. Every one of those names is **Yahuah** ticking off the generations toward a manger, and He is not bored, even if we are. *The Line That Leads To Yeshua* is twelve songs built to make you lean back in on the exact verse you were about to abandon.
The clock nobody reads is still ticking

The opening track, *Every Name Sings*, starts inside the moment I just described, a Sunday morning, a pastor reading Matthew one, a whole room zoning out. And then the narrator catches himself on a name, Salmon, then Boaz, then Obed, and the list stops sounding like a clock and starts sounding like a countdown. That's the hinge of the whole album.

Because Matthew tells you it's a countdown. He organizes the line into three sets of fourteen generations, Abraham to David, David to the exile, the exile to the Messiah (Matthew 1:17). That is not an accident of history. That is an author showing you a design. Fourteen, fourteen, fourteen, and then the One the whole structure was reaching for. **Yahuah** was keeping time across two thousand years, and He did not drop a single generation on the way to Bethlehem.
So the chorus of that first song is not clever. It's just true:
Every name sings, the line that leads to **Yeshua**, Yahuah planned the whole way.
The scandals He refused to delete
Here is where the album stops being a history lesson and starts being the gospel.

If a family were assembling a royal genealogy to impress the neighbors, there are names you would quietly lose. Matthew keeps them. On purpose. And several of them are women, which was already unusual, but look at *which* women.

There's Tamar, whose story in Genesis 38 is one anyone would call a scandal, a widow twice over, wronged by the family, who takes desperate measures and ends up bearing Judah's sons (Matthew 1:3). The song *Judah and Tamar* sits in that tension without flinching, and its whole point is one line I keep coming back to: He did not airbrush the story. He wrote the broken into the gold.

There's Ruth, a Moabite, an outsider by birth, a woman from a nation Israel was taught to keep at arm's length. And she says the most loyal sentence in the Bible: "Where you go I will go... your people shall be my people, and your God my God" (Ruth 1:16). *Ruth Said Yes* is the track, and it ends where her yes ends, as the great-grandmother of King David (Matthew 1:5, Ruth 4:17).

And there's the one Matthew names most carefully of all. He does not write "Bathsheba." He writes that David was the father of Solomon "by the wife of Uriah" (Matthew 1:6). He names the husband. He names the wound. He will not let the reader pretend the worst chapter of David's life, the sin laid bare in 2 Samuel 11 and wept over in Psalm 51, did not happen. *Mercy in the Bathsheba Line* is built entirely on that refusal. **Yahuah** did not erase her name; He named her in.
Do you feel the argument forming? The genealogy is doing gospel work. It is saying, in the driest possible form, a list, that grace is not a mood. It is a fact you can trace by name.
The night the whole album turned on one king
The cinematic peak of the record is track eight, *The Manger Was The Mountain*, and it hangs on a name most people couldn't place: Manasseh.

Read 2 Kings 21 and Manasseh is arguably the worst king Judah ever had. He filled Jerusalem with innocent blood and burned his own sons in the fire. By any human accounting, that name gets struck from the royal line. And yet there he is, right in Matthew's list (Matthew 1:10). Why? Because 2 Chronicles 33 tells the rest of it: in captivity, Manasseh humbled himself, bent the knee, and **Yahuah** heard him and restored him (2 Chronicles 33:12-13).

That is the whole song. The manger, the lowest, smallest place, was the mountain the Messiah climbed to reach us, and He climbed it over the name of a man everyone had written off. And in the second verse I let an ordinary person stumble onto the same truth: if Manasseh made it into the line, then so can the one whose hiding isn't done. The genealogy becomes an altar call. Grace as a genealogical fact.
The line that lands on you
The record does not end at Bethlehem. That would leave you a spectator.

*Mary's Quiet Yes* and *Joseph the Carpenter* carry the line into the first century, a young woman's "let it be to me" (Luke 1:38) and a working man who obeyed a dream, took Mary in, and gave the boy His name, **Yeshua**, which means "Yahuah saves" (Matthew 1:21). And then the finale, *The Line Lands Here*, does the thing I most wanted an album about a genealogy to do. It reaches Galatians 3:29, "if you are Christ's, then you are Abraham's offspring, heirs according to promise." The line does not stop at the manger. It runs on, and it lands on us. Every nation grafted into the same chain of names.
That's why the last chorus is not about ancient Israel at all. It's about the person listening. The line lands here.
Who I made this for
I made *The Line That Leads To Yeshua* for two people.

The first is the one who has quietly decided that parts of the Bible are just filler, the lists, the "begats," the chapters that feel like scaffolding. I want you to hear that the scaffolding is where the tenderness hides. **Yahuah** kept those names because He keeps names. He is the God who tracks every generation through exile and famine and scandal and never loses one.

The second is the one who is sure their own name has been struck off some list. That the file is too thick, the hiding too long, the failure too public to belong in anything called a family tree of God. Tamar is in the line. Ruth is in the line. The wife of Uriah is in the line. Manasseh, Manasseh, is in the line. If those names made the countdown to the manger, hear me: there is room in the story of **Yeshua** for yours.
So next Sunday, when the reader hits the "begats" and the room goes quiet, lean in. Somebody's whole redemption is hiding in a verse you were about to skip. It might be yours.

pieces.excerpt: Hesed is the Hebrew word for a love that never learned how to quit, covenant-love, steadfast mercy. I built a whole dancing record on it, and then I put one quiet song in the middle for the night the music stops in your house. Because that is the night you find out what the floor is really made of.

body.text: There is a word I have spent years trying to get people to feel in their feet, not just understand in their heads.

The word is **hesed**. Your English Bible translates it a dozen ways, steadfast love, lovingkindness, mercy, faithfulness, because no single English word can carry it. Hesed is covenant-love. It's the love that has signed something. It is loyalty that has made a promise and cannot, will not, walk it back. Hesed is the love that never learned how to quit.

And when I finally understood that hesed doesn't quit, I couldn't sit still. So *Hesed That Never Stops* is a dance record, oud, darbuka, a hora pulse, hands clapping. But right in the middle of all that celebration I hid the quietest song on the album, because I wanted you to know the floor holds even after the band goes home.
Why a doctrine had to become a dance

The opening track states the thesis with your body before your mind can argue. *Hesed That Never Stops* calls hesed a floor, the covenant floor you dance on, the ground that does not fall below. That image is the spine of the whole album.

Because most people treat God's love like weather. Sunny today, storms tomorrow, better keep an umbrella of good behavior handy. But hesed is not weather. Hesed is the floor. It was already there before your morning and before your failing, and it will still be there after. The chorus says it the way I'd want it shouted in a full room: His love does not let go, the covenant floor doesn't fall below.

And I can say that with a straight face because of *why* it's true, which the second track spells out. Deuteronomy calls **Yahuah** "the faithful God who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who love him... to a thousand generations" (Deuteronomy 7:9). A thousand generations. That's the song *Faithful, Faithful, Faithful*, and the whole point is that His faithfulness is not a mood He's in. It is who He is. He cannot stop, because to stop would be to stop being Himself.
The most personal line on the record

Track three is where the doctrine gets its knees dirty. It's called *Your Hesed Never Stopped on Me*, and the hinge of it is a small grammatical flip that I think is the most honest sentence on the album:
I stopped on You, but You did not stop on me.
