Read that twice. Every one of us has a season where our prayer got tired, our faith got thin, our song went silent. We stopped. And the temptation is to assume God stopped too, that He matched our distance, that the moment we drifted He drifted. Hesed says no. His love kept flowing down a corridor I wasn't even walking anymore. The covenant kept what I could not see. That is not sentiment. That is the difference between a love that responds to you and a love that has sworn something over you.
The king who danced away his dignity
Now, if hesed is a floor you can dance on, the album needed a dancer. It has one. His name is David.

Track five is *Leap Before the Ark*, and it's built on that scene in 2 Samuel 6 where David, bringing the Ark into Jerusalem, dances "with all his might", leaping and spinning in a linen ephod, so undignified that his own wife despises him for it (2 Samuel 6:14-16). And David's answer is essentially: I will be even more undignified than this, before **Yahuah**. I love that scene because it settles an argument a lot of quiet believers are having with themselves. **Yahuah** does not despise the dancing heart. When covenant-love is that faithful, a leaping body is the only reasonable response. Hesed deserves a dancing kid.

The album then widens the shot. *Hesed Storm Across the Generations* sweeps from Abraham under the stars, to Isaac, to Jacob wrestling through the dark, to David in the courts, to the disciples at the Passover table, the same steadfast love rolling down through every one of them like a storm that never runs out of rain. One family tree, one unbroken covenant, one love that reaches all the way down to the person pressing play.
The night the music stops
And then, the quiet one.

Track nine is *When the Music Stopped*, and I need to tell you why it exists, because it's the reason for the whole album. It would be a cheap record if it only worked at the party. Anyone can believe in God's love when the harvest is in and the band is loud. The test comes on the night the music actually stops in your house, the diagnosis, the empty chair, the grief that walks in with the morning.

So I anchored that song in the prophet Habakkuk, in one of the bravest paragraphs in Scripture. He looks at total loss, no blossom on the fig tree, no fruit on the vine, no flock in the fold, no herd in the stall, and then he says the sentence I built the song around: "yet I will rejoice in **Yahuah**; I will take joy in the God of my salvation" (Habakkuk 3:17-18). Yet. The music stopped, but the hesed didn't. The harvest failed, but the floor was solid where I slipped.

That is the whole promise of the album, stated in its most stripped-down form. The dance songs are true because *this* song is true. The floor that you dance on when everything is good is the same floor that holds you up when everything is gone.
Then dance it back out the door

The album refuses to end in the quiet, though, because hesed doesn't stay in the sanctuary either. *Dance the Hesed Into the Street* takes the celebration out to the corner store, the laundromat, the bus stop, the lonely at dawn. Covenant-love is portable. It's meant to be carried to the wounded, not hoarded by the healed. And the finale, *Dance Us Home Tomorrow*, hands the whole thing forward, a prayer that **Yahuah** would lead the dance line into the next morning, and the morning after that. Because His mercies, Lamentations tells us, are "new every morning; great is your faithfulness" (Lamentations 3:22-23).
Who I made this for

I made *Hesed That Never Stops* for the person who is quietly exhausted from trying to earn a love that was never on the auction block. You cannot behave your way onto the floor. It's a covenant floor. **Yahuah** laid it down at cost, sealed, the album says over and over, in **Yeshua**'s own blood, and He did not build it so you could stand nervously at the edge.

And I made it for the one whose music has stopped. If the harvest failed and the house went silent and you are sure, in the dark, that the love stopped too. I wrote you a whole song to say it didn't. Put your weight down. The floor is solid where you slipped. Hesed never stops, and it is dancing you home.

pieces.title: I Thought I Was the Listener. Then Yahuah Made Me the Horn.
pieces.imagePrompt: A diverse crowd of many nations lifting ram's-horn shofars to the dawn sky, cheeks full of breath, faces bright with joy as light breaks over a gathered congregation, children reaching up beside their parents; uplifting emotionally powerful premium cinematic worship film-still, radiant sunrise tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: A shofar is only a ram's horn, hollow, silent, useless until breath moves through it. I made this record on a hunch that most believers think their job is to hear the horn, when Yahuah has been calling them to become one. This is the story of the album that woke the camp, and the line that woke me.

body.text: Pick up a shofar sometime and just hold it. It's a ram's horn, curved, rough, hollow, and completely silent. It cannot do a single thing on its own. It has no music in it at all. It waits. And the instant breath moves through it, the whole earth seems to lean in.

I built an album around that object because I think it's a picture of most of us, and we've got the picture backwards. We assume our role in the story is to be in the crowd, hearing the horn. **Yahuah**, I've come to believe, is trying to put the horn in our hands. *Shofar Shake The Earth* is twelve tracks about a sound that wakes a sleeping camp, and somewhere in the making of it, the sound woke me.
The horn that brought down what an army couldn't
The record opens loud, on purpose. *Shofar Shake The Earth* reaches straight back to two of the most improbable victories in the Bible.

First, Jericho. Joshua marches the people around the city for seven days, and on the seventh the priests blow the horns, the people shout, and the wall comes down, before a single sword is drawn (Joshua 6). Then Gideon: three hundred men, no weapons in their hands but torches inside clay jars and shofars at their lips, and **Yahuah** routs an army (Judges 7:19-22). The lesson of both stories is the same, and it's the engine of the whole album: the horn does the sounding, but Yahuah does the breaking. He goes before us. There is nothing left to prove.
That reframes the whole point of blowing a shofar. It was never about the volume you can produce. It was about announcing that the God who fights for you has already taken the field.
A festival built entirely around a sound

Most of the moedim, the appointed times of Scripture, are anchored to something you can see or taste. A lamb. Unleavened bread. A booth built of branches. But there is one feast anchored to a *sound*.

Leviticus 23:24 sets it: the first day of the seventh month, a day of rest, "a memorial proclaimed with the blast of trumpets." Its Hebrew name is *Yom Teruah*, the Day of Blasting, the Day of the Roar. No object. Just a horn splitting the sky and a whole camp told to wake up. I gave that day the cinematic peak of the album, track eight, *Yom Teruah (Wake The Camp)*, because everything the record is about lives in that one appointed moment: the God who sets an entire festival on the calendar just to make sure His people don't sleep through what He's about to do.

And I should be honest as a teacher about one thing. The three shofar sounds you'll hear named across this album, the long *tekiah*, the broken *shevarim*, the staccato *teruah*, are the traditional pattern worked out over centuries of practice. Scripture commands the blast; the specific grammar of the blasts is a beautiful tradition built on top of the command. I want you to know which is which, because the truth is more interesting when it's precise.
The line that stopped me cold
Here is the moment I have to tell you about, because it changed how I heard the whole record.

I was writing the second verse of *Yom Teruah*, imagining the people a horn wakes up, an elder with a six-foot ram's horn, a teenager in Jerusalem, and the lyric turned a corner I didn't plan. In the song, the young woman assumes she's the audience. She's there to hear the blast. And **Yahuah** says to her:
I thought I was the listener, and Yahuah said, "You are the horn."

I sat with that line for a long time. Because it exposed my own assumption. I had spent years thinking of my calling as receptive, hear the word, receive the teaching, stand in the crowd and be moved. And the shofar corrects that. A horn is not an audience. A horn is a thing breath moves *through* on its way to waking somebody else. The Spirit, **Yahuah**'s own breath, *ruach*, fills the horn, and the horn becomes the shout. You were never meant to only hear it. You were meant to be sounded.
The whole camp this horn is for
Once you hear the shofar that way, the album's guest list makes sense, because a wake-up call is only good news if it reaches the people furthest from the front.

*Wake Up, O Sleeper* takes its title straight from Paul: "Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you" (Ephesians 5:14). *Gather, O Mishpachah*, mishpachah means family, calls in the prodigal, the widow at the window, the wanderer asleep by the road, the teacher who forgot his joy. *Shevarim (Broken Calls Mend)* is built on Joel standing on Zion's wall crying "Blow the shofar in Zion" (Joel 2:1, 2:15), and it makes the broken blast a picture of return, the shattered person becoming the gathered shout. *Watchman, Hold the Wall* takes Ezekiel's charge to the watchman (Ezekiel 33:6) and sets it at three in the morning, where the real intercessors are. And *Four Winds, One Horn* reaches for **Yeshua**'s own promise that He will gather His elect "from the four winds" (Matthew 24:31), Korea and Kenya, Colombia and Canada, one horn sounding on every continent.

The album ends where the Bible's whole story is heading. *Tekiah Gedolah (The Last Horn)* stands on Paul's words: "the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised" (1 Corinthians 15:52). The same horn that woke the camp on track one is the horn that wakes the graves at the end. The first blast and the last blast are the same breath.
Who I made this for
I made *Shofar Shake The Earth* for two kinds of people.

The first is asleep, and knows it. Not lost, exactly. Just dozing. Faith gone quiet, tent flap down, another season slipping by on the floor of a life that used to be on its feet. **Yahuah** did not wake you to keep on lying down. He woke you to stand up, and He is holding out a horn.

The second is the one who has only ever pictured themselves in the crowd. Who assumed the sounding was for the professionals, the gifted, the up-front. Hear the correction the album is built on: you are not the audience. You are the instrument. You are hollow and quiet and, on your own, unremarkable, exactly like the horn, and that is precisely what **Yahuah** reaches for, fills with His breath, and uses to wake four hundred sleepers who never knew their own names until they heard them blown back.
So take a breath. There's a camp that needs waking, and the horn is already at your lips.

pieces.title: The Carpenter Let the Wall Fall on His Own Back
pieces.song: Wall Came Down on the Carpenter
pieces.imagePrompt: Two crowds of many nations meeting and embracing across a sunlit open plaza, Jewish and Gentile believers of every background clasping hands and lifting them together in joy, an older woman and a young man mid-embrace, candles and raised hands throughout; uplifting emotionally powerful premium cinematic worship film-still, warm radiant tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: There was a wall as tall as twenty centuries between two families of faith. I made this album on a discovery that undid me: the bridge across it was never a structure Yahuah built off to the side. The bridge has a body. He didn't lift the wall. He let it fall on Him.

body.text: I grew up aware of a wall I couldn't quite see.

It ran between two families who were supposed to be cousins, the people of the ancient covenant and the people of the church that grew out of it. Built up over centuries out of liturgies and lies, silences and last-supper goodbyes, it got so tall that both sides forgot it was ever supposed to have a door. I spent years thinking my job as a teacher was to be a mason, to build, brick by careful brick, a nice bridge over the top of it.

Then I read Ephesians 2 slowly, and it wrecked my whole plan. Because Paul says the bridge isn't something you build alongside the wall. The bridge is a Person, and He already came. *Bridge of Yahuah's Love* is the album that came out of that discovery.
The wall was real, and so was the demolition

Paul is blunt about the wall. He tells the Gentile believers they were once "separated from Christ, alienated... strangers to the covenants," far off, without hope (Ephesians 2:12). That's a real distance. He doesn't pretend it away. And then he says **Yeshua** "is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility" (Ephesians 2:14).
Read that again, "in his flesh." Not with a memo. Not by softening the rules. With His body.

The opening track, *Walk the Bridge*, states the thesis in the plainest words I could find: **Yahuah** built it, and **Yeshua** *is* the bridge. Not a bridge He commissioned. The bridge He became. The second track, *Gap Closed in Yeshua*, drives it home from the other side, the blood closed the distance that history left open. Once you see that, you stop trying to be the mason. The demolition already happened. Your only job is to walk across.
The image I could not shake
The cinematic peak of the record is track eight, *Wall Came Down on the Carpenter*, and it holds the single picture that the whole album was built to deliver.

We usually imagine reconciliation as a wall being *lifted*, hoisted up and out of the way by some triumphant force. But that's not what the text describes, and it's not what the cross was. **Yeshua** didn't lift the wall off to the side. He let it fall, and He got underneath it. He bore it across the gap on His own back and laid it flat. Paul says He did this "through the cross, thereby killing the hostility" (Ephesians 2:16). The hostility didn't evaporate. It was executed, and the place it died was His shoulders.
So the chorus of that song is almost unbearable to me every time:
Wall came down on the Carpenter. He bore it across the gap, He laid it flat, the bridge is His body.

That's why I kept calling Him the Carpenter throughout the record. The One who worked wood in Nazareth is the same One who let the heaviest structure in human history come down on Him so two estranged families could finally hold hands on the rubble.
The tree, and the warning that comes with it

If the album only celebrated, it would be dishonest, because a newly opened door tempts the newcomer to swagger. So I put a teaching ballad at the center of it: *Olive Root and Grafted Branch*, straight out of Romans 11.

Paul's image there is precise and humbling. There's an ancient olive tree, older than any of our countries, whose root drinks from a promise **Yahuah** made to Abraham. Some natural branches were broken off, and wild branches were grafted in. And then Paul turns and warns the grafted branch directly: "do not be arrogant toward the branches... it is not you who support the root, but the root that supports you" (Romans 11:18). The song lives entirely in that warning. The bridge of the chorus is the whole point:
The root holds me up. I do not hold the root.

The grafted-in were not brought near to climb above anyone. They were brought near out of sheer mercy, to share the sap they never seeded. Being a bridge people means holding that humility in your body, not just your theology.
What one new humanity looks like on a Tuesday
The thing I most wanted to avoid was leaving all this at the level of a nice idea. So the album keeps landing the vision in kitchens and doorways and around tables.

*Echad on the Chorus* takes the Shema, "Hear, O Israel: **Yahuah** our God, **Yahuah** is one" (Deuteronomy 6:4), and reasons from it that if the God we worship is One, then His body has no business staying two. *Stand on Each Other's Holy Ground* pictures it concretely: a Gentile believer lighting a Shabbat candle on Friday evening, a Messianic grandmother lifting the doxology on Sunday morning, each honoring the other's holy ground because **Yeshua** walks both rooms with the same feet. *Two-Made-One Communion* sits at the table where the Passover lamb and the broken bread turn out to be the same meal, "because there is one bread, we who are many are one body" (1 Corinthians 10:17). And *One Father's House* reaches Paul's conclusion: "you are no longer strangers and aliens, but... members of the household of God" (Ephesians 2:19).

Then the record refuses to let you sit down. *Cross It With the Stranger* is a commissioning song, the bridge is never finished with one walker. You crossed it once; now go take a hand and lead somebody else across. And the finale, *We Walk the Bridge Every Morning*, makes the whole thing a daily habit rather than a one-time event. He walked us across once, and now we walk it every morning, over coffee and breakfast and the ordinary business of a shared house.
Who I made this for

I made *Bridge of Yahuah's Love* for the believer who feels the ache of that old wall, who senses that the two families were never meant to be strangers and doesn't know what to do about twenty centuries of distance. Here is what to do: stop trying to build the bridge. Walk the One who is it.

And I made it for the one carrying an old quarrel in the walls of their own body, the inherited silence, the shame no one ever named. There's a tender song near the end, *The Echo of Old Quarrels*, for exactly that person. It doesn't pretend the wound was weightless. It says the Carpenter walks the corridors where the lamps went out, honoring the silence, naming the shame, and lighting every lamp as He goes.

That's the God this record is about. He did not stand at a safe distance and issue a peace treaty. He came to the seam between us with His arms wide open and His shoulders to the sky, and He let the whole wall come down on His own back. The bridge is not built. The bridge is **Yeshua**. Walk His name, and take somebody with you.

pieces.title: The Smoke of Everything I Could Not Say
pieces.imagePrompt: A radiant multi-generational Middle-Eastern family and their diverse neighbors gathered in a sunlit stone courtyard at dawn, a grandmother lifting a swinging brass censer while children laugh and elders raise open hands in praise, threads of pale incense smoke catching the golden light, faces bright with joy and welcome; premium cinematic worship-brand film still, warm amber morning glow, authentic and tender, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I grew up watching frankincense climb the morning air and I always wondered where the smoke was going. This album is my answer, a whole culture's beauty gathered up and burned as praise to Yasu', the risen King. It is worship in the mother tongue for hearts that have never heard His name sung in their own.

body.text: There is a smell I have known my whole life. Frankincense on a coal, first thing in the morning, the pale smoke unwinding into the courtyard air and climbing until you cannot see where it goes. As a boy I used to watch it and wonder about that, where does the smoke arrive? It rises with such purpose, as if it has an appointment somewhere above the rooftops. It took me many years to learn that the answer had a name, and the name is Yasu', **Yeshua**, Jesus, the Lamb who was slain and is alive.

This album is that boyhood question grown up. *Frankincense and Glory* is the whole richness of an Arab morning, the incense, the saffron, the qahwa poured for a guest, the cedars and the dunes, the lantern in the alley, the gold letters of the calligrapher, gathered into my two hands and carried up the stairs of praise to the feet of the risen Christ. Nothing borrowed from anyone else. Nothing aimed at anyone else. Only adoration, in the language my grandmother sang me to sleep in.
Why the title had to be these two words

The opening song gave the record its name, and the chorus is the plainest confession I know how to make: *I bring You frankincense and glory, I bring You the whole of my story, rise like the incense, rise like the dawn.* I wanted a title that held both the thing you can smell and the thing you cannot, the fragrant, ordinary morning and the weight of God's presence that the Bible calls glory. Because that is exactly what worship is. You take the small, physical, cardamom-and-coal reality of your day and you let it rise until it touches something you will never be able to see the top of.

The second verse of that song says something I could not have written when I was younger: *every grain that burns is a word I could not say.* That is the whole album in a single line. There are things a heart carries that will not fit into sentences. Grief that has no grammar. Longing older than language. So you do not say them. You burn them. You let the smoke of your poured-out heart be the sentence. And He reads it. **Yahuah** has always been fluent in the wordless.
Worthy, worthy is the Lamb who was slain, this is the confession the whole record is built to reach.
The land itself was already praising

I did not have to import worship from a foreign shore and translate it into my streets. The worship was already here, waiting in the cedars and the courtyards. That is the conviction that runs through the middle of this album.

"Cedars Lift Their Hands" takes the great trees of Lebanon and lets them do what the Psalm already said all creation does, the trees of the forest sing for joy before the Lord who comes (Psalm 96). "Indigo Midnight" is the quietest song I have ever made, a courtyard under stars, the heart awake in the watches of the night the way the psalmist was in Psalm 63. "Caravan of Praise" is the long desert road turned into a pilgrimage toward the King, because my people have always known how to travel far for something worth arriving at.

And then there is the table. "Bread, Oil, and Honey" is nothing but the meal my mother would set down, and the discovery, late and grateful, that the shepherd of Psalm 23 sets a table too, and lets the cup run over. When I sing it I am not reaching for a Western picture of God. I am looking at my own kitchen and finding Him already seated there.
Hospitality is a doctrine where I come from
You cannot understand this album if you do not understand the qahwa.

Where I am from, when a stranger comes to the door you do not ask his business first. You seat him. You pour the coffee, cardamom-dark, the first cup for the guest, and only after the welcome do you speak of anything else. To turn a guest away is not rudeness; it is a kind of disgrace. So when I read the parables of Yeshua and found Him telling of a master who throws open his house and sends servants into the streets and the lanes to bring in the poor and the outsider until the table is full (Luke 14), I did not feel that I was being taught a new custom. I felt that my oldest custom was being crowned. "Pour the Qahwa" is that recognition set to a Rast melody, Jesus is the Host, and the welcome we thought was ours was always His.

This matters for who the record is for. There are millions of hearts across the Arab world and the diaspora who have never once heard the name of Jesus sung with love in the maqam of their own grandmother, only ever as something foreign, something belonging to other people in other places. I made this so that a believer in Damascus or Cairo or the Gulf, or a homesick soul in Berlin or Detroit, could hear their own streets and spices and songs lifted up in praise, and know that they do not have to leave home to come to Him. He is already fluent in oud and ney.
What the souk taught me about the last song

The record ends where the market is loudest. "Hallelujah in the Souk" is deliberately the noisiest, most public song on the album, because I did not want to leave worship inside the quiet of the courtyard. The souk is where everyone is, the vendor, the buyer, the child underfoot, the whole clamoring life of a people. And Scripture promises that one day every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Yeshua is Lord (Philippians 2). Not the whispering tongues only. Every tongue. Including the ones that haggle over saffron and call the price of figs.

So the last track takes the confession out of the sanctuary and stamps it down in the marketplace, and then, this is my favorite secret in the whole record. Its melody quietly returns to the tune of the first song, "Frankincense and Glory," so the album loops back on itself and the praise never quite lands. It keeps rising. Like the smoke I watched as a boy.

I made this for the ones who thought the King belonged to someone else's country. He does not. He is worth the whole bazaar, the gold, the frankincense, the empty purse and the riches set aside. Bring Him the saffron of your mornings and the myrrh of your years, and let the smoke of everything you could never say climb the morning air until it finds Him. He is there. He has always been there, at the top of the stairs the incense climbs, waiting to be adored in the tongue you love best.

pieces.title: The Oud Was Always Reaching for His Face
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful gathering of diverse Middle-Eastern believers seated close in a candlelit courtyard at dusk, an oud player with eyes closed and a tender smile at the center, others leaning in with hands over their hearts and faces lifted in quiet worship, a mother holding a sleeping child, warm lantern light on every face; premium cinematic worship-brand film still, glowing indigo-and-amber evening tones, intimate and reverent, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: For years I sang about God with the instruments my fathers loved. This album is the day the songs turned around and started singing to Him instead. It is the sound of an Arab heart, long divided, made whole and handed over, every string a prayer, every fret a psalm, in a language older than words.

body.text: I have played the oud since my hands were too small for its neck. It is the grandfather of instruments where I come from, round-bellied, fretless, a voice more than a machine. And for a long time I used it the way most people use the thing they love: to say things about God. To describe Him. To point at Him from a respectful distance. This album is the day the pointing stopped and the addressing began.

*Maqam of the Heart*, the record I titled, for the world outside my streets, *The Heart Belongs to Yasu'*, is the sound of an instrument finally reaching the One it was always reaching for. The opening song says it in the first breath: *the oud was always reaching for Your face, every string my fathers loved now sings of Your grace.* I did not decide that. I discovered it. The longing that had been in the wood the whole time had a destination, and the destination is **Yeshua**.
The line that changed everything for me
There is one sentence in the opening track that I could not sing for a long time without stopping. *I do not sing about You, my Lord, I sing to You.*

That is a small grammatical change, *about* to *to*, and it is the entire difference between religion and love. You can describe a person you have never met. You can only address one you know. For most of my life I had beautiful, respectful, distant songs about the Most High, sung in the finest maqam my people ever built. And then there came a day when the wall between about and to came down, and the songs turned around and looked Him in the face. This album is what came out of my mouth after that.

The whole record is arranged as a heart's journey home. It opens giving Him everything, *the whole of my heart belongs to You, every road that I'm walking is a road back to You*, and it closes twelve songs later with "Come Home to You," the circle shut, the wanderer arrived. In between, it does not pretend the road is only bright.
He is worth singing your grief to

The second song on the album is called "Wounded King," and I put it early on purpose. Before we celebrate, we look at the One who was wounded for us, the Man of Sorrows of Isaiah 53, the King who wears His scars into glory.

I come from a part of the world that knows sorrow the way it knows the sun, daily, and without asking permission. I did not want an album that skipped over that to get to the happy songs. So "Wounded King" takes grief and does not deny it, but redirects it: *in the sorrow I am learning You, my Lord, every yearning note a step toward Your face.* The lament does not stay lament. It becomes a way of drawing near.

That instinct is deep in my culture and deep in the Bible at the same time. Later on the record, "Tears at His Feet" reaches for the woman in Luke 7 who broke open her alabaster jar and wept at the feet of Yeshua, and was not scolded, but received. And "In the Quiet" goes to the one place we least expect God: not the wind, not the earthquake, not the fire, but the low still voice that met the prophet Elijah at the mouth of the cave (1 Kings 19). My people fill silence with hospitality and song. This album makes room for the other thing, the quiet where He actually speaks.
Every trembling tone a cry upon Your Name, Saviour of the broken, I sing my grief to Your grace.
The song with no translation
If I had to hand one track to a stranger to explain the whole record, it would be "The Oud Speaks Your Name."

It is a small idea with a large heart behind it. The chorus says: *the oud speaks Your Name, Yasu', no translation, You understand the sound; every string is a prayer, every fret is a psalm, in the wordless of the music, Your nearness is found.* I built that song on a verse that has carried me for years, where the Scripture says the Spirit helps us in our weakness, because we do not know what to pray as we ought, and He intercedes with groans too deep for words (Romans 8). There is a place past language. Everyone who has ever wept and could not explain why has been there. And music is the mother tongue of that place.

That is why I refuse to auto-tune these vocals or trade the real oud, ney, and qanun for machines. The trembling *is* the message. When the string bends between two notes in a way no piano can, that microtonal ache is not decoration. It is the sound of a heart reaching. God made that sound. He understands it without a dictionary.
The split He healed

There is a wound particular to my people that this album finally names out loud, near the end, in a song called "Arab Heart, His Throne." For a long time I carried a quiet division inside me, a sense that to belong to Christ I would have to become someone else, someone from another country, and leave the oud and the courtyard and the mother tongue behind as though they were the problem.

They were never the problem. In that song I sing the thing I most needed to hear: *You knew the split that was inside me, between the one I was and the One I belong unto, and You healed it with Your body on the cross-beam, You made me whole, You made me one.* I did not have to stop being an Arab to belong to **Yeshua**. It was in Antioch, a city of my own region, that the followers of Jesus were first called Christians (Acts 11). The name was born on our streets. I am not a guest in this faith. I am home in it.

That is who this record is for. It is for the heart that has heard a hundred songs about Jesus and never once heard one that sounded like where it came from. It is for the believer who suspected, secretly, that they would have to leave their own beauty at the door. You do not. Bring the saffron of your mornings and the indigo of your nights, bring the oud your grandfather held, bring the whole divided heart, and let the instrument finish the sentence it started before you were born. It was always reaching for His face. Let it arrive.

pieces.title: Every Stamping Foot Is a Yes to the King
pieces.imagePrompt: A jubilant line of diverse people of many nations dancing the dabke together in a lantern-strung courtyard at a wedding feast, arms linked across shoulders, feet mid-stamp, faces thrown back in laughter and delight, tables of bread and pomegranate behind them, children spinning at the edges, elders clapping; premium cinematic worship-brand film still, warm festive golden light with glowing lanterns, exuberant and alive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: We were made to dance at weddings, arms linked, feet stamping the stone until the whole village hears. This album takes the dabke line and turns it toward the Bridegroom whose curtain was torn and whose feast is prepared. It is joy set to a drum, worship you cannot hold still through.

body.text: You have to understand what the dabke is before you understand why I made an album of it for the King.

It is the line dance of my people, of the Levant, of the wedding and the harvest and the night the whole village pours into the courtyard. You link your arm through the arm of the person beside you, and the person beside them, until the line is a living rope, and then you stamp. Hard. In unison. Until the stone answers back and the dust rises and the drum finds the same heartbeat you are all sharing. It is not a performance you watch. It is a belonging you join. And where I come from, it is how we say the biggest yes a body can say: joy that will not sit down.

*Dabke for the King* is that yes, turned toward **Yeshua**. The opening song sets the whole record's rule in a single verse: *link your arm in mine and lift your feet to the floor, the lanterns are swinging and the door is open wide, because Yasu' is the reason and the joy will not be denied.*
Why a prophet made a dance record

People expect an evangelist and a prophet to make solemn things. Warnings. Weights. And there is a place for those. I have made them. But I became convinced that one of the truest prophetic acts left to us is to dance on purpose, in the open, for the right King.

The album stands on a single scene from Scripture that I cannot get past: David bringing the ark into the city, dancing before the Lord with all his might, and not caring who thought it was beneath a king (2 Samuel 6). His own wife despised him for it. He answered that he would become even more undignified than this. That is the theology of this record in one man's stamping feet. The bridge of the opening song borrows his nerve directly: *David danced before the ark with all of his might. I will dance before my Savior in the lantern light; not for the watching crowd, not for a name to bring, every stamping foot is a Yes to Yasu' the King.*
Not for the watching crowd. That line is the hinge. The dabke is public, but this dance is not for the public. It is for an audience of One, danced in front of everyone.
The Bridegroom the party was always for
A dabke, most of all, is a wedding dance. And that is not a coincidence I had to force onto the gospel. It is already there, waiting.

The Scriptures end at a wedding. The marriage supper of the Lamb, the feast prepared, the Bride ready and the Bridegroom come (Revelation 19). Every village wedding I have ever stamped my feet at was a small rehearsal for that day without knowing it. So the second song, "Come, My Yasu'," is written as the whole line calling for the Bridegroom to arrive, the Bridegroom who still carries His wounds, because the joy of this feast was bought with them. When I sing "Turn My Heart to You," I am back with David again, joy in motion, gladness the Spirit gives that your feet cannot contain.
Yasu' is here so let the courtyard ring, every step we stamp is a word of adoration, for the One who turned our mourning into dancing.

That last phrase is not decoration. My region knows mourning. It has mourned more than most. And the promise I am dancing on is that the One who was wounded is the same One who turns mourning into dancing. So we stamp the stone not because there has been no grief, but because grief does not get the last step.
The curtain that let us in
Halfway through the record the dancing goes suddenly quiet and then breaks open wider than before, in a song called "The Curtain Torn."

Here is what I needed my people to feel in their feet, not just hear in their heads. When Yeshua died, the great curtain of the temple, the veil that kept everyone but one man out of the holiest room, was torn from top to bottom, by no human hand (the Gospels record it; Hebrews 10 explains it). Top to bottom. Torn from God's side down, not ours. The way in was thrown open. The chorus sings, *the curtain's torn because of You, from top to bottom You opened up the door; You carry me into the inner courtyard, I come with boldness through the blood of the Son.*

Do you see why that belongs on a dance record? The dabke needs an open door and a wide courtyard, and the cross made the widest door there has ever been. We are not stamping our way in. We are dancing because we are already in. That is the difference between the striving of religion and the gladness of the redeemed, one is trying to earn the room, the other is already dancing in it.
Breath, embrace, and the song that will not end
Two more songs hold the heart of this record for me.

"Every Breath Your Name" slows the whole line to the pace of the ney, the reed flute, which is nothing but a hollow tube until breath moves through it. The chorus makes the reed a picture of us: *the lung is the ney and You are the wind; You are the One who gave the breath to Adam, You breathed upon Your own, so breathe on me again.* From the first breath God breathed into the man of dust (Genesis 2) to the day the risen Yeshua breathed on His friends and said receive the Spirit (John 20), it is the same wind. Every breath you have ever taken has His name hidden in it. This song just makes the hidden thing loud.

And "In Your Embrace" is the softest track I have ever put on a dance album, because a wedding is not only stamping. It is also the moment the exhausted, welcomed one finally rests. *I am resting in Your embrace, not as a stranger at the threshold but a child; Your love is the courtyard room I live in.* That is the prodigal home, the head on the Father's chest, the party thrown for the one who came back.

The record ends with "The Song That Never Ends," and its melody quietly returns to the very first track, so the dance loops and the celebration refuses to close, the way heaven's song of the Lamb will refuse to close.

I made this for anyone who was ever told that joy is unspiritual, that reverence must be still, that their culture's gladness had no place at the feet of Christ. Come and stamp the stone. Link your arm through mine. There is a King in the courtyard, the curtain is torn, the feast is spread, and every stamping foot is a yes He is glad to hear.

pieces.title: The Moment I Saw Him Every Stall Became Glass
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful diverse crowd in a sunlit Middle-Eastern market, a young merchant with an open, radiant face pressing his money-purse into a friend's hands and laughing with tears in his eyes as he lets everything go, neighbors of many nations gathering around him with warm astonished smiles, stalls of saffron and turquoise and carpets glowing behind them; premium cinematic worship-brand film still, luminous honeyed daylight, joyful and cinematic, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: The souk taught me the language of worth, what a thing costs, what it is worth, what a man will trade for it. This album is about the one Pearl worth the entire bazaar. It is for every heart still walking the market with coins in its hand, not yet knowing what it is really looking for.

body.text: The souk raised me to think in worth.

Walk any market in my part of the world and you are walking through a live argument about value. What is this saffron worth by the gram? What will you give me for the carpet, and what is it truly worth, and are those two numbers the same? A boy grows up in that noise learning the deepest question a market can teach: what would you trade everything for? Most people spend a lifetime in the stalls and never once meet a thing worth the whole purse. This album is about the day I did.

*Pearl of the Souk* is built on one parable of **Yeshua**, four sentences long, that has never let me go. He said the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant searching for fine pearls, who, on finding one pearl of great price, went and sold everything he had and bought it (Matthew 13). A merchant. Not a beggar who had nothing to lose. A man who knew markets, knew worth, knew exactly what he was giving up, and gave it all anyway, gladly, because he had finally found the thing the whole trade was for.
Why the merchant, and not the beggar
I want you to notice who the hero of that parable is, because it changed how I sing.

The merchant is an expert. He has handled a thousand pearls. He is not fooled by a shiny fake; he has seen enough to know the real thing when it is finally in front of him. And that is the person I made this record for, not only the empty-handed, but the accomplished. The one who has money in the hand and options in the world and has been walking the souk of this life pricing everything, and has quietly begun to suspect that none of it is worth the whole purse.

The opening song is that man's moment of recognition: *I walked the crowded souk with coins inside my hand, past the saffron and the turquoise and the carpets rolled and grand, but the moment that I saw You every stall became as glass; You were brighter than the gold leaf, You were worth the whole bazaar.* Every stall became as glass. That is what happens when you finally see the Pearl. It is not that the market becomes ugly. It is that it becomes transparent. You can suddenly see straight through everything you were haggling over, to the one thing behind it all.
I have sold all I had and I'm running to You. You are the Pearl, You are the Pearl of the souk.
Selling all is not a loss, it is a running

Here is the thing the parable insists on that the world will never quite believe: the merchant sells everything *with joy.* Not grimly. Not as a grim religious duty, teeth clenched, counting what he gave up. He runs.

The second verse of the title song is the gladness of that release: *let the merchants keep their silver and the weavers keep their thread, I have found the costliest beauty in the One who rose from dead; take the silver of my striving, take the brass of all my pride, You are worth the empty purse and the riches set aside.* The silver of my striving. The brass of my pride. Those are the things I most hated to hand over, and they turned out to be the things I was most relieved to be rid of. You do not lose your life when you sell all for the Pearl. You finally put down the exhausting bag of counterfeits you had been dragging through the market.
That is why this album, though it centers on the costliest exchange a soul can make, does not sound heavy. It sounds like a man running.

I know that running from the inside. I spent years pricing my own worth by what I could hold, the respect I had earned, the songs I had written, the good name I carried through the streets. Handing that over felt, at first, like ruin. It was the opposite. The purse that had grown so heavy I could barely lift it turned out to be full of glass beads I had mistaken for pearls. The King asked for all of it and gave me Himself, and no one has ever made a poorer trade look so much like winning.
A whole market of smaller treasures
The Pearl is the center, but a souk is full of other beauties, and I let them each have a song, because every one of them turned out to point back to Him.

"Pour the Qahwa" is the coffee of welcome, Jesus the Host who fills His house from the streets and the lanes (Luke 14). "Saffron Morning" is the dawn, and the mercy that the book of Lamentations says is new every single morning, never running out no matter how dark the night was (Lamentations 3). "Bread, Oil, and Honey" is the set table and the overflowing cup of Psalm 23. "The Lamp in the Fanous" is the lantern in the dark alley, the word that is a lamp to the feet (Psalm 119) and the Light that darkness cannot master. And "Letters of Gold" is the calligrapher's art turned toward Scripture itself, the words the Psalm calls sweeter than honey, sweeter than the honeycomb (Psalm 19).

Each of these is a real treasure. The saffron is genuinely precious. The bread is really sweet. I am not pretending the market is worthless. I love the market; it is my home. I am saying that every good thing in it is a smaller pearl, and behind them all is the one Pearl they were all rehearsing for. When you find Him, you do not despise the saffron. You finally see what the saffron was hinting at.
The souk goes silent, then it shouts

The album ends the way the market ends its day, but not in exhaustion. "Hallelujah in the Souk" takes the confession public, out among the vendors and the buyers and the children underfoot, because Scripture promises a day when every tongue confesses that Yeshua is Lord (Philippians 2). Even the tongues that spent their whole lives calling out prices will one day call out His name. And the tune of that last song circles back to the very first, so the record does not close so much as loop, the merchant is still running, the market is still being redeemed.

I made this for the one still walking the stalls. You have coins in your hand and you are good at this. You know worth, you have priced a thousand things, and something in you is tired of never finding the thing worth the whole purse. It is here. It has a name, and the name is **Yeshua**. When you see Him, the stalls go to glass, and you will do the strangest, gladdest thing a market-wise heart can do, sell all you have, laughing, and run.

pieces.title: The More I Drink, the More It Pours
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful diverse crowd gathered around a flowing courtyard fountain in the heat of a Middle-Eastern afternoon, people of many nations cupping their hands to catch the water and laughing, a mother lifting a cup to a child's lips, elders and youths with faces bright and refreshed, water sparkling in the sun and spilling across warm stone; premium cinematic worship-brand film still, radiant sunlit blues and warm sand tones, refreshing and full of life, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: In the desert, water is the whole conversation. This album is about the well that never runs dry, the living water Yasu' promised a thirsty woman at noon, and the endless exchange between a heart and its God. It is for everyone still carrying a cracked cup to a world that keeps selling water that runs out.

body.text: If you have never been truly thirsty, this album will be hard to understand. Where I come from, water is not a background fact. It is the whole conversation. You measure a place by its well. You greet a traveler by offering it. A fountain in a courtyard is not decoration. It is the sound of life not running out. So when **Yeshua** sat down at a well in the heat of the day and told a thirsty woman about water that would become a spring inside her, welling up forever, He was not reaching for a poetic image. He was speaking the one language a desert people never mishear.

*The Eternal Conversation*, the record whose opening song I named "The Fountain Never Ends", is my attempt to live inside that promise for twelve songs. It is about the well that does not run dry, and the endless back-and-forth between a heart and the God who fills it. Because that is what living water finally is: not a single drink you take and leave, but a conversation that never has to end.
The cracked cup at noon

The whole album begins with an honest admission. The opening verse is me arriving exactly as I am: *I came to the courtyard with a cup that was cracked and dry, I came to the well in the heat of the day with nothing but a thirst.*

That is drawn straight from the fourth chapter of John, the woman who came to draw water at noon, the hottest and loneliest hour, the hour you choose when you are avoiding the other people at the well. She came with an empty jar and a life full of thirst that water could never touch. And Yeshua, breaking every social rule to speak to her at all, offered her a different water, one that would end the endless trips back to the well, because it would become a spring inside her own chest.

I love that He met her at noon. The desert at noon is where you are most exposed, most parched, most alone. That is precisely where the Fountain chose to sit down and wait. So the album opens there, not clean, not full, not impressive. Cracked cup, dry throat, wrong hour. And the discovery that follows is the engine of the whole record.
The paradox in the title

Here is the strange thing I found, and could not stop singing about. With ordinary water, the more you drink, the less there is. The well goes down. The jar empties. Everything the world pours for you works that way, the pleasure, the success, the applause, the next thing. You drink and it drains.

But the water Yeshua gives runs backward. The chorus of the opening song holds the paradox: *the fountain never ends, the fountain never ends, the water that You give me is the love that never bends; pour it in the courtyard, let it run across the sand.* And the second verse pushes it further: *the more that I am drinking, Lord, the more it pours and bursts.* The more you take, the more there is. Your capacity grows as you drink. That is not how any market fountain works. That is only how God works.

The bridge names the contrast the desert taught me: *whoever drinks the water that the world is always selling will thirst again, will thirst again before the day is done; but the spring that You have opened in the garden of my spirit is rising up forever to the glory of the Son.* I have drunk from the world's fountains. They are real, and they are salt. You drink and you are thirstier than before. Only one spring has ever left me less thirsty the more I drank.
The clay jar at my shoulder is too small to hold this mercy, so I lift the cup and drink again, I drink it like the morning.
Why I called it a conversation
I could have named this record simply after the water. I named it after the exchange, because a fountain that never ends makes something else possible: a relationship that never has to be rationed.

Much of my life I treated God like a well you visit. You go, you draw what you need, you carry it away, you ration it until the next trip, and you are always calculating whether you have enough to last. The living water ends that arithmetic. If the spring is inside you and it never runs dry, then you are never carrying a fixed supply that might run out before morning. You are in an unbroken conversation with the Source itself. You can drink now and drink again in an hour and drink again at midnight, and the well is not lower. That changes how a soul breathes.

The songs on the record are that conversation moving through a whole day and a whole culture. "Pour the Qahwa" is the welcome of the Host who never sends a guest away thirsty (Luke 14). "Saffron Morning" is the mercy that is new every morning, the well refilled before you even wake (Lamentations 3). "Indigo Midnight" is the heart still talking to Him in the watches of the night (Psalm 63), because the conversation does not close when the sun does. "The Open Courtyard" throws the fountain open to the outsider, the one who assumed the well belonged to someone else. From dawn qahwa to midnight stars, it is one continuous drink, one unbroken exchange.
For the ones carrying a cracked cup

I made this album for the thirsty who have stopped believing there is any water that lasts. For the ones who have drunk from every fountain the world sells and are standing in the heat of noon with an empty jar, certain that thirst is simply the human condition and there is nothing to be done but keep hauling water that always runs out.

There is another well. It is not in a far country or a foreign tongue. **Yeshua** is still sitting at it in the hottest hour, still willing to break every rule to speak to the one who came at noon to avoid the crowd, still offering the water that becomes a spring inside your own chest. Bring the cracked cup. Bring it to the courtyard. Drink, and then, this is the whole secret of the record, drink again, and find there is more than before. The fountain never ends. The conversation never has to. Come and be thirsty here; it is the one thirst that answers itself.

pieces.title: The Loveliest Sound We Have Opens Downward
pieces.song: The Phrase They Said Was Most Beautiful
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful, globally diverse circle of friends and family gathered on a warm wooden staircase and landing inside a candlelit home, faces lit with tender wonder and relief as they listen together with hands over hearts, soft golden light pooling from below as if rising up the steps toward them; cinematic worship-brand film still, bright and emotive, premium and radiant, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: There is an old story that the most beautiful-sounding phrase in the English language is "cellar door", two syllables that mean almost nothing and sound like a hymn. I could not let it go, because the loveliest sound we have is a doorway that opens downward. So I made a whole album about the descent, and about the One who was already waiting at the bottom of the stairs.

body.text: There is a story linguists love to tell, and I have never been able to send it back.

The story goes that if you strip a phrase of its meaning and listen only to the pure music of the sound, the vowels, the way the tongue rolls the soft consonants, the loveliest phrase in the whole English language is not *love*, not *dawn*, not *mother*, not any of the words we would nominate if we were thinking about what they mean. It is *cellar door*. Two plain syllables that open low and descend, that fall like water down a small flight of stairs. Say it slowly. *Cellar door.* It sounds like a lullaby. And it points at a hole in the ground under a house.

I am a woman who has given her life to the wonder of sound, and this undid me. Because it means that beauty, real beauty, the kind that stops a linguist in a quiet room and makes him close his eyes, beauty does not live only in the bright, shining, upward things we would expect. The most beautiful sound we have opens *downward.*
The title is a doorway, not a decoration
I called the album **Cellar Door** because I could not get over that descending sound, and because I realized it was telling the truth about my own life that I had spent years refusing to hear.

We all have a cellar. The basement of memory. The lower room where we have stored the grief we never gave space to, the wound that shaped us, the secret we swore we would never say out loud. And the sound of that door, the soft, definitive click of anything that opens low, is a sound most of us have learned to *fear.* In the opening song, "The Phrase They Said Was Most Beautiful," I sing the line exactly as it came to me: *I have learned to fear the sound of anything that opens low.* That is the honest starting place. The stairs going down feel like a falling.

But the whole record turns on a single reversal, and it is the reversal the gospel keeps making. What if the descent is not a punishment? What if the loveliest sound in the language is telling us something the Maker has been saying all along, that He calls *the lowest places lovely, the buried rooms a song, the threshold of my hiding the threshold You walk down?*
Why I had to make it

I built this album out of one verse I underlined years before I understood it. The prophet Isaiah records **Yahuah** saying, *I will give you the treasures of darkness, riches stored in secret places* (Isaiah 45:3). I read that for the longest time like a pretty line for a page. Then a season came when I had to go down my own stairs, and the verse changed my age.

Because here is the wonder that the physics of sound had already been teaching me: a low note is not an empty note. The deepest tones a voice can make are the ones you feel in your chest before you hear them in your ears. The bottom of the range is not the absence of music. It is where the music gets *bodily.* And when I finally went down into the rooms I had been avoiding, I did not find the monsters I feared. I found, as I sing it in "What I Found in the Dark," *small things wrapped in linen that the Lord had stored down here*, a name I had stopped saying, a song I used to hum, a truth I had tried to bury, shining, unburied, raw. He had gone down before me and left me lanterns, left me letters, left me bread.
That is the heart of the album. The descent that I dreaded turned out to be the descent He had already made.
The Word that did the longest walking
The centerpiece of the whole record, for me, is a quiet song called "The Beautiful Words," and it holds the reason the title matters at all.

A word, I have come to believe, is only a sound *until the soul has paid for it.* You can read the syllables *cellar door* and hear nothing but a shape. But live the descent, walk the small stairs, sit in the lower room, and the same two syllables answer back, awake. Meaning has to find a sound the long, slow way.

And this is exactly what the Scriptures say the eternal Word did. *In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God* (John 1:1). Then that Word did the longest walking any Word has ever done. He came down. He took the lantern down every stair there is, all the way into the basement of a doubting human heart, and He made the cellar door *sound like home.* **Yeshua** is the loveliest sound we have precisely because He is the One who opened downward, who descended into our lowest room and did not flinch at what was stored there.

Maybe beauty is not what shines on top. Maybe beauty is what waits underneath for someone brave enough to listen, two syllables, one descending breath, and the Lord at the bottom of the stairs already knowing my name.
When I first sang that bridge I had to stop and breathe, because it is the truest thing I know how to say about grief and about God in the same sentence.
For the one afraid of the basement
I made this for the person who has a door in their chest they have kept locked for years.

The album walks the whole descent honestly. There is a song, "The Door That Locked Behind Me," about the panic of feeling shut in with your own buried things, and its whole comfort is drawn straight from the night the risen **Yeshua** walked through a locked room to His terrified friends and said *Peace* (John 20:19). The door your fear shuts tight is not too thick for Him. And there is "The Cellar Becomes a Chapel," where the lowest room in the whole house turns into a sanctuary, because a chapel was never a building the carpenters arrive to raise. A chapel is wherever a soul kneels down. And by "Coming Back Up Different" and the closing benediction, "Cellar Door, Cellar Door," the phrase the linguist gave me has changed its meaning completely. It is not a threat anymore. It is a hand on the shoulder. It is the Father saying, *welcome home from the lower room, beloved, well done.*

I am not asking you to enjoy the dark. I am telling you what the sound already told me. The prayer underneath the whole album is the oldest and bravest one there is: *Search me, God, and know my heart; test me and know my anxious thoughts. See if there is any offensive way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting* (Psalm 139:23-24). That is a prayer that consents to the descent. It hands Him the lantern and lets Him lead down the stairs.

So the next time you hear that soft click of something opening low, and your whole body tightens the way it has been trained to. I would be very slow to trust the fear. The loveliest sound we have opens downward. And there is Someone already at the bottom of the stairs, holding a light, and He has known your name longer than you have been afraid of the dark.
Say the phrase. Say it slow. *Cellar door.* It was a benediction the whole time.

pieces.title: God Skipped the Earthquake and Chose the Whisper
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful, globally diverse gathering of people of many nations seated quietly in a sunlit garden and on a worn wooden bench, eyes softly closed and faces turned upward in listening peace, morning light slanting golden through cedar branches over a candle and an open book, hands resting open in their laps; cinematic worship-brand film still, hushed and radiant, tender and emotive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: A prophet stood on a mountain and God sent a wind that split the rocks, an earthquake, and a fire, and was in none of them. Then came the smallest sound in the world, and that was Him. I made an album about the strangest fact in all of sound: that the quietest thing can carry the most. This is the story behind The Listening Place.

body.text: Here is the fact that started the whole album, and I still find it almost too strange to believe.

A prophet named Elijah, running for his life and empty to the bone, climbs a mountain to meet God. And God, we are told, *passes by.* First comes a wind so violent it tears the mountains apart and shatters the rocks, *but the LORD was not in the wind.* Then an earthquake, *but the LORD was not in the earthquake.* Then a fire, *but the LORD was not in the fire.* And after the fire, the text says, there came *a still small voice.* A gentle whisper. In the old Hebrew it is stranger still, a phrase that means something like *the sound of a thin silence.* And *that*, that almost-nothing, that hush you would miss entirely if you had not gone quiet, that was Him (1 Kings 19:11-13).

Think about what God did there. He had at His disposal the three loudest sounds creation can make. Wind, quake, fire. Every one of them the kind of sound we would call *the voice of God* if we heard it. And He let them all pass, and He spoke instead in the register we are least equipped to hear.
I have spent my whole life on the wonder of sound, and I cannot get over this. **Yahuah** skipped the earthquake and chose the whisper.
The quietest sound carries the most
We assume, always, that loudness equals significance. The big sound must be the important one. But it is simply not true, not in music and not in God.

A whisper carries less force than a shout. And yet a whisper can carry things a shout never could. You do not whisper a threat; you whisper a secret, a name, a love. The very quietness *is the meaning.* It says: this is only for you, come close, I am not performing, I am telling you the truest thing I have. In "Still Small Voice," the song at the heart of this record, I sing it the only way I found honest, *You who could have thundered chose the smallest sound. You who could have shaken chose the holy ground of a heart that learned to listen for a Word the noise won't drown.* The smallness is not a limitation on God. It is a tenderness *from* God.
And so the whole album, before it says anything about God at all, has to say something about us. If He speaks in the quietest register, then the problem was never His volume. It was our attention.
The title is a discipline, not a place
I called it **The Listening Place** because I became convinced that hearing God is less about His willingness to speak and more about our willingness to build a room quiet enough to catch a whisper.

The opening song is literally the sound of a room being prepared, a broom on wood, a candle lit, a phone left outside the door. *I am building something quieter than I've ever built before.* Not a temple, not a tower. Just a little swept square of floor where *my hurry comes to perish.* Because here is the physics of it, and the theology of it, in one breath: a whisper is drowned not by God's absence but by ambient noise. Turn the room loud enough and the most important sound in the universe is simply *masked*, present, real, unheard. We are not usually deaf. We are usually just loud.

That is why the record moves the way it does. "After the Wind, the Fire" walks straight through Elijah's mountain and lands on the line I most needed to learn, *after the noise has had its will,* there is a smaller kind of glory that a louder one can't fill. "Breath Prayer" strips everything back to an inhale and an exhale, because when the words have all gone empty, the body still knows how to pray, *the lungs become a chapel and the diaphragm the bell.* "The Bell at the Hour" is about letting a single far-off sound interrupt your rushing and call you back. Every one of them is a discipline of getting quiet enough.
What you hear when you finally stop
The turn of the whole album comes in a song called "What I Heard When I Stopped," and it holds the thing I most want you to know.

Because we are afraid of silence. We assume that if we stop the noise, what we will meet is emptiness, or accusation, that the quiet will *scold* us for everything the busyness has been outrunning. And I found the opposite. When I finally stopped the noise of working and the noise of news and the noise of explaining myself, *the quiet didn't punish and the silence didn't scold. It just sat down beside me like a friend grown soft and old.* And the first thing I heard was not thunder and not fire. It was *a love I'd been outrunning*, a Voice that had been there always, underneath the noise of my fears.

This is the promise of the oldest invitation in the Psalms: *Be still, and know that I am God* (Psalm 46:10). Not *strive.* Not *achieve.* Not *get loud enough to be worthy.* Be still. The knowing is on the other side of the stillness.
The listening place is portable as the heart that turns to hear. And the cedar bench is anywhere the Shepherd's drawing near.

That is the closing line of the record, and it is the whole hope of it. The place is not a corner by a window. The place is a willingness, to turn the volume down and remember His kind Name, on a train, at a kitchen sink, in a hospice room with your hand against the pane.
For the ones worn thin by the noise
I made this for the person who is so tired of being loud.

The one who has confused a busy life with a full one, and a full inbox with a heard prayer. The one who suspects, somewhere underneath, that if the noise ever stopped they would have to face how far they have drifted, and who is more afraid of the silence than of anything the silence holds. I want to tell you what the mountain told the prophet and what the stillness told me: the God who chose the whisper is not waiting on the far side of the quiet to shame you. He is *in* the quiet, already coming toward you, and He has been speaking the entire time in a register the noise kept masking.
He breathed the first breath into the first human's quiet clay (Genesis 2:7), and He is breathing inside you now, every undefended day. That is how close the whisper is. Closer than the air.

So build the small room. Sweep the corner, set the chair, light the candle, leave the phone outside the door. You are not manufacturing His presence. You are only turning down the interference on a signal that never stopped transmitting. Get still enough, stay long enough, and the smallest sound in all the world will lift out of the silence and you will realize with a rush that it was singing over you the whole time.
He skipped the earthquake for a reason. He wanted to be near enough to whisper.

pieces.title: The Veil Is a Trembling Membrane, Not a Wall
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful, globally diverse company of pilgrims and worshippers of many nations standing together on a windswept green sea cliff at golden dawn, faces lifted and radiant with awe, some with arms open to the light breaking over the water, a small stone chapel behind them; cinematic worship-brand film still, luminous and emotive, sweeping and reverent, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: The Celtic monks had a word for the moments when heaven leans so close you can feel it, thin places. I have spent my life listening for how the holy comes near, and I have become convinced the veil between us was never a thick stone wall. It is a thin, trembling membrane, the way a drum-skin trembles when a sound moves through it. Here is the story behind Thin Places.

body.text: The monks who walked the islands off the coast of Scotland and Ireland had a phrase for it that they never bothered to explain, because everyone who had felt it already knew.

They called them *thin places.* Moments and locations where the distance between heaven and the ordinary world seems to shrink to almost nothing, where, as the old saying goes, the veil grows so transparent you could almost put your hand through it. A hush after a service. A river in the rain. A headland at dawn. The air goes lucid, and you know, with your whole body and not just your mind, that you are not alone. They did not build a system out of it. They simply named the ground and said: *here is a doorway; listen for the sound.*

I have given my life to the wonder of how the holy draws near, and that little phrase reorganized everything for me. Because it means the barrier between us and God was never what we assumed. We picture a wall, thick, permanent, sealed. But the monks were describing something else entirely. Something that *thins.* Something that, in the right moment, you can feel *trembling.*
A membrane, not a wall
Here is the image I could not escape, and it is the one the album is built on.

A wall does not move. But a membrane, a drum-skin, an eardrum, the thin surface of water, a membrane *trembles* when a sound passes through it. That is, in fact, the whole physics of hearing: a sound reaches you only because a wave crosses the air and sets a thin membrane vibrating. The barrier and the medium of contact are the *same surface.* The thing that separates is the exact thing that lets the sound through.

And I began to suspect that the veil between heaven and earth is far more like a membrane than a wall. In the song at the center of this record, "The Veil Trembling," I put it as plainly as I could, *the veil is not a curtain of impossible thick cloth. It is a thin trembling membrane that the Spirit can flow off.* Not a barricade. A drum-skin. Something built precisely so that Presence can pass through it and set the whole thing ringing.

This is not sentiment. It is what happened at the very center of the story. When **Yeshua** gave up His breath on the cross, *the curtain of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom* (Matthew 27:51), the thick veil that had walled off the Holy of Holies, torn open, top down, by a hand that was clearly not human. The letter to the Hebrews says He opened *a new and living way for us through the curtain* (Hebrews 10:19-20). The wall we thought was permanent turned out to be a thing that could be rent. He tore the cloth Himself, as I sing it, *that I might see His face.*
The title is a map of where He shows up
I called the album **Thin Places** because I wanted to teach the ear where to listen, and because the answer surprised even me.

You would expect thin places to be dramatic. And some of them are. There is a song on the record called "Iona at Dawn," about standing on the shore of a small Hebridean island where fifteen hundred years of morning prayers have been sung, where *the sea is a chalice, the rocks are an altar, the sky is the roof of an open hall.* There is "The Cliff Above the Sea," four hundred feet of basalt with the Atlantic below, where the wind is so enormous it can carry every word you ever held that you should have let go, and I stand there and confess, straight out of Job, *You set the bounds of the ocean, You named the deep its place* (Job 38:8-11). Those are the postcard thin places. The grand ones.
But the album's whole argument is that the veil trembles just as thin in rooms with no view at all.

There is a song called "Holy Ground at the Kitchen Sink," and it is the one people write to me about most. Because I had asked God for a sign in a chapel, for a vision, a wonder, a burning bush, and He met me instead at the supper dishes, in the soap and the rind, in the soft yellow lamp above the saucers. Brother Lawrence, the old Carmelite who found God among the pots and pans, knew this. Moses knew it: he took his sandals off in a wilderness, because the bush that would not burn up had made an ordinary patch of dirt into holy ground (Exodus 3). *Every dish a kind of altar. Every soap-sud a small prayer.* The veil is as thin at the sink as on the cliff.

And there is a song I could barely record, "The Hospice Room Was a Thin Place", about a bedside, a communion cup, a father's breathing slowing like a tide, and the certainty that heaven was leaning into that small yellow room. If the veil is a membrane and not a wall, then it is thinnest exactly where we thought God was most absent.
When bread becomes body
The wonder for me is that the thin place is not always a lightning strike. Often it is a *rhythm*, something the faithful step into on purpose.

That is what "When Bread Becomes Body" is about. Every Sunday of my whole life, the same small wonder takes hold of me at the communion rail, wheat that grew in one field, grape that swelled on a vine, gathered onto a table and, by ancient words, made into the nearness of God. *This is the regular thin place. This is the door we walk through.* You do not have to understand the mystery. He never asked us to dissect the gift, only to come and receive it.

Jacob said it first at Bethel: *Surely the LORD is in this place, and I did not know it. How awesome is this place! This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven* (Genesis 28:16-17).

That is the verse the whole album stands on. A man on the run, sleeping on a stone, wakes from a dream of a ladder between heaven and earth and realizes the doorway was there all along. He simply had not known it. *Heaven has a thousand doorways, and every one of them is blessed.*
For the ones who feel the veil is stone
I made this for the person who has decided God is behind a wall.

The one for whom prayer feels like talking to sealed rock, who has concluded that if there was ever a doorway it has long since been bricked over. I want to tell you what the torn temple curtain says, what the trembling membrane says, what every thin place I have ever stood in says: the barrier is not what you think it is. It thins. It trembles. It was torn from the top by a Savior who wanted your face against His, and the Spirit still flows off it like sound off a drum-skin.

And the best news of the album is its closing song, "Carry the Thin Place Home." You do not have to stay on the island to belong. *The kingdom of God is portable*, as near as your breath, as thin in your kitchen as on the holy shore. Jacob carried Bethel with him all the long years of his life; every tent he pitched afterward was a doorway past the strife. You can carry yours too.

There is a day coming, the last song promises, when *heaven touches down* and the veil is not thin but gone, when every headland and every kitchen is lit with an unsetting sun and the whole earth is the thin place forever (Revelation 21). Every trembling doorway we have known was a whisper of that view.

Until then: listen for the sound. The wall you have been leaning against, exhausted, is thinner than you know. Put your hand out. It is trembling, because Someone on the other side is very near, and He has never once stopped leaning in.

pieces.title: The Whirlwind Was Not an Answer but a Face
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful, globally diverse group of honest seekers of many nations gathered in a warm lamplit chapel at night, some with heads bowed and others with faces lifting into relief and wonder, one person's hand resting on another's shoulder in comfort, a second chair pulled close in golden light; cinematic worship-brand film still, intimate and emotive, tender and hopeful, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: A man buried in grief demanded answers from God, and God answered, out of a whirlwind, in a voice, with a hundred questions of His own about stars and storms and the sea. He did not solve it. He showed up. I made an album for everyone who came to God with a legal pad full of accusations, and I called it The Interrogation. This is why.

body.text: I want to tell you about the loudest sound in the whole Bible, and what it turned out to actually be.

There is a man named Job who loses everything, his children, his health, his whole world, for reasons he is never told. And for chapter after chapter he does the thing we are all quietly warned not to do: he demands an explanation. He wants God in the witness box. He builds his case. He will not be comforted with slogans. And then, at last, God answers him. But not the way anyone expects. *The LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind* (Job 38:1), out of a storm, in a voice, and what He says is not a single explanation. It is a torrent of questions. *Where were you when I laid the earth's foundations? Have you commanded the morning? Can you bind the chains of the Pleiades, or loose the cords of Orion?*

I have spent my life on the wonder of sound, and I have never gotten over the fact that when God finally speaks the answer everyone is waiting for, *the answer is a voice out of a storm that does not answer anything.* It solves nothing. It explains nothing. And Job, who had cross-examined heaven, covers his mouth with dust and says the strangest thing: *My ears had heard of You, but now my eyes have seen You* (Job 42:5). He got no explanation. He got a Presence. And it was enough.
That is the seed of the whole album. The whirlwind was not an answer. The whirlwind was a face.
The title is an invitation, not a threat
I called it **The Interrogation** because I wanted to name the thing most of us are too ashamed to admit we are doing.

We come to God with a list. In the opening song I sing it exactly as it happened to me, *I came in with a legal pad, every line a thing You had not said.* The doubt I did not throw out. The fear I never told. The questions the chapel could not hold. And I braced, the way we all brace, for God to flinch, to be offended, to withhold the room, to punish the honesty. And what I found instead is the reversal the whole record turns on: *You did not laugh, You did not leave. You pulled the second chair up close. You said, beloved, ask Me anything.
