I have been waiting for this most.*

That is not sentimentality. It is the pattern of Scripture. Moses argued with God at the burning bush. Abraham argued with Him over a city. Habakkuk stood on his watchtower and refused to come down until he got an answer. Jeremiah wept and accused Him to His face. And **Yahuah** did not strike a single one of them down. He *leaned in.* There is a song on the record called "The God Who Argues Back," and its whole confession is this: *a God who can be argued with is a God who can be truly known.* The interrogation is not the opposite of faith. Sometimes it is the front door of it.
Where were You
The hardest song I have ever written sits early on the album, and it is just one question repeated. "Where Were You."

Where were You the night the call came. Where were You when the doctor's mouth turned the room into disaster. Where were You when the prayer was good and the answer was a stone. I did not want to write a resolution for that song too quickly, because grief does not resolve on a schedule and I refuse to lie to the grieving. *I am not asking for a verse,* the song says. *I am asking for a face. I am not asking for a fix. I am asking for the place.* That is the truest thing about lament. It is not, at bottom, hunting for information. It is hunting for *company.* The Psalms taught me this. *My God, my God, why have You forsaken me* (Psalm 22:1). *How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever?* (Psalm 13:1). Those are in the songbook of the faithful. God kept the accusations *in the worship book.*

And what I found, what Job found, is that the answer to *where were You* was never a diagram. It was a companionship in the dark. *You did not hand me a why. You sat down in the silence with me. And somehow that was more like love than any rescue, any power.*
The wonder that made me small enough
Here is what the physics of the whirlwind taught me, and why the sound of it matters so much.

A storm is the loudest thing most of us will ever stand near. And when God chose to answer the deepest human demand for meaning, He did not send a page of reasons. He sent a *sound so large it reorganized the man standing in it.* He walked into Job's deposition and turned the question into flame. Every argument I had rehearsed in the car, every point I had practiced at night, when the door clicked shut and the wind came through, they simply *took flight.* Not because they were shamed. Because they were suddenly the wrong size.

In "The Whirlwind Answer" I sing the thing I most needed to learn: *the whirlwind did not break me down, the whirlwind made me small enough to fit inside the love that holds the galaxies, the dust, the rough.* That is the gift hidden in the storm. Awe does not humiliate you. It *right-sizes* you. It takes a soul that had swelled up with its own need to understand everything and gently shrinks it back down to the scale where it can finally be held.
The whirlwind answer was not an answer, the whirlwind answer was a face. You did not solve, You did not soothe. You filled the courtroom with Your grace.
The questions that get to stay
I need you to hear how the album ends, because it is the whole pastoral point.

The wrestling does not tie every question off. There is a song called "The Questions That Stayed," and it is about waking up after the long night to find that some questions are still sitting at the table, *but they had lost their teeth somehow. They sat like friends, not enemies.* Why the child. Why the cancer. Why the prayer that fell so flat. *I do not know,* the song admits. *I have stopped pretending that I do. But I know the One who knows, and that is enough to walk me through.* Faith, it turns out, is not the absence of the question. Faith is the carrying of the load, loving still the Author of the chapter that came late.

The whole record is framed by another man who wrestled through a night: Jacob, alone at the ford of the Jabbok, gripping a Stranger until daybreak and refusing to let go without a blessing (Genesis 32:24-30). He got his blessing. He also got a new name, Israel, *one who strives with God*, and a limp he carried the rest of his life. There is a song called "The Limp I Left With," and it blesses the wound: *the slow, uneven walking that became my praying task.* You can leave an honest wrestling with God marked. That mark is not your defeat. It is the proof He was really there.
For the one holding a legal pad
I made this for you, the doubter, the deconstructor, the griever who is furious and faithful in the same breath.

If you have a list of accusations you have been too afraid to say out loud in church, bring it. Bring the page, bring the pen, bring the part you cannot mend. **Yeshua** is not the God of the polished and the smiling. He is the God who argues back and loves you all the while, who has been pulling a second chair up close since who knows when. He will not flinch. He will not flee. He may not hand you the explanation you came for. But He will do the thing that turns out to matter more. He will fill the room with His face.

You do not have to solve Him to be held by Him. You only have to stop running long enough for the wind to come through. And when it does, you will find what Job found and what I found: the whirlwind was never an answer. It was Someone, at last, in the room. And He had been waiting for this most.

pieces.title: He Knows the Name of Every Star and Still Learned Mine
pieces.song: You Know the Name of Every Star
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful, globally diverse family and friends of many nations lying back together on a car hood and blankets in an open field beneath a vast star-filled night sky, faces glowing with wonder and tears of joy, arms pointing upward, the Milky Way arched overhead; cinematic worship-brand film still, awe-struck and radiant, deeply emotive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: The Scriptures say God counts the stars and calls them each by name. Every deeper look we take into the dark finds more galaxies pouring out. I used to think a God that vast would crush a soul as small as mine. I made an album to say the opposite, that His vastness is the safest home I have ever found. This is the story behind The Vastness of You.

body.text: There is a line in the Psalms that I did not believe for years, even as I sang it.

*He determines the number of the stars and calls them each by name* (Psalm 147:4). I would read that and quietly file it under poetry, a lovely exaggeration, the kind of thing worship writers say. Then one night I drove an hour out past the streetlamps, parked at the edge of an empty field, lay back on the cold hood of the car, and looked up. And the sky was not a sky I had ever known. Every deeper look humanity takes into the dark, the great telescopes reaching past what any eye can see, finds *more.* Another field of galaxies pouring out of the black, and past those, more, and no floor to it that anyone has found. I lay there in the cold trying to hold the size of it, and I could not fit it inside my chest.

And I did the thing the shepherd-king David did under a different sky three thousand years before me. I asked the question that this whole album is built on: *When I consider Your heavens, the work of Your fingers, the moon and the stars which You have set in place, what is man, that You are mindful of him?* (Psalm 8:3-4).
The vastness was the thing I was afraid of
I have to be honest about where I started, because it is where a lot of people are stuck.

For most of my life the size of God frightened me. I assumed that a God vast enough to fling a hundred billion galaxies would have to be, by definition, *uninterested* in me. Too big to bend down. Too occupied with the machinery of the cosmos to notice a small woman sweeping a small kitchen at three in the afternoon. The numbers did not comfort me; they *erased* me. If He is that enormous, I reasoned, then I am a footnote nobody bothers to cite.

That is exactly the fear the album walks straight into. There is a song called "Smaller Than a Speck and Loved," and it names the terror before it names the mercy: *I have read the numbers and they did not fit inside my chest. I should be a footnote nobody bothers to cite.* Because the Milky Way is a speck in the cosmos, and the solar system a speck in the Milky Way, and the planet a speck in that, and us a speck on the planet. By every honest measure, I should be paralyzed by my own smallness.
And then the whole record turns, because the same Scriptures that tell you how vast He is tell you what He *does* with the vastness.
He bent down
Here is the wonder that undid the fear, and it is the exact center of the album.

The very same voice that Job heard from the whirlwind, *Can you bind the chains of the Pleiades? Can you loose the cords of Orion?* (Job 38:31), the voice that hung the Hunter in the winter sky and set the seven sisters wheeling, that voice *learned a human name.* In the song "You Know the Name of Every Star," I sing the thing I finally came to believe out on that car hood: *the One who names the trillion stars above has named me too, and the name is love.* There is no anonymous galaxy in His library of light. And there is no daughter on a back porch with her coffee growing cold whose name He has not carved beside a star upon the line.

This is not me being sentimental about astronomy. It is the plainest claim of the gospel, and the album says it as bluntly as it can in "The God of Galaxies." The hands that scooped the seas held a tiny finger. The voice that sang the spheres into their orbits cried in the night. *The God of galaxies was a baby in a barn beneath the Bethlehem starlight.* The letter to the Colossians says of **Yeshua** that *by Him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible*, and that *in Him all things hold together* (Colossians 1:16-17). And that same One emptied Himself, took the form of a servant, and bent all the way down (Philippians 2:6-7). The vastness did not stay remote. It *stooped.*
The heavens are not silent
The reason I could only make this album is that the sky, to my ear, has never been quiet.

There is a Psalm that has followed me my whole life: *The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of His hands. Day after day they pour forth speech; night after night they reveal knowledge. There is no speech or language where their voice is not heard* (Psalm 19:1-4). Read that slowly. The sky is *speaking.* Not in words, the Psalm is careful to say there is no actual language, no syllable, and yet its voice goes out to the ends of the earth. The whole cosmos is a sermon preached without a single word, and every human being who has ever looked up has been in the congregation.

That wrecks me, as someone who listens for a living. The stars are not decoration. They are *proclamation.* In the song "The Heavens Declare" I sing it the only way I can, *every sunrise is a salutation, every sunset is a benediction, every star is a small confession of allegiance.* The cosmos has been preaching the same conviction since the first morning, and the wonder is not that it is loud. The wonder is that it is *constant,* and free, and pointed the whole time at the tenderness of the One who made it.
You are big enough to be uninterested. You are great enough to overlook. But He bent down. Oh, He bent down. He bent down to the speck and wrote her in His book.
The vastness is the safe place
Everything on the album empties into its final song, and I want to give you its whole reversal, because it is the thing I most want you to carry.

The song is called "Vastness," and it begins with the old fear stated one more time: *I used to be afraid of the vastness of God. I used to think the size of Him would crush the size of me.* And then it turns, and does not turn back: *But the vastness of God is the safest place I have ever known. The vastness of God is the wideness of a Father's arms. The vastness of God is the room for every wound to be welcomed.* A small God, a God the size of my understanding, would run out of room. He would have a limit I could reach, a mercy I could exhaust, a patience I could wear through. But a God as wide as the cosmos has *space* in Him for everything I am and everything I have done and everything I have not yet dared to bring.

The apostle Paul stakes his whole life on it: *I am persuaded that neither death nor life, nor angels nor principalities, nor things present nor things to come, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord* (Romans 8:38-39). *Height nor depth.* He reaches for the biggest words he has, the scale of the universe itself, and says not even *that* is large enough to get between you and the love that holds you.
For the one who feels too small to be seen
I made this for the person lying awake feeling like a footnote.

The one who has done the math on their own insignificance, the vast sky, the vast history, the billions of other faces, and concluded that of course God has not got time for a soul as small as theirs. I want to tell you what the field of stars told me on the hood of that car. The size of Him is not your erasure. It is your welcome. He counted the tears that fell in the dark and *saved them in a vase* the same night He set the Pleiades wheeling. He is not too holy to bend, not too high to stoop, not too good to enter the kitchen of the lost.

So go outside tonight, if you can, and look up until the size of it starts to frighten you a little. And then remember: the One who knows the name of every star out there leaned all the way down through all of it to learn yours, and He has been whispering it, over your small and beloved life, since before the oldest light up there began its journey to your eyes.
You were never a footnote. You were the reason He bent down.

pieces.title: The Cross Came Down Off the Wall and Into the Street
pieces.song: La Cruz Que Baila (The Cross That Dances)
pieces.imagePrompt: A jubilant Latin American village procession in a sunlit plaza, a wooden cross carried high at the front, families of many ages dancing cumbia in the dust, an abuelo holding his hat to his chest, an accordion player mid-stride, grandchildren spinning, candles and bright ribbons, believers of many nations joining the dance with hands raised, joy on every face, cinematic worship-brand film still, warm golden light, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I grew up watching the Cross hang silent on a wall, beautiful, holy, and completely still. Then I saw a whole village carry it into the plaza and dance. This album is what happened when I finally believed the Cross was not a monument but a victory, and victories in my culture are never celebrated sitting down.

body.text: For most of my growing-up years, the Cross was something that hung on a wall. It was carved, it was gilded, it caught the candlelight, and it never moved. We venerated it in a hush. We lowered our voices when we passed it. And somewhere along the way I absorbed a lie so quiet I never even noticed I was carrying it: that the holiest thing in the room was also the stillest.

Then, one May, in a dusty little pueblo where the streets are cobblestone and the accordion is louder than the church bell, I watched them lift the Cross off the wall and carry it out the door. It went down the street on the shoulders of ordinary men. The güiro started scraping on every beat. An old man put his hat to his chest and began to step. And the whole village, abuelas, teenagers, babies on hips, started to *dance behind the Cross.*
I have never been the same. **La Cruz Que Baila**, *The Cross That Dances*, is the record that came out of that street.
What the title actually means
*La Cruz Que Baila* means "The Cross That Dances." Not the cross that decorates. Not the cross that scolds. The Cross that *dances.*

I built this album on cumbia on purpose, and I need you to understand why. Cumbia is the one rhythm the whole Spanish-speaking world already knows in its feet, Colombian, Mexican, Peruvian, Argentine, Salvadoran, Bolivian. It is the music of every wedding, every quinceañera, every backyard birthday where the asado smoke drifts over the patio. It belongs to the abuelos and to the babies at the same time. So when I wanted to sing the Cross into every village at once, cumbia was the only language wide enough to hold it.
The opening track says the thesis out loud in the first thirteen seconds: *"My people! The Cross is not a monument, the Cross dances!"* And then the chorus lifts:
The Cross that dances! Christ in the rhythm, and the village starts to rise.
That word, *rise*, is doing everything. Because a Cross that only hangs on a wall asks you to be quiet. A Cross that dances asks you to *get up.*
Why I had to make it
Here is the thing nobody told me for years: the Cross is not sad news. The Cross is the sound a cancelled debt makes.

Paul wrote it plainly, *"God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ"* (Galatians 6:14). He was not glorying in a defeat. He was glorying in the single most decisive victory in the history of the universe. **Yeshua** *"humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross"* (Philippians 2:8), and then He walked out of the grave and left it empty.

In my culture, we do not celebrate a victory by holding still. When the team wins, we pour into the street. When the daughter marries, we dance until the sun comes up. When the prodigal comes home, we kill the fattened calf and the whole barrio hears the music. So why, *why*, had we agreed to treat the greatest victory of all as if it were a funeral?

I made this album to break that agreement. I made it so that the next time a village carries the Cross through the plaza on the Day of the Cross, they would have a song that finally matches what actually happened on that hill.
The songs, and the heart under them

"Procesión de la Cruz" is built on one of my favorite sentences in all of Scripture. When the ark of the covenant set out, Moses would cry, *"Rise up, LORD"* (Numbers 10:35), *Arise, O Yahuah, lead.* That is a marching order. So the procession song puts the Cross at the *front*, and the whole village walks behind it into the morning, candles cupped in their palms, because the Cross is not the thing you leave behind in the building. It is the thing that goes ahead of you into the day.

"Cristo en Nuestra Plaza" plants Him right in the town square, the fountain with the cracked tile, the vendor selling elote, the children running between the trees. I anchored it to Acts 17:17, where Paul reasoned *in the marketplace daily* with whoever happened to be there. The plaza is not a lesser place than the sanctuary. **Yeshua** is Lord of the fountain and the food cart too.

Then the album travels, because Latin America is not one place. "La Cruz en la Frontera" takes the Cross to a Mexican-norteño beat and a border crossing, where a grandmother lifts her prayer over a wire fence. "Chicha de la Resurrección" climbs into the Peruvian Andes at dawn and sings the empty tomb over electric cumbia. "Villera de la Salvación" slips into an Argentine villa, up a narrow alley, a gospel tract sliding under a third-floor door. And "La Cruz en el Velorio", this one still makes my throat tight, brings the Cross into a wake, a vallenato accordion played softly by a cousin in the corner, a grandmother who prayed to **Yeshua** without ceasing to her very last breath. Even there, *especially* there, the Cross does not stand still. It sits down with the grieving and it does not let go.
By the time you reach "Toda la Tierra Baila la Cruz", *the whole earth dances the Cross*. I wanted you to feel every one of those villages join hands at once.
The bridge I keep coming back to
There is a line in the title track that I sing four times, and I mean it more each time:
The Cross dances with us, and we dance with the Cross.

That is the whole gospel in one sentence. He came down to us first. The Cross moved *toward* us before we ever moved toward it. And now the invitation is simply to fall into step. King David understood this. He *danced before Yahuah with all his might* (2 Samuel 6:14), and when someone told him it was undignified, he said he would become even more undignified than that. I love him for it. Dignity is a small price for joy this size.
Who this album is for

This one is for the church patio on a Saturday afternoon, the plastic chairs and the portable speaker and the asado smoke. It is for the wedding reception that wants the gospel without losing the dance floor. It is for the abuelo who has carried the Cross in the procession every May of his life and has never once heard it sung in the rhythm his feet already know.

And it is for you, the cousin who came for the food and figured you would slip out before the worship. Stay. The Cross came down off the wall. It is out here in the street now, in the dust, in the güiro, in the accordion breathing open to the morning. It is dancing toward you. All you have to do is stop watching from the shadow of the doorway, and step.
The village is rising. Come rise with us.

pieces.title: The Celebration Was the Commissioning All Along
pieces.imagePrompt: A jubilant, globally diverse multi-generational Latino congregation mid-celebration in a bright church hall, a beaming young believer being presented at the center with arms lifted, a father's proud hand on the shoulder, abuelas and cousins and children dancing with tambourines and raised hands, accordion and horns glinting, confetti light and joy on every face, believers of many nations celebrating together; cinematic worship-brand film still, radiant and euphoric, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: At every quinceañera there is a moment when the music stops, the spotlight finds the floor, and the father walks his daughter out to present her to the whole world. I made a merengue record because that exact moment is what the Father does with every one of His children, and He does it at a party. This is the album where the dance floor turns out to be the throne room.

body.text: There is a moment at every Dominican *quinceañera* that stops the whole room, and I have never gotten over it.

The band cuts. The güira goes quiet. The spotlight finds the center of the floor. And the father walks out, in his best suit, the one he has been saving, and he takes the hand of his fifteen-year-old daughter, and he turns her to face the crowd. Everyone she has ever known is in that room. And he *presents* her. Not as a little girl anymore. As a young woman. As someone the whole community is now responsible to receive and to send. The *tías* start crying. The *abuelas* are already crying. And then the accordion detonates, the tambora cracks, and the entire family floods the floor to dance.

I grew up watching that moment, and one day it hit me so hard I had to build a whole album around it. Because that presentation, that exact thing, is what **Yahuah** does with every single one of His children. *And He does it at a party.*
What the word actually means

*Quinceañera* means "the girl who is turning fifteen." In our culture it is the great rite of passage, the day the family throws everything they have into a celebration that says *you are grown now, you belong to us, and we are launching you.*

So I called the album **Quinceañera del Espíritu**, the coming-of-age party of the Spirit. Because there is a moment in every believer's walk that is exactly this: the day you stop being a spectator to your family's faith and step into your own. Fifteen years in the Spirit. Grown up in **Yeshua**. And I gave the record a subtitle I will defend to anyone: *Mi fiesta es de Cristo.* My party belongs to Christ.

Let me be clear about the center, because it matters. I am not baptizing a tradition and calling it done. The dress is not the point. The candles are not the point. Remove **Yeshua** from this record and it collapses into a birthday party with an accordion. But leave Him at the center, where He belongs, the One the whole celebration is *for* and *from*, and the merengue becomes worship. The party is His.
The night I realized the party was a sending
Here is the engine of the whole album, and it is the moment I built everything else around.

For the first seven songs, the record just dances. First confession of faith. First testimony. First baptism. First communion. Each one its own merengue, its own celebration. And then comes the song at the peak, "El Padre Presenta," *The Father Presents*, and the music pulls back, and the Father's own voice speaks over the floor: *My son. My daughter. I present you to the world. This party. It was never just a song. It was your commissioning all along.*

That line is the thesis of my life right now. **The celebration was the commissioning all along.** We think the party and the sending are two different events, that you celebrate on Sunday and then get to work on Monday. But at the quinceañera, the presentation *is* the launch. The father doesn't throw the party *and then* send her out. The party *is* the sending. The dance floor lifts, and it turns out to have been the throne room the whole time.

And this is not sentiment I invented. It is straight out of the letter to the Romans: *those who are led by the Spirit of God are the children of God. For you did not receive a spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, "Abba! Father!"* (Romans 8:14-15). We are adopted, named, and then presented as heirs. The Father steps to the floor and introduces you, not because of your bloodline, but because His Spirit led you home and He is proud to claim you in front of everyone.
Heaven's default response is a fiesta
If you still think God is the sober one in the room, the One who tolerates joy but doesn't really trust it, then you have not read how **Yeshua** described His own Father.

He told a story about a boy who took his inheritance, wasted it, and came crawling home expecting to be a servant. And the father *ran.* He put a robe on him, a ring on his finger, and he said the most important sentence for understanding the heart of God: *Bring the fattened calf and kill it. Let us eat and celebrate. For this son of mine was dead, and is alive again* (Luke 15:23-24). The homecoming was not met with a lecture. It was met with a *party*, music and dancing so loud the older brother heard it from the field. **Yahuah's** reflex, when a child comes home, is to throw a fiesta. Heaven itself does it: *there is rejoicing in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner who repents* (Luke 15:10).
This is why I make the music I make. The longest-running party in the universe is not out in the world. It is the Kingdom. And you were not invited as a guest. You were presented as family.

The prophet Zephaniah saw it centuries early and could barely hold the words: *The LORD your God is in your midst... He will rejoice over you with gladness... He will exult over you with loud singing* (Zephaniah 3:17). Do you hear that? He does not just love you quietly. He *sings over you, loud.* The God of the universe has a celebration voice, and you are the reason He uses it.
The songs, and the rites they dance
Every track on the record is one coming-of-age moment turned into a merengue.

"Yo Confieso" is the first public confession of faith, a fourteen-year-old shaking in the back of a youth room, saying it out loud for the first time, straight from *if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord... you will be saved* (Romans 10:9). "First Time at the Mic" is the testimony anchor, the moment somebody hands you the microphone and Cristo hands you the words, and the first sentence out is *"He lifted me out of the pit,"* which is David's own testimony: *He drew me up from the pit of destruction... and set my feet upon a rock* (Psalm 40:2). "Down in the Water" is the baptism dive, *buried with Him... so that we too might walk in newness of life* (Romans 6:4). "La Mesa Tiene Mi Lugar" is the first time you realize the communion table has a place set with your name on it, and Cristo Himself is the Host.

And then the record does what a good party does. It does not keep the celebration for itself. "Toma el Micrófono Tú," *You Take the Mic Now,* is the moment the one who was just presented turns around and hands the microphone to the next trembling teenager, saying *yo te tengo*. I've got you. The chain does not break. And the finale, "Vamos al Mundo," sends the whole thing out the door: *twelve songs ago the party began, and now we're going to the world.* The fiesta was never meant to stay in the room. It was always meant to be carried into the office, the school, the neighbor's house.
For the one who thinks they missed the party
I made this for the person who believes joy belongs to everybody else.

The one who thinks following **Yeshua** is the sober, colorless thing you settle for after the real living is over. Hear me: you have the story backwards. The world's party ends when the lights come up. This one is just getting started, and it runs forever.

I made it for the one who feels too old, who thinks their coming-of-age moment passed them by unnoticed. There is no expiration on being presented. The Father can step to the floor for a fifteen-year-old and a fifty-year-old in the same breath.

And I made it, most of all, for the one who never had a family to present them, no father in the suit, no crowd that showed up, nobody who stood them up in the light and said *this one is mine.* I have news that I would stake my whole ministry on. You have a Father who has been waiting to do exactly that. He knows your name. His Spirit has been leading you home this whole time. And the day you step onto the floor, He will present you to the whole watching world without a shred of shame, *my son, my daughter*, and heaven will do what heaven always does.
It will start the music. *Vamos.* The party is His, and it has your name on it.

pieces.title: The Kingdom Did Not Arrive in a Limousine
pieces.song: El Reino No Vino En Limosina
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful gathering at the edges of a Latin American city, a long shared table stretching down a humble street past where anyone could count, working families with calloused hands raised in praise, a night-shift worker still in uniform welcomed with an embrace, an abuela on a bright floral couch surrounded by neighbors, children laughing, believers of many nations feasting together, warm dignified light, cinematic worship-brand film still, bright and emotive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: The city forgets certain people on purpose, the night-shift worker, the woman on the yellow couch, the ones no program ever counted. This album is my argument, sung in sertanejo, that God did not merely visit the margin. He was already living there when we arrived.

body.text: There is a woman named Doña Carmen. She is a composite of a hundred real ones, and she has a yellow floral couch in a little barrio chapel, and on the arm of that couch sits a Bible worn soft and a prayer list pinned where she won't lose it. The city she lives in does not know she exists. No census of importance has ever counted her. No program ever put her name on a slide. And she has been holding that whole neighborhood together with intercession for thirty years.

I wrote a record about her, and about everyone like her. **Dios en el Margen**, *God in the Margin*, is that record. And the thesis is not the polite one the church usually offers. We usually say God *reaches down* to the margin, God *sends help* to the margin, as if the center were where He lives and the edge were where He does outreach. I am telling you something more dangerous and more true: **Yeshua** was *already in the margin* when the rest of us finally showed up. He never left. He was born there.
What the title means

*Dios en el Margen* means "God in the Margin", the margin being the edge of the page, the part the eye skips, the place the city forgets on purpose. The people who live there in my songs are specific: the night-shift worker clocking out at 6:32 in the morning with his boots heavy, the man selling honest work for honest pay, the grandmother on the couch, *"los nombres que la ciudad olvidó"*, the names the city forgot.

I set the whole thing to sertanejo, the Brazilian countryside music of *dueto* harmony, two male voices singing in thirds and sixths like brothers who have worked the same field. I did that because sertanejo is not city music. It is the music of the people the city drives past. The viola caipira, the accordion warm as fresh bread, this is the sound of the overlooked, and I wanted the overlooked to hear their own music carrying the highest news there is.
Why I had to make it
Because I got tired of a gospel that treated poor people as a *project* instead of *family.*

There is a track on this album called "Familia, No Proyecto", *Family, Not a Project*, and it is the beating heart of the whole thing. The handshake you give a project turns into an embrace you give a family, and the difference is everything. The margin does not need to be *studied.* It needs to be *sat down with.* And when you sit down with it, you discover **Yeshua** got there before you.

He told us this plainly. He stood up and said, *"Blessed be ye poor: for yours is the kingdom of God"* (Luke 6:20). Not *blessed are the poor because one day we'll get around to them.* Theirs *is* the Kingdom. Present tense. It already belongs to them. That is why one of the songs is simply called "El Reino Pertenece a Ellos", *the Kingdom Belongs to Them*, and it modulates up a whole key right at the twist, because the twist is the good news itself.
The song that names the whole record
The title I would put over this entire album is a track called "El Reino No Vino En Limosina", *the Kingdom did not come in a limousine.*

Think about how **Yeshua** actually arrived. He *"humbled himself"* (Philippians 2), He was laid in a feed trough, He grew up on a dust road, He had nowhere to lay His head. The King of everything skipped the motorcade entirely. He came in on foot, in the dust, at the level of the people the parade route never passes. So when I sing that the Kingdom did not come in a limousine, I am not being clever. I am reading you the birth certificate.

And if that is how the King came, then that is where the King still is. Not idling at the front gate of the nice part of town. Out at the margin, on foot, knocking on the doors nobody official ever knocks on.
The table, and the door
Two images run through the middle of this album, and they are the two images I would build a whole ministry on.

The first is the door. "La Puerta Abierta," the *Posada Anthem*, reaches back to our old Christmas tradition of the posada, the reenactment where Mary and Joseph go door to door looking for room. I flipped it. In my version the door *opens.* It leans on Hebrews 13:2, *"Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares."* Every stranger at the door might be carrying more of heaven than you are. Open it.

The second is the table. "La Mesa Está Servida", *the Table Is Set*, and "El Pan Partido," the broken bread, the leftovers from when **Yeshua** fed thousands out of a boy's lunch and *twelve baskets were left over* (Matthew 14). The Kingdom's table has a way of stretching past the number of people you counted. You set it for the ones you invited, and it feeds the ones you forgot. That is not bad planning. That is how His table has always worked.
Set the table longer than your guest list. The Kingdom always eats past the count.
The saints nobody canonized

There is a song near the end called "Santos Que Nadie Llamó Santos", *Saints Nobody Called Saints.* The night-shift cleaner. The grandmother on the couch. The man with calloused hands who was made in the image of God and never once got told so. I put them inside Hebrews 11, that long roll of the faithful, because the writer of Hebrews ran out of room and just said *"time would fail me to tell"* of all of them. Heaven's list of the faithful is longer than earth's list of the famous, and the two lists barely overlap.

"Trabajo Honrado", *Honest Work*, sings that man's dignity back to him, straight from Genesis: he is made in the image of the Maker (Genesis 1:27), and his calloused hands are not a mark of his lowness but a signature of his likeness to a God who also builds.
Who this album is for

This one is for the barrio chapel with the folding chairs. For the worker who clocks out when the rest of the city clocks in. For Doña Carmen and her yellow couch and her pinned-up prayer list. For every believer the church has quietly filed under *outreach* when God has already filed them under *family.*

And it is for the rest of us, the ones who assumed the center was where God lived. Come out to the edge of the page. Come sit on the couch. Come eat at the table that stretches past the count. He is already here. He never came in a limousine, and He never will. He came on foot, into the margin, and He is still here, and *"aquí está el reino"*, here is the Kingdom.
Pull up a chair. There's room. There was always room.

pieces.title: The Ones We Remember Are More Alive Than We Are
pieces.imagePrompt: A luminous evening remembrance turning into resurrection joy, a Latino family around a candlelit ofrenda with marigold petals and framed photographs, faces shifting from tender grief to radiant hope, a mariachi ensemble with trumpets raised, believers of many nations with hands lifted, warm marigold-orange light and candle glow, a sense of dawn breaking over a cemetery, cinematic worship-brand film still, emotive and bright, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: Every November my people light candles, lay marigold paths, and set out photographs for the ones who have gone. I did not want to erase that ache. I wanted to answer it. This album takes the Day of the Dead and, with a full mariachi and a trumpet blast, turns it toward the Day of the Living.

body.text: Every year in early November, my people go to the cemetery. We bring flowers the color of fire, *cempasúchil,* the marigold, and we lay the petals in a path, because the old belief is that the scent guides the dead back home for one night. We set out photographs. We light candles in a semicircle. We tell the stories again. We laugh and we cry at the same table, and it is one of the most beautiful and most aching things my culture does.

I did not want to argue my people out of that ache. The ache is *love,* and love is holy. But I could not stand to leave it unanswered either, because I know something about where the dead in **Yeshua** actually are, and it is so much better than a path of petals could ever promise.

**Vivos en Cristo**, *Alive in Christ*, is the album I made to answer the ache. I set it to full mariachi, violins and vihuela and guitarrón and the trumpet, because if I am going to sing you the resurrection I am not going to whisper it. I am going to blow the horn.
What the title means
*Vivos en Cristo* means "Alive in Christ." The subtitle of the closing song says it even plainer, *Los Santos Viven,* the saints *live.* Present tense. Right now.

The whole record is built as a turn, the Day of the Dead becoming the Day of the Living. There is literally a song in the middle called "El Día de los Vivos," the Day of the Living, and everything before it is walking toward that pivot and everything after it is dancing away from it. Because for the believer, death is not the end of the story. Paul said it without flinching: *"For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain"* (Philippians 1:21). *Gain.* Not loss. The song that carries that verse, "Morir es Ganancia," has the whole congregation shouting the phrase back, because it is the most defiant good news a grieving people can sing.
Why I had to make it
Because I have stood at too many gravesides where the only thing on offer was a memory.

A memory is precious, but a memory cannot hold you up at 4:18 in the morning when the grief comes back. I needed to sing something *truer* than memory. So this album leans its full weight on the thing **Yeshua** said standing outside a tomb, four days too late by human reckoning: *"I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live"* (John 11:25). The song "Yo Soy la Resurrección" puts that sentence in His mouth and lets the congregation answer *"vivirá, vivirá"*. He shall live, he shall live, until you believe it in your chest.

I made this record for the aunt who cannot stop crying, and for the grandchild standing in front of the ofrenda looking at a black-and-white photo of an abuelo in his white guayabera. There is a song for exactly that, "Abuelo's Photo on the Ofrenda", and the testimony under it is that Cristo held that old man's hand as he crossed over. The photo is not all that is left of him. He himself is more alive right now than the grandchild staring at his picture.
The songs, and the shape of the hope

The album starts in restraint. The opener, "El Cementerio en Noviembre," deliberately holds the trumpet back, a mariachi record with *no trumpet* on track one, because there is a reverence you owe the graveside before you are allowed to celebrate. "Los Cempasúchiles" walks the marigold path. "Te Recordamos" says *we remember*, but it adds the two words that change everything: *with hope.*
Then the turn comes, and the trumpet is finally allowed in, and the whole thing lifts.

"Lejos del Cuerpo, Cerca del Señor" takes its title straight from Paul, *"absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord"* (2 Corinthians 5:8). That is the actual address of the believing dead. Not wandering. Not waiting by a petal path for one night a year. *Present with the Lord.* Home already.

"La Gran Nube de Testigos" pulls in Hebrews 12:1, that *"great cloud of witnesses"*, and I staged it like a stadium, because that is what the passage describes: a packed arena of the faithful who ran their race and are now cheering ours. Your abuela is not gone. She is in the stands. She is *loud.*

And then the two songs I wrote to be shouted at a funeral until the funeral changes its mind. "La Trompeta Sonará", the trumpet shall sound, from Paul's promise that *"the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible"* (1 Corinthians 15:52). And "Dónde Está, Muerte, Tu Aguijón," where the whole congregation taunts the grave with Paul's own words: *"O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?"* (1 Corinthians 15:55). I gave the trumpets a call-and-response on that taunt on purpose. Death does not get the last word on this record. It gets *mocked.*
We do not gather to say goodbye. We gather to say *hasta luego*, until later, because in Christ there is a later, and the later never ends.
What I am not saying

Let me be honest and careful, because I love the truth more than I love the tradition. I am not telling you the marigold petals bring anyone back. I am not telling you to pray to the dead. The dead in **Yeshua** do not need our petals to find their way. They are already home, already in the presence of **Yahuah**, already more alive than we are. What I *am* doing is taking the beautiful, aching instinct of my people to remember and honor their loved ones, and pointing it at the only place that instinct can finally rest: the empty tomb.
Remember them. Light the candle. Tell the stories. But remember them *forward*, toward the resurrection, not backward toward a grave that Christ has already emptied of its power.
Who this album is for

This one is for the family at the cemetery in November. For the grandchild in front of the ofrenda. For the aunt whose grief is still raw. For every believer who has buried someone they cannot wait to see again.

Play it at the wake. Play it at the graveside. Play it loud. Let the violins mourn for a while, and then let the trumpet come in and tell the truth: the ones we remember are not behind us. They are ahead of us, in the great cloud, cheering, waiting, *alive.* And one day the trumpet on this record is going to be a small echo of a real one, and the graves are going to open, and *los santos*, the saints, are going to stand up and dance.
Until later, then. Not goodbye. *Hasta luego.* We will finish the song together.

pieces.title: Christ Moved Onto Our Block, and the Whole Street Started Singing
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful urban Latino block party at dusk, a church's double doors thrown open spilling light onto the sidewalk, families dancing salsa in the street, a grandmother singing from a third-floor window, teenagers on a stoop joining in, a bodega owner leaning out to listen, string lights and warm lamppost glow, believers of many nations with hands raised in celebration, cinematic worship-brand film still, vibrant and emotive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: The bodega, the laundromat, the stoop, the third-floor window where abuela prays over her coffee, this is the barrio, and I refuse to believe God only shows up once you leave it for somewhere nicer. This salsa record is my testimony that Christ moved onto our block, and the whole street woke up singing.

body.text: Seven o'clock on a summer evening, the lamppost at the corner throws its yellow halo onto the sidewalk, someone is frying platanos, and the church on the block has thrown its double doors wide open so the sound spills straight out onto the street. Up on the third floor, an abuela leans on her windowsill with a cup of coffee and a steady prayer. Down at the corner store, the bodega owner leans out to hear what all the music is about. And on the stoop, a couple of kids with a dented boombox stop what they are doing, because the whole *calle*, the whole street, has started to sing.
That block is where I am from. **La Calle Canta**, *The Street Sings*, is the album I made to prove that God never asked me to leave it.
What the title means

*La Calle Canta* means "The Street Sings." Not the cathedral. Not the arena. The *street*, the sidewalk, the stoop, the fire escape, the laundromat with the flickering fluorescent light and the buzzer at the end of the cycle. I built this record on salsa, on the cowbell and the mambo and the piano montuno, because salsa is the sound of the city barrio, the sound of the block party, the sound that gets people out of their apartments and onto the sidewalk. If the street was going to sing, it was going to sing in the rhythm the street already dances to.

There is a lie the church accidentally taught a lot of us who grew up in the barrio: that you have to *make it out* to get close to God, move up, move away, find a nicer neighborhood with a nicer building. This whole album is my rebuttal. God is not waiting for you in the suburb you cannot afford. He moved onto *your* block.
Why I had to make it
Because of one sentence in the Gospel of John: *"the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us"* (John 1:14).

*Dwelt among us.* He did not visit. He did not commute in from somewhere nicer. He moved in. He took an apartment on the block. That is the truth behind the song "Cristo Es el Vecino Nuevo", *Christ Is the New Neighbor.* He is the one who moved in down the hall, and He knocks on the door, the peephole, the chain, the deadbolt click, and He is *the* neighbor you actually want to let in.

I made this album for everybody the fancy worship playlists forgot. The single mother in her kitchen apron packing a lunchbox at 7 AM. The father with the worn jacket who is out of work and ashamed of it. The teenager on the stoop who thinks nobody is coming to sit with him. I needed them to hear their own laundromat, their own bodega, their own kitchen, sung as holy ground, because it *is.*
The songs, and the streets in them

"Bendición en Cada Puerta", *Blessing on Every Door*, is built on a blood-red doormat that just says *Blessings,* and under it runs the echo of Exodus 12, the night the blood went on the doorposts and death passed over the house. Every door frame in the barrio can be a marked door. The plague passes over the ones He has covered.

"La Lavandería Está Llena de Gloria", *The Laundromat Is Full of Glory*, is maybe my favorite, because it is the least glamorous place I could think of. Fluorescent light, the hum of the dryer, quarters in the slot, a grandmother folding a school uniform. And I am telling you the glory of **Yahuah** fills that room as surely as it ever filled a temple. He is not too holy for the spin cycle. He is *right there* in it.

"Cantamos en la Bodega" takes it to the corner store, the bell on the door, the platanos hanging from the ceiling, the Cuban coffee steaming, the transistor radio behind the counter. I anchored it to the book of Acts, where the gospel got argued out *in the marketplace,* right where people actually buy and sell and live. **Yeshua** is Lord of the marketplace, cowbell and all.

"Los Jóvenes de la Esquina", *The Kids on the Stoop*, is the tender one. The concrete stoop with the chipped corner, the dice on the second step, the streetlight buzzing into dusk. And the whole point of the song is that **Yeshua** *sits down* with those kids. He does not lecture them from across the street. He comes and sits on the step, the same way He always sat down with the ones the respectable people would not touch.

Then "La Cocina de Abuela" slows the whole party down to a bolero-salsa ballad in a grandmother's kitchen, the yellow table with the floral plastic, the rice and beans steaming, a worn Bible open to Psalm 23 with the corner curled from use, her hands folded in prayer beside the salt. *"The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want."* That grandmother has been the reason the whole block held together, and she never once left the kitchen to do it.
The block party is the point

By the time you get to "El Barrio Entero Baila", *The Whole Barrio Dances*, the church doors are open, three old men are leaning on the lamppost with their hats in their hands and tears on their cheeks, the dice game has stopped mid-throw, and the grandmother on the third floor is leaning out her window singing every single word. That is not a fantasy. That is a revival, and revivals in the barrio look like block parties.
Salvation did not ask me to leave my block. It moved onto it, sat on the stoop, filled the laundromat, and turned the whole street into a choir.

And it does not stay put. "Lleva la Bendición", *Carry the Blessing*, sends the whole thing to the next neighborhood, chairs stacked, instruments packed, the bus pulling up to take the joy one block over. Because a street that has learned to sing cannot keep it to one street.
Who this album is for

This one is for the barrio. For the single mother and the out-of-work father and the kid on the stoop. For the abuela in the third-floor window. For everybody who was ever made to feel that God lived in a nicer zip code than the one on their mail.

He does not. He moved onto your block. He is the new neighbor. He is in the laundromat and the bodega and the kitchen and He is sitting right down on your stoop next to you. So open the double doors. Let the sound spill onto the sidewalk. Lean out the window and sing.
The street is singing tonight. It's singing His name. Come out and join it. You already know the words.

pieces.title: The Name the Wind Was Carrying Before the Book Arrived
pieces.song: Grandfather Whispered Yeshua in His Sleep
pieces.imagePrompt: A globally diverse gathering of joyful believers standing on a high wind-swept ridge at dawn, elders and children together with hands lifted toward a breaking golden sky, grass bending in the wind across an open plateau, cinematic worship-brand film still, warm and bright and emotive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I grew up being told my people were found the day a book arrived. This album is my answer, that Yahuah was already speaking His Son's Name across the high country long before any ship, any page, any preacher. He knew us before we knew Him. That is not romance. That is the gospel.

body.text: There is a lie I carried a long time up the mountain, and I want to set it down where you can see it.

The lie is this: that a people are lost until someone hands them a book. That the Creator waits at the edge of the map, arms folded, until the right voice arrives with the right pages. I was raised on the far end of that story, the end where you are supposed to feel grateful you were found, and quietly ashamed of everyone who came before you. This whole album is me climbing back down to tell you the truth I finally heard in the thin air: **Yahuah** was already speaking. He was speaking your Name and His own long before the ship was ever sighted from shore.
Why I Had to Make This One
I did not want to write an argument. I wanted to write a homecoming.

For years I met people, good, faithful, weathered people, who believed their grandparents were in the dark. That the prayers their great-grandmothers lifted at the river bend went nowhere, because the "right words" had not crossed the ocean yet. And every time, something in my chest broke a little, because I do not believe in a God who is late.

The apostle Paul stood on a hill in Athens, looked at an altar inscribed *to an unknown god*, and did not say, "You are lost." He said, in effect, the One you have been reaching for in the dark, *Him I proclaim to you* (Acts 17:23). He told them that in **Yahuah** we live and move and have our being (Acts 17:28). Paul did not bring God to Athens. Paul named the God who was already there.
That verse is the spine of this record. I built twelve songs on it because one was not enough to undo a lifetime of being told you were a stranger to your own Maker.
What the Title Means
*The Word Was Always Speaking.* Not "started speaking." Always.

John opens his Gospel with the oldest sentence there is: *In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God* (John 1:1). Then, four verses of glory later, *the Word became flesh* (John 1:14). The same Word who spoke light into the dark spoke over the high plateau, over the tall grass turning at the crease, over every people on every shore. Paul told the Colossians that in this Son *all things hold together* (Colossians 1:17). If that is true, and I have staked my life on it, then there was never a square foot of this earth where the Word was silent.

So the opener, *The Voice the Wind Carried*, is not a metaphor I invented for a pretty melody. It is a confession: the syllable the wind had spelled was the Name no scribe had yet held. The breath before the book was the same breath.
The Heart Behind the Songs
Let me take you inside three of them, because the doctrine only becomes a home when it has a face.

*They Knew You Before the Ship Sighted Shore* is about a grandmother walking at dawn with a child on her hip, turned toward a fog thicker than the weather knew, carrying a Face she had not seen yet. And underneath the whole song runs the deeper truth that undoes all our pride: *You knew them first. You wrote the note.* We think our reaching is the beginning. It never is. The reaching is already an answer.
Then there is the song this article is named for, and the one I can barely sing without stopping.
Grandfather whispered Yeshua in his sleep,  a Name no one in the family had taught.

I wrote it around an old man at the end of his days, three nights unopened, and then his mouth shaping a sound older than English and older than the old speech, **Yeshua**. The Hebrew name of the Son. A Name he had never heard pronounced, never seen spelled. And the Scripture I laid it on is Joel's promise that *your old men shall dream dreams* (Joel 2:28). I am not asking you to believe every detail of one man's passing. I am asking you to believe in a Spirit who can lay a Name on a tongue no preacher ever reached. Because if He can do that, then no one you love is beyond His speaking.

*The Vision the Elder Saw in 1825* stands on the ledge above the run, where an old man sat ten mornings without food, waiting. The storm came, and the voice was not in the storm. The earthquake came, and the voice was not in it. The fire came, not there either. This is Elijah on Horeb, exactly (1 Kings 19:11-12). *And after the fire a still small voice.* I put my people on that same mountain because the mountain is my lane, and because the God who met Elijah in the thin quiet is not a regional God. He speaks in the low whisper on every high place where a hungry heart will wait for Him.
The Ground It Stands On

I am careful here, so hear me clearly. I am not telling you the old ways were secretly Christianity. I am not baptizing everything a people ever did or believed. Scripture is the judge of all of it, mine included.

What I am telling you is what Hebrews tells me: *Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke*, *and in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son* (Hebrews 1:1-2). Many times. Many ways. One Son. The morning mercies did not begin the day the message arrived by boat; Lamentations says His compassions are *new every morning* (Lamentations 3:22-23), and mornings are older than any of our arrivals. That is why *Before Contact, You Were Faithful* had to be on this record. He was faithful every dawn that ever broke over the dry land, whether or not anyone yet had the breath to say His Name aloud.

And one day, Revelation shows it, *a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, tribe, people, and language*, stands before the Lamb (Revelation 7:9). Every tongue a different door, and He walks through all of them. Your grandmother's tongue is one of those doors. It always was.
Who This Is For
This album is for the one who was made to feel like a latecomer to their own Father's house.

It is for the person who loves **Yeshua** with everything and still carries a quiet grief that the people who raised them "missed it." Hear me: *We Were Not Lost. You Were Already Speaking.* The altar you did not have a Name for was already His. The prayers the wind carried were never lost. He held every one in His hand, the way John saw the golden bowls of incense that are the prayers of the saints (Revelation 5:8).

And it is for the worn-down believer standing on their own high ledge tonight, hungry, waiting through the storm and the fire for a word, sure everyone else got the loud dramatic sign and you got silence. Friend, the silence *is* where He speaks. Keep waiting on the thin still air. The Name is already in the room.

The closer, *The Cloud of Witnesses Sings Too*, is where I finally let the whole mountain sing at once, the grandfather who whispered, the elder who saw, the great-grandfather whose prayer rose like smoke, all of them at the table now, none of them gone, none of them silent (Hebrews 12:1). When you lift your voice, you are not starting the song. You are joining one that has been climbing since before the first ship, and will not stop when the last star burns down.
You were never lost to Him. You were already being spoken. Come up the mountain and hear it.

pieces.title: The Roll Call No Ledger Could Keep
pieces.imagePrompt: A tender multigenerational gathering of globally diverse families reunited in warm open country at golden hour, grandmothers embracing children, people of many nations with faces lit by relief and joy, a small home with an open door behind them, cinematic worship-brand film still, emotive and bright, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: This is the hardest record I have ever made and the one I am most sure of. It is about the children who were sent away, and the Father who counted every face on the platform. I refused to make it a song of despair. Christ never asked anyone to forget, and He keeps the only complete list there has ever been.

body.text: I have to tell you up front that I set out to make this album afraid.

Afraid I would say too much, or too little. Afraid that if I sang about the trains that carried children away, I would leave people in the dark with the grief and never bring them back up into the light. So before I wrote a single line I made myself a rule: every road down into this valley has to end at the Father who was standing on the platform, counting faces. I was not going to leave anyone at the depot. Not the listener. Not the child.
This is that album. It is the heaviest thing I carry, and it is the surest I am of anything I have made.
Why I Could Not Leave This Unsung

There are wounds that families pass down like a folded blanket. You inherit it before you understand what it is. The children who were taken from home and marched into schools designed to erase their names, their language, their songs: that is a wound still living in the bones of people I love. And too often the church has handled it in one of two wrong ways. Either we look away because it is uncomfortable, or we pick at it until the wound itself becomes the only god in the room.

I refused both. I wanted to name what was done, plainly, without pretending it did not happen, and then lift my eyes to the only Shelter that did not fail. That is the exact turn of *The One Who Did Not Protect Me*: *I will not call evil good, and I will not curse him either. I will name what was done*, and look up. Psalm 27 gave me the ground to stand on: *though my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will take me up* (Psalm 27:10). That is not a slogan. On the mountain and in the valley, it is the last handhold when every human one has broken off in your grip.
What the Title Means
*He Remembers Every Child.* Every one. The named and the unnamed.

Somewhere above the iron track, the Father of every child was leaning down, counting each small face looking back, hearing each small mouth still meaning the words they had been forbidden to speak. That image runs through the whole opener, *The Ones Who Were Sent Away*, because it is the difference between a record of despair and a record of hope. Human ledgers were partial. Some were burned. Some were never made. But **Yahuah** keeps a roll no agent ever saw and no fire ever reached.

The title track is the seal on the album: *He has the only complete list there has ever been, the file the agent did not see, the roll only His ink could light.* I hung it on the words of **Yeshua** Himself about the little ones: *their angels always behold the face of my Father* (Matthew 18:10). No child was beneath His notice. Not one.
The Heart Behind the Songs
Let me walk you through the ache and the answer, because they are braided together on purpose.

*He Kept the Count* is about a six-year-old in a barber's chair, feet not reaching the floor, watching hair fall that a grandmother had blessed. And the Scripture that saved that song from being pure grief is small and enormous at once: *even the hairs of your head are all numbered* (Luke 12:7). What they could cut, He had already counted. The floor was full; heaven was not bereft.

*I Hid My Name* undid me. A child whispers the name they were given at sunrise into a closed palm, and holds it for three long years against the school's command. And then the reframe. There was a larger Palm, a wounded one, and the child's name was on the back of it before the child ever learned to fold his own hand.
I was engraved on His palms before I was hidden in mine.
That is Isaiah, word for word: *Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands* (Isaiah 49:16). Nothing they typed on a roll could out-hold that.

And *What the Children Did to Survive*, the smallest things: a pressed leaf folded in a handkerchief, a word whispered against the rule, a piece of bread traded bunk to bunk. I set it beside the midwives of Egypt who feared God and quietly saved the children in a system built to destroy them (Exodus 1). The Father bent above the bunks. Not one small act of survival was wasted. Not one fell.
From the Valley Up to the Light
I promised you I would not leave you in the dark, so here is where the record turns, and it turns hard.

The centerpiece is *Christ Never Asked You to Forget*. This is the hinge of everything I believe about this history. Whatever anyone was told they had to surrender to belong to God, the word for water their grandmother taught them, the song a daughter should inherit, **Yeshua** never asked for it. *The school asked. The policy asked. The agent at the door asked. He did not.* The hands of Christ are not the hands the system used; the cross is the rebuke of every hand that abetted the forgetting. You can be fully His and fully who He made you. He never required the loss. He never has. He never will.

Then come the homecomings. *Returning to the Home I Knew* puts a survivor on the long road back with two names on him, the school's word on his papers, his grandmother's word still folded in his palm, and Christ above the two. And before he reaches the porch, the Father is already running down the road. That is the prodigal's father exactly: *while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and ran* (Luke 15:20). He did not walk. He ran.

*The Song Comes Back in His Mouth* is a grandmother of sixty-three who has not sung the old song since she was six, and a four-year-old who asks one small question, and the Spirit who had been keeping the song all along gives it back. Joel's promise made audible: *I will restore to you the years that the locust has eaten* (Joel 2:25). And *The Keepsake My Grandmother Hid* is a blanket buried behind a cottonwood for forty years, dug up the year a new daughter is born, Jeremiah's word that the children *shall come back to their own border* (Jeremiah 31:17).
Who This Is For
This is for the survivor and the grandchild of the survivor. For the person who carries a grief they did not cause and cannot name.

It is for anyone who has ever wondered whether God was watching when the worst was done. Genesis says a brother's blood cried out *from the ground*, and the Lord heard it (Genesis 4:10), so *The Names the Records Did Not Keep* is sung slowly, with held breath between the syllables, because the God who hears blood from the ground hears every unmarked place on this land. He was not at one of the schools. He was at every one.

And it is for the tired believer who needs to know they are remembered when no one else remembers. That is why the closer, *He Remembers Every Child*, is led by children's voices, gentle, never triumphal, before the whole intergenerational family rises behind them. The roll the Father calls is whole. There is not a child He has forgotten. Not one. And the door is open for every name on it.
Come home. He counted your face on the platform, and He has been holding your place ever since.

pieces.title: The Day the Music Stopped Hurting
pieces.imagePrompt: Globally diverse worshippers on a mountain ridge at sunrise with arms raised toward the first light cresting the peaks, drums and open hands, faces radiant with joy and relief, mist in the valley below, cinematic worship-brand film still, bright and emotive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: Some of us were taught that the drum, the song, the very music in our blood was the enemy's. This album is my reclaiming of it, the morning the Sun of Righteousness rose over the ridge with healing in His wings. The song was never wrong. It was always His good gift. And one morning it stops hurting.

body.text: I want to tell you about a sound that used to make my hand shake.

Not a frightening sound to anyone else. Just music, a rhythm coming across a field. But for years it arrived tied to the worst of what I had lived, and the two came in on the same beat, twenty-six years knotted tight. And then one morning, in a room full of ordinary worship, the knot came loose. The first note landed clean. My hand did not shake. And I understood something I have spent this whole album trying to give away: the music was never the problem. The hand was carrying a wound. And **Yeshua** came to take the wound the sound used to find.
Why I Made This Record

Some of us were taught, with real conviction, by people who loved the Son, that the drum was dangerous. That the old songs, the rhythms carried in our blood, belonged to the enemy and had to be laid down to be holy. My own great-grandfather set the music down out of fear and shame. He did it because he loved Christ, and because he was told it was required.
It was not required. And I could not carry that misunderstanding one more generation.

So *Healing in His Wings* is my reclamation, but I want to be precise about the spirit of it. This is not rebellion; it is restoration. On the song *It Was Always Good* I sing, *we do not hate the ones who taught us wrong; we lay the wrong down and pick up the song.* I name the teaching as wrong. I do not name and shame the teachers. That distinction matters to me more than almost anything on the album, because bitterness is just another wound looking for a beat to ride in on.
What the Title Means
The title comes straight off the page of my grandmother's worn Bible, from the prophet Malachi: *the Sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in his wings* (Malachi 4:2).

There is a play in that verse that never stops thrilling me, the Sun that rises and the Son who rose are, in Him, the same sunrise. *The Healing Has Come* is built on that dawn breaking over the eastern ridge, the first light on the high country, my grandmother's God who is my God, the same One. She prayed for that Sun on her knees; and the morning I sing about is the morning her prayer crested the ridge.

This is where my own mountain comes into it. I am named for a mountain, and I have learned that the high places in Scripture are always healing places, Sinai where the Law was given, Horeb where a broken prophet was fed and met by the still voice, the mount where **Yeshua** was transfigured in light, the hillsides where He withdrew to pray (Luke 5:16). Healing keeps happening on the high ground. The first light finds you there first.
The Heart Behind the Songs
Let me open the record for you, because it is built like a sunrise, dark to dawn to full day.

*The First Light* begins before I have even earned the morning: *the first light of the morning is not mine; the first light is His mercy, new, on time.* That is Lamentations again, *his mercies are new every morning* (Lamentations 3:22-23). The day is His before my mouth is His. I only have to wake into what He already started.

*Heartbeat Under My Own* is the quietest thing here, and maybe the most important. I wrote it about the night my mother died, lying below my own ribcage with my pulse uneven, and hearing, underneath it, another heartbeat, older than my bone. Psalm 139 was open on the floor beside my hand: *you knitted me together in my mother's womb* (Psalm 139:13). When my own strength was flat against the wall, the strength I needed was the deeper pulse inside my chest. *When mine cannot, His can. When His holds, mine is held.*

Then comes the reclaiming center, *It Was Never Wrong*. I stand on Paul's plain word to the Romans, *nothing is unclean in itself* (Romans 14:14), and on the oldest verdict in the Book, from the day the world was made: *and it was very good* (Genesis 1:31). The song was on the list when the world began. It was never the enemy's gift. The teaching was wrong; the worship wears His crown.
Where the Joy Breaks Loose
I did not want this album to end quietly reclaimed. I wanted it to end *dancing.*
You have turned my mourning into dancing.

That is Psalm 30:11, and *Dancing for the Risen One* is where the whole record breaks into the open. The round stone moved. The tomb was disproved. The mourning of three generations finds its answer in the feet of the Risen One, and the joy simply cannot stop. Right beside it, *When the Music Stopped Hurting* tells the truth I opened this letter with, twenty-six years late, but the morning came, because *joy comes with the morning* (Psalm 30:5).

And *The Cross the Old Man Carried* is the testimony I hold closest: an elder who whittles a small wooden cross all winter, and a young woman who comes on a Saturday in March with hands she cannot still, and holds the cross once while the old man prays in the Name of **Yeshua**, and the shaking does not come back. The Carpenter Christ stilling a hand through a carpenter's small carved cross. Whose hand stilled her hand? His. From the start, His.
Who This Is For
This is for the worn-down believer who was made to feel that some good gift in them was too dangerous to bring to God.

It is for the one whose worship got tangled up with a wound, so that the very thing meant to heal you became the thing that hurt. Hear me: the music is not your problem. Bring the wounded hand to the One who takes wounds. He is the Sun rising over your ridge with healing in His wings, and He is patient with a knot that took decades to tie.

And it is for anyone in a dry season, standing on their own high country waiting for the light. *Calling, Lamb Answering* is my picture of it, a lone voice at the canyon edge at dawn, singing the worship a grandmother handed down, and the wind carrying it out, and the Lamb answering, because *my sheep hear my voice* (John 10:27). The song is the call. The wind is the carrier. The Lamb is the answer. You are not shouting into an empty canyon.

The album closes with *The Song Will Not Stop*, because the kingdom of our Lord is *forever and ever* (Revelation 11:15). Past sunset, past this age, past the rolling up of the heavens, the song does not stop, and neither does the healing that started the morning it stopped hurting. Lift your eyes. The first light is already His, and it is already yours.

pieces.title: The Song That Made Two Villages One Again
pieces.imagePrompt: A large joyful gathering of globally diverse Pacific-island families singing together on a green windward coast at golden hour, two groups joined as one with arms around each other, elders and children, ocean and open sky behind them, cinematic worship-brand film still, warm and radiant, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: Lōkahi is the Hawaiian word for oneness, and this album is my prayer that the walls we build would come down under one Aloha, one Lord. It rises to a true-to-life picture of two feuding villages who had not sung together in forty years, brought back to one voice at a dying woman's graveside. This is what Christ does.

body.text: I am a mountain man by name and by nature, but I have spent enough time listening to the music of the islands to know that the ocean preaches a sermon the peaks cannot. The mountain teaches you to climb alone into the quiet. The ocean teaches you that no one crosses it alone. This album is the second sermon.

*Lōkahi* is a Hawaiian word for oneness, harmony, unity, many made one. And I made a whole record around it because I have watched the church, and I have watched families, and I have watched whole peoples build walls so tall and so old that everyone forgets the reason they were ever raised. I wanted to sing those walls down. Not with my strength. With His.
A Word Before I Begin

Let me be honest about who is singing. I am a mixed-heritage believer who loves the music and the heart-language of the Pacific. I do not speak for the Hawaiian people and I claim no authenticity I have not earned. Every island word on this record is used with care and with an English gloss beside it, and every song of praise points to one Person only, never to a wind, never to a sea, never to anything made. I say that plainly because *lōkahi* itself demands honesty; you cannot sing about oneness while quietly taking what is not yours.
With that said, let me tell you why the oneness had to be sung.
What the Title Means
*Lōkahi, one in Him.* Not one in agreement. Not one in blood. One *in Him.*

The whole record stands on two Scriptures. The first is the psalm the opener quotes directly: *Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers dwell in unity* (Psalm 133:1). The second is the prayer **Yeshua** prayed the night before He died, *that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you* (John 17:21). Read that again. Our oneness is not a project we manufacture; it is a participation in the oneness the Father and the Son have always had. That is why every unity song on this album routes through Christ in the middle and never around Him. Take Him out of the center and the circle collapses. He *is* the center that holds.
The Heart Behind the Songs
I built the album out of the everyday pictures of island life, because that is where unity is either real or it is nothing.

*One Canoe, One Crew* is the outrigger, *hoe*, paddle, together or we do not move at all. One side slacks and the whole canoe stalls. Paul's body of Christ, *many members, one body* (1 Corinthians 12), turned into a paddling song, with the Captain who never lost a single soul. *Weave Us Together* is the lauhala, the leaf woven strand by strand by a grandmother's patient hands, one frond alone tears and splits, but woven close it holds a basket's heart. That is Ephesians 4, one body and one faith, and Christ the Weaver who *never wastes a single strand.*

*Lei of Many Flowers* is my picture of gifts that differ, plumeria and pīkake and ʻilima gold, every flower different, but the string runs through them all and they hang as one. *The orchid doesn't envy how the rose was made.* And *The Reef Stands Together* is the one with the turn I love most: a billion coral polyps, each too soft to stand alone, building a reef that breaks the strongest tide, and here is the cinematic truth of it, *the reef that breaks the wave still gives the lagoon its peace.* The unity is not only strength against the storm; it is shelter for the little ones swimming behind it. That is Ecclesiastes, *a threefold cord is not quickly broken* (Ecclesiastes 4:12), with Christ the cornerstone.

And *No Walls in His House* is the reconciliation at the heart of the whole thing, straight out of Ephesians: *he himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down the dividing wall* (Ephesians 2:14). The hand that hammered the wall sky-high is the hand He let be nailed down. Where the wall once stood, there are flowers in bloom.
The Song This Article Is Named For
Every record I make has one song that is the reason for all the others. On this one it is *The Day Two Villages Sang.*

It is a true-to-life picture drawn from the kinds of stories the islands know too well, two small churches on a green windward coast, two valleys that meet, forty years of silence between them over a boundary stone and a word said wrong long ago.
