Neither side would greet the other. And then an old grandmother, a tūtū named Leilani, lay dying, and she called both pastors to her bedside with one last wish:
Sing me home together or don't sing at all.

So two choirs that had not sung together in forty years came stiff and slow to a graveside. One choir started low. The other found the third. And the harmony rose like nothing they had heard, old men who had not spoken gripped each other's hands and wept on the green of the windward land. They buried her to one song, and the two became one ʻohana forever. They built one church on the very boundary stone they had fought over, and carved *John seventeen* into the wood of the door: *that they all may be one.*

I honor Leilani in that song as a faithful witness, not as anyone who saves. **Yahuah** alone reconciles. But He is not above using a dying woman's last request to do what forty years of arguing never could. God alone did what no man could do. Two became one, and the old was made new.
Who This Is For
This is for anyone standing on one side of a wall that has been up so long no one alive remembers laying the first brick.

It is for the church split down the middle, the family that stopped speaking, the two believers who both love **Yeshua** and cannot sit at the same table. Hear the reef: what one alone could never do, the many built together break right through. And hear the canoe: *no man left swimming when the storm comes round. We reach an arm and we pull him to the sound.*

And it is for the worn-down soul who feels like a stranger at the edge of every gathering, back row, outside, second class. *No walls in His house. Come on in.* There is no outside in the Father's house. The dividing wall is already broken low; you only have to walk through the door He is holding open.

The album ends where it began, on purpose, *One in Him Forever*, the log-drum heartbeat that opened the record isolated again at the close so it loops right back to the start. Because that is the shape of it: the multitude from every tribe and tongue, standing as one before the Son (Revelation 7:9), a circle that comes all the way around and does not end. Many islands. One Aloha. One shore.
Come sing the wall down. He has been holding the door the whole time.

pieces.excerpt: Kuleana is the Hawaiian word for your sacred responsibility, the calling that is yours to carry and no one else's. This album is an island-hip-hop charge to the ordinary faithful: sweep the floor like it's the throne room, don't bury the gift, and answer to the Maker alone. It ends with a corner boy named Keoni coming home to his calling.

body.text: Most of the people I most admire will never be famous.

They are the ones who show up. Who sweep the hall in the quiet of the night before anyone comes. Who carry a calling nobody claps for. I made a whole record for them, and I built it out of island hip-hop and reggae-pop over a ʻukulele instead of my usual mountain hush, because a charge this direct needed a beat you could stand up to. This one is not a whisper on the ridge. This one is a shout on the block.

The word at the center of it is *kuleana*, a Hawaiian word for your sacred responsibility, the calling that is yours to carry and no one else's. And the whole album is one message turned twelve ways: do not bury it.
A Word Before I Begin

The same honesty I owe on every island record I owe here. I am a mixed-heritage believer who loves this music and this heart-language; I do not speak for the Hawaiian people and I claim no authenticity I have not earned. The island words are used with care and glossed in plain English, and every line points to **Yeshua** alone. *Kuleana* is too weighty a word to borrow carelessly. So I carry it the way it deserves, as a trust.
What the Title Means
*My Kuleana*, my calling, my sacred charge, mine to own.

It stands on two Scriptures that have shaped my whole life of work. The first is Paul to the Colossians: *whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men* (Colossians 3:23). The second is his word to Corinth: *it is required of stewards that they be found faithful* (1 Corinthians 4:2). Put those together and you get the spine of the title track, *not for the clout, not the likes, not the view*, but *whatever my hand finds, I do it for the King.* The Father handed me a role. Not too big, not too small, just right for my soul. My kuleana is my honor, never my escape.

That is the thing I most want to hand you: your calling is not a burden you got stuck with. It is a dignity you were entrusted with. Nobody else can carry what was set for you, and you cannot carry theirs. That is not a limitation. That is a design.
The Heart Behind the Songs
I wanted this record to preach faithfulness the way real life delivers it, in small, unglamorous, daily pieces.

*Faithful in the Small* is the cornerstone. **Yeshua** said, *one who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much* (Luke 16:10). So I sing about sweeping the floor like it is the throne room, mopping the deck of the canoe with nothing to prove, because the Boss is always watching and He sees the heart. The mountain is made of pebbles, one by one. The harvest is made of faithful mornings in the sun. And the only review I want when I am done is the one from Matthew 25, *well done, good and faithful servant* (Matthew 25:21).

*Hands to the Plow* takes its title straight from the Lord's own words: *no one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom* (Luke 9:62). The row does not dig itself. And I lean on Philippians for the strength to finish, *he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion* (Philippians 1:6). He never gave a calling He will not help you bear.

*Use What He Gave* is the parable of the talents (Matthew 25) turned into a warning I needed myself: the servant who buried his gift out of fear lost the very thing he thought he was protecting. None of us got nothing, that is a lie from below. Find the gift He gave you and let it go. *Carry My Brother* widens the calling outward, because kuleana is not only what I do alone, Paul says *bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ* (Galatians 6:2). And the turn in that song is one I have lived: the day I carried him, he carried me. The strong and the weak keep trading places, and the Christ who carried the heaviest tree carries me carrying my brother.

*Steward of the Land* grounds it in the very first job description humanity ever received, *the LORD God took the man and put him in the garden to work it and keep it* (Genesis 2:15), and Psalm 24, *the earth is the LORD's* (Psalm 24:1). I care for the ground not because it is a god, but because it is a gift, and I want to hand it to the next generation better than I found it. And *Light to My Block* is the reminder that the mission field is where your two feet stand today, *let your light shine before others, that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father* (Matthew 5:16). You do not have to cross an ocean to obey.
The Song That Ties It Together
Every album I make has a testimony at its heart, and on this one it is *Keoni Came Home.*

Keoni is a true-to-life picture of the young man everyone wrote off, dropped out, a record and a count against him, slinging on the corner where the streetlight died, wasting every gift the Maker put inside him. His grandfather prayed for him on his knees every night: *Lord, bring my moʻopuna back into the light.* And in a county cell one day, Keoni could not shake a verse he had heard once, *a steward, prove faithful*, pounding in his head next to a sentence he could not silence: *you got a kuleana that you left for dead.*
He picked up a broom before he ever picked up a mic.

That is the whole gospel of this record in one line. He came home and swept out the hall in the quiet of the night, faithful in the small thing, the corner boy becoming a kuleana man. Now he runs the youth night, telling the lost ones, *I was you, but the Maker called me.* And his grandfather wept in the front row watching the grandson he prayed for preach. The Father ran to meet him on the road, took the weight of every wasted year, and the gift the streets had stolen, Christ gave back whole. I honor the grandfather in that song as a faithful witness who prayed, never as a savior. **Yahuah** alone restores. But He loves to restore through a grandmother's kitchen and a grandfather's knees.
Who This Is For

This is for the faithful nobody claps for. The one showing up when the fire is low and nothing feels inspired, because *the calling ain't a feeling, it's a faithful thing*, Paul's word to *be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord* (1 Corinthians 15:58). *Show Up Anyway* is your anthem. The faithful are not the ones who never doubted. They are the ones who kept showing up.

And it is for the worn-down soul in a dry season who has started to believe their gift is too small or too buried to matter. Hear me: the small thing done in love is never small. Do not bury the talent in the backyard sand. *Pass the Mic* is the reminder that a calling which ends with you is a calling that dies, the kūpuna passed it down so you could stand, and now you hand it to the keiki, hand to hand, with the cloud of witnesses cheering from the shore.

The record ends on *Kuleana for Life*, because this is not a season or a phase. It is a lifelong carry, straight through to the day you hope to hear *well done* from the risen Son. You will answer to the Maker for what you did with the gift in your hand (Romans 14:12), not the gossip, not the applause of men, but Him. And that is not a weight. That is the honor of your life.
Pick it up. It has your name on it, and it always did.

pieces.title: The Wall of Water Was a Doorway All Along
pieces.song: He Made the Sea a Doorway
pieces.imagePrompt: A vast diverse crowd walking forward on dry ground between towering luminous walls of water at dawn, a grandmother holding a small child's hand, faces turning from fear to awe, a woman lifting a tambourine at the far shore, cinematic worship-brand film still, bright and emotive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: Israel stood pinned between Pharaoh's chariots and an ocean with no bridge. What looked like the dead end was the door. I made a whole album on the night the sea cracked open, and on the strange freedom of being told to stand still while Someone else fights.

body.text: Pinned Between the Army and the Ocean

Picture the worst position a rescued people ever stood in. Behind them, six hundred chariots throwing up dust. In front of them, the Red Sea, no boats, no bridge, no shallows. On both flanks, wilderness. Israel had walked out of Egypt free on Friday and by the next morning looked utterly trapped. The math said they were finished.

I have stood in versions of that spot, and so have you. The diagnosis on the counter with the army of what-ifs behind it. The courtroom date. The bills stacked against a wall of water you cannot cross. And the cruelest lie in that moment is the one that says the obstacle in front of you is the end of your story.
I made a whole album about the night that lie drowned. Because what Israel could not see is the thing I most want you to see: **the wall of water was a doorway all along.**
The Strange Command in the Panic

Before the sea ever moved, Moses said something that makes no sense to a cornered heart. Exodus 14 records it: *Do not be afraid. Stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD. The LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be silent.*
Stand still. Of all the instructions to give people with an army bearing down, stand still.
The Lord will fight. You hold your peace. Salvation's near, the chains release.

That is the hinge of the whole record, and it upended how I understand deliverance. We are trained to believe rescue is something we muscle our way into. But at the sea, **Yahuah** did not hand Israel swords. He handed them stillness. The one job of the delivered was to stop striving long enough to watch the Deliverer work. The pillar of cloud slid between them and Pharaoh, and the same God who heard their groaning in Egypt became the wall at their back while He opened the wall in front.
What's Behind You Stays Behind You

There is a song on the record about the rearview mirror, because deliverance is never only about what is ahead. Israel could still hear the chariots. Six hundred of them, wheels loud, dust rising, the entire machinery of their old slavery bearing down. And the pillar of cloud slid in between the army and the people and simply *stood there*, a wall of glory holding the past off the redeemed.
The chorus names it plainly: "What's behind stays behind us. We are walking through the night."

I wrote that verse for the addict on the highway out of last year's house, for the survivor with the paperwork finally settled, for the person who keeps flinching at a life they already left. Pharaoh's army looked enormous in the rearview, but a drowning army cannot drive. The same **Yahuah** who opens the water ahead of you posts Himself between you and everything that used to own you. You do not have to keep turning around. What is behind you stays behind you, because He is standing in the gap you keep trying to guard yourself.
The Warrior Who Does the Fighting

There is a line in the Song of Moses that I built a centerpiece around. After the sea closed over the chariots, Israel sang, *The LORD is a warrior; the LORD is His name*, Exodus 15, verse three. Not *we are warriors.* Not *look what we pulled off.* The LORD is a warrior.
The centerpiece song shouts it back over and over, "He fights the fight we cannot fight; Faithful Father, He wins the night", until the truth sinks past the panic.

I need you to hear the relief in that. So much of religious exhaustion comes from believing the war is ours to win. But the testimony of the sea is that the horse and rider went into the water by a hand that was not human. Later, when King Jehoshaphat faced three armies with no strategy, the prophet told him the same ancient truth, the battle is not yours, but God's, and Judah marched in singing instead of swinging. Praise became the weapon precisely because the fighting belonged to Someone stronger. That is not passivity. That is knowing whose arm actually parts seas.
The Obstacle Was the Exit
Here is the revelation the whole album is built to arrive at, and it still undoes me.

Pharaoh looked at the sea and saw a trap. Israel looked at the sea and saw a wall. But **Yahuah** looked at the very same water and saw a *gate.* The obstacle that was supposed to end them became the road that saved them. The thing in their way was the way out.
What looked like the wall was the way. He made the sea a doorway. He knew the day.

Sit with that against your own impossible water. The counter where the diagnosis sits. The wall of a marriage that looks past saving. The account that will not stretch. What if the barrier you are staring at, convinced it is the terminus of your story, is the exact place God intends to make a doorway? He does not always take the sea away. Sometimes He splits it and walks you through the middle of it on dry ground, so that the very thing that terrified you becomes the testimony you tell forever. He did not trap Israel against the water. He delivered them *to* the door.
Miriam Already Had Her Tambourine

I could not end this record on the far shore without a woman I love. Exodus 15 says that when Israel came up out of the sea, Miriam took a tambourine in her hand, and all the women followed her out with dancing.

She did not wait to process the trauma quietly. She did not schedule the celebration for a more composed season. Sand still wet on her feet, Egypt's smoke still hanging in the air, she picked up the tambourine early and led the women in the shout.
The song leans in with the line I most want you to keep: "Every breakthrough has a tambourine, pick it up, sister; the women are waiting."

That is the posture I want to leave you in. You may be mid-crossing right now, walls of water on your right and your left, heart still pounding from the army behind. Stand still long enough to watch the Warrior work. And when your feet touch the far shore, even before the sand dries, reach for the tambourine. Because the God who split the sea still reigns, forever and ever, and the doorway He made in the impossible was never the exception. It is exactly who He is.

pieces.title: The Altar Can Hold Your Hardest Question
pieces.imagePrompt: A diverse crowd at a night worship gathering with hands open and lifted, some faces streaked with honest tears turning to joy, warm light like flame washing over a multigenerational congregation, a young man and an older woman side by side at an altar rail, cinematic worship-brand film still, bright and emotive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: We keep telling people to leave their doubts at the door of the church. I made an album that says the opposite, bring the question inside, lay it on the altar, and watch what the fire does with it. The upper room was full of people who did not have their answers yet.

body.text: The Worst Advice We Give Doubters

Somewhere along the way the church started handing out a piece of advice that has quietly wounded a generation: *leave your doubts at the door.* Come in clean. Sing like you are sure. Save the questions for a private crisis you will manage alone.

I made a whole album to say the exact opposite. Bring the question *in.* Carry it up the aisle. Lay it on the altar with your name still attached to it. Because the God I serve has never once been threatened by an honest question, and the altar was built to hold heavier things than your certainty.
Bring the question, lay it at the altar. Fire is the answer. Holy Spirit's listening, every doubt a dancer.
That is the thesis of the record, and it starts where the church actually started, with a room full of people who did not have their answers yet.
The Upper Room Was Not Full of Answers

We remember Pentecost for the fire. We forget the ten days before it. Acts tells us that after **Yeshua** ascended, about a hundred and twenty of His followers went back to an upper room and simply waited, devoting themselves to prayer. They did not have a plan. They had a promise they did not fully understand and a thousand unresolved questions about what came next.
They did not leave the room because the answer was slow. They stayed *in* the room with the questions unresolved, and that is where the fire fell.
One line keeps circling back: "Don't leave the room because the answer hasn't come, Spirit at the altar, and the altar is a drum."

I put a whole song on the waiting itself, because I think we have made an idol of the arrival and despised the wait. But the wait is not the enemy of faith; the wait is often the womb of it. The upper room is proof that **Yahuah** does some of His deepest work in the people who are willing to hold a question open long enough for Him to answer it His own way.
Honest, Not Polished

There is a temptation, even at the altar, to dress the prayer up. To translate the rage into something churchier. To swap the real cry for the acceptable one. And the Spirit's answer to that, all through this record, is tender and blunt at once: *tell Me the truth.*
I wrote a verse about that exact reflex: "Tried to dress the prayer in language I didn't believe; the Spirit said, tell Me the truth, let the lies grieve."

Think of the woman in Mark's gospel who had bled for twelve years, twelve years of an unanswered question about her own body, and pushed through a crowd to touch the edge of **Yeshua's** cloak. He did not scold her for the desperation. He called her *daughter* and made her whole. Hebrews says we may approach the throne of grace boldly, not because we have polished ourselves, but because of the One who opened the way. Honesty is not the risk at the altar. Honesty is the whole point of it.
The Silence That Broke Into Yes

The cinematic peak of the album is a moment I still cannot sing without a lump in my throat. It is built on a single line from Romans 8, that the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words. Every question you have ever whispered and could not finish, the Spirit was already carrying to the Father before you found the syllables.
In the song, the whole band drops out. Everything goes silent. And a whisper lands: *every question we have whispered, the Spirit has whispered yes.*
The silence broke open in the middle of the prayer. What we have been asking, Spirit was already there.

Not yes to every demand exactly as we framed it. But yes to the deepest thing under the question, *am I heard? Are You there? Do You see me?* The Spirit's answer to that, spoken over Calvary and Pentecost and every honest altar since, is yes. And in the song, the silence detonates into a stadium of voices, because the moment a soul realizes it was heard all along, the only thing left to do is get loud.
The Fire That Consumes but Does Not Destroy

There is a song near the end of the record about Moses and the burning bush, and I put it there on purpose, because it answers the fear underneath every honest question: *if I bring this to God, will it burn me down?*

Moses was on the back side of the desert, a man full of doubts and a stammer and a past, when he saw a bush wreathed in flame, and the strangest thing was that the fire burned and burned but the bush was not consumed. That is the exact nature of the holy fire I am inviting you into. It is not a fire that reduces you to ash. It is a fire that refines without destroying.
The song says it the way I need to hear it: "Every question consumed, but the listener remains, every doubt refined, every fire kind."

The voice from that bush said, *take your sandals off, this is holy ground*, and then it spoke the great Name: *I AM that I AM.* You can bring the hardest thing you carry into the presence of the great I AM, and the fire will burn away the lie without burning up the you. Doubt handled by God does not incinerate the doubter. It refines them. Take your sandals off. The fire is kind.
From Kindling to Flame

There is a reason I called the record what I called it. The questions are not the opposite of the fire. The questions are the *kindling.* Peter, on the day of Pentecost, stood up and quoted the prophet Joel, that God would pour out His Spirit on sons and daughters, and they would prophesy. The same people who had huddled with their doubts in a locked room walked out and set a city ablaze. The doubt did not disqualify them. Once it was surrendered, it became fuel.
That is the turn the whole record makes: "Question becomes praise, Spirit-set on fire, every doubt is the kindling, every prayer is the choir."

So here is my invitation, and it is the one I most wish someone had given me earlier. Do not perform your certainty. Do not abandon the altar because you arrived with a fistful of hard questions. Bring them. Lay them down where the fire falls. Stand at the burning bush, where the flame consumed but did not destroy, and let **Yahuah** turn the very thing you were afraid to say out loud into the thing that finally sets you free. The altar can hold your hardest question. It was built for exactly that.

pieces.title: I Am the One Part of Creation That Can Hear the Rest
pieces.song: I Am Made Of Listening Dust
pieces.imagePrompt: A diverse group of people standing in awe on a hillside at golden sunrise, arms open toward a sky streaked with light, mountains and trees behind them, a child pointing upward while a grandfather smiles, birds rising over a valley, cinematic worship-brand film still, bright and emotive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: The mountains have been singing longer than I have. The cedars clap, the whales rumble their praise below the range of my ears. But there is one thing they cannot do that I can, hear it. I made an album about being the strangest instrument in creation's choir: dust that was given breath and taught to listen.

body.text: The Sermon I Heard Before the Coffee

I walked outside one morning and the sunrise had already started preaching. A ridge of cumulus across the kitchen window. Light coming up peach over the hill. And before I had poured a single cup of coffee, I had heard a sermon that used no words.

That is not poetry. It is Psalm 19: *The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of His hands. There is no speech, nor are there words, yet their voice goes out through all the earth.* The sky has been talking since the fourth day of Genesis, and it has never once stopped. I built a whole album on the strange, glorious fact that creation is a choir that has been singing far longer than any of us have been alive.
But that is not the part that undid me. The part that undid me is what I realized about *myself* standing in the middle of it.
Everything Is Singing, But Almost Nothing Can Hear

The deeper I got into the record, the more staggering the choir became. Psalm 104 says God plants the cedars; Isaiah says the trees of the field clap their hands. The mountains rise at His command and wear His name across their granite. Out in the deep, the humpback sings at a frequency below what a human ear can even register, a praise going up that I will never hear, but the Father hears every low note of it.
The chorus states the strange arithmetic of it: "Mountains sing but cannot hear; cedars clap but cannot say."

And there it is. The mountain sings, but the mountain cannot hear the cedar next to it. The whale rumbles its praise, but it cannot hear the storm answering back. Every piece of creation is pouring out worship, and almost none of it can perceive the rest of the song. It is the most magnificent choir in the universe, and its members are, in a sense, deaf to one another.
Except one.
The Difference Was Breath

Genesis 2 tells us something happened to one handful of the ground that did not happen to the rest of it. *The LORD God formed the man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life.* The mountains were spoken. The cedars were spoken. But this dust, **Yahuah** leaned down and breathed into it Himself.
The dust was different. Father blew the breath that learns to pray.

That is the whole revelation the album is built to arrive at, and I called the peak of the record after it: *I am made of listening dust.* I am not more valuable than the mountain because I am louder. I am not the lead singer of creation because my voice is better. I am dust, the same stuff as the ridge and the riverbed. But I am dust that was given breath, and breath is what learned to *hear.* I am the one part of creation that can stand in the middle of the choir and actually take it in. The stones sing without knowing it. I get to sing while knowing exactly Whom I am singing to.
The Evening I Heard Him in a Field

There is one song on this record where the wordless sermon of creation becomes a spoken word, because sometimes the God who preaches through the sky decides to preach through it *to you specifically.* It is a testimony about a person at twenty-seven whose company had failed in the spring, who walked out into a hayfield in September just to think, and sat down in the cut grass with the orange light going long across the hill.

And in that field a voice came that did not sound like their own kind of thinking, *clearer than my mind and kinder than my drinking*, and it said: *this is not the ending. This is the ground of the next thing.*
The voice in the song speaks it directly: "This is not your story's ending, this is your ground for the next thing; you are still on it, look at the orange light."

I love that the pulpit was a field and the sermon came with the smell of cut hay and a grasshopper on the knee. Creation is not only a choir singing generally to everyone. Sometimes it is the room **Yahuah** chooses to meet one grieving person in particular. The skies declare His glory to all the earth, and every so often, standing in the middle of that declaration, you hear your own name in it.
Not the Soloist, a Row in the Choir

Here is where it got humbling, and I needed it to. I have spent years as a worship leader with a microphone and a face pointed at a crowd. And somewhere in making this record, the Father gently rearranged my seat.
I am not the soloist, the mountain has been. I am not the conductor, that's the Father at the rim. I am not the audience. There's no audience to win.

The mountains have been holding the alto part longer than I have been alive. The forest ran its dawn chorus every morning before I learned the words. I am not the star of this thing. I am not even the conductor. I am one row in a choir that started long before me and will keep singing long after, and my job is not to be impressive. My job is to *join.* To take the breath I was given and add my voice to a song creation was already singing, and to be the member of the choir that gets the unspeakable privilege of hearing it.
The Song That Will Not Stop

I ended the album where the choir never ends. Because Paul writes in Romans 1 that God's invisible attributes have been clearly seen since the creation of the world, in the things that were made, the sky has been a witness with no excuse for anyone to miss. It was singing before Scripture was written, and it will still be singing past the last page of Revelation.
The closer chants it out past the horizon: "Past the end of every age, skies won't stop; past the last of every page, skies speak out."

So the next time you step outside and the morning is doing something wordless and enormous over the hills, do not just admire it. Recognize what you are standing in. You are inside a choir older than the human race, and you, dust with breath in it, are the one voice in it that can hear the rest and answer back on purpose. That is not a small thing. That is the reason **Yahuah** breathed into the dirt in the first place. Add your row to the song. Everything else already has.

pieces.title: You Were Prayed For Before You Had Ears
pieces.imagePrompt: A warm multigenerational family of diverse background gathered in prayer around a kitchen table at dawn, a grandmother with her hand on a young mother's shoulder, small children with hands folded, an older man smiling with eyes closed, soft golden morning light through the window, cinematic worship-brand film still, bright and emotive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: Someone was praying your name before you had ears to hear it. The floor under your knees was warm because a grandmother knelt there first. I made an album about the prayer chain that runs across generations, the one you were born into, and the one it is now your turn to carry.

body.text: The Prayer That Came Before You Did

Here is a thought that will reorder your whole sense of yourself if you let it land: before you could speak, before you could hear, before you had a name anyone had said out loud, someone was already praying for you.

A mother holding an ultrasound photo up to the kitchen light, whispering your name over a cup of coffee at six in the morning. A father with his hand on the curve of her, asking God to write your story before the first chapter began. **Yahuah** heard those prayers before you had ears to hear anything at all.
The song puts it in a single breath: "He heard her before I had ears; He loved me before there were years."

I made a whole album about that, about the prayer chain you were born into without your permission or your knowledge, and about the strange, holy weight of realizing you are the answer to prayers prayed by people who may already be in glory.
You Are Somebody's Answered Prayer

The testimony at the heart of this record is a scene I cannot shake. A young woman comes home on a college break and walks into her grandmother's kitchen before dawn. The linoleum is still warm where the old woman's knees had been. The Bible is open and smudged at Psalm 22. And the granddaughter kneels down and puts her own knees, for the first time, right into the imprint her grandmother left.
The floor under your knees was warm because I was here first.

Do you understand what that means about your life? You did not arrive on the scene as a self-made spiritual pioneer. You walked onto ground that was already warm. Somewhere behind you is a grandmother in 1952, a father with a worn-out rug in the corner of a room, a mother with a marked-up Bible, people who prayed for a person they would never fully meet. Psalm 145 says one generation shall commend God's works to another. You are downstream of a river of intercession you did not start. The prayers that hedge your life were rising before you knew what prayer was.
The Prayers Do Not Die When the Pray-er Does
This is the revelation the album is built to arrive at, and it is the one that brings comfort to the grieving. We assume that when a praying grandmother dies, her prayers die with her. They do not.

The book of Revelation shows John a scene in the throne room: golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints. Not the prayers of the living saints only, *the prayers of the saints.* Every quiet request she ever made is kept. **Yeshua** did not spend them like a single coin and toss them aside. They are still before the throne.
Grandma went to glory, but the bowls are still on fire. Prayer outlives the pray-er, every word goes higher.

I have watched that truth undo rooms of grieving people. The intercessor you lost is gone from your kitchen, but her prayers are not gone from heaven. That fourteen-year-old cry you whispered decades ago through a broken bedroom door, still rising. The praying is not lost. It accumulates. And some of the answers you are living inside of right now are prayers somebody prayed before you were even born.
The Coal That Never Went Cold

The chain does not only run through your bloodline. There is a song on the record about a fire older than any family, an altar that has never once gone cold in two thousand years. The coal was lit at Pentecost, when tongues of fire settled on the believers in the upper room. And it got carried, hand to hand, into the second-century catacombs, through the nineteenth-century brush-arbor camp meetings, into the twentieth-century gospel choirs, all the way down to a twenty-first-century dorm room where a college student whispers a prayer at midnight.
The chorus carries the fire forward: "The coal was lit at Pentecost; the coal is glowing in my chest, the altar will not rest."

I find enormous courage in that. Whatever you are praying today, you are not praying it into a vacuum. You are adding a coal to a fire that has been burning without interruption since the day the Spirit fell, a fire that survived persecution and exile and every century's worth of people who were sure the faith would not make it. The altar did not cool through any of it. And it is not going to cool on your watch either, because the same Spirit who lit it at Pentecost is the One keeping the embers alive in you.
Now It Is Your Turn to Carry It

But a chain is not just something you receive. It is something you hand on. The album turns, in its final act, from *being prayed for* to *becoming the one who prays*, and it borrows a picture from the prophets to do it.

When Elijah was taken up, his mantle fell, and Elisha picked it up off the ground and carried the same anointing forward. Isaiah describes watchmen on the walls who never keep silent day or night. The prayer chain only continues because, in every generation, somebody bends the same knees on the same kind of floor and takes up the same mantle.
Another song turns it into the charge: "Lay the mantle down, and the next one picks it up to pray, same knees, same God, every age, same place."

That is the sober, beautiful assignment. You were prayed into being. Now there are names, children, nieces, students, strangers at the bus stop, waiting for someone to warm a floor for them the way one was warmed for you.
The Chain Runs Forward, Too

I closed the record looking not backward but ahead, at a great-grandchild none of us will ever meet, kneeling in some kitchen decades from now, prayed for by the same Spirit who prayed us through. The chain does not end at us. It runs forward through people whose faces we will never see.
The final song stretches it forward: "Was, and is, and is to come, the prayer that never stops; generations still pray."

So if you feel spiritually alone today, I want you to reconsider the evidence. You are standing on warm ground. You are living inside answered prayers older than you are. And you are being handed a mantle to carry for someone who is not born yet. Bend the knees. Warm the floor. **Yahuah** heard the ones who came before you, He is holding their prayers in golden bowls right now, and He is not about to let the chain go cold. You were prayed for before you had ears. Go be that for somebody else.

pieces.title: He Didn't Tear the Curtain So You Could Peek
pieces.imagePrompt: A diverse congregation walking forward with hands lifted into a room flooded with warm light, faces lit with wonder and relief, a young woman stepping across a threshold with tears of joy, elders and children together moving toward the light, cinematic worship-brand film still, bright and emotive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: The temple curtain tore the moment Yeshua died, and it tore from the top down, which means no human hand did it. He didn't rip it open so we could nervously peek inside. He tore it for a home. I made an album for everyone who still stands at the back, afraid to walk in.

body.text: The Direction of the Tear Tells the Whole Story

For centuries there was a curtain in the temple, thick, tall, woven blue and scarlet, hanging between the people and the Holy of Holies, the room where the presence of God dwelled. Only one man, one day a year, could go behind it, and not without blood. The message of that curtain was unmistakable: *stay out. You cannot come in here.*

Then, at three in the afternoon on the day **Yeshua** died, Matthew tells us the veil of the temple was torn in two, *from top to bottom.* And that little detail is the sermon. Sixty feet of temple curtain does not rip itself. And it certainly does not tear from the top, where no human hand could reach. The direction gives away the author. This was not man clawing his way up into God's presence. This was heaven reaching down and ripping the barrier open from above.
The song makes the point unmistakable: "The Father's hands made the curtain fall to the ground; the path is open. There's no more middle ground."
I made a whole album on that torn curtain, and the first thing I had to settle was *why.* Why tear it at all?
He Tore It for a Home, Not a Peek

Here is the wrong way to read the torn veil, and it is the way a lot of us secretly carry it: as if God cracked the door so we could cautiously peek inside, hold our breath, and hope we do not get struck for being there.
That is not why He tore it.
He didn't tear the curtain so we'd peek. He didn't tear the curtain for the meek to stay weak. He tore it for a home. He tore it for a heart.

The book of Hebrews says it plainly: we now have boldness to enter the holy place by the blood of **Yeshua**, by a new and living way that He opened for us through the curtain, that is, through His flesh. His own body was the veil that tore so that yours could walk through. He did not open the way so you could stand in the entrance and apologize for existing. He opened it so you could come *home.* The room that was off-limits for the whole history of the world now has your name on the door.
The Woman Who Was Afraid of the Altar

The tender center of the record is a testimony I could not stop thinking about, because it is so many of us. A woman who grew up terrified of the front of the church. The carpeted altar step felt too steep, the brass kneeler rail too holy for hands like hers. She sang about God's presence from the back pew. *Don't touch the ark* was the rule she lived by, until the day the Spirit said, *the curtain is torn, daughter. Walk in.*
Her knees buckled at the step. She braced for the strike she was sure she deserved.
I thought He'd say, "You don't belong." He said, "The curtain is gone, child, and the chair is yours."

He did not strike her. He *held* her. That is the whole difference between religion and the torn veil. Religion keeps you at the rail, hoping not to be turned away. The torn curtain says the Father stood up when you walked in, like He had been waiting in that room the entire time for you to finally believe you were allowed. Hebrews invites us to draw near with confidence, not because we cleaned ourselves up, but because the blood already did.
Not a Peek Through Glass, Face to Face

The album climbs to a moment built on Paul's line in First Corinthians 13, that now we see through a glass dimly, but then face to face. And the revelation at the peak is almost too tender to sing: **Yeshua** is not hiding.
The peak of the record lands there: "He's not hiding. He's standing in the open; the veil is torn, the room is wide and open."

We carry this quiet suspicion that God is elusive, that He tore the curtain but is somehow still tucked away in the dark at the back, difficult to find, reluctant to be seen. The gospel says the opposite. He did not tear the curtain in order to keep residing in the unreachable place. He tore it and stepped into the open. When Moses spoke with God it was face to face, as a man speaks with his friend, and in **Yeshua**, that same access is handed to every believer, north to south, young and old. There is one Mediator, and through Him the throne is not a place you sneak up on. It is a room where the Father's eyes light up when you enter.
What You Behold, You Become

There is a quieter song late on the record where the Father Himself speaks, and it names what actually happens to a person once they stop being afraid of the room. Paul writes in Second Corinthians 3 that when anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is removed, and then all of us, with unveiled faces, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image, from one degree of glory to another.

Read that slowly, because it is the mechanism of the whole Christian life. You are not changed by striving harder at the back of the room. You are changed by *beholding*, by finally walking in and looking at His face.
In the song the Father says it plainly: "Child, what you behold is what you become, keep your eyes on My face, the veil is undone."

That is why the torn curtain matters so much for who you are becoming, not just where you are allowed to stand. As long as the veil kept you at a distance, transformation stayed out of reach. You cannot be changed by a face you are not allowed to see. But the curtain is torn, and now the beholding is yours, and the beholding is the becoming. **Yahuah** is not only letting you into the room. He is remaking you in it, glory to glory, by the simple grace of letting you look.
From the Veil to the Throne

I closed the record on the whole arc compressed into one breath, from the curtain that tore at Calvary to the throne where a formerly-terrified believer now stands. From the carpet step she would not cross to the chair beside His hand. From a room you could enter once a year, if you were the right person, with the right blood, to a daily walking-in.
The finale compresses the whole arc: "From the Holy of Holies once a year, to the daily walking in; veil to throne, bold and steady."

So if you are still standing at the back, still convinced the front of the room is for holier people than you, hear me. The curtain did not tear so you could peek. It tore from the top down, by a hand that was not human, so that you could come all the way in and stay. The chair is yours. The Father is already standing. Walk in.

pieces.title: Your Bank Statement Is a Kind of Confession
pieces.imagePrompt: A warm kitchen table at golden hour where a diverse young woman lays a paper receipt flat and smiles, a coffee cup and a small handwritten list beside her, while behind her a joyful multigenerational Latino family passes plates and a father presses a folded bill into a daughter's hand at a doorway, everyone glowing with generosity and belonging; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, warm amber and honey tones, authentic and alive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I used to think my heart was one thing and my money was another. Then I read my own statement like a diary and realized they were never separate. Where the Money Goes is the album I wrote about the quietest confession any of us make, the one written in receipts.

body.text: I used to believe my heart lived in one room of my life and my money lived in another.

The heart room was where I kept the real me, my loves, my prayers, the people I would die for. The money room was just plumbing. Boring. Numbers. Bills. I would never have said the two were connected, and I certainly would never have called a bank statement a spiritual document. Then one Sunday afternoon I opened my banking app and, half by accident, I read it the way you read a diary, top to bottom, slowly. Coffee for my sister. Books for my mind. Twenty dollars sent to my mama. And it stopped me cold, because I was reading a love letter I did not remember writing.

That afternoon became the whole album. I wrote the thesis almost as a dare to myself: *show me your receipts and I'll show you your soul.* Because it turns out the two rooms were never separate. There is only one room, and the receipt is the confession you make in it without meaning to.
What "Where the Money Goes" Actually Means
The title is not really a question about budgeting. It is a question about worship.

Every dollar you spend is a small vote for what you believe is worth something. String a year of those votes together and you get a portrait more honest than anything you would ever post, because you can curate a feed, but you cannot curate a statement. It has already happened. It is already true. That is why one of the songs is called "Receipts Don't Lie": you can *say* you love your family, but the numbers quietly tell the story of where you actually stood. Not to condemn you. The record is careful about that, the numbers don't judge, but the numbers don't pretend. A receipt is just a mirror that already went off.
Don't tell me you love it if you never paid for it. The heart follows the treasure. It always has.
The Album Is a Room Full of People, Not Numbers
Here is the turn that surprised even me as I wrote it: when you read your spending as love, the money almost disappears and the *people* walk in.

"Coffee for My Sister" is four dollars at a corner shop, pumpkin spice, walked five blocks in the cold and set down at her door, because the receipt was small but the love was tall. "The Lunch I Bought You" is twenty-six dollars at a diner that I would frame if I could, because the lunch was the cheap part and the talk was the gold. And "Show Me Your Calendar" widens the whole thing, because time is a currency too, maybe the truer one. *Where the hours go is where the heart aligns.* You can audit your week the same way you audit your wallet, and it will tell you, gently, who you have actually been choosing.

Then the album reaches its quietest, holiest song, "Dad's Last Twenty." It is a memory of a father who reached into his back pocket on a prom night and pulled out a folded twenty, the only one he had, and pressed it into his daughter's palm with *"for the shoes, mija."* She did not understand until fifteen years later, when she was a parent herself, that he had an empty refrigerator on the other side of that bill. *He skipped his dinner so I could feel like a queen.* Daddy didn't preach. The receipt was the sermon.
The Verse Written Under Every Receipt
Here is the Scripture the whole album is built on, and once you see it you cannot un-see it in your own spending.

**Yeshua** said it in one sentence that has never let me go: *where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.* Notice the direction of it. He did not say put your heart in the right place and your money will follow. He said the opposite, that your heart trails after your treasure like a body after its center of gravity. Which means your spending is not just evidence of what you love; it is one of the ways your love gets *formed*. Move the money toward a person and, over time, your heart leans that direction too. That is terrifying and it is hopeful, both at once.

And He was not impressed by the size of the gift. He watched rich men drop loud sums into the temple treasury, and then a widow put in two tiny copper coins, and He said she gave more than all of them, because she gave out of her poverty everything she had to live on. That is "Dad's Last Twenty" written two thousand years earlier. Heaven does not read the *amount* on the receipt. Heaven reads the *cost*. The folded twenty from an empty wallet weighs more in that ledger than a fortune given from the overflow.

So the album refuses to end in guilt. It ends in freedom, in a song called "Spend It Like You Love." Because the good news underneath all of this is that **Yahuah** is the most generous spender in the universe, the One who gave freely, extravagantly, His very best, and told us that what we've freely received we get to freely give. A generous heart is not a heart that has more. It is a heart that has learned where its treasure lives.
Every dollar is a name, and every name is a kiss. Heaven doesn't read the amount. It reads the love.
Who I Made This For
I made *Where the Money Goes* for anyone who has quietly split their life into a heart room and a money room and hoped no one would connect them.

For the person who says they value their family but can't remember the last thing they spent on them. For the one who feels guilty about money and doesn't know that guilt was never the point, alignment is. For the dad with the folded twenty and the empty fridge, who thinks nobody sees the cost. For everyone who has been managing their finances but never once let their receipts preach back to them.

Read your statement like a love letter this week. Read your calendar the same way. You will find the truth about your own heart sitting right there in the small purchases, and it is not a verdict. It is an invitation. Move a little more of your treasure toward the people and the God you say you love, and watch your heart follow it home. Pay what you love. The receipt is the confession, and grace is standing at the register.
Mira, spend it like you love.

pieces.title: The Feeling Arrived Before the Word Did
pieces.imagePrompt: A diverse young woman dancing slowly alone in a fog-lit apartment at dawn, eyes closed and at peace, hand over her heart, soft light through a misted window; around the scene other people in quiet in-between moments, someone journaling a blank page, someone breathing on a train, a friend sitting with another in comfortable silence, all held and unhurried and unafraid; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, warm amber and honey tones, authentic and alive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: There are seasons where something real arrives in you and the dictionary just goes gray, no name for it yet, only the weight. No Word for It Yet is the album I wrote for the in-between, and for the quiet mercy that heaven hears the prayers we cannot spell.

body.text: Something arrived in me one day, and the dictionary went gray.

I don't have a better way to say it, which is fitting, because that was exactly the problem. There was a real thing in my chest, a weight, a color, a weather, and every word I reached for slid off it. I opened the notes app and typed nothing. I stared at the blank page like it owed me an answer. I kept grabbing for the line and the line kept moving with my mind. And the culture I live in has no patience for that. It wants you to name it, brand it, caption it, and move on. But some things do not come with a name attached. They come first, and the word comes later, if it comes at all.
That gap is where the whole album lives. I wrote the first line as a confession and a small act of defiance: *I got no word for it yet, but I'm gonna dance til I do.*
What "No Word for It Yet" Actually Means
The key word in the title is not "no." It is "yet."

I did not want to write an album about being lost. I wanted to write one about being *in process*, which is a completely different thing that looks almost identical from the outside. Lost says the thing will never resolve. *Yet* says it hasn't resolved so far, and that is allowed. So the record is a permission slip for the season when you cannot explain yourself, not even to yourself. When someone asks how you are and the honest answer is a shape with no name. The songs give that shape somewhere to stand. "The Feeling Has No Door" is about knocking on your own inside wall and finding no frame to it, *no door, no name, but it's here in the hallway just the same.* "Color With No Number" is the paint chip the chart forgot to print, honored anyway: *don't need a name to honor what I see.*
The feeling is often older than the language we use for it. Not knowing the word is not the same as not being real.
The Album Is a Slow Turn From Chasing to Receiving
The middle of the record is where I stopped fighting the fog and started trusting it.

"Half-Time Heart" is about keeping your own slow pulse inside a world that counts double-time, a whole song about Sabbath pace disguised as a drum-and-bass track, learning to *slow down inside the storm* until the storm becomes something you can stand in. "The Almost Word" is the fox in the fog, the thing on the tip of your tongue that runs when you chase it, and the surrender that finally catches it: *I'll catch it when I let it go.* And then the hinge of the whole album, a song called "Stop Asking, Start Listening." It is about a year of hurling questions at the ceiling, journaling pages of question marks, asking until my mouth was sore, and the night I finally sat down on the kitchen floor at midnight and heard the answer in the silence between two breaths. *I stopped chasing the word, and the word started walking toward me.*

The tenderest song is the peak, "The In-Between." It is a funeral program still in a wallet six months later, a 2 a.m. mirror, a season with no name because grief doesn't hand you one. And the line I most needed to sing: *it's not the end, it's not the start. It's the place that re-shapes the heart.* Some seasons are not detours between two named things. They are the workshop where you are quietly being remade.
The Verse in the Wordless Place
Here is the Scripture the whole album is leaning on, and it is the one that made me brave enough to write it.

I grew up thinking prayer required the right words, that if I couldn't articulate it, I couldn't bring it. And then I really sat with what Paul wrote to the believers in Rome: that the Spirit helps us in our weakness, because *we do not know what to pray for as we ought*, and that the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words. Sit with that. The Bible names a category of prayer that has no vocabulary. Wordless groans. The exact thing I was ashamed of, that I had a feeling with no language, is not a failure of faith. It is a described, honored, Spirit-carried form of prayer. Heaven has a channel for the prayers you cannot spell.

That is why the record trusts the pause instead of panicking in it. There is a line in an old psalm, *be still, and know that I am God*, and stillness there is not passivity, it is a kind of knowing that comes only when you stop striving to name everything. **Yahuah** is not waiting for you to compose the perfect sentence before He'll listen. He was already listening in the fog, already translating the groan, already forming the word inside you before you could hear it. The last song is called "I'll Name It Tomorrow," and it is a trust-fall: *the word will arrive. I trust the trance.* The vocabulary is coming. It was already in you, waiting to appear.
The prayer with no words is still a prayer. He hears the groan and knows the whole of it, long before you find the sentence.
Who I Made This For
I made *No Word for It Yet* for the person in a season they cannot explain.

For the one typing nothing into a blank note at midnight. For anyone grieving something with no clean name, living in the in-between and afraid the fog means they are broken. For the person who thinks a prayer doesn't count unless it's articulate. For everyone who has been told to have it all figured out and just, quietly, does not.

You are allowed to not know the word yet. The feeling arrived before the language, and that does not make it less true. It might make it more true, older and deeper than anything you could caption. So slow your heart inside the storm. Stop chasing the word and let it walk toward you. And know that the One who searches the fog is already holding the thing you can't name, already interceding with groans too deep for words, already forming tomorrow's vocabulary in the quiet of your chest. You are not lost. You are being re-shaped in the in-between.
No word for it yet. I'll name it tomorrow.

pieces.title: Heaven Doesn't Sleep Through the Night Shift
pieces.imagePrompt: A diverse night-shift nurse in scrubs pausing to smile in a softly glowing hospital corridor at 3 a.m., and around the frame other unseen night workers held in warm light, a security guard on rounds, a bus driver on an empty road at dawn, a young mother swaying with a baby by a nursery window, a janitor and a toll attendant nodding to each other, dignity and quiet holiness on every face; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, warm amber and honey tones, authentic and alive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: While the world sleeps, a whole hidden congregation keeps it running, nurses, guards, drivers, night-feeding mothers. Three A.M. Saints is the album I wrote to put a halo on the name tag, and to say the thing the dark most needs to hear: heaven is awake with you.

body.text: There is a whole congregation that meets at three in the morning, and almost no one knows it exists.

They do not gather in a building. They are scattered across a sleeping city, the nurse on the polished floor of room 412, the guard watching sixteen screens, the driver on an empty highway at first light, the mother on the nursery rug with a baby in her arms and cold coffee at her side. The world is on pause. The applause is off. And they keep the wheel turning anyway, in the dark, for people who will wake up tomorrow and never know their names. I have loved these people my whole life, and one night I realized nobody had written them a hymn. So I did. I wrote the first line like a benediction over the badge: *heaven knows the hours we put in the darkness.*
What "Three A.M. Saints" Actually Means
I chose the word "saints" on purpose, and I did not choose it lightly.

We reserve that word for the stained-glass few, the spectacular holy. But the oldest meaning of it is simpler and far more generous: a saint is just someone set apart, someone doing sacred work whether or not anyone claps. And there is a particular sacredness to labor that happens where no one can see it, the work with no audience, no spotlight, no recognition beyond a time card and a fluorescent hum. So the album puts a halo where the world would never think to look. *Halo on a name tag, halo on a badge, halo on the lunchbox at the bus pad.* Because the hours you keep in the dark are not lesser hours. They might be the holiest ones you have, precisely because you are the only one who knows you kept them well.
The world doesn't see it. But the work you do where no one is watching is the truest measure of who you are.
The Album Is a Shift, Start to Sunrise
I built the record to move like a real night, clock-in to clock-out, because I wanted it to walk beside somebody through the actual hours.

It starts with the badge clipped and the boots tied at eleven, duty calling, *me llama el deber.* It rolls through "Coffee at Two," the break-room Bunn machine and the styrofoam savior getting you to the far side of the wall. It salutes the nurses in "Hospital Glow", *healing in the hands, holding in the land*, the ones who whisper "you're gonna be just fine" to a stranger at three on the dot. It honors the guard walking an empty lot with a flashlight, keeping watch over a world that will never thank him: *quiet hero work, unseen.*

There is "Coffee at Two" for the second wind and the co-worker who clinks your cup and says salud in the break room. There is "Two-Cup Breakfast" for the strange dawn when your shift is over but your body is still on, eggs cold, family asleep, the kitchen finally yours, *empty kitchen, full heart, that's the night-shift art.* And it has a song for the drive home that only night workers understand, "Empty Highway Home," six a.m., sun not up yet, the toll attendant's nod through the glass, the strange fellowship of the few who are awake. *Bus driver wave, gas station glow, that's how I know I'm not alone.* But the heart of the record is "Mama on the Floor," 3:17 a.m. on a nursery rug, an off-key lullaby sung by someone too tired for the tune, singing anyway because it's the only thing she can do. It carries the line the whole album exists to say: *nadie te ve, pero el cielo te ve*. Nobody sees you, but heaven sees the holy thing you are.
The Verse Awake in the Dark
Here is the Scripture the whole album is built on, and it is the most comforting thing I know to tell a night-shift saint.

**Yeshua** taught that there is a Father who *sees in secret*, who watches the good done quietly, off-stage, with no witnesses, and that this hidden seeing is the reward that matters. The night shift is the most literal version of that promise I can imagine. The work you do at three in the morning is not invisible to everyone. It is only invisible to us. And Scripture also says that whatever you do, you can do it heartily, as unto the Lord and not for people, which means the clock-in itself can be an act of worship, the twelve-hour stand an offering, the folded lunch a liturgy. You are not just keeping a wheel turning. You are, in the deepest sense, keeping it turning *for Him.*

But the line that undoes me most is the promise in the psalm about the One who watches over you, that *He who keeps you will neither slumber nor sleep.* Think about what that means for the person reading this at 3 a.m. You are not the only one awake. The One keeping you never once closes His eyes; there is no night shift in heaven because heaven never goes off duty. So while you keep watch over a sleeping ward, a quiet lot, a fevered child, **Yahuah** is keeping watch over you, wide awake, through every hour the daylight ignored. You have never once kept the night alone.
Nobody sees you, but heaven sees. And the One who keeps you does not sleep, so you have never held the dark by yourself.
Who I Made This For
I made *Three A.M. Saints* for everyone the daylight world overlooks.

For the nurse and the guard and the trucker and the janitor and the baker and the dispatcher. For the mother on the floor at three-seventeen who feels like the whole world depends on her and no one can see her holding it up. For the person who apologizes for being tired, for being "behind," for living on a different clock, and needs to hear there is nothing to apologize for. *Sin disculpa.* You are not behind. You are on a sacred and different time.

You do not need a stage. You had the floor. And when the sunrise finally comes and you hand off the light to the day crew, *buenos días, have a good one*, know that the hours you kept in the dark were seen, and counted, and called holy by the only audience that finally matters. Put your head down at dawn in peace. Heaven was awake the whole time, keeping watch over the ones who keep watch.
Three A.M. saints. Heaven never slept.

pieces.title: Home Turned Out to Be a Verb
pieces.imagePrompt: A diverse young woman lying peacefully on the hardwood floor of a nearly empty sunlit apartment on moving day, a single suitcase by the door, smiling up at walls washed in warm morning light with faint height-marks on the doorframe; through the window a new front door waits, and glimpses of the life the room once held, friends around a small kitchen table, a cat on a window seat, glow softly in memory; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, warm amber and honey tones, authentic and alive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I thought home was the address I was about to leave. On the last night, lying on the empty floor, I understood it was never the building at all. The Apartment is the album I wrote about the walls that witnessed my becoming, and the home you carry out the door with you.

body.text: On my last night in that apartment I slept on the floor, because the bed was already gone.

The rooms were empty and enormous the way rooms only get when you're leaving them. The radiator clicked in the corner like a metronome keeping time for nothing. There was a suitcase by the door waiting for morning, and there was the doorframe with the faint height-marks still penciled into it from a season I could barely remember starting. And lying there on the bare hardwood at 11:47, I felt the whole place saying the years back to me. Every corner held a chapter I had never given a name. That night is the entire album. I wrote it as a thank-you note to a building, and by the end, I understood I had gotten the whole thing backwards.
What "The Apartment" Actually Means
For most of the record I sing to the apartment like it is the hero of the story, the keeper of my memories, the witness to who I was becoming.

And it was. The walls don't talk, but the walls were listening the whole time. "The Kitchen Knew" is about the tile with the chip by the fridge and the knife that learned my grip, the place I burned a year of toast and slowly became someone who could host a table, *every breakfast made me a little more myself.* "The Window Seat" is the faded cushion where I read a thousand evenings and, living alone for the first time, discovered I had become someone who looked forward to her own company. There is "The Kitchen Knew" for the meals that made me, and "The Last Night" for the empty-room gratitude, and a whole song for the bathroom mirror that heard more of my true voice than any stage ever did. The apartment held all of it. It was a real witness to a real becoming, the plaster quietly keeping every chapter I never bothered to name.
But the title is a trick I set for myself, and the record springs it at the very end. Because the last song is not called "The Apartment." It is called "Home Was a Verb."
The walls don't speak, but the walls remember. And what they remember is not a building. It's who you became inside them.
The Album Is a Move-Out That Becomes a Revelation
The turn happens in the peak, a song called "The Last Night", the empty-room gratitude, the radiator, the suitcase, the whole place wrapping its arms around the years as I lay on the floor.

And what I realized on that floor is the thing the whole album had been walking toward: I was not losing home. I could not lose it, because it had never been the square footage. Home was everything that *happened* there, the hosting, the healing, the becoming, the being-known by my own four walls. And all of that was leaving with me. It was already packed, invisibly, in the suitcase by the door. So the closing songs stop grieving and start carrying. "Carry the Walls" is exactly what it sounds like, the discovery that the architecture I loved was interior all along. "Next Front Door" turns the whole ache into propulsion, toward a threshold I hadn't crossed yet. And "Home Was a Verb" lands the plane: home is not a place you live. It is a thing you *do*, a way of loving, tending, becoming, and being-with. You don't leave it behind. You take it with you and you build it again.
The Verse Under the Floorboards
Here is the Scripture the whole album is quietly resting on, and it reframes every move any of us will ever make.

The people of faith in the Bible were, almost to a person, tent-dwellers. Scripture says Abraham lived in tents his whole life, in a land he'd been promised but never fully possessed, and it explains why: he was looking forward to *a city with foundations, whose designer and builder is God.* It goes on to say that the faithful confessed they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth, people seeking a homeland, longing for a better country, a heavenly one. That is the theology under this whole album. The reason no apartment ever feels permanent, the reason every home is a little bit temporary, is not a design flaw. It is a homing signal. We were built to carry home and to seek Home at the same time.

And there's a line **Yeshua** spoke on the night before He died, to friends about to lose everything familiar: *in my Father's house are many rooms, and I go to prepare a place for you.* He did not promise them a fixed address. He promised them a place being prepared, a belonging that no move-out could cancel. An old psalm says it plainly too, *unless the LORD builds the house, those who build it labor in vain.* The walls I loved were real, and they witnessed real things. But the One who was actually building me was **Yahuah**, and He does not leave His work in the drywall when the lease ends. He carries it, carries *you*, to the next front door, and the next, all the way to a Home with foundations that finally cannot be left.
Every home is a little temporary on purpose. The ache to belong somewhere permanent is a homing signal pointing at a house being prepared for you.
Who I Made This For
I made *The Apartment* for anyone standing in an empty room on a last night, afraid they're losing the place that made them.

For the person packing boxes with grief in their chest. For the one who thinks that when they close this door, the version of themselves that lived here disappears. For everyone who has confused an address with a home and is scared of the next threshold. And for the pilgrim in all of us who has always felt, underneath every move, a little bit like a stranger looking for a country.

You are not losing home. It was never the building. Everything that made those walls holy, the becoming, the hosting, the being-known, is already in the suitcase, already inside you, ready to be built again at the next front door. So thank the room, and then carry it out with you. Home turned out to be a verb the whole time. And the One who has been building you never once leaves His work behind. He's preparing a place with foundations, and He'll walk you all the way there.
Home was a verb. Carry the walls.

pieces.title: You Can Always Tell Who Has Been Loved
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful diverse street scene at golden hour where love is visibly rippling outward, a young woman laughing on the phone with her mom, a passerby helping an elderly man gather dropped groceries and both smiling, friends hugging at a corner cafe, a grandmother waving from a kitchen window with a jar of soup for a neighbor, warmth spreading person to person down the block; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, warm amber and honey tones, authentic and alive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: We treat love like a risk to be warned about. But when I read the label on the love I'd been given, every single side effect was good. I slept better, called my mom, made a friend of a stranger. Side Effects of Love is the album I wrote about the evidence love leaves behind.

body.text: We hand each other warnings about love like it's a medication that might hurt us.

Guard your heart. Don't get too invested. Read the fine print before you fall. And I understand where the fear comes from, people have been burned. But one ordinary week I decided to actually read the label on the love I had been *given*, the way you'd read a prescription bottle, and I started laughing, because every warning on it was good news. *May cause smiling for a day. May cause peace. May cause sleep. May cause shine.* Side effect one: I called my mama last night. Side effect two: I forgave someone I'd planned to fight. Side effect three: I'm sleeping like a kid. That was the whole album, right there in a joke that turned out to be true. Love does come with a warning sticker. It's just that all the warnings are things you'd want.
What "Side Effects of Love" Actually Means
The title is a reframe, and the reframe is the whole point.

A side effect is something you can measure from the outside, evidence that the medicine is actually in your system. And that turned out to be the truest thing I could say about love: you cannot really see love itself, but you can always see its side effects. You can tell who has been loved by the way they move through a grocery store. Love is not a feeling you announce; it's a change other people notice before you do. So I built the record as a pharmacy label with the danger stripped out. The world sees a warning on the bottle and runs. *Smart folks read it and they take what's done.* Because the wise one knows that when it comes to real love, the warning label is not a threat. It's a promise of exactly the symptoms you've been aching for.
You can't see love. But you can always see its side effects, and that's how you know it was ever really there.
The Album Is a List of Symptoms, and Every One Is a Gift
The middle of the record is just me cataloging the evidence, one joyful symptom at a time.

"Sleep Better" is about three years of not falling asleep before two in the morning, holding a grudge like a clenched fist, and the Tuesday I finally wrote the letter and let it go, and slept eight hours straight the very next night. *The grudge was the alarm, the love is the snooze.* Forgiveness turned out to be a health intervention no doctor could prescribe. "Called My Mom" is a ten-minute phone call about a tomato plant and a bad joke, and the way it left me standing tall the rest of the day. "Helped a Stranger" is an old man's dropped groceries at a corner store, fifteen minutes on a bench, and a friendship I still have, *walked away with a friend I didn't have before.* "Smiling All Day" is the mirror catching me grinning at the sink until a cashier asks if I'm getting married. These are not big miracles. They're symptoms. They're what love looks like once it's actually in your bloodstream.

The heart of the album is the quietest song, "My Grandmother's Hands." She stood at her kitchen window every afternoon, waving at the mailman, keeping a pot of soup on the stove and a brown-paper jar at the door for whichever neighbor needed it. When Mr. Smith got sick, she brought him soup until his eyes cleared. When Mrs. Garcia's husband died, she just showed up and didn't say a thing. *She never once said "love your neighbor" out loud. She just did it every day.* And that is where the record turns from cataloging symptoms to naming the source. Because I finally understood: I was not born generous. I caught it. Her hands taught me the math of a love that expands, and she taught it entirely without words.
The Verse Behind Every Symptom
Here is the Scripture the whole album is quietly built on, and it turns the joke into a theology.

**Yeshua** said you will know people by their fruit, that a good tree cannot help but produce good fruit, and you recognize the tree by what grows on it, not by what it claims. That is "side effects" said two thousand years earlier. You don't detect a loving heart by its announcements; you detect it by the harvest hanging off its branches. And Scripture gives the actual list of fruit that grows when the Spirit is at work in someone, and the very first item is *love*, and right behind it, *joy, peace, patience, kindness.* Read that list next to my album and it's almost embarrassing: sleep better (peace), smiling all day (joy), helped a stranger (kindness). I thought I was writing a fun garage-pop record about good vibes. I was accidentally writing about the fruit of the Spirit.

And there's the deeper question the album keeps circling: where do the symptoms *start*? Because I did not manufacture my own kindness any more than a body manufactures its own medicine. Scripture answers it in one of the plainest sentences in the whole Bible: *we love because He first loved us.* Every ripple has an origin, and the origin is not me. My grandmother's hands were passing along a love she had received, and so am I, and so are you when it's working. That's why the record ends in multiplication, not addition, *one small flame and the whole block is bright.* **Yeshua** said to let your light shine in front of people so they'd see the good and give the glory to your Father. That is the entire strategy of this album. Don't preach the love. Show the symptoms, and let people trace them back to the Source. And the Bible is blunt that this is the real thing: love not with words and speech, but *with actions and in truth.* My grandmother never gave the speech. She gave the soup. **Yahuah** is the love we first received; the soup is just the side effect.
We love because He first loved us. Every ripple has a source, and the soup on the neighbor's doorstep is quietly pointing back to Him.
Who I Made This For
I made *Side Effects of Love* for the person who has been so warned about love that they've forgotten it's good medicine.

For the one still carrying a three-year grudge that's stealing their sleep. For anyone who thinks they're just not a warm person, when the truth is they've never been shown where warmth comes from. For the grandchild who inherited a kindness they've never traced back to its source. For everyone who has been guarding their heart so carefully they've quarantined themselves from the one thing that heals.

Read the label. Don't peel it off, don't run from the warnings. They're all favorable. Forgive the person and get your sleep back. Call your mom on a Tuesday for no reason. Help the stranger and watch a friend appear. And when people ask why you're glowing, you don't have to preach, just let the symptoms show and let them wonder about the Source. You can always tell who has been loved. Go be someone they can tell about.
Side effects of love. Every one of them is a gift.

pieces.title: You Didn't Inherit Their Strength. You Inherited Their God
