pieces.imagePrompt: A radiant multigenerational gathering of African, Caribbean, and diaspora believers in a warm storefront church, grandmothers in white hats, mothers, and children of many nations standing shoulder to shoulder, an old family Bible open, hands lifted, golden light pouring over faces marked by dignity and joy, a great cloud of witnesses feeling; tender, cinematic, premium worship-brand film still; wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: People keep telling me I'm strong like the women who came before me, and for years I let them, because it sounded like honor. Then I made "Ancestral Strength" and had to tell the truth: my grandmother didn't have the strength. She had the God. And He is the only thing I actually inherited.

body.text: People keep telling me I am strong. Strong like my mother. Strong like her mother before her. And for a long time I wore that the way you wear a compliment you have not fully examined, gratefully, and without asking what was underneath it. Then I sat down to make an album about the women who raised me, and the whole thing nearly came apart in my hands, because I realized I was about to tell a lie.
The lie is that strength is something you inherit in the blood. It is not. I made *Ancestral Strength* to say the truer and far better thing.
The Compliment That Was Almost an Idol
Here is the confession at the center of this record, in the song **Same God of My Grandmothers**:
Grandma didn't have the strength. She had the God. Auntie didn't have the strength. She had the God.

I need you to feel how close that sits to something dangerous. In a culture that rightly honors its elders, it is the easiest thing in the world to slide from *honoring* the ancestors to *venerating* them, to start believing that the power to survive was in their genes, their grit, their bloodline, and that I am simply the next strong woman in a strong line. It flatters me. And it is false.

Because I watched these women up close. My grandmother knelt at a storefront-church altar rail until she wore a print into the wood. That was not a woman relying on her own reserves. That was a woman emptying herself before Someone stronger, every single morning, for sixty years. The strength people praise in me was never a family trait passing down the line. It was **Yahuah**, held onto by one generation and handed to the next, not as a bloodline, but as a faith.
What the Bible Actually Puts in the Family Tree

Scripture is careful about this in a way we usually are not. When Paul writes to young Timothy, he does not say, "You come from strong stock." He says he is persuaded of *the unfeigned faith that is in thee, which dwelt first in thy grandmother Lois, and thy mother Eunice* (2 Timothy 1:5). Notice what got handed down. Not temperament. Not toughness. *Faith.* The inheritance was a way of trusting God, carried by real women with names.

That is the whole thesis of the song **Family Tree in the Bible**, the leather-bound King James on the parlor table with four generations of names written inside the cover, and the line that turns the whole thing right side up: *I'm not standing on the strength of bloodlines, I'm standing on the faith that they kept.* The names matter because of the God they trusted, not the other way around.

And this is why, when **Yahuah** wanted to remind His people who He was, He did not point them to their own pedigree. He said, *I am the God of thy father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob* (Exodus 3:6). One God, across three generations of very flawed men. The constant in that sentence was never the patriarchs. It was the God who kept showing up to each of them.
The Songs They Sang in Chains

You cannot make an honest album about African-diaspora heritage and skip the hardest ground, so I did not. **Cotton-Field Hallelujah** and **Wade in the Water Still** reach back to the spirituals, the songs the ancestors lifted where a master could not stop them, *Steal Away to Jesus* hummed low over a Mississippi row, *Go Down Moses* moving down the field.

I want to be precise as a teacher here, because this matters. The power in those songs was never that suffering is noble. Suffering is not noble; it is a wound. The power was that praise turned out to be the one thing chains could not confiscate. When Paul and Silas sat in a Roman prison at midnight, beaten and bound, *they prayed, and sang praises unto God* (Acts 16:25), and the foundations shook. The ancestors knew that secret in their bodies long before I read it in a book. The hallelujah was unchainable because the God it was aimed at was unchainable. Again: the strength was never in them. It was in the One they sang to.
The Cloud Is Cheering, Not the Genes

There is a picture I built the finale around, **Cloud of Witnesses March**, and it comes straight from Hebrews. After a long chapter naming the heroes of faith, the writer says: *Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses... let us run with patience the race that is set before us, looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith* (Hebrews 12:1–2).

Read that carefully. The cloud of witnesses is not there to be worshiped. They are in the stands. The eyes stay fixed on **Yeshua**, the *author* who started the faith in your family and the *finisher* who will complete it. The grandmothers are cheering. They are not the finish line. He is. And the same **Yeshua** who was *the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever* (Hebrews 13:8) for my grandmother at that altar rail is the same for me, which means I am not running on borrowed strength that will eventually run out. I am running to the same God who never has.
Who I Made This For

I made *Ancestral Strength* for the one who is tired of being called strong. For the person carrying a family and a legacy and a quiet fear that when their own strength gives out, the whole line breaks with them. It will not. You were never the source. You were only ever a link, holding on to the same God the ones before you held.

And I made it for the opposite person too, the one estranged from their line, without a praying grandmother in the story, wondering if they missed the inheritance. Hear me. The inheritance was never the bloodline. It is the God. And He is not a family heirloom that only some people get. He is offered, fresh, to you, today, *the same God* who met every generation before you and is standing ready to be met by you.

So when someone tells you that you are strong like the women before you, you can smile and let it pass. Because you and **Yahuah** both know the real testimony. You did not inherit their strength. You inherited their God, and He is the only strength that was ever going to hold.

pieces.title: The Rescue That Came Onto the Dance Floor
pieces.song: He Pulled Me Off the Floor
pieces.imagePrompt: A jubilant Caribbean and diaspora youth congregation worshipping with hands raised in a warm storefront church at night, faces of many nations lit with relief and joy, an older mentor embracing a young person, freedom and belonging radiating from the middle of the room, tambourines and lifted hands; vivid, warm, cinematic, premium worship-brand film still; wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: The lie is that you have to clean yourself up first, walk back to the church door, and hope He'll take you. I made "Dancehall Redemption" because that is not how it happened for anybody I know. He didn't wait at the steeple. He walked out onto the floor, into the strobe and the bass, and pulled us off it, without shaming us.

body.text: The lie goes like this: clean yourself up first. Get your life presentable. Then walk back to the church door and hope God is still willing to take a returning mess. I have watched that lie keep people out in the cold for years. I made *Dancehall Redemption* to burn it down, because it is the exact opposite of how the rescue actually happens.

He does not wait at the steeple for you to come crawling back. He comes out to where you are, into the strobe, into the bass, onto the floor, and He pulls you off it. And here is the part that undoes me every time: He does it without shaming you.
The Night He Walked Into the Noise

The center of this album is a song called **He Pulled Me Off the Floor**, and it is a scene I have lived and watched too many times to count. A club at two in the morning. The sub-bass kicking your rib cage. A tear in your eye you are trying to hide from friends who never notice you leave.
He didn't wait at the church steeple. He walked onto the floor of the people. Reached through the strobe and the bass. He pulled me off, that was grace.

I anchored that on the eighth chapter of John, on the woman they threw at **Yeshua's** feet, caught and humiliated, expecting stones. What did He do? He did not pile on. He straightened up and said, *Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more* (John 8:11). He got her off the ground without adding one ounce of shame to what she was already carrying. That is the God I know. He reached through the crowd and pulled her up, and the reaching was the whole gospel.
Same Bass, Brand-New Heart

People assume an album about the dancehall must be about leaving the culture behind, turning the volume down, trading the riddim for an organ. That is not what happened to me, and it is not what this record says.

The opener, **Kingston Bass Salvation**, tells it straight: *same speakers, same bass, new heart.* When **Yeshua** found me, He did not confiscate the low frequencies. He rewrote what they were pointed at. The energy that used to run toward everything that was quietly killing me. He redirected it, whole, toward Him. That is what **Bass Drop, Soul Stand Up** is about: *same body, brand-new King.* Redemption is not amputation. It is re-aiming.

Because the chains were real, and I name them on **Chains Beneath My Feet**, the drinking chain, the lying chain, the fear chain, each one dragging at the dance. **Yeshua** walked them down to the cross. This is exactly the ministry He announced for Himself when He stood up in the synagogue and read the scroll: *He hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives... to set at liberty them that are bruised* (Luke 4:18, from Isaiah 61). Liberty to the captives. He was never squeamish about where the captives were being held.

And that liberty is not a Saturday-night novelty that fades by Sunday afternoon. **Saved Like Sunday Morning** carries the whole record into daylight, the same person who walked out of the far country now sitting in a pew with the light coming through the windows, made new. Redemption is not just a dramatic rescue in the dark. It is the ordinary Sunday that follows, and every ordinary Tuesday after that, held by the same hand that first reached through the strobe.
The New Name Nobody at the Dance Ever Called You

There is a moment on this record I hold as tenderly as anything I have made, **New Name on the Riddim**. The old name, what the dance crew called you, what your past kept calling you, what you started to believe was the truest thing about you, goes down into the water. And a new one comes up.

That is not a metaphor I invented. **Yeshua** promises the overcomer *a white stone, and in the stone a new name written, which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it* (Revelation 2:17). A name only He and you will ever fully know. Because when a person comes to Him, *old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new* (2 Corinthians 5:17). The bio changes. The story changes. The name the strobe lights knew you by does not get to follow you home.
Old name washed at the cross, new name on the riddim now.
The One at 2:47 in the Morning

The testimony I am most protective of on this album is the quietest one, **Riddim of My Repentance**. It is a real hour: a prodigal walking the long block home at 2:47 in the morning, streetlight low, first whispered prayer rising up before they even reach the door. And the line I built the whole song to deliver: *Jesus meets you where you stand, whether it's the altar or the dancehall sand. He doesn't wait for you to come.*

That is Luke 15, the father who *when he was yet a great way off... ran* (Luke 15:20). He did not stand at the gate with his arms folded, waiting for a proper apology. He ran down the road, undignified, to a son who still smelled like the far country. The running is the point. God is always the one who closes the distance.
Who I Made This For

I made *Dancehall Redemption* for the one who thinks they are too far gone, too deep in it, too many nights into a life they cannot see a way out of. For the returner walking in with the night still warm on their skin, bracing for the church to wince. For anyone who believes the rescue is conditional on cleaning up first.

Hear me, and hear me as a pastor: you have the order backwards, and it is keeping you on the floor. He does not wait for you to get up. He comes down to where you fell, reaches through everything you are ashamed of, and lifts you, and only after you are standing in His arms does the cleaning up begin, and even that He does with you, not to you. That was grace on the dance floor. It is grace right now, wherever you are reading this.
You do not have to make it back to the door. He already walked out to meet you. Let Him pull you off the floor.

pieces.title: The Defiant "Yet" at the Heart of Haiti
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful multigenerational Haitian and diaspora congregation in warm morning light, grandmothers, families, and children of many nations praising with tanbou drums and lifted hands, a Miami-Caribbean kitchen and storefront church glowing gold, faces radiant with resilient hope and defiant joy after hardship; tender, cinematic, premium worship-brand film still; wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: There is one small word that carries the whole weight of a faith that refuses to quit, the word "yet." I made "Haitian Heartbeat" around the tanbou pulse and Habakkuk's impossible sentence, because I have watched a people say "though everything failed, yet I will rejoice," and mean it, and it is the bravest thing I know.

body.text: There is one small word I built a whole album around, and most people read right past it. Three letters. It sits in the middle of one of the boldest sentences in all of Scripture, and everything turns on it. The word is *yet.*

I made *Haitian Heartbeat* to the pulse of the tanbou drum, but its true heartbeat is that word, because I have watched my people say it with their whole chest, in seasons when nothing on paper gave them the right to, and mean it. That "yet" is the bravest thing I know.
The Sentence That Should Not Be Possible

Listen to the prophet Habakkuk, and do not soften it: *Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls: yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation* (Habakkuk 3:17–18).

Count the losses first. The fig tree, the vine, the olive, the field, the flock, the herd, that is not one setback, that is total collapse. Everything a person could lean on for provision and future, gone. And then, at the bottom of the ruin, the word turns: *yet.* I wrote the song **Though the Fig Tree** to walk that exact arc, the verses honest about the empty field, the accordion in a minor key, and then the flip to major on the one line that changes everything: *yet I will rejoice.*
From the "though the fig tree" to the "yet I will rejoice", same chapter, same mouth, same season.
That is the miracle. It is not two different days. It is the same breath. The lament and the joy live in the same sentence, and the joy does not require the circumstances to improve first.
Why This Album Had to Sound Like Haiti

I did not choose the Haitian heartbeat as decoration. I chose it because I do not know another people who preach that verse with their bodies the way the Haitian church does. I want to say this plainly and with honor, and without a trace of the tired pity that so often gets aimed at Haiti: this is a people who have buried more than most nations will ever be asked to, and who still fill storefront churches from Port-au-Prince to Little Haiti to Brooklyn with a praise that could raise the dead.

So the tanbou keeps beating under every song, and the rara horns blast, and the accordion shimmers, and none of it is spectacle. It is theology you can dance to. When I sing **Yet I Will Rejoice** with the diaspora named city by city, Miami, Brooklyn, Boston, Montreal, Port-au-Prince. I am not asking anyone to pretend the fig tree bloomed. I am saying the God of the salvation is bigger than the failed harvest, and the joy is aimed at *Him,* not at the yield.

I want to be clear that the tanbou and the rara belong in the sanctuary. Some have been taught to be ashamed of these instruments, as if the drum itself were suspect. But the psalmist commands the opposite: *praise his name in the dance* (Psalm 149:3). On **Dance With the Tanbou** I hand the drum straight to the King, because a redeemed people do not leave their own rhythms at the door. They carry them in and lay them on the altar. The heartbeat God gave Haiti was always meant to keep time for His praise.
The Joy Is a Person, Not a Mood

Here is where I have to teach carefully, because "just choose joy" can become a cruelty in the wrong mouth. The defiant joy of Habakkuk is not positive thinking. It is not pretending the diagnosis did not come or the visa did not get denied. Habakkuk names the disaster out loud before he rejoices. Honesty comes first.

The joy holds because of *where* it is aimed. Look at how the prophet ends the chapter one verse later: *The LORD God is my strength* (Habakkuk 3:19). The joy does not come from the situation improving; it comes from the God who does not change when the situation gets worse. That is why, on the album's peak, **Heart Inside the Heart**, I stop chasing and start receiving, because I read Galatians 2:20, *Christ liveth in me*, and understood that the rhythm keeping me alive in the dry season was never my own resilience. It was **Yeshua**, beating inside a chest that had run out of its own strength.
Weeping May Endure, But Watch the Morning

I close the record where the whole thing is headed, **Joy Cometh Morning**, and I let two verses carry it home. First, the promise the diaspora has clung to across every crossing: *weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning* (Psalm 30:5). And under it, the mercy that makes each new morning survivable: *they are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness* (Lamentations 3:22–23).

Notice the shape of that hope. It does not deny the night. It says the night is real, and it has a length, and it has an end that God Himself sets. The "yet" of Habakkuk and the "morning" of the psalmist are the same faith facing two directions, one refusing to let go of joy in the dark, the other certain of the dawn. Between them there is no room for despair to take up permanent residence.
Who I Made This For

I made *Haitian Heartbeat* for the one in the silent season, the visa still pending, the diagnosis on the page, the field that yielded nothing this year. For the person who has been told their faith must be weak because they are still in pain, when in truth their faith is doing the hardest thing faith ever does: rejoicing without proof.

You do not have to wait for the fig tree to blossom before you say *yet.* That is the whole point of the word. You say it standing in the empty field, with your losses named honestly and your eyes fixed past them onto the God of your salvation. **Yahuah** has not forgotten you in the dry season. The morning He has appointed is coming, and it is not in doubt.
So beat the drum anyway. Say the defiant "yet." Joy cometh in the morning, and until it does, the God who is your strength is beating inside the very heart that thought it had none left.

pieces.title: Scattered Is Not the Last Word Over You
pieces.imagePrompt: A tender reggae-warm healing service of Caribbean and diaspora believers of many nations gathered close in golden light, a shepherd-like pastor with a hand on a weary young person's shoulder, families and elders drawn together from many places into one room, faces of relief and belonging, wounds being bound with love; cinematic, warm, premium worship-brand film still; wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: The word "diaspora" literally means scattered, seed thrown to the wind. I made "Healing Diaspora" for everyone who has felt like that: pulled apart between two homes, two accents, two griefs. But scattered was never meant to be the last word over you. The Shepherd gathers, and He heals, and He calls the scattered by name.

body.text: The word "diaspora" is not a warm word. Strip it back to its root and it means *scattered*, seed flung to the wind, thrown far from where it started, landed who-knows-where. I have carried that word my whole life without stopping to feel its edge. Then I made *Healing Diaspora,* and I had to sit with it: what does the gospel say to people whose defining condition is being scattered?
It says a great deal. It says scattered was never meant to be the last word over you.
Two Homes and a Grief Nobody Sees

Let me name the actual wound first, because a healing album that skips the wound is a lie. The scattering is not abstract. It is the Bronx morning and the Kingston ache in the same body. It is the office accent and the granny accent, and the low-grade grief of never being fully home in either. It is the visa season, the diagnosis morning, the broken family, the homesick displacement at the kitchen sink that I put into the song **Scattered Diaspora Cry**, *Bronx but missing Kingston, diaspora, feels alone.*

I did not want to rush past that. Some worship gets to the victory too fast and leaves the wounded feeling unseen. So the record sits in the cry for a while, because **Yahuah** does. But it does not stay there, because in the very same psalm that names the scattering, the answer is already waiting.
The Verse That Holds Both Halves

Here is the sentence the whole album is built on, and I love it because it refuses to separate two things we usually keep apart: *The LORD... gathereth together the outcasts of Israel. He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds* (Psalm 147:2–3).

Read those two verses as one breath, because that is how they were written. In the same motion, **Yahuah** *gathers the scattered* and *heals the broken.* The regathering and the healing are not two separate programs. They are the same tenderness. He does not fix your heart and leave you scattered, and He does not gather you into a crowd while your heart stays in pieces. He does both, together, with one hand.

That is why the opening song is called simply **Healing Diaspora**, *Father binds the broken, Spirit's covering.* And the healing has a source; it is not sentiment. It is Calvary. *With his stripes we are healed* (Isaiah 53:5). The binding of every diaspora wound was paid for on a cross, which means the healing is not a wish. It is a purchase already made.

I set that healing on a reggae one-drop for a reason. The scattered are also the rooted, if the roots run to the right place, and on **Roots Run to Jesus** I lean on the promise that the one who trusts the Lord is *as a tree planted by the waters... her leaf shall be green; and shall not be careful in the year of drought* (Jeremiah 17:7–8). You can be transplanted a thousand miles from where you started and still be deeply, unshakably rooted, as long as the roots are sunk in Him and not in a piece of ground you can be moved from.
Found Before I Knew I Was Lost

The peak of this record reframed my whole understanding of how I got here, and I put it in a song called **Good Shepherd Found Me**. For years I told my testimony as a story of my searching, how *I* went looking for God, how *I* found my way back. Then I read the tenth chapter of John more slowly.
You didn't wait for me to find You. You came across the diaspora field. Good Shepherd, called me by name.

**Yeshua** says of the Shepherd, *he calleth his own sheep by name, and leadeth them out* (John 10:3). And through Ezekiel, **Yahuah** says something that reorders the entire search: *I, even I, will both search my sheep, and seek them out... As a shepherd seeketh out his flock... so will I seek out my sheep, and will deliver them* (Ezekiel 34:11–12). Do you see it? The scattered sheep is not the one doing the finding. The Shepherd is. I did not find my way home through the diaspora field. He crossed it, found me, and called my name before I even understood I was lost.
He Knows Your Name, Not Just Your Category

This is the mercy that undoes the whole ache of being scattered. When you are one of millions displaced, one more name on a migration map, it is easy to believe you are a category to God, a demographic He is generally fond of. Scripture will not let that stand.

I close the album with **Gathered By Name**, on the strength of one of the most personal verses in the Bible: *Fear not: for I have redeemed thee, I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine* (Isaiah 43:1). By thy name. Not "the diaspora" in general. You, specifically, the particular scattered one reading this. And **Yeshua** completes the picture: *other sheep I have, which are not of this fold: them also I must bring... and there shall be one fold, and one shepherd* (John 10:16). Bronx, Brixton, Kingston, Toronto, Miami, one fold, one Shepherd, and not one name lost in the gathering.

And once gathered and healed, you are not meant to hoard it. **Healed and Sent** takes the man **Yeshua** freed and repeats His commission over the diaspora: *Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee* (Mark 5:19). The healing was always meant to travel back through the very family you were scattered from.
Who I Made This For

I made *Healing Diaspora* for the one holding two homes and belonging fully to neither. For the person who has read their whole life as a story of loss and distance and has never once considered that a Shepherd was crossing the field toward them the entire time. For anyone who hears the word "scattered" and feels it land as a verdict.

It is not a verdict. It is a condition, and it is temporary, because the God who scattered the nations is also the God who gathers them, one named sheep at a time. You were found before you knew to look. You were called by your own name, not your category. And the wound of the scattering was bound up at a cross before you were ever born.
Scattered is real. But over you, it is not the last word. **Yahuah** has spoken a later one, and it is your name.

pieces.title: The Tuesday Morning After the Parade
pieces.imagePrompt: A vibrant Caribbean and diaspora praise celebration of many nations, a Brooklyn parade-style church tent and storefront church alive with soca brass, steelpan, dancing families, grandmothers and children stomping and clapping in golden light, radiant sanctified joy overflowing; bright, cinematic, premium worship-brand film still; wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: Anyone can rejoice on carnival Sunday with the brass blazing and the whole street moving. I made "Island Joy" for the other day, the quiet Tuesday after the parade, when the costumes are packed away and the heart goes flat. Because that is where I learned the thing Nehemiah knew: the joy of the Lord isn't the reward for strength. It's the source of it.

body.text: Anybody can rejoice on carnival Sunday. The brass is blazing, the whole street is moving, the steelpan is ringing off the buildings, joy on a day like that costs you nothing. I love those days. I made a whole loud, foot-stomping album for them. But that is not actually where I learned what joy is.

I learned it on the Tuesday. *Island Joy* is a celebration record, but its true center is the quietest song on it, and it is about the morning after, when the costumes are packed away, the parade is over, and the heart goes flat.
When the Carnival Heart Goes Quiet
I put that exact feeling into a song called **Carnival Heart Quiet**, and I did not dress it up:
Carnival heart quiet now, Father, where did the joy go? Brooklyn parade is over, Tuesday morning, the diaspora slow.

Every one of us knows that Tuesday. The high recedes and something underneath it is exposed, the burnout, the loneliness, the ordinary grey of a life that cannot stay at parade pitch. And here is the trap so many believers fall into: we decide that the flat Tuesday is the real us and the joyful Sunday was the performance. We start to think joy was a mood we borrowed for a weekend, and now the bill has come due.
That is exactly the moment Nehemiah was written for.
What They Learned on Their Worst Day

Picture the scene in Nehemiah 8. The people of God have gathered, the law is read aloud for the first time in generations, and they understand it, and they break down weeping, because they realize how far they have fallen. It is a low, exposed, Tuesday-morning kind of moment. And their leaders say something that sounds almost impossible: *Mourn not, nor weep... neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength* (Nehemiah 8:9–10).

Sit with the order of that sentence, because I built the album's peak, **Joy Is My Strength**, entirely on it. We assume you need strength first, and then, if things go well, joy shows up as the reward. Nehemiah says the reverse. *The joy of the LORD is your strength.* The joy is not the payoff at the end of a strong week. It is the fuel the strong week runs on. Joy is upstream of strength, not downstream.
Not strength first and joy as the reward, joy of the LORD is the source. Strength flowing from the rejoicing.

That is why it can come to you on the flat Tuesday. If joy depended on the parade, the empty morning would be the end of it. But *the joy of the LORD* does not depend on your circumstances. It depends on **Yahuah**, who does not pack up and go home when the celebration ends.
Gladness Is a Command, Which Is Good News

Here is where I have to teach as a pastor, because "be joyful" can sound like pressure. It is not pressure; it is permission, and it is provision. Psalm 100 does not suggest gladness, it commands it: *Serve the LORD with gladness: come before his presence with singing* (Psalm 100:2). I built **Serve the Lord With Gladness** on that, and on the freeing truth two verses later, *it is he that hath made us, and not we ourselves; we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture* (Psalm 100:3).

Do you feel the relief in that? The reason you can be commanded into joy is that the joy was never something you had to manufacture out of your own flat heart. You did not make yourself. You are His, the sheep of His pasture, as I sing on **Sheep of His Pasture**, which means the source of the gladness is *outside* you, in the Shepherd, and it does not run dry when your energy does.

And notice what those weeping people were told to do next: to eat the fat, drink the sweet, and *send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared* (Nehemiah 8:10). The very first act of Nehemiah's joy was generosity toward the ones with nothing. That is how you know this joy is not a private high. It overflows. Real gladness in **Yahuah** always reaches for the person beside you who has less. The parade was never the point; the caring was.
Even the Foot-Stomp Belongs to Him

Now, do not hear me diminishing the loud days. The parade belongs to God too. When *David danced before the LORD with all his might* (2 Samuel 6:14), stripped of his royal dignity in the street, he showed us that the whole body, feet, hands, hips, breath, was made for praise. I reclaim all of it on **Wine to the King** and **Foot-Stomp Glory**: the soca, the carnival road, the shout-drums, every bit of it aimed back at the King who gave us bodies that know how to move. Psalm 47 opens with it: *O clap your hands, all ye people; shout unto God with the voice of triumph* (Psalm 47:1). And Psalm 150 closes the whole songbook with *let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD.*
The point is not to trade the loud joy for a quiet, serious faith. The point is that the loud Sunday and the flat Tuesday are both held by the same source, so the joy survives the trip between them.
Who I Made This For

I made *Island Joy* for the one on the Tuesday. For the person who felt God at the parade, at the conference, at the retreat, and now sits in an ordinary week wondering if it was ever real. For anyone running on empty, trying to grind up enough strength to feel joyful again, when the whole thing works the other way around.

Stop trying to build strength so you can afford joy. Go to **Yahuah** for the joy first, the joy that is *His,* not yours to generate, and let the strength flow out of it, the way Nehemiah said it would. You do not have to wait for a good day to rejoice. The joy of the Lord is your strength on the flat Tuesday exactly as much as on the loud Sunday, because its source never once depended on the parade.
Pack away the costumes. The joy was never in them. It is in Him, and He is still here on Tuesday morning.

pieces.title: Go Where Nobody Is Staking Their Name
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful, diverse street gathering at golden hour outside a weathered roadside meeting place, a preacher with dust on his boots embracing the poor and the overlooked, people of many nations sharing bread and lifting hands in gladness, an accordion and an acoustic guitar in the circle, warm forgiving light on worn but radiant faces; cinematic worship-brand film still, bright and emotive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: The respectable churches sit on respectable streets, but the ones who need the gospel most are out where the kingdom feels unsafe. I made a whole record about being sent to the margins with dust on my boots and conviction for a credential.

body.text: The respectable churches sit on respectable streets. I have preached in some of them, and I am grateful for them. But I could not shake a thing I kept noticing: the people the gospel came for most were almost never the people in the building.

So I made a record about leaving it. *The Outlaw Apostle* is my honest confession that the call of God does not always point you toward the polished sanctuary. Sometimes it points you the other way, toward the honky-tonk, the cellblock, the trailer park, the roughest terrain in town, the places nobody is staking their name.
Why I had to make it

I got tired of a gospel that had grown comfortable. The opener says it plain: "They got respectable churches on respectable streets, but the prophets aren't there, where the broken folks meet." That is not a jab at the faithful. It is a map. I was reading my Bible, and I noticed the pattern is almost embarrassing in how consistent it is.

**Yeshua** stood up in His hometown synagogue, opened the scroll of Isaiah, and read His own job description: the Spirit of the Lord is upon me, He said, to preach the gospel to the poor, to proclaim liberty to the captives. That is Luke chapter four. Then He spent the rest of the Gospels doing exactly that, eating with tax collectors, touching lepers, letting the wrong kind of woman wash His feet. When the religious crowd complained, He told them straight: I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance. That is Matthew chapter nine.

If that is where the Master went, I could not in good conscience make a record about staying safe. The apostle Paul said it was his whole ambition to preach where Christ had not yet been named, to build on no other man's foundation, out past the edge of the comfortable map. That is not a personality quirk. That is the shape of the sending itself.
What the title means
"Outlaw" is a hard word, and I chose it on purpose, but I want to be careful with it. I do not mean lawless. I mean *the ones the respectable world writes off.*

An outlaw, in the old West, was a man outside the protection of the establishment, and that is exactly the ground the apostle is sent to. The whole second track leans into it: my past is my proof, my wreck is my warrant. I am not credentialed by a diploma from a place that would never have let me in the door. As the opening song puts it, "my credential's conviction, my commission is this, go find the forgotten, and tell 'em they're home."
An apostle is not somebody the establishment approves. An apostle is somebody the Master sends. Those are not the same credential, and they never have been.

That is why the record keeps naming the prophets, Jeremiah crying in the street, John the Baptist out in the wild, men fired by a vision too big for the temples to hold. Every one of them was pushed to the edge, and every one of them found God waiting there.
The heart under the songs
The center of this album is a sending, and it moves through three deliberate stages.

First comes the going. *Go to the Margins* and *Go Feed the Poor* are boots-on-the-ground marching orders, and I built them on Matthew chapter twenty-five, where **Yeshua** says the King will one day tell the righteous: I was hungry and ye gave me meat, I was a stranger and ye took me in, inasmuch as ye have done it unto the least of these, ye have done it unto me. That verse rearranges everything. It means the poor man at the margin is not a project. He is where Christ is hiding, waiting to be met.

Then comes the wilderness. *Wilderness Calling* and *Return to the Ground* are the songs about being emptied before you are useful. Every apostle starts in the wilderness, even **Yeshua** Himself, driven out to a solitary place to pray, as Mark chapter one tells it. I wanted the record to admit that the road to the margins runs through your own desert first. You cannot carry a gospel of liberty to captives while you are still performing for the respectable crowd. The wilderness burns that need right out of you.

And then comes the fire and the answer. *Apostolic Fire* draws on Pentecost, Acts chapter two, the tongues of flame, because the sending is not powered by grit alone. And the record ends where Isaiah's whole ministry began. In Isaiah chapter six the prophet hears **Yahuah** ask, "Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?" and answers with the only words that matter: "Here am I; send me." That is the closing track, *Send Me*. The entire album is a long, dusty walk toward being able to say those three words and mean them.
Who I made this for
I made *The Outlaw Apostle* for two kinds of people, and they are usually sitting far apart.

The first is the one at the margin, the man in the cellblock, the woman in the trailer park, the addict, the outlaw, the one who has already been told a hundred times that the kingdom door is closed to the likes of him. Hear me: the God they say denied you will be found in the kneeling. **Yeshua** did not come for the people who had it together. He came for you, on purpose, by name, and the whole record is one long way of telling you that you are not too far gone to be sent for.

The second is the one who has grown comfortable in the building and can feel, somewhere underneath the comfort, that God is nudging him toward the door. Maybe you have felt a pull toward the rough part of town, the jail ministry, the neighbor everyone else avoids, and you have talked yourself out of it because it is not safe and it is not respectable. It was never supposed to be. The record of Scripture is that **Yahuah** loves to save the people the establishment gave up on, and He loves to do it through people willing to leave the safe street.

So here is the commission, the same one I wrote into the first song and the same one Isaiah answered on the day the coal touched his lips. There is a margin near you where nobody is staking their name. There are forgotten people there who have never once been told they are wanted.
Go find them. Tell them they are home.
And when you get there, do not be surprised to discover that **Yeshua** was already standing among them, waiting on you to show up.

pieces.title: The Barroom Where the Church Told the Truth
pieces.imagePrompt: A tender, diverse congregation gathered at dusk moving from a worn barroom out toward a bright bluegrass circle, people of many nations kneeling and then rising with relief and joy, some embracing in reconciliation, hands open and faces wet with grateful tears turning to gladness, warm restorative light breaking across the room; cinematic worship-brand film still, bright and emotive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I set the whole first half of this record in a honky-tonk because that is the one room where people still tell the truth about themselves. It is a corporate confession, the church owning what it broke, and it does not stop at sorry. It pays something back.

body.text: I set the whole first half of this record in a honky-tonk, and I want to tell you why. It is not because I love a barroom. It is because a barroom is one of the last rooms left where people still tell the truth about themselves.

Nobody at the end of the bar is pretending to have it together. The mask is already off. And I had come to believe the church needed to learn how to talk the way people talk when the mask is off, honestly, out loud, about what we have actually done. So *Honky Tonk Repentance* opens on a sawdust floor with a confession, and it does not let up until the confession has grown a spine.
Why I had to make it

Most repentance records I have heard are private. Just me and my sin and my Savior. And that is true and good as far as it goes. But I kept running into a harder kind of repentance in the Scripture, one we mostly skip, the kind a whole people does together, out loud, for what they did as a people.

Daniel prayed it. Nehemiah prayed it. And **Yahuah** framed the whole thing in Second Chronicles chapter seven: "If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land." Notice it is *my people*, plural. A community owning what a community broke.

So the opener is not "I broke the covenant." It is "*We* broke the covenant." The church broke it. The nation broke it. And the very first line of restoration is the willingness to say so without flinching. King David modeled the personal version of it in Psalm fifty-one, after the prophet Nathan cornered him: "against thee, thee only, have I sinned." No excuses, no spin, a man naming the exact thing he had done. This record just takes David's honesty and lets a whole people sing it together.
What the title means
Honky-tonk repentance means repentance that happens in the room where you actually are, not the room where you would like to be seen.

The confession side of the album walks through the hard specifics, *We Stole the Land*, *We Abandoned the Poor*, *We Silenced the Prophet*, *The Church Ignored the Widow*. I named those on purpose, because a confession that stays general is a confession that costs nothing. Joel chapter two says, "rend your heart, and not your garments." It is easy to tear your shirt for show. It is another thing entirely to let the truth tear something on the inside.
Vague repentance is just guilt with good manners. Real repentance names the thing it did, out loud, in the room where it happened.

But here is the mercy woven all through it: Isaiah chapter one has **Yahuah** say to a people drowning in exactly this kind of sin, "Come now, and let us reason together: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow." The honesty is not the end. It is the door. First John chapter one promises that if we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us, and to cleanse us. The barroom is dark, but the light is already reaching for it.
The heart under the songs
The most important thing on this record is a single structural move, and I built the whole album around it.

For six tracks, it is honky-tonk, barroom upright bass, a lonesome Telecaster, the sound of a man on a stool telling the truth. Then track seven, *Restitution Begins*, the banjo rolls in and the whole thing turns to bluegrass. That is not a production gimmick. That is the theology of the album in a chord change. Because the song says the thing I most wanted to say on the entire record: "Confession alone is not enough. Repentance requires action. Restitution demands that we return what we stole, restore what we broke, honor what we silenced."

I stand that on Zacchaeus. In Luke chapter nineteen, the little tax collector meets **Yeshua** and does not merely feel bad. He says, "if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold." He gets out the checkbook. And **Yeshua** answers, "This day is salvation come to this house." Salvation and restitution walked in the same door. That is why the record refuses to end at "sorry."

From there it climbs. *The Church Kneels*, *The Road Back*, *Restoration Ahead*, and it lands on new creation, because that is where genuine repentance always lands. Second Corinthians chapter five: if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature; old things are passed away, all things are become new. Revelation chapter twenty-one puts the same promise in the mouth of the One on the throne, "Behold, I make all things new." The album that started on a barroom floor ends with a whole people made new, and I wanted you to feel the road between those two rooms in your own chest.
Who I made this for
I made *Honky Tonk Repentance* for the church, honestly. For us.

For every believer who has felt the low, uncomfortable ache of knowing that our house has not been innocent, that there are peoples and poor and prophets and widows we looked past, and that saying a soft, general "we've all made mistakes" is not the same as telling the truth. This record is permission to tell it. Not to wallow in it, to walk *through* it, because the far side of honest confession is the cleanest ground there is.

And I made it for the individual on the stool, too. The one who is sure he is too far into the wreck for the church to want him. Hear the deepest note on the album: the Lamentations chapter three promise that His mercies are new every morning; great is His faithfulness. New every morning. Not new if you clean yourself up first. New at dawn, over the same tired sinner, again and again, for as long as it takes.

So go on and tell the truth in whatever barroom you are sitting in tonight. Name it. Do not soften it. And then do the thing the honky-tonk turns to bluegrass to say, get up, go back, and start returning what got broken.

Because the God who told a scarlet people they could be white as snow is still, this very morning, faithful and just to forgive. The confession is the hard part. But it was never the end of the song. It was only the first verse.

pieces.title: God Has Only Ever Built With the Broken
pieces.imagePrompt: A radiant, diverse group of people rising at dawn from a place of ruin and rubble into golden light, faces of former prisoners and the once-broken lifted in astonished joy, hands reaching upward, dust turning to light around them, believers of many nations helping one another up, green shoots breaking through cracked ground; cinematic worship-brand film still, bright and emotive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I made a record for the ones in the rubble, the imprisoned, the addicted, the fallen, everyone the system wrote off as no hope. It stands on the plainest fact in Scripture: God has never built anything out of anything but dust, and dust is exactly where resurrection begins.

body.text: I made this record for the people in the rubble. The ones the system already filed under "no hope." The imprisoned, the addicted, the fallen, the ones who fell into a place so low that respectable folks stopped reaching for them.

And I built the whole thing on the plainest, most stubborn fact in all of Scripture: **Yahuah** has never once built anything out of anything but dust. That is not a limitation. That is the good news. Because if dust is His raw material, then the very place you think disqualifies you is the exact place He does His best work.
Why I had to make it

I have sat with too many people who believe their bottom is the end of their story. The cell, the relapse, the wreckage of a life that came apart in public. And I noticed that the church sometimes agrees with them by accident. We celebrate the polished testimony and quietly step around the ones still covered in the dust of the fall. We like our resurrections clean. We prefer the part where the man is already standing. But Scripture never skips the dust, and neither should we, because the dust is where the miracle starts.

So the opener just says it, flat and unashamed: "I am dust, dust and ashes, dust and breaking, but dust knows its Creator." I wanted the first thing you heard on this record to be the thing the world tries hardest to make you forget, that dust is not garbage to God. Dust is the stuff He reaches for when He is about to make something alive.
What the title means

Go back to the beginning. Genesis chapter two says **Yahuah** formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life. The first human being was dirt with God's breath in it. That is the whole species. Dust that got loved into life.

And then Genesis chapter three, after everything breaks, He says the hard word too: "dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return." We spend our lives running from that sentence. But the record turns it over and finds the hope hiding underneath it, because the God who started with dust the first time is not the least bit intimidated by dust the second time.
Your lowest place is not a disqualification. It is raw material. God has been building glory out of dust since the first morning of the world.

That is the arc of the album, right there in the title. *Dust and Resurrection.* Not dust *or* resurrection, dust *and* resurrection, because in His hands the one becomes the doorway to the other. The bridge of the opening song says it as clear as I know how: out of dust God made humanity, out of dust **Yeshua** rose, out of the dust the gospel is alive.
The heart under the songs
This record is a gallery of people the world buried, and every one of them gets up.

*Prison Cell Prayer* is for the man behind the bars, praying in the one place the system swears is the end of the line, and I wrote it remembering Paul and Silas, who at midnight in a Philippian jail prayed and sang until the foundations shook and the doors flew open. *The Prodigal Returns* is Luke chapter fifteen: the son who spent it all, hit bottom in a pigpen, and found that the father had been watching the road the whole time and ran to meet him while he was yet a great way off. *The Gospel in Recovery* and *Rising From the Ashes* are for the ones clawing their way back one day at a time, who need to know that the climb itself is holy ground.

And then there is *Scars as Resurrection*, which may be the truest thing on the album. When **Yeshua** rose from the grave, He did not come back unmarked. He kept the scars. In John chapter twenty He shows Thomas the holes in His hands and His side, the risen Lord wearing the wounds of the worst day of His life, now glorified. That is the whole promise of this record in one image: resurrection does not erase where you have been. It transfigures it. The scar becomes the proof. The very mark of your breaking becomes the evidence of your rising.

I anchored the sound of the album in one of the strangest, most hopeful passages the prophets ever wrote, Ezekiel chapter thirty-seven, the valley of dry bones. **Yahuah** sets the prophet down in a valley full of the deadest things imaginable and asks, "Can these bones live?" And then He tells him to prophesy, and the bones come together, and the breath comes into them, and they stand up, an exceeding great army. That is what I wanted this record to do, to prophesy to whatever the world has buried in you and call it back to its feet.
Who I made this for
I made *Dust and Resurrection* for anyone who has been written off, most of all by themselves.

For the one reading this from a place they are ashamed to name. For the one who has relapsed so many times they have stopped believing the next morning could be different. For the one whose life fell apart where everyone could see it, and who is convinced that the dust they are sitting in is the final chapter. It is not. First Corinthians chapter fifteen promises a body sown in corruption, raised in incorruption; sown in weakness, raised in power. The sowing is real. But so is the raising, and the raising gets the last word.

Hear me on this, because it is the reason the record exists. The tomb was not the end of **Yeshua**, and the rubble is not the end of you. He came out of the ground, and He came out still wearing the wounds, which means He is not embarrassed by yours. He specializes in exactly the thing you are most afraid He will turn away from.

So if you are in the dust tonight, do not despise it. It is the one material the Maker has always used. Let Him breathe on it. Let the breath come into the dry bones. Let the scar become the testimony. Stop apologizing for the ground you are lying in and start listening for the voice that asks whether these bones can live, because when He asks it, He is not mocking you. He is about to answer His own question with your name.
Because the God who has only ever built with dust is not finished building you, and everything He has ever made out of the dust, He has made to rise.

pieces.title: The Devil Never Comes in His Own Clothes
pieces.imagePrompt: A jubilant deliverance celebration at dawn in an Appalachian holler, a globally-diverse crowd of freed and joyful believers of many nations dancing with hands raised as morning light burns off the mist, broken chains on the ground, a fiddle and banjo lifted high, radiant faces full of relief and triumph after a long night; cinematic worship-brand film still, bright and emotive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: Deception never shows up looking like deception. It comes dressed pretty, smiling gold, smelling like an answered prayer. I made a whole record about the one thing that tears the costume off every lie, the truth of Jesus, and the discernment His Spirit gives.

body.text: My grandfather used to tell a tale about a stranger who came down the mountain at dusk. The stranger walked in a fine skirt and smiled a smile like gold, but the old preacher in the story saw the snake beneath the husk. That tale is the seed of this whole record.

Because here is the thing my grandfather understood that a lot of us forget: the devil never comes in his own clothes. He does not show up ugly. He shows up beautiful, smiling, smelling like the very thing you have been praying for. And *Devil in a Skirt* is my record about the one force in all creation that can tear that costume off, the truth of **Yeshua**, and the discernment His Spirit gives a watchful heart.
Why I had to make it

Let me say plainly what the title is and is not, because it matters. The "skirt" on this record is not a woman. It is a costume. It is the disguise the deceiver wears, the beautiful dress pulled over an ugly thing. The whole album treats it exactly the way Scripture does, as the wolf's borrowed wool, the angel-of-light glow the accuser puts on when the lamps are dim.

I had to make it because I watched too many good people get taken by something they never saw coming, precisely because it did not look like anything to fear. Sin that announced itself would be easy to refuse. It never does. Paul warned in Second Corinthians chapter eleven that Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light. **Yeshua** warned in Matthew chapter seven to beware of false prophets who come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves. The danger was never the thing that looks dangerous. The danger is the honey on the lips of the lie you would happily keep.
What the title means
The opener says it in a single line I keep coming back to: "the devil don't never come in his own true clothes, he comes in the dress that he thinks will deceive."

That is the whole warning of the record. Deception is, by definition, disguised. If you could see it plainly you would not be deceived. So the question is never "does this look good?" The question is "what is underneath it?" And you cannot answer that with your own eyes. You answer it with the Word and the Spirit. As the chorus of the opener puts it: the Lamb of God strips every disguise, the truth of His Word turns the lie to light, the Spirit of **Yeshua** exposes the counterfeit.
The devil's whole strategy is the costume. God's whole answer is the light. You do not out-argue a disguise. You drag it into the light of Christ and watch it fall off.

That is why First John chapter four does not tell us to trust every warm feeling. It tells us to try the spirits, whether they are of God. Discernment is not suspicion and it is not fear. It is a watchful love that refuses to let a pretty lie walk off with the people **Yeshua** died for.
The heart under the songs
The first half of this album is a frontier watch, a man learning to see.

*Wolves in the Wool* and *Angel of Light* name the disguises. *Try the Spirits* is First John four set to a fiddle. *Guard Your Heart* stands on Proverbs chapter four, keep thy heart with all diligence, for out of it are the issues of life, because the counterfeit always aims at the heart first. *Armor of Light* is Ephesians chapter six, the whole armor of God, so a man can stand against the wiles, the *schemes*, of the devil. And *The Mountain Watchman* is Ezekiel chapter thirty-three, the watchman set on the wall who will answer for the souls he fails to warn. I put a lot of vigilance on the front of this record on purpose, because you cannot resist what you refuse to recognize.
But I did not want an album that only warns. A record that leaves you scared of the dark has failed. So the whole thing turns, hard and glad, at the deliverance.

The cinematic peak is *Jesus Strips the Disguise*, and it opens with the plain words of Revelation chapter twelve: now is come salvation, and strength, and the kingdom of our God, for the accuser of our brethren is cast down. The song stands the deceiver at the foot of the cross and watches the costume fall. It leans on Colossians chapter two, where Paul says **Yeshua** spoiled principalities and powers and made a public show of them openly, triumphing over them in His cross. That is the frontier preacher's old refrain built right into the song: there is no disguise that can stand at the foot of the cross, no costume of the devil that can stay on his frame when the Lamb of God shines through.

And it goes back further still, all the way to the first promise in the Book. Genesis chapter three, the serpent in the garden was a disguise too, and **Yahuah** swore that the Seed of the woman would bruise the serpent's head. The bridge of the opener sings exactly that: the heel of the Seed crushed the head of his lies. Every mask in the record was already doomed the day that promise was made.

Then comes the party. *Deliverance Holler* is the morning after the long night of warfare, "the deliverance song is the song of the morning, and the praise of the Lamb sweeps the dark away." Chains falling, captives leaping, every nation gathered at the holler of grace. And the finale, *Truth Walks the Mountain*, ends the whole record not with the enemy but with the King, Truth Himself walking the high road forever, the wolves and the false lights all bowing at His feet, and word going out to the cabins and the cradles and the watchmen: the new day has come.
Who I made this for
I made *Devil in a Skirt* for two people.

The first is the one who got fooled. The one who danced with something that smiled like gold and only later saw the snake beneath it, and who is now drowning in shame, certain they should have known better. Hear me: the whole point of a disguise is that you were not supposed to see through it alone. That is not your failure, that is what a counterfeit is. And Revelation chapter twelve says how the brethren overcame the accuser: by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony. Not by being clever enough. By the blood. The costume that fooled you has already been torn off at the cross. Come stand there and watch it fall.

The second is the watchman, the believer God is teaching to see. Maybe you have felt a check in your spirit about something everyone else is celebrating, and you have wondered if you are just being difficult. You may be a watchman on the wall. James chapter four gives you the promise to stand on: resist the devil, and he will flee from you. He flees. The disguise has no power once the light hits it.
So do not be afraid of the dark, and do not be dazzled by the pretty lie. Keep your heart. Try the spirits. Stand on the rock and hold the sword of the Word.

Because the devil never comes in his own clothes, but there is not a costume in all of hell that can stay on his frame when the Lamb of God walks up the mountain in the truth of His Name. The night of warfare ends. The deliverance holler always comes at dawn. And the last thing standing on that mountain is not the disguise. It is the King.

pieces.title: The Fire Is Older Than Our Names
pieces.song: Gather Around the Fire of God
pieces.imagePrompt: A warm nighttime campfire circle of diverse travelers and families of many nations gathered close under a vast starry sky, faces glowing gold in the firelight, coffee cups and an old guitar and a harmonica, no one sitting alone, expressions of deep belonging and quiet joy, an empty chair being filled by a newcomer welcomed in; cinematic worship-brand film still, bright and emotive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I built a record around a campfire because that is where Jesus sat with His men. It is about covenant belonging, a circle of the tired and the wandering gathered not around each other, but around the Fire that is older than any of our names.

body.text: I built a whole record around a campfire, and I want to tell you why a fire and not a cathedral.

Because a fire is where **Yeshua** sat with His men. After everything, after the cross, after the empty tomb, after Peter had denied Him three times, the risen Lord met His disciples on a beach at dawn, and John chapter twenty-one says there was a fire of coals there, and fish on it, and bread, and He said, "Come and dine." That is the picture I could not get out of my head. Not a throne room. A campfire. The King of glory cooking breakfast for the men who had failed Him, gathering them back around the flame.

So *Campfire Covenant* is my record about that fire, about covenant belonging, about the circle of the tired and the wandering drawn in out of the dark. And the deepest thing it says is right there in the title of this piece: the Fire is older than our names.
Why I had to make it

I have watched a lot of lonely believers. People who are technically in the church but have never once felt like they *belonged* to anyone. And I have watched us try to fix that with programs and small groups and name tags, gathering people around each other and wondering why the loneliness does not lift.

The record makes a quiet correction that I believe is the whole cure. In the opening song the circle sings, "We don't need another idol, we don't need another shrine, we just need the One who sat with men at the fire, by the sea, that time." We do not gather around each other. We gather around Him. Belonging is not something a circle of people manufactures. It is something that happens to a circle of people when they all turn and face the same Fire. Two men on the road to Emmaus felt it without even knowing who they were sitting with, their hearts burned inside them while He talked, long before they recognized His face. That is the secret of every true fellowship. The warmth was never coming from the circle. It was coming from the One in the middle of it.
What the title means

The Fire in this album is a Person, and the Scripture is not shy about it. Hebrews chapter twelve says plainly, "our God is a consuming fire." He met Israel that way at Sinai, in Exodus chapter nineteen, the whole mountain wrapped in smoke because **Yahuah** had come down in fire. He is not a warm feeling we generate. He is a holy flame that was burning long before we showed up cold and looking for somewhere to sit.

That is why the bridge of the opener sings straight to the Father: "the Fire is older than our names, but our names, in You, have come home." I wrote that line, and then I sat with it a long while, because it holds the whole gospel. You did not start the Fire. You did not earn a chair by it. But the Fire has been burning since before you had a name, and when you finally come in out of the dark, you discover it was keeping a place for you the entire time.
You do not build the belonging. You come in out of the cold and find that the Fire was already burning, and your chair was already there.
The heart under the songs
A covenant, in the Scripture, is a bond cut in blood, and this record never lets you forget that the warm campfire and the costly covenant are the same thing.

In Genesis chapter fifteen, when **Yahuah** made covenant with Abraham, He passed between the pieces as a smoking furnace and a burning lamp, binding Himself to His promise by fire. The album stands on that: the covenant You cut in Your own blood is the One we are here about. And it reaches its fulfillment in *Jesus, the Covenant Word* and *Jesus, You Are the Promise*, because Hebrews chapter nine calls **Yeshua** the mediator of a new covenant, the One in whom every old promise to Abraham, Moses, and David finally comes true. Jeremiah chapter thirty-one had prophesied it centuries before: a new covenant, no longer written on stone but written on the heart.

But the tenderest tracks are the ones about the men around the fire who almost were not there. *Jesus, I Broke the Covenant* is Peter's song, the disciple who denied his Lord at one fire of coals, restored by his Lord at another. That is not an accident in John's Gospel; the man who failed at the fire is remade at the fire. It preaches the whole hope of the record: the campfire is where the covenant-breaker gets a chair again. And *Belonging to Jesus* and *Jesus, You Keep Forever* land the promise Paul makes in Romans chapter eight, that nothing, not height nor depth nor anything else, shall be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ **Yeshua**. Once you are in that circle, the night can be as long as it wants. You are not going anywhere.
Who I made this for
I made *Campfire Covenant* for the ones out on the highway in the dark who are not sure anybody saved them a seat.

For the believer who serves and shows up and still goes home feeling like a stranger. Hear the bridge of the very first song: "no man here is a stranger, no chair here sits alone." For the one who broke faith and is sure the circle would never take them back, when the whole record is proof that the fire is exactly where **Yeshua** restores the one who failed. And for the tired soul who has been trying to earn belonging, who needs to lay that burden down and simply come in out of the cold and sit, because the Fire is older than your name and it has been waiting.

Hebrews chapter thirteen says **Yeshua** is the same yesterday, today, and forever. The Fire that warmed the shepherds and burned on Carmel and cooked breakfast on that beach is the same Fire burning tonight. It has not gone out. It is not going to.
So come on in. The coffee is hot, the wood is dry, the stars are coming slow. There is a chair by the flame that has had your name on it since before you were born.
And the Man tending the Fire, the One who cooked breakfast for the ones who let Him down, is looking up, right now, glad you finally came home.

pieces.title: The Three Things No Thief and No Year Can Steal
pieces.imagePrompt: A tender elderly couple of warm brown skin seated together in golden evening light on a porch, surrounded by three generations of a globally-diverse family, a daughter's hand resting over her aged parents' joined hands, faces full of peace and enduring love though the years have marked them, a worn Bible nearby; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still warmth, luminous and moving, love that outlasts everything made visible; wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: The years take your eyesight, your strength, sometimes even the name of the person sleeping beside you. I made this album about the three things that no year, no thief, and no grave can ever reach, and about why the last of them is the greatest.

body.text: I have sat at a great many bedsides in my life, and I have learned to watch what a person reaches for when everything else has already been taken. Because the years are thieves. They come slow and polite, and they take a little at a time, the eyesight, the hearing, the strength in the hands, the names of the streets you grew up on. And if you live long enough, the years will eventually walk right into the room and take the one thing you swore they never could.

I made **All That Remains** for the hour when the subtraction is nearly finished, and a soul is trying to find out what, if anything, is left. And I built the whole record on the most examined verse the church owns: *"So now faith, hope, and love abide, these three; but the greatest of these is love"* (1 Corinthians 13:13). Abide. That is a word for what stays when everything else has gone home.
What the years cannot take

The song I want you to sit with is "What the Years Cannot Take," and I will tell you plainly where it comes from, because I do not build songs on air. It follows a woman watching the long disease take her husband, watching him forget her own face across the kitchen table. And the line that breaks me every time I sing it is not a complaint. It is a discovery: *I have watched my husband forget my face in the long disease, but I have watched the Lord still walk into the room with ease.* The years take memory, the years take strength, the years take everything. *But the Lord remains, and the soul remembers what to sing.*

That is doctrine, sung from the far edge of a life. The anchor under it is Hebrews 13:8, *"Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever."* Everything else in your life is on a moving belt, sliding away a little each year. He is the one fixed point in the room. So when the song says *what the years cannot take is the Name above every name*, it is not sentiment. It is the only sane place left to set your feet when the floor is being pulled up plank by plank.

The husband forgets, the children move away, the body fails, the doctor has nothing left to say. But the Lord of yesterday, today, forever is the same, and what the years cannot take is the Name above every name.
Faith and hope will one day be out of a job
Now let me teach, because there is a glory hidden in Paul's little word *abide* that most people rush past.

Faith and hope are magnificent, and this album spends its first songs on them, "Faith Remains," "Hope Remains." Hebrews 11:1 calls faith *"the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen,"* and Hebrews 6:19 calls hope *"a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul."* An anchor. A conviction. These are the muscles that carry you through every dark season you will ever cross. But here is the wonder: faith and hope have an expiration date, and it is a happy one. Faith is for what you cannot yet see, and one day you will see. Hope is for what has not yet come, and one day it will come. On that day, faith becomes sight and hope becomes possession, and the two of them, their work finished, quietly retire.

Love does not retire. Love is the one of the three that is already doing on earth exactly what it will do forever in heaven. That is why Paul says the greatest of these is love, not because faith and hope are small, but because love is the only one of the three that never has to stop being what it is. When the album's final song lands on *"All That Remains Is Love,"* it is making a theological claim, not a greeting-card one: at the far end of everything, when faith has become sight and hope has become home, love is still standing in the room, because love was the thing God was the whole time.
Where the treasure actually is

The middle of the record turns from the losing to the keeping, and I want to be exact about it. "The Treasure Untaken," "Incorruptible Inheritance," "What Lasts Forever", these are not vague comforts. They are **Yeshua's** own economics.

He told us where to put what matters: *"Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal, but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven... For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also"* (Matthew 6:19-21). Notice He does not deny that earth's treasures get stolen. He assumes it. Moth, rust, thief, the years, by other names. His counsel is not to grip the perishable tighter but to move your treasure to a vault the thieves cannot reach. Peter names what is stored there: *"an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you"* (1 Peter 1:4). And Paul gives the whole album its sightline: *"the things that are seen are transient, but the things that are unseen are eternal"* (2 Corinthians 4:18). We spend our lives staring at the transient and calling it real. The eternal things have been the real ones all along.
Who this is for

This album is for the caregiver in the long disease, sitting beside a face that no longer knows hers. It is for the widow who has already buried most of what she loved and wonders what is even left to hold. It is for the aging saint taking inventory of a body that keeps handing things back to the years. And it is, quietly, for the young and strong who have not yet been robbed of anything, because the time to move your treasure is *before* the thieves arrive, not after.

Here is the whole record in one sentence: the years are going to take nearly everything, and they cannot touch the three things that were the point the entire time. Faith will carry you home and then rest. Hope will bring you to the door and then be filled. But love, the love **Yahuah** poured out at the cross, the love He has set in you toward Him and toward every soul at your table, that one goes all the way through, out the far side of the grave, and keeps on going.

So hold what remains. The husband may forget your face. **Yeshua** never has, and He never will. And when the years are finally finished taking, you will find that what is left in your hands was the treasure the entire time, and the greatest of it is love.

pieces.title: He Does Not Move, So Neither Do I
pieces.imagePrompt: A resolute multi-generational group of globally-diverse believers standing together in bright open daylight, an older woman at the front with a lifted, unafraid face and a hand over her heart, younger believers of many nations standing shoulder to shoulder behind her with quiet courage, wind moving through a field beyond them; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still warmth, bold and luminous, steadfast conviction made visible; wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I have swallowed the word God pressed into my chest so many times I forgot it was there. This is the album I made about the fire in the bones that will not stay buried, and about the strange steadiness of a believer who does not move because the Rock beneath her never does.

body.text: There is a sentence God pressed into the middle of my chest a long time ago, and I have swallowed it so many times I nearly forgot it was there. Every meeting, I rehearsed it and said nothing. Every hallway, I revised it down to something safer. And I told myself that swallowing the word was humility, when the honest name for it was fear. **Courage and Conviction** is the album I made when I finally understood that a called woman holding her silence is simply a woman not yet heard, and that the word in my bones was never mine to keep down.
The fire that will not stay swallowed

The record opens with a song called "Speak Your Word in Me," and it does not begin with boldness. It begins with a confession: *Jesus, You put a sentence in the middle of my chest, and I have swallowed it so often I had forgotten it was pressed.* Anyone who has ever been given something true to say and then talked themselves out of saying it knows exactly what that feels like.

The prophet Jeremiah knew it best of all. He tried to quit, decided he would not speak in the Lord's name again, and found he could not: *"there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I am weary with holding it in, and I cannot"* (Jeremiah 20:9). That is the engine of this whole album. Conviction is not, first of all, a personality trait. It is a fire. And a fire that is fed and covered does not go out; it just burns the one holding it in. The courage the record is after is not the courage to manufacture something bold. It is the courage to stop suffocating what **Yahuah** already lit. As the opening song prays it: *the mouth is mine; the message, Lord, is the message You made.*
A called woman holding silence is a woman not yet heard. Jesus, You are the Word made flesh, come and loose the word. I am only a vessel for the voice of the only Lord I follow.
Courage is not the absence of fear. It is a different foundation

Now let me teach, because there is a lie about courage that keeps timid believers timid: the idea that brave people simply do not feel afraid. That is not the Bible's picture at all. Scripture never tells the fearful to feel differently; it tells them *whose they are* and *who goes with them.*

When the Lord commissioned Joshua to lead a nation into everything that could go wrong, He did not say *feel confident*. He said, *"Be strong and courageous. Do not be frightened, and do not be dismayed, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go"* (Joshua 1:9). The command to courage is welded to a promise of Presence.
