And Paul says the same to a young, frightened pastor: *"God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control"* (2 Timothy 1:7). Power *and* love *and* a sound mind, which is why the courage on this album is never reckless or harsh. The chorus of the opening song asks for a word that is *"clear and kind, undiluted, unhedged, unafraid."* Kindness and clarity are not opposites. The bravest thing is usually also the most loving thing said plainly.

Look at how the first believers were described. When the council saw *"the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were uneducated, common men, they were astonished. And they recognized that they had been with Jesus"* (Acts 4:13). Their credential was not training or temperament. It was proximity. They had been *with Him*, and the boldness came off Him onto them. Courage, in the kingdom, is contagious. You catch it by staying close.
You do not move because the Rock does not move

The hit single at the heart of this record is "You, Lord, Do Not Move," and it holds the whole thesis in one line: *You, Lord, do not move, so I don't. Christ the Rock beneath me, and the Rock is where I stand.* I want to be exact about why that order matters, because we get it backwards constantly. We try to summon steadiness *from ourselves*, grit our teeth, stiffen our spines, resolve to be unshakable. And we shake anyway, because a person standing on their own resolve is standing on sand.

The steadiness the song describes is borrowed. *"No one can lay a foundation other than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ"* (1 Corinthians 3:11). **Yeshua** told us the wise builder digs down and builds on rock, *"and the rain fell, and the floods came... but it did not fall, because it had been founded on the rock"* (Matthew 7:24-25). The house does not hold because it is a strong house. It holds because of what is under it. So when the weather comes and the letter comes and the room goes silent and the phone goes cold, the very costs the song names. You are not asked to be immovable by willpower. You are asked to stand on the One who is immovable, and let His steadiness become yours. Hebrews calls that hope *"a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul"* (Hebrews 6:19). An anchored ship still feels the storm. It just does not drift.

And there is a cost, which this album refuses to hide. The song's bridge weighs it out loud, *if it costs me platform, title, friendship.* Conviction that has never cost anything has never really been tested. The world will always offer the softer door: *you could be a little softer, and they'd let you through.* But Paul drew the line where it has to be drawn: *"Am I now seeking the approval of man, or of God? ... If I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ"* (Galatians 1:10). You cannot serve two audiences. At some point every faithful believer has to choose whose face she is living toward.
Unashamed, and building the next brave one

The song that lands hardest for me is "Unashamed of Jesus," because shame is the quiet thing that keeps more good people silent than outright fear ever does. *A daughter does not apologize for the One who set her free.* That is Romans 1:16 with dirt under its nails: *"I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes."* Not ashamed of the message, the call, the Cross, or the blood-bought claim, the shame, the song says, goes in the grave where it belongs.

But courage was never meant to end with the one brave person, and neither does the album. It closes with "Teaching Them Jesus" and "Strong in the Lord Forever," because the whole point of finding your voice is to help the next frightened believer find hers. The armor Paul describes, *"be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might... put on the whole armor of God... that you may be able to stand"* (Ephesians 6:10-13), is issued to a whole army standing shoulder to shoulder, not a lone hero. And at the end of it all, the goal is Paul's own last words: *"I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith"* (2 Timothy 4:7). Kept it. Handed it on. Still standing.
Who this is for

This is for the believer with a true thing to say who has swallowed it one too many times. It is for the one being told she would go further if she were softer about **Yeshua**, sister, the Door you are standing for is the only Door worth losing the other doors over. It is for the tired, the outnumbered, the ones who feel the fire in their bones and are weary of holding it in.

Hear the whole record in one sentence: you do not have to generate your own steadiness. He does not move, so, standing on Him, neither do you. Let the fire out. Say it clear and kind and unafraid. The first time always shakes. But He is not shaken, and He is what you are standing on.

pieces.title: The Kitchen Floor Was Holy Ground the Whole Time
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful globally-diverse family gathered in a sunlit kitchen at morning, a grandmother kneading bread while children set a table and a young father lifts a laughing toddler, warm light pouring across worn wooden floorboards, an open Bible on the counter, faces full of belonging and everyday holiness; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still warmth, radiant and homey, the sacred ordinary made visible; wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I used to think the church was the holy place and the house was where I rested from God. Then I learned the first Christians had no steeples, only a table and a loaf and rooms with Him in them. This is the album I made about the sacredness of an ordinary home.

body.text: One morning I took my shoes off at the doorway of my own kitchen, and I could not have told you why. No one had asked me to. But I felt the floorboards hum under my feet, and I understood, all at once, that I had been standing on holy ground for forty years and calling it linoleum.

That is where **Homemaking Faith** came from. Because somewhere I had absorbed a lie so common we do not even notice we believe it: that the church building is the holy place, and the house is merely where I rest *from* God until Sunday brings me back into His presence. This album is my repentance from that lie, sung twelve times over. **Yeshua** never left the kitchen. I just had not been paying attention.
Take your shoes off in the kitchen

The opening song is called "Jesus, You Are Home," and it says the thing straight out: *I used to think the church was the holy place, and the house was where I rested from You. Now I know. You never left the kitchen.* The doctrine under it is one of the oldest scenes in Scripture. When **Yahuah** met Moses, the first word out of the fire was not a command about worship. It was, *"Take your sandals off your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground"* (Exodus 3:5). The ground was not holy because of the geography. It was holy because He was on it. And that changes everything about your house, because the same Presence that made a patch of desert holy is standing in your kitchen while the coffee brews.

The first believers understood this in a way we have nearly lost. They had no cathedrals, no steeples, no sanctuaries. What they had, Luke tells us, was this: they were *"breaking bread in their homes"* and *"day by day, attending the temple together and... received their food with glad and generous hearts"* (Acts 2:46). The church was a house with His table in it. Paul greets *"the church that meets in their house"* over and over (Romans 16:5). So when my song says *the first Christians had no steeples. They had Your table, they had Your loaf, they had rooms with You in them*, it is not poetry. It is the actual floor plan of the early church.

Before I hang a single picture, before I light a single lamp, before I bake a single loaf, Jesus, let me say it out loud: You are the holy ground. You are the sanctuary I am standing in. And You built this house, not me.
He is in the ordinary rhythms, not just the crisis
I built the middle of the record to walk a person through an ordinary day, because that is where most of a life is actually lived, and I refuse to let the ordinary be treated as the un-spiritual.

There is "Jesus in the Kitchen," because He called Himself *the Bread of Life* (John 6:35) and then handed real bread to tired people again and again. There is "The Lord Tends the Garden," because He said *"I am the vine... my Father is the vinedresser"* (John 15:1), and a woman on her knees in the dirt is closer to that parable than she knows. There is "Jesus in the Daily Rhythms," because the holiness of a home is not built in dramatic moments but in ten thousand small faithful ones. Remember Mary and Martha: Martha was *"anxious and troubled about many things,"* and **Yeshua** did not scold her for keeping a home. He gently called her to keep it *at His feet*, where *"one thing is necessary"* (Luke 10:38-42). The homemaking is holy the moment He is the center of it and not the competition for it.

And I will not pretend a home is only warmth, so the record has its hard song too. "Jesus Outlasts the Roof" sits on the hardest confession a household ever makes, Job's: *"The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD"* (Job 1:21). Roofs fail. Homes are lost. Families scatter. But Hebrews reminds us *"here we have no lasting city, but we seek the city that is to come"* (Hebrews 13:14). The house you love is a rehearsal, not the destination, which is exactly why you can love it freely and still hold it with open hands.
Who is really building the house

Here is the turn that keeps the whole album from becoming a hymn to domesticity for its own sake. A home is not made holy by the woman who works herself to the bone keeping it. It is made holy by the Lord who dwells in it.

Psalm 127:1 is blunt about this: *"Unless the LORD builds the house, those who build it labor in vain."* I have watched good women exhaust themselves trying to *manufacture* the peace of a home by sheer effort, and it cannot be done, because peace is a Presence, not an achievement. Your body, Paul says, is already *"a temple of the Holy Spirit within you"* (1 Corinthians 6:19), so you carry the sanctuary into every room you enter. You are not building God a house from scratch each morning. You are keeping house *with* the One who already lives there.

And the door of such a home swings outward. "Jesus Sets One More Chair," I called one of the songs, because a house where **Yeshua** is truly at home cannot stay closed. He said, *"I was a stranger and you welcomed me"* (Matthew 25:35). The holiest kitchens I have ever stood in were the ones with a place always ready for one more.
Who this is for

This is for the homemaker who suspects her real work is invisible and un-spiritual, sister, you have been ministering on holy ground the whole time. It is for the single person in a small apartment who wonders if a home even counts without a crowd in it; it does, because the Presence does not require a crowd. It is for the family that lost the house, and for the one just moving into a new one wondering how to make it a place where God dwells. You do not make Him welcome. You wake up to the fact that He is already there.
So take your shoes off in your own kitchen. The floorboards are humming. The ground you have been calling ordinary was holy the entire time, because **Yeshua** is home, and He never once left it.

pieces.title: A Hurried Yes Is a Future No in Disguise
pieces.imagePrompt: A diverse group of ministry leaders of many nations gathered in prayerful stillness around a wooden table in warm lamplight, an older woman with a hand laid gently on a younger leader's shoulder as heads bow before an open Bible, faces calm and unhurried, the weight of a decision carried in peace; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still warmth, grave and hopeful, wisdom sought before action made visible; wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I have known the leaders who decide without God, and I have buried what they broke. This is the album I made about the first work of every faithful leader, kneeling before the gavel, waiting for the Lord to decide in you before you decide for anyone else.

body.text: I have buried what hurried leaders broke. I do not say that to be dramatic; I say it because I have lived long enough to attend the funerals of good ministries, good marriages, and good churches that did not die of scandal. They died of speed. Somebody lifted the gavel before the Lord had spoken, made a fast yes to look decisive, and the whole house paid for it years later. So when I sat down to make **Leadership Wisdom**, I did not build it around vision or charisma or strategy. I built it around the one discipline almost no leadership book teaches: how to *wait* before you decide.
The first work of the faithful is not deciding. It is kneeling

The opening song is called "Deciding Well," and it does not start with a decision. It starts on the knees: *Jesus, which chair, which word, which meeting, before the voices are heard. I will not decide before I have knelt. Father, speak the weight before the gavel is dealt.* That is the whole thesis of the record in one verse. Leadership, in the kingdom, begins as surrender, not initiative.

James gives the reason, and it is astonishingly practical: *"If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach, and it will be given him"* (James 1:5). Notice, wisdom is not primarily something you develop by experience. It is something you *ask for*, from a God who gives it generously and without shaming you for needing it. And Paul locates that wisdom in a Person, not a principle: *"Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God"* (1 Corinthians 1:30). This is why the song's refrain is not *I will be wise* but *Jesus, You decide in me.* The wise leader is not the one with the best judgment in the room. She is the one most surrendered to the One whose judgment is perfect.

A hurried yes without You is a future no in disguise, but a leader yoked to the Lord will not outrun His eyes. I have sat with the yes till You softened it to a no; I have sat with the no till You told me where to go.
Listening is a decision you make before all the others
The third song is called "Listening First," and I put it early on purpose, because most bad leadership is not a failure of courage. It is a failure of hearing. We decide loudly and listen last.

The model is the boy Samuel in the dark, taught by old Eli to answer the voice with the only posture that ever produces wisdom: *"Speak, LORD, for your servant hears"* (1 Samuel 3:10). Servant first, decision second. On this record I even let the music preach it. There is a moment where a single fiddle note holds while everything else falls away, twenty seconds of enacted silence, because I wanted the listener to *feel* how uncomfortable and how necessary the pause is. We are so frightened of the quiet before a decision that we fill it with noise and call the noise leadership. But *"trust in the LORD with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding; in all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make straight your paths"* (Proverbs 3:5-6). The straight path is on the far side of the listening, not the far side of the hurry.
Wisdom wears two faces: truth and kindness
I called the fifth song "Truth and Kindness," and it corrects the two ditches leaders fall into, because wisdom is not just *knowing the right thing*. It is knowing how to carry it.

Some leaders have truth and no tenderness; they are right and they wound. Others have kindness and no spine; they are warm and they mislead. But the Lord we follow *"came... full of grace and truth"* (John 1:14), both, at full strength, in one Person, with no dilution of either. And the wisdom that comes down from Him is described exactly this way: *"the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy"* (James 3:17). Pure *and* peaceable. That is the whole art of it. This is why the album's picture of authority is not a raised fist but the King's own self-description: *"I am gentle and lowly in heart"* (Matthew 11:29). "Authority Gentle," I named that song, because the strongest leaders I have ever known held the most power with the softest hands.

There is also a song on this record called "Breaking Barriers," and it stands at the altar-peak of the whole album for a reason. Because there come decisions no amount of careful waiting can resolve by human means, walls that will not move, doors that will not open, situations where the wise thing and the possible thing seem to be two different things. And **Yeshua** says of exactly those moments, *"I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved and will go in and out and find pasture"* (John 10:9). The wise leader does not batter down the barrier with her own force. She waits at the Door, and lets Him open what no committee, no budget, and no clever strategy ever could. Some of the most important yeses of my life were doors I could not have forced in a hundred years, the Lord simply opened them, in His time, after the waiting.

And real wisdom multiplies itself. The record does not end with the leader deciding well alone; it ends with "Commissioning Others" and "Teaching Leaders," because a wise leader who trains no one has misunderstood the job. **Yeshua** promised, *"where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I among them"* (Matthew 18:20), leadership in the kingdom was always meant to be shared, done in the midst of others, never hoarded by one gifted person at the top.
Who this is for

This is for the pastor with a hard meeting on the calendar and a decision she is dreading. It is for the ministry leader, the business owner, the mother of a household, anyone who holds a gavel over other people's lives, which is nearly all of us. It is for the young leader in a hurry to prove herself, and for the tired one who has been burned by her own fast decisions and needs to be reminded that the pause is not weakness; it is the first work of the faithful.

Here is the sentence I want you to carry into your next decision: the room will wait if the One speaking is the Lord. You do not have to outrun His eyes, and you do not have to lift the gavel before He has spoken. Sit with the yes until He confirms it or softens it to a no. Because a hurried yes is only a future no wearing today's clothes, and a leader yoked to **Yeshua** has all the time in the world to decide well.

pieces.title: You Provide It; I Only Get to Hold It
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful multi-generational farming family of many nations gathered at a laden harvest table outdoors in golden light, open hands passing bread and baskets of produce, a grandmother lifting her face in gratitude while children share food with a visiting stranger, fields glowing behind them; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still warmth, abundant and thankful, provision and open-handed stewardship made visible; wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: Before I count the dollars in the drawer, I sit on the porch floor and lift my eyes to where the Father looks. I made this album about the God who saw the ram before Abraham saw the thicket, and about the freeing truth that I am only ever the hands that hold what already belongs to Him.

body.text: Every month of my life there has come a morning when the figures did not add up on paper, and I have learned to do one thing before I do anything else with them. Before I count the dollars in the drawer, before I write the figures in the book, I sit down on the front-porch floor and I lift my eyes to where the Father looks. **Resource and Stewardship** is the album that came out of that porch floor, a whole record about money and provision and the strange, freeing arithmetic of the kingdom, where the God who owns everything hands it to people who own nothing and calls them faithful.
Jehovah-Jireh saw the ram before Abraham saw the thicket

The record opens with the oldest name for provision in the Book. When Abraham climbed the mountain with his son and the knife, trusting God for what he could not see, **Yahuah** caught a ram in a thicket behind him, and Abraham named the place forever: *"The LORD will provide"*, Jehovah-Jireh (Genesis 22:14). The song is built on the tense of that mercy, and I want you to feel it: *You saw the ram inside the thicket when I could not see. You see the rent before the paycheck. You see the bread before I knead.* The provision was already caught in the bush before Abraham ever turned around. God's supply is not a reaction to your crisis. It was set in place before your crisis arrived.

That is why the album refuses to worry the way the world worries. **Yeshua** pointed at the birds, *"Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap... yet God feeds them"* (Luke 12:24), and drew the only sane conclusion: *"Look at the birds of the air... are you not of more value than they?"* (Matthew 6:26). The song sings it plainly: *the ravens never sowed a single seed, the lilies never spun a single thread, yet You feed them, Father, every one in need, and You have never left me unfed.* This is not a promise of luxury. It is a promise of a Father, and a Father who feeds ravens does not forget His own children.
I am only the hands that hold it

Now here is the hinge of the whole record, and it is the difference between provision and stewardship. It is one thing to believe God supplies. It is another, deeper thing to believe that what He supplies was never yours to begin with.

The chorus of "Jehovah-Jireh" makes the confession that reorganizes a person's entire relationship to money: *Father, You are the Provider. I am only hands that hold. Every gift inside my keeping is a gift that You controlled.* That is straight from David, at the height of Israel's wealth, praying over the offering for the temple: *"But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able thus to offer willingly? For all things come from you, and of your own have we given you"* (1 Chronicles 29:14). Of your own have we given you. And **Yahuah** says it Himself through the prophet: *"The silver is mine, and the gold is mine, declares the LORD of hosts"* (Haggai 2:8). If you believe that, really believe it, the whole weight of ownership lifts off your shoulders. You are not a proprietor defending a hoard. You are a steward holding, for a while, something that belongs to Someone kind.

Before I count the dollars in the drawer, before I write the figures in the book, Father, I sit on the front-porch floor and I lift my eyes to where You look. I am only hands that hold; every gift inside my keeping is a gift that You controlled.
What the hands are for

If the resource is His and I am only the hands that hold it, then the songs have to answer the obvious question: hold it *for what*? And the record spends its middle answering, because a steward who only clutches has missed the calling entirely.

There is "Jesus, Multiply It," built on the boy who handed over five loaves and two fish and watched **Yeshua** feed thousands, because in the kingdom, what you release multiplies and what you hoard rots. There is "Jesus, I Sit Down First," on His own counsel: *"Which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost?"* (Luke 14:28). Stewardship is not reckless generosity; it is *counted* generosity, wisdom and open hands together. And the Lord who owns it all still asks us to give it back cheerfully: *"Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver"* (2 Corinthians 9:7). He does not need your money. He wants your heart, and He knows the two travel together, *"where your treasure is, there your heart will be also."*

And He measures it upside down from the world. When the widow dropped in her two small coins, He said she *"put in more than all"* the wealthy givers, *"for they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty put in everything she had"* (Mark 12:43-44). The kingdom does not count the size of the gift; it weighs the size of the trust behind it. That is the freedom of the record's final songs, "Jesus, Teach the Children" and "Father, You Are the Forever Giver", because the surest sign a steward has understood the lesson is that she is unafraid, generous, and already teaching the next generation to hold with open hands.
Who this is for

This is for the family staring at a budget that does not close, doing the porch-floor math before the paycheck comes. It is for the person who has enough and is quietly terrified of losing it, sister, you cannot lose what was never yours; you can only steward it or hoard it. It is for the giver and the tither and the one who has nothing but two coins and wonders if they even count. They count the most. And it is for anyone raising children who need to learn, early, that the drawer was never theirs.

Remember how the parable of the talents ends. Not with an audit of net worth, but with a word over a servant who was *faithful*: *"Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a little; I will set you over much"* (Matthew 25:23). Faithful over a little, because *"one who is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much"* (Luke 16:10). That is the whole assignment. He provides it. You only get to hold it. So hold it well, hold it open, and lift your eyes to where the Father looks before you ever count the drawer.

pieces.title: On the Worst Day of My Life, Grace Walked In Without Knocking
pieces.imagePrompt: A diverse circle of people around a warm kitchen table at dawn, one man exhaling with his head lifted and shoulders loosening as friends of many nations lean in with steady, unshaming faces, morning light pouring through the window onto open hands and a worn Bible, quiet relief breaking into smiles; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, warm amber and soft-gold tones, tender and freeing, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: This is the album I wrote for the person hiding in the dark at 2 a.m. with the bathroom light off, carrying a shame they have never said out loud. It is a slow walk from hidden to standing tall, built on the audacious arithmetic of Romans 5: where sin increased, grace increased all the more. The weight you mistook for humility was only condemnation. You can lay it down.

body.text: There is a version of me I used to keep alive only on Sundays, the one who kept the lights on and the smile steady. And there is the me at 2 a.m. at the kitchen table with the bathroom light off, rehearsing a secret I had never said out loud to anyone. *Grace Redeems* is the album I wrote to get that second man into the light.

I made it because I got tired of preaching a healing I did not yet have. This is a record about shame, the real thing, the specific thing, the thing you have buried under Monday smiles, and about the grace that meets it there and does not flinch.
Shame thrives in silence, so the album begins by breaking it

The opener is called "Honest Reckoning," and it is exactly that. No band. Just a Rhodes chord, a fingerpicked guitar, and a man saying the thing at last: *Father, here is the truth I buried. I am tired of pretending.* I anchored it to the plainest promise in the New Testament, *if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us and to cleanse us* (1 John 1:9), and to David's dangerous prayer, *search me, O God, and know my heart* (Psalm 139:23–24). Because shame's whole strategy is silence. The naming is the first half of the freedom. You cannot be met in a room you refuse to admit you are standing in.

Then, on "The Weight Lifts," I sing the part that took me years to understand. I had carried something strapped to my back like a second spine, and I had mistaken it for conviction, mistaken it for humility. It was only condemnation. There is a difference, and the difference is everything: *there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus* (Romans 8:1). Conviction is the kind hand of **Yahuah** turning you toward home. Condemnation is a bag He never asked you to hold. On this record a man finally sets it down and discovers he is breathing different, lighter, not because he minimized the sin, but because the Son already bore it.
I mistook it for conviction. I mistook it for humility. Father, it was only condemnation.
Grace is loudest on the worst day

The center of the album is a single sentence I would put on the wall of every hiding heart: *grace met the worst day.* That is the song, and it is the testimony compressed to five words. **Yeshua** did not wait for me to clean up before He arrived. On the worst day of my life He walked into the room without knocking, hands open, His name on the air, and the worst day got smaller in His light. This is the scandalous math of Paul: *where sin increased, grace abounded all the more* (Romans 5:20). Not grace that matches the sin, grace that overwhelms it. And when I begged for a healing that felt like fireworks, what I got instead was the quiet word of the Lord: *my grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness* (2 Corinthians 12:9).

From there the record hands you back your future. "The Failure Is Not the Future" is built on the truth that the past does not get to write the next page, the Author does. *Forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead* (Philippians 3:13–14), and *neither things present nor things to come* can separate you from His love (Romans 8:38–39). The failure is a paragraph. It is not the title page.
A new name, and the courage to stand up

Then comes the turn I love most. On "New Name Spoken," the Father does not name me by what I had done. He names me by what He had paid. I built that song on the promise in Revelation, *to the one who conquers I will give a white stone, with a new name written on it that no one knows except the one who receives it* (Revelation 2:17), and Isaiah's word that *you shall be called by a new name that the mouth of the Lord will give* (Isaiah 62:2). The old name was the failure I had repeated in my own head for twenty-two years. The new name has authority the old one lost the moment it landed.

And "Standing Tall" is the body finally agreeing with the testimony. It is a man in a church basement, on a folding chair, standing up in a small group and saying it all out loud, and the room does not shrink back; the room leans in. The standing is not pride. It is restored dignity. *Having done all, to stand* (Ephesians 6:13), and the promise that undergirds the whole thing: *the Lord is able to make him stand* (Romans 14:4).
Who I made this for, and why it does not end with you

The last movement of the album refuses to let redemption be private. "Lifting Others Out of Hiding" is a man across a diner booth at 11 p.m., pouring the second cup and listening while a friend finally says his own secret, because *confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be healed* (James 5:16). The freed become the freeing. And the finale, "Grace Forever," ends the only way redemption can, which is to say it does not end: *for by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God* (Ephesians 2:8–9). Grace keeps moving because the freed keep passing it forward. Leave the porch light on. Pour the second cup. Save the folding chair for the next saint.

So hear me, whoever is reading this at 2 a.m. with the light off: the room you are afraid of is the room where He finds you. You do not have to say it perfectly. You just have to say it. The weight you have called humility for years was only condemnation, and it was never yours to carry. Name it, lay it on the table, and watch what grace does with the worst day of your life.

pieces.title: The Mercy That Does Not Hurry
pieces.imagePrompt: A tender scene of diverse friends sitting close with a grieving man in a softly lit room, one hand resting on his back and another holding his, faces patient and unhurried, a cup of tea going cold on the table as first light warms the walls, the quiet comfort of people who will not rush him; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, warm amber and dawn-blue tones, gentle and safe, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I wrote this album for the person everyone keeps telling should be further along by now. It is a record for the wound that is still here, sung by a pastor who refuses to preach a healing he does not have. Grace does not always look like lightning, sometimes it looks like God pulling up a chair on the long Tuesday afternoon and simply staying.

body.text: Somebody told me I should be further along by now. They meant it kindly. They pinned a verse to me the way you pin one to the version of a person who is fine. And I decided, standing there, that I was done preaching a healing I did not actually have.

*Healing Wounds* is the album that came out of that decision. It is a record for the wound that is still here, the anniversary that still arrives, the grief still sitting on the edge of the mattress at 3 a.m., and for the God who has not flinched once at any of it.
The wound is still here, and He is still here

The opening song is simply called "The Wound Is Still Here," and it is the most honest sentence I have ever put first on a record. *I am done preaching a healing I do not have, Lord, so here is the honest thing: the wound is still here. And You have not flinched once.* I built it on the oldest promise of healing in the book, *by his stripes we are healed* (Isaiah 53:5), and on the God who *heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds* (Psalm 147:3). Notice the tense. Not *were healed and moved on*, but *being* healed. The anniversary comes and **Yahuah** does not shame the tears. He never once asked me for a timetable.

Because here is what the healing industry does not tell you: some healing is a sprint, but most of God's repair is a walk. "Slow Mercy" is the song at the heart of the album, and its whole claim is that His mercy reads a different calendar than the one the world hands you. *At the pace of breath and blood and tears, You meet me in the years.* There is a grace that does not look like lightning. It looks like **Yeshua** pulling up a chair on the long Tuesday afternoon when nothing at all happens, except that He stays. And His staying is the miracle.
The miracle is not the speed. He is the miracle. And He is staying.
He does not fix me too fast

The most counterintuitive prayer on the record is on "Stay With Me": *Jesus, do not fix me too fast. Do not rush me past the part I do not understand.* I mean that prayer. Most of the sermons I have actually needed were not sentences at all. They were His face across from mine, a chair pulled up, a door not closed. He is *the God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction* (2 Corinthians 1:3–4), and He is *near to the brokenhearted* (Psalm 34:18). He does not hand you a verse and leave. He sits down beside you and He does not explain. He just does not leave.

And He does it in the dead hours. "Three Forty Seven" is set at the exact minute the wound wakes up, the hour when the grief you thought you had sent to bed is sitting on the edge of the mattress. The song calls Him an insomniac of love, because *he who keeps you will not slumber; behold, he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep* (Psalm 121:3–4). I used to fight the grief at the door. Now I set a chair for it, and I find He is already seated there, awake, keeping the night watch in my room.
The room around me, and the balm that is a Person

I could not make an honest healing record without the church, because I did not heal alone and neither will you. "The Room Around Me" is about the body of **Yeshua** as the actual bandage the Spirit uses, the casserole on the porch, the hand on the shoulder, the friend who showed up at six months and two years, long after the polite window had closed. He healed me *inside* His body, not off by myself. And the album's peak, "Balm for Gilead," takes the ancient cry, *is there no balm in Gilead?* (Jeremiah 8:22), and answers it with a Person. The balm is His body broken and His blood poured out. The Healer is not a technique. He is a Man with scars who does not leave the room.

Which is the whole turn of the record. On "Scars Become Songs," the wound that almost ended me becomes the very vocabulary the Spirit gives me to love the next hurting person, because one day someone I love reached the 3 a.m. hour I had reached, and I had nothing to give them except the scar His hands had already touched. He *comforts us so that we may be able to comfort those in any affliction* (2 Corinthians 1:4). The scar is not the shame. It becomes the song.
Who this album is for

It is for the one who buried a parent, a child, a marriage, a self, and is quietly ashamed it is taking so long. For the person whose faith promised a fast fix and delivered a long walk instead. For anyone worn out by well-meaning people counting the months. Hear me: you are not regressing. You are being healed, and *the inner self is being renewed day by day* even while the outer wastes (2 Corinthians 4:16).

The album ends on "The Road Home," and it does not pretend the scar is gone. It calls us a caravan of the still-being-healed, walking with a God whose home is not where the wound ends but where the wound is held, because *the Way* Himself is both the home and the road (John 14:6). So take His pace. Lay down the striving. He is not in a hurry, He is not going anywhere, and the mercy that will not rush you is the mercy that will get you all the way home.

pieces.title: Every Curse on This Family Stops at My Generation
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful multigenerational, multiethnic family gathered around a long kitchen table with the leaf pulled out, grandparents and grandchildren laughing together as a father blesses a small child with a hand on the head, a porch light glowing warm through the window, faces bright with belonging across four generations; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, warm golden and honey tones, tender and celebratory, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: This is my album about the family tree, the rooms in you that you did not decorate, the voices in you that you never hired. It is about the sharp tone you swore you would never use leaking out of your own mouth, and the God older than the bloodline who breaks the curse and turns the hearts of fathers back to their children. The blessing runs forward from here.

body.text: We all came from somewhere, and that somewhere came from somewhere before. There are rooms in me I did not decorate and voices in me I never hired. *Family Blessing* is the album I wrote about that inheritance, the part of the family tree you carry whether you chose it or not, and about the God who is older than the bloodline and speaks louder than it.
I did not write it as a nostalgia record. I wrote it as a chain-breaker. Because somewhere along the line, one person has to decide that what got handed down does not get handed down any further.
The bloodline speaks, but He speaks louder

The album opens with my grandfather's voice, unpolished, over a held chord: *Child, before you hear a word I sing, hear me tell you this, Jesus wanted you. The Father wanted you before you were born.* Then the song "Bloodline" does the honest work of naming what we carry, and it stands on a promise from the very last page of the Old Testament: *he will turn the hearts of fathers to their children, and the hearts of children to their fathers* (Malachi 4:6). And it stands on Paul's word that **Yeshua** was *born under the law to redeem those under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons* (Galatians 4:4–5), and that *he redeemed us from the curse* by becoming it for us (Galatians 3:13). The bloodline gets the last word it pretends to have only until the Father speaks.

Then the record gets specific and uncomfortable, the way it has to. "The Tone I Swore I Wouldn't Use" is a man hearing the old sharpness leak out of his own mouth at the kitchen mirror at 6 a.m., the sigh he inherited, the door-slam he memorized, the words his father never had for him that he almost did not have for his son. This is where cycles actually break or don't: at the sink, in a single sentence, with the Spirit moving your tongue back. *Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up* (Ephesians 4:29). I asked **Yahuah** to retune the instrument of my mouth, and He did, not by shaming the broken thing, but by teaching it a new sound.
The bloodline speaks, but You speak louder. Father, You turn the hearts of fathers to the children.
The empty chair, and the Father who takes it

Some of us grew up staring at an empty chair at the head of the table. "Empty Chair" is that song, and it rests on the tenderest name for God in the Psalms: *a father to the fatherless, a defender of widows, is God in his holy dwelling, God sets the lonely in families* (Psalm 68:5–6). The Father did not arrive late to that table. He sat down in the empty chair and then pulled mine right up next to His, because *every family in heaven and on earth is named* from Him (Ephesians 3:14–15). If the chair at the head of your childhood table was empty, hear this carefully: it is not empty now.

And the blessing has to be handed forward on purpose, in small repeated holy things. "Pass It Down" is a verse taped to a fridge in 1989, the card yellow now, the tape brown, the verse the same, the inheritance that outran three moves and a will. That is the actual mechanism God gave us: *these words shall be on your heart; you shall teach them diligently to your children, and write them on the doorposts of your house* (Deuteronomy 6:6–9), the faith that *dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice* (2 Timothy 1:5).
The blessing breaks, and the whole house breathes

The turn of the album, and the song I would hand anyone who is the first believer in their line, is "The Blessing Breaks." It is a man calling his sister at 9 p.m. and saying the words out loud: *Beth, every curse on this family stops at my generation.* And the phone goes quiet a long time, and then she says, *I receive that. I receive that. I receive that.* The next morning she calls back, her son slept through the night. That is not superstition; that is what happens when one mouth in a family finally breaks a silence in the name of the One who *redeemed us from the curse* (Galatians 3:13). The curse hits the bedrock of the Son and it shatters. The blessing breaks because He broke first.

And once it breaks, it multiplies. "The Table Is Long" is the blessing become a climate, a table that keeps growing because the Father keeps adding chairs, the leaf pulled out for the cousin who left, the neighbor who never darkened a church door, the man who used to be an enemy. *Compel them to come in, that my house may be filled* (Luke 14:23). "Prodigals Welcome" keeps the porch light on for the one who left at nineteen, because the father in the parable *saw him while he was still a long way off* and ran (Luke 15:20).
Who this album is for

It is for the one who swore they would parent differently and heard the old voice come out anyway. For the first believer in a hard line, wondering if the past gets a permanent vote. For the person who inherited a silence and is deciding, right now, whether to pass it on or break it.

The album ends where it began, with my grandfather's voice, and then the blessing handed to the next mouth: *the Lord bless you and keep you; the Lord make his face shine upon you* (Numbers 6:24–26). *One generation shall commend your works to another* (Psalm 145:4). So decide it today. As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord (Joshua 24:15). The curse stops here. The blessing runs forward. And the God who is older than your bloodline has already carved a place at the long table for the children who come after you.

pieces.title: The Wall Had My Address for Thirteen Months
pieces.imagePrompt: A jubilant, globally diverse crowd bursting through a broken-open wall into wide morning sky, arms raised and faces radiant with release, broken chains falling to the ground at their feet as light floods over people of many nations mid-shout of joy, dust and dawn glowing gold around them; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, warm amber and open-sky blue tones, triumphant and alive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I wrote this album from the foot of a wall I had sat at for thirteen months and four days. It is a record about deliverance that refuses to pretend, the chain that turned out to be a costume, the barrier you baptized as caution, the walls you built to protect yourself that only kept God out. From Jericho to the open sky, this is the sound of what you cannot move coming down.

body.text: I sat at the foot of that wall for thirteen months and four days. I had prayed every angle I knew how to pray. The wall had my address by then, the wall and I were on familiar terms. *Breakthrough* is the album I made from that spot, and it is a record about the exact moment what you cannot move finally comes down.

I did not want to write a triumphalist record that skips the wall. So this album names the wall honestly before it ever names the break. Because the God of Scripture is not embarrassed by the seasons we spend sitting in front of things that will not budge.
Name the wall before you name the break

The opener, "Breaking Through," starts at the kitchen table with a man who has run out of prayers, and the Lord standing up beside him and saying, *Son, watch what I am about to do.* The whole album stands on the day David called Baal-perazim: *the Lord has broken through my enemies before me, like a breaking flood* (2 Samuel 5:20). And on the wall at Jericho that fell not to a battering ram but to obedience and a shout (Joshua 6). And on the line I keep taped to my own life: *by my God I can leap over a wall* (Psalm 18:29). The first stone is already in His hand. What I cannot move, **Yahuah** can.

But here is the confession the album makes on "When the Walls Fall Down", some of the walls I was praying against, I built myself. I had fortified my heart. I had kept myself shielded from the dark and the pain, and the very wall I raised to protect me was the wall that kept God out and kept me lonely. Then He said, *let the walls down; let Me love you.* He promised through Isaiah to *swallow up death forever and wipe away tears from all faces* (Isaiah 25:7–8), and He meant the inner rooms too. Sometimes the breakthrough is not Him tearing down an enemy's fortress. It is you opening a door from the inside.
Son. You don't have to keep the wall up to keep My love. I have been on both sides of it the whole time.
The chain was a costume

The song I would hand anyone who feels permanently bound is "Every Chain Released," and its central image undid me when I wrote it: the Holy Spirit walking into the room where He found me and saying, *Son, the keys never fit. The chain was a costume.* So much of what binds us is a limitation we baptized as identity, a prison the world insisted was permanent. And **Yeshua** unbuckles what we could not unbuckle, because *if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed* (John 8:36), and *for freedom Christ has set us free, stand firm, then, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery* (Galatians 5:1). Every link that named me before He renamed me is on the floor now.

And I could not write a deliverance record that made freedom feel like a performance you keep up. "Walking Into Rest" flips the whole striving on its head: sometimes rest is an action, and the bravest decision you make all week is at the kitchen table on a Tuesday night, letting go. *Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest* (Matthew 11:28). *There remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God* (Hebrews 4:9–11). The rest of God is louder than my striving.
He held me the whole time

The tender center of the album is "His Arms Around Me," and it reframes everything that came before. **Yeshua** did not arrive at month thirteen to demolish the wall while I white-knuckled the wait. He was already holding me at the foot of it the whole time, *the eternal God is your dwelling place, and underneath are the everlasting arms* (Deuteronomy 33:27); *fear not, for I am with you; I will strengthen you, I will uphold you with my righteous right hand* (Isaiah 41:10). The breakthrough was never me finally earning His attention. It was me discovering His arms had been around me since before the first crack appeared.

And the album's peak, "His Faithfulness Endures," says the truest sentence I know how to sing over a hard season: *the story is not "you held on through it." The story is: He held you. He always held you.* Because *his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness* (Lamentations 3:22–23), and *if we are faithless, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself* (2 Timothy 2:13).
Who this album is for

It is for the one who has prayed every angle and is still sitting at the wall. For the person who built the wall themselves and calls it caution. For anyone wearing a chain they have started to believe is their name. For the believer who is more than a conqueror through Him who loved us (Romans 8:37) and cannot feel it yet.

The album ends on "Breakthrough Proclamation," and it does not let the open sky stay private. It sends you to call the next person into it, because the breakthrough is a doorway He holds open, not a trophy you keep. *For a vision awaits its appointed time; though it tarries, wait for it; it will surely come* (Habakkuk 2:3). So if you are at the wall tonight, hear me: the wall has your address, but it does not have the last word. He knows the seam. He has been studying it longer than you have. The first stone is already in His hand, and there is open sky on the other side.

pieces.title: The Shake in My Voice Was Never the Disqualifier
pieces.imagePrompt: A warm front-porch gathering at dusk with diverse neighbors of many nations pulled up in chairs, one man leaning in mid-story with an open hand while another rests a steadying grip on his shoulder, coffee mugs and an open Bible on the step, lantern light glowing gold as faces listen with tears and smiles; premium worship-brand cinematic film-still quality, warm amber and honey tones, intimate and courageous, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: This is my dobro-and-harmonica album about being terrified to tell your story and telling it anyway. It is for the person whose hands shake at the thought of speaking the name of Jesus out loud, a record that insists the trembling is not the disqualifier, the trembling is the altar. You do not need a stage. You need a screen door, a cup of coffee, and the courage to say the part you want to hide.

body.text: The microphone was taller than I was that night. My sermon notes were shaking in my hand. I had underlined His name nine times and still could not get my mouth open. *Faithful Witness* is the album I wrote out of that exact terror, and out of the truth I learned on the other side of it: the shake was never the thing that disqualified me.

This is a dobro-slide, harmonica, brushed-kit record, front-porch music, because the kind of witness I most believe in does not happen on a stage. It happens across a kitchen table, on the steps at dusk, in a diner over coffee gone cold.
The mic and the knees are both His

The opening song is "The Mic and the Knees," and it does not hide the fear. It consecrates it. *The mic and the knees are both Yours, Lord. Father, let the shake be the sermon tonight.* I built it on the great crowd in Hebrews, *since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us run with endurance, looking to Jesus* (Hebrews 12:1–2), and on Peter's charge to be *prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you, yet with gentleness and respect* (1 Peter 3:15). The shake is not the disqualifier. The shake is the altar.

And the second song says the thing I most want a nervous believer to hear: you do not have to wait for a feeling that may never come. "Tell It Anyway" is a man who was waiting on the wind and got an elder's hand on his shoulder instead, *son, the witness doesn't wait on the wind; He'll meet you in the telling.* When **Yeshua** healed the man among the tombs, He did not send him to seminary; He said, *go home to your friends and tell them how much the Lord has done for you* (Mark 5:19). And the apostles, hauled in and ordered to stop, could only answer, *we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard* (Acts 4:20). The testimony does not need a stage to land. It just needs a mouth willing to shake.
The shake in the voice is the song. Jesus, You'll do the work in the silence between the lines.
Front porch gospel

The heart of the album is a picture I would put over every anxious evangelist's desk. "Front Porch Gospel" is a screen door slapping at six, a neighbor sitting down with his coffee and his griefs, and a man who *did not preach*. He poured him a cup, and **Yahuah** did the rest. The porch became the pulpit, the cup became the chalice, and the gospel walked from chair to chair. *Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden* (Matthew 11:28) handed across a step. Because *we are ambassadors for Christ* (2 Corinthians 5:20), and an ambassador does not need a sound check. He needs a doorway and a willingness to sit in it.

Then the record does something I needed it to do: it honors the quiet, unglamorous witness that never trends. "The Long Haul Honesty" is about the testimony that ages out of the spotlight, my grandfather preached forty-one years in the same small town, no album, no platform, just the elder's hand on every shoulder, and *forty-one years of front-pew faithfulness sing louder than the stadium.* That is the witness Scripture actually crowns: *I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith* (2 Timothy 4:7). Not the flash. The kept candle.
Faithful through repetition

The album's peak is a song called "Faithful Through Repetition," and it may be the least glamorous thesis I have ever built a track around, and the truest. The same sermon notes for the four-hundredth Sunday. The joy not new today, and the witness getting up anyway. *Faithfulness is a kind of repetition, the same Name on my tongue until the tongue forgets to question it.* The Father's own word in the bridge is the whole permission I wish someone had given me at twenty-three: *son, you don't have to dazzle the room to witness for Me. Just say My name today. Say it again tomorrow. That's the witness.* Paul closes his resurrection chapter exactly there: *be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord* (1 Corinthians 15:58); *let us not grow weary of doing good* (Galatians 6:9).

And it multiplies down a bloodline. "Teach Them the Telling" is a man sitting his daughter down with her coffee and saying *the testimony doesn't skip a generation in this house*, teaching her to tell the very part she was tempted to hide, because *you shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house and when you walk by the way* (Deuteronomy 6:7). The testimony is a torch, not a trophy.
Who this album is for

It is for the believer whose hands go cold at the thought of saying His name out loud. For the person convinced they need a platform, a title, or a certain confidence they do not have. For the one who has been outsourcing their own story to polished men in suits, when the rough draft they lived is the very gospel God wants to preach through them.

The finale, "Witness Forever," names the listener as the next faithful witness and sends them out, because *they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony* (Revelation 12:11), and *let the redeemed of the Lord say so* (Psalm 107:2). So say it, wherever you are. You do not need a stage; you need a screen door and a cup of coffee and the nerve to tell the part you want to hide. Let the shake be the sermon. He will meet you in the telling. He always does.

pieces.title: You Circle Six Days to Shout on the Seventh
pieces.song: When We Shout, The Walls Fall Down
pieces.imagePrompt: A jubilant globally-diverse street congregation in full praise-break motion, believers of many nations packed on a sunlit avenue, hands thrown up, a young drummer on congas, elders clapping, a great crowd caught mid-shout as light pours between buildings, tambourines lifted, pure collective joy, cinematic worship-brand film still, bright and euphoric, warm gold and amber tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I put a DMV go-go pocket under the oldest deliverance story in the book, because Jericho was never about a battering ram. It was about a shout. Six days of silence, and then the sound the wall could not survive. This is why the praise break is our whole address.

body.text: Put a go-go pocket under it, congas, cowbell, the rototom, the pocket bass walking deep on the sixteenth-note ghost notes, the Hammond spinning on a fast Leslie, the horns answering every line, and then hand the oldest deliverance story in the Bible back to the people it was written for. That is what I made *Go-Go Praise Break* to do.

Because Jericho was never a story about engineering. There was no battering ram. No siege tower. No ladder against the wall. The most fortified city in the land came down to a *sound*, and I wanted the whole DMV to feel that in their feet before they ever argued it in their heads.
The Wall Did Not Fall on Day One

Here is the part we skip when we want the miracle without the marching. **Yahuah** told Joshua to take the whole army around the city once a day, in silence, for six days. Six days of walking a perimeter and watching nothing happen. Trumpets in the front, the ark on the shoulders of the men, and not one brick moving.

*"And it came to pass on the seventh day, that they rose early about the dawning of the day, and compassed the city after the same manner seven times... And the people shouted with a great shout, that the wall fell down flat"* (Joshua 6:15, 20).

I wrote a whole song just for the waiting, *"Seven Days Around the Wall"*, and I built the DMV day-count right into the bridge, because that is the part that breaks people. *Day six in your waiting, child, the answer's almost here.* Don't quit on day six. The silence of the first six days is not **Yahuah** ignoring you. It is the discipline that makes the seventh-day shout mean something. Most folks abandon the march one lap short of the wall.

And notice the marching order Israel kept. The trumpet went in the *front*, the ark of the covenant on the shoulders of the men, the presence of God carried right into the perimeter of a city that had not budged. They were not circling a wall. They were carrying the presence around it, six days running, trusting a promise they could not yet see keeping. That is the real work of the silent days, not proving your patience, but keeping His presence in the center of the march while nothing visible changes.
The Shout Is a Weapon, Not a Mood

Now hear me carefully, because the culture has trained us to think a shout is just excitement. It is not. At Jericho the shout was the *weapon*. It was the thing **Yahuah** chose, on purpose, to bring down what no army could.

So on *"When We Shout, The Walls Fall Down"* I take the seventh-day shout and I aim it at your living room. *What you been staring at for thirteen years can fall tonight.* The name of **Yeshua** carries more authority than any obstacle's might. That is not hype. That is the standing pattern of a God who prefers to topple the impossible with a sound His children make in faith.
Concrete crumbling all around, the same God who walked into Joshua's story walks into a praise break, and the walls have never learned to tell the difference.

And then Act Two of the record turns the shout loose on the real walls. *"Shout the Anxiety Out"* stands on Philippians 4:6, *be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God*, and answers the 3 AM phone call from worry with an eviction notice. *"Shout the Addiction Out"* takes the twelve-step circle of folding chairs and puts **Yeshua** in the middle of the room, on the word He gave in John 8:36: *if the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.* *"Shout the Old Story Down"* hands the abuse survivor a new page, because *if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature; old things are passed away* (2 Corinthians 5:17). Every wall in the deliverance act falls to the same weapon that dropped Jericho.
Why I Took It to the Parking Lot

The center of gravity on this album is a track called *"Holy Ghost Block Party."* Watch Night, hour seven, and the Spirit says: *take it out, the parking lot needs the light.* The deacon runs a cable from the truck to the bass. Somebody rolls the Hammond out the storefront's side door. The neighborhood comes out in their pajamas under the streetlight, and the brother who spent years too afraid of all the tears to come inside gets touched on the shoulder on the asphalt, and the chains break in his own words.

That is the whole reason for the go-go. Go-go is DMV street music, call-and-response, the congregation *is* the band, the pocket never stops. And that is exactly what a Holy Ghost people are. So on *"Where My Holy Ghost People At?"* I stop being the caller and I turn the microphone around: I have called for six straight tracks, now the sanctuary answers back. The deliverance was never meant to stay on the platform. Once you have shouted a wall down, *you* are the deliverance team.
Who I Made the Shout For

I made it for the one still marching on day six, convinced the wall is permanent because it did not move on the first lap. For the one who has been staring at the same obstacle for thirteen years. For the survivor carrying an old story in somebody else's voice. For the brother on the corner who has watched the church for years and is sure the tears would swallow him if he stepped inside.

And I made it because the shout does not stop at the wall. Listen to how the record ends. *"The Shout Is Our Address"* claims the whole identity, the world wants a denomination and a street number, and we tell them we are *from the praise break, where the chains come undone.* Then *"The Shout Don't Stop"* lifts the eyes all the way up, because Revelation 7:9 shows a great multitude *which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues* standing before the throne with a shout that has no end. Jericho was just the opening lap. The same shout that dropped the wall is already rising around the throne, and it is on the map from here to eternity.

So circle your six days, beloved. Keep marching when nothing is moving. Hold the silence without quitting. And when the seventh dawn comes and the trumpet finally sounds, open your mouth with everything in you. The wall in front of you was built by men and reinforced by years, but it has never once survived the sound of a people who believe **Yahuah**. Shout, and deliver. The wall is closer to falling than it has ever been.

pieces.title: He Gave Me Eyes for What the City Keeps Ignoring
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful globally-diverse street procession at first light, a New Orleans-style second-line of many nations dancing behind a brass band, believers lifting white handkerchiefs, trumpets and trombones raised, elders and children marching together down a sunlit avenue, radiant faces caught mid-celebration, cinematic worship-brand film still, bright and jubilant, warm golden dawn tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I woke at 4:47 with a vision and a brass band in my chest, and I made a whole second-line record out of it. The seer doesn't sit in a tower guarding secrets, the seer walks. This is the story of the procession that carried prophecy down Esplanade and into the streets.

body.text: Four forty-seven in the morning, the blinds still on the wall, and I sat up in the dark with the Hammond from somebody's radio already in the hall and a vision already in my chest. Before I lit the air, the Lord was showing me pictures. And the strangest part was not the vision. It was the brass band that woke up with it, the tambourine coming on slow, the whole procession assembling in my spirit while the streetlamp was still the only light on the corner.

That is where *Eyes Wide (The Seer Walks)* was born. And I set it to a New Orleans second-line, trumpet, trombone, sousaphone, the zydeco accordion, the frottoir rubboard scraping the backbeat, because I needed you to understand one thing the church keeps getting wrong: the seer is not a person who *sits.* The seer *walks.*
The Old Word for Prophet Was "Seer"

There is a little verse most people read right past. *"Beforetime in Israel, when a man went to enquire of God, thus he spake, Come, and let us go to the seer: for he that is now called a Prophet was beforetime called a Seer"* (1 Samuel 9:9). Seer. One who *sees.* Before we had the word prophet, we had a word about the eyes.

And the eyes have a rule. The seer does not manufacture the vision. She receives it, and then she has to *wait* for it, and then she has to *walk* it. That is Habakkuk's whole assignment: *"I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower... And the LORD answered me, and said, Write the vision, and make it plain... For the vision is yet for an appointed time... though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come"* (Habakkuk 2:1–3).

So the album opens on the watch. *"Eyes Wide Open"* is the seer the Lord wakes at dawn, and the line I could not stop singing became the title of everything I want to say here: *He gave me eyes for what the city has been ignoring.* Then *"What I See Is Real"* is the seer at the kitchen table at eleven at night, Habakkuk open, the coffee gone cold, second-guessing, until the validation comes in slow. **Yahuah** does not hand out visions just to make you feel something. He shows you what He shows you so you will not shut up about it.
The Procession Is the Prophecy

Here is why I built the whole thing as a second-line and not a solo. In the culture that raised this music, the procession *is* the message. You do not read the prophecy off a page. You walk it down the street, and the whole block falls in behind the brass.

So on *"The Procession Has Begun,"* the seer lifts a handkerchief pressed white the night before, and steps off the sanctuary floor with the trumpet on the lead-note and the sousaphone on the back. The middle of the record is one long walk, and the seer's eyes sweep across everything she loves. *Over the sanctuary*. I see the wind, I see the wave, the glory getting ready to fall on Sunday. *Over the marriage*. I see the husband on his knees and the wife finally letting go of the key she carried too long, and the Lord loosing what was bound *at the speed of slow.* *Over the next generation*, the teenagers at the altar, the prophets in their twenties already being built.
The seer does not walk to keep the vision. She walks so the whole street can catch what heaven has been trying to show it.

And then *"Over the City (NOLA Walk)"*, Treme to the Lower Ninth, handkerchief in the air, the intercessors behind the brass, the sister at the storefront setting her broom against the chair to watch the procession pass. This is where the prophetic stops being private. The seer walks the actual blocks and calls out over each one what the Lord let her track.
What the Seer Is Really Looking For

Do not miss where the eyes finally land, because it tells you the heart of the whole gift. After the city and the nation, the vision narrows down to the ones nobody else is looking at. *"Eyes for the Hidden"*, the orphan in the system, the widow at the back, the forsaken on the corner the family stopped tracking. The Lord opens the book on the overlooked.

That is what prophetic sight is *for.* Not to impress a room. Not to guard secrets in a tower. **Yeshua** Himself walked into every crowd and saw the one, the woman in the press, the man up the tree, the blind beggar the disciples wanted to hush. Real seeing always ends up at the person the world has agreed to ignore.

And the burden is not meant to be carried alone. On *"Over the Nation,"* the vision gets heavier than one set of shoulders can hold, the weight of a whole country at dawn, and the seer does the only faithful thing: she lays it at the prophetic throne and calls the whole community in. *We are the seers, and the burden is the Lord's to be known.* Sight that stays private curdles into pride. Sight that gets shared becomes intercession, and intercession is what a procession was always for.
Who I Made This Walk For

I made it for the one who woke at 4:47 with something in her chest she could not explain and no category to put it in. For the seer at the kitchen table second-guessing the vision because the coffee is cold and the doubt is loud. For everybody who was taught that "prophetic" belongs to a special few standing on a stage, when the last-days promise was poured out on all of us.

Because the record does not end with one seer. *"We All Are Seers Now"* stands right on the ground Joel gave us: *your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions* (Joel 2:28). I stepped back from the front line, pointed at the whole congregation, and watched the aunties see the vision and the teenagers in the back row name the brave. And then *"The Whole City Will See"* lifts it to the end of the story, *behold, he cometh with clouds; and every eye shall see him* (Revelation 1:7). Twelve songs that started with one seer at dawn end with a city, and then a world, whose eyes are all about to open at once.

So if He has been showing you pictures in the dark, if you have felt something over your sanctuary, your marriage, your children, your city, do not file it away and go back to sleep. Lift the handkerchief. Fall in behind the brass. The seer was never meant to keep the vision. She was meant to walk it down the street until the whole city sees what He gave her eyes to see. And beloved, He gave you those eyes on purpose.

pieces.title: The Same Carpenter Turns Every Corner of Every Age
pieces.imagePrompt: A jubilant globally-diverse crowd of city-dwellers erupting in praise on a bright urban avenue and subway platform, believers of many nations with hands lifted, a woman mid-shout, elders and young people and a mother with a stroller radiant together, warm light flooding the scene, pure collective joy, cinematic worship-brand film still, bright and celebratory, warm gold and amber tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I set the miracle stories of the Gospels on a Bronx subway platform and let the funk carry them, because the Carpenter who worked Galilee is working the 149th Street line right now. Same hands. Same power. Different century. This is the record about a God who never stopped.

body.text: Eleven thirty-eight at night, the 149th Street and Grand Concourse platform, MetroCard down to two dollars and ninety cents, the last of the pay, and the landlord already called. That is where I opened *Miracle Worker (Subway Funk)*, not in a cathedral, but on a Bronx platform under the fluorescent light, with a clavinet funk-stab and a Hammond punch and a bass walking deep in the pocket.

Because I got tired of hearing the miracles of the Gospels talked about like they closed with the first century. They did not close. The same Carpenter who worked Galilee is working the 149th Street line, and I built a whole funk record to say it in the language of the block.
Same Carpenter, First Century to This One

The title track puts the thesis right in your ear: *same Jesus, first century, same Jesus, twenty-first century.* And the anchor is one dismissive little question the hometown crowd threw at Him in Mark. *"Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary?"* (Mark 6:3). They meant it as an insult, just a tradesman, just a working man's boy. But that is exactly the glory of it. The hands that built tables also raised the dead. The Carpenter turns the corner of *every* age.

And He handed the works forward. This is the promise the church keeps flinching away from: *"He that believeth on me, the works that I do shall he do also"* (John 14:12). So on *"Miracle Worker (149th Street)"* the city becomes the choir, shouting back *yeah, He works!*, because the works were never retired. **Yeshua** stopped for blind Bartimaeus at the Jericho gate; He stops for the corner you navigate. Same stopping. Same mercy. Different pavement.
The works of the Carpenter did not end at the edge of the New Testament. They walked out of it, straight onto the rush-hour block.
The Miracles Have a Bronx Address
I took the actual miracle stories and gave each one a real address, because that is how you know a God is present-tense: He shows up in a specific place, at a specific hour, for a specific person.

*"Walk (Gate Beautiful Now)"* is Acts 3, Peter and John at the temple gate, and the lame man asking for change. Peter says the line that reorganized the early church: *"Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth rise up and walk"* (Acts 3:6). I moved the Gate Beautiful to the 149th subway gate, because the man on that bench is the same man, and the Name is the same Name. *"Open My Eyes (Lincoln Hospital)"* takes Bartimaeus, *Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me* (Mark 10:47), into a fourth-floor corridor at 11:18 at night, where **Yeshua** deals not in fifty-fifty odds but in opened eyes.

And *"Lazarus Come Forth (Project Tower)"* is the one I could not sing without weeping. John 11, the tomb at Bethany, and the shortest, heaviest verse in the Bible: *Jesus wept* (John 11:35). He wept *first,* and then He spoke, and *Lazarus, come forth* emptied a grave (John 11:43). I mapped it to a project-tower funeral on the fourteenth floor with the elevator broken, because the same Voice that broke the bonds in Bethany climbs the stairs of the Bronx. He is not embarrassed by your human tears. He honors the grief, and then He speaks.
The Miracle Rides the Rush-Hour Train

There is a track on this record called *"Praise Break on the 6 Train,"* and it carries the whole idea further than any of the others. Friday, 7:43 in the evening, the doors sliding back at Union Square, and the Holy Ghost steps onto the car with the rush-hour crowd. The lady with the shopping bag starts humming. The brother in the corner has his Bible on his knee. And by the time the train passes Twenty-Third and Twenty-Eighth and Thirty-Third, the whole car is standing with hands lifted.

I wrote it that way on purpose, because the church has quietly agreed that the encounter belongs to the sanctuary and the sanctioned hour. It does not. The Carpenter does not keep office hours. If the works were handed to *believers*, then the believer at the bus stop, the cubicle, the corridor, the moving train is carrying a portable miracle. The 6 train becomes a moving sanctuary the moment somebody on it believes He is present, because He is.
Do not wait for Sunday to expect Him. He is on the train.
The City Itself Becomes the Testimony

The tenderest thing on the record is a track called *"What God Has Done,"* built around a storefront church on White Plains Road and a mother named in the song who stood at the altar rail and passed the microphone to her four children, one by one: *tell what God has done.* And they did. *He healed my mama. He fed us when the cupboard was bare. He stopped the eviction at the door. He brought my brother home.* A whole family line reading its receipts out loud.

That is the architecture of the whole album, provision on *"Ravens at My Window,"* where the church-lady's grocery bag becomes the literal fulfillment of *I have commanded the ravens to feed thee* (1 Kings 17:4–6); restoration on *"Years the Locust Ate,"* standing on the mercy of *I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten* (Joel 2:25); and the commission of *"Signs Shall Follow,"* where **Yeshua** promises *these signs shall follow them that believe* (Mark 16:17), and the signs are not for the platform alone, but for the believer in the church and the home.
Who I Made This Record For

I made it for the one on the late platform with $2.90 and a landlord's voicemail, sure that the dramatic miracles happen to other people in other centuries. For the family in the corridor being handed odds instead of hope. For the recovering one counting the years the locust ate and wondering if any of them can come back. For everybody who reads the Gospels like a closed museum and never once believed the Carpenter would turn *their* corner.

Because the record ends where it began. *"The Streets Still Sing"* reprises that first platform cry, *I needed a miracle on track one*, and answers it: the works ain't done, the Carpenter is still walking, and the whole city is the choir now. And underneath all of it stands the sentence Gabriel spoke to a teenage girl in Nazareth, the one I built an entire song around: *"For with God nothing shall be impossible"* (Luke 1:37).

Nothing. Not the rent, not the diagnosis, not the years you lost, not the grave you are standing over. The platform is a chapel when the chest is tight, the fluorescent is the chandelier, and the same Carpenter who worked first-century Galilee is turning the corner of your century right now. Make the call, beloved. He still works.

pieces.title: The Offerer Became the Offering
pieces.imagePrompt: A radiant globally-diverse congregation lifting open hands at a warm altar of light, believers of many nations with faces upturned and streaming with joy, some kneeling, some with arms raised high, glowing embers and golden light rising around them, a sense of release and homecoming, cinematic worship-brand film still, bright and emotive, warm amber and gold tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
