pieces.excerpt: I made a whole altar record about the one thing I would not put on the altar. You can bring a thousand offerings and still hold back the one that's naming you from the inside. This is the story of the night I learned the fire was never punishment. It was the kindness of God.

body.text: I built a whole altar record around the one thing I would not lay on the altar.

For nine years I would not say the name. The bitterness wore my face like a second skin, and I brought **Yahuah** a thousand other offerings. I served, I sang, I gave, I showed up early and stayed late, and the one thing I refused to name was quietly naming *me* from the inside. That is where *Burn It All* comes from. Twelve songs about a truth I had to learn the slow way: you can worship at the altar for years while carefully keeping the real offering in your pocket.

I set it to a contemporary band-led praise break, Hammond on the fast Leslie, kick-snare drive, brass punching every modulation lift, because I wanted the surrender to feel like release, not loss. The altar is loud on this record. It should be. Something is finally coming off.
The Altar Is Set to Take More Than Your Stuff

The record opens with the match. *"Fire Fall (Burn It All)"* is the offering laid on the wood, *every weight I dragged inside, every name I hid behind*, and the one line that governs the whole album: *what survives is what was Yours.* That is the promise and the warning together. The fire does not destroy what belongs to Him. It only burns what was never built to hold.

Then comes the hard part, the part most of us skip. *"Lay Down the Crown"* names the throne I carved out of my own pride and called freedom, a crown built from my own gold, my own name in the band, handed over to the only King who ever wore thorns. *"Tear Up the Blueprint"* takes the plan I drew in my own ink and hands the pen to the Architect who sat down at my kitchen table, because *"a man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps"* (Proverbs 16:9).
I kept bringing the altar my things. The altar kept quietly asking for me.
The Refiner Sits Down and Waits
The center of the whole record, the song I put in the frontmatter, is *"What Survives the Fire,"* and it is the most honest thing I have ever recorded.

The anchor is a picture from Malachi that changes how you see every hard season: *"he shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver"* (Malachi 3:3). *Sit.* He does not rush the fire. The refiner sits over the metal and waits, waits until the dross rises and the gold goes clear, waits until He can see His own face reflected in it. And Peter says the same thing about your trials: *"that the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire"* (1 Peter 1:7). The fire is not proof He left. The fire is proof He is *sitting right there,* refusing to leave until the gold blushes.

For nine years I brought Him everything but the bitterness. And on that song I finally said the name out loud, the lyric says *minute forty,* and that is true to how it happened, and the shoulders I had carried dropped like stone. Here is what I learned in that moment, and it is the whole revelation of the album: *the offerer became the offering.* I came to the altar carrying a thing to give, and the altar wanted *me.* Romans 12:1 had been in front of me the whole time: *"present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service."* Not your stuff. *You.*
Everything on the Altar Has a Name

I did not want this to stay abstract, so the middle of the record names the specific things we hide. *"Burn the Fear Down"* takes the 3 AM ceiling-stare, the list of worries on the chair, and stands on *"perfect love casteth out fear"* (1 John 4:18), Love as a Person filling the room like incense. *"Burn the Bottle"* names the thing at 2 AM we drink or scroll or swallow to numb the pain, and lets the chains drop in the flame. *"Burn the Anger Out"* is the slow-burn coal I fed for years, handed back to the only One who can hold it, *"Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord"* (Romans 12:19).

And *"Burn the Lust Away"* does something I think the church needs more of: it does not kill desire, it *purifies* it. The heart was built for Him and Him alone. Augustine, not Scripture, but a saint who knew, said it best: our hearts are restless until they rest in Thee. The fire on that track is not shame. It is a want made holy.

There is one more thing on the altar that surprises people, and *"Burn the Wheel"* names it: control. The white-knuckled grip on a road you cannot see at midnight, the plan you steer by fear. Proverbs says it straight, *"Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths"* (Proverbs 3:5–6). The grip is an offering too. The road only opens when the hands finally let go of the wheel.
Who I Made the Fire For

I made it for the faithful one who has been to a thousand altars and still walks around with the real thing sewn into her chest. For the one carrying a name she will not say, a grudge she keeps rehearsing, a plan she cannot release her grip on. For everyone who thinks the hard season is punishment when it is actually the Refiner sitting down, patient, over gold He refuses to lose.

Because the record does not end in ashes. *"Living Sacrifice Walks Out"* takes the whole self off the altar and back onto the street as the offering. *"Ashes Singing Back"* watches the ash pile start to sing, because *"they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony"* (Revelation 12:11), the very thing that burned becomes the weapon. And the capstone, *"Walk Away Light,"* re-frames the entire fire: it was never anger. It was the kindness of the cross. Greater Love walked in on the first song and walks out on the last, and the same Hand that lit the fire is the Hand holding the gold He pulled from the ash.

So bring Him the one thing, beloved. Not the thousand substitutes, the one you have been protecting. Lay it on the wood and step back. The fire in front of you is not here to consume you. It is here to give you back to yourself, holy and whole, with the gold finally showing. You will not walk away burned. You will walk away *light.*

pieces.title: The Delay Was the Dressing Room
pieces.imagePrompt: A jubilant globally-diverse crowd at radiant daybreak looking upward with joy, believers of many nations, hands raised, faces lit gold as a brilliant sunrise splits the sky, some dancing, a great multiethnic celebration caught mid-shout of joy under breaking dawn light, cinematic worship-brand film still, bright and hope-filled, warm gold and rose dawn tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I put the second coming on a steelpan and a drill beat because the return of the King is the best news a scared generation could hear. He's coming back, and the long wait you've been calling wasted was never a delay. It was the dressing room. This is a record about watching the sky with joy instead of dread.

body.text: I put the return of the King on a steelpan and a drill beat, and I would do it again. *Any Day Now* is a record about the second coming, and I refused to make it sound like a warning siren. Because the church has handed my generation the blessed hope wrapped in dread, and I wanted to hand it back the way the New Testament actually gives it: as the single best piece of news a frightened world will ever hear.

He's coming back. And when I finally understood what that meant for all the waiting I had been calling wasted, it undid me. So I made twelve songs to say it. The delay you have been resenting was never a punishment. It was the dressing room.
Any Day Now, Hope, Not a Countdown to Fear

The whole album lives in three words: *any day now.* That is not date-setting, and I was careful to say so right in the songs, *I don't need a date, I just keep my lamp aglow; Father, You set the hour.* **Yeshua** was plain that the timing is not ours to calculate: *"Watch therefore: for ye know not what hour your Lord doth come"* (Matthew 24:42).

But listen to how He framed the not-knowing. Not *be terrified,* but *watch*, the way you watch for someone you love to come up the walk. Paul called it *"that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ"* (Titus 2:13). The *blessed* hope. And when **Yeshua** left, the two men in white did not tell the disciples to brace for doom; they told them *"this same Jesus, which is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go"* (Acts 1:11). Same Jesus. Same face. Coming back.

That is why the opener is a dance and not a dirge. *Any day now, You're coming back*, eyes on the seam where the gold breaks the ground, lacing my shoes for glory before the morning even yawns. He told me to watch. So I'm dancing through the night.
The Waiting Was the Wedding
The turn that broke the record open, the song I put in the frontmatter, is *"The Waiting Was the Wedding."*

Picture it: the dress in the garment bag on the door, the ring turned and turned on a nervous finger, the calendar crossed out in red, and a heart that had started to believe the long wait was a punishment for every night it prayed. That was me. And then the Spirit whispered something that flipped the whole thing over, *every day of longing was a getting-ready-for-You.*

That is the theology under the whole album, and it comes straight from the wedding at the center of the Bible's last chapters: *"Blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper of the Lamb"* (Revelation 19:9). If the end of the story is a wedding, then the waiting was never dead time. It was bridal preparation. The tears were the fitting. The longing was the veil being sewn.
I was counting the days as empty. He was calling them a feast. Not one day I waited fell forgotten to the floor.

That is why I titled this the way I did. The delay was the dressing room. And **Yeshua** told us plainly why He was gone so long: *"I go to prepare a place for you. And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again, and receive you unto myself"* (John 14:2–3). He is not late. He is *preparing.* And so, it turns out, are we.
Trim the Lamp, Lace Your Shoes, Watch the Sky
Ready is a posture, not a panic, and the middle of the record teaches it three ways.

*"Trim the Lamp"* is the ten virgins of Matthew 25. Five kept oil and five leaned on the sand, and at the midnight cry only the burning lamps went in. So the song is not anxious; it is *tending*, feeding the flame with worship till the morning breaks in white, because **Yeshua** said *"Watch therefore, for ye know neither the day nor the hour"* (Matthew 25:13). *"Lace Up Your Shoes"* is the get-up song for everybody stuck in *someday, maybe, soon*, double-knot them tight, the Bridegroom is on the doorstep. And *"Watch the Sky"* is for the whole scrolling generation with their faces to the floor: *me, I'm looking up, where the angels made it plain, same way that He left is the same way He'll reign.*

But readiness is not only trumpets and rooftops. The tenderest track, *"Every Ordinary Morning,"* is where the record does its quietest work. Soap bubbles catching gold on the window, the 7:42 train door, a toddler's lost sock under the chair, and the confession that if He came right now, He'd find me *right there.* The mother nobody sees, folding little laundry like she's folding it for Him. He does not measure by the loud; He measures by the true. So the way you get ready for the King is not to quit your Tuesday. It is to be *faithful in the small* until He comes, a citizen already, because *"our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour"* (Philippians 3:20).
Who I Made This Record For

I made it for the ones who were taught to be scared of His coming, who flinch at the word *rapture* because somebody used it to frighten them as a child. For the tired saint who is sure the wait has been wasted. For the generation staring down at cracked screens, drowning in headlines, who has never once been told that the best news in the universe is that this is not the end of the story.

Because the record does not stay in the waiting room. *"Trumpet on the Downbeat"* erupts on the promise that undoes death itself: *"In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump... the dead shall be raised incorruptible"* (1 Corinthians 15:52), when *"the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout... and the dead in Christ shall rise first"* and the living are caught up to meet Him (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). Then *"Even So, Come"* becomes the whole church's final prayer, one candle passed hand to hand until the room is on fire, *"The Spirit and the bride say, Come... Even so, come, Lord Jesus"* (Revelation 22:17, 20). And the finale, *"The King Returns,"* opens the sky like a sheet of golden paper and seats us at a banquet table running further than the eye can see, every tear I cried turned to a diamond in the atmosphere.

So lift your head, beloved. The One who promised *"Surely I come quickly"* has never broken a word. The dread was never yours to carry. If you are still waiting, for the promise, for the healing, for the day it all makes sense, hear the good news in the groove: the waiting is not wasted, the delay is the dressing room, and the King is coming for a bride He has spent the whole long season getting ready. Keep your lamp burning. Watch the road with joy. He could come any day now, and when He does, may He find you dancing.

pieces.title: Every "Thou Shalt" Is Hiding a "My Beloved"
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful multi-ethnic congregation gathered around an open scroll in warm morning light, faces lit with delighted discovery, an elder and a child tracing the letters together, others dancing softly with hands lifted; uplifting emotionally powerful premium cinematic worship film-still, warm golden tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: For years I read the commands of God the way you read a bill, a list of what I owed, a wall between me and the day. Then one Sabbath morning the ink seemed to lift off the page and sing, and I heard something I'd been missing my whole life. This is the album I made when the law turned out to be a love letter.

body.text: I need to confess how I used to read the Bible, because it's the reason this album exists.

I read the commands of God like a debt. Like a bill that came in the mail with my name on it and a total I could never quite pay. Every "Thou shalt" landed on me as a wall, one more brick between me and an ordinary, unbothered Tuesday. I could recite the instructions. I just experienced them as weight.

And then one Sabbath morning, sitting over challah crumbs with the scroll open, something happened that I can only describe the way the album describes it: the ink began to lift off the page like sparks. The wall I'd been staring at turned out to have hinges. *Torah Sings Back* is the record I made to tell you what I heard when the law finally opened its mouth and sang.
The wall was a window all along

The opening track states the whole thesis in its first breath. I read the words I thought I'd seen, and discovered I'd never really seen them. What I had filed under "law" was written in the grammar of love. That's the line the whole album turns on:
What I thought was law is a wedding song.

Here's the reframe, and I want to be careful and clear as a teacher about it. The Hebrew word **Torah** does not primarily mean "law" in the cold, courtroom sense. At root it means *instruction*, *teaching*, the guidance a father gives a child he adores. When you read it that way, the commands stop sounding like a fence and start sounding like a hand on your shoulder pointing you home. The wall was a window all along. I had just never walked up close enough to look through it.

And **Yeshua** is the One who handed it back to me brand new. He said plainly He did not come to abolish the Torah but to fulfill it (Matthew 5:17), not to throw the instruction out, but to live it out in front of us and then move it inside us. When I finally believed that, every page changed color.
Delight is not a thin thing
Track four is called *Delight, Delight*, and it fixed a lie I'd believed about joy.

I used to think delight was flimsy, sugar on a counterfeit grin, the kind of shine that the first storm sweeps off. But then I read David. Psalm 1 says the blessed one's "delight is in the law of the LORD, and on his law he meditates day and night" (Psalm 1:2). The great Torah psalm says it over and over, "I delight in your law" (Psalm 119:70). And David was not a man untouched by storms. His delight was iron-deep, a joy the weather could not reach, because it wasn't built on his circumstances. It was built on the Instruction of a God who never lied to him.

The bridge of that song reaches for the oldest image in the book: the Word is honey. "Sweeter than honey and drippings of the honeycomb" is how the psalmist describes the ordinances of **Yahuah** (Psalm 19:10). Not a diet. Dessert. When was the last time you approached a command of God expecting it to taste like honey? I hadn't. Now I can't unremember it.
The command that is a kiss
This is the heart of the record, and it's why I named the whole thing around one song: *Mitzvah Is The Love-Line*.

People told me the mitzvot, the commands, were a wall. A pile of chains. There is even a beloved tradition that counts them at six hundred and thirteen, and I'll flag that number as exactly that, a rabbinic tradition rather than a verse you can point to, but the point stands: to a certain kind of ear, that sounds like six hundred and thirteen ways to fail. That's how I heard it, too. Until I picked the scroll back up slowly and re-read the lines I thought I knew, and I found a Father bending down to tie the fringe on His child's garment with His own hands.
That's the whole song, and I'll say it as plainly as it deserves:
Every "Thou shalt" is a "My beloved."

Every instruction is covenant intimacy in disguise. He commanded rest, because He loves you and knows you were killing yourself trying to earn a Sabbath He wanted to give you free. He commanded remembrance, because love keeps saying *don't forget what I did for you*. He bought your rest by being slain, and He bought your joy in the storm and the rain, and then He handed you the commands not as "obey me" but as "love you, love you, love you." Once you hear a command that way, you stop trying to escape it. You lean in.
What only the Spirit can do
I don't want to make this sound like I merely adjusted my attitude and everything softened. It went deeper than that, and two tracks tell the truth about it.

*Stone To Flesh* is built on Ezekiel's promise: "I will give you a new heart... I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh" (Ezekiel 36:26). Because here was my real problem. For years I could read the Torah end to end and not feel a single line. Stone in the chest, stone in the spine. No amount of trying loves a scroll. It took the **Ruach HaKodesh**, the Spirit, moving in soft and slow, chisel work no one else could do, to make a heart that could actually delight in what it read.

And *The Law On The Heart* stands on the promise that gathers the whole album up. Jeremiah heard **Yahuah** say, "I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts" (Jeremiah 31:33), the New Covenant, quoted again in Hebrews 8:10. Notice: He never says He'll throw the instruction out. He says He'll relocate it. Off the stone tablet on the wall and into the beating chest. **Yeshua** sealed that move with His own blood. The song puts it the way I'd want it sung in every congregation:
Not a tablet on the wall, a Torah singing in the chest.
Who I made this for

I made *Torah Sings Back* for the believer who has quietly decided that most of their Bible is homework. Who reads the commands with a tired, dutiful heart, bracing for a bill. Hear me: you have been reading a love letter as if it were a summons. The Father who wrote it is not standing over you with a ledger. He is bending down to tie the fringe on your garment.

And I made it for the person whose heart has gone to stone, who can recite the truth and feel nothing, and is frightened by the numbness. That is not a character flaw you have to fix by trying harder. It is exactly the thing the Spirit came to do. Ask Him. He does chisel work no one else can, and He does not rush it, and He does not quit.

The scroll is not a wall. It has hinges. Open it, and listen. Some morning, when you least expect it, the ink is going to lift off the page and start to sing, and you are going to realize that behind every "Thou shalt" there was a "My beloved" the whole time.

pieces.title: The Organ and the Ram's Horn Are One Spirit's Two Voices
pieces.imagePrompt: A jubilant, globally-diverse congregation mid-celebration, an organ player and a shofar-blower side by side, hands raised across a crowd of many nations, faces bright with revival joy, warm light flooding a packed hall; uplifting emotionally powerful premium cinematic worship film-still, radiant warm tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: A Hammond organ swirling in a Pentecostal room and a ram's horn blasting over a Hebrew-roots gathering have been playing what sounded like two different songs for a hundred years. I made this album because I became convinced they were never two songs. The Body of Messiah fell asleep on top of her own roots, and the roots never stopped keeping the heat.

body.text: Stand in the right room on a Sunday and you'll hear a Hammond B3 organ swirl up under an altar call until the whole place is on its feet. Stand in a different room and you'll hear a ram's horn split the morning open over a gathering that keeps the ancient appointed times. For about a hundred years those two sounds have kept to their own buildings, as if they were playing two different songs, for two different peoples, headed two different directions.
I made *Hebrew Roots Rising* because I stopped believing that. The album's second track says it as bluntly as I know how, and it's the sentence the whole record is built to prove:
The Hammond and the shofar are the same Ruach's two voices.
The roots never went to sleep. She did

The opening track, *The Roots Wake*, sets the frame. It pictures the Body of the Messiah dozing in the pew for generations while, down beneath the floorboards, the root system kept the heat true. That image matters, so let me be careful with it. The roots didn't wake up because they'd been dead. They were awake the whole time. It was the Body who slept on top of them, forgetting what she was drinking from.

And **Yahuah** is the Gardener who never once stopped the watering. That's the good news under the whole album. The recovery we're living through is not us inventing something clever. It's a family remembering an inheritance that was always in the account.
The tree she forgot she was joined to
The theological spine of the record is Romans 11, and it runs through the track *Body Remembers Her Tree*.

Paul's picture there is exact and humbling. There is an ancient olive tree. Some natural branches were broken off, and wild branches, that's the nations, that's most of us, were grafted in. And Paul turns and warns the grafted branch: "do not be arrogant toward the branches... it is not you who support the root, but the root that supports you" (Romans 11:18). For centuries the Body was told the root was old, the branches were now the whole story, the tree could be left behind. Romans 11 never left the page. The grafted branch is still held up by a root it did not plant.
So when the album shouts "the Body remembers her tree," it isn't nostalgia. It's Romans 11 waking up in a congregation that had quietly stopped reading it.
Two voices, one breath
Here's where the Hammond and the shofar come in, and why I gave them a whole song.

The organ is the voice of a stream of the church that has always known the Spirit falls, that worship can go from a whisper to a roar, that **Yahuah** still moves on a room. The shofar is the voice of a people who never let go of the appointed times, the Hebrew of the Scriptures, the feasts and the fasts and the ancient shape of the calendar. For a long time each side eyed the other. And I've become convinced they are two instruments of the same Spirit, breathing through two horns.

The album makes that case with a story it dares to tell out loud in track eight, *Acts 2 in the Upper Room*. A Pentecostal pastor realizes, after thirty years of preaching Acts 2, that the day the Spirit fell, "when the day of Pentecost arrived" (Acts 2:1), was the Hebrew Feast of Weeks, **Shavuot**, the fiftieth day, set on the calendar centuries before by **Yahuah** Himself (Leviticus 23:15-16). The tongues of fire fell on an appointed time. The Pentecostal fire and the Hebrew feast were never two events. They were one room. The Spirit He poured out is the same Spirit who wrote the calendar it fell on.
I'm not asking either side to give anything up. I'm saying the organ and the horn were always meant to be in the same band.
The remnant nobody wrote down
An album about recovery could get triumphant and forget the cost. This one doesn't, and I love it for two quieter tracks.

*Daniel Prayed Toward Jerusalem* remembers a man in exile who kept his windows open toward home and knelt three times a day, even when a royal decree made it a death sentence (Daniel 6:10). That's what faithfulness looks like in a foreign land, not loud, just oriented. Facing home when everything around you faces the other way.

And *The Long Way Home* honors the believers in every century who saw the Hebraic roots and reached for them tenderly, whose names are in no book we own. The song leans on the great roll call of faith in Hebrews 11, the ones "of whom the world was not worthy", and the cloud of witnesses that surrounds us (Hebrews 12:1). Most of them walked a long dusty road no one recorded. **Yahuah** saw every torch they carried. The recovery has a genealogy, and it's longer and more faithful than we know.
Rebuilding what was ruined
Two more tracks give the album its working hands.

*Nehemiah's Wall Goes Back Up* takes that scene of a man riding the broken wall at night by torchlight, surveying the rubble, and then organizing a whole city to build, half the people working, half the people guarding, everyone with a tool in one hand (Nehemiah 4:17). Recovery is not a mood. It's masonry. Stone by stone, and never alone.

And *Living in the Rebuilt House* lands where Paul lands in Ephesians 2, no longer strangers and aliens, but "members of the household of God," built on a foundation with **Yeshua** as the cornerstone the builders rejected (Ephesians 2:19-20). The wilderness season is over. The Father rebuilt the house. And the house is big enough that the Hammond can play the doxology on the kitchen-table chair while the shofar waits on the mantel for the next time it's called.
Who I made this for

I made *Hebrew Roots Rising* for the believer who has felt, in the quiet, that something got lost somewhere, that the faith they inherited was pulled up out of a soil it forgot it grew in. You're not imagining it, and you're not being divisive to notice. The root is real, and it has been holding you up the whole time you didn't know its name.

And I made it for the two rooms that have been eyeing each other across a hallway for a hundred years, the ones with the organ and the ones with the horn. Hear the album's whole argument: you are not two songs. You are one Spirit's two voices, and He has been trying to get you into the same room so the whole Body can finally get up off the pew and stand on her feet.
The Gardener never stopped watering. The roots were awake the whole time. It's morning now, and the Body is rising.

pieces.title: The First Word of the Book of Comfort Is Said Twice
pieces.imagePrompt: A tender, globally-diverse gathering at dawn, a shepherd-hearted man with hands open in comfort, people of many nations embracing and consoling one another, an older woman being held, soft light breaking over grief turning to peace; uplifting emotionally powerful premium cinematic worship film-still, warm gentle tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: When God finally spoke tenderness to a people He knew were headed into exile, He did not say the word once. He said it twice, Nachamu, nachamu. I made this album for the ones who need to hear a doubled word, because I have sat at enough bedsides to know that comfort, when it is real, always comes singing.

body.text: There is a moment in the book of Isaiah where the whole tone of the scroll changes. The chapters before it are heavy with warning; a people are headed toward exile, toward loss, toward a long night. And then chapter forty opens, and **Yahuah** speaks the first word of comfort, and He does not say it once.

He says it twice. "Comfort, comfort my people, says your God" (Isaiah 40:1). In Hebrew: *Nachamu, nachamu, ami.* I built an entire album on that doubling, because I have learned something at bedsides and gravesides that the grammar of that verse already knew: some words have to be said twice before a broken person can hear them at all.
Why He said it twice

The opening track, *Nachamu, Nachamu, Ami*, begins with a single unaccompanied voice, no band, no drum, just breath, because that is how comfort actually arrives. Not with a fanfare. With a voice that gets to you before anything else does.

And I want you to feel the tenderness of when this word came. It is spoken to people who had learned to expect that the night was long. Wounded ones who lost the song a long time ago. The doubling is not filler. It is the sound of a God who leans down and repeats Himself because He knows the first time didn't land. *Nachamu* breaks the silence that the loss made strong. And notice what He calls them in the same breath, *ami*, "my people." He didn't comfort them as strangers. He comforted them as His own.
Comfort that levels the road
Comfort in Isaiah 40 is not a soft blanket that leaves you where it found you. It comes to *move* you, and two tracks carry that.

*Lift Your Voice With Strength* takes the herald of good news up the high mountain: "lift up your voice with strength... say to the cities of Judah, 'Behold your God!'" (Isaiah 40:9). Comfort has a volume. It's meant to be carried up a ridge and announced. And *Every Valley Lifted* stands on the promise that "every valley shall be lifted up, and every mountain and hill be made low... and the glory of the LORD shall be revealed" (Isaiah 40:4-5). The valley of depression I lay in too long, the mountain of pride that grew too strong, the Comforter is a road crew, grading the heart flat so the glory has a way to come through.
That's the thing about this comfort. It doesn't just sit with your sadness. It builds a road out of it.
The warm side of the cloak
The cinematic peak of the album is track five, and it holds the tenderest picture in all of Isaiah 40. It's called *He Carries Lambs Inside His Cloak*.

The verse is this: "He will tend his flock like a shepherd; he will gather the lambs in his arms; he will carry them in his bosom" (Isaiah 40:11). A shepherd's wool cloak is rough on the outside, where the cold pasture wind hits it. But inside, against his chest, it is warm, and that is where the lamb rides. The lamb doesn't feel the wind. It only feels the heartbeat. The song sets that image beside a chaplain's hand at 3:47 in the morning and a mother in the dark of a fever-night, reaching for the one verse she can still hold:
He gathers the lambs, inside His cloak.
Cold pasture wind on the outside, but the lamb is carried on the warm side of the cloak. I have watched that verse be the only thing a person could hold onto, and I have watched it be enough.
Comfort that has a face
There's a turn on this album I planned carefully, and it happens on track eight, *Get Up On The High Mountain*. For seven songs, the Comforter of Isaiah 40 is a Voice. Then the Voice gets a face.

Because the Shepherd who carries lambs in His arms in Isaiah 40 said, in the flesh, "I am the good shepherd" (John 10:11). The Comforter and the Carpenter are the same. The tenderness that broke seventy years of coming silence has a Galilee shore and a name, **Yeshua**, "Yahuah saves." That's not a stretch across two Testaments; it's one Shepherd stepping out from behind the curtain of a prophecy He was always the answer to.

And the record does not shy from the long grief, either. *First Notes After The Years* sits in a widow's dim bedroom five years on, where the old songs no longer fit, and it leans on Psalm 56:8, "you have kept count of my tossings; put my tears in your bottle." What looked like silent grief was a kept-and-quiet cradle the whole time. He was gathering every tear before you knew He was counting.
Comforted, so we can comfort
Here's where I most wanted the album to land, and why it doesn't end at the bedside.

The last stretch, *Sit With The Next One Weeping* and *Comforted, We Comfort Now*, turns the whole thing outward, and it stands on one of the most practical promises Paul ever wrote: **Yahuah** "comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted" (2 Corinthians 1:4). Comfort is not a thing you receive and keep. It's a thing you receive and *pass*. The comfort that found you at your worst hour is meant to become the comfort you carry to the next person in theirs.

Sometimes that just means sitting there. The album remembers Job's friends at their best, before they started talking, "they sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him" (Job 2:13). Presence in the pew, a hand on a shaking shoulder, no easy verse forced too soon. That is ministry. That is the God of all comfort working through an ordinary person who once needed the same.
Who I made this for

I made *Comfort Comes Singing* for the one in the long night, the exile of grief that has gone on longer than anyone else's patience. Hear the doubled word: *Nachamu, nachamu*. He is not saying it once and moving on. He is leaning down and saying it again, because He knows the first time didn't reach you, and He calls you *ami*, His own.

And I made it for the one who has been comforted and doesn't yet know what to do with it. You do this: you go sit with the next one weeping. The comfort that carried you on the warm side of the cloak was never meant to stop with you.
Comfort, when it is real, always comes singing. And the song is older than your sorrow, and it knows your name.

pieces.title: The Kingdom Isn't a Someday. It Already Walked In
pieces.song: The First Time The Kingdom Walked Into My House
pieces.imagePrompt: A radiant, globally-diverse throng celebrating a coronation of joy, people of many nations with hands lifted and knees bowing, a sense of a King present among ordinary families at their tables and in the streets, bright banners and light; uplifting emotionally powerful premium cinematic worship film-still, vivid warm regal tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: We file the Kingdom of God under "later", a distant coronation, a someday sky. I made this album to argue two things at once that only sound like a contradiction: the King is enthroned in cosmic glory over every nation, and He walks into ordinary kitchens on ordinary weekday afternoons and takes the empty chair.

body.text: Ask most believers where the Kingdom of God is, and you'll get a direction: *up there*, and a time: *later*. A distant throne, a someday sky, a coronation scheduled for the far end of history. We file the whole thing under "eventually."

I made *King Yeshua Reigns* to hold two things at the same time that only sound like a contradiction. The King is enthroned in cosmic, blazing, every-knee-will-bow glory. And that same King walks into an ordinary kitchen on an ordinary weekday afternoon, pulls out the empty chair, and sits down. The album refuses to choose between the throne room and the kitchen table, because the gospel doesn't.
Not far off, not later, here

The second track, *The Kingdom Is Here*, plants the flag. **Yeshua** did not preach a Kingdom you could only find in the future or the past. He said, "the kingdom of God is in the midst of you" (Luke 17:21), and He opened His ministry announcing that it was "at hand" (Mark 1:15). The song hammers the present tense until you can't miss it:
Not far off, not later, here. Not someday, not maybe, here.

That is not wishful thinking. That is the plain grammar of how the King spoke about His own reign. It has arrived. The **Ruach** has fallen. The work has begun. Whatever else is still coming, the Kingdom is not only a "will be." It is a "here."
The day it walked into a kitchen
The emotional center of the record is track seven, *The First Time The Kingdom Walked Into My House*, and it's why I chose it as this album's anchor song.

Picture it, a Tuesday in November, a messy kitchen, unopened mail, yesterday's news, a Bible on the table you keep meaning to read. And a daughter asks a small, enormous question: "who is **Yeshua**?" And the quiet in the room gets loud. The King doesn't knock. He walks in like He always belonged there, takes the chair across the way, and the house you built for yourself quietly becomes a home that belongs to **Yahuah**.
That's the whole point of the song, and it says it as tenderly as anything I've written:
He came home to me, and I came home to Him.
This is what "the Kingdom of God is at hand" feels like on a weekday. Not a parade. A presence. The most cosmic reality in existence, walking through your kitchen door without a sound.
But make no mistake. It is a coronation

Now, if the album only did the kitchen, it would be sentimental. So the record surrounds that intimate moment with the full, blazing coronation, because the King who sits at your table is the King before whom the universe bends.

*Every Knee Bows* takes Paul's great hymn: because **Yeshua** humbled Himself and died, "God has highly exalted him... so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow... and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord" (Philippians 2:9-11). *Lift The Gates* sings Psalm 24, "Lift up your heads, O gates... that the King of glory may come in... the LORD of hosts, he is the King of glory" (Psalm 24:7-10). And *Melech HaMashiach* stands in the throne room of Revelation, where twenty-four elders fall down and the Lamb takes the scroll no other hand could open (Revelation 5). *He Reigns From Zion* draws on Psalm 2, where the nations rage and "he who sits in the heavens laughs," having set His King on His holy hill (Psalm 2:4-6). This is not a small King who fits in your kitchen because He's modest. This is the King of kings who fits in your kitchen because He wants to.
The crown ended up on the wounded One
There's a track I have to point you to, because it holds the strangest and best thing about this King: *The Crown Is On The Lamb*.

In the throne room John saw, the One worthy to take the scroll and receive the crown was "a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain" (Revelation 5:6). Read that again. The universe-crown does not sit on a warrior with an unmarked face. It sits on the Wounded One, the Lamb who was despised and killed, now wearing the marks of slaughter *and* the crown of everything. Heaven's anthem is "Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power" (Revelation 5:12). The King who conquers wears the scars of the cross He conquered by. That is the only throne in all of literature where losing everything is how you win the crown.
And it means the Kingdom that has come is not a Kingdom of raw force. It's a Kingdom of a King who bled for the people He now reigns over.
He shares the throne
The album refuses to end with us as spectators, and this is the part I most want a listener to hear.

*Daniel Saw The Saints Receive The Kingdom* takes Daniel's night vision, the Son of Man coming on the clouds, given everlasting dominion by the Ancient of Days, and then the astonishing turn: "the saints of the Most High shall receive the kingdom" (Daniel 7:14, 7:18). And the finale, *We Reign With The King*, stands on **Yeshua**'s own promise: "The one who conquers, I will grant him to sit with me on my throne, as I also conquered and sat down with my Father" (Revelation 3:21). He made us "a kingdom, priests to our God" who will reign on the earth (Revelation 5:10). The King who walked into your kitchen is preparing to hand you a seat beside Him. Not because you earned it. Because that is the kind of King He is.
Who I made this for

I made *King Yeshua Reigns* for the believer who has quietly relegated the Kingdom to the far horizon, who prays "your kingdom come" as if it's entirely a future weather report. Some of it is future, yes. But the King is at hand. He is at your door on a Tuesday. Stop waiting for a someday sky and set an extra chair.

And I made it for the one who cannot imagine that a King that big would want a table that small. Hear the album's whole argument: the Lamb who wears the universe-crown is the same One who walks into a messy kitchen and blesses the coffee like it's Sabbath. He does not visit your life as a formality. He comes home to you, so that you can come home to Him.
The Kingdom isn't only a someday. It walked in on a Tuesday. And the King who took the empty chair intends to share His throne.

pieces.title: The Land Was Always a Picture of a Face
pieces.song: The Inheritance Was Yeshua All Along
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful, globally-diverse procession crossing a river at dawn into a sunlit land, people of many nations stepping forward together with lifted hands and glad faces, a sense of homecoming and arrival, warm light over green hills; uplifting emotionally powerful premium cinematic worship film-still, radiant warm tones, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: A whole people spent centuries reaching for a Land, crossing a river to get into it, singing over its hills, setting their tents down on its promise. I made this album about the moment the inheritance came into focus and turned out to be a Person. The Land was real. It was also, the whole time, a picture of a face.

body.text: For most of the Bible, a whole people is reaching for a piece of ground.

They're promised it under a night sky full of stars. They carry the promise out of slavery, across a wilderness, up to the edge of a river. They cross the river to get into it. They sing over its hills and set their tents down on it and bury their dead in it and weep for it when they're carried away from it. The Land is the ache that runs through the whole story.

I made *The Promise Walks In* about the moment that ache comes into focus, and the inheritance everyone was reaching for turns out to be a Person. The Land was real. It was also, the entire time, a picture of a face.
A promise with feet

The opening track sets the whole tone. **Yahuah** spoke to Abraham at the oaks of Mamre, showed him a sky and said "your descendants will be like the stars" (Genesis 15:5), and the album's claim is that the promise He made then never stopped keeping pace. It's still walking. It walks in to where you're sitting still.

That's the picture I wanted: a promise that isn't a document in a drawer but a living thing with feet, closing the distance between an ancient oath and your ordinary Tuesday. Every promise Abraham held, every promise Jacob knew, still on the move, still arriving.
The river in front of every promise
The second track, *Cross The Jordan*, tells the crossing, and it holds a detail I never want a believer to miss.

The Jordan was at flood stage, "the Jordan overflows all its banks throughout the time of harvest" (Joshua 3:15). The water was high and fast. And the river did not part *before* the priests moved. It parted when the first foot stepped in. "As soon as those bearing the ark... dipped in the brink of the water... the waters coming down from above stood and rose up in a heap" (Joshua 3:15-16). The song draws the line straight to your life:
Yahuah does not wait for the river to recede. He parts the river when the first foot steps in.

There is a Jordan in front of every promise. A wilderness ending where a Land begins. And the God who owns the water waits for a foot in the current. That is not recklessness. It's covenant. He had already sworn the Land was theirs; the crossing was simply the moment they let their weight prove they believed Him. Faith almost always looks like a foot going into water that hasn't moved yet.
The name at the front of the crossing
Track three is where the whole album quietly turns, and it turns on a name.

Moses brought the people to the edge of the inheritance, but Moses did not take them in (Deuteronomy 34:4). The one who led them across was **Joshua**, and here is the thing every teacher should say slowly. *Joshua*, Yehoshua, means "Yahuah is salvation." It is the very same Hebrew name as **Yeshua**. The man whose sandals stepped first into the Jordan carried the name of the One whose nail-pierced feet would one day lead a far larger people into a far greater inheritance. When Joshua met the Captain of the host of **Yahuah** at Jericho and was told to take off his sandals because the ground was holy (Joshua 5:14-15), the pattern was already being drawn. The leader who goes first, into the water, into the Land, bearing the name that means salvation.
The inheritance was Yeshua all along
The revelation the whole record is built toward lands in track eight, *The Inheritance Was Yeshua All Along*, and it stands on one of the most honest paragraphs in Scripture.

Hebrews says of the patriarchs: "These all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar" (Hebrews 11:13). They were looking, it says, for "a better country, that is, a heavenly one" (Hebrews 11:16), a city "whose designer and builder is God" (Hebrews 11:10). Even after Joshua led them into the actual Land, the writer of Hebrews insists there remained a rest still ahead of them (Hebrews 4:8-9). The ground was real. But it was never the whole promise. It was pointing.

And **Yeshua** said it Himself: "Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day. He saw it and was glad" (John 8:56). Abraham, under that sky of stars, was ultimately seeing a face. The song puts it the way I most want it remembered:
The Land was a picture, Yeshua was the promise.
Every step you take is that ground now
If the inheritance is a Person and not only a place, then something changes about where you're standing right now, and two tracks carry it home.

*Every Step We Take Is Holy Ground* remembers Moses at the burning bush, told to take off his sandals because the ground was holy (Exodus 3:5). But the ground was holy because **Yahuah** was there. And now, the song reasons, the **Ruach HaKodesh** lives inside His people, so the holiness travels. Every place you set your foot is sanctified, because the Presence that made that bush-lit dirt holy now walks every road you walk.

And *The Inheritance Is Sealed* rests on Paul's promise that we were "sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is the guarantee of our inheritance" (Ephesians 1:13-14). The deposit is already down. No power can break the seal. The finale, *We Are Home*, gathers it all: we are home in the Land the patriarchs reached for and home in the Messiah the Land was prophesying, one inheritance, held in one Person, at last.
Who I made this for

I made *The Promise Walks In* for the believer standing at the edge of their own Jordan, a promise on the far bank, a flooded river in the way, waiting for the water to drop before they'll move. It won't drop first. The God who owns the current is waiting for your foot in it. Step in.

And I made it for the one who has spent their faith reaching for a *place*, a circumstance, an address, an arrival they were sure would finally feel like home, and kept coming up short. Hear the album's whole discovery: the inheritance was never mainly a place. It was a face. Every promise **Yahuah** ever made was pointing to **Yeshua**, and in Him the whole thing comes home together.
The Land was always a picture of a face. And the moment you see the face, you realize the promise has been walking toward you the whole time, and it just walked in.

pieces.title: One Long Story, and His Face Fills Every Word
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful circle of diverse believers of many nations gathered around an open illuminated manuscript in a sunlit stone hall, an elder tracing a golden line of calligraphy while young and old lean in with wonder and delight on their faces, hands lifted in quiet praise, warm light falling across the pages; premium cinematic worship-brand film still, luminous honeyed daylight, reverent and radiant, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I used to read the Scriptures like a shelf of separate books. Then I saw one face looking back at me from every page. This album walks the whole library from the Garden to the Gospel and finds Yasu' hidden in each shadow, until the reading turns into worship.

body.text: For a long time I read the Scriptures the way you walk through a souk of separate stalls, a book of law here, a book of poetry there, a shelf of prophets down the lane, and the story of Yasu' waiting at the far end. Sixty-six stalls, each with its own keeper. Then one day the whole market rearranged itself in front of me, and I saw that it had never been separate stalls at all. It was one long road, and one face was waiting at every turn of it. This album is that discovery set to the oud.

*Every Page Sings Your Name* is my attempt to walk the entire library out loud, from the first page to the last, and show what I finally saw, that the Scriptures are not a collection of religious documents that happen to mention a Messiah at the end. They are one story, and **Yeshua** is the meaning the whole thing was reaching for. Remove Him and it does not merely lose a chapter. It loses its plot.
The promise older than the prophets

The record opens in the Garden, on the oldest promise in the Book. "Seed of the Woman" goes back to the moment right after the fall, when the Lord speaks to the serpent and says the seed of the woman will crush his head, though his heel will be bruised (Genesis 3:15). The old teachers called that verse the first gospel, the whole rescue announced in a single sentence before a single prophet was born. The opening verse of my song says it plainly: *the Seed of the woman who would crush the snake, every page of Scripture was written for Your sake.*

From there the album refuses to treat the early Scriptures as a warm-up act. Adam is called a shadow of the One to come, and Yasu' the Last Adam, where the first man fell, the true Man stood and rose (that is the language of 1 Corinthians 15:45). Abraham's promised seed turns out, the apostle Paul insists, to be singular, and the singular is Christ (Galatians 3:16). I did not invent these connections in a studio. They are the reading the earliest believers were already doing.
From the Garden to Calvary, one long story, and Your face fills every word.
The shadows that were always Him

The middle of the album is my favorite country to travel, because it is full of the images my people already love, the desert, the lamb, the lifted standard, and each one turns out to have been a portrait all along.

"The Bronze Serpent" takes the strangest scene in the wilderness, where a snake of bronze was lifted on a pole and the dying who looked at it lived (Numbers 21), and Yasu' Himself said that just as Moses lifted up the serpent, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever looks to Him might live (John 3:14). "Passover Lamb" walks straight into the night of Exodus, the blood on the doorframe, the firstborn spared, because the apostle says outright that Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7). "Suffering Servant" sits down in Isaiah 53 and does not flinch, the man despised and acquainted with grief, wounded for our transgressions.

These are not clever overlays I pressed onto the text. They are the shadows the text was already casting, waiting for the light that would explain their shape. That is why the music modulates from a minor maqam up into major right at the heart of the record, the shadow is real, and then the sun clears it.
The road where the reading caught fire
Everything on this album bends toward one afternoon on a dusty road, and the song at the album's peak is "Emmaus Road."

Two travelers are walking away from Jerusalem, crushed, sure the story is over, and a stranger falls into step with them. And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, He interprets to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning Himself (Luke 24:27). They do not recognize Him until He breaks the bread, and then they say the thing this whole record is named for: *did not our hearts burn within us while He opened the Scriptures to us?* (Luke 24:32).

That is what I want this album to do. Not to win an argument about the Bible, but to reproduce that burning. To let a listener feel the sensation those two men felt, the slow, astonished realization that the book they thought they knew had been about a Person the entire time, and that the Person is now walking beside them. The single "Every Page Sings Your Name" is the whole record in a chorus: *from Genesis to Malachi, the Law and the Prophets proclaim, Jesus, You are the Word made flesh, every page sings Your Name.*
Where the whole library was heading

The album ends where the Gospel of John begins, with "The Word Made Flesh", in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God, and the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:1, 14). All the scrolls, all the shadows, all the promises older than the prophets, gather into a face you could look at, a voice you could hear, a Man who pitched His tent in our streets.

I made this for two kinds of hearts. One is the believer who has read the Scriptures dutifully for years and found them a set of disconnected rooms, the law heavy, the prophets strange, the poetry beautiful but far away. I want you to see the corridor that runs through every room, and Whose it is. The other is the seeker from my own part of the world who has heard the Scriptures spoken of with respect but always as someone else's book, a foreign anthology with no thread running through. There is a thread. His name is **Yeshua**, and He is not a foreign figure inserted at the end. He is the reason the first page was written.

Open the Book anywhere. Read slowly. Watch for the face that keeps appearing in the margins of every story, in the lamb and the ladder and the lifted pole and the suffering servant. It is one long story from the Garden to the empty tomb, and His face fills every word. When you finally see it, the reading stops being a duty and becomes what it was always meant to be, a fire in the chest, and a Name on the lips.

pieces.title: The Name My Whole Heart Was Made to Look For
pieces.imagePrompt: A jubilant crowd of diverse people of many nations in a lantern-lit courtyard at dawn, faces turned upward and radiant, hands lifted high in unified praise, a mix of young families, elders, and children all caught mid-song with joy and tears, warm gold light rising behind them; premium cinematic worship-brand film still, glowing amber sunrise tones, exultant and tender, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: In my language a name is not a label. It is a destiny, a prayer, a door. This album is twelve songs built on a single Name, the one lifted higher than every other, the one that heals and saves and calms the storm. It is for the heart that has been searching its whole life without knowing what it was searching for.

body.text: Where I come from, a name is never only a label. It is a destiny folded into a few syllables, a prayer the parents pray every time they call the child in from the street. We name our sons for mercy, for light, for the beauty we hope their lives will carry. So I did not make this album about a word. I made it about a Name, the one Name that carries more destiny, more mercy, and more power than every other name that has ever been spoken. The Name is **Yeshua**, Yasu', Jesus, and this whole record is built on it the way a house is built on rock.

*The Name Above Every Name* takes its title and its foundation from one sentence in the letter to the Philippians: because He humbled Himself to death, God has highly exalted Him and given Him the Name that is above every name, that at the Name of Jesus every knee should bow and every tongue confess that He is Lord (Philippians 2:9-11). That is not a slogan. That is the architecture of the universe. And I wanted to sing it in a way my people could feel in their chest.
Why a Name and not a lecture

I could have written an album of arguments. Instead I wrote an album that mostly repeats one Name, on purpose, because that is what the heart actually does when it finally finds what it was looking for.

The opening song lifts the Name like the frankincense of the morning: *Abba lifted Him to the highest of the dawn, gave Him the Name that the morning is sung upon, higher than the cedars, higher than the gold of the souk, the Name that the whole of my heart was made to look for.* That last line is the confession the whole record is built around. I did not decide to want this Name. I discovered that I had been made wanting it, that the searching in me, the reaching that no success or pleasure ever satisfied, had a shape, and the shape was Name-shaped. Every restless heart is looking for a Name it cannot yet pronounce.

That is why the second song simply chants it, *Yasu', Yasu', Yasu'*, as the refrain of a heart at rest. In my culture we know the power of repetition in devotion, the way a beloved name said again and again is not empty but full. This record leans into that. It says the Name until the Name becomes home.
The Name that does what no argument can
The heart of the album is a series of songs about what this Name actually does, because a name in Scripture is never decoration. It is power at work.

"The Name That Saves" stands on the boldest claim the early believers ever made: there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). The chorus is almost nothing but that truth, repeated like a heartbeat, *the Name that saves, the Name that saves, Yasu', the Name that saves.* "The Name That Heals" remembers how the first apostles prayed for healing to be done through the name of the holy servant Jesus (Acts 4:30). "The Name That Calms the Storm" puts us in the boat on the night the wind was tearing at the sail, and the Man asleep in the stern stood and spoke, and the sea went flat as glass (Mark 4:39). "The Name of Unshaken Power" remembers that on the cross He disarmed the powers, making a public spectacle of them (Colossians 2:15).
The Name that saves, the Name that saves, Habibi, the Name that saves.

I want to be careful and honest here, because this matters: I am not claiming a name is a magic word to be waved over trouble. I am confessing that a Person stands behind this Name, and that when His people call on Him, the Person Himself answers. The power was never in the sound. It is in the One who owns the sound.

The old songs of the church reached for this too. They called Him the balm that heals the wounded, the peace that stills the raging sea. Those are the pictures of devotion, and they are true to the Person, even when they are the language of hymns rather than the words of a single verse. I hold them the same way: as the heart's own way of confessing what the Scriptures declare, that this Name carries a Person, and the Person carries all the power there is.
Every knee, and every tongue
The record climbs to a single peak, a song called "At the Name of Yasu', Every Knee," and I built the whole album's arc to arrive there.

Because the promise in Philippians is total. Not some knees. Every knee, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth. Not some tongues. Every tongue. And the very next song, "The Name In Every Tongue," celebrates exactly that, the Name confessed in every language of the earth, which for me is not an abstraction but the burning center of my whole calling. I sing so that the Arab tongue, the Turkish tongue, the tongues of the whole Middle East and its scattered children, would have their own confession of this Name, in their own maqam, not borrowed from another country.
There is a day coming when the confession will be universal. But the invitation is now. That is the difference between the two, and the whole reason I sing.
For the searching heart
The album ends the way it began, with a benediction that circles its melody back to the first song, so the Name does not stop but keeps rising, because the praise of this Name has no last day.

I made this for the one whose heart has been looking its whole life and could never say for what. You have chased the beauty of the souk, the respect of the village, the love that was supposed to fill you, and something in you kept reaching past all of it. That reaching is not a defect. It is a compass. It was pointing, the entire time, at a Name, the Name lifted higher than the cedars and the gold, the Name that heals and saves and calms the storm, the Name your whole heart was made to look for.

Say it slowly. **Yeshua.** Yasu'. The Person behind it has been waiting to answer to it longer than you have been alive. There is no other name like it under heaven, and there never will be. Lift it, and find that the reaching in you finally has somewhere to arrive.

pieces.title: Out of the Wadi He Raised Me a Rose
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful group of diverse desert-dwelling people of many nations standing in a wadi after rain, wildflowers blooming across the sand around their feet, faces lifted in astonished delight as they lift their hands, a shepherd carrying a lamb on his shoulders among them, warm low sunlight raking across the dunes; premium cinematic worship-brand film still, golden desert light with fresh green shoots, tender and triumphant, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I know what it is to be a dry stretch of sand with nothing growing and nothing in the hand. This album is about the rain that came where rain never goes, and the bloom that rose out of the wadi. It is for every heart the desert has worn down, sung in the language of dunes and dawn.

body.text: I have been the desert. Not the poetry of the desert, the actual thing. A dry stretch with nothing green, nothing growing, nothing in the hand, the kind of inner wilderness where you stop even expecting rain because rain does not come to places like that. This album was born out of the memory of being that, and out of the astonishment of what happened next. Because rain came where rain never goes, and out of the dry riverbed something impossible bloomed.

*Desert Rose* opens with that exact confession: *Yasu', I was a thirsty stretch of sand, nothing green, nothing growing, nothing in my hand, then You came like rain where the rain never goes, and out of the wadi You raised me a rose.* The whole record grows out of that one image, a flower rising from a dry wadi, because that is the truest picture I have of what **Yeshua** did to me, and of what He is still doing across a whole region that the world too often writes off as barren.
The Rose that grows in the dust

The title reaches for one of the oldest and most tender names devotion has ever given the Beloved. In the Song of Songs, the beloved says, *I am the rose of Sharon, the lily of the valleys* (Song of Songs 2:1), and for centuries believers have sung that line over Christ Himself, the fairest, the fragrant One, the beauty that outshines the whole field. That is a devotional reading, a song the church has long sung, and I sing it here with the same love.

But the desert bloom is not only tradition. It is direct prophecy. Isaiah promised that the wilderness and the dry land shall be glad, and the desert shall rejoice and blossom; it shall blossom abundantly and rejoice with joy and singing (Isaiah 35:1-2). A blooming desert is not a sentimental idea in Scripture. It is a promise with the weight of God behind it. So when I sing that Yasu' is the desert rose, I am holding both, the Beloved of the Song, and the fulfillment of the promise that the driest ground would one day break into flower.
Blooming in the dust where the dry wind blows, deeper than the dune, sweeter than it knows, Yasu', in my desert You rose, You rose.
That doubled word at the end, *You rose, You rose*, is not an accident. It is the flower and the resurrection in one breath. The Rose that grows in the dust is the One who rose from the grave.
The cross planted in the sand

The record does not stay in gentle imagery, because a real desert is a place of death, and the deepest song on the album knows it. "The Cross in the Sand" is the proclamation at the album's heart, and it refuses to be vague.

*The cross in the sand, the blood of Yasu', truly bled, truly died, truly rose, the cross in the sand, the Lamb of God, bearing the weight of every soul He chose.* I wrote it that way on purpose. Truly. Truly. Truly. Because the beauty of the desert rose is not a mood or a metaphor for feeling better. It grows out of an actual grave, an actual death, an actual body that an actual tomb could not keep. The whole record leans on the confession the Scriptures make of the Lamb who was slain and is worthy (Revelation 5). The bloom is real because the cross was real and the rising was real.

That is what separates this from a pretty desert song. The comfort is not that the sand is secretly nice. The comfort is that the King came down into the sand, bled in it, and rose out of it, and now He raises roses out of ground that had given up.

I have watched this happen in real lives, not only in my own. I have seen the driest people I know, hardened by loss, by exile, by years of being told nothing would ever grow in them again, kneel at that cross in the sand and come up changed, the green shoot pushing through where everyone had stopped looking. The desert does not bloom because it worked hard at blooming. It blooms because rain finally reached it. That is grace, and grace is the only thing that has ever made barren ground rejoice.
The Shepherd who crosses the dunes
If the cross is the ground the rose grows in, the Shepherd is how it gets found. "Shepherd of the Dunes" is the most personal song on the record, because it is about being carried.

My people have herded flocks across hard country for longer than anyone can count. We know what a shepherd does when one is lost in the dunes. He does not shrug and count his losses; he goes out into the killing heat and he does not come back without it. That is exactly the picture Yasu' painted of Himself, the shepherd who leaves the flock to go after the one that wandered, and lays it on His shoulders and carries it home rejoicing (Luke 15). The chorus is that rescue: *Shepherd of the dunes, Yasu', calling the wanderer home, no more to wander and roam.* Every soul I have ever met in the diaspora, homesick in a foreign city, and every soul at home who feels far from God under a familiar sky, this song is for the wanderer in both.
For the ones the desert wore down

The album carries on through the qahwa of welcome and the wedding joy of henna and the overflowing table, and it ends in the marketplace with hallelujah on every tongue. But its heart never leaves the wadi where the rose came up.

I made this for the ones the desert has worn down. For the heart that has been dry so long it has stopped expecting anything to grow. For the region so often described only by its hardness, its heat, its loss, and never by the astonishing thing God delights to do in exactly such ground. I want you to know that the driest place you carry is not disqualified from blooming. It is the very kind of ground the promise was made for. The wilderness shall rejoice and blossom. That is not wishful thinking. That is a word older than your dryness.

So bring Him the sand. Bring the empty hand and the riverbed that has not run in years. **Yeshua** is the rain that comes where rain never goes, the Rose that grows in the dust, the Shepherd who crosses the dunes to carry you home. Out of the driest wadi He can raise a rose. He raised one out of me, and He rose Himself out of a sealed tomb, and He is still in the business of making deserts bloom out loud.

pieces.title: I Refuse to Hand Them My Likeness
pieces.imagePrompt: A moving scene of reconciliation and shelter among diverse people of many nations, two people of different backgrounds embracing with visible relief and dignity on their faces, others gathered close with open hands and healing smiles under a sheltering archway, warm protective light wrapping the whole group; premium cinematic worship-brand film still, warm golden refuge-light, tender and hopeful, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I know the word spat across the street and the welcome that never came. This album is for everyone wounded by hatred for who they are, how you heal without becoming the hate aimed at you, and how you find a shelter that does not deny the harm but outlasts it. Yasu' is that refuge.

body.text: I know the word. The one spat across the street at someone who looks like me, or prays like me, or comes from where I come from. I know the glance that says you do not belong here, and the silence where a welcome should have been. I did not learn about prejudice from a book. I learned it the way most people from my part of the world learn it, on the skin, in the gut, in the pause before a door that does not open. This album was written out of that wound, and out of the harder question the wound forces: what do you do with the hatred once it has found you?

*Refuge in God* is the most vulnerable record I have ever made. It is not a theology lecture about shelter. It is the walk itself, the wound named, the anger owned, the healing begun, the refuge finally found, for anyone who has been hated for who they are and does not know how to survive it without either shattering or turning to stone. And its answer, the only one I have found that holds weight, is a Person: **Yeshua**, Yasu', who does not offer escape from the harm but grounding underneath it.
He names the wound before I do
The record opens with the thing most of us were told never to do: it says the wound out loud.

"Jesus, You Name the Wound" refuses the lie that faith means pretending you were not hurt. *You see the word they spit across the street, You see the glance that said I don't belong, You see the silence where a welcome should have been. I don't have to pretend it didn't happen, Lord.* That last line was the hardest and freest thing I ever wrote, because so much religion asks the wounded to bury the wound in a hurry and call it forgiveness. This album will not. The One I follow is the Man of Sorrows of Isaiah 53, acquainted with grief, and He is the Lord who stood at the grave of His friend and wept (John 11:35). He does not tell you to be quiet about your pain. He weeps with the rejected before He heals them.
You are the Christ who bleeds with the rejected. I lay the wound at Your pierced feet tonight, and You do not look away.

And He sees. The third song reaches for one of the tenderest names for God in all Scripture, given by an outsider in a desert, Hagar, the Egyptian slave woman, hated and driven out, who met God in the wilderness and called Him El Roi, *the God who sees me* (Genesis 16:13). She was foreign, low, and cast off, and she was the first person in the Bible to give God a name. That is not an accident this album could pass by. The God who sees is the God of exactly the ones the world refuses to see.
What to do with the anger
Then the record does something I have rarely heard a worship album dare. It gets angry, and it does not apologize for it. It hands the anger up.

Because if you have been truly hated, you know that pretending you feel no rage is not holiness; it is a slow poison. So "Jesus, Carry This Anger" brings the fire to God instead of swallowing it or aiming it: *I cannot be its keeper, I will not let it become my god, I will not let it make a stranger of my face. You are the Lion, You are the Lamb, You know what to do with the fire.* This is the wisdom of the Scriptures, not a denial of it. The apostle wrote that we are to leave room for God's wrath, for it is written, vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord (Romans 12:19). Handing the anger up is not weakness. It is refusing to let the hatred conscript you into its own army.

And that leads to the line the whole album turns on, the one I named this reflection for. "Jesus, Keep My Face Like Yours" is a prophetic refusal set to melody: *let Your meekness settle in my jaw, let Your mercy settle in my eyes. I refuse to become what wounded me, I refuse to hand them my likeness.* That is the real danger of being hated: not only the harm done to you, but the temptation to be remade in the image of the ones who harmed you, until your face hardens into theirs. I will not. I was made in the image of God (Genesis 1:27), and I will not trade that likeness for the likeness of my enemies. The deepest act of defiance a hated person can make is to keep a merciful face.
The refuge that does not deny the harm

The center of the record, its title song, is where the shelter finally opens. "Jesus, You Are My Refuge" is built on the oldest refuge-poetry we have: *under the shadow of Your wing I hide, Lord, in the hollow of Your palm I rest, Psalm 91 is singing over me again.*

I want to be careful about what kind of refuge this is, because I am not selling escapism. The Psalms that overflow with refuge language are not promising that the harm is not real. Psalm 91 does not say no arrow flies; it says the One who dwells in the shelter of the Most High abides under His shadow through the flying of it. God our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble (Psalm 46), present *in* the trouble, not instead of it. So the chorus does not pretend the wound away: *safe in Your arms, beyond this harm, beyond this shame. You are the Rock that does not move.* The refuge is not a denial that harm happened. It is the affirmation that harm does not get the last word over a life hidden in God.
That is the difference between hiding from reality and being grounded in ultimate reality. One is a locked room. The other is a fortress with the door open and the King inside.
Healing without waiting for the haters to heal

The album's last movement is the one I most needed to sing for my own people, and for anyone the world has taught to hate back. It refuses two false endings, the numbness that pretends it never hurt, and the bitterness that lets the hurt become the whole self.

"Jesus, You Are Justice and Mercy" holds the paradox the prophet Micah held: to do justice, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God (Micah 6:8). *You weigh the scales I cannot weigh, You render the verdict I cannot render, vengeance is not mine, Lord, it is Yours; forgiveness is not easy, but it is Yours too.* I do not have to become either the judge or the doormat. I can hand both the scales and the forgiveness to the One who can actually carry them. And the record ends gathered, "Jesus, You Gather Us," one flock out of every wounded people, and beyond it the healed tomorrow, the city where the hating finally ends. The old spiritual called Him the balm of Gilead, the healing for the sin-sick soul; that is the church's song reaching for the same hope the prophet voiced, and I sing it with them.

I made this for the ones the world has hated for who they are. For the immigrant and the outsider, for the diaspora heart in a cold city and the wounded heart at home, for anyone who has felt a door close in silence. You do not have to bury the wound, and you do not have to become the hate to survive it. There is a God who sees you the way He saw a cast-off woman in the desert, a Man of Sorrows who bleeds with the rejected, a Rock that does not move. Hide in Him, hand Him the fire, and keep your face like His. **Yeshua** is a refuge that does not deny the harm. He simply outlasts it, and He means to heal you whether or not the ones who wounded you ever do.

pieces.title: I Lift the Lanterns While the Dark Is Still Drawn
pieces.imagePrompt: A serene gathering of diverse people of many nations in a courtyard just before sunrise, each holding a small glowing lantern lifted toward a paling sky, faces peaceful and expectant in the blue pre-dawn light, an elder and a child side by side, the first warm gold breaking over the far wall; premium cinematic worship-brand film still, tranquil indigo-to-amber dawn tones, quiet and luminous, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: Before the souk opens and the village wakes, there is a stillness that belongs to God alone. This album lives in that hour, the lamps lit before sunrise, the first prayer of the day laid down while the courtyard is still dark. It is for anyone who wants to give Yasu' the morning before anyone else takes it.

body.text: There is an hour in my part of the world that belongs to almost no one. It comes before the muezzin of the day's busyness calls anyone to anything, before the souk unlatches its shutters, before the village smells the first bread. The courtyard is still dark. The lantern wicks are still smoking from the night. And into that hour, if you are willing to rise for it, you can lay the whole of your morning down before God while nobody is watching and nothing is demanding. This album lives entirely inside that hour.

*Lanterns at Dawn* is my record of the first prayer of the day, the lamps lifted before the sun, the heart turned toward Yasu' before the world can turn it toward anything else. The opening song is exactly that scene: *Yasu', the courtyard is dark and the wicks are still smoking, so I lift the little lanterns till they catch the first gold; the night was so long and the oil was running low, but You are the dawn that I waited for, the warmth in the cold.*
Giving Him the morning first
The whole conviction of this album fits in one small decision: whom does your morning belong to?
