Everyone's morning gets claimed. The phone claims it, the market claims it, the worry you fell asleep holding claims it before your feet touch the floor. The songwriter-king knew this temptation three thousand years ago and made a discipline against it, *in the morning, O Lord, You hear my voice; in the morning I lay my requests before You and wait expectantly* (Psalm 5:3). In the morning, and wait. Before the day can spend you, you spend the first of it on Him. The pre-chorus of the opening song is that exact turning: *before the saffron light has spilled across the wall, I am turning every flame toward You, my first and my all.*
I did not want a record about squeezing God into a busy schedule. I wanted a record about beating the schedule to the punch, meeting Him in the stillness before the stillness is stolen.
Lanterns at dawn, lanterns at dawn. I lift them to Yasu' while the dark is still drawn, the fanous is burning and the night is withdrawn.
The mercy that is always waiting at first light
There is a reason the dawn, and not the noon, anchors this album. Because morning in the Scriptures is where mercy keeps its standing appointment.

The prophet, sitting in the ashes of a ruined city, still found the ground to say that the steadfast love of the Lord never ceases, His mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning, great is Your faithfulness (Lamentations 3:22-23). New every morning. Not recycled from yesterday, not rationed, not dependent on how well you slept or how the day before went. A fresh mercy, delivered before you wake, waiting in the dark like a lantern already lit. So the second track on the record, "Saffron Morning," is nothing but that discovery, the sunrise as the daily proof that God's compassion did not run out overnight.

That is why the dawn hour is not a burden but a gift. You are not rising early to earn God's attention. You are rising to receive a mercy He already prepared while you were asleep. The lantern was burning in the archway before you came down the stairs.

And there is a tenderness in meeting Him at that hour that the crowded day can never give. In the stillness before the souk, before the first voice calls and the first errand pulls, it is only you and Him and the smell of the cardamom rising. The heart hears more clearly in that quiet, the way the psalmist, awake in the watches of the night, found his God nearer than his own breath (Psalm 63). The early hour is not merely disciplined. It is intimate. It is the one part of the day nobody else has touched yet, offered whole.
The lamp that outlasts my little flames

There is an honesty in the imagery I want to name, because it keeps the album from being sentimental. My lanterns run low. The opening verse admits it, *the oil was running low.* Any flame I light will gutter and need refilling. That is the truth about every discipline of prayer I have ever kept: it flickers.

So the record moves, by its tenth song, to a greater lamp than any I can hold. "The Lamp in the Fanous" reaches past my little wicks to the One who called Himself the Light of the world, and to the Word that the psalmist said is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path (Psalm 119:105). My lanterns are real and worth lifting, but they are only ever reflecting a Light that never gutters, never runs low, never needs me to refill it. I light my small flames at dawn precisely because there is a Sun rising behind them that will still be burning when every wick I own has gone out.

The bridge of the opening song already reaches for that, quietly borrowing heaven's own song: *worthy is the Lamb who outshines the rising sun.* The Lamb of Revelation 5 outshines the very dawn I am lifting my lanterns toward. My flames are a welcome for a Light far greater than themselves.
For the ones who want to give Him the first of it

The album carries on into the waking day, the qahwa brewing, the bread warming, the souk about to open, the cedars and the courtyard and the road. But it never forgets where it began, in the dark before the gold, with a handful of lanterns lifted toward the One who is the true dawn.

I made this for anyone tired of handing their mornings to everything but God. For the one who keeps meaning to pray and keeps getting beaten to it by the noise. For the diaspora heart in a cold northern city, and the heart at home under a familiar sky, both wanting to give **Yeshua** the first of the day before anyone else takes it. You do not need a full lantern or a steady flame. You need only to rise into the stillness while the dark is still drawn, lift what little light you have, and turn every flame toward Him.

The mercy is already new. The dawn is already on its way up behind the wall. And **Yeshua**, the Light no night has ever put out, is waiting in the quiet courtyard for the ones who love Him enough to come before the sun. Lift the lanterns. He is worth the early rising, and the morning He gives back is always brighter than the one you gave Him.

pieces.title: He Swapped My Stone Heart for a Drum
pieces.imagePrompt: A packed Friday-night youth worship concert of many nations, teenagers and young adults with hands on their chests feeling the bass, faces lit with joy under stage light, a diverse crowd jumping as one, an older abuela and small children among them, hands raised, sweat and confetti and pure celebration, cinematic worship-brand film still, vivid and emotive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I spent years with my heart beating for a hundred empty things, the chain, the fame, the dream that never paid out. Then one Friday night at a youth concert the bass dropped on the four, and I felt God trade me a heart of stone for a heart that finally had a beat. This dembow record is the sound of that new pulse.

body.text: For years my heart was beating hard for nothing. The music, the dream, the chain hanging out of my shirt under the lights, the weight of a fame that never once weighed anything real. My pulse was fast and it was pointed at a hundred empty things, and I thought that was just what it meant to be young and alive.

Then, on a Friday night, at a youth concert with the bass cabinet out on the sidewalk shaking the chain-link fence, the kick hit the one and something in my chest answered it. And I heard **Yeshua**, quiet under all that volume: *Son, your heart is Mine forever more.* I did not get quieter that night. I got *louder.* Because I finally had something worth the beat.

**Corazón Latino (Late Para Ti)**, *Latin Heart (It Beats for You)*, is the record that came out of that night. It is a dembow album, boom-ch-boom-chick, sub-bass you feel before you hear it, and every song is built on one discovery: God did not calm my heart down. He gave me a *new one.*
What the title means

*Corazón Latino* means "Latin Heart." And *Late Para Ti*, that is the part that undoes me, means "It Beats for You." Not *it beats for the party,* not *it beats for the grind.* It beats *for You,* meaning for **Yeshua.**

I built this on dembow on purpose, because dembow is the heartbeat of a whole generation of young Latinos, the rhythm in the earbuds on the train, the thump out the Honda in the church parking lot. And a heartbeat is exactly the right picture, because the promise God made through Ezekiel is a heart transplant: *"A new heart also will I give you… and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh"* (Ezekiel 36:26). He did not renovate my old stone heart. He took it out. He put in one that could feel, one that could beat, one that had a rhythm, and the rhythm was Him.
The opening track says the thesis in one line I still shout:
A hundred reasons for the heart to beat, but only One is the truth, Christ is the rhythm.
Why I had to make it
Because I watched it happen to the people I love, and I could not keep it to myself.

There is a verse in that first song about my cousin. She used to listen to the same dembow on the train, and her heart was in pain. Now Cristo is on her playlist and the pain is gone. There is another cousin who used to play the dice game on the stoop and now plays bass for the worship band. And there is the kid with the chain still hanging out of his shirt. I did not make him hide the chain. I just watched it start pointing at a different cross. *The heart that was beating for nothing, beats for Christ somehow.*

That is what I needed the world to hear. **Yahuah** is not in the business of giving young people a smaller life with the volume turned down. He is in the business of taking a heart that was pounding away for empty things and re-aiming every single beat. King David knew he could not manufacture that himself, so he begged for it: *"Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me"* (Psalm 51:10). That is not a request for behavior modification. That is a request for a transplant. And **Yeshua** grants it.
The songs, and where the beat points

"Mi Corazón Despierta", *My Heart Wakes Up*, is the 6 AM song. The alarm hits on the kick, the Bible on the nightstand is still open from last night, the tile is cold underfoot, and God says *wake up, life is real and rare.* The new heart does not sleep in.

"Boom-Ch-Boom Para Cristo" is the most unashamed thing on the record. I take the signature dembow pattern itself and hand it to **Yeshua.** Paul told us to *"present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God"* (Romans 12:1), and I decided that if my body is the offering, then the rhythm my body already loves belongs on the altar too. The beat is not the enemy. The beat is the offering.

Then the album widens the heart outward. "Mi Amor Es Tuyo" and "El Corazón de la Familia" take that same pulse to the dinner table, the mother's hand reaching across, the friend's text at 11 PM that says *praying for you,* the neighbor across the hall. Because **Yeshua** said the second command sits right next to the first: *"Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself"* (Matthew 22:39). A heart that beats only for itself is still a stone heart with better production. The new heart beats *out.*

And "Late Por Otros", *Beats for Others*, is where it lands. A heart of flesh cannot stay private. It starts beating for the cousin who hasn't heard, for the friend on the subway you slip an earbud to, for the whole block.
The quiet track in the middle of the loud album

There is one song I made deliberately soft, a dembow-bachata that pulls the whole thing down to a whisper. The bedroom ceiling at 11 PM, the streetlight through the blinds, headphones on the pillow with no music playing, the Bible closed tonight. Because sometimes the new heart still aches, still lies awake, still forgets to open the Book. I wanted that honesty on the record. Even David, with his transplanted heart, still cried out like the deer that *"panteth after the water brooks"* (Psalm 42:1). A new heart is not a heart that never thirsts. It is a heart that finally knows *Who* it is thirsty for.

And then Sunday comes, "Domingo en la Mañana", the coffee steaming, the car stereo on the way to church, the whole congregation's voices stacking up, because the new heart was never meant to beat alone. The Scripture is plain about it: *do not forsake "the assembling of ourselves together"* (Hebrews 10:25). Hearts keep better time in a crowd.
Who this album is for

This one is for the Friday-night youth concert with the bass out on the sidewalk. For the second-generation kid with the chain and the airpods who thinks God only speaks in slow songs and old hymns. For the cousin on the train. For anyone whose heart has been pounding hard for a long time at a hundred empty things and is starting to suspect it was built to beat for something more.

Hear me: **Yeshua** is not asking you to flatline. He is offering you a transplant. He will take the stone out and hand you a heart with a beat in it, and then, I promise you, you will feel the kick hit the one, and you will know exactly Who your heart was made to run for.
*Corazón Latino.* It beats for You. Only for You. Come feel it start.

pieces.title: The Cross Went Over the Line First
pieces.imagePrompt: A hopeful dawn crossing scene, a diverse group of travelers and families walking forward with light breaking over a river and distant hills, a wooden cross carried ahead of them, footprints in the dust leading the way, an accordion player among them, hands reaching to help one another across, then a great multitude of many nations gathered at a long shared table in warm light, joy and relief on their faces, cinematic worship-brand film still, emotive and bright, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I came to the crossing trembling, with dust on my boots and fear at my back, and then I looked down and saw a footprint already pressed into the ground where I was about to step. This vallenato record is built on one discovery: whatever line you are afraid of, the Cross went over it first.

body.text: I came to the crossing trembling. Dust on my boots, the line up ahead, the fear at my back. You know the feeling even if you have never stood at a literal border, that moment where the thing in front of you is bigger than you are, and there is no way around it, only through. And then I looked down at the ground where I was about to put my foot, and there was already a footprint there. Someone had crossed this exact spot before me.

That is the whole album in one image. **La Cruz Cruza**, *The Cross Crosses*, is a vallenato record about the discovery that no line you are afraid of is a line **Yeshua** has not already gone over first.

I set it to vallenato because vallenato is the folk music of the Colombian crossing country, accordion breathing like a pair of lungs, the *caja* drum, the scrape of the *guacharaca*, the music people actually carry on the road. If I was going to sing about a road, I wanted the music of the road.
What the title means
*La Cruz Cruza* means "The Cross Crosses." And the opening track adds the word that changes everything: *Primero.* First. *La Cruz Cruza Primero*, the Cross crosses *first.*
The chorus is a shout, and I mean every syllable of it:
The Cross won't wait on the far side of the river, the Cross steps in first to the depth of the cold. Before the wall, before the fear, before the checkpoint, the Man already crossed.

Think about who did the crossing. The Carpenter of Galilee, the Son of the Father. He *"humbled himself, and became obedient unto death"* (Philippians 2:8), that is a crossing from heaven to earth, the widest border ever traversed. Then He crossed a second line no one else could: from holy to sin-bearing, taking on our guilt as His own. *"God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us"* (Romans 5:8). He crossed from the Father all the way out to the orphan, and He did it carrying the whole weight of our fear.
Why I had to make it
Because too many of the people I love are living at a border of one kind or another, and they think they are facing it alone.

Some of them are literally at a line, the checkpoint at dawn, the wire fence, the dust on the family's shoes. But most of the borders that terrify us are not on any map. The diagnosis. The empty bank account. The estrangement that has lasted years. The grave. Every one of those is a crossing, and every one of them feels like a place where you have to step out first, into the cold, with no idea what is on the other side.

I made this record to tell you the truth about every one of those lines: *He has already crossed it.* The footprints in the dust are His. And the promise on the far side is not a scary unknown. It is a homecoming. *"If thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved"* (Romans 10:9). That is the only crossing that finally matters, and He made the way through it Himself.
The songs, and the road they walk

"Amanecer en el Checkpoint", *Dawn at the Checkpoint*, catches the first light hitting the wire, the moment of most fear, and answers it with the accordion opening like the sun coming up. "Río de Misericordia," the *River of Mercy,* takes the whole thing down to a ballad at the river bend at dusk, just voice and accordion, because some crossings you make quietly, holding onto nothing but the fact that He is in the water with you. Psalm 23 said it first: *"Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me."*

"Cocina de Abuela" and "El Rosario de la Abuela" bring the grandmothers into it, the way they always are, praying without ceasing over everyone who has to travel (*"Pray without ceasing,"* 1 Thessalonians 5:17). "Cristo Cruza Conmigo", *Christ Crosses With Me*, is the companion truth to the whole record: He did not only go *before* me, He comes *with* me. That is the double comfort of the gospel, His footprint is already ahead of me on the ground, and His hand is already around mine as I step. "Hermanos al Otro Lado," *Brothers on the Other Side,* sings toward the family already waiting across every divide. And "Una Sola Mesa," *One Single Table,* is where the album is heading the whole time, hermanos on both sides of every line, sitting down together at last, the accordion still going, nobody counting who came from where.
The voice on the bridge
The moment that breaks me every time I sing it is the bridge of the title track, where the music strips down and the voice is no longer mine. It is the Father's, answering the trembling traveler:

Child. I've already crossed the river. Already crossed the wall, already crossed the cold. Every border that you fear, I crossed it safe. Every line of your whole life, I signed it with the blood of the Lamb.

That is the gospel with dust on its boots. Whatever you are standing in front of tonight, afraid to step, He has already been through it and come out the other side, and He signed the whole crossing in His own blood.
Where the road ends

The last song is called "Frontera Sagrada", *Sacred Border*, with the subtitle *Fiesta Sin Frontera,* the party with no border. Because here is where all the crossing leads. John saw the finish line and wrote it down: *"a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues"* standing together before the throne (Revelation 7:9). Every line crossed. Every wall down. One festival, every language, no checkpoint left to clear.
Who this album is for

This one is for whoever is standing at a line tonight, the real ones and the invisible ones. For the family in the dust at dawn. For the person facing the diagnosis, the bill, the goodbye. For anyone who has to step out first into a cold they cannot see the bottom of.

Look down. Those are His footprints. Look up, those are His stars. Go ahead, hermano; go ahead, hermana. He has gone before you, and He is going with you, and He has already signed your crossing in blood. The Cross went over the line first.
The far side is a fiesta. Come across.

pieces.title: Every King I Crowned Before Him Fell
pieces.imagePrompt: A vibrant night worship celebration in a Latino barrio, young people with hands raised toward a single point of light, joy on their faces, phones and earbuds set down, a diverse crowd of many nations united in praise, warm street-lamp glow mixing with stage light, a sense of every lesser idol falling away, cinematic worship-brand film still, bold and emotive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I tried every name the street was selling, the money, the fame, the sneaker parade, the kings trending on the timeline. Every one of them fell. This reggaeton record is my testimony that after all the counterfeits collapsed, only one Name was still standing.

body.text: I tried every name on the radio play. I chased every name the street ever sold, the money, the fame, the sneaker parade, the whole line of kings the world hands you and tells you to bow to. And I need you to hear the testimony plainly, because I paid for it: *nothing ever filled me. No one could hold.* Every king I crowned collapsed under the weight of the crown.

Then one Friday night, His Name walked in, and the dembow itself seemed to surrender to the Light. **Solo Tú, Jesús**, *Only You, Jesus*, is the reggaeton record I made the morning after every counterfeit fell and only one Name was left standing.
What the title means

*Solo Tú, Jesús* means "Only You, Jesus." It is the most exclusive claim a person can make, and I make it on purpose, over an 808 and a dembow kick, because the barrio needs to hear that the gospel is not shy. There is a track literally called "Reyes Que Caen", *Kings That Fall*, and it is the honest one, the inventory of every throne I built for something that could not sit on it.

The world will offer you a thousand names to worship. Isaiah heard **Yahuah** answer all thousand of them at once: *"I am the first, and I am the last; and beside me there is no God"* (Isaiah 44:6). And Peter, standing in front of the whole council, refused to soften it: *"Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved"* (Acts 4:12). That is not narrow. That is *rescue.* When you are drowning, one rope is not narrow-minded. One rope is everything.
There's no other Path, no other Way. There's no other Name, no other day. Only You, Jesús, only You can save.
Why I had to make it
Because I watched a generation crown TikTok kings and come away empty, and I have been that generation.

There is a verse in the opening track about a kid on the block with the airpods in, chasing kings on the timeline all week, and then the real King walks in *through the algorithm's bend.* **Yeshua** on the feed. That line makes people laugh and then it makes them quiet, because they know exactly what it describes. We are the most-entertained, most-marketed-to, least-satisfied generation in history. We have crowned more idols than any people who ever lived, and every one of them has fallen.
I made this album to say: stop rebuilding thrones for things that keep collapsing. There is a Name that does not break. *Every other name will break, only Yours can hold.*
The songs, and the "I AM" that answers everything
This whole record is really a tour through the great **Yeshua** self-declarations, the "I AM" statements, set to reggaeton so the barrio can chant them back.

"Camino, Verdad, Vida" is John 14:6 turned into a hook you cannot get out of your head, *"I am the way, the truth, and the life."* "Una Sola Puerta" and "La Puerta del Pastor" plant the flag on John 10, *"I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved"* (John 10:9), and *"I am the good shepherd"* (John 10:11). The door and the Shepherd are the same Person, and He is the only way into the fold and the only One inside it who will lay His life down for you.

"Nombre Sobre Todo Nombre", *Name Above Every Name*, takes the crown off every fallen king and puts it where it belongs. "En el Barrio Tu Nombre," *Your Name in the Barrio,* plants that one Name on the block I am from, on the corners where all the other names were sold to me first. And "Altar en la Calle," *Altar in the Street,* refuses to keep any of this indoors. The barrio corner is an altar. **Yeshua** is *"the light of the world"* (John 8:12), and light does not stay in the building. It goes out to the very street where the counterfeit kings are still being advertised, and it names the real One.

"Lleva Tu Nombre Conmigo", *I Carry Your Name With Me*, is the commissioning song, and it settles the difference between an idol and the Lord in one line. You carry an idol; it never carries you, and eventually the weight of it breaks your back. But His Name carries *you.* You do not prop Him up. He holds you up. Every king I ever crowned needed me to keep it standing. **Yeshua** is the first one who kept *me* standing instead.
The most intimate song on a loud record

There is one track that pulls the whole party down to a whisper: "Solo Tú Me Conoces", *Only You Know Me.* Under all the ad-libs and the 808s, this is the quietest confession on the album, and it leans on Psalm 139: *"O LORD, thou hast searched me, and known me."* The world crowned a version of me it invented, the image, the followers, the highlight reel. But only **Yeshua** knows the real one, the one behind the phone. Only He can be Lord of a person He actually knows. Every other king was ruling a stranger.
That is why He is the only One worth the crown. The idols demanded I perform for them. He already knows me all the way down and calls me His anyway.
Where it's all headed

The album does not end with me. It ends with the world. "El Mundo Te Conocerá", *The World Will Know You*, reaches back to Paul standing in Athens in front of an altar marked *TO THE UNKNOWN GOD,* saying, *"Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you"* (Acts 17:23). Every city is full of altars to unknown gods, kings that will fall. My job, our job, is to walk up to those altars and finally name the One they were reaching for the whole time.
Who this album is for

This one is for the kid with the airpods in, chasing kings on the timeline. For the person who has crowned money, or status, or a relationship, or their own image, and watched the crown crush the thing it sat on. For everyone exhausted from bowing to names that keep breaking.

Here is the good news, loud, over the dembow: there is a Name that does not fall. Every king I crowned before Him collapsed, and then **Yeshua** walked in, and He is still standing, and He always will be. Take the crown off the counterfeit. Put it where it holds.
*Solo Tú, Jesús.* Only You. Let His Name lead.

pieces.title: The Grin That Would Not Come Off
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful Caribbean carnival of faith, a steelpan player mid-song, a diverse crowd of many nations laughing and dancing in bright daylight, a former cynic beaming with unguarded joy, brass and iron and color everywhere, hands raised, genuine grins on every face, sunlight and celebration, cinematic worship-brand film still, radiant and emotive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: The world hands you bad news with a serious face and a cynic on every corner saying nothing ever changes. I made a steelpan record to answer them, not with a frown, but with a grin the darkness could not wipe off. Because the truth is not grim. The truth already won.

body.text: The world handed me bad news with a serious face. The anchorman frowning like a frown could win the race. The cynic on the corner saying *nothing ever change.* And for a long stretch of my life I agreed with him. I figured the smart people were the sad ones, and joy was just what you had before you found out how things really are.

Then I met the actual Truth, and He was *grinning.* He walked into the room I had already decided was dark, and He was not wringing His hands. So I made a record to answer every serious face and every corner cynic, not with a bigger argument, but with a smile they could not explain and could not wipe off.

**Truth Wears A Smile** is that record. It is a rapso album, Trinidadian calypso groove under spoken-word commentary, steelpan lead, iron and brass and a big crowd shouting back. Calypso was always the music of the sharp-tongued street commentator. I just redeemed the tongue.
What the title means
*Truth Wears A Smile.* Not truth *pretends* to smile, not truth *forces* a smile through gritted teeth. The truth itself is smiling, because of how the story actually ends.
Here is the whole thesis, straight off the opening track:
They sell me the panic, they sell me the gloom, but You walk grinning, Lord, right into the room.

Most people think faith is the frown you put on to seem serious about God. I think that gets it exactly backwards. **Yeshua** said, *"I am the way, the truth, and the life"* (John 14:6), and the same **Yeshua** told His followers, *"In my presence is fulness of joy"* is what David sang of Him (Psalm 16:11). Nehemiah stood in front of a weeping people and told them to stop, because *"the joy of the LORD is your strength"* (Nehemiah 8:10). Joy is not the reward for getting through the truth. Joy is what the truth is *made of.*
Why I had to make it
Because cynicism is the cheapest costume in the world, and I wore it for years, and it nearly cost me everything.

There is a track called "Cynic Turned Believer," and another called "The Comedian's Confession," and another called "Same Joke, Sober Now", and they are all the same man, which is to say they are all a version of me. The mocker who used bad news as material. The comedian who could make a whole room laugh and go home empty. What changed the mocker? The answer the crowd shouts back is the only one that ever works: *Jesus changed the mocker.*

I had to make this album because the church too often hands the world the truth with the exact serious face the world was already drowning in. And meanwhile the enemy gets to look like the fun one. That is a lie, and I wanted to name it. **Yeshua** told us who invented lying in the first place: the devil, *"a liar, and the father of it"* (John 8:44). The very first lie in the Book was a question dressed up as concern, *"Yea, hath God said?"* (Genesis 3:1). Every gloom the world sells you is a descendant of that first lie. The Light exposes it: *"In him was life; and the life was the light of men. And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not"* (John 1:4-5).
The songs, and the sound of the grin

"Steelpan Says His Name" hands the melody to the instrument itself, that bright, unmistakable Caribbean shimmer answering back the moment I call out to **Yeshua.** "Loud in the Daylight" refuses to keep the good news whispered in the shadows, because He said it plainly: *"Ye are the light of the world… let your light so shine before men"* (Matthew 5:14-16). Light is not shy, and it is not for after dark only.

"Who Told You That Lie" is the detective song. It takes the panic the world sold you and traces it back to the liar who first wrote it. "Light Switch in My Chest" and "Grin That Won't Come Off" are the testimony of what happens next: the switch flips, and the grin will not come off, no matter how hard the old cynicism tries to scrub it. That is not naivety. That is Galatians 5:22, *"the fruit of the Spirit is… joy"*, growing where it was planted.

And "Bad News Ran Out of Road" is my favorite, because it is Paul's taunt in a calypso hook. When the resurrection is true, the bad news finally hits a dead end: *"O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?"* (1 Corinthians 15:55). The worst news the world has, the grave, ran out of road at an empty tomb.
The rule I sing by
There is a line in the opening track that is the ethic of the whole album, and I hold to it:
No angry finger pointing at the man, just point at the Lie and hold out Your plan. I call out the liar, but I love the human.

That is the calypso wit redeemed. The street commentator's job was always to name what is wrong. I just refuse to name a *person* as the enemy. I name the *lie,* and I love the human every time. Truth with a grin does not shame you into the light. It disarms you into it.
Where the carnival ends up

The album climbs toward "Carnival of the Redeemed," and I built that one straight out of Revelation, *"a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues"* (Revelation 7:9). Because that is the real party at the end of history: every culture, every steelpan and every drum, one enormous carnival of people the bad news could not keep. And the closer, "Last Laugh Belongs to Jesus," is exactly what it says. The cynic thought he had the last word. He doesn't. **Yeshua** does, and it is a laugh.
Who this album is for

This one is for the cynic on the corner. For the comedian who goes home empty. For the exhausted believer who thinks holiness means never smiling again. For anyone who has been handed the truth with such a grim face that they assumed the good news must be bad news too.

It isn't. The Man from Galilee walked out of the grave. The Light is here and the dark cannot dim it. So I don't do the frown, and I don't do the fear. I grin at the darkness, because the story already ended, and it ended well.
Go ahead. Try to wipe the grin off. You can't. It won't come off. That is what the truth does to a face.

pieces.title: The Bandoneón Cries, and the Father Sings
pieces.song: Cristo No Se Va (Even When the Night Arrives)
pieces.imagePrompt: A tender late-night scene opening toward dawn, a lone figure at a kitchen window at 3 AM with a kettle and a single lamp, the Father's presence felt in the room, then the same family embracing as first light breaks over the city, a bandoneón player in warm shadow, faces moving from grief to hope, believers of many nations holding one another through the dark into morning, cinematic worship-brand film still, intimate and emotive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: This is my night record, the 3 AM kitchen, the hospital corridor, the money that doesn't come, the phone that never rings. I set it to Argentine tango because the bandoneón knows how to cry. But every time it weeps, the Father sings back, because He does not leave when the night arrives. He was already at the window before I prayed.

body.text: Eleven thirty-three at night. The kettle not on yet. The chair pulled out from the table but nobody sitting in it. The silence in a dark kitchen is a heavy thing, and if you have ever sat in it, waiting on a phone call, or a test result, or a paycheck, or just for the fear to loosen its grip, then you already know the sound this album is trying to make.

I set **Cristo No Se Va** to Argentine tango, to the bandoneón, because the bandoneón is the one instrument I know that cries like a person. It opens like a window, it breathes in and out, and it sighs the exact sigh you sigh at three in the morning when you cannot name what is wrong. I wanted an instrument that would not pretend the night is fine. And then, over top of every one of those cries, I put the answer the whole record exists to give: the Father, singing back.
What the title means

*Cristo No Se Va* means "Christ Does Not Leave." That is the whole thesis, and I built it on a single verse the way you build a house on a single rock. **Yeshua** made a promise and He did not soften it: *"I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee"* (Hebrews 13:5). The title track sings it plain:
He's not the friend who shows up on the easy day. He's the One who never goes away.

Tango is usually the music of the one who *left*, the lover gone, the door closed, the empty room. I took that grieving, gorgeous music and turned it inside out. On this record the tango is not about who walked away. It is about the One who *stayed.* The bandoneón weeps the way grief actually weeps, and the Father does not tell it to stop. He just refuses to leave the room while it does.
Why I had to make it
Because most of the real crises of a life happen at night, with no audience, and the church does not always have a song for that hour.

We have plenty of songs for Sunday morning with the lights up. But the diagnosis comes at 11:47 PM in a hospital corridor. The panic comes at 3 AM at the kitchen table. The loneliness comes when the phone sits silent on the counter and does not ring. I needed to make a record for *those* hours, not to explain the pain away, but to sit inside it and testify to the one thing I have found to be true every single time: He was already there before I said a word.

The opening song, "El Bandoneón Abre," says it over and over until you believe it, *the Father was in the window before the prayer. The night arrived, but He arrived before it.* That is the good news for the dark: you are not waking Him up with your 3 AM cry. He was already awake. He was already standing there. Scripture says even the dark is not dark to Him, *"the night shineth as the day: the darkness and the light are both alike to thee"* (Psalm 139:12). The night that terrifies you does not so much as dim His sight of you.
The songs, and the long night
The album walks through the specific nights, one at a time, and refuses to be vague about any of them.

"El Corredor del Hospital", *The Hospital Corridor*, is the fluorescent-lit walk at almost midnight, and its subtitle is the whole comfort: *Cristo Camina Conmigo,* Christ walks with me. Down that hallway you are never actually walking alone.

"Cuando el Dinero No Llega", *When the Money Doesn't Come*, is for the believer who is ashamed to bring their empty bank account to God, as if He only handles spiritual things. He handles the rent too. He is Lord of the corridor and the kitchen and the unpaid bill.

"El Teléfono Que No Suena", *The Phone That Doesn't Ring*, is the loneliest one, the silent phone on the kitchen table at 9:47 PM. And its subtitle is the turn: *El Padre Llama,* the Father calls. When the call you were waiting on never comes, there is Another who is already calling your name.

Every one of these songs does the same thing. It names the night honestly, no fake cheer, no rushing past the ache, and then it points to the Presence that was already in the room before the ache started.
The mercy that shows up at dawn
Then the record turns, and it turns exactly where the Bible turns: at the morning.

"El Padre Es La Luz" is built on Lamentations 3, a book of *tears,* which is the point. Right in the middle of the saddest scroll in Scripture, the prophet writes: *"It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness"* (Lamentations 3:22-23). The Scriptures open at three-twenty-two, the kettle goes on again at 6:14 AM, and the mercies that got you through the night are already fresh for the day. **Yahuah** does not ration His mercy. He bakes a new batch every single morning.
Weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning (Psalm 30:5). The night is real, and it is not the last word.

And "Cuenta Las Estrellas", *Count the Stars*, reaches back to the night **Yahuah** took Abram outside and said, *"Look now toward heaven, and tell the stars, if thou be able to number them… So shall thy seed be"* (Genesis 15:5). Notice the timing: God gave His biggest promise *at night.* He did not wait for the sun. He used the dark itself, the very thing Abram was afraid of, as the canvas for the promise. Your dark sky is not empty. Count it. It is full of what He has promised.
We danced in the dark anyway

There is a song near the end I could not make this record without: "Bailamos en la Noche," *We Dance in the Night.* Because here is what I have learned as a man who leads worship in a culture that dances at every wedding and every wake. You do not have to wait for the morning to dance. The joy of **Yahuah** shows up *before* the sunrise, in the dark, and you can dance right there in it while the bandoneón is still weeping. The album's last track is called "El Amanecer", *The Dawn*, and its subtitle is the testimony of the whole night: *We Never Stopped Dancing.* The morning did not start the joy. The joy was there in the dark the whole time, because He was there in the dark the whole time.
Who this album is for

This one is for the 3 AM kitchen and the almost-midnight corridor. For the person staring at a phone that will not ring, or a bill that will not shrink, or a chair that will not be filled again. For everyone who has decided, quietly, that the night is proof God left.

He didn't. He was at the window before you prayed. He walks the corridor beside you. His mercies are already rising for the morning you cannot see yet. **Cristo no se va**, Christ does not leave, and I would stake my whole life on that sentence, because I already have.

Let the bandoneón cry. It's allowed. Just listen underneath it, and you will hear the Father singing back. And if you have any strength left at all tonight, get up, in the dark, and dance. The dawn is coming, and He never once left the room.

pieces.title: He Engineered the Voice You Cannot Bear to Delete
pieces.imagePrompt: A globally diverse gathering of people of many nations holding phones and headphones to their ears with faces lit by wonder and tearful joy, a young Black woman smiling as she listens, an older Asian man with eyes closed in peace, a Latina mother and daughter sharing one earbud and laughing, a family embracing in warm lamplit living-room glow, hands lifted softly toward gentle light, cinematic worship-brand film still, bright and emotive, high-key golden light, shallow depth of field, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: There is a saved message on ten million phones that no one has the heart to erase. I made a whole album about that small blue square, because a recorded voice is captured breath, and the God who invented the larynx does not lose a single voice He ever made. This is the story of why grief kept the sound, and why the Shepherd keeps it too.

body.text: There is a message saved on a phone in your pocket, or in a drawer, or in a phone you never traded in, and you cannot bring yourself to delete it. Someone's voice is in there. Nine seconds, maybe thirty. *"Hey, it's me, just calling to say."* The little trash icon waits like a question, and you leave it sitting in the queue, unmarked, year after year.

I wrote a whole album about that small blue square. I called it **The Voicemail**, and it is the tenderest thing I have ever made. But I want to tell you the part underneath the grief, the part that made me, a person who spends her life in awe of sound, sit very still at my desk and worship.
What is actually saved when you save a voice

Think, for one honest moment, about what a voicemail *is*. When someone you love speaks, they push air up out of their lungs and across two small folds of tissue in the throat, and those folds tremble, hundreds of times a second, and shape the trembling into your name. That trembling is who they are. No two of them are alike. Your mother's voice is not a picture of her; it is a piece of her, still moving.

And a recording catches that moving air and holds it. A cassette does it in rust and plastic; a phone does it in a pattern of ones and zeros; but both of them are doing the same astonishing thing, *keeping a breath that has already left the room.* One of the songs on the album says it plainly, sitting on the attic floor with a thrift-store player: **Yeshua**, You invented the human larynx, You invented the way love takes shape. I did not write that as a poem. I wrote it because it is true. Every voice you have ever loved was His idea first.

So when grief refuses to press delete, grief is not being sentimental. Grief is doing theology. It is insisting that a voice matters, that sound is not nothing, that the person is not gone the way a signal is gone. And I believe grief is right.
Why I had to make it
I made **The Voicemail** for the people who keep the sound.

I made it for the woman in *The Voicemail I Couldn't Delete*, clearing the photos off a full phone at one in the morning so she can keep the recording, *storage full, so I clear the photos, I keep the sound.* I made it for whoever is stuck in *Replay*, pressing the same small arrow at two a.m., knowing each pause and breath and laugh line, wondering if that loop is holy or just a wound. I wrote that song to sit on the edge of the bed beside them and say: the God who prays through us when we have no words is *in* the loop, not ashamed of it.

I made it for the daughter in *Her Voice Still On Record*, who finds a cassette her mother left for a seventh birthday and hears her stumble over the word "anointed" reading Psalm 23 aloud. And I made it for the one in *The Message I Saved for Years* who finally, after seven Januaries, taps play on a message she was too afraid to hear, and it turns out to say, *I forgive you.*
Every one of these is a true shape of the same thing: a human being holding onto a voice because a voice is love you can still hear.
The verse the whole album is built on

There is one sentence **Yeshua** said that I could not get out of my head while I wrote, and it became the eleventh song, *He Knows My Voice.* He said that His sheep know His voice, that a lamb can pick the one who feeds it out of a thousand bleating others. Shepherds outside Bethlehem really could do this; the flocks would sort themselves by the sound of the one they trusted.
But turn it over. If His sheep know His voice, then He, in turn, knows *theirs.*
He knows the cry you make at three in the morning. He knows the laugh, the sigh, the small designs. He knows the voice beneath your voice on Sunday, and the voice you keep beneath your pride.

We have built machines that unlock when they recognize us. Your phone knows your face; an assistant answers when you speak the name. But the kingdom of **Yahuah** is not facial recognition and it is not a database. The One who knit the larynx into your body hears the tone you cannot hide. The psalmist marveled that before a word is even on his tongue, **Yahuah** already knows it completely. That is not surveillance. That is being *known*, which is the thing we were all secretly aching for under all that grief.

And here is the mercy that undoes me: the same God who keeps a record of every voice keeps something even more tender. Scripture says He collects our tears in His bottle, writes them in His book. He is not a God who erases. He keeps the cup of tears, keeps the count of hairs, keeps the names of all His sheep. He is the great Keeper. Nothing true is ever lost with Him, not a tear, not a name, not a voice.
For the one who is afraid the sound will fade

There is a quiet terror in grief that no one warns you about. It arrives the morning you wake and cannot quite hear them anymore. You remember the words, the laughter, but the exact pitch has gone dim. I wrote *When Voice Becomes Memory* for that exact morning, because I have had it. And what I found there is the only thing strong enough to stand on: the God who spoke the world into being, who whispered a prophet out of a cave, who called a dead friend out of a tomb by name. He does not run out of voice. Even when the sound of someone fades in you like an old photograph, He can speak them clearer than the day they last spoke. He is the Memory beneath your memory.

The album ends where mine nearly ended for real. *The Voicemail That Saved Me* is about thirty-one seconds, a friend leaving a message she didn't know why she was leaving, on the worst night of a life, and a floor that stayed underneath because of it. I will not tell you the details of that Tuesday. I will only tell you that the Shepherd uses voicemails. He uses friends. He whispers to someone, *call her now, do not wait*, and a phone rings at the exact second the dark had almost won.

So if you are reading this and there is a person you love and a phone in your pocket: leave the message. Record the *I love you* on purpose. Send your mother the voicenote that just says you were thinking of her. You are not being silly. You are leaving a small inheritance of sound in a world where sound is one of the truest things we have.

And if what you are holding is a voice already gone, keep it. Press play when you need to. It is not weakness; it is the way love refuses to be small. The One who made that voice has not misplaced it. He knows it better than your own mother knew it on the phone. He has been listening every year.
The gate is open. And the God who invented the larynx is still saying your name.

pieces.title: The Longest Note God Ever Played Was a Silence
pieces.imagePrompt: A globally diverse congregation of many nations sitting together in a candlelit sanctuary at dawn with peaceful, deeply moved expressions, an older white woman and a young Middle Eastern man holding candles with quiet tears of relief, a Black father resting a hand on his daughter's shoulder in stillness, soft first light breaking through tall windows onto upturned faces, hushed reverent hope turning to gentle joy, cinematic worship-brand film still, warm and emotive, low-key candle glow lifting into dawn light, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: For fourteen months the sky did not answer, and I made an album out of the quiet. Here is the thing I learned that no one tells you: in music, the rest is not the absence of sound. It is part of the composition. This is the story of a record that never raises its voice, and why God's longest silence turned out to be the note that shaped my whole soul.

body.text: Every musician knows a secret that most listeners never think about: the silence is written in.

Open any score and you will find rests, little marks that command the player to stop, to lift the bow, to let the air go empty for a beat, or two, or a whole measure. A novice thinks the rest is where the music isn't. A master knows the rest is where the music *breathes.* Take the silences out of a great piece and you do not get more music. You get noise. The pause is not the enemy of the song. The pause is part of it.
I learned that the slow way, in a season I would not have chosen. And out of it came the quietest record I have ever made. I called it **The Long Silence.**
Fourteen months of a phone that would not ring

I want to be honest about where this album comes from, because pretending would help no one. There was a stretch, more than a year, when I prayed and the ceiling did not answer, when I knelt where I had always knelt and the hallway did not echo back a prayer. The first song is just the oldest question in the Bible, the one the psalmist asked and I asked after him: *how long, O Lord.* I had asked it now for fourteen months.

I built the second song, *The Phone That Doesn't Ring*, around a feeling anyone who has waited on **Yahuah** will recognize, checking the screen, telling yourself today will be the day you feel the tug, hear the name, and the screen staying dark. But the refrain that surfaced surprised me:
The phone that doesn't ring is still the phone I love.

That was the turn. I was not going to delete the contact. I was going to be the woman by the door, the lamp left on through the night, the one who keeps the kettle warm because absence is not the same as gone, and silence is not the same as wrong.
When worship goes quiet inside of you
Here is the part of the story I most needed to tell, because the church often will not.

There is a Sunday, maybe a year of Sundays, when the song begins, the people lift their hands, and you move your mouth and nothing in you stands. The chorus swells and you are dry. You cannot remember the last time you cried. I wrote *When Worship Goes Quiet* for that person in the cold pew, and the whole song is one stubborn decision: *I will not leave the room. I will let the choir sing what I cannot. I will let the liturgy hold what I forgot.*

Because the song is not the proof of love. The proof of love is that you came, and sat among your people again, and whispered, even, just His name. Scripture tells us not to give up meeting together, and I have come to believe that command is a mercy for exactly these seasons, when your feeling has gone silent but your body can still carry you into the room where the saints are singing your part until you can sing it again.

That is not weakness. That is *faith without feeling*, and the eighth song argues, gently, that it is the deeper kind. The warmth in the chest was never the proof that **Yahuah** was near. Love that only stays when love is felt is not yet love; it is only what was dealt. The vow that holds when the honeymoon is gone, the mother nursing through the longest dawn, the friend who shows up though the room is cold, that is the love that does not need to be told. And a faith refined past feeling is a faith that has learned to love a God it cannot, at that moment, find.
The dark night is not the night of sin

A long time ago a Spanish contemplative named John of the Cross gave this experience a name, the dark night of the soul, and I set his idea to a slow processional in the fourth song. His insight is one the anxious heart desperately needs: there is a darkness that is *not* punishment. Not the night of sin, but the night of grace, where **Yahuah** empties the lamp to widen the place. It is the long, unlit hallway of the saints, where the eye lets go and the heart awakes.

I know how that sounds when you are in it. It does not feel like formation; it feels like abandonment. But I keep coming back to the mountain where the prophet stood waiting for God, and the wind tore the rocks and God was not in the wind, and the earthquake came and God was not in the earthquake, and the fire came and God was not in the fire, and then, after all the loud things had exhausted themselves, there was a low whisper, and *that* was Him. Sometimes the reason you cannot hear **Yahuah** is that you are still braced for thunder, and He has chosen the quiet.
The silence was composing something

Then, slowly, the record turns toward dawn. The tenth song, *The First Word After*, is the truest thing on it. When the silence finally broke for me, it was not a thunderclap or a vision. It was a quiet sentence, on an ordinary Tuesday morning, a line I read that suddenly warmed, and I sat down on the kitchen floor and cried the way the long-bereaved cry. I had imagined trumpets. I had hoped for fire. What came was softer than desire: a simple sentence about being loved. And He did not shame the long unanswered years. He did not scold the asking through the tears. He simply spoke, and what He spoke was love, and every absence was understood in it.

Looking back, I could finally see what I titled the eleventh song, *The Silence Was Speaking.* The hush had been holding more than it withheld. The absence had been teaching me that presence cannot be earned. The years without a word had been hollowing out a chamber in me, widening the soul to hold a word too large to fit when everything was easy and bright. What I had called abandonment was a kind of school. The Master who instructs by withholding was teaching me a love that needs no proof.

So the album ends not with a finish but with a fold, a coming home into an always-held. **The Long Silence** does not resolve with a triumphant key change and a wall of sound, because that would be a lie about how these seasons actually end. It ends the way a long night ends: not loudly, but truly, like a friend who returns and does not need to explain, who simply sits and stays and stays again. The last note of the record is one held breath, and then real silence, six seconds of it, on purpose.
For whoever is in the quiet right now

If **Yahuah** feels silent to you, hear this from someone who sat in that pew a long time: the rest is part of the song. The pause is where the music breathes. He is not gone; He is holding the longest note He has ever held over your life, and it is doing something in you that the loud seasons never could.

The asking is a kind of faith. The asking is the proof you stayed. A heart that questions has not left. And the silence you are enduring is, I promise you, speaking, hollowing the chamber, widening the soul, loving you the long and patient way, until the morning comes without announcement and you find, waiting in it, a deeper God than you had known to find.

pieces.title: The Ground Settles Long Before the Body Does
pieces.imagePrompt: A globally diverse group of people of many nations in a warm therapy-circle and worship gathering, faces moving from weariness into gentle relief and belonging, a young South Asian woman exhaling with a soft smile, an older Black man with a steadying hand on a friend's back, a mixed-race support group holding hands in a sunlit room, tears turning to quiet laughter, soft warm daylight through wide windows, cinematic worship-brand film still, tender and hopeful, high-key natural light, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: Six months out, a door slammed two apartments over and my whole chest went black. I made an album about the tremors that keep coming after you think the earthquake is done, and about a stranger truth: your body is a resounding instrument, and the God who built it to shake can also teach it to ring in tune. This is the story of Aftershocks.

body.text: Seismologists will tell you the aftershock is not a new earthquake. It is the same one, still settling. The ground heaved once, the fault slipped, and for weeks or months afterward the earth keeps ringing down toward stillness, sending up smaller tremors long after everyone has folded the blankets and gone home.
I named an album after that, because I have lived it in my own body, and because I think the church badly needs a language for it. I called it **Aftershocks.**
The door that slammed two apartments over

The opening song is a true story wearing a slightly changed coat. Six months out from a hard thing, I thought the ground had settled. I had given the casseroles back. And then a door slammed two apartments over, and my whole chest went black. I had forgotten I was still standing on a fault line.

For a long time I called that weakness. I wondered why my Bible could not lift this dust, why my prayer life had a hidden leak, why my faith felt strong but my body still felt weak. And then a doctor said a word, the clinical name for what happens to a soul that survives more than it was built to carry, and something in me eased. I wrote a whole song about that easing, *PTSD Is Not a Failing*, because the shame slid off like rain off a windowpane. A diagnosis is not a punishment. The wound is not the blame.

Here is the sentence I most want you to hear, and it stands at the center of that song: **Yeshua** does not love you less for the way you tremble. He did not say *strong.* He said *come.* He did not say *healed.* He said *home.*
Your body is an instrument, and it keeps resounding
Now let me tell you the thing that makes me, of all the family, the one who had to write this record, because I cannot stop marveling at how **Yahuah** built us.

Your body is a resounding thing. Strike a bell and the metal goes on vibrating after the hammer lifts; that ongoing ring is not a malfunction. It is what the bell *is.* And your nervous system, it turns out, works something like that. The mind forgets what the muscles still recite. Your shoulders climb to your ears in a checkout line for no reason you can name, because your back already knew the song. A stranger's cologne in an elevator, and suddenly you are exactly where the old harm was. The body remembers. The body keeps the score.
I wrote *The Body Remembers* to hold that plainly, and then to turn it toward the One who made the wiring:
You knit me together, You know the wiring under the skin. Teach my body the Sabbath my mind has been asking for. Teach the muscle the mercy of an unlocked door.

The psalmist marveled that **Yahuah** knit him together in secret, that he was fearfully and wonderfully made. That is not a greeting-card verse when you are shaking on the kitchen tile. It is a lifeline. The same God who designed the nerve that is misfiring is not surprised by the misfire, and He is not above the tools we make to heal it. In *EMDR Sessions* I sang about the buzzers pulsing left, then right, then left, and the honest confession that **Yeshua** is not threatened by the science, by the buzzer in the hand. He is the One who taught us how to understand. And in *My Nervous System Needs Jesus* I got even plainer: none of the breathing, the low humming tone, the cold cloth on the wrist is unspiritual. He made the nerve. He made the breath. When He breathed into the dust, the dust became a living soul, the same breath, the *ruach*, that hovers over your chest when it will not calm.
The healing is not a closing door

The great lie about healing is that it is a single closing door: walk through, shut it tight, never look back. I believed that lie, and the album's turn away from it, *Healing in Layers*, was the first time the record lets itself breathe wide. Healing is an onion. Healing is a rose. Layer by layer, the way the morning grows, naming, then grief, then the body learning to believe in relief, then forgiveness, then the laugh. And there is a layer you have not reached yet, and that is not failure; you are walking the path. **Yahuah** did not make the world in a single afternoon. He took six unhurried days. He is not in a hurry with the work He has started in you either.

That reframe is what let me sing *The Tremor Still Comes* without pretending. A year out, the tremors visit less but they still visit. I do not have a timeline. I do not have a cure. What I have is a promise, that He will not abandon what He endures. Forty years in the desert, and the manna still fell. The tremor is not a sign that He has walked away; it is the very place He keeps meeting me, day by day by day.
Not free from the shaking, free inside it

I did not want this album to end with a miracle it could not honestly promise, so it ends with a benediction. *The Tremors Are Teaching Me* is the quietest song on the record, just a cello and a voice, like the close of a service. The tremors came as enemies, and they are leaving as guides. They are teaching me to listen for the quiet sides of the Spirit.

And this is the whole of what I have learned, so I will hand it to you exactly as I sing it: healing is not the absence of the wound. It is the wound made luminous. The wound becoming *tuned.* You are not promised freedom from the shaking. You are promised something better and stranger, freedom *inside* the shake, because **Yeshua** is the Stillness that the storms can never break.

There is a scientific phrase, *post-traumatic growth*, for the gold that sometimes comes not in spite of the wound but through it, the way certain pine cones only open in the heat. I will not tell you the trauma was a gift; it was not. But what the Lord has done with it, the Lord has done. Joseph said it to the brothers who sold him: what you meant for harm, God wove into good. The cracks running through me turned out to be the places He holds, and He painted glory through the very places where I broke apart.
For the one still inside the quake

So to you, still on the kitchen tile, counting backward from a hundred, tired of explaining it to anyone, hear the bridge I wrote straight to you: you are not alone, beloved. He has gathered every tear into the bottle of His care, the ones you cried when the ground came back and no one saw. He is closer than the breath. He is nearer than the air.

The ground settles long before the body does. That is not your failure. That is just how aftershocks work, and He stays for the quake, and He stays for the silence, and He stays for the tremor, and the one after, and more.

pieces.title: Grace Knocks Softer Than You Brace For
pieces.albumTitle: The Night He Came for Me
pieces.imagePrompt: A jubilant globally diverse crowd of many nations bursting into praise in warm golden light, a young Black woman with arms flung wide and face radiant, an older Latino man laughing with tears streaming, an Asian family embracing at an open front door as light pours in, a mixed congregation clapping and singing with open mouths and lifted hands, rain-washed street glowing behind them, cinematic gospel-worship film still, exuberant and bright, high-key golden light, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I was not looking for Him. I had a wall of good reasons and a kettle on for nobody. Then, at ten o'clock on an ordinary rainy Tuesday, three soft knocks, quieter than I thought heaven would ever be. This is the story of the loudest gospel-soul record I have ever made, and why the sound that changed everything was gentler than the God I had braced myself against.

body.text: I make a lot of quiet records. This is not one of them. **The Night He Came For Me** is the most extroverted thing I have ever recorded, Hammond organ, brass stabs, a full gospel choir, a whole album that ends in a shout. But I want to tell you about its softest sound, because that is the sound the whole record turns on. It is a knock.
The night before the night you remember
Every testimony has a night you talk about, the night you finally opened the door. But there is a night before that one, and heaven remembers it even if you don't.

I wrote the opener, *The Night Before the Night*, from that hidden angle. There was an ordinary evening: same chair, same hum, a kettle on for nobody and a TV on for none. The rain was on the window like it had been for years. I did not know that tomorrow was the door He'd come through. I called it Tuesday. I called it tired. I called it fine. But somewhere out past the streetlights, past the highway, past the years, a Shepherd had already left the ninety-nine and turned His face toward my street.

That is the gospel **Yeshua** told about Himself, the shepherd who leaves the whole safe flock to go after the single lost one, and does not stop *until He finds it.* I built the entire record on that one phrase. Because the thing the parable insists on, the thing I most needed, is that the searching started on His side, long before it ever started on mine.
I wasn't looking for Him

Let me be honest about the woman I was. I had not asked for **Yeshua**. I had a list of reasons built up like a wall, the hurt, the church I had left, the friend who wounded me when I called. I was not reading Scripture or humming any hymn. I was scrolling through my phone with the volume on slim. If you had asked me what I needed I would have said "another hour," not "the carpenter from Galilee with resurrection power."

The second song is a call-and-response between those two facts, and the choir sings the truer one back at me: *I wasn't searching the sky, but He was searching for me. I wasn't lifting my eyes, but He was lifting toward me.* There is a line in Paul's letter to Rome where **Yahuah** says, through the prophet, that He was found by people who were not even looking for Him, revealed to those who did not ask. That verse used to trouble me. Now it is the ground I stand on. You cannot earn a knock you did not know was coming. He did not wait for me to pretty up the porch.
The first knock
And then, the sound.

*The First Knock* is the hinge of the whole album, and I produced it so the kick drum lands like a heartbeat in the wood. Three soft knocks on the door at ten, and the world bent in. Not loud, not angry, not the kind you fear, the kind that asks, quietly, whether anyone inside is good. I froze the way a deer freezes near a road. And I thought: *who knocks like that in the rain? Who knocks like mercy at ten o'clock at night?*
The first knock, quieter than I thought heaven would be. Holier than anything had ever sounded to me. Not a fist, not a force, not a demand, just the patient, holy patience of a nail-scarred hand.

**Yeshua** said it about Himself in the last book of the Bible: *behold, I stand at the door and knock.* I had heard those words once on a Sunday-school felt board and never thought they would come true on a Tuesday, on the porch of a woman who had ignored the Lord. But there He was, patient as the moon above the trees, not breaking down the door, not shouting through the wood, just asking, *will you open up for Me?*

This is what I most want you to hear, because I think many of us are braced against the wrong God. We expect thunder, a demand, a shaming. We have steeled ourselves for a fist. And grace knocks softer than that. He could have kicked the door wide open. He could have summoned wind and fire. But love is gentle. Love is patient. Love just keeps on knocking higher, until the heart admits it.
The chain I almost left in place

There is a song on this album I could barely finish writing, because it names how close I came to missing everything. In *The Door I Almost Didn't Open*, my hand is on the chain, my forehead is on the cold glass, and I am counting all the reasonable reasons to let the moment slip. *It's late. I'm tired. I don't know who that is. I'll regret this. I'll cry.* And every single reason was a small and reasonable lie, and every single reason was the enemy standing nearby.

If that is you tonight, with your hand on the chain, let me say it to you the way the bridge says it: He is the kindest knock you will ever hear. The voice on the other side of the glass is love, not fear. Slip the chain. Turn the latch. You are already standing on heaven's porch, do not let the morning come and find Him gone.
He came in my worst hour, not my best

When I finally opened, He did not come in glory-thunder. He sat down on my hand-me-down couch like He had always been invited, took the cup I poured, and laughed at something small I said, the God who flung the stars across the dark, sitting in a living room where a cheap lamp made the wall go red. He asked about the photograph of my grandmother in her Sunday-go hat and said, *she prayed for you, and tonight her prayer is being answered in this room.*

And He came, I have to tell you, at my *worst* hour, not the polished, cleaned-up version I would have chosen. He did not wait for me to wash my face. He did not wait for me to dress the place. The Shepherd comes for the lost sheep in the field of her deepest mess, and He turns the whole hour into holy ground. He knew every secret without my telling Him, Scripture says **Yahuah** searches us and knows us completely, and He did not recoil and He did not list them. He just held the whole of me up like a song, and being known like that is the thing that finally told me I belonged.
The smallest word that changes everything

The album's loudest moment is built on its smallest word. Three letters and a held breath. *Yes.* I had spent a lifetime not saying it, and He did not pressure and He did not preach. He just waited, patient as a father at the end of the prodigal's road, for the smallest word my trembling mouth could carry. And when it came up from somewhere underneath, the chain I had nailed across my chest snapped like a thread, and the whole room lit up like sunrise on the wall.

So I will end the way I end the record, in the song that gives it its name, with the oldest confession the rescued have ever sung: *I was lost, and now I'm found. I was bound, and now I'm free.* And the reason I made a whole loud, brass-and-organ, choir-shouting album out of one quiet knock is the reason of the very last song, *tell the story.* The Shepherd does not find the lost so they can keep the finding quiet.

There is someone still on the hillside tonight. Someone with a kettle on for nobody, sure that nothing is coming for them. He is already crossing the field. And when the knock comes, it will be softer than they braced for. Open the door.

pieces.title: Truth Out Loud Changes the Weight of the Air
pieces.imagePrompt: A globally diverse group of people of many nations in a sunlit room exhaling into relief and courage, a young Black woman speaking with tears and a growing smile as friends lean in and listen with warm faces, an older Pacific Islander woman nodding and holding her hand, a supportive circle of many nations under bright window light, faces opening from heaviness into freedom and belonging, cinematic worship-brand film still, tender and luminous, high-key natural light, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: There is a kind of silence that is not holy, the swallowed sentence, the folded truth, the weight that lives behind the tongue. I made an album about the day a sealed voice finally makes a sound, because the strangest, truest thing I know about that day is physical: the room actually gets lighter. This is the story of Breaking Silence.

body.text: I have made a record about the gift of silence, the holy rest, the pause where the music breathes. So I want to be careful and clear here, because this is a record about the opposite thing: the silence that is not a gift at all. The swallowed sentence. The folded truth. The weight that lives behind the tongue, heavier than a raised hymnal, that some of us have carried since we were children in a Sunday-best dress, memorizing the ceiling tile so the hour would pass. I called this album **Breaking Silence**, and it may be the bravest thing I have ever set to music.
Not every hush is holy

The opening song is a confession of a hush I rehearsed for years. *The Silence I Kept* is about learning to hum through the dinner prayer, to swallow the shape of a name, to fold the truth like a napkin nobody asked to unfold, and to sweep it, week after week, under every Sunday hallelujah. That kind of silence disguises itself as peace, even as reverence. But it is not the quiet of trust. It is the quiet of a stone laid over a sleeping soul.

The whole album stands on one sentence **Yeshua** spoke: *the truth will set you free.* We usually quote it about doctrine. But a person who has kept a secret to survive knows it in the body, that the unspoken thing is a cage, and the said thing is a door. The very first line of the record is that verse read at a whisper, because for some of us freedom does not begin with a shout. It begins with a syllable we can barely get out.
The physics of a sentence finally spoken

Here is the thing I cannot get over, the thing that made me, of all people, need to write this. When a held truth is finally spoken out loud, *the room changes.* Not metaphorically. Physically. I wrote a whole song about it, *The Room Got Lighter*, and every detail is true to the experience:

The lamp had not changed bulbs, the curtains had not moved, no one had cracked a window, and yet the room got lighter the moment the sentence left my chest. I did not know that air had weight until I felt it lift.

Think about what is actually happening when you speak. You take breath, the same breath **Yahuah** first exhaled into dust to make a living soul, and you press it up through two small folds of tissue in your throat, and you shape the moving air into a word. A word is not nothing. It is force. It is a wave that leaves your body and enters the world and *does* something to it. Scripture opens with **Yahuah** speaking light into being; the whole universe begins with a voice, not a hand. And we are made in that image, down to the astonishing fact that we can push air into meaning. So when a survivor finally says the true thing, they are doing, in miniature, the most God-like act there is: they are speaking, and by speaking, changing what the world contains.

That is why the chest feels like a gate swinging open. That is why the shame slides off like rain off a windowpane. The lungs had been a low, shuttered room, and the air you were holding turned out to be the seed of your own bloom.
The first word out is a hairline crack

It rarely comes out clean. *The First Word Out* is set at a kitchen sink on an ordinary Tuesday, the kettle still on, a sister stirring a mug, and the word slips past the tongue crooked, one syllable, half a name, half a sigh, and the floor seems to tilt because it knows why. What made the second word come easier than the first was not courage. It was a witness. *She set the spoon down very slow. She did not interrupt. "Tell me," she said, "I'm not going anywhere", and the rest came out like rain that had waited.*

I want to say something plainly to anyone who has ever been on the *hearing* end of that moment, because the album insists on it: to believe someone is a holy act. In *The Ones Who Believed* I named them one by one, the aunt at the kitchen table, the youth pastor who was actually able, the stranger in the bathroom, the woman in the support-group circle when I finally said the date. They did not require my proof. They did not require my poise. They made themselves a quiet roof above a smaller voice. They were the lamp-stems that held the wick this long. **Yeshua** built His whole ministry believing the people the crowd would not, and every time you sit in the chair and stay, you are doing His work.
When the room does not believe you

I did not want to lie about how often that goes the other way, so the record does not. *Believing Me Was Not Guaranteed* is the soberest song on it, and it ends without a resolving major chord on purpose. Telling the truth is not a contract that the hearer will receive it. Some turn away. Some change the subject. Some ask, *are you sure that's true.* And into that unverified room the song plants its one unshakable footing:
**Yeshua**, You believed me first. You believed me before the word, and that was the well that quenched the thirst when no one else had heard.

That is the deepest wonder of hearing in the whole album, and it is not about a human ear at all. Before you ever risk your voice on a listener who might fail you, there is already One who has heard the words you never said and read the page you never let anyone read. He wept inside the house where the secret was kept, the shortest, heaviest sentence in the Gospels is simply that **Yeshua** wept, and He knew the names you would not say long before you found the breath to say them. You do not speak into a void hoping to be heard. You speak toward the One who has been listening the entire time.
The voice was never the wrong shape

The album climbs, song by song, the letter finally sent to a small blue mailbox, the therapist's forty-eight minutes of grace, the ceremony of *Naming What Happened*, where a fog with no proper noun is finally given the courage of the verb and the noun without the gauze. Because naming is half the healing; the other half is being heard. And then it turns outward. *Breaking It for the Next* is about the girl you have never met who will need this story told, the chain that breaks somewhere or it breaks no one, ending with a mouth that speaks.

And it lands, at last, on a benediction I could barely sing without my own voice shaking: *My Voice Is Mine.* It took the woman in that song thirty-something years to come home to her own throat, to learn the difference between the fear and the actual note. And the truth she arrives at is the truth I want to leave with you:

This voice was never the wrong shape. It was only the held breath. **Yeshua**, You gave me the cords I sing with, You knit them in the womb, my voice is mine, the truth is the gift that walked me out of the tomb.

The psalmist marveled that **Yahuah** knit him together in secret, wonderfully made. That includes the instrument in your throat. He built it. He tuned it. It belongs to no one who ever tried to silence it, not the family's brand, not a careful church tone, not the person who handed you a script that was not your own.
