So if you are carrying a stone-covered silence tonight, hear this from someone who lay under one a long time: not every hush is holy, and the sentence you are afraid to say is a door, not a bomb. You do not have to shout. One crooked syllable at a kitchen sink is enough to start the river running. And when you finally say the true thing, watch the room. The lamp will not change bulbs and no one will open a window, but the air will get lighter, because a voice **Yahuah** Himself knit into you just did the most God-like thing a body can do. It spoke. And the truth, exactly as He promised, begins to set you free.

pieces.title: The Names He Knew Before They Were Born
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyful multigenerational gathering of globally diverse families outdoors at golden hour, grandparents lifting laughing children toward the sky, four generations standing together in warm open country, faces bright with hope, cinematic worship-brand film still, radiant and emotive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: I made this album standing at a riverbank where I will one day teach children not yet born. It is about handing down the only inheritance no policy can confiscate, Christ Himself. She is His before she is ours. He knew every name before the stars did. And the song does not stop when we do.

body.text: I stood at a river once, thinking about a child who did not exist yet.

Not a hypothetical child, a real one, coming someday, to be carried down to that same water and taught the prayers my grandmother taught me by name. And the strange, holy weight that settled on me at that riverbank became this whole album. Because I realized the most important thing I could ever hand a child is not a name, not a house, not a language, not even a song. It is a Person. And that Person already knows the child's name, knew it before the river, before the birth, before the stars were hung.
Why This Record Had to Exist

I come from people who had things taken. Land signed away under a lie. Wages kept. Years spent and counted as rent. A whole inheritance drained across a century the way you take a breath. When you carry that history, you learn to ask a hard question about anything you try to pass down: *can this be stolen too?*

That question is the engine of this record. I wanted to sing about the one inheritance that no agent can stamp a paper on. On *The Inheritance That Cannot Be Taken*, I name what was lost plainly, and then I sing the thing that outlasts every theft:
No system erased the Lamb,  the inheritance is Christ Himself.

Paul told the Colossians the mystery was *Christ in you, the hope of glory* (Colossians 1:27), and Peter said we have an inheritance *imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you* (1 Peter 1:4). Kept. Not by us. By Him. They took the cabin; they could not take the Christ. That is the future I want to leave a child.
What the Title Means
*Children's Future.* But the future I mean is not a career or a college fund. It is a Name that was spoken over them before they drew breath.

The opener, *The Baby Born This Morning*, lands on a line I built the whole album around: *she is His before she is hers.* We lifted her by her own name, yes, but under the Name above her name, the way **Yeshua** was named on the eighth day (Luke 2:21). And on *When She Asks "Who Made the Stars,"* a four-year-old points at the brightest one and asks the oldest question there is, and her father does not rush. Psalm 8 and Genesis 1 are open in his hands. The answer he has been holding for her is this: the Father made the stars, the Son holds them in place, and the Spirit knew *your* name, daughter, *your name first, the stars second.* That is not sentiment. That is Isaiah's God, who says *I have called you by name, you are mine* (Isaiah 43:1).
The Heart Behind the Songs
Let me walk you through the ache and the joy of it, because a real inheritance is honest about both.

*What I Want Them to Know* is a grandfather on a kitchen floor, doing what Moses commanded, *teach them diligently to your children* (Deuteronomy 6:6-7). And he boils a whole life of faith down to a chant a child can carry: *Jesus. The Cross. The Spirit. The song.* Christ first, always. *First Words I'll Teach Her* is tenderer still, water, milk, song, light, Father, but under the first words is the first Word: **Abba**. Paul says the Spirit Himself cries *Abba, Father* in us (Galatians 4:6). A child's first true word is His, crying in her chest before her mouth can shape the sound.

But I would not let this album pretend the road is smooth. *The Stories We Will Not Hide* is my vow to tell the family history straight, the hard years, the losses, the graves, because I serve a God who tells His own story straight. *The Cross is over the wound, not in place of it.* And *We Will Not Lose Another* is the line I draw with my whole body: we have lost cousins to the road, brothers to the load, the uncle to the bottle, the sister to the dark, and by the grace of God, *not one more.* I stand that ground on the promise of **Yeshua**: *no one will snatch them out of my hand* (John 10:28), and on Malachi's ancient word that He turns *the hearts of fathers to their children* (Malachi 4:6). The Father holds the cycle. And so we hold the children.
The Ones Not Yet Here

There is a song on this record I could barely finish. *The Names of the Yet-to-Be-Born* holds two things in the same hand: the names of children coming, and the names of children who never came, a daughter's loss, a sister's two. I wrote it for the arms that are empty and aching. And the only comfort strong enough is the truth of Psalm 139: *in your book were written every one of them, the days that were formed for me, when as yet there was none of them* (Psalm 139:16). He has known every name from the foundation. Not one came late. Not one is lost. If you have grieved a child you never got to hold, that song is for you, and so is that verse. He keeps the Book. He has known.

The centerpiece, *The Child Sings First*, flips the whole thing on its head. A boy sings lead, and the elders hum underneath, not behind him, *under* him, holding him up. Because **Yeshua** said God has *prepared praise from the mouths of infants* (Matthew 21:16). The child sings first because the Father called first. The little one already knows what the elders had to walk a long road to find out: *You see me. You know me. You called me by my own name.*
Who This Is For
This is for the young parent standing at their own riverbank, terrified of everything they cannot protect their child from.

It is for the grandmother who has kept setting a plate for a boy who has not come home yet, *The Boy Who Came Back* is for her, and the Father in that song is already running down the road while the rest of us stand still, exactly as He ran in Luke 15:20. It is for the family fighting to break a pattern that has run four generations deep. And it is for anyone who feels they have nothing worth handing down. Hear me: you have Christ, and He cannot be confiscated.

The album ends with *Every Generation Singing*, a great-great-grandfather of ninety-four and a great-grandson of two singing the same Name, because *one generation shall commend your works to another* (Psalm 145:4). The eighth generation is not born yet, and the tenth is only in His book, but the Name does not stop. On the final song, *We Hand Them Christ and the Song*, I say it as plainly as I know how: Christ first, the song follows, both kept under Him. Give a child everything you can. But give them Him first. He knew their name before the stars, and He will be holding it long after you and I have gone home.

pieces.title: The War Was Over Before I Knew There Was One
pieces.imagePrompt: A jubilant crowd of globally diverse worshippers gathered on a high mountain ridge as the sun blazes over snow-capped peaks, hands raised in triumph, faces lit gold with awe and joy, banners of light across a vast alpine dawn, cinematic worship-brand film still, epic and euphoric, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: This is my loudest record, arena worship-rock made to preach one settled fact off the face of the mountain: the victory is already finished. Long before I feared the dark, the Light of the World had already walked out of the tomb. I am not fighting for the win. I am standing in a win that was won without me.

body.text: I spent years fighting a war that had already been won, and nobody had told me the news.

That is the confession this whole album grew out of. I would wake up bracing for a battle, against the fear, against the old chain, against the dark that whispered my verdict before I even walked into the room, as if the outcome were still up for grabs. And then one morning it broke over me like the sun over a ridge: the war was over. It was finished on a cross and sealed at an empty tomb, and it had been finished long before I ever laced up for the fight. So I made the loudest record I have ever made, full arena worship-rock, a wall of electric guitar, drums like thunder, because a truth this settled deserves to be shouted off the top of a mountain.
Why I Made a Victory Record

Most of us do not doubt that Christ is powerful. We doubt that the matter is *settled.* We live like the verdict is still pending, like our worrying is somehow load-bearing, like if we stop straining the whole thing might come apart.
I know that exhaustion from the inside. So I built *Christ Already Won* to preach the difference between striving *for* a victory and standing *in* one:
What is finished cannot be unfinished. What is won cannot be unwon. I'm not fighting for the victory,  I'm standing in the victory already done.

**Yeshua** did not say "I'll try." From the cross He said *it is finished* (John 19:30). Scripture piles the proof high: through death He *destroyed the one who has the power of death* (Hebrews 2:14); He *disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, triumphing over them* (Colossians 2:15); *the reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil* (1 John 3:8). The battle was over before I knew there was a war. That is not denial. That is the gospel finally read in the right tense.
What the Title Means
*Light on the Mountain.* I am named for a mountain, Tahoma, the great snow-capped one, and I have watched a thousand sunrises catch its face pink and gold before a single climber was awake to see it.

That is the whole picture. On the opener, I sing: *long before the cameras, long before the climbers, the Maker's light was already on the mountain. Long before the dark could whisper my name, the Light of the World had already come.* Scripture says God *has delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son* (Colossians 1:13), and John promises *the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it* (John 1:5). The mountain has been preaching the finished victory since before I opened my eyes. Every ridge a pulpit. Every dawn a hymn.

The high places have always been where **Yahuah** shows His glory, Sinai wrapped in fire, the mount where **Yeshua** was transfigured until His face shone like the sun, the ridges where He withdrew alone to pray. I stand in that long line when I say the light on the summit is not a metaphor. It is a witness.
The Heart Behind the Songs
Let me take you up the trail, because the album climbs on purpose.

*Fear Has No Throne* is the song I most needed to write. For years I let fear sit at the head of my table, served him like he was the ruler, let him deliver the verdict before I walked into any room. And then the Lord flipped the chair. The verse I built it on is Paul's word to a frightened young pastor: *God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control* (2 Timothy 1:7). Fear gets evicted. Fear gets the door. And nothing, *neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor height nor depth*, can separate me from the love that is seated on the throne (Romans 8:38-39).

*Lamp for Every Step* is the quieter climb. Up the trail in the dark, the headlamp only throws a small circle, *I cannot see the summit, I cannot see the bend; I can see the next stone where my boot will land.* The Lord does not hand you a floodlight for the whole road. He gives *a lamp to my feet and a light to my path* (Psalm 119:105), and *the path of the righteous is like the light of dawn, shining brighter and brighter until full day* (Proverbs 4:18). You do not need the whole map. You need the next lit stone.

And *Sunrise Over Tahoma* lets the mountain preach without a single human word, *the heavens declare the glory of God* (Psalm 19:1), *his invisible attributes... clearly perceived in the things that have been made* (Romans 1:20). The marmots and the eagles already know who the Maker is. The forest holds its breath until the first ray comes. Creation has been testifying to the finished glory all along.
The Dawn After the Longest Night
I built this record with a cinematic turn at its center, because the finished victory has to be able to reach the darkest night.

*Dawn Breaks the Darkness* opens stripped bare, a single soft heartbeat in the dark, and it holds the vigil honestly: *we prayed through the long night, we sang into the dark, we did not know when the morning would come.* But it stands on the promise of Psalm 30: *weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning* (Psalm 30:5). And then the whole band explodes into the sunrise, because the morning turned out to be a Person: *the morning was the Lord standing in our place.*

*Glory on the Ridge* lifts my eyes off my own summit to the whole earth, *the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord as the waters cover the sea* (Habakkuk 2:14), and *Light to the Nations* sends it out, because the Servant was given *as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth* (Isaiah 49:6; Acts 13:47). The light does not stay on my mountain. It runs.
Who This Is For
This is for the worn-down believer who is exhausted from fighting a war they were never told was already won.

For the one who wakes up bracing, who lets fear render the verdict before the day even starts, who has been straining as if the outcome depended on the strength of their grip. Hear me: loosen your hands. *The Day He Found Me* is my own testimony on this record. I did not find Him; He was the Shepherd who left the ninety-nine and came into the dark of my disgrace, and *the one who comes to me I will never cast out* (John 6:37). And *Sons and Daughters of Day* is the identity the finished victory hands you: *you are all children of light, children of the day; we are not of the night or of the darkness* (1 Thessalonians 5:5). The dark has no claim on you anymore.

The album ends where every climb ends, *Morning on the Summit*, the whole family gathered at the top, the air thin, the light on the snow, realizing the Lord was the One who taught every step of the trail. We climbed all night. But the war was over before we started. Come up the mountain and see the light that was already there.

pieces.title: The Morning the Chain Hit the Floor
pieces.imagePrompt: A jubilant crowd of globally diverse people outdoors in bright morning sun, hands thrown high in celebration and freedom, faces radiant with joy and relief, dancing together in an open sunlit square after rain, cinematic worship-brand film still, vivid and euphoric, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: This is my freedom record, gospel reggae built around the sound of metal hitting the ground. It is about the year of Jubilee that never ends, the prison door that swings open from the outside, and the one key that could turn a lock nothing else would budge. The key was not silver or gold. The key was His blood.

body.text: I want you to imagine a single sound: metal hitting the ground.

The exact moment a chain that has been on someone's wrists for twenty years slides off and lands on the floor. That sound is the whole reason this album exists. I made a gospel-reggae record, hand drum, skank guitar, warm bass on the one, brass stabs, because freedom needs a groove you can throw your hands up to. The mountain taught me the quiet. But some mornings, when the chain finally comes off, quiet is not enough. Some mornings you need a drum.
Why I Made a Freedom Record

I have watched too many people try every key the world has on offer. The bottle. The powder. The reform program. The willpower. The religion of just trying harder to walk out of your own broken storm. And I have watched the locks refuse to turn, one after another, until a person is convinced their cell has no door at all.

That is who I made this for. Because the gospel is not self-improvement. It is a jailbreak. On the opener, *Chains Off, Hands Up*, I sing about a man who comes to the river with iron on his hands, and **Yeshua** does not lecture him or turn him away. He just bends down and breaks the metal like clay. *What the bottle could not give, what the shame had welded shut, Jesus opened with His hand.*
What the Title Means
The chorus of the whole record is two motions: chains off, hands up. The chain comes down; the hands go up. That is the shape of the freed life.

And it stands on the sermon **Yeshua** preached in His own hometown, when He unrolled the scroll of Isaiah and read: *the Spirit of the Lord is upon me... to proclaim liberty to the captives... and the year of the Lord's favor* (Luke 4:18-19, from Isaiah 61). That last phrase is the whole album. The year of the Lord's favor is the Jubilee, the year in Leviticus 25 when every debt was forgiven, every slave set free, every lost inheritance returned home. On *Jubilee Drum*, I take that ram's-horn command and set it to a reggae bass, because *Christ is our Jubilee, the year that never ends.* Once every fifty years the trumpet sounded in Israel. But in **Yeshua** the Jubilee never stops.
The Heart Behind the Songs
Let me take you through the jailbreak, because it happens key by key.

*Walk Out of the Cell* is Peter in prison in Acts 12, the angel comes, the chains hit the floor, the sandals go on, and the iron gate of the city swings open on its own. And here is the line I built it on: *he thought he was dreaming, the dream was the chain. The freedom was real and it had a name.* Whatever **Yeshua** opens, no one closes again. *No Going Back* is the resolution of the freed man, straight out of Romans 6: the old self drowned in the baptismal water, and I am not crawling back to pick up what He took off me.

But the song at the center, the one I named this whole article for, is *The Key Was His Blood.* It opens stripped down to a single hand-drum heartbeat, no bass, no brass, and it tells the truth every other key failed to tell:
The key was not silver. The key was not gold. The key was His blood. Let the story be told.

That is Peter's own word: *you were ransomed... not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ* (1 Peter 1:18-19). I asked the elder, the counselor, the doctor, the friend. They could all help, but they could not mend. Only the Lamb who was slain could turn the key in the lock of time. He turned it from the other side. The cell of my shame is opened wide.
The Groove of the Redeemed
I did not want this record to only mourn the chain. I wanted it to *dance* about the freedom.

So *Reggae for the Redeemed* is a pure celebration, a party for the bought-back, standing on the truth of Revelation 5:9 that He redeemed people *from every tribe and language and people and nation.* Let the elders sing it, let the young men shout it, let the children answer, let the islands and the plains join the reggae of the broken chains. And *Rise Up Standing* takes Ephesians 2 straight to the dance floor: we were *dead in our trespasses,* and God, *rich in mercy, made us alive together with Christ*, the dead do not stay dead when **Yeshua** is Lord.

*Hands Up High (Thank You, Jesus)* is the gratitude explosion, hands that were tied with the rope of my own choice, now raised to the sky, because the Carpenter took these hands in His own and taught them to lift again. And *Whole Again* leans on Joel's promise, *I will restore to you the years the locust has eaten* (Joel 2:25), because the Healer does not only break the chain. He heals the wrist where the chain left its mark.
Who This Is For
This is for the one in the cell right now who is convinced there is no door.

For the addict at the end of the line. For the elder carrying the wound of forty years. For the young woman silenced by what was done to her. *Bondage Broken* is my own testimony on this record, the same chain finding its way back at twenty-three, thirty-three, forty-three, and the **Yeshua** who came down to the very place I thought was past His reach, and stayed in my breach. If you are hearing this and the chain is still on, hear the bridge of that song: *He's coming to your river. He has not gone.*

The album ends where every freedom ends, *Free in the Morning*, the sun coming up on a freed man, walking out into the light with the One who broke the chain in the dark. Whom the Son sets free is *free indeed* (John 8:36). Not a maybe-free. Not a slowly-free. Free in the blood, free in the name, free in the morning, never the same. Throw your hands up. The chain is already on the floor.

pieces.title: The Strength That Shows Up When Yours Runs Out
pieces.imagePrompt: A determined and joyful group of globally diverse hikers cresting a mountain ridge at dawn, helping one another up the last steps, arms raised as the sun breaks over distant peaks, faces weathered and radiant, cinematic worship-brand film still, triumphant and emotive, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: This is my long-trail record, for the ones still walking when their own strength ran out miles ago. It is built on a promise that sounds backward until you have lived it, that His strength is made perfect in weakness. It walks past Elijah's cave, past the finish line, all the way home to the morning.

body.text: I am named for a mountain, so let me tell you what the mountain taught me: nobody makes the long climb on their own strength. They only think they do until the air gets thin.

This is my walking record. It is for the ones who are still on the trail when their own legs gave out miles back, the ones putting one foot in front of the other on a road that has cost them more than they ever planned to pay. I did not build it out of my usual mountain hush. I built it as a full worship-band anthem, drums driving, choir answering, because some seasons you do not need a whisper. You need a cadence to keep walking to. And the cadence of this whole record is one word repeated until you believe it: *walk on.*
Why This Record Had to Be Loud

Quiet is for the summit. But most of life is not the summit. It is the switchback in the cold, the stretch where you cannot see the bend or the rise, where the only honest prayer is *I am so tired.* I have been on that stretch. And I found out something there that I could not have learned anywhere else.

The engine of this whole album is one verse that sounds backward until the day you need it. Paul begged God three times to remove a thorn, and God answered: *my grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness* (2 Corinthians 12:9). So Paul made the strangest boast in Scripture, *I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me.* That is the title track, *Strong Heart Walking*: not the strong-of-the-tall, but the weak-made-strong. *My strength has run out; His strength is enough.*
What the Title Means
*Strong Heart Walking.* But read it right, the strong heart is not mine. It is His, beating underneath a heart that has nothing left.

On *By His Strength*, I sing Paul's other great line, *I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me* (Philippians 4:13), and I anchor it to Zechariah so nobody mistakes it for self-help: *not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the Lord* (Zechariah 4:6). This is not a record about digging deeper and finding hidden reserves. There are no hidden reserves. This is a record about what shows up *after* your reserves are gone, the strength that is not yours, arriving exactly when yours runs out.
The Heart Behind the Songs
Let me walk you along the trail, because it is honest about how hard the walking gets.

*Grace in the Weakness* is the quietest song here, and it names the real places: *my anxiety is the place of His peace. My sleeplessness is the place of His ease. My family wound is the place of His healing. My addiction history is the place of His feeling the weight of the cross.* Where I am weak, He is mighty in me. And *Step After Step* is the one I reach for when the whole road feels impossible:
I do not need the whole map of the road,  I need the next step under my own load.

That is Galatians 5:25, *if we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit*, and Psalm 37:23, *the steps of a good man are ordered by the Lord.* You do not have to see the bend. You have to take the next step. The Spirit goes ahead, at your side, and behind you where the dust would hide.

*Long Road Saints* lifts my eyes to the ones who walked before, Abraham without knowing the land, Moses with a staff, the martyrs through fire, the grandmother on her knees every dawn. Hebrews 12 calls them *a great cloud of witnesses,* and the album is careful here: they are runners we follow, not intercessors we pray to. They finished the race. We run the same place. And *Heartbeat of Hope* strips all the way down to a single kick-drum beating alone, revealing that the rhythm under every gathering was always meant to be *His* heart, Romans 15:13, *the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing.*
The Song for the Ones About to Quit
There is one testimony on this record I need you to hear, because it might be the reason you keep going.

*I Almost Quit* is Elijah at the cave. The prophet who called down fire from heaven collapsed under a broom tree and prayed *it is enough; now, O Lord, take away my life* (1 Kings 19:4). And here is what wrecks me every time: God did not lecture him. God did not condemn him. God sent bread and water and let him sleep, and then came, not in the wind, not in the earthquake, not in the fire, but in *a still small voice* (1 Kings 19:12). I put myself in that cave in this song, a Tuesday in November, having told nobody, nothing left to remember. And the Lord came the same way He came to Elijah. If you are at the cave right now, hear the verse this song hangs on: He is coming for you with bread and with water. He is not done with His sons and His daughters. The still small voice is for the broken-through.

*Run to the Finish* pulls me back to my feet with Paul's last words, *I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith* (2 Timothy 4:7), and *Heart of a Pilgrim* reminds me I am *a stranger and a pilgrim on the earth* (Hebrews 11:13; 1 Peter 2:11), not building my city on the road but carrying the lamp toward home.
Who This Is For
This is for the worn-down believer in the driest season of their life, still walking when everyone would understand if they stopped.

For the one who got the diagnosis. The one who lost the work, the marriage, the brother, and still laced up the next morning. *I Keep Walking* is your anthem, built on Isaiah's promise that *they who wait for the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings like eagles, they shall run and not be weary, walk and not faint* (Isaiah 40:31). Not by your strength. By His, showing up right where yours ran out.

And the record ends where every long trail ends, *Home in the Morning.* The road is over, the morning is breaking, and the Lord at the door says the only words worth walking a whole life to hear: *well done, good and faithful servant* (Matthew 25:21). You did not walk it on your own strength. You never could have. You walked it on His, and it carried you all the way home.

pieces.title: The Offering Was Never the Point. He Was
pieces.imagePrompt: A joyous crowd of globally diverse worshippers of every age dancing and celebrating together in bright open-air daylight, hands and drums lifted high, colorful regalia and flowing garments, radiant faces full of exuberant joy, cinematic worship-brand film still, vivid and celebratory, wide cinematic 16:9 widescreen landscape, no text, no letters, no words, no numerals, no logos, no watermarks.
pieces.excerpt: A celebration record of embodied worship, drum and dance and lifted hands, built on one careful line I refuse to blur: the drum is not the prayer. The drum is the floor the praise is lifted on. Everything we carry gets laid down before the King, because He, not the ritual, was always the point.

body.text: I made a record with drums loud enough to shake a floor, and its whole reason for existing is one sentence I refuse to let anyone blur.
*The drum is not the prayer. The drum is the floor the praise is lifted on.*

I say it that plainly because embodied worship, the dance, the drum, the lifted hand, the color and the movement, is beautiful and biblical and joyful, and it is also the exact place where a heart can quietly slide from worshiping the King to worshiping the celebration itself. This album, *Honor the King*, is a full-throated feast of praise, and it spends all twelve songs making sure the honor lands where it belongs. Everything we carry into His presence gets laid down at His feet. The offering was never the point. He was.
A Word Before I Begin

Let me be honest about who is singing. I am a mixed-heritage believer who loves the drum and the dance and the gathered celebration, and I hold these forms with care. On this record they are offered *to* Christ, never venerated, never the recipient. The Grand Entry is a grand entry for the King. The regalia is laid before Him. Every drum bows to Christ. That is not a disclaimer tacked on the end; it is the spine of the whole thing.
Because you can lift your hands to the wrong throne. So I wanted to make joyful, dancing, drum-driven worship that never once forgets Who it is for.
What the Title Means

*Honor the King.* The album is one long honor song, and it opens by walking through the gates the way the psalmist commands: *enter his gates with thanksgiving, and his courts with praise* (Psalm 100:4).
But listen to how carefully I frame it on *Sing and Celebrate for Jesus*:
The song is not the recipient, the Lord is. The praise is not the destination, Jesus is.

Every drumbeat is a heartbeat *for the King.* The drum is the floor; the prayer is addressed to the Lord. Psalm 150 tells us to *praise him with tambourine and dance* (Psalm 150:4), and David danced before **Yahuah** with all his might (2 Samuel 6:14), embodied, unashamed, physical praise. This record says yes to all of it, and then aims every bit of it at **Yeshua**, the Lamb who was slain. That is the honor. The movement is real; the recipient is settled.
The Heart Behind the Songs
Let me carry you through the celebration, because each song lays something different at His feet.

*Dancing in the Joy of the Risen Lamb* is the dance clothed in the right garment, *he has clothed me with the garments of salvation, he has covered me with the robe of righteousness* (Isaiah 61:10). And the line I keep coming back to keeps the ownership straight: *the dance is to Jesus, the dancer is His.* I do not dance to display my own righteousness. I dance because He put His robe on my back. The colors on me are the colors of His promise.

*Lay It All Before Him* is the beating heart of the album's theology, and it is drawn from one of the most staggering scenes in Scripture. In Revelation, the twenty-four elders, crowned, honored, seated near the throne, *cast their crowns before the throne, saying, "Worthy are you, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power"* (Revelation 4:10-11). Every gift I carry, talent, treasure, strength, song, is beautiful, but the gift is not what the Lord is after. He wants the heart behind the offering, laid all the way down. The crowns come off. He wears the crown.

*Honor Song for the Lamb* is the record's summit, built on the great anthem of heaven: *Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing* (Revelation 5:12). The drums roll slow under that one, deliberate and weighty, because some honor is not fast and loud, some honor bows low. And *Circle of the Redeemed* gathers the whole nations-wide multitude John saw, *from every tribe and language and people and nation,* around the one center: the Lamb. Not the circle at the center, the Lamb at the center. *Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb* (Revelation 7:9-10).
When the Praise Runs Past Words
I did not want this to be only a loud record. Some of the deepest honor happens when the words run out.

*When Words Become a Hymn* is the quietest thing here, a wordless humming that is not a technique or an incantation, but the heart's cry when language fails. It stands on one of the tenderest promises Paul ever wrote: *the Spirit helps us in our weakness... the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words* (Romans 8:26). When you cannot find the sentence, the Spirit shapes your sighing into a prayer the Father receives. The honor rises even when the vocabulary collapses.

And *The One Who Met Jesus on the Road* is the testimony that keeps the whole record from becoming a performance, a gifted young man whose talent was perfect and whose heart was empty, until the Lord met him on a road he did not know, the way He met Saul on the way to Damascus (Acts 9). The line lands the album's thesis one more time: *the talent did not save him; the Lord did. The gift did not save him; Jesus did.* Same voice, new heart. The gift was never the point. The Giver was.
Who This Is For
This is for the worshiper who loves to bring everything they have, the drum, the dance, the color, the whole body, and wants to be sure it is all landing on the right throne.

And it is for the worn-down one who feels they have nothing impressive enough to offer. Hear the record: He never wanted the impressive gift. He wanted *you,* laid down. *Healing in Christ* says it about the very music itself, *the music does not heal; the Lord does; the Lord is the Healer above the buzz* (James 5:14-15). Even our best offering is only ever the floor the praise stands on. The Healer is the Risen One, not the ritual.

The album closes twice, on purpose. *Go in Peace* sends the people home under the oldest blessing there is, *the Lord bless you and keep you; the Lord make his face shine upon you and give you peace* (Numbers 6:24-26). And then *Every Heart Bows to Christ* lands the whole feast where all things finally land: *at the name of Jesus every knee should bow... and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father* (Philippians 2:10-11). Bring the drum. Bring the dance. Bring the loudest, most joyful thing you have. And then lay it down, because He was always the point, and every honor was only ever on its way to Him.
